The accusation assumes that 魔術 must be called “Magecraft,” without demonstrating an English category collision here. “Organizes” is compatible with administrative oversight, which the next sentence explicitly describes.

The prestigious lineage signaled by 名門 is inadequately conveyed by personal distinction and an unspecified “history.” The number accusation does not survive: “they” can refer to the preceding singular magus, with a singular title.

Kiritsugu’s ignorance is explicitly present in Original and in the appropriate English branch. The repeated “magus” results from flattened alternatives; the remaining awkward connective does not establish a material error.

Japanese says Shirou lacks a magus’s knowledge, while English substitutes insufficient practical skill. Retain that semantic difference, but remove the grammar accusation: “have not the skill” is a valid construction.

“Commit a crime” falls within a defensible contextual reading of 事件を起こす. The heretic-hunting description supports an adverse response directed at the perpetrator; the finding overstates both the added intentionality and the specificity of “come after.”

Retain the failure to translate the spoken cold complaint: さむ becomes “Hm.” The page still mentions morning chill, and habitual early rising does not prove that a complaint about mornings is contradictory.
The alleged invented sentence is present in Original, including childhood non-use and the judgment about alarm clocks. This finding relies on the shorter later-edition witness.

The English does not identify the rolled dashi omelet or the leftover konnyaku simmered with bonito flakes. Generic “broth egg and broth boil” materially loses the stated preparations and ingredients.

その加減 elaborates the distinction between defeating and killing rather than unequivocally introducing a separate lesson. In the stated sparring context, learning that difference can convey practical awareness of the degree involved; a material omission is not established.

殺し合い denotes a struggle in which participants attempt to kill one another. “A murder” does not convey that reciprocal combat, which is central to identifying what kind of confrontation Shirou has entered.

“Prepare my mind” does preserve mental readiness, so saying 覚悟 disappears entirely overstates the case. The narrower omission is the capacity to resolve immediately when actually facing mortal danger.

“Kiritsugu” preserves the explicitly written referent in narration. The familial ruby adds coloring, but selecting the name does not materially change the death, relationship, or account of the dojo’s use.

The English describes learning through physical sparring, not merely learning vocabulary. その加減 can elaborate knowing the difference between defeating and killing; the finding does not establish that an independent practical lesson has been removed.
The Japanese alternative is reciprocal lethal fighting. “A murder” changes it into a killing event and fails to convey the mutual combat that Shirou must recognize.

The English omits readiness to respond promptly upon encountering mortal danger. However, preparing one's mind for death does convey 覚悟; claiming that resolve disappears entirely overstates the error.
Blood flow is explicitly among the bodily processes monitored. The English instead assigns the flow to the Magic Circuit and never mentions blood.

“Weights” already conveys ウェイト, so both readings were not discarded. “Mental shackles” faithfully renders the written metaphor; not reproducing the additional hurdle reading does not establish a material mistranslation.

Butterflying is omitted, and a broad square striking surface becomes four flat sides. Narrow the finding accordingly: flattening is explicitly retained on the following page, and Japanese does not specify the tool's total number of faces.

Retain the ingredient error: さやインゲン means green beans in their pods, whereas ordinary English “kidney beans” suggests shelled beans. 酒 does not unequivocally specify sake, and pan-cooking reasonably conveys the surface-cooking step.
The mock-reverent personification and enthronement are genuinely lost. Remove the claimed connection to “two-suns rhetoric”: the supplied passage mentions two main dishes, not two suns.
Japanese omits the subject. Praising Shirou as “perfect again today” naturally praises his performance in the immediately established breakfast context; it need not assert personal perfection.

Read together with “I’ll make my own,” “can I help?” functions as a request to join the lunch preparation. Her participation and intended self-provision remain clear, as does Shirou's subsequent offer to share.
The explicit contrast between being unhurried and working efficiently is omitted. “Quick movements” conveys briskness but leaves out the independently stated composure.

学校前 specifies when the cooking occurs. “For school” instead specifies its purpose, losing Shirou's objection to cooking before the school day; the lunches' destination does not translate that temporal relation.
“Coming back” can mean responding or countering in conversation. “No matter what I say” and Sakura's preceding reply support precisely that idiomatic reading, without implying renewed visits.

The page links Sakura's archery hobby to shooting-range language and Shirou's realization that he is being targeted. The English preserves competitive progress but removes that linked joke from both dialogue and narration.

虎視眈々 and targeting someone's head are conventional figurative expressions. Pursuit and enmity preserve the competitive complaint, while the opening statement that he taught her cooking retains the teacher–pupil reversal.
“You can’t be better than me” can express that his superiority is unacceptable. It neither establishes that Sakura currently leads nor reverses the competition; this matches ダメ in context.
“Shrewd” can mean sensible or practically astute, not necessarily socially cunning. That overlaps with しっかりしている sufficiently that the alleged assignment of a new, manipulative trait is unsupported.

The complete Japanese explicitly includes 呆然, supporting “in a daze.” Combined with blank staring and the following question, the English reasonably compresses her apparently unselfconscious behavior rather than inventing impairment.
Retain the omitted hand withdrawal: looking down does not express pulling the hand back. Remove “defensive,” since neither the sentence nor the adjacent discovery establishes that motive.

The Japanese explicitly conveys strong unease or revulsion toward his own hand, which “looks bad” leaves vague. Limit the claim to that weakened reaction; an omen or supernatural interpretation is not required by the wording.
淹れすぎる can describe excessive tea preparation or pouring; overfilling is plausible. Drenching with soy sauce reasonably conveys the mishap, and 卵焼き does not grammatically establish a singular omelet.

“Cheerful” is less vivid than はりきる, but her immediately preceding offer to help and the retained “admirable junior” preserve the willing enthusiasm. The claimed material loss of determination exceeds the evidence.
Taking a dish from the back implies reaching, and the same English page explicitly says she leaned forward when her wrist became visible. The causal staging has not disappeared.

The cited sentence belongs to page9, supplied elsewhere in the data, not page5. There, displeasure is replaced by merely feeling like hitting her. Do not insist that the omitted object of 気にくわない must be Sakura herself rather than something she did.
Sakura denies her own entitlement to his anger on her behalf. “You can’t get mad” retains the practical plea but removes that explicit self-directed judgment and beneficiary relationship.
Both judgments explicitly occur in Original, including the supplied raw Original witness. Their absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
Retain the evidential change from “I heard” to “I think.” Treating someone as an enemy is a defensible rendering of 目の仇; the claimed loss of a necessarily persecutory fixation is overstated.

“Indecent” shifts the scar's visual unattractiveness toward impropriety, and the modest qualification is lost. However, “certainly” has support in たしかに; it is not independently an invented intensifier.
Original expressly includes Sakura looking upward as though wanting to say something. The accusation results from using the shorter edition rather than the governing Original witness.

Original explicitly places a brief vacant pause before her answer, so an immediate response is not the governing reading. “For a while” is less precise about brevity but does not establish the alleged invented, prolonged stare.

Narrow this to the missing force of 女丈夫, describing a strong, formidable woman. “Insightful” is within 達観's range, and the following English sentence explicitly preserves her maturity beyond her years.
English “made someone quit” can express a caused consequence without intention or a direct order. The Japanese explicitly uses the boy's departure as evidence of how excessive Shinji's conduct was.
The English explicitly retains the gathered female audience and the forced shooting. “He laughed at him” does not mean only Shinji laughed or that the humiliation was private.

“Very harshly” loses the explicit judgment that his severity exceeds necessity. Narrow the finding to that concession; “make fun of people like that” can refer back to the already described public humiliation.

Surprise can express disapproving disbelief. “You really are like that,” Shirou's response about thinking badly of him, and the ensuing retort retain the negative judgment; 呆れた need not receive one prescribed English label.

The following explanation identifies Rin's rejection of Shinji as what now makes sense. The English instead explicitly makes the first sentence endorse the nickname, changing the object of his acceptance.

The supplied raw Original calls Shinji 癇癪持ち, supporting the Original English branch about a nasty temper. The all-ages wording also permits losing one's temper in this anger-driven context. The joined English alternatives are extraction artifacts.

The Japanese specifically contrasts previous displaced aggression with doing something to Rin herself this time. Generic “something really bad” loses that target and escalation, leaving another attack on someone else possible.

Shirou interprets the comment as hostility toward Rin, but アイツ is ungendered and Shinji remains a plausible target of Ayako's remark. These witnesses cannot rule out Shirou misunderstanding her; the alleged definite referent reversal is not established.
弓 can denote archery metonymically, and 弓の調子 can mean how one's shooting is going. Nothing here establishes an equipment inspection, making the accusation's exclusively literal reading unwarranted.

“That part of her” naturally points to Ayako's briskly ending the exchange and moving on. The description is less explicit, but the preceding action, affection, and resulting calmer mood preserve the contextual meaning.
典座 is the temple role responsible for meals. Becoming its cook fits the dispute over food; running away to join a circus introduces an unrelated action and replaces the joke's premise.

托鉢 is more specific, but the full page retains receiving donated food, solemnly calling it religious training, bowing, and the priest's-son punchline. The generalization does not remove the act or establish a materially different joke.
二丁目 identifies a numbered neighborhood subdivision, not a numbered avenue. The English changes the kind of geographic location being named.

“Sword” is a defensible generalization of 日本刀 and preserves the inference from a long weapon to a sword. The surrounding reconstruction does not establish a material dependence on its specifically Japanese subtype.
The comparison to a street sword-slaying adds a characterization beyond the fact of murder. The English omits it entirely, losing the suggestion of indiscriminate sword violence.

A “nasty expression” can be a fierce, angry, or forbidding look without implying malice. The murder discussion and Issei's apology support that reading; a changed moral assessment is not demonstrated.

“Addresses” does not necessarily restrict speech to a greeting, and the next sentence expressly describes a talk and Issei's relaxed manner. Reduced vividness does not establish the claimed loss of conversational engagement or trust.

“I cannot go anywhere as I have work” conventionally excludes discretionary outings. The next sentence explicitly specifies going directly to work, resolving the scope; the accusation imposes an unnecessarily literal prohibition on all travel.
“No sign of life” is a normal English idiom for no apparent occupants or activity. In an apparently empty classroom it does not assert death or materially darken the scene.
“Lifeless” commonly means lacking energy or animation. Its comparative use and the surrounding concern about illness support that figurative meaning, not a newly asserted deathlike appearance.

Shirou is already holding her hand, so pulling it also pulls her arm. “Back” fits stopping her passage, and “dragging” can describe a forceful pull without prolonged movement. The alleged staging changes are not necessary readings.

“Nii-san wants me to, so I have to go” naturally communicates that her brother has requested her attendance and she feels obliged. Reading “wants” as merely an uncommunicated preference ignores the complete utterance.

The full Japanese expressly mentions complicated Matou family circumstances. The English condenses that sentence, while the immediately preceding exchange identifies the relevant sibling relationship. It does not substitute an unrelated household issue.
無責任 adds a judgment about speaking without bearing responsibility for the consequences. Merely being an outsider does not convey that qualification, which explains Shirou's reluctance to intervene.

The exchange contrasts attending with actually shooting, as Sakura's answer confirms. “Only going to watch” is a reasonable contextual paraphrase of nonparticipating attendance; 顔を出す does not itself establish a specifically brief visit.

Authority can be interpersonal or familial, not necessarily institutional. Preserving an older brother's authority by honoring his request is a defensible contextual rendering of showing him deference or saving his face.

The specific cover story—that she spent time refusing Shirou's invitation—is lost, including her asserted resistance. However, “held you up” means delayed you and does not establish direct or physical detention.

The emphatic insistence on absolute truth is reduced to a plain denial of lying. Retain that tonal omission; the supplied context does not establish a carefully framed deception or a definite sophistry joke.

The preceding English explicitly mentions stealing tea. Sakura’s response clearly refers to that proposal, and 'get into trouble' naturally covers being scolded. Compressing the repeated proposal does not materially obscure her concern.
The instruction specifically asks Sakura to lean back and lounge in her chair. 'Wait here' loses both the physical image and the teasing invitation to relax.

The isolation among people is translated defensibly, but 'outside the crowd' gives the gaze the wrong spatial reference. Her current gaze at the sunset anchors the contrast to looking outside versus inside.
Knowing one another is reciprocal here. The English preserves Shinji’s role in enabling their exceptional relationship; changing grammatical perspective does not reverse agency or the relationship.

'A small girl' can naturally mean a young child, particularly in a passage contrasting her former childish appearance with growing maturity. It does not necessarily assert short stature or import Shirou’s height motif.

'My place' followed by how she is 'at home' clearly distinguishes Shirou’s house from Sakura’s own household. Replacing the household name with this natural reference does not erase the boundary in his knowledge.
The Japanese explicitly presents an audible chuckle. A smile cannot convey that sound, and the following sentence does not restore it.

'Pole' can denote the long rod serving as the crossbar. The supplied English already identifies high jumping, and the next page describes jumping over the elevated pole. 'Crossbar' is more precise, but a change to pole vaulting is not established.

Retain the loss of being put through strenuous drills: the passive しごかれる is stronger and more specific than 'practicing.' However, the English does not explicitly say practice is voluntary, and 居残り alone does not establish forced detention.
Sakura explicitly describes the attempts as frightening to watch. The English preserves repetition and lack of complaints but entirely omits her fearful reaction.
'That’s some ending' naturally works as a sarcastic response to an anticlimax. The immediately preceding failure makes that reading clear. A possible falling echo does not establish a mistranslation.

His dismissive description of what she witnessed, averted eyes, and stammered response support self-conscious embarrassment. The English is a defensible contextual paraphrase rather than an unsupported declaration of shame.
A ringing bell can interrupt speech by drowning it out. The Japanese does not exclude an acoustic interruption, and 'as if' preserves the figurative framing.

手をあげる here means physical violence against Rin, not merely anger. The next page restores the violence explicitly, limiting the overall loss, but this sentence still substitutes a materially different action.
Original explicitly includes both discomfort at imagining the scene and a resolve to intervene. Their absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence of English invention.
Original explicitly says he suddenly turns around. 'Spin around' is ordinary English for that abrupt turn and need not mean a complete bodily revolution.
Both the snort and the turned gaze appear explicitly in Original. The finding relies on the shorter edition witness.

Retain the mistranslation of 女生, read にょしょう, as 'schoolgirl'; the marked designation concerns women, not school attendance. 'Fox' remains defensible with 'the woman' and the supernatural context. The claim that the term is a coinage is not established.
悪いことは言わないから introduces supposedly beneficial advice. Rendering it as a promise not to say bad things misrepresents the idiom and its connection to the following instruction.

The complete speech denies that his remarks constituted slander and recasts them as personal wariness. とりわけ does not require an admission of partial slander; the English preserves the same evasive self-justification.

The genuine issue is the repeated substitution of 'schoolgirl' for 女生 read にょしょう, which changes the expression Shirou objects to. The supplied evidence does not establish a newly coined word or require calling the English logically nonsensical.
Retain the loss of the conspicuously hearty, ringing laugh in かんらかんら. Romanizing the conventional shout as 'Katsu' is not itself an accuracy error, and an explanatory gloss is not mandatory.
Narrow this to the misleading 'City' rendering of 深山町, described here as a residential area. The supplied passage does not establish the asserted administrative relationship to Fuyuki.

The English omits the specified trees and lawn and replaces this park’s holiday use with an expectation about parks generally. The raw Original also distinguishes the perpetually deserted section from the surrounding park, reinforcing the concrete description.
呆れた expresses exasperation or incredulous dismay at the continued neglect. 'Sad' substitutes sorrow for that evaluative reaction.
整地 means preparing or leveling the ground. 'Retiled' introduces replacement tiles unsupported by the neglected earth and proposed grass planting.
Original explicitly supplies childhood and the difficulty of retaining the scene as possible explanations. The accusation mistakes an edition omission for an English insertion.

Within this recollection of fatal outcomes in the conflagration, failing to escape expresses the deaths of those left behind. 'Died' is a defensible contextual explicitation rather than an invented outcome.

The Japanese omits the subject; it does not grammatically require an impersonal reading. Continuing the first-person perspective of wanting to see people safe with a potential reading of 成し遂げられなかった is defensible.
くってかかった describes an angry or combative challenge to Kiritsugu. 'Denied it' conveys disagreement but drops the explicitly confrontational manner, which the adjacent ぶちまけた reinforces.
The source explicitly contrasts hearing these words only once with their continuing strong impression. Lasting memory alone does not convey the stated frequency.

正義の味方 can designate the familiar heroic or superhero archetype. The surrounding definition retains the ethical problem of selective rescue; requiring the literal word 'justice' is terminology preference, not a demonstrated error here.
'Superhero' is a defensible rendering of the heroic archetype, and the sentence preserves the restriction to chosen beneficiaries. The argument about the limits of saving everyone remains intact.
'Geez, I’m hopeless' can be a dry, locally directed self-reproach about his bleak imagined ending. It does not necessarily assert global inadequacy or despair, as the finding assumes.
Original contains the illuminated buildings and the comparison to an elaborate illumination display. 'Festival of illumination' is an expansive rendering of that comparison, not an invented scene.

最上階 literally identifies the highest floor, but the supplied sequence subsequently locates this same figure on the roof. 'Rooftop' is contextual specification of the same visual target; the alleged material relocation is not established.

The source describes her turning away before reporting her absence. The English repeats disappearance and omits the observable bodily action. This is an action omission, without implying that the English necessarily depicts teleportation.

Retain the narrower place-name issue: 'City' mislabels 深山町, described as a residential area. Neither the English nor the supplied Japanese establishes that Miyama is being made coextensive with Fuyuki.

The concrete tree-and-lawn landscape is lost, while this park’s recurring holiday crowds become a generic expectation. The raw Original’s distinction between the park and its deserted section supports the specific reading.
His reaction to the unchanged, neglected ground is mild exasperation or disbelief. 'Sad' changes that expressly identified reaction to sorrow.
The proposed work is ground preparation or leveling, consistent with planting grass. Retiling introduces an existing tiled surface and a different operation.
The disputed explanation is explicitly present in Original, including its speculative wording. Its absence from the other editions cannot support an insertion accusation.

The whole passage recalls people dying in the fire, and those unable to escape are another example. Rendering that contextual implication as 'died' is defensible; the Japanese does not establish the finding’s proposed bounded uncertainty.

An omitted Japanese subject is not necessarily impersonal. The preceding first-person wish supports taking 成し遂げられなかった as his inability to achieve it; the accusation treats an alternative reading as mandatory.
The verb specifies snapping back or aggressively challenging someone. A bare denial loses that confrontational behavior, supported by the subsequent description of his outpouring to Kiritsugu.
The only-once qualification is explicit and absent from the English. It establishes a contrast with the words’ enduring impact, regardless of any proposed use in cross-scene analysis.

'Superhero' can convey 正義の味方 as an idealized rescuer. The explicit definition and its exclusionary implications remain translated; omission of the literal component 'justice' does not establish semantic collapse.

The colloquial self-reproach can refer specifically to his inability to imagine a hopeful outcome. Reading 'I’m hopeless' as necessarily global inadequacy or despair overstates what the English says in context.

Original explicitly describes the lit buildings and compares them to an elaborate illumination display. The accusation follows the shorter edition witness and incorrectly labels the comparison unsupported.

Although 'highest floor' is lexically closer, the supplied continuation places the same observed person on the rooftop. There is no demonstrated change of target or consequential premature revelation.
The bodily turn is an explicit part of the departure, followed by her disappearance from view. The English drops that action and replaces the sequence with repeated absence.
Narrow the finding to rendering 深山町 as 'Miyama City' rather than a town or neighborhood designation. The claimed identification with all of Fuyuki is not established by the supplied wording.
売れない means commercially unsuccessful, not notorious, and 演歌歌手 specifies an enka singer rather than an idol. Both the performer category and the nature of the dismissive description change.

The supplied raw Original passage explicitly says 自衛隊 and identifies recruitment for its members. The page’s originalJa field reproduces the altered youth-association wording; this is an edition/witness mismatch, not the alleged replacement by English.

The English preserves the dazed, repetitive seeing-stars outburst. The Japanese-to-English lexical switch cannot remain the same switch in an English translation; absence of compensatory wordplay alone does not establish a material accuracy error.

The comparison specifically concerns cutting wooden chopsticks with their paper sleeve, explaining his speculation about a paper weapon. Generic 'skill of a master' omits the substantive comic comparison.
なんまいだぶ is a colloquial Buddhist invocation, used here with his joking fear of being killed. 'How true' turns that mock prayer into agreement and changes the joke’s action.

The Japanese already predicts losing dinner if Shirou objects to Fuji-nee. Her depriving him of it is a plausible contextual interpretation. The finding's alternative explanation—that their communal dinner cannot get underway—is not established.

町 can designate a town or an urban district. This page does not establish Miyama's administrative relationship to Fuyuki, so the claimed promotion to an independent municipality needs a geographical witness.
'Strange' can convey suspicious or unsettling behavior in this context. The surrounding check for abnormalities preserves the concern; behavioral suspicion has not demonstrably disappeared.

孫の頼み explicitly attributes a request to the grandchild. The following threat is also Japanese. Neither version establishes that Sakura specifically requested violence against Shirou; Zouken is treating him as the reported suspicious outsider.

The neutral reference to a question omits the explicit juxtaposition of cheerful delivery and menacing statements. The preceding dialogue retains the threat, but not this characterization of its delivery.

様子 has no expressed possessor here. Shirou introduces his connections to both siblings, and Zouken immediately offers to summon both. Although Sakura motivates his visit, plural reference in this public explanation is defensible.

The apparent displeasure is genuinely omitted. However, its precise cause is not established: Zouken has not yet given Shirou his name, and subsequently explains his introduction as reciprocal courtesy.

The explicit noun 座 and the assessment of its workmanship or outcome disappear. However, 'it' can refer back to the Einzbern discussion; 'no possible antecedent' overstates the problem. The precise lore referent remains unestablished here.

お爺ちゃん explicitly identifies Sakura's grandfather. Possessive 'your old man' conventionally means father or husband, making it misleading here even though the earlier mention of a granddaughter helps readers recover the relationship.
ガッカリ describes disappointment or dejection, reinforced by the sigh and failed expectation. 'Shocked' substitutes a different emotional reaction.
隠居しておる describes an existing retired or secluded state. 'Will go away' substitutes a future action. 'Do not reserve yourself' also obscures the invitation to visit without feeling constrained.

孫たちと善くしてやってくれ naturally asks him to maintain good relations with the grandchildren. Given their established acquaintance, 'stay friends' is a defensible social equivalent. An 'unsettling breadth' is interpretive.

'Shed' generalizes the storage outbuilding, while 'practice my daily routine' conveys recurring practice or training. The phrasing is awkward and less specific, but the alleged grammatical or material change is not established.

The sentence identifies his exhausted, rescued childhood self as the dream's endpoint. English replaces that identification with an awkward clause about how he is rescued. The preceding ten-year reference does not fully preserve this construction.

'Metal weight inside my chest' preserves the oppressive internal heaviness of the lead metaphor. Calling it an external weight misdescribes the English. Original explicitly contains this sentence despite its omission from the other editions.

Omitting a routine vocative is defensible English adaptation. Sakura's offer remains polite, and the next page explicitly identifies Fuji-nee's school-club role. No material relationship change is demonstrated.
Konnyaku is an explicitly named ingredient alongside lotus root. The English dish description retains lotus root and chicken but drops konnyaku entirely.
寝覚めが悪い can describe waking in an unpleasant mood. 'Grouchy' is a plausible colloquial rendering in Shirou's reassurance that nothing else is wrong; the Japanese does not exclude irritability.
ムキになる includes becoming heated, upset, or defensive. 'Shouldn't get mad about it' reasonably conveys having no reason to react that way to Fuji-nee's apparent indifference.

The Japanese qualifies recovery by a specific ability: brushing off the dream afterward. 'Well over it' makes a substantially broader claim of recovery, even though the English retains that ability as supporting evidence.

弟分としては explicitly frames Shirou's reply as coming from her unofficial younger brother, answering the preceding big-sister stance. This reciprocal role-based joke is absent from English; 'sweet' itself is defensible.

The back-of-hand endpoint and palm-directed comparison are genuinely generalized to 'hand.' However, the English preserves the overall shoulder-to-hand direction, so claiming that direction itself is erased is excessive.

Following 'I'm fine,' 'How about you?' asks whether Shirou is well. Her immediately following concern about his appearance and worsening injury makes the health question explicit. This is a defensible conversational compression.

The raw English contains mutually exclusive edition branches, not shipped duplicate fragments. Original also contains both clearing his thoughts and the building's apparent lack of vitality. 'Lifeless' is therefore supported, not an invented contradiction.
ごまする means flattering or currying favor. 'Sticking up for' means defending someone, changing the substance of Shinji's accusation about obtaining favorable school reports.
The target-mound cleanup is a separate unfinished task. Neither the general description of disorder nor the English reference to bowstrings communicates it.

'I don't know' can function as a hesitant objection to 'It's fine, right?' rather than a literal statement of ignorance. The girl still dissents and adds a practical objection, preserving the disagreement.

The specific etiquette point—that even stringing another person's bow would be discourteous—is omitted. However, declining because the bow is not his retains ownership-based restraint and implies an etiquette concern.

The carbon-bow discussion is present in Original, including active raw Original prose about price and club funds. Its removal or commenting-out in the other Japanese edition does not make the Original English unsupported.
The English omits both named locations and the observation that dirt remains in smaller details. Those details explain the additional cleaning after the general tidying was already completed.

Original explicitly describes drawing his body in against the cold. The raw English restricts this sentence to the corresponding edition. Its wording is awkward, but the bodily gesture is not invented.
'No sign of life' is an ordinary English idiom for an apparently deserted place. It does not assert death and is appropriate to the school's absence of people and bustle.

向かってしまった conveys ending up going, with retrospective regret. It does not establish contemporaneous knowledge that he must not go. The later speculation about instinct likewise does not establish that knowledge.

The Japanese itself retrospectively qualifies the impression as initial and distant. English can express the same limitation and anticipation of a closer discovery; it does not necessarily give Shirou prior knowledge of their nonhumanity.

The explicit inference of bladed, cutting combat is generalized to weapons. However, 'fighting' in context still conveys combat between opponents; the claim that reciprocity also disappears is overstated.
'Dangerously armed' preserves menace but omits the substantial description of armament beyond anachronism and too formidable to dismiss as a joke.
The comparison explicitly places these weapons far beyond kitchen knives and other knives. English retains their lethal purpose but entirely omits that comparison of lethality.
'My heart stops' conventionally describes a moment of terror figuratively. In this fear-response passage it need not assert cardiac arrest. The finding improperly literalizes the English idiom.
持つ identifies people possessing magical energy. 'With knowledge of' changes that condition to intellectual familiarity, which is not equivalent.

The page already twice states that the red fighter will be killed. 'Survive it' expresses that predicted consequence of an indefensible strike; it does not introduce the alleged new certainty of death.

淀む describes blood stagnating, not coagulating, so 'clots' is a genuine change. 'Exploded' can loosely compress breaking apart and scattering blood; treating it as a separate literal explosion is less secure.
Retain the substitution of brief duration for the pause's explicit strangeness. The fragment itself is not an independent grammatical error: the Japanese also deliberately uses a fragment.
のか can mark a dawning realization as well as a question. Hearing his own breathing supports 'must still be alive' as an inference, not an asserted medical fact.
The explicit blood-soaked condition is omitted. Limit the finding to that physical detail: the claims about intimacy and cost are interpretive, while the English preserves contact without hesitation.

'Reforge' suggests remaking the existing organ, whereas 偽造して代用 describes fabricating a substitute while the heart is repaired. Retain that distinction; 'in the process' can still convey concurrent activity and does not necessarily reverse the sequence.

Sentence-final じゃない can be rhetorical affirmation ('isn't that instant-admission level?') or literal negation ('beyond that level'). The supplied unvoiced text does not securely distinguish them, so the claimed deletion of a higher benchmark is unproven.
The page first describes returning sensation, then returning bodily functions. Repeating 'feeling' for the second statement removes the explicit broader physiological recovery.

The image of heat sufficient to startle his dead body is genuinely omitted. However, melting can continue the source's frozen-blood metaphor; it does not necessarily assert a literal healing mechanism.

Retain the omitted stunned awakening and throat-focused nausea. 'Feel sick' adequately conveys nausea, and 'whole body' can colloquially summarize pain in various places rather than establish a distinct new distribution of injury.
'Cold' omits being chilled through to the point of shivering. This removes an explicit degree and physical manifestation of his condition.
The English omits that the uniform is torn specifically at the chest and that his blood heavily stains or adheres to the corridor floor. Both concrete descriptions are present in Original.
With the preceding throat nausea, holding back what rises describes suppressing vomit or nausea. 'Bearing the pain' substitutes a different symptom.
雑巾 identifies a wiping rag, whereas a floor mop normally denotes a different implement. Retain the object error, but remove the alleged contradiction with wiping the floor: a mop can also do that.
The Japanese describes lack of strength in both upper and lower limbs. English restricts the condition to hand steadiness, omitting the leg weakness and changing the expressly described impairment.

The kitchen-knife comparison and deep penetration are genuinely omitted. The chest location, however, remains explicit in the immediately preceding English sentences, so it has not disappeared from the remembered event as a whole.
下がっていく describes symptoms subsiding progressively. 'Vanish' asserts complete disappearance, which the Japanese does not establish.
In conjunction with possessing substance, 直接干渉 describes directly affecting living humans. 'Associate directly' suggests company or social contact and fails to convey the relevant capacity.

The agentive 押し入った already invokes the perpetrator within the incident description. Recalling the local robbery-murder through its murderous burglar is a defensible metonymic paraphrase, not necessarily a changed event or agency.

掻きむしる describes clawing or scratching, substantially stronger than holding. The self-derogatory qualifier つまらない is also omitted from this act of self-restraint, although nearby English retains his shame.
叩き出す specifies forcibly driving the intruder out. 'Counter' conveys opposition but omits expulsion as Shirou's concrete objective.
The English is awkward but grammatical and retains words suggesting reconstruction of the speaker. Reduced clarity about autosuggestion does not establish a material mistranslation.
構成材質 identifies the material constituting the object. “Basic quality” replaces that concrete object of analysis with a generic property, obscuring what this technical stage examines.
“Trace, off” follows the expressly supplied ruby. Using the spoken incantation is defensible, and the surrounding termination and success narration preserves its completion function.

“Metal” is less specific, but defensibly conveys this ordinary comparison of reinforced paper with hard metal. The passage does not establish a technical distinction requiring an exact iron benchmark.
“Stand up” omits his explicitly stated position in the middle of the room. Retain the spatial omission; a deliberate decision to wait for the intruder is not established here.
In this farewell before another attempted killing, 迷う naturally evokes failing to pass on or wandering after death. “Don’t come back this time” defensibly conveys that taunt.

The preceding English explicitly says the lance is swung sideways. Combined with the face target here, the attack remains clear; the finding incorrectly treats its direction as absent from the narration.
Retain the missing full-swing commitment. The sweeping geometry is substantially conveyed by the beautiful arc and attack from the other side, so its wholesale removal is overstated.

The explicit involvement of both arms is incorrectly reduced to one. “Broken” is a defensible approximation of damaged, crushed bones here; calling it an “ordinary break” adds an unsupported severity distinction.
After the preceding attempt to flick the shaft away, “only moves slightly” naturally describes the limited displacement achieved. It does not materially replace the deflection with unrelated motion.
“Armed fight” suits an exchange involving a sword and lance. “Good” explicates Lancer’s plainly expressed disappointment with Shirou’s performance rather than inventing a quality judgment.
The Japanese describes allowing Shirou to strike at him, whereas “let me hit him once” represents a landed hit on the man. The supplied action instead records contact with his lance.

The Japanese specifies acting without confirmation, not without thought. The next page explicitly confirms an expectation, making the distinction between an unverified prediction and an unthinking action consequential.
Retain the omitted comparison to being kicked like a ball. The interrupted word is intentional: both raw scripts end the thought with a dash command as the wall impact interrupts it.
The English omits the back-breaking intensity attributed to the wall impact and replaces the subsequent sliding fall with a crash. The Japanese does not assert that his back actually breaks.
Original explicitly identifies the shed as his destination. The English apposition is understandable and grammatical; the supplied witnesses provide no evidence of a corrupted mixed variant.
The source specifies charging directly at Shirou. “Approaches” omits the manner and straight course of this urgent attack, even though the next page retains his imminent arrival.
Generic recovery drops the specific image of forcibly rallying a heart that seems about to stop. That bodily distress is explicit, whether literal or figurative.
もしやとは思うが can introduce a tentative, seemingly unlikely possibility. “It’s unlikely, but maybe” is defensible; the finding’s claim of an already developing suspicion is not required by the Japanese.
埋まる can describe the process of becoming embedded, so metal entering his body is defensible. 鉄 also functions as a material description of the weapon; the English says “into,” not “through.”

Retain the omitted breaking-through of the ribs. 刺さる is nonpast and permits imminent or projected action; the surrounding suspended attack does not establish that chest penetration has already occurred.

Retain the omission of the back of the left hand. Grabbing or clutching the painful hand can reasonably render 押さえつける; a fundamentally different action is not established.

The curse-like characterization is compressed, but the preserved accusation “Coward” and angry complaint retain hostility. “Complains” does not make the speech mild or erase its abusive content.

The clearest error is changing “for the sake of this instant” into suppressing strain “for an instant.” The leg metaphor need not be literalized, and the Japanese does not establish a separate preparatory action.
“Twirls her body” conveys rapid bodily rotation and can compress the spinning-top simile. It does not inherently mean a weak or gentle movement; that tonal contrast is imposed by the finding.
The generic execution of a blow omits なぎ払う, the sweeping action connecting her rotation with the opponent being knocked away. Whole-body involvement alone does not specify that action.

The supplied passage does not establish that 槍剣 denotes a distinctive hybrid weapon rather than a broader spear/blade expression. The alleged contrast with Lancer’s weapon requires lexical or contextual support not supplied.

“Slow” can characterize his current failure to react or understand. In this taunt it need not assert a permanent intellectual deficiency, and 惚けている itself permits an unflattering description of his awareness.
The English omits the concrete basis for Lancer’s insult: his Master will not show himself. Generic cowardice does not preserve that information about the Master’s absence.
“To prove my point” is a normal narrative idiom for an event confirming the preceding assessment. It need not attribute an intention to Saber, and 事実 performs that confirming function here.

The English preserves the expressly supplied spoken name and its two-beat invocation. Translating a named attack through its ruby is defensible; requiring a simultaneous descriptive gloss is a presentation preference here.
Bleeding badly does not itself convey a pierced chest. The English omits the specific penetrating injury stated at this point, though later narration supplies further information about the strike.

The English compresses targeting into use against the victim. The complete passage still describes the opponent’s predetermined heart wound; it does not establish a different activation mechanism or an untargeted effect.

The page already calls her extraordinary, then expresses astonishment at her abnormal capabilities. “Too strange” is defensible colloquial incredulity here and need not introduce disapproval or replace the magnitude judgment.

Retain the overstatement from diminishing hostility to disappearance. Annoyance and a later conditional threat do not independently prove that hostility could not temporarily disappear, so remove that supporting argument.
Neither the Japanese nor the English establishes an exclusive transmission time. “He’s telling me” can report an operative instruction, and the Original raw witness itself uses ぬかしてやがる.
“Be prepared to die” expresses readiness to face death, not a factual prediction that death is certain. It directly conveys the resolve demanded by 決死の覚悟.
Naivety can mean innocent simplicity or lack of sophistication. Applied to her face within a description of youthful appearance, it need not allege intellectual deficiency.
The supposedly invented rationale appears explicitly in Original, including strength, armor, and girls having to fight. The accusation relies on the later-edition omission.
Original explicitly describes her quiet voice on this page. The later witnesses omit the sentence, which does not make its English translation unsupported.

English “master” already carries the ordinary meaning of lord or person with authority over a servant. It preserves both the system designation and the everyday meaning of 主人.
痺れ can denote a painful tingling or electric sensation, and the immediate exclamation explicitly marks pain. “Pain” is less specific but does not demonstrably misrepresent this experience.
Original supplies both the intended question and the sudden change in her demeanor. The English rearranges the interrupted question naturally; neither element is invented.

“Only healed the outside” conveys superficial closure with deeper damage unresolved. The Japanese does not establish a separate nonhealing covering mechanism that would make this paraphrase materially wrong.

Disrupting an opponent’s guard is a defensible contextual rendering of breaking his fighting posture. The Japanese, including Original’s 態勢 variant, does not require a distinct loss-of-balance event.

“Cuts off” can mean terminates or stops an effect without physical cutting. The supplied continuation explicitly says Saber nullified the magic, so the alleged replacement of magical negation is not established.
The ruby explicitly reads オヤジ, supporting a paternal form of reference. “Father” neither treats the title as a personal name nor requires biological parenthood.

“Thank God” is an ordinary idiom of relief and need not imply religious belief. It compresses the psychological benefit into an emotional reaction; the lost tentativeness does not establish the alleged material change.

Retain the loss of the explicit necessity: stopping her would require confronting her with full effort. The Japanese does not say that even full effort might fail; its negative prediction is conditional on not exerting it.
The genuine change is from feeling sympathy for an attacker to being willing to release one. The English states a hypothetical disposition under negation, not an actual release decision.
Putting strength into the sword is a physical response, reinforced by her later relaxing her hand. Concentrating attention on the sword substitutes mental focus for that action.

Retain the stronger accusation of disloyalty introduced by “betray” where the immediate issue is defying an instruction. Betrayal does not necessarily mean changing allegiance, so that part of the explanation is false.

“Relaxes” loses the precise hand movement, but the following English sentence preserves the inferred putting away of the sword. The Japanese does not establish a specific weapon-dismissal mechanism whose loss constitutes a material error.

The raw English places the two occurrences of “definitely” in alternative branches. The supplied raw Original also contains the exclaimed recognition, so neither duplication nor an invented scream is established.
The narrower loss of qualitative praise survives: a “big smile” conveys にっこり but not 極上. The claims about an unnervingly perfect social mask or deliberately polished expression exceed the Japanese.
“Glares” already conveys an angry or hostile look, especially after this warning. A separate “with hostility” is not necessary to preserve the meaning.

The English does lose Shirou’s qualification of his admiration. However, past 憧れていた does not independently establish that his admiration has ended, and an unqualified statement need not imply wholly unreserved admiration.

Keep the substitution of summoning for using or commanding the familiar. “Transfer part of their body into something” is a defensible, less precise description of transplantation, particularly with the animal hosts explained immediately afterward.

使役 concerns employing or controlling a familiar, not summoning it; the surrounding discussion concerns sustained control. Drop the separate numerical accusation: Japanese 魔術回路 does not explicitly specify singular or plural here.
The raw English selects the personal and family versions through mutually exclusive branches. The personal version corresponds to Original; the apparent combined statement is an extraction artifact.
The narration explicitly registers Rin’s pleasure and Shirou’s uncertainty about its cause. Neither observation appears in the English; her preceding dialogue alone does not preserve them.
“Takes a look” compresses the manner of inspection and can naturally describe a brief examination. The reduced detail does not demonstrably alter the action or establish a material timing error.

Addressed directly to the person who helped, “I’m glad you fixed it” naturally communicates appreciation. The accusation incorrectly treats this conversational acknowledgment as merely private satisfaction.

“Usually” introduces an unsupported temporal contrast and weakens the specific connection between beauty and intimidating silence. But the English still connects beauty causally to scariness; it does not necessarily say she has ceased to be beautiful.

半端 disparages the selected magecraft as limited or unsatisfactory, whereas “odd” principally calls it unusual. Narrow the finding accordingly: the grammar does not specifically establish that Rin is judging his execution of Strengthening as incomplete.

“That is a separate issue” can naturally become “that doesn’t matter right now” in this objection. The English retains his insistence that he has worked seriously; the Japanese leaves the exact referents of それ and これ implicit.
The opening is awkward, but the same English passage explicitly says the mark overrides the Servant’s will and enforces “your command.” Command authority and its holder are therefore preserved.

倒す can mean killing an opponent in lethal conflict. Rin is directly affirming Shirou’s question about being killed, so this rendering is contextually defensible; the lexical substitution alone does not prove an invented formal rule.

The complete sentence explicitly describes mutual killing and a struggle for survival. Rendering 倒す as “kill” within that description is defensible; the finding isolates it from the governing lethal context.

実感 concerns the explanation feeling real or concrete to Shirou. “Too brief for me to understand” instead presents inadequate comprehension, losing the distinction between hearing the information and internalizing its reality.

“Artificial gods” can describe divinity produced through worship without implying deliberate manufacture. The narrower issue is that the English states categorically what Rin presents with conjectural qualification.

The specific examples concern spirit invocation and mediumship, which “supplicating ghosts” does not accurately identify. “Ghost Magic” itself is a defensible broad label for magic dealing with spirits, so that terminology objection should be removed.

The Japanese makes the Heroic Spirit itself the familiar. “Familiars of the heroes themselves” ordinarily assigns the familiars to the heroes and fails to communicate this identity, central to the contrast with borrowing their power.

The supplied raw Original explicitly includes decapitation. The English outcomes occupy alternative branches, so the apparent competing insertion results from edition conflation and flattened extraction.

In Rin’s continuing simplified account, already characterized as 殺し合い and eliminating other Masters, the lethal sense of 倒す remains defensible. “All” is also established earlier. The finding does not demonstrate that the translator independently invented an exceptionless rule.
知るべき事でもない disclaims responsibility or an obligation to know. The English instead asserts that Rin does not know, changing her stated grounds for declining the question.
風格 evaluates Saber’s dignified bearing or stature. “A good personality” replaces that particular appraisal with a general judgment about temperament or likability.
悔しい can include anger or vexation over a frustrating loss. Her preceding regret supplies that cause, and “with anger” assigns no different target. The gesture is also explicitly present in Original.
容赦がない means merciless or unforgiving. “Shows no openings” describes invulnerability or guardedness and changes the judgment prompted by Rin’s blunt insult.

Saber identifies insufficient knowledge, supporting the proposed explanatory visit. “Experience” substitutes practical familiarity for that information deficit and also loses the explicit excessive degree.

“I want you to be stronger” can function as a serious directive in English. The preceding contractual framing remains, and the narration explicitly locates Saber’s concern in Shirou’s welfare; no separate contractual duty is established here.

“Pervert” is a defensible contextual rendering of 痴漢 and retains the sexual implication. The narrower loss is the explicit attack condition: 襲われたら describes them being attacked, whereas “appears” merely states arrival.
Original explicitly describes Rin’s lively, happy delivery while looking up at the bridge. Its absence from the other editions does not make the English an insertion.

The park is firmly established in the adjacent English. Omitting its repetition here slightly compresses the proposed atmospheric explanation but does not remove the setting or demonstrate a material distortion of the attraction beat.
Rin’s ascent is explicitly narrated in Original. The accusation relies on the shorter edition rather than the governing witness.

“Compelling” is imprecise, but paired with “towering over its visitors” it can convey a forceful, imposing presence. The entire sentence does not establish the claimed conversion into attraction or persuasion.
似て非なる explicitly juxtaposes resemblance with a difference in nature. “Barely similar” instead minimizes the resemblance, losing the idiom’s central relationship between the organizations.

The malformed coordination is real and obscures how the church custodian exemplifies the general principle. Drop the claim that “should” necessarily makes this optional advice; it can express an expected condition here.

“Inseparable relationship” conveys the persistent bond, while the immediately following wish never to have met him supplies its unwanted character. Reading the complete exchange rules out the alleged positive closeness.

“Must have” marks an inference rather than directly witnessed fact and is a normal rendering of this explanatory のか. Kirei has already answered their conversation, making inferred awareness especially natural.

覚えはない can idiomatically reject an imposed status, much like “I didn’t sign up for that.” Shirou already knows the label and is resisting it; the accusation unnecessarily restricts the Japanese to recollection or awareness.

The bored-looking expression is genuinely omitted. However, the Japanese does not establish that her boredom is performed, and Kirei’s explicit claim about her relying on him occurs later, not on this page.
Original explicitly narrates Kirei laughing with apparent amusement. The English action is supported; the accusation arises from using the shortened edition.

元通り specifically promises restoration to a previous state. “As you desire” substitutes general wish fulfillment. The later reference to starting over preserves related imagery but does not make this substitution accurate.

The translation changes both the image’s bodily location and its action: words penetrate the chest or heart and cling viscously, rather than enter the brain and coagulate. This alters the expressly described sensation.
The proverb concerns kindness benefiting its giver, which Kirei’s enjoyment and Rin’s follow-up explicitly support. “Not good for others” gives a different meaning and breaks that connection.

The repeated term and the question’s referent are the Holy Grail itself. Adding “War” makes the first question ask about the conflict, creating an unnecessary referent shift before the question about the actual cup.

In this recollection of the familiar Holy Grail and its collection of sacred blood, Christ is a normal contextual identification of 聖者. Japanese omission of an explicit name or article does not make that identification unsupported.

眉唾 can dismiss a story as bogus or a tall tale, not merely suspend judgment. In Shirou’s skeptical narration, “just an invention” is a defensible expression of that dismissal rather than a claim of independently verified fabrication.

聞かない limits the assertion to what Shirou has heard about actual existence or successful reproduction. “Doesn’t exist and isn’t possible” replaces that evidential limitation with categorical denial, especially of possibility.

The genuine issue is “almost”: Kirei says the miracle can be classified as 魔法, while the English leaves it short of that classification. “Sorcery” can serve as the distinct English term for 魔法 and is not itself evidence of conflating categories.
真贋 concerns whether something is genuine or counterfeit. “The object’s unreality” instead attributes unreality to it, changing the argument that authenticity is irrelevant beside demonstrated power.

“Reach” can broadly express inability to make contact. Shirou immediately restates the restriction as “Only spirits can touch spirits,” so the complete English page preserves the precise reason Servants are needed.

The Japanese describes outrageously formidable swordsmanship, not merely possession of sword skill. The English drops the exceptional degree in one of Shirou’s explicit reasons that defeating Saber is impossible.

潰される can mean being killed in this context. The next page explicitly identifies killing the Master as the tactic being deduced. Rin’s earlier distinction concerns what is required, not whether Kirei is now discussing that lethal tactic.

Shirou is summarizing the preceding passage, which explicitly describes killing Masters. “Killing” is therefore a justified contextual sense of 倒す, and calling it effective does not make it a formal necessity.

The English states an ongoing ability for as long as Command Spells remain, with no one-contract limit. The following page explicitly explains replacement contracts and reentry, so the alleged loss of that mechanism is not established.

The English is more explicit, but Shirou has just voiced the proposal Kirei now ridicules. Ordinary insight into that stated intention is contextually available; this does not materially establish new access to concealed thoughts.

The broken fragments result from flattening mutually exclusive English branches. Original explicitly contains mockery and a rough, irritated narration, supporting the longer English version and its colloquial anger.

Here なったつもりはない rejects having knowingly assumed the role. “No intention of being a Master” defensibly conveys that stance and need not refer only to the future; the following offer to abandon the role confirms willingness is at issue.

The English weakens explicit priority into the size or importance of a responsibility. However, 最優先事項 does not establish that this must be the uniquely singular top priority, and “as the supervisor” retains the institutional framing.

末端 can legitimately refer to a low organizational echelon. The narrower error is structural: the Japanese places the church within the special bureau, whereas “the lowest of the special agencies” makes it one agency ranked among others.
Narrow to reduced emphasis on extreme severity. Recurrence is explicitly retained earlier on the page, and indiscriminate killing preserves the violence; neither is removed wholesale.
戒める includes warning or admonishing. A supervisor can formally caution rule breakers; the Japanese does not require punitive enforcement here.
The courteous gesture is genuinely omitted. However, laughter already suggests amusement, and 慇懃 does not by itself establish insincere or performed politeness.
In this challenge about a disaster, 'not troubled by' defensibly expresses lack of concern. The claim that it presupposes a particular trauma response overinterprets the English.
'Looked terrible' naturally refers back to Rin's immediately preceding 'You're pale white.' The concrete pallor and reason for her concern remain explicit in context.
The narration explicitly describes Kirei's apparent enjoyment while prompting Shirou. The neutral English invitation omits that characterization; the dialogue does not otherwise establish it.
一時的に modifies the Grail's becoming genuine within the relative clause. English instead attaches 'temporarily' to obtaining it, losing the stated temporary manifestation.

Japanese explicitly denies reaching completion. 'Imperfectly completed' instead describes defective completion, obscuring the distinction between manifestation and completion developed in the surrounding explanation.

甘ちゃん criticizes softness or naivety, whereas 'chicken' specifically alleges cowardice. Retain that distinction, but remove the unsupported insistence that the word establishes an idealist motivated by excessive mercy.

The genuine shift is from whether mental readiness already existed to deciding whether to prepare. 'Prepare' need not mean practical preparation, and the next page retains the discussion of readiness.
'He doesn't need to ask' can convey that Shirou needs no prompting because his response is already settled. Converting the passive idiom into an active English sentence does not reverse agency.

先日 is less specific than 'yesterday,' but yesterday can fall within its reference. The supplied pages do not establish Archer's summoning date, so contextual explicitation cannot be distinguished from an incorrect date.
兄弟子 specifically identifies a senior fellow disciple. 'Fellow pupil' retains shared training but omits seniority, a relevant part of Shirou's appeal for a more respectful farewell.
'I feel like' retains a subjective, nonliteral experience rather than asserting an actual completed blackout. The small aspectual difference does not establish the claimed material perceptual event.

'Insecure' can mean unstable or lacking firm foundations, especially when applied to an abstract wish. The following reference to inconsistent ideals supports that reading rather than personal lack of confidence.

理想 is not grammatically marked as singular. The surrounding conflict between protecting something and desiring its threat permits plural 'ideals'; 'inconsistent' need not exclude internal contradiction.

'Worries' is broader than 葛藤, but here refers directly to the preceding distress over contradictory desires. The supplied context does not establish a material change from inner conflict to an unrelated concern.
'Kill or be killed' idiomatically conveys entering a world of lethal participation. The surrounding statements that his world changes and he is now a Master preserve the change in status.
泥仕合 describes an ugly, discreditable struggle; it does not require a deadlock or literal mire imagery. 'Dirty killings' defensibly compresses that condemnation in an established mutual conflict.

Kirei explicitly asks whether Shirou will fight. 'He doesn't even need to ask me' naturally expresses the firmness of Shirou's already determined answer; refusal to accept instruction is not mandatory.

構わない can be rendered 'I don't care' in this exchange. The next sentence explicitly preserves Rin's restraint because it is Shirou's choice, and Kirei's reference to guilt undercuts literal emotional indifference.

The challenged sentence belongs to the mature English branch, while supplied raw Original nearby already specifies an arm. Its corresponding Original aftermath paragraph is missing, so the shoulder and bleeding details cannot responsibly be classified as inventions.

'Assisted suicide' is a broad but defensible explanatory rendering of カイシャク here. The Original English branch immediately specifies seated beheading, preserving the cultural mechanism of the distorted joke.

The lung and distance occur only in the mature English branch. No corresponding raw Original passage is supplied, and nearby witnesses demonstrate substantive edition differences; the repeated page fields do not resolve that alignment problem.

The alleged duplication is demonstrably branch flattening. The remaining accusations concern the mature branch, whose matching raw Original is absent; nearby edition differences prevent certifying those details as unsupported additions.

'Senses' can denote reason or mental faculties, as in losing one's senses. This figurative sentence does not necessarily assert cessation of hearing or feeling, so the claimed contradiction is not established.

'Senses' can encompass consciousness or awareness. In this passage about remaining aware despite injury, it need not restrict the meaning to individual sensory faculties; magical causation is not specified by the quoted sentence.

'Hope' follows the explicit ruby reading, while the preceding English retains frozen rationality. Losing the visual double meaning is a presentation tradeoff, not by itself a demonstrable material mistranslation.
簡単には qualifies the likelihood or ease of attack. English removes it and states enemies will not attack at home, overstating the protection; the preceding English likewise drops まず's qualification.

Retain the loss of being caught unawares in generic 'beaten.' 寝首をかく can be figurative and need not promise literal assassination; 'potential' can mean fighting capability in this explicit combat context.

In direct response to the claim that he cannot keep secrets, 'I can take care of myself' defensibly asserts competence in handling that situation. It does not necessarily change the subject to physical defense or general self-care.

The specific instruction to stop attempting strategic maneuvering is lost in reassurance. However, the preceding English already criticizes his inability to conceal things, so the judgment of unsuitability is not wholly removed.

'Would happily' can mean 'would readily/without scruple,' fitting やりかねない in this accusation of untrustworthiness. It asserts neither an actual sale nor habitual behavior, and 人の can refer indignantly to Rin's own information.
親しみ includes fondness and affectionate warmth. 'A bit of affection,' qualified by 'seem,' preserves both modest degree and Shirou's uncertainty without implying romantic love.
白い describes the visible whiteness of exhalation. 'Cold' substitutes temperature and omits that visual detail from the list of memorable sensory impressions.

The homeward destination is explicitly omitted from this sentence. Narrow the finding accordingly: the next page preserves their respective homes and impending separation, and Japanese does not require one shared final destination.
The silence is explicitly present in both the supplied Original page and raw Original. Its absence from later-edition prose cannot establish an insertion in the Original comparator.
やられる commonly means being killed in lethal combat. Shirou has just said he will die before Saber, making that reading natural; this warning does not assert that every possible defeat must be fatal.
腹 identifies the abdomen or belly, not the chest. English changes the location of the knife in an otherwise closely rendered physical comparison.
All three allegedly added thoughts appear in the supplied Original and its raw witness. Their omission from the later editions is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
The English is redundant and awkward, but it accurately conveys the large disparity; this is editing criticism, not a translation error.
それも僅かな物 limits how much composure Rin has; “come to nothing” instead predicts that her readiness will prove futile.
The English clause is grammatically malformed and fails to state clearly that Rin should recognize the full name.

This is an edition/branch artifact. The supplied raw Original witness has 「じゃあ殺すね」, directly supporting “I’ll kill you”; the public text flattened that branch together with the later 「じゃあいくね」 version.
クセに marks an unexpected contrast—his body is paralyzed yet his mind works calmly. “That’s why” reverses this into causation.
弾ける itself permits “burst” or “explode.” The following no-scratch statement establishes that the magical eruption caused no lasting injury; it does not make that lexical choice demonstrably false.
Although stiff, “cannot compare to” can idiomatically mean “cannot match,” which conveys 敵うはずのない.
The Japanese depicts fresh blood scattering; a stationary accumulated “pool of blood” is an unsupported change to the image.
“Unconsciously” can mean while unconscious, and the surrounding sentence makes that reading clear. The accusation relies on a possible secondary ambiguity rather than an actual contradiction.
The raw English shows mutually exclusive edition branches flattened into the supplied display. In the Original branch, the inference appears only once, split for dramatic pacing.
The Japanese asks which single person will be defeated and immediately identifies her; “the ones getting killed” wrongly pluralizes that referent.
弟子一号 is the numbered dojo title “Disciple Number One,” not “senior student”; the recurring hierarchy is changed.
肝 with こそ presents the dojo as Fate’s very core or essential point. “An important part” materially weakens the climactic boast.
The raw Original Japanese specifically says Shirou’s lower body is flattened and only his head remains. The supplied English merely exposes Original and later-edition branches together.
“Genocide of love” is a compressed but defensible rendering of genocide rationalized as affection’s reverse expression; the central comic contradiction remains.
In this answer-rejection exchange, “Unsatisfactory!” naturally means unacceptable or not approved. It preserves the immediate mock-authoritarian rejection.
With じゃんじゃん選びなさい, “you’ll die a lot” naturally conveys the repeated result of choosing those options; the availability/prediction distinction is not material here.

The two displayed clauses are mutually exclusive script branches, not two printed translations in one edition. The Original branch’s penetration also accords with the next page’s sword lodged in Rin’s chest.
ごほ is the cough-like sound itself. The English invents a separate pained voice before separately reporting the blood cough.
The translation preserves the opening but omits the concrete route: Shirou passes along Berserker’s right side.
A bush hammer remains a heavy masonry hammer image, and “arm,” following “not with the sword,” adequately conveys an unarmed blow. The proposed distinction is too fine to establish a material error.
The source threatens repeated killing until Berserker reaches his final remaining life. “Kill you to your last one” is grammatically broken and does not communicate that mechanism unaided.
よう marks Illya’s inference from appearances. The English promotes that limited observation into an unqualified claim that Shirou cannot use Magecraft.
“You can’t call me alive anymore” idiomatically means his technical survival no longer counts as living, which is a defensible rendering of survival being mere cold comfort.
Being “turned into something that is not me” reasonably conveys the ongoing, identity-destroying change and implies inability to return; it does not state a completed transformation.
理性 is his last remaining rational faculty during mental destruction. “Last thoughts” instead suggests generic final thoughts and loses that specific persistence of reason.
A fallen person in this context is plainly someone needing help, so the paraphrase preserves the operative meaning. The apparent “Ican’t” is a stripped line-command artifact.
In context, “can’t leave the girl” naturally means he cannot leave the injured Saber as she is. The present condition remains recoverable without literal repetition.
The Japanese proceeds to identify Saber, Rin, and Illya as sources, so English plural “voices” is normal explicitation rather than a number error.

The English lines are explicitly separate mature/all-ages branches flattened together. No raw Original Japanese block for this page establishes which anatomical wording belongs to the Original branch, so neither insertion nor contradiction can be certified.

The explicit remains and euphemistic remains are separate mature/all-ages English branches. Without the corresponding raw Original Japanese page, the witnesses cannot establish that the explicit branch medicalizes this Original-edition line rather than translating an edition variant.

A narrower omission survives: “that sword” drops the grotesque comparison to an enormous hatchet. However, “blown out” still conveys wholesale violent loss of the abdomen, so the physical-action accusation is overstated.
“That won’t happen again” gives the contextual force of the Buddha-patience idiom: Shirou cannot expect another miraculous reprieve. Replacing an idiom with its meaning is defensible.
The English omits the sound of festering or sloughing decay and then misreads “it was all of those” as “sound is all there is.”
The translation truncates the progression after flesh, omitting the worms reaching bone, entering nerves, and continuing upward; it also reduces sucker-like proboscises to suckers.
The supplied raw Original Japanese says 「腐った肉の匂い」, directly supporting “the smell of rotten meat.” The duplicated nonspecific odor is a flattened later-edition branch.

The raw Original Japanese explicitly describes a human’s bones and organs being replaced and the body collapsing as boneless skin. The second, milder line is a flattened all-ages branch, not a contradictory Original translation.
The conditional says the entity eats worms; it does not say worms are its exclusive diet. “Only” adds an unsupported biological restriction.
English requires a reflexive form to express 自ら, and using the contextually known gender is ordinary pronoun explicitation, not a change in who performed the summoning.
The apparent fusion comes from stripping the line-dash command: the archived clause reads coherently as “But one thing—that ‘thing’ created after a lot of work—has been completed perfectly.”

“Afterbirth” commonly denotes the placenta, sometimes together with associated membranes. It preserves the deliberately dehumanizing reproductive-tissue reference and is within the word’s acceptable range.
The English retains destruction but omits the distinct possibilities of losing the battle and becoming nonfunctional before disposal.
The English omits 胎盤 entirely, obscuring that the speaker specifically sought a placenta possessing excellent Magic Circuits; it also reduces the plural technical attribute to one circuit.
昏い specifically identifies the subject’s dark emotions as the transformative key. Generic “emotions” materially broadens the mechanism.
依り代 frames the candidates as vessels or hosts. Replacing that with the ordinary war role “Masters” erases the speaker’s technical, objectifying conception of Rin.

The apparent “changea” fusion is a stripped dash command, not a source error. A narrower claim survives: “emotion of evil” moralizes 負の感情, and “fills” loses the image of the feeling flickering to life.
The English removes the scales being tipped, leaves the result clause without a coherent referent, and changes a slight strain or creak into a physical crack.

“The rotten meat” and “It” are explicitly mature/all-ages branches flattened together. No corresponding raw Original Japanese block is supplied for this page, so whether the mature noun is an Original-edition variant cannot be established responsibly.
The Japanese directly addresses the player who has just died and promises retraining from scratch. The English instead describes a generic service for people prone to dying.
弟子一号 is the forcibly assigned title “Disciple Number One,” not “senior student”; both numbering and dojo hierarchy are lost.
Tora-shinai is a defensible romanization of the mock weapon name, and “demonic sword” plus the item notification preserve its function. Explaining the compound would be a localization preference.
ちぇすと is a stylized striking cry here, immediately accompanying Taiga’s blow. Rendering it as the anatomical noun “Chest” breaks the action.
“Kills out of love” concisely conveys affection leading to murder. The exact transformation wording is compressed, but the comic causal contradiction is preserved.
After being ordered to drive the cat away, “I made it go somewhere” awkwardly but clearly reports causing it to leave. Repeating “strange cat” is not necessary for accuracy.
Being put in an unfavorable position after Saber’s attack is a natural contextual paraphrase of having one’s stance broken; no contrary event or agency is introduced.
“Behind that man” states only location and omits that Archer is actively shielding Rin from Saber.
喉を鳴らす describes producing a throat sound, and Shirou has just uttered 「や」. “Call out” is defensible; the accusation’s claim that the attempt necessarily failed is not in the Japanese.
In this sword-fight context, “attack her” naturally covers 斬りかかる. The omitted weapon manner is readily supplied by Saber’s established action and is not a material mistranslation.
軽い explicitly makes the pain slight or mild; “sharp pain” materially increases its intensity.
The English omits that the disappearing engraved mark is specifically on the back of Shirou’s left hand, a concrete part of the Command Spell reveal.
The Japanese describes an absolute stop as though the armor turned to stone. “Hesitates” instead suggests a voluntary moment of indecision.
The archived English contains a line-dash command between “guy” and “he’s.” The run-together form is an extraction artifact, not the translated presentation.
In a past counterfactual, “should have been able to defeat” naturally expresses Saber’s confident assessment that victory was available. The difference from 確実に is not material here.
斬り殺す explicitly culminates in Rin’s death. “Slash at” retains the attack but omits the lethal result that motivates Shirou’s horror.
