“The man she could not slay” can describe the situationally unsuccessful attempt interrupted by the Command Spell; the preceding context already establishes that she otherwise could have won.
仕留める can mean bring down or decisively defeat as well as kill. “Defeat her here” is a defensible combat rendering, not demonstrable euphemistic error.

In 「そんな事は知らない」, 知らない can idiomatically dismiss the matter as not one’s concern. Shirou separately states his actual lack of understanding in the next sentence, so “I don’t care about that” is contextually sound.
The narration is present in the supplied Original Japanese but omitted/commented out in the later witnesses. Its English inclusion is an Original-edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The English lists Rin beside Archer but omits her physical action of pushing past him and stepping forward, removing her initiative in entering the exchange.
The missing space is an extraction artifact: the raw script has a pause command between “Then” and “if,” not a translation-level word join.
“Big smile” conveys an emphatic smile but loses the exceptional quality in 極上 and some of the intensification. The claim of specifically “calculated perfection” is not established by the Japanese.
“Almost forget about all these strange events” is a defensible natural paraphrase of those events beginning to feel unreal or untrue in the face of an ordinary greeting.
Although awkward English, “Man, how difficult” retains Archer’s complaint that Rin is undertaking another troublesome matter; no material mistranslation is demonstrated.
Archer actually disappears, and “literally” functions as colloquial emphasis. It drops the illusion simile, but does not falsely describe the event.
The omitted object of イヤ is naturally supplied from 全部教えてあげる; “even if you say you don’t want to know” accurately expresses her refusal to accept an objection to being told.
“Isn’t like the previous one” adequately expresses that her present expression is distinct from the earlier smile. “Altogether different” would only strengthen the wording.
“Now is one of those times” is an idiomatic and accurate rendering of “now is that kind of occasion,” with the mortal danger supplied by the preceding sentence.
“Totally unlike” naturally conveys the idiomatic 180-degree reversal; preserving the numerical image is optional.
Calling the singular 学校のアイドル the school’s “number-one idol” is a reasonable explicitation of Rin’s pre-eminent school-idol status, not a meaningful invented ranking here.
The transfer direction is substantially recoverable—magi transfer a body part into something—but 使役される means the resulting familiar is employed or controlled as a double, not subsequently “summoned.”
In this Master–familiar context, “control” is a natural contextual rendering of figurative 縛り付ける and preserves the binding relation.
使役する concerns employing or controlling a familiar, so “summon” changes the stated deficiency. The Japanese does not independently establish the finding’s singular-versus-plural objection.

The English is clumsy, but “something else than a familiar” preserves Shirou’s conclusion that Saber is not truly the same kind of being as an ordinary familiar. Loss of the resemblance idiom is not material here.
The ruby explicitly instructs the reading オヤジ (“Dad/old man”) over 切嗣, so “my father’s generation” follows the performed Original text rather than erasing unsupported information.
習っている describes Shirou currently learning or being taught magecraft. “Knew magic” instead asserts possessed knowledge or ability and removes the ongoing, limited instruction.
新鮮 can describe something as novel or unfamiliar to the speaker; “I am not used to this Japanese style” is a defensible natural rendering.
“Takes a look at it” conveys the examination and is compatible with its brevity. It is less vivid than まじまじ but does not omit the action.
“In a matter of seconds” conventionally means within only a few seconds and adequately conveys the very short repair time; the difference is not material.

まさかとは思うけど expresses disbelief that the suspected fact could be true while checking it. “Even though it’s impossible” incorrectly makes impossibility an asserted fact and produces a different logical relation.
In context, “this” can refer to Rin falling silent, and the English still makes her beauty the reason she appears especially frightening. The alleged causal reversal is not established.
半端 criticizes Strengthening as incomplete, middling, or half-baked. Calling it “odd” changes the substance of Rin’s appraisal.
“It doesn’t matter right now” naturally conveys Shirou’s claim that his immaturity is separate from the issue presently under dispute.
呪文 here is the spoken incantation needed for activation. Rendering it as another “spell” obscures the distinction and clashes with the preceding description of the Command Spell itself.

Although 倒す alone can mean “defeat,” the immediate exchange begins with Shirou being killed and proceeds into an explicitly described 殺し合い. “Killing” is contextually licensed rather than demonstrably false.
The English omits the explicitly stated defining function of the prize: the Holy Grail fulfills the winner’s wish.
The same sentence calls the contest a 殺し合い, so interpreting 倒す as killing in this lethal battle is contextually defensible.
潔かった characterizes the voice as strikingly resolute, forthright, or cleanly decisive. “Pure voice” shifts that defining quality toward tonal or moral purity.
In direct response to Rin asking whether his resolve is settled, 覚悟ぐらいちゃんと知ってる pragmatically supports “I’m already prepared.” It does not necessarily mean only abstract knowledge of resolve.

Both texts are deliberately interrupted fragments. “Someone certainly—” is awkward and adds emphasis, but it retains the recollection that an unknown person did something to or for him; the alleged removal of the rescuer is overstated.

主役 is not translated explicitly, but identifying Shirou as one of the seven Masters of the war already conveys that he is a principal participant rather than an observer. This is compression, not a material error.
“Uses his or her Servant” preserves the operative Master–Servant hierarchy. Omitting the conventional “hands and feet” metaphor is stylistic compression rather than a factual loss.
潰す can mean crush, eliminate, or destroy, and the surrounding explanation repeatedly frames the war as lethal. “Kill” is a defensible contextual choice.
実感を得る means acquiring a felt sense that the account is real, not merely intellectually understanding the explanation. The English collapses that important distinction.
“Glance” accurately conveys the brief look. 盗み見る adds furtiveness, but its omission is a minor manner nuance rather than a material error.

The Japanese explicitly requires the legendary hero to be dead, including one drawn from the modern era. Omitting 死亡した permits the materially different reading that a living contemporary hero could be summoned.

“The Holy Grail does the rest,” immediately after the Master’s summoning role and before discussion of giving a soul shape, adequately refers to the Grail’s materialization work. It is condensed, not contradictory.
Within a passage explicitly discussing materialization and giving souls form, “give it a body” is a defensible contextual interpretation of fixing or stabilizing the reproduced soul.
English “any” functions naturally within the generalization over humans, animals, and machines; it does not demonstrably lower the requirement that the achievement be great.
“Artificial gods” is within the lexical range of 擬似的な神さま in this explanation of beings made godlike through worship. Deliberate manufacture is not necessarily implied.
降霊術 and 口寄せ are distinct examples—spirit invocation and mediumistic summoning/channeling. “‘Ghost Magic’ such as supplicating ghosts” obscures both and invents a quoted English category.
The English omits that ordinary spirit arts borrow only part of a Heroic Spirit’s power, eliminating the explicit contrast with bringing the Heroic Spirit itself.

The Japanese says the Heroic Spirit itself is brought directly and made into a familiar. “Familiars made from” Heroic Spirits instead suggests a derived construction, undermining the passage’s core contrast.
“Give them form” is a natural rendering of materializing an entity currently in spirit form, and the surrounding sentences clearly establish the two states.
こっち naturally means “our side,” and saying “we can attack them” in the condition where attacks can land accurately expresses 当たる. The possibility of defeating them remains separately qualified.
Paired with “But I’m not convinced,” “Technically, yes” naturally marks merely propositional or verbal understanding, preserving Shirou’s contrast with acceptance.
悪趣味 is Shirou’s explicit condemnation of the war as grotesquely tasteless. Reducing it to neutral “such a thing” removes that judgment.
“All you can do now is fight” directly expresses that fighting is the sole remaining option; it is not meaningfully looser than “no choice but to fight.”
The whole clause is framed as what Rin can tell him, and “you should use yours wisely” naturally conveys her directive to use the powerful familiar effectively.
“Give me form” is an ordinary rendering of 実体化させる. The Japanese itself does not explicitly say “keep me materialized,” so the finding’s preferred wording adds interpretation.
敵 specifically identifies Rin as an enemy and frames the disclosure as a tactical concession. Generic “others” removes that adversarial relationship.
“Our situation” conveys the information represented by こちらの手札—their capabilities and weaknesses. Loss of the card-hand metaphor is not itself a material accuracy error.
風格 evaluates Saber’s distinguished bearing, presence, or dignity. “Good personality” instead evaluates her character and is substantively different.

悔しそう indicates frustration, chagrin, or rueful envy rather than straightforward anger. The additional accusation that Japanese specifies exactly one fist is unsupported because 拳 is not decisively numbered here.
へっぽこ calls Shirou inept or useless in the practical role under discussion. “Idiot” redirects the insult toward intelligence.
In this comic rebuke, “any normal person” is a defensible pragmatic rendering of a decent or feeling person; both accuse Rin of casually saying something others would hesitate to say.
鬼みたいに容赦がない plainly means demonically merciless. “Shows no openings” introduces combat-style vigilance absent from the Japanese and loses the lack-of-mercy judgment.

“It’s already late, so…” leaves Shirou’s travel-distance concern implicit, and Rin’s immediate answer about the neighboring town resolves that implication. This is defensible ellipsis rather than a material omission.
Rin’s direct “But what about you, Saber?” already shows that she is soliciting Saber’s independent view. Omitting なぜか removes only Shirou’s brief surprise marker.
The Japanese expressly limits Servants’ universal temporal adaptation to eras within the human world. “Any time” removes that domain restriction from a technical explanation.
Saber identifies a shortage of knowledge, the very defect the proposed instruction will remedy. “Experience” instead denotes insufficient practice and changes her diagnosis.
強くなってもらわなければ困ります expresses necessity—Saber needs Shirou to become stronger or will be in difficulty. “I want” reduces that obligation to preference.
“Evil smile” is a common playful rendering of 意地の悪い笑み, and the next sentence makes clear that Rin is teasingly enjoying Shirou’s confusion rather than being morally evil.
寝静まった町 denotes a town settled into sleep and therefore silent. “Silent town” preserves the immediate nocturnal condition, merely dropping personification.
“Really strong” conveys the emphatic とんでもなくお強い in ordinary English. A stronger intensifier would be stylistic refinement, not correction of a material error.

返り討ち predicts that the attacker will be defeated when Saber turns on them; “counterattacked viciously” describes retaliation without clearly preserving that result. The adverb is interpretive, but not the central problem.
In this context, “pervert” is a normal colloquial rendering of 痴漢, and Rin’s hypothetical clearly concerns a sexual nuisance threatening the girls.
助ける covers both “help” and “rescue/save.” The surrounding hypothetical attack supplies the protective role reversal, so “help us” is defensible.
ツカツカ adds a brisk, purposeful gait, but “follows me” preserves the action. Omitting this manner detail is not a material translation error.
“I don’t want to walk alongside them” naturally expresses Shirou’s strong reluctance. 非常に supplies degree, but its reduced emphasis does not materially change the action or motive.
The English omits that the park is by the river, but the bridge route is immediately stated. This minor scenic compression does not create a false geographic account.
The characters’ presence in the park is already explicit on the adjacent page, so “because it’s nighttime” naturally invokes the nighttime-park atmosphere without materially changing the cause.
A face seen while its owner looks up at the bridge can naturally denote her profile in context. “Face” is less compositionally precise but not materially inaccurate.

“Bridge” is a defensible contextual shortening. The surrounding pages establish that this is the bridge and its pedestrian route; omitting the compound’s explicit “pedestrian” does not create a demonstrable geographical error here.
The English retains the fear of collapse but omits the stated basis for it: the construction seems insufficiently sturdy. That concrete causal observation is not otherwise conveyed.
最たるもの means the foremost example among the old-fashioned streets just described, not necessarily the chronologically oldest district. “The oldest of all” changes the claim.
The Japanese describes a gently continuing slope. “Hilly roads” both loses that gradual, continuous geography and appears in malformed agreement with “There’s.”
The distant object is explicitly something resembling a cross, not a generic building. The following fragment identifies the church separately.
寄りつきもしなかった emphatically says Shirou had never even gone near the church, conveying longstanding avoidance. “Visit for the first time” preserves only the neutral fact of no prior visit.
The apparent concatenation is an extraction artifact: the supplied raw script places a line/pause command between the words. It is not evidence of a missing boundary in the translation itself.
ほとんど means “most” or “almost all,” while “the whole top” removes the estimate and overstates the grounds’ extent.

“Compelling” does not directly render 威圧, so the explicit intimidation is lost. The accusation should be narrowed, however, because “towering over its visitors” still preserves part of the looming, oppressive image.
“Leave you” directly identifies Saber, and “when we’ve come up here together” makes her exclusion clear. Adding “alone” would be more explicit but is not necessary for accuracy.
Saber is inferring that Shirou will not travel any farther because the church is his destination. “You should not” changes that prediction into advice or prohibition.
Shirou infers daytime attendance specifically from the number of seats. The English substitutes the chapel’s overall size, changing his stated evidence.
人格者 denotes a person of notably good moral character. “Distinguished” ordinarily indicates eminence or social standing and loses the premature moral judgment that supplies the irony.

Although awkward, “my senior as an apprentice” conveys that Kirei is Rin’s senior within their shared apprenticeship, and the next line explicitly clarifies that this is magical training. No substantive relationship is reversed.

“The other side of religion” is imprecise, but the continuation—“the side you wouldn’t see while living a normal life”—preserves the hidden institutional side, and “Holy Church” identifies it. “Beyond recognition” is unsupported.
The Japanese says chosen saints learn miracles; the English instead says miracles are given to them. This changes the Church’s controlled instruction into passive allocation.
The English clause is syntactically broken and turns the descriptive inverse relation—greater divine protection entails greater distance from magecraft—into advice that one “should” stay away.

In the preceding occult exposition, こっち側 means the hidden supernatural world. “Our side” instead naturally suggests factional allegiance, which is misleading because Kirei belongs to the opposing Church institution.
難しい顔 can describe a troubled, uneasy, or uncomfortable expression. Given Rin’s evident discomfort concerning Kirei, “an uncomfortable expression” is within the phrase’s contextual range.

“Inseparable relationship” conveys the enduring, unwanted tie, while Rin’s immediately following wish that they had never met supplies the negative attitude. The complete English is not neutral closeness.
English “must have noticed” is an epistemic inference, not a statement of certain fact, and appropriately renders Shirou’s conjectural 気が付いていたのか.
決まり is singular here, and the English construction “it was the rules” has a demonstrable number-agreement error. The intended meaning is “that was the rule.”

In this contrast, “He’s not scary at all” defensibly expresses that Shirou finds no identifiable frightening quality or hostility despite feeling Kirei’s pressure. It does not negate the unease described immediately afterward.

なった覚えはない idiomatically disclaims having knowingly become or signed up to be something. After admitting the contract but rejecting the imposed Master label, “I haven’t agreed to this” is a defensible natural paraphrase.
The supplied raw script contains a long-pause command between the surname and given name. “EmiyaShirou” results from stripping that command, not from a missing boundary in the underlying translation.
最後まで extends Kirei’s prediction through to the end—effectively, that Rin would never have come. The English only says she would not have come on this occasion and loses that temporal finality.

Japanese permits an omitted addressee/agent here, and Shirou is directly speaking to Kirei as the apparent authority. “A better person” is also licensed by the immediately stated contrast with a “proper magus.”
The English reports only that Rin prompts Kirei, omitting her explicitly displayed reluctance to do so.
The English removes both marked tonal details: Kirei chuckles in evident enjoyment, and Shirou grows increasingly—not merely generally—uneasy as he listens.
元通り means everything returning to its former state. “Everything will be as you desire” instead promises general wish fulfillment and loses the restoration claim.
The English sentence is grammatically malformed and fails to present the invasive image cleanly: all the mud accumulated inside Shirou can be dredged out.
The Japanese places the words in Shirou’s chest and says they cling thickly like blood. The English relocates them to his brain and changes adhering into clotting.

回りくどい means circuitous or indirect, and in context Kirei is digressing instead of explaining the rules. “Don’t go off topic” is a defensible functional paraphrase; the Japanese does not itself explicitly say “manipulative tactics.”

The proverb means kindness ultimately benefits the giver. “Compassion is not good for others” states the familiar mistaken interpretation and directly conflicts with Kirei’s explanation on the next page.

争奪戦 is a contested struggle for possession, and “all out war” is a defensible contextual rendering within an explicitly named Holy Grail War. The surrounding discussion already supplies the object being contested.
Shirou explicitly says Kirei keeps repeating “Holy Grail,” the object he then asks to have defined. The English incorrectly quotes him as repeating the full name “Holy Grail War.”

Within the conventional definition of the Holy Grail as the chalice that received sacred blood, identifying the otherwise omitted holy person as Christ is normal contextual explicitation, not a material unsupported insertion.
“Makes wishes comes true” has a clear subject–verb construction error. The Japanese definition itself is straightforward and singular.
Shirou says he has never heard that the Grail existed or was reproduced. The English converts this evidential limitation into categorical nonexistence and impossibility.
Kirei says the miracle can qualify as 魔法, the setting’s true Magic. “Almost sorcery” instead places it short of that classification.
真贋 is the distinction between genuine and counterfeit. “The object’s unreality” presupposes unreality rather than saying authenticity is irrelevant.
The supplied raw scripts place a line/pause command at this boundary. “Warthe” is produced by command stripping and is not an underlying translation error.
The English calls it only a ritual of mutual killing and entirely omits 降霊, which classifies it specifically as a spirit-invocation ritual.
“I guess” explicitly marks the statement as Shirou’s inference from Kirei’s words. It therefore preserves the attributional uncertainty conveyed by 言いたいのか.

降霊 means invoking or summoning a spirit, not materializing it; “materialize” also conflicts with the next page’s statement that the summoned Grail remains intangible. The run-together portion of the accusation should be dropped because the raw script contains a pause command there.

“Very skilled with her sword” is a defensible rendering of extreme sword ability, and the complete passage already says defeating her is impossible and magic is useless. The accusation depends chiefly on preferred intensity.
潰される can mean being crushed, taken out, or killed. In this lethal-war context—immediately followed by an explicit argument for killing Masters—“if the Master dies” is a defensible reading.
Although 倒す can be broader than killing, death is a valid contextual sense here: Shirou is paraphrasing the immediately preceding statement that killing the Master is the efficient method.
The plural “form a contract with Servants” does not convey 幾らでも, which expressly permits repeated or unrestricted re-contracting while Command Spells remain.

The Japanese condition covers any Servant who has lost a Master. “Whose Masters are killed” narrows that technical state to one particular cause, despite other contract-loss mechanisms in the surrounding explanation.

After the preceding sentence explains that the Master has been killed, “abandoned Servants” can naturally mean Servants left without Masters; it need not imply deliberate emotional abandonment. The technical state remains understandable.
最優先事項 identifies protection as the supervisor’s highest or foremost priority. “One of my biggest responsibilities” makes it merely one major duty among several.
The church is described as a peripheral or lower-echelon unit of one Special Bureau. The English instead makes it the lowest-ranked member among plural “special agencies,” changing the hierarchy.
査定 emphasizes assessment, but “investigate” is defensible because the next sentence expressly defines the task as determining authenticity, recovering the real object, and rejecting the false one.

The Japanese itself designates the target as the “726th Holy Grail”; it does not say “candidate.” In context, “has appeared” can render a detected manifestation, while the following real-or-false test preserves its unconfirmed authenticity.
The raw script contains a pause command after Shirou’s interrupted な. Its removal creates “Whaare”; the underlying translation indicates an intended broken-off exclamation followed by the question.

In the immediate exchange, “people” naturally refers to the historical participants just under discussion, not humanity in general. The deictic hostility of 連中 is softened, but responsibility is not reassigned.

“Terrible” is a broad but defensible description of the past wars’ extreme brutality, which the following clause specifies as indiscriminate killing. Treating a stronger adjective as mandatory is preference policing.
戒める includes admonishing, warning, or cautioning against misconduct; it does not necessarily entail punishment or forcible restraint. “To caution them” lies within its lexical range.
“Fundamentally bad” conveys that the war is bad in its underlying nature, which is the force of 性質が悪い here. “Appallingly pernicious” is a stylistic intensification, not the sole accurate rendering.
The English omits both おかしそうに and 慇懃な仕草: Kirei laughs with amusement while displaying elaborately courteous manners. Those details materially sharpen his mockery.

無様 can denote an awkward, clumsy, humiliating, or pathetic condition. “My clumsy inability to accept” is not an unsupported competence claim and adequately conveys Shirou’s perceived undignified state.
In context, 参考にする means taking Kirei’s proposed course as guidance and potentially adopting it. “Will you not accept it?” is a natural, if less literal, rendering of that taunting invitation.
In the context of a contest for the Grail, “winner” is a defensible contextual rendering of the person who obtains it; it does not materially change the hypothetical.
“Whether I want it or not” naturally expresses disregard for Shirou’s feelings or wishes here; it does not specifically introduce a consent dispute.
事実 can be rendered as either “facts” or collective “truth.” Nothing in the English morally privileges Kirei’s statements beyond the Japanese.
In this context, being “not troubled by” the catastrophe communicates the charged indifference expressed by 関心を持たない. The distinction alleged is not material.
The two English lines form one sentence, so capitalizing “That” after the comma is a visible grammatical error.
The surviving issue is narrower: “lose concentration” incorrectly mentalizes the visual 焦点, although “can’t focus my eyes” then restores much of the intended visual disturbance.
崩れ落ちる describes the body collapsing or giving way, appreciably stronger than merely stumbling; the next page confirms that Shirou arrests that collapse.
“Looked terrible” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of looking extremely pale, particularly because Rin has just explicitly described his face as white.
“Smacks me in the head” preserves the physical and comic force. Omitting 容赦なく is a minor compression, not a demonstrable material mistranslation.
The English closely reproduces the Japanese idiom: 叩きたりない顔 literally describes a look suggesting she has not hit him enough.
“Tended to” can mean kept or maintained under care, and the vessel/replica distinction is explicitly supplied immediately afterward. The finding also inserts “vessel” before the Japanese does.
“Well-made replica” conveys 精巧に作られた. The lost intensifier 極めて is a modest degree reduction, not the substantial factual change alleged.
The Japanese says the Grail never reached completion; “was imperfectly completed” instead asserts that completion occurred in a flawed state.
“The previous pressure” is a concise contextual rendering of Kirei’s prior overbearing manner, not an incompatible ambient force.
甘ちゃん characterizes the former Master as naive or softhearted. “Chicken” specifically attributes cowardice, an inference drawn from his refusal to fight rather than the word used.
The speaker has just said he was protected by his father, so “Father died” unambiguously retains the relationship. Capitalization is a normal English convention for this familial use.
“Stands the symbol of worship” naturally covers both the symbol’s presence and 礼拝されるべき as its function. Rendering 聳える as “stands” is mild compression, not a material error.
Within the stated qualification for obtaining the Grail, “those who have Servants” plainly denotes Masters possessing Servants under their authority. No consequential status change results.
The English omits 高みから見下ろして entirely, losing the explicit image of Kirei looking down from above as he demands Shirou’s decision.
“Accept this” can naturally refer to acknowledging the newly arisen motive and will described in the preceding sentence. 認める permits that rendering without implying only an external proposal.
The Japanese asks whether mental readiness was already established. “Whether to prepare” changes that state into a prospective voluntary choice.
“Superhero” is a defensible idiomatic localization of 正義の味方, a stock heroic ideal. “Ally of justice” is not the uniquely governing English rendering.
“I can’t let it happen again” already expresses active prevention and recurrence; “again” supplies the second-occurrence sense of 二度も.
The supplied raw Original witness contains the breath, so it is an Original-edition line absent from the base page rather than an unsupported insertion.
“As a man, I said I will fight” preserves the masculine self-rule, while the following English explicitly says he must not go against his word. The binding commitment is therefore retained.
魔術戦 specifically authorizes magical warfare; reducing it to “the battle” removes the formal declaration’s explicit occult scope.
先日 is an imprecise recent-day expression that can include yesterday, and “yesterday” is consistent with the surrounding summoning chronology. The witness does not demonstrate that the date is false.
おそらく……だろう expresses a probable prediction, whereas “may” states only possibility and materially lowers Kirei’s confidence.
ズカズカ adds a brusque gait, but the English retains her abrupt departure and lack of farewell. Its omission is minor tonal compression rather than a material error.
兄弟子 identifies a senior disciple under the same teacher. “Fellow pupil” retains the shared tutelage but incorrectly drops Kirei’s seniority.
The subject of 用はない is omitted, and Rin has just directly ordered Shirou to leave. Reading it as “you have no business here” is contextually defensible; a collective “we” is not compelled.
After sensing someone behind him, “turn around” is a natural rendering of たまらずに振り返った. The explanation overstates this startle response as bodily aversion to Kirei.
足は勝手に explicitly makes the retreat involuntary—his feet move on their own. “I back off” presents it as an ordinary deliberate action.
“Superhero” is a viable idiomatic equivalent for the stock expression 正義の味方, and the need for an evil or villain to defeat is preserved exactly.
なりそうだった marks an impending blackout that had not occurred. “Has turned black” presents the visual change as already completed despite the prefatory “feel like.”
“Insecure” can mean unstable or not firmly grounded, and the following line still identifies the contradiction in Shirou’s ideal. The alleged new psychological diagnosis is not established.
The Japanese has one pursued ideal, 理想, whose internal contradiction is at issue. “The target ideals” wrongly pluralizes it and produces unclear English.
葛藤 is an inner conflict, not merely generic worries, and とても正しい evaluates it as properly human rather than just statistically normal.
The English omits 愉しげに, which explicitly states that Kirei smiles with pleasure while exposing Shirou’s conflict.

The Japanese says Shirou has become a person belonging to the class of those who kill and are killed. “At the point of kill or be killed” recasts that lasting changed position as an immediate dilemma.
言葉が投げかけられた is a conventional image for words being addressed or called after someone; “He says so as I quickly make my way out” preserves the event and timing without a factual error.

The narrower surviving omission is the explicit contact with Shirou’s cheeks and the cold being sharper still. “Sharp chill” does preserve the basic severity, so saying the whole sensation disappears overstates the loss.
“It’s a bit windy now” is a natural weather rendering of 風が出ていた, with “now” suggesting the changed condition. The mild qualification is not a material temporal error.
“Comes closer and looks up at me” naturally conveys Saber leaning toward Shirou and looking intently at him; the upward angle is ordinary spatial explicitation, not a consequential invention.
他人事じゃない says Shirou’s choice directly concerns Saber. Saying it determines her fate promotes that personal stake into a substantially stronger causal claim.
The source itself says 深呼吸, literally a deep breath. 軽く merely qualifies how he does it, so “deep breath” is not an invented intensification.
The parallel with 判らない shows that 知らない expresses Shirou’s lack of knowledge. “I don’t care” instead asserts indifference toward the relationship.
“Have our first greeting be in style” is a loose but defensible idiom for making the greeting properly or with due form. The earnest wish for a proper first greeting remains clear.
The causal “Saber is really serious, so I nod” retains the effect her seriousness has on Shirou. Losing the nuance of つられてしまった is not material here.
頼む is a request meaning “please” or “I’m counting on you.” In response to Saber’s vow, “yes, please” is awkward but retains his acceptance and request.

The chilled hands are a concrete sensory detail omitted from an otherwise accurate description, but the winter setting and handshake remain; the finding does not establish a material translation error.
完全に asks whether Shirou now trusts Saber completely. Omitting that degree changes the pointed question, especially given his qualified answer on the next page.
わたしたち explicitly includes Rin and Archer as the opposing pair. “I won’t” assigns the threat to Rin alone and changes the stated number of actors.
気持ちよく戦えない concerns Rin’s own ability to fight without lingering discomfort over the debt. “Fight him fairly” converts that subjective compunction into procedural fairness.
カタチはどうあれ concerns the form or manner the intervention took, not its reason. The English changes the logical qualification.
The English retains Rin turning away defensively. Omitting the brief snort is a minor performance detail, not a material mistranslation.
In context, accompanying Shirou and Saber back to town is the concrete way Rin will 面倒みる them. Her reluctance is retained by “Um” and “at least.”
“Without looking at us” directly communicates the avoidance of eye contact. The Japanese makes the deliberateness slightly more explicit, but the English does not omit the behavior.
ずんずん adds an emphatic gait, but “follow Tohsaka” preserves the action and the next page states that she walks ahead. This is minor manner compression.
The Japanese place name is 深山町, not a city designation. Capitalized “Miyama City” assigns the location the wrong geographic category.
“Concerned with” can mean occupied or preoccupied with, not only emotionally worried about. It is awkward but remains within the lexical range of かまけて.
捜し物の一つも is idiomatic minimization meaning to do some searching, not necessarily complete one countable search task. “I’ll go look while I’m here” conveys that intention.
殺し合い explicitly defines the Holy Grail War as mutual killing. “Battles” removes that lethal characterization.
仕留める means bring down or finish off the other Servant. “Take it out on” instead denotes venting frustration against someone and does not communicate the intended defeat or kill.
“I can’t go home now” is a natural concise rendering of going home not being an option. It loses 大人しく and the rhetorical question, but preserves Rin’s operative refusal.
Although “a magus” omits 一人前 locally, the very next sentence says her mind and knowledge are complete as a magus. The complete page preserves the full-fledged judgment.
“Supported me, understanding the situation I’m in” reasonably conveys both taking Shirou’s uninformed position into account and siding with him; “acted fairly” preserves the stated principle.
手を取る is readily figurative here—extending aid or taking someone in hand. “Helped me out” accurately conveys the action’s contextual meaning; a literal hand-taking is not required.
“Sour, cranky, unapproachable” is loose but lies within the pejorative range of きつい and ツンケンしていて近寄りがたい. The public/private contrast remains intact.
情が移る describes affection or attachment developing over time. “Feels empathy for me” is a different and weaker emotional relation.
“Suburbs” is acceptable for 郊外, so the claimed loss of the marginal setting does not survive. The narrower issue is that “silent” does not explicitly preserve 人気の絶えた, the absence of people.
In combat, やられる can mean being taken out or killed, and a Servant’s loss normally entails destruction. “Gets killed” is a defensible contextual reading, not demonstrably too narrow.
The English retains the sigh but omits the explicit exasperated-seeming manner of Rin’s reaction.
“Glances” conveys brevity but not the expressly sidelong manner encoded by 流し見た.
In context, “I don’t like it” defensibly expresses Shirou’s reluctance to accept or rely on the advice; it does not unambiguously mean he dislikes the advice itself.
“Soft” generalizes the specifically stated risk of becoming emotionally involved or attached.
The English omits the explicit destination of Rin’s departure.
In this combat warning, “strong” is a defensible contextual rendering of Saber being 優れている; the accusation demands unnecessary lexical breadth.
“Gloomy” does not preserve the setting’s explicit blue-pale coloration.
“A figure that should not be there” naturally conveys a forbidden or intolerable presence in context; reading it as merely being at the wrong location is not compelled.
異質さ denotes alien or categorical otherness, whereas “dreadfulness” substitutes a generic fearful evaluation.
Although “bad” is not separately lexicalized, the surrounding chill, monster, and grotesque mismatch make the adverse dream quality unmistakable; this is not a material mistranslation.
The Japanese says their gazes have not met; the English instead describes Shirou not staring, changing reciprocity and agency.
In a comparison of Servant combat parameters, “raw power” is a defensible idiomatic rendering of 単純な能力 rather than a demonstrable narrowing to muscular strength alone.
The English is awkward but intelligibly preserves Rin’s spirit of refusing to lose; the finding identifies style rather than an accuracy failure.
“Learnt more than enough” retains the aversive excess of イヤって言うほど and is a defensible natural paraphrase.

The surrounding references to fighting and being accepted as Saber’s Master make “good enough for you” naturally mean adequate to serve as her Master; no material personal-role substitution is established.
覚悟 can denote resolve, preparedness, or readiness; “ready or not” is acceptable in Archer’s tactical statement.
“Spirits” is a reasonable concise rendering of 霊体 here, and the adjacent sentence expressly discusses turning into spirit form; the alleged categorical distortion is not material.
“Complete Master” is stiff but directly conveys 完全なマスター and is contextually contrasted with Shirou’s deficient capabilities, not Rin’s personal completeness.
“A part unlike a magus” preserves the contrast between Rin’s humane excess and magus conduct; demanding “diametrically opposed” is chiefly intensity policing.
“My vision is drawn” naturally means his line of sight or visual attention is drawn upward and does not materially change the looking action.
“Head on” reasonably conveys reliance on direct force, while “unique style” conveys Archer’s own characteristic method; the tactical contrast remains clear.
The supplied raw Original witness explicitly has Illya lift her skirt hem before bowing, which supports identifying the action as a curtsy; the shorter page text reflects an edition difference.
“If I make that” is genuinely malformed and obscures Illya’s point that stating her full name should secure recognition.
The Japanese describes a faint movement or sway, not bodily stiffening; the visible reaction is changed.
異形 has a lexical range including strange, abnormal, or grotesque form; “strange shape” is somewhat plain but defensible in the already threatening context.
The English loses the explicit downward fall in 落下してくる, but “from the top of the hill” does not establish that it became a specifically horizontal leap.

“Shooting through the giant” ordinarily asserts passage through his body, whereas the Japanese describes the arrows striking or shooting into the descending target before their ineffectiveness is revealed.
岩盤 is bedrock or a rock mass; generic plural “rocks” materially lowers the stated destructive benchmark.
蜂の巣にする specifically evokes riddling houses with holes; “mow down” substitutes destruction by flattening or sweeping aside.
The Japanese explicitly says Berserker received the arrows in his body, while moving through a “rain” does not establish direct bodily hits.
The English preserves blocking and parrying but reduces the final active 切り崩していく to merely facing the assault.
The immediately preceding English already states that Saber is flung away; rendering the continuation as her sliding avoids redundant repetition without losing the attack sequence.
The Japanese says the arrows are defeated by Berserker’s body; their literal disappearance is an unsupported replacement, even though the preceding sentence preserves their ineffectiveness.
The ongoing charge and emergency block make its sudden reflexive character clear; omission of 咄嗟に here is not a material factual change.
The English omits the explicit landing position halfway down the slope.
The apparent “balland” junction corresponds to a supplied line-control command between the words, so it is an extraction artifact rather than demonstrated source grammar.
Obsidian is commonly treated as a gemstone or ornamental jewel, and Rin is visibly using such stones for magecraft; “obsidian jewels” is defensible contextual explicitation.
“Bravely” reasonably transfers the gallant composure expressed by 凛々しい視線 into natural English; losing the literal gaze image is not a material change here.
“Plows into” remains a violent impact, and “open terrain off the road” is a defensible contextual rendering of 荒れ地; both alleged weakenings are overstated.
Berserker has just been repeatedly characterized as a monster; using that contextual referent for 相手 is normal English explicitation, not a material insertion.
In context, “not obedient enough to follow” naturally conveys Shirou’s refusal simply to accept Rin’s sensible advice; the distinction alleged is too fine to establish an error.
The joined words derive from a line-control command, while “even if I go” adequately conveys going to the battle; no material surviving claim remains.
The joined “hillfrom” is a stripped line-control artifact, and “open area” is a defensible description of the cemetery ground in the adjacent context.
Omitting the ordinary size adjective 広い does not alter which cemetery or battle space is meant and is not a material accuracy error.
これからよろしく is a conventional partnership greeting whose natural force can be localized as undertaking to work or try together; the English is defensible in the new Master–Servant context.
“She shook the hand I held out” preserves the offered and reciprocated handclasp; omission of the firmness adverb alone does not substantiate the claimed material weakening.
The apparent “stillI” junction results from a stripped line-control command and is not demonstrated grammar in the game text.
In this decision context, “there’s nothing else I can do” naturally communicates that the choice is already obvious or settled; it does not materially erase agency.
“Open land” is a defensible contextual rendering of the rough, open cemetery ground denoted by 荒れ地; “wasteland” is not uniquely required.
“Heavy gravestones” preserves the operative fact; 冗談のように adds astonished intensity but its omission does not create a material factual error.
The English preserves the repeated gravestones being violently flung; omitting the onomatopoeic ドンドン is a compression of sound texture, not a material mistranslation.
“You’ll get hit if you’re there” naturally warns that he will be caught by the battle’s spillover; it does not require an intentionally directed strike.
“Really angry” preserves both the emotion and heightened degree; the finding primarily demands more vivid prose rather than correcting a factual error.
The apparent “UmI” junction corresponds to the supplied line-control command and is an extraction artifact, not demonstrated malformed dialogue.
腹は立たなかった specifically means Shirou did not become angry; “I don’t feel bad” can instead mean no guilt, sadness, or discomfort and changes the stated emotion.
“Had a different face on” is awkward but conveys an assumed school persona or facade; the deliberate contrast is not reduced to a merely accidental difference.
The sentence expresses Rin’s strongly grounded conclusion, and conversational English may state that conclusion directly; dropping the light だろう hedge is not material here.
“As long as I’m alive” is a natural idiomatic rendering of 体があるかぎり; the claim that Shirou uniquely conceptualizes his body as a tool is not established by this sentence alone.
やらせる accuses Rin of making or having another person do it, not merely requesting it; her following admission of 強制 confirms the coercive force.
強制する explicitly means force or compel, so “asking” materially softens Rin’s admission.
“Attacks Berserker” accurately conveys delivering the sword attack; omission of the single-stroke packaging 一刀 is not material in this action sequence.
神業 literally denotes godlike or divine skill, and “a divine work of utmost excellence” is stylistically stiff but semantically faithful.
The English preserves lethality but omits the explicit, graphic result of being instantly reduced to a lump of flesh.

“Match even a fierce god” defensibly conveys being able to contend with 鬼神 alongside Saber; the asserted loss of supernatural force is false, and the endurance nuance does not alone establish a material error.
In combat, 剣を受けた naturally means receiving or catching the sword attack, and the preceding action shows Saber doing so with her sword; “blocked on purpose” is defensible.
The source’s whirlwind is a metaphor for Berserker’s desperate sweep; recasting it as the already monster-like attacker lashing out is normal English paraphrase, not a material new characterization.
Following her backward dodge, “holds her sword with both hands” naturally conveys taking up the new two-handed posture; the reset is sufficiently implied.
The Japanese foregrounds Shirou’s feet moving, suggesting bodily action before conscious narration; “I act instantly” makes it generalized and deliberate.
The English preserves drawing Berserker away but omits both Saber’s bodily self-endangerment and the benefactive force toward Shirou.
在りもしない makes the imagined pursuer nonexistent, whereas “unknown pursuer” implies a real but unidentified threat.
The preceding English sentence already says Shirou never looked back while running, so the final compression avoids repetition without losing the forward-only psychological action.
English epistemic “must have” still marks an inference rather than witnessed certainty and is a defensible rendering of Shirou’s tentative explanation.
The reconstructed pane is being checked for missing-area gaps caused by the leftover pieces; “crack” describes a different defect.
Each 誰か evokes one individual—Rin and Saber—whereas “the people” grammatically creates plural groups in both clauses.
Although は can give a lower-bound nuance, “it’s been thirty minutes” is commonly approximate rather than mathematically exact; no material timing error is demonstrated.
The English changes dull numbness into sharp pain, broadens the back of the left hand to the hand, and omits that the sensation vanishes.

Treating the contract sign as proof that he is Saber’s Master is contextually defensible, but the English genuinely omits the specifically red radiance and removes the qualified “could be called” framing.
感情に任せて identifies emotion as the force driving Shirou; “follow my instinct” substitutes a distinct psychological faculty.
“Stabbed in the heart” naturally entails penetration and adequately renders 心臓を貫かれた; requiring “pierced through” is intensity preference rather than correction.

In the perspective of a mortally wounded narrator, “I can’t see very clearly” is a defensible naturalization of seeing yet failing to see; calling the visible agent “someone” does not materially alter the scene.
時点で marks the point after which Shirou is vulnerable; it does not say the killing occurs at that very instant. The English adds simultaneity.
一人になってしまった means he ended up alone, whereas “secluded myself” implies a deliberate act of isolation.
ようなもの explicitly makes this “as good as over,” not a literal simultaneous loss of life.
“Should be able to” retains both the if-condition and an epistemic modal, and is a defensible natural rendering of the cautious double negative.
The English omits 身を挺して, which says Saber risked herself bodily, and changes “away from me” into “away from here.”
のなら is itself conditional; “If she was protecting me” is a defensible rendering, with the protection already established by the preceding sentence.
在りもしない explicitly says the pursuer was nonexistent, not merely unidentified.
The immediately preceding English already says he never looked back. “Desperately ran here” compresses the repeated forward-only image without losing the asserted conduct.
English “must have” commonly marks a conjectural inference rather than certainty, so it is defensible for なのか here.
隙間 can denote an opening, fissure, or crack; “crack” is defensible for a repaired pane and is clarified by the following reference to missing pieces.
Each 誰か evokes one person, and その二人 confirms exactly two individuals. Recasting each as plural “people” changes the number and focus.
The particle は does not obligatorily encode a strict lower bound here; “thirty minutes have passed” is a normal rendering.
The source describes dull numbness specifically on the back of the left hand and says it vanished; the English changes it to sharp pain in the hand and omits its cessation.
Calling the contract sign proof that Shirou is Saber’s Master is defensible in context. The narrower genuine loss is that the radiance is explicitly red.
感情 means emotion, not instinct. The distinction is especially clear because the preceding sentence separately uses 直感的 for instinctive understanding.
“Stabbed in the heart” is a normal English rendering of 心臓を貫かれた; 貫く does not require an explicit through-and-through formulation here.
The Japanese presents a paradoxical failure to apprehend something visibly present. Ordinary unclear eyesight does not fully convey that perceptual contradiction.
時点で establishes the point after which Shirou will be killed, not death at the exact instant Saber is lost.
The Japanese says Shirou ended up alone; “secluded myself” incorrectly supplies deliberate self-isolation.
ようなもの marks an “as good as over” judgment, which the English incorrectly literalizes as his life already being lost.
The supplied raw English contains a line-control marker between “Then” and “I.” Their joining in flattened text is an extraction artifact, not a mistranslation.
The raw witness places a line-control marker between “Geez” and “What.” The joined display is an extraction artifact rather than malformed translated dialogue.
“Ignoring” or putting aside hesitation and fear is a defensible natural paraphrase of breaking through or casting them off; the alleged characterization change is overstated.
見栄 means concern for appearances or showing off, not “force.” The English therefore loses one of Shirou’s explicitly self-conscious motives.
“Must have been hiding” is an ordinary inferential rendering of 隠れていたのか, not a categorical claim of witnessed certainty.
“Great in all aspects” is broad but naturally encompasses the mental and technical excellence expressed by 心技共に最高. The objection is chiefly one of preferred specificity.
The prediction is expressly conditional on nobody interfering, and that condition is wholly absent from the English.
肉薄する can mean closing aggressively to attack at close quarters. In this combat context, “rushes in and attacks” is defensible and does not assert a successful hit.

The supplied raw English contains the page’s translated sentences under a duplicate page label. This establishes a labeling/alignment problem, not elimination of the Japanese text from the translation.
神業 literally denotes godlike or superhuman workmanship or skill. “Divine work of utmost excellence” is awkward English but preserves the idiom’s meaning rather than creating a factual error.
The source gives the concrete consequence of being reduced instantly to a lump of flesh; “fatal destruction” removes that specific bodily image.
戦い抜ける means fighting through to the end. “Match” instead asserts parity with the opponent and omits the endurance/completion sense.
In combat, a sword or blowを受ける can naturally mean receiving, meeting, or blocking it. “Blocked Berserker’s sword” is within the phrase’s lexical range.
坂道 itself leaves direction unstated, but the supplied Japanese does not show that the contextually explicit “down” is false. Treating every such explicitation as an error is unwarranted.
“Must have … or must have …” remains an unresolved pair of epistemic alternatives; it does not assert that both events necessarily happened.
The desperate sweeping whirlwind is Berserker’s attack, so making the implicit attacker explicit as “the beast” is a defensible contextual paraphrase.
After Saber jumps back, “holds her sword with both hands” reasonably conveys adopting the two-handed guard. Omitting the literal ‘again/reset’ is not a material factual change.
足が動く presents his feet moving before a consciously narrated decision. “I act instantly” both generalizes the motion and supplies deliberate agency.
踏み込む toward an enemy is a committed offensive advance. Describing Saber as stopping her attack is a defensible contextual rendering, not an assertion that a blow landed.
The English reproduces Saber’s sharp spoken protest immediately before “I ignore her.” Omitting the narrator’s label 叱咤 does not erase the warning’s force from the scene.
The leap is plainly evasive in context, and the following action confirms withdrawal from danger. “Jump away” is normal English explicitation.
向き直る explicitly describes Berserker physically turning back after judging the arrow unworthy of defense. “Ignores it” preserves the judgment but omits the spatial action.
The source identifies vibration of the air shaking Shirou’s body, not movement of the ground.
The plural fragments are scattered in every direction and grammatically continue into striking Shirou’s back; the English reduces the impacting shrapnel to one piece.
The English preserves the consequential impact by saying a fragment pierces his back. Dropping the accompanying onomatopoeic heavy sound is a minor texture loss, not independently material.
Surviving the destruction naturally entails weathering it without a fatal wound. The English is broader but accurately conveys the asserted outcome.
The immediately preceding English already says Shirou threw himself on top of Saber. Their physical positions therefore remain established despite not being repeated on this page.
炎上 means the cemetery caught fire or was set ablaze. “Razed” instead says it was leveled or destroyed.
破壊 means destruction; “abolition” is semantically inapplicable to physical devastation and produces broken English.
ランクＡに該当する means falling within or corresponding to Rank A. Calling it “a Rank-A Noble Phantasm” is a natural classification, not a demonstrable change of rank.
“With a noise” loses the hard clattering quality, but the object’s approach and audible impact remain intact; this is minor descriptive compression rather than a material error.
In this bow-shot context, using the sword as a projectile is precisely what makes it function as an arrow. The English is a defensible explicitation, not an unrelated broadening.

The raw witness places display-control markers around the pause, and the capital follows an extended page-level visual break. This is presentation formatting, not a Japanese-to-English accuracy error.
口元を歪める can describe curling or twisting the mouth into a hostile smile, and the next sentence explicitly says he laughed/smiled. “He’s smiling” is defensible, though less vivid.
The comparison explicitly includes feeling ready to vomit, which the English sentence omits entirely.
Illya orders Berserker to return immediately before the English says he retreats. The response relation is already clear from the sequence; only the source’s ‘as if’ wording is implicit.
いらない can naturally mean either “do not need” or “do not want.” In Illya’s contrast with her new interest in Archer, “I don’t want Saber” is defensible.
The English omits both the identifying description 白い and the concrete departure beyond the flames; these are two genuine visual details, not an edition difference.
“Let go of me now” conveys the timing carried by そろそろ. The alleged omission is not present.
The raw English has a line-control marker between “Oh” and “Yeah.” Their fusion in flattened text is an extraction artifact.
ぐらぐら describes a reeling or unsteady head, whereas “throbbing” describes pulsating pain and changes the sensation.
“Fall on my butt” already carries an undignified, comic quality in ordinary English. Adding an adverb for みっともなく is not required to preserve the effect.
The raw witness contains a line-control marker between “well” and the second “Shirou.” The fused words result from flattening, not the translation itself.
ずくん denotes a sudden painful throb and can reasonably be conveyed as a sharp pain. The objection demands a more literal sound description without establishing material error.
“Sharp pain” conveys substantial severity, so that portion of the accusation is overstated. The genuine loss is the explicit intermittent, flashing-on-and-off pattern of 点滅している.
The raw English contains a line-control marker between the cry and “You’re.” The joined public text is an extraction artifact.
特殊 means unusual or peculiar, not especially unpleasant. The English changes the kind of sensation into a judgment of severity.
かもしれない explicitly marks possibility, while “I’m sure” asserts confidence.
A wound visibly closing is naturally described in English as healing. The rendering does not materially exceed what Saber observes.
“Difficult magic” is a defensible contextual rendering of high-level 魔術. Without an immediate contrast with 魔法, the terminology objection does not demonstrate a material mistranslation.
Unmarked Japanese future statements often express practical prediction rather than certainty. “Might come” is a defensible English modal for Rin’s warning.
地面を蹴る here is kicking off from the ground to launch into pursuit; merely planting a foot does not express that motion.
ほとんどの機能 refers broadly to most functions shutting down. Limiting the collapse to all senses materially narrows it.
鼓動 can denote a heartbeat or pulsation, and the page immediately identifies the remaining phenomenon as a headache pulsing like one. “This throbbing within me” preserves that ambiguity.
“Continues to throb” preserves the heartbeat-like pulsation, and the preceding sentence supplies exclusivity. The narrower genuine omission is the feverish quality 熱病めいた.
身を乗り出して adds the distinct bodily action of leaning out toward Saber; merely reaching out a hand does not preserve that risky extension.
それで察してくれたのか is an observational inference naturally rendered “She must have understood.” The withdrawal issue is separately addressed and does not make this inference erroneous.
The adjacent Japanese explicitly describes Saber jumping back like a spark. “Jumps away with all her might” therefore conveys the physical form and urgency of her attempted withdrawal.
The first English sentence already says Berserker tries to pursue Saber; saying he ignores the arrow then naturally implies that pursuit continues. The page does not lose the action as alleged.
The Japanese identifies vibrations traveling through the air and shaking Shirou’s body; “shaking of the ground” changes both medium and object.

English retains numerous objects flying, so the whole shrapnel field is not reduced to one object. The narrower error is that plural fragments striking into Shirou’s back become one vague piece, while the four-direction detail is lost.
The heavy impact sound is explicitly present but wholly absent from the English.
Surviving the destruction naturally entails weathering it without a fatal wound. The English is less anatomically explicit but faithfully conveys the operative result.
Although “俺の下で” is not repeated here, the immediately preceding English says Shirou threw himself on top of Saber. Their physical relation therefore remains established in context.
炎上 describes the cemetery catching fire or becoming engulfed in flames; “razed” instead says it was leveled or demolished.
“Abolition” is semantically inapplicable to physical destruction and does not render 破壊.
A Noble Phantasm that 該当する to Rank A can naturally be called “a Rank-A Noble Phantasm”; the English does not demonstrably impose a different classification.
“With a noise” omits both the hard quality and clattering onomatopoeia that signal the approaching object’s material character.
In this context an object used as an arrow is being used as a projectile, and the English still concludes that it is an “arrow.” This is defensible functional explicitation.

The Japanese and supplied raw witness deliberately split the dramatic continuation across a display break. Capitalizing the resumed fragment is at most presentation style, not a material mistranslation.
口元を歪める commonly describes twisting one’s mouth into a smile or smirk, and the following sentence explicitly calls the expression laughter. “He’s smiling” is contextually supported.
The English carries over the burning spine but omits the associated feeling that he is about to vomit.
The English places Berserker’s retreat immediately after Illya orders him to return, so the response relation remains clear without translating the explicit “as if.”
In this dismissive choice, セイバーはいらない can idiomatically mean either “I don’t need Saber” or “I don’t want Saber.” The English is defensible.
English omits both the identifying description “white girl” and the specific image of her disappearing beyond the flames.
大した qualifies the injury as not serious; “I’m not wounded” incorrectly denies injury altogether.
The Japanese describes most of Shirou’s functions shutting down, whereas the English substitutes total sensory loss, changing both scope and kind.
鼓動 can denote a pulse or throbbing, and “this throbbing within me” is reinforced by the subsequent repeated “throb.” Calling it an unidentified sensation is too strong.

The repeated English “throb” substantially preserves the heartbeat comparison, and the preceding sentence supplies exclusivity. The definite surviving error is omission of the headache’s feverish quality.
Although “tumultuous” is closer to 激動, “shocking” is a plausible loose description of a route marked by dramatic upheaval, not a demonstrable material error.
The Japanese apologizes for feeding Taiga bogus information without establishing that the falsehood was deliberate; “I lied” adds that intent.
跳梁 here means running rampant or acting unchecked, not physically jumping. The literalized English is nonsensical and loses the complaint.

“Role theft” is a loose meta-comedy adaptation of the production shake-up implied by テコ入れ and the surrounding complaint about other characters becoming prominent. It is not a factual mistranslation requiring correction.
In the immediate account of one choice, “Shirou was a coward” can naturally paraphrase 臆病風に吹かれた without necessarily asserting a permanent trait.
The Japanese specifies that Shirou was killed by a surprise attack; English replaces that manner with an unsupported claim about instantaneous death.
A hastily formed “alliance” is a reasonable description of the improvised Rin–Archer combination. The political sense alleged by the finding is not compulsory.
The Japanese preserves comic partial recognition—Taiga feels she may understand while not wanting to—whereas English categorically says she does not understand.
“Close to the truth” idiomatically conveys a remark approaching the core of the matter; the difference from “hits the core” is not materially demonstrable here.
縁側 is a veranda-like passage along the house’s open edge and can be described as a corridor. The moon-viewing context prevents a firm inference that English relocated them indoors.
“The weather wasn’t cold” is a natural English paraphrase of the temperature not being very low, and the next sentence preserves the slight chill.
のんびり describes staying home and taking things easy; “carelessly” adds an unsupported judgment of negligent behavior.
“Yearning” can describe nostalgic longing for something in the past. In this deathbed reminiscence it remains within the reasonable range of 懐かしむ.
むっとする can mean becoming angry, offended, or annoyed, while the retort itself is phrased as questions. The English stays within the source’s range.
形にする means to realize or actualize something; “make [the dream] come true” is an idiomatic and accurate rendering, not a loss of substance.
The marked spelling 微笑った with the reading わらった permits a restrained “laughed” as well as “smiled.” The accusation imposes a preferred English affect.
The supplied raw English has a line-control marker between “Yeah” and “I’m relieved”; the apparent fusion results from stripped formatting rather than the underlying translation.
The child’s belief that Kiritsugu looked as though he would wake in the morning is a normal explicitation of the simile explaining why he did not raise an alarm.
サッパリした describes feeling cleared out or relieved after crying. “There was nothing” is incomplete and can instead suggest absence or emotional emptiness.

The English relative clause can grammatically attach to the immediately preceding “me,” and the next sentence explicitly identifies the unconscious burned child. The claimed role reversal is not established.
“How to become one” makes the goal becoming a superhero and omits both 早く and the distinct idea of becoming fully fledged or competent.

Both languages deliberately trail off at the waking transition, and the raw English contains a line-control dash marker after “really.” The displayed fragment is not evidence of an accidental unfinished sentence.
The Japanese itself calls what enters どろっとした空気, and the English immediately precedes “thick air” with the supposition that blood filled his mouth. The causal link is retained.
熱が出てきた refers to heat or fever arising; “headaches” substitutes a different symptom.
The raw English places line-control dash markers between and after the cries. “OwOwww” is a flattened-display artifact, not the actual punctuation of the translated script.
斬り捨てられた specifies cutting or slashing away the abdominal region. “Blew away my stomach” changes both the attack mechanism and anatomical scope.
English retains Shirou’s defensive questioning and Rin’s sigh, so it does not delete his reaction wholesale. It does omit the specifically ostentatious, weary quality of her sigh.
“It worked out like that” can neutrally mean “that is how it ended up,” especially after “just happened.” It does not necessarily imply a favorable outcome.
“Wouldn’t take risks” accurately translates the operative meaning of the chestnut proverb. Preserving its source-language imagery is not required for accuracy.
“Again” loosely presents Rin as returning to a better mood after anger. Any unsupported temporal implication is minor and does not materially alter the tentative mood assessment.
“It’s stupid not to ask” colloquially conveys that failing to ask would be unreasonable when he wants both answers. It is a defensible paraphrase of practical necessity.
“Wow, you’re pretty smart” can carry exactly the backhanded sarcasm of Rin noting that Shirou’s head works properly after all.
The Japanese graphically specifies his blown-out insides; generic “wounds” removes the extraordinary bodily damage central to Rin’s observation.
Japanese is counterfactual and retrospective: had Shirou learned such healing, Rin would not have needed to puzzle over the cause. English incorrectly turns this into present reassurance.
多少の傷 means some, modest, or relatively minor wounds. “Major wounds” reverses the scale and narrows Rin’s warning.
The Japanese says Shirou gets himself hurt and thereby receives or takes something from Saber. English removes his unilateral agency and makes Saber intentionally help him.

In context, “I won’t allow myself to be wrong” is a comic localization of Rin insisting that magecraft must consume money because otherwise her personal losses would be intolerable. The surrounding grudge remains clear.
Both formulations say Shirou has not reached an answer about what to do. “I haven’t made my mind up yet” is a natural contextual paraphrase, not proof that he has developed a conscious choice.
“I’m not too sure about” idiomatically expresses the dubious or objectionable judgment conveyed by どうかと思う; it need not denote mere factual uncertainty.
The Japanese explicitly names other Masters as the targets. English substitutes other Servants, contradicting the following explanation about neutralizing Masters.

The preceding English already says eliminated Servants return to where they belong, so “can’t be killed” is naturally read as inability to kill them permanently. The temporary-death distinction remains available.
息絶える describes expiring or ceasing to live, even if provisionally. “Disappeared” replaces that death-like event with its aftermath and weakens Shirou’s stated objection.
The supplied raw English contains a line-control dash between “still” and “I’m.” The apparent fusion is caused by stripped formatting rather than a script typo.
The Japanese rejects fighting for the purpose of killing. “Fight to the death” is broader and can include the lethal self-defense Shirou expressly accepts on the next page.
The inability is explicitly limited to people without spiritual perception; English incorrectly universalizes it to all humans.
自然災害 is a natural disaster, not a natural death. The substitution changes the comparison’s causal meaning.
The supplied raw English contains a line-control dash after “Servants,” marking Shirou’s self-correction. “Servantsno” is a flattened extraction artifact.
The Japanese itself says 魔術を連発できる, directly supporting “use magic repeatedly.” The finding imports a preferred technical gloss not demanded by this line.

The English opens Rin’s speech but does not close it before the next page begins a new quotation. The Japanese visibly closes this explanation, so this is a genuine typography defect rather than a continuing quote.

The supplied raw witness shows “mass murderer” and “tyrant” as mutually exclusive conditional variants. Their simultaneous appearance is the warned-about branch-flattening artifact, not an inserted translation claim.
呆れる covers dismayed, fed-up, or exasperated reactions; “disappointed” is imperfect but defensible here and does not demonstrably create a material factual change.
The apparent duplication comes from flattened conditional English branches; the archived script selects either “I’ll” or “Then I’ll,” so this is not a playable translation error.
In context, 考えがおよばない means he has not worked out an answer; “I haven’t made my mind up yet” naturally conveys that unresolved state without asserting a formed decision.
どうかと思う is a mild expression of doubt or disapproval. “I’m not too sure about” preserves that restrained judgment and is not merely factual uncertainty.
The object is explicitly 他のマスター, other Masters. The English substitutes other Servants, changing who Servants independently target.
The full English already says eliminated Servants return to where they belong. In that context, “can’t be killed” plainly means they cannot die permanently and adequately conveys 死んでも死なない.

Although 息絶える is literally dying or ceasing to breathe, the immediately preceding “temporary death” preserves the death-like event; “disappeared from this world” is contextually defensible for a defeated Servant returning elsewhere.
The missing separation is caused by stripping the supplied [line3] script command, not by the underlying translation. The archived English retains that break.
相手を殺すため specifies a battle whose purpose is killing. “A fight to the death” instead describes its possible outcome and conflicts with Shirou’s following allowance for lethal self-defense.
The Japanese limits invisibility to people without spiritual perception. Unqualified “Humans can’t see” incorrectly includes spiritually perceptive humans.
自然災害 is “natural disaster,” not “natural death.” The mistranslation replaces the comparison to an unseen calamity with a kind of death.
The correction is separated by the supplied [line3] command in the archived English. “Servantsno” is an extraction artifact caused by stripping that command.
Shirou himself says 魔術, whose ordinary translation is “magic.” The surrounding exchange makes clear that he is applying this shorthand to Servant abilities, so “use magic repeatedly” is defensible.
“Mass murderer” and “tyrant” are conditional edition variants in the supplied English script, not text displayed together. Their apparent coexistence is branch flattening.

The Japanese itself contrasts other Servants with his own—他のサーヴァントだけでなく、自分のサーヴァント. The English preserves his conclusion that attacks by both are unacceptable; it need not assert formal command authority over every Servant.
腹 commonly denotes the belly or stomach area, while “blown away” can idiomatically describe its wholesale destruction without alleging an explosion. The rendering preserves the severe abdominal loss.
そうみたい accepts that Rin’s account appears correct. “It sounds like a lie” reverses that tentative acceptance into disbelief.
ぶっ飛んだ中身 refers vividly to his displaced or destroyed insides. Reducing this to generic “wounds” removes the extraordinary internal damage Rin says he restored.
悩む必要はなかった is a past counterfactual: if that explanation were true, Rin would not have needed to puzzle over his recovery. “I’ve nothing to worry about” turns it into present reassurance.
多少の傷 means some or relatively minor wounds. “Major wounds” reverses the scope of the complacent belief Rin tells him to abandon.

The accusation overstates intentionality, since “helping” can describe an unintended benefit. A narrower error survives: the English loses かってに and the sense that his unilateral injuries consume or take something from Saber.

Rin says that if magecraft did not consume money, she personally would not forgive that state of affairs. “I won’t allow myself to be wrong” replaces the financial-grievance joke with simple obstinacy.

“Poking a sleeping dragon awake” is a natural English localization of provoking a dangerous dragon. The following line still supplies its wrath, so changing the exact anatomical image is not a demonstrable factual error.

逆鱗 is conventionally an idiom for provoking terrible wrath. Rendering its idiomatic meaning instead of the literal reverse scale is acceptable, especially after the preceding English retains the dragon image.

The definite surviving problem is grammatical: “felt more like dangerous” improperly uses the adjective after “like.” The separate claim that past tense materially changes the danger is not established.
The temple is part of the lateral forehead region, and “a vein in your forehead” is a normal English rendering of this anger cue. The minor anatomical generalization is not material.
“Intense smile” conveys its force, while answering “in bits and pieces” conveys that Shirou is overwhelmed and halting. The causal pressure remains readily apparent.
The Japanese describes Shirou actually retreating with his tail tucked. The English changes this action into merely wanting to escape and removes the comic submission image.
正座 specifies the formal kneeling posture. “Sit there, Japanese-style” is too vague to communicate the disciplinary pose, and the following generic “sit down” does not repair it.
ぶっ飛んだ中身 identifies his blown-out or destroyed insides. “Wounds” suppresses this unusually severe internal damage.
The Japanese is a past counterfactual about why Rin previously had to puzzle over the recovery. The English instead presents current freedom from worry.
多少の傷 refers to modest or minor injuries, not major ones. The English therefore warns against the wrong expectation.

Calling it Saber “helping” is not necessarily intentional, so that part is overstated. The narrower omission is real: かってに and 何かを貰ってる frame Shirou as unilaterally getting hurt and thereby taking a resource from Saber.
The Japanese joke is that Rin personally would not forgive magecraft if it failed to consume money. The English substitutes a refusal to admit that she is wrong.
考えがおよばない says he has not arrived at an answer or thought the matter through. “Haven’t made my mind up yet” is a natural contextual equivalent, not proof of an already formed decision.
どうかと思う is deliberately mild and can naturally be rendered as “I’m not too sure about.” The English still expresses his objection to risking his life for something unwanted.
The Japanese explicitly makes other Masters the targets. The English incorrectly changes them to other Servants.

The preceding English sentence states that eliminated Servants return to their proper place. Consequently, “They can’t be killed” communicates the lack of permanent death rather than erasing provisional defeat.
The English explicitly retains “temporary death” immediately beforehand. In that context, disappearance from this world defensibly describes the result of 息絶える for a Servant who returns elsewhere.
The apparent fusion results from removing the supplied [line3] formatting command. It is not present as an unseparated word in the archived translation script.
The source rejects fighting for the purpose of killing, leaving room for the lethal self-defense described next. “Fight to the death” instead rejects combat defined by its lethal endpoint.
The source qualifies the humans as those without spiritual perception. The English incorrectly makes the inability universal.
自然災害 means a natural disaster or calamity. “Natural death” is a different concept and breaks the comparison.
The supplied archived English separates the self-correction with [line3]. “Servantsno” is produced only when that script command is stripped.
The Japanese expressly uses 魔術, so “magic” is not an unsupported narrowing. The preceding discussion supplies the Servant-power context.
The archived English shows “mass murderer” and “tyrant” as mutually exclusive edition branches. Printing both in the supplied mirror text is a flattening artifact, not the playable sentence.
倒す means defeat or take down and does not by itself specify killing. Rendering both occurrences as “kill” makes Shirou’s stated policy categorically lethal.
以上 ties his obligation to the firm declaration he just made. “As a man, I have to listen” removes that causal commitment and substitutes a generic masculine duty.
The source identifies what he touches as the trace of a greatsword blow. “It was pretty much instant death” retains lethality but omits both the weapon and the bodily trace.

The English says Saber has no problem but is made less useful because her Master drags her down. That preserves the distinction between an excellent Servant and the deficient Master limiting their side.
The archived English places [line3] between “Guh” and “but.” Their fusion is caused by stripping that presentation command, not by the translation text.
