先輩 can denote a more experienced senior or mentor. Since Rin has just offered to teach him Master knowledge and inspect his magecraft, “reliable teacher” is reasonable contextual explicitation.

The governing Original Japanese contains both disputed rationale lines as active prose. Their absence or commented status in another edition cannot make their Original-edition translation an unsupported insertion.
“In comparison” explicitly relates Shirou’s scratched hand to Rin’s soft hand, and “ill-suited” naturally expresses 不釣り合い. The comparison is not unresolved.
“She” supplies an explicit subject, and the English preserves the sequence of puzzlement, knowing exclamation, and malicious expression. It is neither a fragment nor a lost escalation.

強く permits a sense of strong or forceful physical contact, and “touched a girl so strongly” preserves that reading despite being stylistically awkward. Emotional intimacy is not the only governing possibility.
The archived English itself has “show you feelings,” where the required possessive is “your.” This is a genuine textual typo rather than a branch or command-stripping artifact.
The English omits どこに隠し持っていたのか, which marks Shirou’s surprise at the book’s concealed provenance and is part of the reveal action.
In this context, “full Master” readily means a complete or fully qualified Master. “Full-fledged” would be more idiomatic, but the supplied wording does not materially change 一人前.

The English retains the core mechanism: a suitable class is prepared and the actual Heroic Spirit is called into it. “It” is clumsy but recoverably refers to the Grail, and the following page explains the container analogy.

筐 with the reading ハコ denotes a box, casing, or container. “Case” is therefore a defensible literal rendering; preferring the established fantasy term “vessel” is terminology preference, not a demonstrable mistranslation.
Singular “they/their” is standard contemporary English and can agree with “each class.” The sentence accurately conveys that the classes respectively possess distinctive traits.
“Spirits” is a defensible rendering of 精霊, and the English still contrasts them with “divine spirits.” The accusation overstates the loss.
The Japanese presents a generic hypothetical hero; masculine singular “he” is dated and inconsistent with the preceding plural, but does not materially alter the proposition.
“Just because of that” naturally renders それだけで, and “that” clearly refers to being from the Age of Gods. Any dismissive coloring is minor.
The ruby explicitly reads 英霊 as サーヴァント, so “Servant” follows the supplied Japanese presentation. “In their life” is awkward but intelligible.
In this context, “what history it has” adequately conveys 曰く—its story, associations, or provenance. The objection is chiefly terminological preference.
The English adds “divine,” making 神秘 specifically sacred or god-related when the Japanese merely names Mystery. This materially narrows the technical concept.
“Sorcery” can function as the distinct English label for 魔法, especially where 魔術 has already been rendered differently. It does not inherently collapse the distinction.

“Fantasia race” is clumsy, but it still communicates a fantastical species or race and preserves the claim that dragons are its strongest members. Malformed terminology alone does not establish a material mistranslation.
万里 conventionally signifies an immense distance; “far and wide” is a normal nonliteral rendering and preserves the legendary range.
The English is stylistically awkward and repetitive, but still states that Servant battles center on battles between Noble Phantasms. The tactical thesis remains clear.
Although 断つ literally emphasizes cutting or severing, a sword stroke that destroys a mountain conveys substantially the same extraordinary feat here. This is not a material factual change.

“Identify” can mean recognize or determine what a Servant is; Japanese 判断 does not itself limit the judgment specifically to displayed status or capability. The narrower governing reading is unproven.
倒れている means defeated or down, not necessarily dead. “Once” also converts one arm of a whether-or alternative into a completed temporal precondition.
The supplied raw witness contains a line command between “So” and “it’ll”; the fusion is a flattening artifact rather than translation text intended as “Soit’ll.”
一人前 means fully competent or fully fledged, not that Rin has attained her maximum potential. “Full potential” makes a materially stronger claim.
In context, “You are a Master now” directly validates Shirou’s status. It weakens the emphasis of 歴とした but does not materially change Rin’s point.

The subject is established before the intervening dialogue, and the later fragment completes that interrupted construction, just as the Japanese sentence spans the quotation. It is awkward but recoverable.
The supplied raw English has a line command between “night” and “when.” The fused display is an extraction artifact, not a translation error.
させられない is causative: Shirou cannot make Saber assume spirit form. “I can’t do that” instead most naturally makes Shirou himself the performer.
“Sitting in a Japanese-style” is grammatically incomplete and fails to express the specific formal sitting posture 正座.
The supplied raw witness places a line command between “So” and “I,” so “SoI” is a display-flattening artifact.
Here “surprisingly” can naturally express the striking degree conveyed by ひどく. The voice’s strong suitability to the dojo remains intact.
In context, becoming conscious of Saber’s “womanhood” reasonably conveys awareness of her as the opposite sex. It is somewhat abstract but not a demonstrable material distortion.
“I’m troubled” is loose, but the surrounding sentences make Saber the obvious cause of Shirou’s discomfort. It remains a defensible contextual paraphrase of 苦手.
The raw witness has “Wha” followed by a line command and “don’t,” representing an interrupted false start. “Whadon’t” results from command stripping.
“I’ll thank you for that” can be a present performative declaration, and the preceding “I’m grateful” removes any real ambiguity about when the thanks is given.
“No room for me to question her” can mean no room to doubt or challenge her resolve, which is a natural rendering of 疑問を挟む余地などない. It need not mean she forbids questions.
“Reached the rank of gods” is a plausible figurative rendering of climbing into 神域, a divine or godlike level. It does not necessarily assert literal deification.
卓越した means outstanding or exceptional. “Supernatural” adds a categorical claim that all such abilities exceeded nature, which the definition itself does not state.
The English entirely omits the sentence explaining that the vessels provide anchors through which Heroic Spirits can exist in this world.
“Receive these classes” conveys assignment but omits the explicit image of a Heroic Spirit wearing a role as a shell, an important part of the manifestation explanation.
セイバー can denote the class here, and the surrounding discussion concerns the class selected for sword ability. The English class-level reading is contextually defensible.
白兵戦 specifically means close-quarters or melee combat. General “combat” broadens the condition and weakens the contrast with alternative tactics.
Both Japanese and raw English deliberately break off mid-utterance at a line command. “Fightin—” represents interrupted speech, not accidental truncation.
息の根を絶つ explicitly means ending the enemy’s life. “Beat them” removes the lethal force of Shirou’s realization.
“Lack ability” can mean being deficient in ability rather than possessing none at all, and it reasonably conveys 能力に劣った. The proposed confrontation-specific restriction is contextual inference.
The supplied raw script shows “an” and “a special” as mutually exclusive conditional branches. Printing both in the flattened page is an extraction artifact, not the translation’s active sentence.
機会 denotes an opportunity or chance for a sure-kill blow. “Guaranteed fatal attack” turns that potential opening into certainty that the attack itself will kill.
The raw witness places a line command between “Noble Phantasm” and its appositive, representing a dash or pause. The apparent fusion is caused by flattening.
桁違い describes magnitude on an entirely different scale. “Strange amount” changes overwhelming quantity into mere oddness.
“Recitement” is awkward and uncommon, but the sentence still communicates that uttering the true name is required to awaken and activate the Noble Phantasm. No material mechanism is lost.
The preceding explanation establishes that speaking the weapon’s name reveals its owner’s identity. In that immediate context, “revealing the name” is acceptable metonymy for 正体を明かす.
The Japanese says that failure also exposes the Servant’s flaw or vulnerabilities; it does not say every weakness is comprehensively exposed. “All” is an unsupported overstatement.
The raw witness separates “Uh” and “um” with a line command, marking hesitation. “Uhum” is a flattening artifact rather than an assent chosen by the translator.
魔力 is magical energy or power, not plural acts or systems of magic. “Powerful magics” changes the reason Servants can be sensed.
The apparent “Ughthat” fusion comes from a stripped line command, but “could be true” genuinely weakens それはそう, which concedes that the statement is true.
“Its only natural” incorrectly uses the possessive “its” where the contraction “it’s” is required. This is a genuine source-text grammar error, not a removed line-command artifact.
Classifying or distinguishing according to animals substantially conveys a personal animal-based visualization. The loss of the explicit simile is minor and does not change the mechanism.
冷徹 can describe cool, dispassionate composure, and the following “allows no disagreement” preserves the gaze’s severity. “Calm” is weaker but defensible in the complete sentence.
In a returned-gaze confrontation, “trying not to lose” naturally expresses refusing to be overawed or borne down. It does not materially recast the action.
The Japanese says Shirou cannot remain both inactive and unscathed. Omitting 無傷で changes this into the stronger claim that doing nothing necessarily prevents survival.
実感が湧かない means the Grail lacks felt reality or concreteness for Shirou. “I don’t feel anything toward” instead states emotional indifference.
無関係な人 means uninvolved people or bystanders. “Unnecessary people” evaluates their usefulness and changes Shirou’s ethical concern.
Although the base text names 切嗣, its supplied ruby reads オヤジ, meaning “my old man” or father. “My father” follows the spoken ruby rather than improperly deleting a name.
緊張の糸が切れる is an idiom for tension giving way or disappearing. The English loses the thread image but preserves the causal relaxation.
The supplied raw English shows “magus” and “magus to want it” in mutually exclusive edition branches. Their apparent duplication is caused by branch flattening.
“Cheating myself” is a reasonable natural paraphrase for Shirou feeling that taking such a shortcut would be cowardly or unfair. It preserves his personal moral aversion.

“Expectations” genuinely mistranslates 思惑, which means motives, intentions, or designs. However, “defeat your enemies” is a defensible contextual rendering of pushing rivals aside in the chair-game analogy.
“Get up” can mean raising oneself from a lying position and does not necessarily assert that Shirou stands. The next page separately establishes standing.
The English exclamation remains an irritated complaint that Rin omitted the crucial point. It softens rough markers such as ヤツ and やがって, but not enough to establish a material tonal error.
The causative させられない says Shirou cannot make a Servant enter spirit form. “I can’t do that” instead suggests Shirou cannot personally perform the transformation.

The scene is explicitly about Saber and Shirou’s role as her Master, so “just how am I a Master?” retains the relationship-specific doubt through context. Repeating “her” is unnecessary explicitation.
The allegedly inserted analogy is present in the governing Original Japanese; its absence from base and all-ages witnesses is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
柱 specifically means a pillar or post. The English changes the concrete object Shirou strikes to a wall.
“Complaint” is a plausible contextual rendering of 弱音 as a weak or dispirited utterance, while “How rotten of me, idiot” retains the self-reproach. The alleged characterization loss is overstated.
The adjacent Original Japanese explicitly establishes Saber sitting in seiza. Adding “sitting” here is harmless contextual explicitation, not an unsupported event.
The posture sentence is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its omission or commenting-out in later witnesses cannot make the Original-edition translation an unsupported insertion.
ためらう事なく describes decisive action without hesitation. “Mercilessly” instead asserts lack of mercy and imposes a harsher moral characterization.

“Completely accepted Saber” defensibly folds 全て into “completely”; the immediately preceding page already frames her as a girl. This is condensation, not a demonstrable loss of the whole-person scope.
“Surprisingly” adds a reaction or violated expectation not expressed by the Japanese; the sentence simply says her voice suits the dojo.
The archived English is “Y[line3]Yeah,” so the apparent fusion results from stripping a line/dash command; it represents the Japanese hesitation rather than a source typo.
The approach is present verbatim in the governing Original. Its absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported English insertion.
The allegedly removed narration is active in the governing Original Japanese. Empty base/all-ages witnesses do not make its translation erroneous for this comparator.
“Sit down and talk” is a conventional English paraphrase for having a settled, unhurried conversation and need not assert a literal seating action here.
The raw English reads “Wha[line3]don’t,” marking a broken-off objection. “Whadon’t” is produced only by extraction that removes the command.
The raw English contains “And[line3]if”; the apparent missing space is an extraction artifact caused by stripping the line/dash command.

In context, “no room for me to question her” naturally means that the certainty of her resolve cannot be challenged. It preserves the force of the Japanese rather than changing her will into mere conversational restraint.

Although “steeled myself” would be closer, “convinced myself that I have to fight” still conveys accepting the necessity of battle and forming the corresponding resolve. The accusation overstates a tonal preference as error.
弱音 commonly denotes weak complaints or whining, and “stop whining” is a defensible idiomatic rendering of suppressing that impulse. The narration need not describe audible whining.
The comparison is explicitly with what happened yesterday, whereas the English says tomorrow may resemble today. This changes the referenced battle.

The broken syntax follows the Japanese’s deliberate interrupted construction and an intervening visual transition. The stray “And” corresponds to the suspended あんな rather than evidencing a mistranslated causal relation.

The speech is intentionally cut off, as the next page explicitly says Shirou cannot finish. Ending mid-word is a defensible English device for that interruption, not an accidental loss of the ethical example.

“Not a possibility” is immediately defined as a moral impossibility by “I can only do those things I will allow myself to do,” her beliefs, and the knightly oath. The complete English does not imply merely physical incapacity.

“Treading inside me” is awkward but intelligibly preserves the Japanese metaphor of intruding into Saber’s inner self; the surrounding forced-order and Command Spell context establishes the violation of will.
The English retains her lack of doubt but omits 強さ, one of the two stated reasons Shirou had viewed her as a fighting machine. Adding “cold” does not restore that missing basis.

“Until you become a suitable Master” still presents an endpoint Shirou must develop toward and is a defensible contextual rendering of maturing into the role. The harsher alleged judgment is not compelled by the English.

“About an hour after Berserker left” normally locates completion roughly one hour after his departure and is compatible with treatment taking about that long. The proposed distinction is too fine for a demonstrable error.

The raw script has mutually exclusive conditional variants—“healed” for one edition and “healed easily” for another. Their consecutive appearance in the supplied mirrorMoon field is branch flattening, not duplicated player-facing translation.
“Sigh in admiration” is an ordinary English expression of impressed wonder, and “in admiration” prevents a reasonable reading of weary exasperation. It is acceptable naturalization of the reaction.
Persuading the neighbors that Saber is Kiritsugu’s relative still describes maintaining a false cover, and “I would have to do so anyway” preserves Shirou’s recognition that he has no alternative.

The Japanese itself has Shirou characterize the Servant system as magecraft that summons and employs Heroic Spirits. “Magics” is dated and awkward terminology, but the alleged conceptual insertion is present in the source.
The archived English is “Then[line3]you”; removing the line/dash command creates the apparent fusion. It is not a source-text spacing failure.
存在意義 can mean raison d’être or why one exists in a particular setting. “Why I am here in this time” is a defensible natural paraphrase of Saber’s class-defined purpose.

“Not a name to represent my real identity” preserves the operative contrast between a class designation and an individual identity. Omitting the illustrative “like Shirou” comparison is minor condensation, not a material mistranslation.
“Master and Servant are one” is a standard, concise English equivalent of 一心同体, and the following secrecy sentence supplies the functional interdependence. No material weakening is established.

In this casual internal voice, “I don’t care about it” is within the contextual range of not being especially interested. The difference in bluntness is tonal preference rather than a demonstrable factual change.
The English is grammatically defective: the count expression requires “a” in “That’s a bit unexpected.” This is not caused by a script command or edition difference.

Context has already established Shirou’s weakness and inexperience as a Master, so “Your Master is weak” is permissible explicitation. “Try everything” loosely but defensibly conveys Saber devising compensating measures.
The raw English contains “And[line3]from.” The apparent “Andfrom” fusion is created by stripping the line/dash command.
不覚を取る can mean to suffer defeat as well as to be caught off guard or suffer a reverse. Given Saber’s incapacitation in the encounter, “suffered defeat” is within its defensible range.

The raw English places “The” and “Still, the” in mutually exclusive edition branches. Printing both in the supplied flattened field is an extraction artifact, not a duplicated sentence in a single active script path.
The archived line is “Ah[line3]hold on,” so the apparent fusion arises from removal of the line/dash command and represents Shirou’s interrupted outburst.
“One bed” is a natural localization of one futon set, and the immediately following line explicitly identifies the joke as sharing the same bed. The arrangement and joke remain clear.

The English is stiff, but it still communicates Shirou’s accusation that Rin is saying outrageous things while he remains silent. The more idiomatic proposed wording is an improvement, not proof of material inaccuracy.

In this context, “calling me by my name” conventionally signals first-name address, and the surrounding dialogue supplies “Shirou” and the later “Emiya-kun” reversal. Explicitly explaining the missing honorific is not required for accuracy.
After the preposition “for,” the coordinated pronoun requires object case: “for Shirou and me.” The supplied English uses the nonstandard subject form “I.”
In this arrangement, 嫌 can naturally be rendered as not wanting it. The English preserves Saber’s comic distinction between merely being troubled and actually rejecting the proposal.

The English preserves the audible joke—both women repeatedly calling him “Shirou” as if calling a found cat. The kanji/katakana distinction is orthographic and not naturally reproducible in identical romanized names; its loss is not a factual mistranslation.

ふー describes the huffing exhalation accompanying Shirou’s mock threat, so “breathe out hard and intimidate” is a defensible rendering. “Intimidate” can describe the attempted action without asserting success.
外敵 literally denotes an external or foreign enemy, not every neutral outsider. “Enemy” therefore does not improperly narrow the Japanese detection condition.
“Ostentatiously” is a direct and contextually adequate rendering of これみよがしに. Because “Emiya-kun” is quoted immediately after prior first-name usage, the deliberate address reversal remains evident.

The raw script places the one-sentence and two-sentence versions in mutually exclusive classic/non-classic branches. Their consecutive appearance is caused by flattened extraction, not duplication in one active translation.
An engawa is commonly described in English as an open or exterior corridor/veranda. “Open corridor” preserves its spatial function in the directions and is an acceptable alternative.
The archived English is “Wha[line3]this,” representing an interrupted “Wha—this.” The fused form appears only after the line/dash command is stripped.

“An assorted person” is not an idiomatic English description of a personality and leaves Saber’s impression difficult to understand. The Japanese refers to a more miscellaneous, cluttered, or less spare cast of character.

The English condenses exploratory contact with the walls and fusuma into touching the wall, but retains the material action and its purpose. The omitted architectural example is too minor to establish a material translation error.
The English retains the hypothetical comparison through “as if”; it does not assert psychometry as fact. “Understands” is a defensible rendering of figuratively apprehending the object’s memories.

Saying the room “will not change my impression of you now” naturally means it confirms the impression Saber has already formed. The temporal relationship is awkwardly expressed but not materially reversed.

“The spiritual connection we ought to have is not present” accurately conveys the operative condition that the normally connected channel is disconnected. It generalizes the wire metaphor but does not change the technical consequence.

Saber was summoned and fought the cited battles during the preceding night, so “used … last night” remains compatible with the cumulative expenditure reached by last night. No material duration error follows in this context.
“Used up that much” ordinarily means consumed that quantity, not necessarily exhausted the entire reserve. The ensuing question about how much longer she can remain makes the partitive reading clear.
The supplied raw Original witness contains 何より, directly supporting “most of all.” “I have my own life” is also a defensible contextual rendering of having circumstances and commitments of his own.

“Those with inhuman attitudes” reasonably denotes people whose outlook or conduct falls outside human decency. It is less behaviorally explicit than 節度を外した but does not materially change whom Shirou means.
The raw English reads “Masters[line3]if”; the apparent fusion results from removal of the line/dash command during extraction.
“Heroic spirits that attribute to several classes” is grammatically malformed and does not clearly express possession of qualifications or affinities for multiple classes.

万全 describes Saber previously being in full or unrestricted condition. “She was flawless last time” instead naturally claims faultless performance, changing the contrast with her present magical handicap.

The immediately preceding sentence explicitly establishes her blood-covered appearance, and “covered miserably in blood” is a contextual visual paraphrase of the grievously wounded image. The injury is not plausibly erased from the passage.
In Saber’s blunt reassurance, calling the regret “useless” is within the contextual sense of 余分 as unnecessary or serving no purpose. The colder nuance is not enough to demonstrate a material error.

The head movement and serious expression are present in the governing Original Japanese. Their omission from base and all-ages is an edition difference, so the English is not an unsupported insertion here.
The archived English contains “That’s[line3]true”; stripping the line/dash command creates “That’strue.” It is not a source-text spacing error.
“Consider her words in my mind” is plain but still conveys inward reflection on Saber’s words. The more tactile force of 噛みしめる is stylistic nuance rather than a demonstrable material loss.
“Master and Servant are one” is a standard concise equivalent of 一心同体, while the adjacent secrecy and combat sentences make the practical interdependence explicit.
“I don’t care about it” is a somewhat blunter but contextually defensible expression of Shirou’s limited interest. It does not establish a materially different attitude.
The count phrase is grammatically defective: standard English requires “That’s a bit unexpected.” No branch or line-command artifact accounts for the missing article.

“Weak” is a defensible contextual explicitation of Shirou’s self-described inadequacy, while “try everything” reasonably conveys Saber making compensatory efforts. The accusation overstates lexical differences as factual errors.
The archived script has a [line3] display command between “And” and “from”; the fused public text is an extraction artifact, not the translation stored in the script.
不覚をとる can mean suffering a defeat or reverse, not only being caught off guard. “I suffered defeat” is defensible even though Saber survived.
The archived English conditionally selects either “The” or “Still, the.” Both appear together only because the public extraction flattened mutually exclusive branches.
The archived English contains “Ah[line3] hold,” where the command marks an interruption. The alleged fused “Ahhold” is not the stored translation.
“One bed” is a reasonable localization of one futon set, and the following sentence explicitly preserves the joke as sleeping in the same bed.
Although literal and awkward, the English still communicates that Rin says this while Shirou remains silent. The claimed loss of the accusation is not demonstrable.

In this context, “calling me by my name” naturally means switching to his given name; the surrounding use of “Shirou” versus “Tohsaka” supplies the intimacy change. Explicitly explaining 呼び捨て is optional localization.
“For Shirou and I” has the wrong object-case pronoun; standard English requires “for Shirou and me.”
In context, “did not want it” is a natural expression of 嫌だ and remains clearly distinguished from merely being troubled. The comic contrast survives.
The English cannot reproduce the kanji/katakana spelling distinction without intrusive explanation, but it preserves the repeated use of “Shirou” by both speakers and the stray-cat comparison.

うなって specifies a growling or huffing vocal performance, which “breathe out hard” weakens. However, 威嚇する directly supports the threatening/intimidating action, so that part of the accusation should be removed.
外敵 literally denotes an outside enemy or hostile intruder. “Enemy” is within its normal lexical range and does not necessarily imply magical hostility detection.
“Ostentatiously” is a valid rendering of これみよがしに, and the quoted “Emiya-kun” plus surrounding conversation makes the pointed address reversal evident.
The archived script contains mutually exclusive classic and non-classic renderings. Their consecutive appearance is caused by conditional-branch flattening, not duplication in a playable translation.
An engawa is commonly describable in English as an open corridor or veranda. The translation preserves its function as the route along the house.
The archived English is “Wha[line3]this,” with a display command marking the broken-off false start. “Whathis” is an extraction artifact.
“An assorted person” is not idiomatic English for a person’s character and leaves 雑多な人となり semantically opaque rather than conveying a messier or more miscellaneous personality.
The Japanese explicitly has Saber testing walls and fusuma, while the English reduces the exploration to touching one wall and omits the sliding panels.
The English retains the hypothetical simile through “as if”; it does not assert psychometry as fact. “Understands the object’s memory” is a defensible poetic paraphrase of sensing its memories.
“This will not change my impression of you now” substantially conveys that the room accords with Saber’s existing impression. The temporal framing is awkward but not reversed.

Calling the expected spiritual channel a “spiritual connection” that “is not present” conveys the operative fact that it is disconnected. Omitting the wiring metaphor is defensible generalization, not a changed condition.

All three post-summoning battles occurred in the relevant night, so “last night” does not materially contradict the cumulative endpoint 昨夜までで. “By last night” would be more exact but the accusation overstates the difference.
“Used up that much magical energy” means consumed that quantity; “that much” prevents it from naturally meaning her entire reserve. Her remaining manifestation is not contradicted.

The normalized originalJa omits a hierarchy marker, but the supplied raw Original candidate contains 何より, which directly supports “most of all.” Because that candidate is expressly not certified alignment, the conflicting witnesses cannot settle the accusation.
“Inhuman attitudes” is a defensible, if less behavior-focused, paraphrase for people acting outside the bounds of human restraint or decency. No clear reversal of Shirou’s criterion results.
The archived English has “Masters[line3]if,” where the command supplies an interruption boundary. “Mastersif” is produced by stripping that command.
“Heroic spirits that attribute to several classes” is grammatically malformed and does not clearly express possessing qualifications or affinities for multiple classes.
“Correspond to the class of Saber” is awkward but grammatical and intelligibly conveys that Saber matches or qualifies only for that class. Calling it an accuracy failure is preference policing.

万全 can mean perfect or flawless condition. In the explicit contrast with her present wounds and restrictions, “flawless last time” is readily understood as being in full condition rather than never making mistakes.

“Covered miserably in blood,” immediately following the prior blood-soaked image, plainly communicates that the girl was wounded. The injury is not meaningfully erased by describing its visible result.
“Useless” is somewhat colder than “unnecessary,” but both dismiss Shirou’s regret as something he need not feel. This is a tonal preference, not a demonstrable material mistranslation.

The allegedly inserted sentence occurs verbatim in the supplied Original Japanese; only the later-edition base/all-ages witnesses omit it. It is an edition difference, not unsupported content in this comparator.
The archived text is “That’s[line3]true,” with a display command marking the hesitation. The fused public form results from command stripping.
噛みしめる figuratively means reflecting deeply or chewing something over. “Consider her words in my mind” is clumsy and less vivid but retains the core rumination.
“Pisses me off” is an ordinary colloquial equivalent of 頭にくる, and the phrasing preserves the strong inward anger. The alleged register distortion is not established.

The Japanese itself contains a two-part flustered sound, あ[line7]う, and the archived English analogously has “Uh[line5]Uh.” The apparent fusion comes from stripping the interruption command, not duplicating the utterance.
The archived English places a [line3] interruption between “identity” and “oh.” The public extractor removed that boundary; the realization is not fused in the script.

The archived English uses mutually exclusive edition branches: one ends after forced disclosure, while the classic branch continues with the knowledge sentence. Flattening both creates the apparent stray quotation mark.

The categorical plural 私たちは is rendered with the mismatched singular predicate “a tool.” The English should use plural tools or otherwise recast the collective statement; “our Master” also blurs the distributive Masters.
“Porch” is a standard functional translation of 縁側 in natural English. Retaining the Japanese architectural term is optional, not required for accuracy here.
正規 directly supports “official” or “legitimate,” and the surrounding reference to Rin as Shirou’s senior supplies competence. “Official Master” is defensible.
This is a cross-page continuation: the preceding English ends “Tohsaka is…” and the current text completes it with “…is intently searching.” Reading the adjacent page, the sentence has a subject.

The complete supplied Original Japanese explicitly contains the second deep breath. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference and cannot support an insertion accusation against the Original comparator.
The archived script conditionally selects “There’s” or “Anyways, there’s.” Both appear together only after the public witness flattens the edition branch.
ばたんと倒れ込んだ is an abrupt flop or collapse, so neutral “lie down” loses a genuine comic action. Calling the engawa a corridor is defensible, so the location complaint should be dropped.
The audible はあ and repeated breathing can naturally be presented as another sigh. The Japanese does not independently establish the claimed deliberate self-settling action.
“Later” conveys the time transition and the three being in the room adequately conveys their assembly, but the explicit fact that the sun has set is omitted.
“Man…” is a natural English exasperated interjection capable of carrying the force of the written sigh はあ. Reproducing the breath literally is not mandatory.
“About seven o’clock” is a normal approximation for a time shortly before seven. It loses directional precision but creates no material temporal error here.
The archived English has “Uh[line3]sure,” with the command marking Shirou’s stumble. The fused public form is an extraction artifact.
The English agency is correct. In context Shirou accepts alternating dinner duty: if Rin lives there as family, it is natural for her to cook too, which will make things easier for him.
“Irritatedly” is awkward and uncommon but intelligible, and it accurately conveys Rin glaring with visible displeasure. This is copyediting preference rather than a material error.
The comparison is reversed. 遠坂はともかく sets Rin aside and doubts Saber; “Saber, let alone Tohsaka” instead makes Tohsaka the still less likely person to appreciate the food.
The English omits that the grated daikon is used to make the accompanying sauce. Rendering shishito more generally as green peppers is defensible, so only the missing sauce relation survives.
The archived English reads “three of u[line3]no,” representing an interrupted “us—no.” Removing the display command produces the apparent word “uno.”
The compound subject “You, me, and Illyasviel” is plural, so “makes three” is a clear agreement error; standard English requires “make three.”
The archived English contains “still[line3]I,” where the command marks the break corresponding to the Japanese interruption. The missing boundary is an extraction artifact.
“Family lineage” is mildly redundant but grammatical and accurately conveys 魔術師の家系. Redundancy alone is not a translation error.
The archived script conditionally selects “on” or “on without me.” Their consecutive appearance results from flattening the realta/classic branch.

The English reverses both relationships: Japanese says Shirou cannot speak casually to Saber, so Rin consulting Saber helps; the translation instead makes Rin unfriendly toward Shirou and Saber the one speaking to her.
むっと眉を寄せる describes an irritated or sullen frown, confirmed by Shirou immediately wondering why he is angry. “Disappointed” changes the emotion.
“Helped carrying” is grammatically malformed; it should be “helped carry,” “helped with carrying,” or, more specifically here, “helped serve the food.”
Read with the preceding line, this is one deliberately suspended sentence: “Tohsaka goes ‘huh?’, and after that… makes a frightening smile.” The continuation does not lack a recoverable subject.
面子 denotes the present lineup or group. Singular “this member” wrongly turns Shirou’s concern about the three-person group into concern about one unspecified individual.
In context, “swinging around a sword” plainly refers to Saber’s earlier sword fighting and is within the ordinary range of 剣を振るう. Any careless or playful implication is not compelled by the English.
手をつけていない describes a dish Saber has not yet touched during this meal, not food she has never eaten before. The English invents prior unfamiliarity.

In context, 勝った is a triumphant declaration of assured victory in the anticipated cooking contest. “I’ll win” communicates that prospective conclusion; the past form need not mean the contest is already completed.
“Slowly” is a defensible rendering of 地道に here, conveying a gradual, patient search. The complaint concerns lost nuance rather than a factual mistranslation.
The Japanese instructs him to return immediately once the sun has set. “Before dark” instead sets an earlier deadline and removes the stated trigger.
気乗りのしない means unenthusiastic or disinclined; “without interest” is awkward but conveys that lack of enthusiasm, while the following sentence explicitly supplies his resistance.
Saber specifically praises the seasoning, whereas “It was very good” reduces this to generic approval of the meal.
“Can’t you not go to school?” is marked but grammatical English and accurately asks whether Shirou can refrain from attending. The finding identifies awkward style, not a changed meaning.
The narration is present in the governing Original edition. Its absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference, so translating it is not an insertion.
年下 directly means younger than Shirou. “A girl from a younger age” is unnatural and can instead suggest someone from an earlier historical period.
襖 is a sliding fusuma panel, not a small sheet. The English misrepresents the physical partition between the rooms.
The apparent “Uhno” fusion results from stripping the supplied line-break/dash command; the intended hesitation and denial remain distinct in the script.
In the immediate exchange, “Are you fine?” naturally turns Saber’s concern back on her. The reciprocal bodily concern is recoverable from the question and her condition-focused answer.
平均値 is an average benchmark, with no possessive. “My average” specifically changes it into Saber’s personal historical average.
The supplied raw English shows mutually exclusive classic/Realta branches. Printing both “a bluff” and “confidence or boasting” is flattening debris, not the translation as rendered in either branch.
The script contains a line/dash command between the two occurrences, producing a stammer such as “I—I,” not the fused word “II.”
In Saber’s claim that other purposes are extraneous to a Servant’s role, “useless” is a defensible contextual rendering of 余分なだけ. The alleged tonal difference is not a demonstrable factual error.
The raw script places a line/dash command between “this” and “Saber.” Their apparent fusion is an extraction artifact rather than rendered prose.
The Japanese says Saber should possess enjoyment of her own. The English instead makes Shirou the controlling agent who must make her perform an enjoyable activity.
はず expresses Shirou’s prior expectation that he had no interest in her identity. “Shouldn’t have been interested” reads as a judgment that such interest was improper, changing his self-reflection.
A supplied line/dash command separates “Huh” from “you.” “Huhyou” is produced only by command stripping.
“Cut” is a contextually supported specification of how Berserker felled Shirou and does not contradict 打ち倒されました. The supplied Original candidate even uses 両断されました, further precluding this accusation.
The English reads as Saber asking Shirou to understand something. The Japanese says she must ask the question so that she can understand Shirou as a person.
“I understood that I’d be killed” is an unqualified prediction and naturally conveys certainty. The omission of the separate intensifier 絶対 does not materially weaken the premise.
その後の事なんて知らない can idiomatically mean that he did not care what happened afterward. The surrounding priority statements support the English rather than limiting it to mere inattention.
Here 自然に means spontaneously or without deliberation. “Automatically” is a defensible paraphrase of that involuntary response, and Shirou’s mirrored denial remains coherent.
A supplied line/dash command follows “So.” The apparent “Soif” fusion is an extraction artifact.
心にもない means words Shirou does not mean. “Heartless words” instead characterizes them as cruel or unfeeling and misses their insincerity.
道を間違えなければ warns against taking the wrong path. “Do not make any mistakes” changes that directional or ethical warning into general errorlessness.
“Called as cowardice” is ungrammatical in this passive construction; standard English requires “called cowardice.”
“Must be” is an ordinary epistemic inference, not a direct statement of witnessed fact. Although stronger than the terse のか, it preserves Shirou’s inferential stance.
The English omits 味気ない, removing the explicit barrenness or dreariness of the room from the scene’s closing image.
The Japanese merely says bedtime arrived without either conversation occurring. “It’s not like I need to talk” invents Shirou’s judgment that conversation was unnecessary.
深夜 is late or deep night, confirmed by the following eleven-o’clock statement. “Night falls” ordinarily describes the onset of evening.
“On my side” over-specifies 横になった, but the posture is incidental and compatible with lying down. It does not create a material narrative error.
The Japanese itself contains an unfinished complaint followed by the complete rhetorical question. The English mirrors that restart rather than duplicating a completed question.
針のむしろ is a figurative expression for an intolerably uncomfortable situation. “This hell” is a natural, if less image-specific, idiomatic paraphrase rather than a factual error.
The raw English identifies “retreat” and “retreat to my usual place” as mutually exclusive edition branches. Their apparent duplication is caused by flattening those branches.
Shirou first concludes that Saber is surprisingly insensitive, then immediately considers deep sleep as an alternative. “Must be … Or maybe” reproduces that reconsideration.
In English, “must be A or B” scopes the inference over the unresolved alternatives; it does not necessarily certify A. The uncertainty of the Japanese remains intelligible.
A bandage around the hand necessarily covers the palm area, and the next page still identifies the seal on the back of the hand. This mild generalization does not materially alter its placement.
右腕 means the right arm, not the right hand. The English relocates Rin’s Command Spell to a different body part.
The Japanese opening is itself a deliberate noun fragment whose thought is completed by the following sentence. Reproducing that literary fragment is not a translation error.
The English preserves the cold draft as the stimulus for waking. Omitting the incidental contact point “cheek” is ordinary compression, not a material change.
体を起こす means to sit or raise oneself up. “Pick my body up” is markedly nonidiomatic and suggests lifting the body as a separate object.
The raw script contains a line/dash command between “routine” and “after.” The fused form is an extraction artifact.
面倒になった can naturally mean he could not be bothered to return. “Too lazy” is a colloquial contextual rendering of that momentary reluctance, not necessarily a global character judgment.

The failure itself remains explicit in “failed to strengthen,” so that part of the accusation is false. A narrower error survives: 破片 are broken fragments to be cleared away, not intact “things” to straighten up.
深山町 names Miyama Town, a district within Fuyuki. Expanding it to all of Fuyuki City changes the stated geography.
The frost and lawn passage is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its omission from base and all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence that mirror moon inserted it.
抜け出す means to slip, sneak, or get out, and “escaped the room” is a plausible figurative rendering in this context. It does not require literal confinement.
“Must be” marks an inference rather than an observed fact, and the next Japanese sentence itself proceeds on the proposed explanation. The confidence difference is insufficient for a material error.
The grammatical complaint survives: standard English is “scolded for,” not “scolded at for.” The separate claim that “shouldn’t” materially overstates the tentative Japanese is not established.
脱衣所 is the changing or dressing room, while the next page separately mentions a 洗面所 for merely washing one’s face. Rendering both as “bathroom” erases the distinction governing Shirou’s directions.

The governing Original candidate explicitly contains Rin disappearing into the hallway simultaneously with the bell. Its absence from the later Japanese witnesses is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
身内 can denote one’s own close circle or insiders, so “friends” is defensible here. The following page separately preserves Sakura’s family-like status and possession of a key.

Across the complete page, “She never listens, even though I keep telling her she doesn’t need to ring” already preserves Sakura’s repeated bell habit. The next sentence then retains her announcement before entering.

Read with the preceding “There…,” the English deliberately continues the Japanese’s interrupted tableau around Sakura’s interjected “Huh?” It is awkward VN presentation, but the two figures and their actions remain intelligible.

“At the door” is a reasonable natural rendering of Sakura’s position in the genkan. The adjacent lines still preserve Rin looking down and Sakura looking up, so the claimed spatial relation is not lost.
ように expressly gives the manner “as if looking down on Sakura.” The English closely follows that wording; insisting on an unqualified physical action overstates the Japanese.
The exchange visibly occurs in the morning, so “surprised you” retains the apology’s substance without restating the already established time. This is nonmaterial compression.
Both “Suddenly” and the description of Sakura’s small but clear voice occur in the governing Original Japanese. Their absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference.
The raw script contains a line/dash command inside the response, so the fused “Uhhuh” is an extraction artifact rather than its intended rendered form.
The Japanese specifically challenges how Rin knew Sakura had been caring for Shirou. The English’s “it” instead refers most naturally to Sakura coming to the house, changing the fact under question.
小耳に挟む means to happen to hear something, often indirectly. “I heard about it before somewhere” plus “just a coincidence” preserves Rin’s vague, evasive hearsay claim sufficiently.
不機嫌そう describes visible displeasure or a bad mood, and 言い捨てる adds curt force. “With disappointment” substitutes a softer, different affect.
それなりに知っている can naturally mean knowing someone reasonably or fairly well, and “must mean” remains an explicitly inferential construction. The finding overstates the difference.
The Japanese only speculates that they may have had a good senior–junior relationship. “Must have had a friendship” strengthens that possibility and removes the explicitly hierarchical relationship.

The idiom humorously denotes behavior exceptionally unlike the person’s norm; “a special case” preserves that operative meaning. Loss of the source-language image is a localization preference, not a factual error.
“Perverse” can mean obstinately contrary, which is within the lexical range of 意固地 in this context. No sexual reading is required by the sentence.

In context, “the merciless Tohsaka” metonymically describes Rin as the giver of the merciless explanation just mentioned. It is broader in form but does not materially change Shirou’s criticism of her conduct.

The declaration is present in the governing Original edition; its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference. The repeated “now” results from flattening mutually exclusive script branches, not from the translation itself.
The English conveys only an ordinary sigh and omits the conspicuous, deliberately pointed manner expressed by これみよがしに.
The supplied raw script places a line-dash command between “Sakura” and “oh”; “Sakuraoh” is an extraction artifact, not the rendered translation.
言動 includes Shirou’s speech and conduct, while 破綻している describes them as incoherent or breaking down. “Actions are a bit strange” omits the speech and substantially softens the diagnosis.
The raw English has a line-dash command between “Huh” and “am,” so the apparent fusion was produced by command stripping.
薄れている means the tension has diminished, not disappeared. The following surface-only qualification does not restore that lost degree distinction.
卵焼き is tamagoyaki, a rolled omelet, not fried eggs; the English names a different dish.
The allegedly inserted narration appears verbatim in the governing Original edition. It is merely commented out in the later base/all-ages witness.
“King” preserves the royal-aristocrat hyperbole adequately in context; narrowing the broad expression 王侯貴族 is not a material factual change.
The narration that all three bow in their respective manners before eating is wholly absent from the English.
The raw English retains escalating line-length commands before “Gah.” Their disappearance from the flattened witness is an extraction artifact, so the translation did not replace the silence.
The English renders Shirou forcing himself to accept the excuse but omits that he then shovels down his food.
“Sits Japanese-style” is vague and dated, but in this domestic seating context it defensibly conveys 正座; the accusation does not establish a material mistranslation.

“The two’s greetings” is awkward but grammatically possible, and “strange unison” conveys the conspicuous synchronicity. The stronger comic wording is a stylistic refinement, not a demonstrable material error.
飲み干す means Taiga drains or finishes the soup; “takes a sip” reverses the scale and changes the delayed-reaction timing.
風上 specifically places Sakura upwind/on the safe upstream side. “The other side” substitutes an unspecified spatial relationship and loses why she avoids the spill.
The Japanese identifies a hotpot containing simmered tsukune; “food cooked in pot” removes both the dish type and its salient ingredient.
The raw English contains a line-dash command between “me” and “hey.” The apparent compound is caused by stripping that command.
The English omits 同い年, although Taiga’s objection specifically concerns Shirou housing a girl his own age.
“It’s not even funny” naturally conveys both that the joke is bad and that Taiga refuses to laugh at it. The accusation demands closer wording without showing a factual loss.
Tsukune is a formed meatball, commonly chicken but not merely “a piece of chicken”; the English also broadens the precise collar opening to the whole shirt.
“A hot one” conveys temperature but omits 必要以上に, the deliberately excessive-heating formulation that supplies the comic repetition.
Rin’s movement is present in the governing Original edition and only omitted/commented out in later witnesses; it is not unsupported translation content.
In context, “guardian” is a defensible English description of Taiga’s 教育係 role overseeing Shirou’s upbringing and conduct; the broader label does not materially change her asserted authority.
野生の勘 can naturally be rendered “instinct” or “natural instinct.” “Wild/animal instinct” would preserve more comic color, but its absence is not a material error.
寝首をかく is an idiom for attacking someone while vulnerable or off guard; demanding a literal sleeping throat-cut overstates the Japanese. “Get her” is loose but contextually defensible.
優等生 means a model or exemplary student, not merely someone “student-like.” The English loses the exceptional propriety that leaves Taiga unable to object.

Taiga’s deliberately indirect concern is precisely that something improper could happen between the boy and girl; “what could happen” is normal English explicitation, reinforced by her next reference to a 間違い.
“Things to follow up” is loose, but it can denote unresolved points requiring challenge or examination. The surrounding statement that Rin can handle them preserves the argumentative sense.
“Officially has citizenship in my house” plainly remains a household metaphor; “officially” reasonably conveys 晴れて and does not turn it into a literal legal claim.
“Look after us” can naturally mean supervise or keep watch over the arrangement. Context prevents it from being read merely as domestic caretaking.
“Consider me necessary” is stiff English, but it expresses the requested mental recognition of needing Saber. The Japanese does not explicitly say to call aloud or send a formal signal.
異状 is an abnormality or unusual condition in the Master, not “the Master’s danger.” The substitution narrows what Saber senses and makes the preceding danger condition circular.
The Japanese coordinates two actions by Sakura: she cleaned up breakfast and then waited for Shirou. The English instead makes her wait for Shirou to perform the cleanup.
必要ないモノ is recoverably the key under discussion, and English “anything unnecessary” is a normal context-dependent paraphrase rather than a claim about all of Shirou’s conduct.
The omitted ふん would add an audible huff, but the irritated dialogue and face-turn already communicate her reaction. This is minor tonal compression, not a material error.
味がある can mean having character, appeal, or an interesting quality. “Interesting” is within its defensible lexical range in this context.
してもらわないと itself frames Shirou as needing to bring about Sakura’s cooperation. “Make Tohsaka and Sakura be friends” is clumsy but a defensible relational paraphrase, not demonstrably coercive.
The narrator sentence appears in the governing Original edition and is merely commented out in the base/all-ages scripts. It is therefore not an unsupported insertion.
The surrounding references to hair, wrinkles, and dark circles establish that Rin is asking whether she looks strange. “Acting weird” incorrectly changes the concern to behavior.
The supplied English script uses mutually exclusive edition branches for “sleep” and “sleep in an unfamiliar place.” Their simultaneous appearance is branch flattening, not the rendered line.
“This school thing” makes “been here for ten years” reasonably refer to schooling as an institution, not necessarily ten years at this particular campus. The alleged false claim is not established.
The English is awkward, but its incredulous question still clearly says Rin casually ignored the compliment. The infelicity does not create a material accuracy error.
“Coming through the students” omits that Shinji contemptuously treats them as obstructions and physically pushes them aside.
The fragmentation mirrors the Japanese construction, where それを precedes an interrupting greeting and 掴んで止めて follows it. The restraint and greeting remain understandable as simultaneous.
The raw script places a dash command after “You,” so “YouI” is a command-stripping artifact rather than a missing boundary in the translation.
In ordinary English, “hurt himself” commonly means that someone became injured through his own actions; it does not necessarily imply deliberate self-injury and adequately conveys Shinji’s dismissal.

The English source contains mutually exclusive edition branches, and the supplied raw Original witness itself uses 親なし. Printing both variants is a flattened-data artifact, while parentlessness is supported by the Original edition.
強引に連れて行こう naturally implies physically seizing Sakura in order to take her along. “Tries to grab Sakura forcefully” explicates that immediate action, even though “drag away” would be more precise.
“Sorry for eavesdropping” is a conventional pragmatic rendering of admitting 黙って聞いていたんだけど and can be read as Rin’s pointed, insincere politeness. It does not demonstrably contradict her stance.
The raw English places a line-dash command between “Huh” and “Toh…saka”; stripping it produces the apparent fusion.

The full phrase defines the degree of acquaintance by their expected shared commutes. “I know him well enough that…” is a natural restructuring, especially after the preceding sentence already calls both parties acquaintances.
“I must be imagining it” is a normal English expression of the narrator’s self-questioning inference and does not erase the uncertainty inherent in imagining.

“We’re detached now” is nonidiomatic, but the next sentence still conveys Shinji’s claim that using Shirou as an approach offers Rin little benefit. The manipulation direction is implicit in both languages.
The raw English includes a line-dash command between “Uh” and “shut up.” The apparent fusion results from stripping that command.
“Glares” already denotes an angry, hostile look. 忌々しそうに adds resentment, but omitting that adverb is not a material change here.
The lowered-head narration appears in the governing Original edition and was only commented out in later Japanese scripts. It is not an English insertion.
“My mind went up a gear” is awkward but intelligible English and preserves the mental gear-shift metaphor. The missing crispness of スパッと is stylistic rather than materially inaccurate.
The raw English contains a line-dash command between “Ah” and “yes,” making “Ahyes” an extraction artifact.
English epistemic “must” explicitly marks an inference rather than an observed fact, closely matching the narrator’s 安心したのか inference.
“Someday” naturally expresses the unspecified future occasion denoted by 何かの拍子で, while “I know” preserves 目に見えてる certainty. “Get to know each other better” can describe renewed deepening.
The raw English uses a line-dash command between “Yes” and “please”; command stripping creates the apparent fused word.
The narrator line is present in the governing Original edition and only commented out in base/all-ages. Its inclusion is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
Although traditional edited usage prefers “fewer people,” “less people” is widespread and fully intelligible contemporary English. This prescriptive preference is not a translation-accuracy error.
The English retains the operative contrast between a normally crowded rooftop and its emptiness in winter cold. Omitting the explicit summer label is harmless contextual compression.
“Shivering under cover” conveys both visible cold and shelter behind an obstruction. “Huddled” would be closer to 縮こまって, but the supplied rendering is defensible.
The English omits that the coffee is canned and explicitly hot, but coffee offered to someone shivering in winter is naturally understood as hot. The container detail is not material to the action.
The Japanese has Shirou enter the sheltered area while handing Rin the coffee. “Pass Tohsaka” instead says he walks past her and omits that simultaneous movement into cover.
Plural “milk teas” can denote milk-tea drinks or varieties and does not materially alter Rin’s stated preference, though singular would be more idiomatic here.
The English is stiff but preserves the mock-ranking joke: her gratitude’s value goes down for any other drink. The accusation identifies style, not a factual mistranslation.
呆れた denotes exasperation, weary disbelief, or being appalled; “amazed” instead presents surprise and changes Rin’s reaction.
“Heard ... too many times” naturally conveys the meaning of the idiom. Preserving the bodily callus image is a stylistic option, not required for accuracy.
Although the conditional is not explicit, “will ... encircle” already presents the coverage as prospective rather than current, and activation is clear from the surrounding explanation.
“Meat” is awkward for human flesh but remains within the literal range of 肉. This is a register preference, not a demonstrable change of substance.
“Felt a bit strange” is a defensible natural paraphrase for experiencing an indistinct 違和感. Japanese commonly presents such a sensation through the experiencer.
The supplied raw script has “So[line3]there’s”; stripping the line/dash command produces the apparent fusion. This is an extraction artifact, not established translation text.
意識 is awareness or consciousness, not feelings. The English changes Shirou’s attention snapping into focus into an emotional state and is also unnatural English.
In context, “knowledge of magic” can naturally denote knowledge of magecraft; it does not itself identify this as True Magic. The terminology accusation is not established by this sentence.
“Intimate” can mean closely acquainted or maintaining close relations without romantic force. It is slightly awkward but within the lexical range of 懇意.
“Alienated himself from the Association” can mean deliberately distancing or separating himself from it and is defensible for 離反 in this lone-wolf context.
English “must have” functions epistemically here, expressing Rin’s reconstruction rather than certainty. It does not necessarily harden だろう into fact.
The raw English is “W[line3]What,” so the apparent “WWhat” results from a stripped line/dash command representing the stammer.
一人前 can denote becoming mature, fully capable, or full-fledged. In the surrounding magus discussion, “when you mature” can contextually mean becoming competent.
The English preserves that he supposedly lived long but omits Rin’s more specific claim that he completed his natural allotted lifespan, an important part of her stated rationale.
The English actually distinguishes 魔法 as “sorcery” from the surrounding “magus/magic” vocabulary. The supplied witnesses do not establish that this terminology collapses the distinction.
“This must be the actions” mismatches a singular subject with a plural complement. The Japanese simply attributes this particular field to a Servant’s work.
“Rules of humanity” is awkward but can naturally mean the moral rules governing human conduct, which is the contrast Rin draws with Holy Grail War rules.
In context, comprehending Rin’s words is a defensible paraphrase of forming a clear mental conception, and the following page explicitly retains Shirou’s imagining of the worst case.
基点 can be rendered as a source, base point, or anchor of a field. “Sources” conveys the multiple points; the later singular is awkward but does not prove the technical sense was lost.

張られない asks whether the field will not be laid or established, whereas “won’t be activated” silently corrects Shirou. Rin’s next statement expressly distinguishes the already-laid field from its later activation.
“Only optimism” functions here as “mere wishful thinking” and adequately conveys that the hope is convenient and unsupported.
The English closely follows 黙ってても: the field can activate even if the Master remains inactive. The accusation instead inserts an unsupported claim that the enemy personally chooses the moment.

The supplied raw English contains mutually exclusive conditional variants. Their simultaneous appearance in the flattened page is extraction debris, not an established defect in either active translation branch.
The raw text is “and[line2]defeat”; removing the line/dash command creates “anddefeat.” This is an extraction artifact rather than a missing space in the translation.
“The end of school homeroom ends” redundantly makes “end” both the event and verb, producing plainly malformed English.
早いうちに means soon or at an early opportunity, and Shirou immediately proceeds to Sakura’s classroom. “Now” is contextually justified explicitation.

The following sentence establishes that Shirou remains in the hallway and looks into the classroom. Calling the destination the first-year hallway is a defensible contextual rendering of arriving outside the first-year classroom.
The preceding clause says Shirou expected Sakura to be depressed, so “but she seems okay” retains the comparison with that expectation by ordinary English implication.
The apology occurs before Shirou’s still-future departure, so “before I went home” has the wrong tense and conflicts with the scene’s chronology.
The raw English contains “Eh[line3]Senpai,” with the command marking the interrupted delivery. Its removal creates the apparent fusion.
Japanese leaves the possessor of 事情 implicit. Given that Shirou is explaining why Rin must lodge with him, “the circumstances you’re in” is a reasonable contextual resolution.
“And she lets out a sigh” has a subject and finite verb and is not a sentence fragment. The line break after Sakura’s quoted words does not create a factual translation error.
おかしなの refers to the anomalous person included in Shirou’s comic list. “Mixed into that expression” supplies a misleading abstract or facial referent instead of recognizing the odd listed student.
“I’m caught” accurately preserves Shirou’s figurative 捕まってしまった, while the next sentence explicitly retains his voluntary decision to stop because being caught there is safer.
“Really pissed” is coarse but plausible in Shirou’s casual internal voice, and “really” can carry the force of the comic repetition. This is register preference rather than factual error.
The raw English is “Uh[line3]no”; stripping the line/dash command produces “Uhno.” The apparent fusion is not reliable translation evidence.
“Encircle” can mean surround or encompass an area, especially for a boundary field. The adjacent description of humans inside it prevents a reasonable reading limited solely to the perimeter.
Although “flesh” would be more idiomatic for human bodies, “meat” remains a literal rendering of 肉 and does not materially alter what the field takes.
“Felt a bit strange” is a defensible English rendering of experiencing an indistinct 違和感; the Japanese does not require the sensation to be externalized.
The supplied raw English reads “So[line3]there’s.” The apparent fused word results from flattening the line/dash command.

The allegedly inserted sentence is present in originalJa and in the supplied Original script candidate. Its absence from the active base/all-ages branch is an edition difference, not unsupported Original-edition content.
Original Japanese contains Shirou’s interrupted vocal reaction な, while the English leaves only empty quotation marks. This is a genuine omission rather than ordinary punctuation handling.
“Comprehend” reasonably paraphrases Shirou’s effort to form a clear conception, and the next sentence still describes him imagining the worst case and engraving that image within himself.
“Sources” is within the possible functional range of 結界の基点 and retains their plurality. “Anchor points” would be clearer terminology, but it is not the only accurate rendering.

Japanese has Shirou ask whether the field will not be laid, despite its activation having just been discussed. Replacing this with “will not be activated” removes the confusion corrected by Rin’s next answer.
In this contrast, “only optimism” naturally means mere optimistic wishful thinking and adequately conveys Rin’s dismissal of a convenient hope.
“Even if he does nothing” directly renders 黙ってても. The claim that Japanese instead says he waits until personally choosing activation is not supported by this sentence.
野放しにしておけない states that the threat cannot be left unchecked or at large. “Can’t forgive” changes the intended practical need to stop the culprit into Shirou’s personal moral attitude.
む is an ambiguous grunt that can express reluctance, chagrin, or mild irritation. “Geez” is loose but contextually defensible rather than demonstrably false.
“Before the sun goes down” is ordinary English for returning by sunset. Treating the instantaneous endpoint as an excluded extra interval is excessive precision not demanded by the scene.
校庭 is the schoolyard or grounds, not the school building, and 早足 explicitly says Shirou leaves at a quick pace. The English changes the location and omits that motion detail.
“I’ve forgot” is ungrammatical; the required participle is “forgotten.” This mars an otherwise clear reflective sentence.
The gaze action appears verbatim in originalJa and the supplied Original script. It is absent only from the base/all-ages edition, so it is not unsupported in this Original-edition comparator.
“Crumbles on me” is malformed or highly unnatural English for a sense of reality collapsing, and it poorly expresses the clean, complete collapse emphasized by キレイさっぱり.

The surprise-transfer conjecture is expressly present in originalJa and the Original script. Its omission from base/all-ages marks an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion against Original.
“When I will need it the most” is an awkward, nonstandard doubled-future construction here. The Japanese straightforwardly warns that her movement will be sluggish at the crucial moment.
生半可な冗談 describes a casual, inadequate, or half-measure joke failing with Saber. “Doesn’t get normal jokes” generalizes this into a broad deficiency in her ability to understand ordinary humor.
Japanese tentatively infers an altar made to resemble or function as a temple. “An altar chosen as a temple” tangles that relation, while “must” also removes おそらく’s explicit uncertainty.
Japanese omits the unknown Master’s gender, but resolving an animate singular referent with generic “he” was a normal English expedient and does not materially alter this reasoning passage.
止めさせよう is causative: Shirou proposes finding the Master and making that person stop the field. “Let’s ... stop the boundary field” instead assigns the stopping action directly to Shirou and Saber.
昼間 means the daytime or daylight hours, not specifically lunch. The English materially narrows Shirou’s planned search period.

“End the conversation” is a loose but recognizable rendering of breaking the discussion’s flow. In this casual internal narration, the difference from “derail” or “interrupt” is not a demonstrable material error.
The Japanese explicitly completes the legend by saying the internal thorns kill the pierced target. The English mentions the thorns but omits that lethal result.

At this stage Japanese says every tradition retains a passage about piercing the heart; it does not yet say the lance always succeeds. Adding “always” prematurely imports the later guaranteed-function conclusion.
“Must be X or Y” remains an epistemic disjunction: Saber asserts that one of two mechanisms likely applies without deciding which. This is compatible with the Japanese alternatives.
一対一 specifies the number of combatants—one-on-one combat. “Hand-to-hand” instead specifies fighting range and loses the engagement condition reiterated later.
A genuine grammar defect survives: “great amount” requires an article (“a great amount”). The capitalization complaint is merely a consistency/style issue and need not be part of the finding.
堅実に describes securing victories steadily or reliably. “Can definitely win” strengthens that tactical reliability into an unconditional guarantee.
“Heartless” is a standard lexical rendering of 非情 meaning ruthless or merciless. Any broader emotional connotation is insufficient to make the translation factually wrong here.
The English is grammatically defective: singular “heart” requires a determiner here (“through the heart” or “through my heart”).

“Saber’s presence” conveys the ruby’s intended referent, while the following sentence preserves the distinction between sensing her beforehand and freezing upon seeing her. Preserving both surface text and ruby would be optional presentation fidelity, not a demonstrable mistranslation.
In context this is Saber’s opening surprise attack, so “first blow” is a defensible explicitation of 一撃 rather than unsupported chronology.
The translation retains only “protecting him” and omits Saber’s preceding suggestion of fondness or favorable feeling, which leads directly into her anxious question about Shirou preferring Archer.

The immediately following contrast between close and ranged combat makes the intended kind of compatibility unmistakable. “Our compatibility” is a locally clarified paraphrase, not a material broadening.
多くの制約 denotes multiple restrictions affecting Saber’s condition or power. Singular “a burden on you” instead suggests a generic hardship and loses that concrete plurality.

追い詰める means driving or pressing Berserker into a corner, not necessarily defeating him. “Beat” erases Saber’s escalation from difficulty defeating him to possibly being unable even to pressure him that far.
“Magic” is an ordinary and contextually intelligible translation of 魔術. Requiring the later fandom term “magecraft” is terminology preference, not an error established by this Japanese.

Although awkward, the English still says the armor is close to a magical theoretical concept called a conceptual weapon. The alleged technical-category failure is not substantial enough to establish a material mistranslation.

In the conditional identification of Berserker as a great Greek hero, その能力 can collectively denote his capabilities, and ほぼ supports “mostly/nearly.” The Japanese does not unambiguously restrict this sentence to the single defensive ability.
理 read ことわり means a principle, order, or governing law. “Refusal” is the wrong sense and obscures the contrast with physical law.

The divinity explanation is present in the governing Original Japanese even though it is commented out in the base/all-ages witness. Its presence in English therefore is not an unsupported restoration for this comparator.
撤退が大前提 states that retreat remains the fundamental premise of their plan. “Stay away from them for now” changes this into general temporary avoidance and does not preserve the tactical conclusion.
The plural subject “Noble Phantasms” incorrectly takes the singular verb “decides.”
The Japanese makes Berserker the subject protecting Illyasviel. The English makes Illyasviel protect Berserker, reversing the proposed strategy.
The standing action is explicitly present in the governing Original Japanese; its absence from the other editions does not make the English unsupported.
Sakura’s worried gaze appears explicitly in the governing Original Japanese. It is an edition difference, not an English insertion.

The narrower problem is that “fiery” adds fire not stated by the sound-symbolic ジャージャー or 派手な音. The line still conveys conspicuously noisy cooking, so it is not a wholesale misreading of the onomatopoeia.
The allegedly inserted rationale is present verbatim in the governing Original Japanese, though absent from the other editions.

The preceding sentence specifically says Shirou does not know what to talk about with Saber. In that immediate context, interpreting 苦手 as difficulty talking to or dealing conversationally with her is defensible.

ぼんやり is a minor delivery nuance, but “I say that and just stare at the clock” preserves his disengaged action and mood sufficiently. Treating this compression as a material error is preference policing.

腹が立つ can express anger, irritation, or annoyance. “Really annoying me” remains within its ordinary range, and the grammatical subject is the imagined scene of Saber eating alone, not necessarily Saber herself.
The English names the dumplings but drops both the incredulous 何を考えているのか and the comic image of a platter-sized “army,” removing demonstrable narrator voice and humor.
The Japanese describes an unfamiliar, elegant-looking meat-and-vegetable stir-fry as a whole. The English syntax instead makes the meat itself unfamiliar and elegant-looking.

“Salads on the side plates” plus “various follow-ups” conveys that supporting side dishes and details were provided. “Palate cleanser” would be clearer, but the accusation is principally stylistic rather than a material accuracy error.
“When I told that her no one…” has irreparably malformed word order; the intended indirect-object construction is not grammatical English.
“Live her life poking at holes” is an unintelligible literalization. 隙間を突く here jokes about Rin exploiting every available opening or neglected niche.
そっけなく can mean curtly, aloofly, or coldly. “Coldly” is somewhat strong but remains within its lexical range and does not necessarily imply serious hostility.

The English compresses the conventional spoken greeting and accompanying bow into “Everyone bows and eats.” The communal start of the meal remains clear; demanding an explicit transliteration or equivalent is not a material accuracy correction.
The explicit comparison to Taiga as 先生 is absent. Rin is specifically pleased by Taiga’s characteristically straightforward reaction, not merely by an abstract honest response.
In English food contexts, “hot food” can refer to spicy food as well as temperature. The context supports the spicy reading, so the translation does not demonstrably change the meaning.
The English completely omits Shirou’s overtly comic characterization of Rin as crooked-natured, leaving only her triumphant expression.

手の内 means one’s hidden hand, cards, secrets, or capabilities. “Hide your potential” conveys the operative meaning in the cooking-as-tactics joke; loss of the metaphor is stylistic flattening, not a factual error.
The senior–junior relation is rendered in conspicuously malformed English, and 味方 means that Taiga is now on Rin’s side, not simply that they are friends.
“All of us eating right now” naturally describes the group eating together in the same situation. It does not reduce みんなで to unrelated simultaneity.
“I grab Saber’s hand and take her” is a natural compressed rendering of reaching the room while pulling her by the hand. The loss of まま’s explicit continuity does not establish a materially new grab.
The glare is expressly present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence of unsupported English content.
風雲急を告げる is an idiom for an abruptly looming crisis. “A sound of wind” literalizes 風 and loses the narrator’s mock-dramatic sound-effect joke.

In this context, asking the “purpose” or point of Taiga’s proposed test is a defensible pragmatic rendering of asking what 理屈 justifies it. The distinction is too slight to establish a material error.
少しは limits the degree of Taiga’s willingness or confidence—she can entrust Shirou to Saber to some extent. “Just for a bit” normally imposes a short duration instead.

The genuine loss is the marked, disparaging or playful 小手先 wording, which suggests superficial trickery or wordplay around the kendo strike. The English does still preserve 胴 as an attack to the body, so calling the whole strike generic is too broad.
