ヘンなの is a childish derogatory “weirdo/strange one,” not merely an unknown stranger. The English removes Taiga’s insult and comic tantrum voice.
The Japanese explicitly says Taiga shut herself in Kiritsugu’s room with Saber. Omitting Saber obscures who participated in the two-hour conversation.

なぜも何もない conventionally dismisses the demand for an elaborate explanation before giving the simple motive. “No reason. I just…” is clumsy but reproduces that rhetorical structure rather than inventing a contradictory motive.
“The stars are clear” generalizes 星座 and compresses 見渡せた, but it preserves the essential clear winter-sky image. The alleged loss is not material enough to sustain an accuracy finding.
呆れる ranges from exasperation and appalled disbelief to disgust. “Disgusted with me” is stronger than ideal here but remains lexically possible; the claim of a categorical distortion is overstated.
“Magic” is a normal translation of 魔術. This page alone does not require the specialized English label “magecraft,” so the accusation enforces terminology preference.

In context, 小さな自分を積んでいく describes building up the inadequate self through accumulated training. “Refine myself” naturally conveys that practical meaning; loss of the concrete metaphor is not a demonstrable material error.

“Breakfast table” can metonymically mean the meal or social scene around the table. Though slightly awkward, “a complicated breakfast table” communicates the unusually complicated arrangement rather than asserting complex furniture.
Sakura is speaking to Saber, so English “you” is Saber. The list therefore still contains exactly Saber, Tohsaka, and Sakura; no participant disappears.

“Sakura’s” remains an English possessive ellipsis whose omitted noun must be inferred, just as the Japanese leaves the bodily reference unstated. The preceding dialogue already explicitly mentions Sakura’s chest, so this is not unsupported resolution.

Without “on,” the clause is grammatically possible but means something moving in front of him, not what is unfolding there. The surviving issue is semantic and idiomatic mistranslation, not simply a missing-preposition grammar error.
The raw script shows mutually exclusive conditional branches: the player receives either “She” or “Well, she,” not both. The apparent stray word is a flattened-extraction artifact.
The raw English likewise contains mutually exclusive “a” and “another” branches. “A another” exists only in the flattened audit representation, not in an active Original-edition line.

The second unit is a conversational explanatory fragment following “It’s that… right?” Such fragments are normal in dialogue and accurately enumerate people losing consciousness, becoming comatose, and being hospitalized.

The sentence is grammatically structured, but “danger in the victims’ lives” is the wrong English collocation; it should express danger to their lives or say their lives are not in danger. The surviving issue is idiomatic wording, not malformed grammar.

命 can denote life or vitality, and “absorbing half of their lives” is a literal, contextually interpretable rendering. The following page explicitly identifies the harvested energy as life force, so the wording does not demonstrably assert lost lifespan.

A genuine comma splice joins “the speed is slower” to “it doesn’t break…” The phrase “rules of magi” is awkward but still intelligibly denotes rules applying to magi, so the broader governing-relation accusation should be narrowed.
大師父 is Rin’s grand-teacher or great master, and 書庫 is a library/archive. “The master’s room” loses both the person’s title and the kind of place she means to search.
ウツボカズラ specifically denotes a pitcher plant, but a pitcher plant is an insectivorous plant and the following “lid” imagery retains the trap comparison. This is imprecision, not a material change.
本音 means a true feeling or inner motive left unspoken. “The aspect I didn’t say” is both opaque English and fails to convey the contrast between Shirou’s silence and his exposed inner concern.

The English paraphrases the proverb’s operative meaning: Shirou has the relevant aptitude, so Rin assigns him that part. Losing the proverbial wording is a voice tradeoff, not a material mistranslation.
“Unpopular places” can mean places people rarely frequent, so that lexical accusation is overstated. The English does, however, omit the corridor dead end from the list.
“Thick wind” is wooden English, but it directly conveys 濃密な風, and the surrounding suffocation and nausea remain explicit. This is chiefly a fluency complaint.

“Basis point” is an inappropriate established English term for 基点 here; an anchor or base point is meant. The separate complaint about “sign” is not sound because 刻印 is explicitly read サイン in the ruby.
The source assigns the mark a binding or enclosing function, whereas “constructing the boundary field” makes it the agent creating the whole field.
水を差す means to dampen or spoil someone’s enthusiasm. “Alienate me” instead describes damage to the interpersonal relationship.
警戒する is being wary or on guard, not successfully remaining safe. The English changes a mental stance into an outcome.

Although Japanese uses the nonpast 見えない, English narrative backshift to “couldn’t see” is defensible, and the next sentence makes clear that this explains Shinji’s present mistake. It does not establish a one-time missed sighting.
The Japanese explicitly says neither Shinji nor Shirou will get off lightly. “It’ll be no good” removes both affected people and substantially weakens the threatened consequences.

Read with the preceding line, this completes “There is Shinji sitting in a chair, and a figure…”. The page break and capitalization are presentationally awkward, but the alleged standalone fragment ignores the full construction.

The supplied Original-edition witness has 舐めるよう, literally a licking-like motion, while the base/all-ages text has 撫でるよう. The mature English simile reflects an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
冷たい applied to a person can denote emotional coldness, so “coldhearted” is within its lexical range. The following English sentence still contrasts Rider’s “coldness.”
光 is light, physical or symbolic. “Lightness” instead denotes low weight or levity and is a clear lexical misreading.
信用できる means someone trustworthy. “Someone I know” reduces that asserted trust to mere acquaintance, altering Shinji’s appeal.
“Magic” is a conventional English rendering of 魔術 in ordinary dialogue. Insisting on “magecraft” here is terminology preference rather than a demonstrable error on this page.
“We’re the same” is a normal contextual paraphrase of 似たもの同士, meaning people in the same situation. The preceding conditional remains explicit.
“Knows magic” does lose the specific claim that Sakura received instruction. The additional objection to using “magic” for 魔術 is terminology policing and should be removed.
Both 枯れた一族 and “we’re dead” are figurative descriptions of a lineage whose magical capacity has died out. The following explanation prevents a literal-extinction reading.
減っていって describes generational decline, but does not itself state a numeric “circuit count.” “Faded” is imprecise yet conveys the inherited capacity’s gradual disappearance.
Rendering 魔術 as “magic” is an acceptable terminology choice here and does not change the stated fact that the family continues studying it.

先代 points most directly to the preceding head or generation, but in this context the instruction is inherited family teaching. “Previous generations” is a harmless broadening, not a material factual change.
The intended transmission within the family requires “passed down in/through the family.” Omitting the preposition leaves a genuinely malformed construction.
“Knowledge of magic” accurately conveys 魔術の知識. Requiring “magecraft” is a glossary preference, not an independently demonstrable error.
“One” can grammatically stand for “one person,” and the next sentence identifies that one as the eldest son. The recipient construction is awkward but not incomplete.

Despite awkward wording, the English retains the stated consolidation of ten arts into one crystal, its preservation, and the strengthening of the bloodline. The accusation overstates the semantic loss.
In the surrounding explanation of exclusive inheritance, “don’t make exceptions even for family” is a natural paraphrase of not distributing the secret art cheaply even to blood relatives.
“Teach magic only to the heir” conveys the inheritance rule. The objection rests solely on preferring “magecraft” as standardized terminology.
“Given out for adoption” is awkward but intelligible English for a child being sent away as an adoptee. The passive does not erase the family’s deliberate policy in context.
“Thank God” is a conventional English exclamation of relief and does not necessarily assert religious belief. It naturally explicitates 良かった rather than materially changing the event.
A “peaceful world without magic” defensibly paraphrases an everyday life untouched by magic. The shift from 日常 to “world” is stylistic and does not change Shirou’s protective wish.

The supplied Original witness says 殺し合いを強制される, directly supporting the mature branch’s killing language; base/all-ages instead has 戦い. “Without reason” is also a defensible rendering of acting without understanding why.
“Not experienced with magic” conveys 魔術には疎い. The accusation depends only on imposing “magecraft” terminology.

English normally requires an explicit pronoun, and “him” is ordinary contextual explicitation. Epistemic “must be” remains a conjecture matching the rhetorical じゃないの, rather than asserting proven fact.
The source repeatedly identifies Shinji alone as undetectable. “We’re people” invents a plural group and changes the claim’s subject.

The ruby explicitly directs the reader to understand the phrase as “Master,” while the preceding English sentences already explain that Rin detects magical energy. The causal layer is not materially lost across the complete page.
In this combat context 叩く specifically means striking or attacking the threat. “Do something about it” removes the proposed aggressive action.
“The story on this morning’s news” is a natural metonym for the reported incident. The sentence remains readily understood as identifying the cause of those reported events.
“So ordered by Shinji” is stiff but grammatical: the participial phrase correctly modifies Rider, who was ordered and then approaches. It does not obscure agency.
In context, “has nothing to do with me” idiomatically disclaims Shinji’s responsibility once Shirou is outside. It does not require a literal denial that they know one another.
“Clean features” is slightly stiff but can describe neat, refined facial features and falls within the range of 清楚な顔立ち. The accusation is primarily stylistic.
The Japanese itself presents the image directly as a nominal metaphor, “a shrine maiden wet with blood.” English need not add “as if” to preserve its figurative status in this descriptive context.

The supplied raw script shows control commands splitting “curiosity” at the intended comic interruption. The joined “curiosithey” is a command-stripping/extraction artifact expressly covered by the caveat, not translation corruption.
淡々 can describe detached, indifferent, or dispassionate delivery. “Without interest” is an imperfect but defensible characterization, not an invented plot fact.
English “must have” commonly marks an inference rather than certainty. It fits Shirou’s tentative deduction from おかしかったのか.

人が好い carries a naïve or overly trusting nuance that “good person” softens into simple praise. However, “trying to have you on his side” adequately conveys Shinji’s attempt to win Shirou over, so that half should be dropped.
The English entirely omits 隙だらけ, Shirou’s completely unguarded state as he flees, removing the pointed contrast with Rider quietly watching him.

“An hour’s walk to the mountain” is an ordinary elliptical travel description conveying both duration and direction; the following sentence supplies the road and destination. The fragment is stylistic, not materially misleading.
The “Ever since…” fragment explicitly completes the preceding statement that Shirou has not visited recently. Read as continuous prose, the temporal relation is preserved.
“Overanxiety” is unidiomatic, but it still denotes excessive or needless worry and does not alter Shirou’s conclusion. This is a fluency issue rather than an accuracy error.

The sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese and only commented out or absent in the later witnesses. Because Original governs this comparator, the English is not an unsupported addition.
In this explicitly Buddhist context, 精進 can encompass religious self-discipline and purification. “Purify myself more” is a contextual adaptation, not a demonstrably different action.
The English omits Issei’s departing 喝 entirely, removing the emphatic punch line to his mock-ascetic performance.
The Japanese leaves the future addressee unstated, while the English specifies one woman. The subsequent scene has Shirou address both Rin and Saber, so singular “her” is unsupported and misleading.
じゃありません explicitly negates “the taste of the food.” The English removes the negation and makes Rin say the exact opposite.
The English omits the explicit five-person quantity, a concrete detail that establishes the scale of the rice and supports the ensuing excess-food joke.
かちゃかちゃ represents clattering dishes or utensils, not chewing. “Munch, munch” changes the audible action.
An おひつ is a rice tub or rice container, not a generic cooking pot. The wrong vessel weakens Shirou’s concrete correction of Saber’s “cask.”

Yuzu is a citrus fruit, so the hypernym is accurate; 油物 can denote oily or fried food, making “fried things” contextually possible. The wording is awkward but the claimed factual distortion is not established.
昨日今日やってきた人 dismisses a newcomer or recent arrival as an outsider. In Fuji-nee’s possessive outburst, “some stranger” is a defensible natural paraphrase rather than a literal claim of no acquaintance.
我関せず expressly depicts Saber eating as though the commotion has nothing to do with her. The English retains only the eating and loses that contrasted attitude.
The Japanese deliberately recasts Fuji-nee as a 野生の虎. Referring to that imagined animal as “it” sustains the joke rather than mistakenly literalizing it.
In a comparison between battle and peaceful life, “prefer” naturally expresses what Saber gives priority to. It does not necessarily imply enjoyment of violence.
不釣り合い means incongruous or ill-suited. “Is a disparate image” is opaque English and does not clearly convey Shirou’s belief that sword fighting is unfitting for the girl before him.
The Japanese explicitly says Shirou met both Rider and her Master. The English reports only meeting the Master, omitting one participant in the encounter.
呆れる can mean being appalled, amazed, or stunned by someone’s conduct; “stunned” is defensible in this angry context and does not necessarily reduce the criticism to mere surprise.

話を通す covers consulting someone, clearing a matter with them, or obtaining their prior understanding. “Ask you first” is a defensible contextual rendering, not demonstrably a change to unilateral permission.
The Japanese says the proposal was not worth bringing to Rin’s attention; “not something to debate” instead asserts that the matter allowed no discussion.

Because Rider is known to be female, “heroine” can simply be the gendered English counterpart of 英雄. Although potentially awkward or ambiguous, it does not demonstrably turn her into a narrative lead.
The supplied English and archived block open Rin’s quotation but never close it, so this is a genuine presentation error.

“A heroic spirit similar to them” conveys the operative correspondence expressed by それに近い霊殻, which the following wounded-person example immediately explains. Omitting the shell metaphor is not by itself a material error.
“An quick” uses the wrong indefinite article; it must be “a quick.”
深山 and 新都 are two areas within Fuyuki. Calling the former “Miyama City” falsely makes it a separate city and distorts the stated geography.
大魔術 can reasonably be rendered “great magic” in a translation that uses “magic” generically for 魔術. The wording is awkward, but the contrast with wasted magical energy remains intact.
Rendering 魔術 as “magic” is a defensible terminology choice unless the translation has committed to a distinct “magecraft” term; this sentence itself establishes no factual mistranslation.

The subsequent explanation identifies this as where the region’s vital flow runs down. “Fallen ley line” instead sounds like a damaged or morally fallen ley line and leaves the spatial meaning obscure.
Calling the land “sacred” to magi is a reasonable natural paraphrase of land comparable to a temple or sanctuary. It loses the metaphor’s concreteness but not a material proposition.
“Need only to intervene” is an accepted English construction, alongside “need only intervene”; the alleged grammatical prohibition is false.
鬼門 denotes the inauspicious direction or “demon gate” being sealed. “Sealing the ill-omened” supplies no intelligible object and obscures the religious-geographic mechanism.
法術師 are practitioners of supernatural or ritual arts, not healers. The English assigns an unrelated profession and makes the following explanation difficult to follow.

成仏させる commonly means enabling a spirit to pass on or find repose. “Let ghosts go to heaven” is culturally loose, but it communicates that function and is not demonstrably a material doctrinal claim here.
“Enlightened people” is defensible for 覚者, and “Buddhist powers” broadly conveys 神仏の力. The genuine error is “try”: 事を成す says they accomplish the task through that power.
丸め込む means winning over, manipulating, or hoodwinking someone. In context, “control them” can describe that manipulation without necessarily asserting supernatural domination.
文字通り explicitly invokes 鬼門 in its pointed literal or wordplay sense after the earlier discussion of sealing a 鬼門. “Dreadful place” removes that repeated occult concept altogether.
律する includes regulating, controlling, or restraining. “Power to command” is awkward but within that range, and the surrounding explanation makes clear that the subject is the boundary’s effect.
では結論を is an elliptical prompt to move from discussion to a conclusion. Asking for a plan is loose, but contextually defensible, especially since Saber immediately states that only one action remains.
侮る means to underestimate or look down on someone. “Insult me” instead grants permission for verbal abuse, changing the kind of negative judgment Rin accepts.
The supposedly restored action is present in the supplied Original Japanese; its absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The Japanese places Shirou himself opposite the hidden Master on the figurative scales. “Us, the intruders” changes singular 俺 into Shirou and Saber as a group.
緩やかな describes the road’s gentle grade or character, not a winding shape. The English substitutes a different physical feature.
“Leading up to the mountain” naturally describes ascent along it. The omission of the exact midpoint destination is imprecise but does not materially misstate the immediate scene.

The complete supplied Original page contains only the adverse wind and Saber’s warning. The claim about the place being worse than on a previous visit adds history and escalation unsupported by that witness.
Shirou is wondering whether Saber has some concern about the supposed watcher. “There must be something wrong about it” turns that open inference into an assertion about the watcher itself.
門番を下げた is transitive: an enemy deliberately withdrew the guard. Saying the watcher “would depart” makes the guard the departing agent and weakens the deliberate lure or concealment being analyzed.
“See their faces” is understandable English for encountering or identifying the opponent, while “nothing will happen until” loosely conveys 始まらない. The tactical meaning remains clear.
The Japanese itself uses 金の髪 as a visual, metonymic subject of 振り返る. “Her golden hair turns around” is stiff English but mirrors that deliberate image rather than inventing a different actor.
“Magic” is a defensible translation convention for 魔術. This terminology choice alone does not change Saber’s recognition of modern transference techniques.

The Japanese states that Saber kicks off and successfully grabs Shirou’s arm. The English changes arm to hand and presents the grasp only as the purpose of her charge, losing the completed contact before Rider intervenes.
Although ungainly, “sickness” can denote nausea and the comparison to becoming another living thing remains present. The bodily-transformation sensation is not actually omitted.

The supplied Original Japanese describes Shirou’s fingers becoming cold and his consciousness failing; it does not say that his body has no blood left. The mature English branch adds a different death sequence.
低能 primarily insults low intelligence or competence, but “weak abilities” remains within its broader lexical range and does not specifically assert combat ability. The accusation is too narrow.

The supplied raw Original-edition witness explicitly has the dagger cut off Shirou’s left arm. The Command-Spell version belongs to the later witnesses, so the English is an edition rendering rather than an unsupported alteration.
先延ばし means postponing the fight before it begins. “Prolonging a battle” instead means extending a battle already underway.
共倒れ means both parties going down together, and “both you and me defeated” conveys that outcome. The immediately following statement about being gruesomely killed preserves the lethal stakes.
Shirou concedes that he was unfair, albeit bitterly. Adding “if” makes the admission conditional and materially softens his stance in the argument.
The raw Original-edition witness contains the supposedly inactive description that nothing moves and all living things are deeply asleep. Its omission from later Japanese is an edition difference.

“Moonlight to illuminate” naturally conveys the moonlight as the town’s sole recourse in darkness, and “dark sea” retains the governing image. The lost depth and 寄る辺 metaphor are literary compression, not a demonstrable material error.
風が出る predicts or observes the wind beginning to rise. “There is some wind” changes onset into quantity and sits poorly with the explicit statement that the ground is windless.

The English omits the earlobe image but explicitly infers that Saber may hear the otherwise inaudible upper wind. The relevant perception is preserved, making this a stylistic compression rather than a material omission.
在り方を決定づける says the undefeated figure defines Saber’s mode of being. “Proves their existence” substitutes an unrelated claim about existence and introduces an incoherent plural pronoun.

The clear surviving error is the neuter “its” for Saber, whose feminine reference is explicit. “Acting on her master’s order” is narrower than代行する主の意思, but remains a defensible approximation of carrying out the Master’s will.
今宵 is specifically “tonight,” but “today” includes the current nocturnal period and does not change the sequence or outcome. This is minor temporal coloring, not a material error.

The Japanese says Shirou cannot relinquish his 甘さ—his softness, kindness, or naïveté. “Cannot fix his personality” instead labels his whole personality defective and changes relinquishment into repair.
関心はない directly permits “has no more interest.” Reading it specifically as disciplined redirection rather than emotional disinterest depends on context and is not required by the Japanese wording.
屠る is explicitly lethal—slaughtering or killing the enemy. “Defeat” removes that severity from the description of Saber’s battle intent.
中腹 places Ryuudou Temple partway up the mountain. “On top of it” directly relocates it to the summit.
とうの昔に expressly says the pollution occurred long ago. “Already contaminated” communicates a preexisting state but omits the stated historical remoteness.
駆け抜ける has an omitted subject and can describe either the traversed scenery or scenery streaming past. “She runs through the scene” is awkward but contextually defensible and preserves the movement.
The supposedly restored sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese and only absent from base and all-ages. It is therefore an Original-edition line, not unsupported content.
After the preposition “for,” standard English requires the object form “her,” not “she.”

“Fearful” can mean fear-inducing, and the English still distinguishes the man’s features from his weapon. The wording is clumsy, but the accusation of a materially blurred tactical distinction is overstated.
“A way to seize a certain kill” is nonidiomatic, but it still denotes a means of securing a guaranteed kill; the surrounding Saber-focused warning makes the threatened victim recoverable.

それ以上に means “more importantly/more than that,” comparing the positional disadvantage with the difficulty of judging the sword’s reach. “Above it” mistakenly turns that comparison into another spatial relation.
The narration explicitly says Saber needs to learn the samurai’s クラス. “Which Servant are you?” asks for individual identity instead of what kind or class of Servant he is.
In standard edited English, “expect” takes “you to make,” not “expect for you to make.” The supplied construction is a genuine usage error.
慶長 is the named Keichō era. “This large world” is a direct historical misreading and erases the period in which he was reputed peerless.

The Japanese first describes the legendary Sasaki as having been elevated as an extraordinary swordsman’s worthy rival, then says perhaps only the unrecorded foe who defeated him truly knew him. The English reallocates those roles and leaves the relation incoherent.
英霊 is the setting-specific class “Heroic Spirit,” distinct from the preceding 英雄. Rendering both as ordinary “hero” erases that classification.
In this courtesy context, “You have me” naturally expresses being put at an impasse or conceding the point; it need not mean military surrender or capture.
The Japanese explicitly says “this blade alone,” so the plural changes the referent. However, the English still conveys the central point that combat through weapons replaces verbal identification.
深く here intensifies how Saber resets her guard but does not uniquely establish the proposed “deep, committed guard.” Holding the sword close is a defensible physical realization of the stance.
The subject of 傷 is omitted. The direct address to Shirou supports his wounds, while the surrounding story also foregrounds Saber’s unhealed condition; the supplied page cannot decisively assign it.
“Buruma” is a transliteration of the Japanese costume term. It may be opaque localization, but it does not falsely identify the garment or demonstrably mistranslate the line.
“The few spotlights I have” is awkward but intelligibly renders Taiga’s scarce featured moments. The plural and possessive do not create a factual difference.
“There’s isn’t” contains two incompatible finite forms and is an objective grammatical error; the intended conclusion itself is clear from the Japanese.
“Thank God” is a conventional English expression of relief and need not assert religion. It naturally paraphrases 良かった, though it drops the repetition.
“A bit curious” accurately conveys the deliberately minimized degree in ミニマム気になる. Reproducing the conspicuous loanword is a stylistic option, not required for correctness.
カマクラ is itself an unexplained item in a costume list. “Kamakura style” remains comparably opaque; adding “style” merely makes it function naturally as a costume description.

The Japanese specifically invokes a production specification that was already issued or finalized. “A decision they’ve already made” preserves reversal but removes the concrete development-document joke.
In the explicit scenario-cutting joke, 上層部 means the higher-ups or upper management. “Commanders” introduces a military hierarchy not present in that production context.
狼藉者 is a mock-period “ruffian/scoundrel,” and そこになおれ orders the target to sit or kneel and face punishment. “Stay there, you disgrace” loses both the action and theatrical register.
The allegedly inserted symptoms occur verbatim in the supplied Original witness. Their absence from the later active Japanese is an edition/branch difference, not unsupported mirrorMoon content.

The supplied raw Original candidate itself contains the initial entry and a subsequent door-opening entry. The repetition therefore reflects Original text rather than an unsupported English duplication.
Although the later witnesses say 襖, the supplied raw Original candidate says 障子, matching the classic English branch. This is an edition-dependent architectural change.
The obedience complaint is explicitly present in the supplied Original Japanese and only commented out in the later base witness. It is not an English insertion for this comparator.
“Go down the hill with no brakes” can naturally mean descending without braking, just as ノーブレーキ does; it does not necessarily claim the bicycle lacks brakes.

The exact specification “more than five shaku” is omitted. The broader claim that the weapon’s exceptional length disappears is overstated because “longsword” and the surrounding passages still foreground its length.
疾風 ranges from swift wind to gale. “Hurricane” heightens the metaphor, but still supplies the intended violent-wind contrast with Saber’s lightning and is not a demonstrable factual mistranslation.

“Elastic tracks” is ungainly English, but elastic/supple and track/trajectory correspond to しなやか and 軌跡. The following page also explicitly supplies the curved-path contrast, so the mechanics are not lost.
“Go inside on him” is awkward but recognizable combat phrasing for closing inside an opponent’s reach. The sentence retains the tactical meaning of 懐に入る.

In context, “drive” can denote the force or committed impetus of Saber’s attack, reinforced by the remarks about her small, trained body. It is vague but defensible, not necessarily a personality trait.
The wording is awkward, but “There are no stances for that man” closely reflects 構えなどない, and the next sentence immediately explains that he can strike from any posture.
当たりだ can confirm that a guess or attempted contact was on target. “I am correct” awkwardly but defensibly expresses Assassin confirming the invisible blade’s position before measuring it.
The period creates rhetorical fragmentation, but “That…” transparently supplies the object of “Even Saber knows.” The realization and exclusive causal force of 偏に remain intact.
満足に…もいない means they have not exchanged blows fully or sufficiently, not that no exchange occurred. The English absolute contradicts the preceding repeated clashes.

“Fight off your sword” is poor phrasing, but the same passage already says “not locking blades” and then repeats that he cannot lock blades and compete in strength. The head-on-contact meaning remains explicit.

The Japanese itself uses the image of fighting with one’s sword still sheathed as an accusation of holding back. “Fighting with your sheath on” preserves that metaphor; it need not assert a literal conventional sheath.
頭上 literally denotes a position above, and the staircase context makes “being overhead” intelligible as higher ground. The English is awkward but does not establish suspension in the air.
それ refers naturally to Assassin’s warning that Saber will die unless she readies herself. “He’s telling the truth” is normal explicitation of Saber recognizing that warning as fact.

The supplied raw Original candidate contains exactly the charge and Assassin’s readying stance; it is commented out only in the later Japanese witness. This is an edition branch, not an unsupported insertion.

In a combat description, “speed overwhelming Saber” is a compact, contextually clear reference to surpassing her attack speed. The next page confirms she herself is not simply overwhelmed and can block it.
直感だけに任せて directly supports “trusts her instincts,” and 転がり落ちた supports rolling or tumbling down. The following page, also translated, supplies the uncontrolled desperation and absent breakfall.

“Spins her body” is not what 体を倒し says; Saber desperately drops or throws her body down. However, “frantically,” the rolling, and the preceding lack of a breakfall preserve rather than soften her desperation.
The English turns the account into merely thinking about hitting swallows and omits 身に付いた—the fact that he acquired or mastered the resulting technique.
“Apprehend” has a valid, if formal, concrete sense of catch or seize. In the surrounding sword-and-swallow explanation it does not plausibly mean intellectual understanding or police arrest.

“Determination is key to success” is a natural dynamic rendering of the proverb’s point that single-minded resolve overcomes the seemingly impossible. Omitting gods and demons is tonal compression, not factual reversal.

The English preserves both the written technical description and its Kischur Zelretch reading adjacently. Ruby typography is flattened, but the association remains recoverable and no technical term is mistranslated.

The base text identifies the circular trajectory, with 二の太刀 as its ruby reading. Rendering only “the second blow has to be slower” drops the longer curved path and makes simultaneous occurrence sound self-contradictory.
The English generic “battle someone” omits that this is the duel Assassin could never attain while alive, which is the stated reason his summoning becomes worthwhile.
殺し合い explicitly denotes a fight to the death, not merely a battle, and 我が秘剣 is one secret sword technique rather than plural secret attacks. Both distinctions shape Assassin’s enthusiasm.
ほとんどない allows the one narrow response named immediately afterward. “No possible counters” makes the limitation absolute and then contradicts the English sentence identifying a countermeasure.

木々 ordinarily means trees, not structural timbers. In the temple-mountain setting, “trees of the forest” is defensible; the accusation’s conversion into built gate timbers is not established by the Japanese.
一人や二人 is rhetorical, emphasizing how effortlessly humans could be blown away rather than establishing an important count. “A normal person” naturally makes the human-versus-Servant contrast explicit.

合間 can denote a moment or intervening interval. “In that instant” introduces what Saber does amid the wind and does not assert that the bounded field can last only an instant; the next sentence still says several minutes.

Although 戒め evokes binding or restraint, the clause defines the magic by its control of the wind. “Commanding magic” is awkward but conveys that controlling function rather than demonstrably reversing it.
The English omits the serpent-like idiom but accurately retains the wind’s imminent engulfing threat. This is loss of imagery, not a demonstrable material change in action or agency.
The supplied raw Original witness uses the conjectural 渦巻いているのか, matching “must be surrounding.” The assertive version belongs to the later branch; the flattened page displays both.
The causal thought continues into “that image flashes,” so “because” is not substantively stranded across the dramatic break. Only the two-period “..” punctuation is objectively malformed.
身を伏せる can mean lying or pressing oneself low. Doing so against the wind and then moving upward on the steps is coherent crawling, not necessarily contradictory staging.
偶然か presents chance as a question or uncertain possibility. “It must be luck” promotes that uncertainty into a strong conclusion.

The immediately preceding page already identifies the observer as spying on Saber’s secret technique. “Only here to watch” is a natural anaphoric abbreviation and does not obscure the target in context.
気乗りしない means not feeling interested, enthusiastic, or inclined. “This is less interesting now” is a mild but defensible expression of that reluctance.
The preceding lines repeatedly identify the watched 秘剣 as Saber’s. Assassin says he could have experienced its full extent; the English instead makes him the owner displaying his own technique.
よい所 means an exciting or crucial point in the duel. Calling the interruption “at a bad time” evaluates the same timing as unfortunate and does not reverse the event’s practical meaning.

The English preserves the substantive point: Saber independently recognizes the disadvantage rather than merely accepting Assassin’s assessment. The causal phrasing is a defensible contextual interpretation of the discourse marker.
“Your pick-up is here” casually but accurately denotes someone who has come to fetch Saber. The objection is chiefly register preference, not a change of participant or action.
The supplied raw Original witness explicitly speculates that Assassin became a spirit. Its absence from the later active Japanese is an edition difference, not an unsupported mirrorMoon insertion.
ぼう marks blankness, absent-mindedness, or a dazed state. “Quietly stands there” preserves silence and posture but removes the mental impairment that foreshadows her collapse.
とっちめてやる is a comic threat to punish, catch, or thoroughly scold Saber. “Bring it up” reduces that force to merely mentioning the matter.
The Japanese compares Shirou’s expression to that of someone who saw a ghost. Without “as if,” the English conditional incorrectly asks why seeing a ghost would make him look at Rin.

伝わる broadly means be conveyed, reach, or become known. “The Master will be informed” is stiff but compatible with information reaching the Master; the Japanese itself does not explicitly name the bond mechanism.
In contrast with Japanese tea and followed by teabags, “English tea” is readily understood as Western-style black tea. It is dated terminology but not a material substitution in context.

姿 can denote someone’s presented state or manner as well as visible form. “Her usual attitude” is imprecise, but contextually conveys Saber being back to her familiar self and does not assign a new action.
The understood subject remains Saber from 「私は」; 「私たち」 modifies only 「戦い」. “We noticed” demonstrably adds Assassin as a detector.
「～ぐらいなら」 expresses substitution: Shirou will fight instead of making Saber fight. The English conditional can instead permit her fight and add his own.
「この身」 can formally denote one’s body, especially in an argument dismissing bodily sex. “My body is that of a heroic spirit” is a defensible rendering, not a demonstrable identity error.
The English syntax makes the injury occur “in place of saving” Shirou and omits the powerless-self setup, obscuring that someone is hurt as the price of protecting him.
Although literally associated with cutting a sleeping throat, 「寝首をかく」 idiomatically means catching someone completely unawares. “Sneak an attack” preserves that operative meaning in context.
「守り」 permits “defense,” “guard,” or a figurative “shield,” and the paper comparison supports the metaphor. The tactical narrowing alleged is not demonstrably material.

「侮る」 includes treating someone with contempt or disrespect, so “insulting” is within range. The following sentence explicitly retains the underestimation: Shirou thinks a human can defeat a Heroic Spirit.
The supplied Original witness contains 「ダメだ」 before the parallel-lines sentence. “It’s no use” is therefore an Original-edition line, not an unsupported insertion.
The meaning is identifiable, but “It looks this conversation…” is malformed standard English; it requires “looks like/as though” or a direct construction such as “This conversation looks…”.
“Doesn’t want to get you hurt” naturally means that Shirou does not want to cause or allow Saber to be injured. In this argument, that causative responsibility is contextually appropriate.
The English is stiff but transparently preserves Rin’s coined metaphor of emotional excess as mental fat. Calling the mixed wording a factual mistranslation would be preference policing.
“Dangerously” conveys the ominous substance, so no core meaning is lost. A narrower prose-and-tone issue survives: the English is unnatural and does not reproduce the wry 「お二人さん」 framing.
“Magic” is a conventional contextual rendering of 「魔術」, especially in older Fate terminology. No contrast with 「魔法」 on this page makes “magecraft” obligatory.
「汗を流す」 here idiomatically means exercising or training. “Train in the dojo” naturally conveys the promised physical activity; preserving the sweat image is stylistic preference.
「体が資本」 means that health or one’s body is the indispensable foundation. “Everything starts from my body” instead suggests bodily origin and is opaque English.
“Can only rely on the hope” does retain dependence or clinging. The narrower genuine loss is the explicit frailty of 「儚い」, with 「責め苦」 also softened somewhat by “hardships.”
The English’s “just by helping them myself” conveys limited personal assistance sufficiently. The more explicit self-deprecation in 「自分程度」 is nuance, not a demonstrable material error.
“He thought he was a failure” is a natural compression of 「なり損ねた落第者」, and the immediately preceding “superhero to me” supplies what Kiritsugu believed he had failed to become.

“Even though they think like that” gives the concession an unclear indefinite thinker. The Japanese says Shirou consciously accepts the preceding limitation and nevertheless defines justice as saving everyone.
Japanese routinely omits possessors, and Kiritsugu is addressing Shirou directly. Supplying “your” is normal English explicitation and does not complete the unfinished predicate.
The supplied Original witness itself uses dream rarity, so the classic English branch reflects an Original-edition reading rather than inventing one.
The supplied Original witness describes Saber as looking slightly displeased. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
「ないけど」 directly concedes Shirou’s completed claim that Sakura would not consent ordinarily. “It might not be possible” changes that concession into present uncertainty.
The exact count is compressed, but the surrounding English already establishes another attempt and says Rin was burdened “again.” The causal basis of Shirou’s apology remains intact.

The valid issue is that “angry” weakens 「目の仇にする」, which means making someone a persistently hated target. The accusation’s claim that the Japanese necessarily threatens a plural “them” is unsupported.
The Japanese objects to Sakura going out at night too frequently, not to all nighttime movement. “We can’t let her” materially converts a frequency concern into an absolute rule.
In comic English, an “evil face” can denote a mischievously mean expression. Given Rin’s immediate teasing, it is a defensible tonal rendering of 「意地の悪い顔」 rather than a literal moral judgment.
“A big smile” is a normal English rendering of an especially fine, radiant, or emphatic smile. The qualitative nuance of 「極上」 is softened but not materially falsified.
“Give your parents a treat” awkwardly but recognizably means doing something nice for one’s parent, a contextual rendering of 「親孝行」. The finding overstates this as a factual change in relationship.
The unstated recipient of disciplinary dismissal must be Taiga, the employed teacher and guardian, not the student Shirou. The English reverses the experiencer.
“Unfortunately” is a reasonable discourse explicitation of Shirou’s reluctant, embarrassed admission about male nature. It does not contradict or materially alter the joke.
“Smiles” preserves the action and the dialogue already makes Taiga’s delighted teasing evident. Omitting the precise grin manner is a minor tonal compression, not a material mistranslation.
Shirou is addressing Rin as 「おまえ」, so “she” breaks viewpoint and yields ungrammatical English. It should identify Rin as “you.”
「言葉のあや」 can mean a manner of speaking, rhetorical phrasing, or an unfortunate choice of words. “I just used the wrong words” is a defensible face-saving retraction here.
「半熟の玉子」 specifies partially set eggs, and “soft-boiled eggs” is a common breakfast realization of that state. The cooking-method explicitation is plausible and not materially consequential.

In context Shirou is withholding circumstances because they cannot safely be explained. English “can’t tell me” naturally covers that practical inability and does not establish a meaningful agency reversal.
“It doesn’t matter for me” can mean that Shirou’s absence causes Rin no practical problem, matching 「こっちには支障はない」. Personal emotional indifference is not forced by the English.
「手合わせ」 denotes a bout or match, and “contest with someone” falls within that range. It does not imply a materially different formal competition.
The immediately established situation is Saber’s sword-training session, so “what she’ll make me do” has an unambiguous referent. Repeating “sword training” is unnecessary in English.

The narration is not unsupported: it exists in the Original edition. A narrower error survives because 「勝手に自己完結」 means Saber has independently reached her own conclusion—here a mistaken one—not necessarily found a “solution.”
After “I’ll let you decide,” “you can give me anything” conveys unrestricted demands, including unreasonable training. It is loose English but does not demonstrably lose the permission’s extremity.
“Looks at me” omits the sustained intensity of 「まじまじと」, but the action and Saber’s distracted reaction remain. This is minor descriptive compression rather than material error.
“Thank God” is a conventional, often nonliteral English exclamation of relief and naturally renders 「良かった」 here. It does not assert a religious belief or invocation as plot content.
「運動能力」 evaluates Shirou’s overall athletic or physical ability, whereas “strength” ordinarily denotes muscular power. The English demonstrably narrows Saber’s assessment.
Here 「幸いした」 means that Shirou’s training proved useful or paid off. “Good fortune” instead presents luck and sits awkwardly against the following sentence crediting his effort.
「暗転した」 describes the world going dark as Shirou loses consciousness. Turning upside down is a different physical perception.
“Only a bruise” contrasts the contusion with a fracture, while the preceding English explicitly calls it “a bad bruise.” The complete context does not minimize its severity.
The same English page explicitly states that the floor is slippery with sweat. Although the final sentence mentions only fatigue, the unstable footing has not been omitted from the complete page.
「的確」 means apt, precise, or properly chosen, not flawless. “The perfect situation” overstates Saber’s demand beyond seeking tactically suitable circumstances.
「ズキズキ」 specifically describes throbbing or pulsating pain. “Burning” substitutes a distinct sensation, apparently carried over from the preceding description of hot breath.
“Faint slightly” is unnatural English, so a prose defect survives. But 「軽い」 can describe a mild loss of consciousness and does not definitively encode the finding’s claimed brief duration.
「戦力差」 is the overall disparity in fighting power, including physical capability and combat effectiveness. “Skill difference” narrows it to technique or training.
「ビシバシ来る」 conveys forceful, repeated warning intuitions. “Instincts…come at me in numbers” wrongly makes the intuitions countable entities and is unnatural English.
「受け流す」 means parrying, deflecting, or redirecting the shinai strikes. “Elude” instead describes avoiding them, changing Shirou’s defensive action.
The allegedly inserted sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese; it is merely commented out in the base/all-ages witness. It is valid Original-edition content.
「正座」 specifies the seiza kneeling posture. “Sitting in a polite Japanese-style” neither identifies that posture nor forms natural English.
「人間として」 describes Shirou’s own human-to-human mode of regarding Saber. “In everyone’s eyes” changes this into an unsupported universal judgment by other people.

The tranquil-dojo description is explicitly present in the supplied Original Japanese and only absent/commented out in later witnesses. Its English inclusion is an edition difference, not an insertion.
Saber helps Shirou as part of pursuing her own Grail objective because a Master must obtain it. “Helping me to take share in the reward” instead makes Shirou’s reward share the purpose.
「冒涜」 denotes sacrilege, profanation, or a serious affront. “Rude” reduces Shirou’s strong moral condemnation to ordinary bad manners.
“Redo things again” is redundant English, but it conveys Saber’s desire to do things over without changing meaning. The minor tautology is not a material accuracy error.

“A small pain remains in my chest” preserves the persistent emotional discomfort expressed by the thorn metaphor. Retaining the literal image would be preferable stylistically but is not required for accuracy.
The English conflates “what kind of person I was” with “what I was like,” producing a genuinely malformed echo question.
主張した means that Saber asserted or stated her thought; “emphasized” instead describes added rhetorical stress.
The Japanese clearly imagines a finishing move that would let Shirou get by merely by learning it; “lets me do something” loses that shortcut and becomes nearly contentless.
“Japanese-style” roughly signals the culturally specific sitting posture, so it is not wholly wrong, but it fails to identify the concrete seiza posture expressed by 正座.
The rendering approximately indicates Japanese formal sitting, but 正座 specifically orders Shirou into seiza; the surviving issue is imprecision, not total corruption.
The supplied raw English shows mutually exclusive Realta and Classic branches. Their juxtaposition in mirrorMoon is branch flattening, not a duplicated clause in either translation.
三半規管 specifically names the semicircular canals governing balance, not the external or auditory “ear canals”; the following loss of leg strength reinforces that distinction.
The Japanese describes judgment that steers the overall course of battle toward avoiding combat. “Enough judgment to stop yourself” reduces that strategic agency to personal restraint.
The sentence is present verbatim in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported restoration.
“Heal automatically” is a defensible contextual rendering of healing when left alone, especially because 今の俺 explicitly contrasts Shirou’s present condition rather than asserting ordinary recovery.
腕前 can denote ability, prowess, or capability, and the sparring context naturally limits “your powers” to Shirou’s combat capabilities. The broader English is not a demonstrable factual error.
間の抜けた evaluates the sound as foolish or anticlimactic. “Strange” omits that comic judgment immediately before the stomach-growl reveal.
The English preserves the shopping district but entirely omits that it is identified as the center of Miyama Town.
自転車の籠 is the bicycle’s basket. A bicycle cart is a different object and changes the physical staging.
Illya audibly goes “muu” and purses or sticks out her lips in a pout. A generic frown changes the facial action and loses the specifically childish gesture.

The English does communicate a reflexive lowering to facilitate movement, so the stance is not wholly lost. The genuine defect is its malformed bodily agency and failure to express a clean ready stance.
The possessive “her father’s” is left without a natural recoverable object in this construction. Japanese explicitly compares the action to taking her father’s hand.
“Talk friendly” is ungrammatical here; the Japanese clearly asks whether ordinary children are supposed to converse amicably with one another.
振り払われた describes the completed shaking-off as the cause, and 背中から specifies a backward, back-first fall. “Tried to make her let go” and “falls to the ground” lose both details.
“When I notice, I instantly reached” has an irreconcilable tense sequence. 気が付けば…咄嗟に presents the catch as already occurring reflexively before conscious realization.
アンバランスさ directly denotes imbalance, and the preceding description supplies the contrast between Illya’s danger and innocent trust. “She’s really unbalanced” is ambiguous but contextually defensible.
それに負けないぐらい naturally means the other gifts were no less valuable or substantial, not necessarily equal in number. “A lot of things as good as that” is awkward but preserves a defensible comparison.
The supposedly restored narration is present in the governing Original Japanese and absent only from the later witnesses, making this an edition difference.
であろう marks confident narrative conjecture and can defensibly be rendered “I’m sure,” even if “probably” would preserve the modality more literally.
The English closely preserves the Japanese personification of a shock striking the back of Shirou’s head. Its stiffness does not establish that a literal physical attack is being asserted.
“By nature from the core” is redundant and inelegant, but it still plainly conveys that Rin is fundamentally a magus. The alleged loss of the surface/core contrast is not demonstrated.
In context, 自分から describes being voluntarily inclined to kill; “would want to kill others” is a natural, defensible paraphrase of Shirou’s judgment about Illya’s disposition.
The supplied Original witness contains the additional insult “なに、痴呆？” The base/all-ages omission is an edition difference, while the Classic English corresponds to Original.
Both perception lines occur in the governing Original Japanese; they are merely commented out in the later base witness.
The delivery narration is explicitly present in Original Japanese. Its omission from base/all-ages does not make the Classic translation unsupported.
The supplied raw Original witness contains precisely the naked-body denial used by the adult-content English branch, so this is edition-specific text rather than an insertion.
The supplied Original witness includes the delivery cue immediately after this line, although the later edition omits it.
The narration appears explicitly in governing Original Japanese and is absent only from the later editions.
In a scene where Saber’s uncovered body is the immediately visible referent, “my bare body” is a defensible English explicitation of このような場面, not an unsupported new event.
In this construction, “meaningless” naturally means immaterial or of no consequence, which falls within the contextual force of 些末な事. It need not mean literally devoid of meaning.
The adult Original witness intensifies 女の子 as とんでもなく女の子, making “really feminine” a defensible rendering of Shirou’s perception rather than a replacement unsupported by Original.
The supplied Original witness explicitly asks about being seen naked; “your body” belongs to that adult-edition branch, while “you changing” matches the later wording.
A scene “flickering in my mind” is understandable English imagery for an incident repeatedly intruding on awareness. It preserves the effect of ちらついて without a factual change.
Using “magic” as the translation’s term for 魔術 is a legitimate terminology choice unless it creates an actual 魔法/魔術 collision here; this page alone does not establish such an error.
The allegedly inserted entry reaction is present verbatim in governing Original Japanese and omitted only from base/all-ages.

Although distortion is intentional, the English phonetics no longer reliably communicate that Rin asks him to wait because this finishes today’s quota. The substantive latter clause is effectively lost.

Following the explicit comparison of the two teaching types, “putting that aside” can naturally refer to setting aside whether Rin is actually suited to teaching. It is less explicit but contextually adequate.
The sentence does state the inherited specialty as flow and conversion of power, so that content is not obscured. Only the nonstandard plural “magics” and awkward construction survive as defects.
This narration is present in the governing Original Japanese and commented out only in later editions; it is not unsupported for an Original comparator.
溜めやすい describes a capacity to accumulate or retain magical energy. Calling jewels easy “targets” for transfer changes that storage property into ease of directing a transfer.
Rendering 魔術 as “magic” is a consistent and defensible terminology choice. The quotation marks and statement that the jewel itself becomes it preserve the prepared-working distinction in context.
“Large-scale magic” is a plausible rendering of 大魔術 in this activation context. Neither 大 nor the supplied context requires the narrower preferred term “great magecraft.”
The Kiritsugu comparator is present in governing Original Japanese and omitted only from base/all-ages, so its inclusion is edition-correct.
特殊 can mean special, exceptional, or unique, and English “unique” need not assert metaphysical exclusivity here. The translation remains within the word’s ordinary range.
“She murmurs to herself” translates narration found in governing Original Japanese; it is absent only from the later witnesses.
The English question omits 随分前に, losing Shirou’s specific assumption that Rin had noticed long ago—the premise her next reply directly denies.
Rin has already explicitly ordered Shirou to sit there, and “listen up” naturally condenses 腰を落ち着かせて聞く. The posture and attentive lesson command remain established by the complete page.
The repeated “that that” is a clear typographical corruption not licensed by the Japanese.
The supplied English and raw script both leave Rin’s spoken passage without its closing quotation mark.
神秘 is the general technical “Mystery.” Adding “divine” restricts it to religious or godly mystery, a qualification not present in Japanese.
一晩中 means throughout the entire night, whereas “the whole evening” ends substantially earlier.

The quoted metaphor is of magecraft becoming tangible enough to take in hand. English “put one’s hands on” conventionally means obtain or seize, shifting the metaphor and making Shirou’s bodily interpretation awkward.

English lacks a direct counterpart to the aged masculine pronoun ワシ, and the quoted first-person performance remains intelligible. Failure to add compensatory old-man diction is a stylistic preference, not a factual mistranslation.
悪態をついて supports “cursing,” while やれやれ supplies weary disappointment or exasperation. The phrase is stiff but conveys both components without a material change.
矯正器具 broadly denotes corrective equipment or appliances; in a body-altering context, “medical tools” is an imprecise but defensible hypernym. The claimed forced-alignment nuance is not explicit.
わたしたち is explicitly plural and includes Rin’s side or group. “I’m going to suffer” incorrectly reduces the affected party to Rin alone.
The governing Japanese contains only Shirou’s refusal and admission that he is a poor talker. His asserted hatred of Rin-like indirectness is unsupported and makes the reply more hostile.
足音の主 denotes the person responsible for or source of the footsteps. “The cause of the footsteps” turns the approaching person into an unnatural abstraction.
顔を合わせる means to meet or come face to face. “See him face on” instead suggests viewing him frontally and does not naturally express the mutual encounter.
A genuine error survives, but it is aligned to the wrong Japanese phrase. “It’s just not me” mistranslates “it is not only me,” rather than directly mistranslating 肌に合わない.
The two terse Japanese clauses mockingly voice Shirou’s own creed; supplying first person is a defensible English explicitation, and ownership remains clear from context.
The awkward “superhero you are being” fails to convey 気取る, Archer’s accusation that Shirou is posing or styling himself as a champion of justice.
The plurals are clumsy, especially “magics,” but the English still expressly pairs Shirou’s dreams with his magecraft and orders him to discard both. The alleged logical break is not demonstrated.

The accusation of reversal is overstated, since the English still asserts human limitation. It does, however, narrow a general statement that human capability is painfully limited into “that” being the whole of what humans can do.
“The readiness as a magus” is awkward English, but it accurately identifies staking one’s life as a magus’s resolve. This is fluency criticism, not a material mistranslation.

The Japanese presents Shirou’s unexplained impression that those words belonged at the end of Archer’s statement. “Wanted to ask” and “stopped himself” add deliberate intent and action not established by the text.
The governing Original witness contains the gaze-only farewell as active prose. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported mirrorMoon insertion.
Although 指 specifically means fingers, describing the hand holding the shinai as numb is an ordinary, physically compatible broadening and does not materially alter the aftermath.
In this combat lesson, “determination” is a defensible contextual rendering of 勝ち気, which covers assertive, competitive, or strong-willed spirit.
Saber says she looked away expecting Shirou not to be shaken or baited by such a small opening. The English instead makes agitation the result she was testing for.
“Scaled” is unnatural for this idiom, but the sentence still clearly says the two risks need not be compared. No material tactical relation is lost.
打つ can denote making a move or taking action, not only striking a concrete target. “What to do” is broad but defensible in Saber’s discussion of combat decisions.

“Sitting Japanese-style” is vague and dated, but in context it intelligibly conveys the Japanese kneeling posture. Insisting on the loanword “seiza” is localization preference, not a demonstrable material error.
The construction is nonstandard and redundant, but its meaning—what sort of person Saber used to be—is unmistakable. The finding establishes a fluency defect, not an accuracy failure.
主張する can mean assert, maintain, or emphasize a point. In the surrounding contrast between thought and emotion, “emphasized what I was thinking” remains a defensible rendering.

The English does retain the notion of a move useful merely by knowing it, so the alleged total loss is overstated. It nevertheless renders やっていけそう only as vague “do something,” losing the specific fantasy that the move would let Shirou get by.
The wording is awkward and less precise than “seiza,” but it still communicates a Japanese formal sitting posture; this is not a material change of action.
“Sit there in a Japanese style” is poor English but remains an intelligible description of the commanded posture. The accusation principally enforces terminology preference.
The apparent duplicate is produced by flattening mutually exclusive realta/classic conditional branches. The raw English does not display both clauses in a single active edition.
三半規管 specifically denotes the semicircular canals governing balance, not the ear canals generally. The substitution obscures the immediate explanation for Shirou losing his footing.

The Japanese describes judgment capable of steering the course of battle toward a no-fight outcome. “Enough judgment to stop yourself” instead reduces this strategic control to personal restraint or avoidance.
Saber is helping Shirou because assisting the Master advances her own acquisition of the Grail. “Helping me to take share in the reward” wrongly makes Shirou’s share the purpose.

冒涜 is figurative here: Shirou regards the question as an improper affront given his own lack of a wish. “Rude” weakens the rhetoric but remains a defensible contextual paraphrase; literal sacrilege is not required.
“Redo things again” is stylistically redundant but preserves the meaning of wanting to do things over. It is not a material translation error.
A lingering small pain in the chest is a natural rendering of the thorn metaphor’s meaning. The image is flattened, but no material state or implication is lost.

The English partially conveys an easy shortcut through “just because I know it,” so the finding overstates total failure. Its vague “lets me do something” nevertheless omits the specific idea that learning the move would let Shirou get by.
The wording is imprecise and awkward, but it intelligibly describes the formal Japanese kneeling posture. Requiring “seiza” is not necessary for accuracy.
Despite poor phrasing, the English communicates that Saber orders Shirou into a Japanese formal sitting posture. The concrete action is not materially changed.
The displayed duplication comes from combining mutually exclusive conditional translations. It is an extraction artifact rather than corruption present in one active script branch.
The Japanese explicitly names the balance organs, whereas “ear canals” denotes a different anatomical structure and weakens the causal joke about Shirou’s legs giving out.
Saber means the strategic judgment to direct the battle toward a situation where Shirou need not fight. The English recasts that as merely stopping himself from entering such a situation.
The Japanese makes Shirou’s assistance instrumental to Saber obtaining the Grail through her Master. The English instead appears to make Shirou’s share of a reward the beneficiary or goal.
In context 冒涜 is a figurative moral affront, not necessarily literal religious sacrilege. “Rude” is milder but defensible and does not falsify Shirou’s judgment.
The double marking of repetition is inelegant but semantically faithful. The accusation identifies redundancy only, not a material error.
Rendering the small thorn as lingering chest pain conveys the metaphor’s ordinary sense. Loss of the exact image is a stylistic compression rather than a demonstrable factual error.
The English question is awkwardly formed, but it still unambiguously asks what kind of person Saber used to be. This is not a material semantic error.
主張した permits “asserted” or “emphasized,” and the following exchange still distinguishes Saber’s articulated thought from unfiltered feeling. The alleged conceptual loss is not established.
The English invents generic tastiness while omitting ほくほく, the dumpling interior’s distinctive hot, fluffy or steaming texture, and the separately piping-hot shrimp.
籠 is the bicycle’s basket. “Bicycle cart” normally denotes a different attached or trailing object and therefore changes the concrete staging.

In context, saying Illya “didn’t seem like an enemy” is a natural compression of her not having appeared in the role or manner of an enemy during the encounter. It does not assert that Shirou knows she is harmless.
“The taste is coarse” is awkward, but roughness in the seasoning naturally manifests as a coarse or rustic taste, and the English preserves the contrast with evident care.
The passive construction makes Shirou the agent who might cut off Saber’s meals. “If I stop eating” reverses agency and breaks the mock starvation-siege premise.

甘い can mean soft, naive, lax, or indulgent. In a joke about becoming dependent on Shirou’s cooking, “too indulgent” is contextually defensible even if “soft” would better preserve the martial register.
The governing Original Japanese expressly includes the park-and-braking sentence. Its being commented out in later witnesses is an edition difference, so the English is supported for this comparator.
The groceries remain in the bicycle basket, not a cart. The English substitutes a materially different object.

The scene remains recoverable, so the accusation overstates how fully the inversion obscures it. A narrower error survives: “the park I passed” misrenders the park Shirou deliberately detoured into, and the resulting English sentence is malformed.
The description is present in the governing Original edition. Its omission or commenting in base/all-ages cannot make the mirrorMoon line unsupported here.
The governing Original explicitly contains the narration that Shirou calls out. Later editions commenting it out is not evidence of an Original-edition insertion.
Illya’s widened-eye reaction is active in the supplied Original Japanese. The finding incorrectly treats a later-edition deletion as governing.
Both reaction lines occur in the governing Original witness. Their absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported staging.
Taiga is actively picking up an apple while speaking. The English replaces that action with merely looking, disrupting the setup for her immediate bite.

“Necessary” conveys the imposed daily requirement, and the comic excess remains evident from three apples per person. Requiring the noun “quota” is a wording preference rather than a material correction.
“Loosely” is awkward, but it reasonably conveys Taiga speaking casually or blithely. The carefree tone is weakened rather than materially contradicted.

The alleged missing boundary is largely an extraction artifact: the raw line command marks the self-correction. A narrower omission remains because “garbage” drops the specific insult that it resembles a dumping ground for prize-grade stuffed animals.

知人 can be a restrained “acquaintance,” but “friend” is contextually defensible: the preceding narration explicitly identifies Issei as a school friend. The accusation overstates a register preference as error.
The turnaround is active in the governing Original Japanese. Its deletion in base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported restoration.
人見知り directly covers shyness or bashfulness with unfamiliar people. 激しく intensifies it, and the following clause separately supplies his coldness; “really bashful” is therefore defensible.
In this covert probe for abnormalities, “tentatively” can naturally express cautious questioning. It is less literal than “carefully” but does not demonstrably replace vigilance with mere indecision.
問いただす means to press, question, or interrogate. Issei has noticed suspicious points but chooses not to question Shirou; saying they need not be considered erases that deliberate restraint.

神仏 is a collective expression for sacred beings, and Issei’s illustrative singular “a Buddha” preserves the comparison’s operative meaning. The number and religious-range narrowing is not material here.

佇まい denotes bearing, appearance, or presence, whose beauty can naturally be summarized as the person being beautiful. The immediately preceding spiritual comparison keeps the praise from becoming purely physical.

無愛想 covers unsociable, curt, or unfriendly outward manner. “A little antisocial” is somewhat broader in modern English but remains defensible in a passage immediately explaining that Saber does not smile.
ムスッ describes a sullen, displeased, or sulky expression. “Troubled face” instead suggests worry or distress and changes the outward emotion Shirou attributes to Saber.

悩め can mean worry, agonize, or struggle over something. “Torment yourself” is forceful, but Issei’s mock-admonitory register and the following appeal to self-questioning make it a defensible exaggeration.
The English substitutes a substantially smaller ball and changes the stated size of the mask.
サスペリア evokes “Suspiria” and gives the phrase a horror-film flavor; “suspicious” replaces that deliberate reference with an ordinary adjective.
“I never gave up” conveys persistence but entirely omits the explicit two-hour duration that drives the joke.
The Japanese explicitly lists a rhinoceros between the cow and snake, but the English inventory does not.
“Linked to dragons” retains only a vague association, losing the singular dragon and Saber’s emblematic identity as one who bears it behind her.
“And all” suppresses the explicit, comically escalating third action—leaping or flying—rather than translating it.
Although 出来ることなら does not itself say “allowed,” the preceding 預かっていた describes temporary custody, so an external constraint or permission is a defensible contextual explicitation.
惜しい describes Shirou’s reluctance to give up the vision; calling the dizziness “special” does not express that desire to retain it.
勧めてくれた is an appreciative reference to Shirou recommending or encouraging the bath; “insisted” adds materially stronger pressure.
The Japanese announces an extremely bad premonition or suspicion. “Guess about something bad” is both unnatural and changes the object of Shirou’s comic dread.

In the immediately established punching context, “gave Shinji some knuckles” is an intelligible stylized expression for ナックルパート. The alleged bare/bear exchange is not present in the supplied Japanese.
The English is awkward, but “lineage of a magus family” followed by “retain the blood of it” still communicates that Tohsaka preserves that bloodline; the meaning is not materially obscured.
懲りずに means that Shinji keeps approaching despite not being discouraged by rejection; “never gets enough” instead suggests enjoyment or appetite.
Rin says she must make the first move herself. “Setting the mood” introduces a different romantic-emotional idea and weakens her competitive agency.
On this page 魔術 has no supplied contrast with 魔法 or another term requiring a distinct English label. “Magic” is a defensible translation here, even if a terminology scheme might prefer “Magecraft.”
The governing Original Japanese expressly contains Rin’s displeased departure. Its omission or commenting in later witnesses does not make the English sentence unsupported.
Iron is a kind of metal, and “burning metal rod” preserves the concrete bodily image. Losing the precise material is a minor generalization, not a demonstrable material mistranslation here.
The shoulder-drop narration is present and active in the governing Original Japanese; its absence from later editions cannot support an insertion accusation.
食道 specifically locates the stinging in the esophagus after swallowing. “Throat” moves the stated internal sensation to a different anatomical area.
しれっと marks Rin’s unconcerned or nonchalant manner, whereas “straightforwardly” describes directness and misses the comic composure.

The English retains both the lump-like concentration and its location in Shirou’s back. Rendering the symptom dynamically as entering during its onset is awkward but does not materially alter the bodily event.

The allegedly nonhuman contrast is already literal in 魔術師と人間, and the same English passage subsequently clarifies the latter as “a normal person.” The accusation demands an interpretive correction rather than identifying an unsupported change.
保温瓶 is a heat-retaining flask or thermos. “Insulator” is not the concrete second vessel and disrupts Rin’s pot-versus-flask analogy.

ずっとそのまま can mean remaining that way indefinitely, and both Japanese and English immediately qualify the state by explaining that Shirou can turn it off himself. In context, “forever” is not an irrevocable condition.
いいヤツ is a judgment that Rin is a good person. “Cute” replaces that appreciation of her character with romantic or aesthetic appeal.
The English generalizes both にやり, a grin or smirk, and 詰め寄る, pressing in on someone, materially weakening Rin’s mock-menacing approach.
“The strengthening failed” accurately states failure, while the preceding page explicitly says all thirty objects broke. The zero-success outcome remains clear in the supplied context.
With no 魔法 contrast on this page, translating 魔術 as “magic” is defensible. A preferred franchise terminology convention alone does not establish a factual translation error.
“Ten magical energy” is unidiomatic English, but the sentence still unambiguously presents the Japanese ten-versus-one quantitative comparison. The claimed material obscuring is not established.
縁側 denotes the engawa or veranda, not a doorway; the English relocates where Saber is waiting.
補強する means reinforce or shore up weak points. “Enforcing the weak spots” names a different operation and makes the practical advice incoherent.
“He is so correct” is unidiomatic, but it still plainly conveys that Archer is right and Shirou consequently cannot answer. This is not a material accuracy error.
二束三文 means for a trifling or dirt-cheap price, not for no charge. “Free” changes the explicit extension of the buy-a-fight joke.
The missing article is a minor grammatical defect, but “exchange of blows” still communicates 殴り合う accurately and unambiguously.
甘さ can denote soft-heartedness or excessive kindness, and in the stated context “Rin’s kindness” defensibly expresses the leniency Archer reproaches himself for sharing.
やけに means oddly, unusually, or strikingly. “Horribly” adds an adverse emotional evaluation rather than expressing the words’ unusual persistence.

A narrower omission survives: English loses 今の and the name/self ruby’s explicit present-self framing. However, first-person “my oldest memory” still identifies the memory as Shirou’s, so the finding overstates how completely the identity connection disappears.
生かす can mean put to use, make effective, or keep alive. In this philosophical context “make use of what has gone away” is a defensible reading, not necessarily utilitarian exploitation.
The duration question is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its later commenting-out is an edition difference and does not make the Original-edition English unsupported.
The extra description of Saber is present in the governing Original Japanese. Later editions comment it out, but that cannot support an insertion accusation against this comparator.
立場 commonly means position or standing. “My position will be in question” is awkward but defensibly conveys that Saber’s standing in her role would be compromised.
“Explodes” is a normal figurative English rendering of Taiga suddenly erupting in loud protest, reinforced by ずがーん and her shouted dialogue; it need not be read literally.
舐める here means to treat lightly or with contempt. “An insult to the bread” is a comic localization that preserves Rin’s claim that the skimpy meal disrespects bread-based breakfast.
出来レース is more precisely a rigged contest, but “unfair match” preserves Shirou’s accusation that Taiga’s supposed vote was not legitimate. The reduced precision is not a material factual reversal.
懲りずに describes attacking again undeterred; “even stronger” invents greater force and omits Shirou’s defining persistence.
The generic “What are you saying?” omits Saber’s explicit judgment that asking for rest is unlike Shirou’s usual behavior.
今まで compares this morning’s Shirou with the person Saber has known up to now, not merely with the previous day.
The preceding narration establishes that Rin’s gaze distracts Shirou from sparring. “Worried about Rin” instead assigns him concern for her welfare.
The forceful shinai grip is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its commenting in later editions does not make it unsupported in an Original-edition comparison.
素麺 names the specific dish somen; “white noodles” replaces it with an imprecise visual category and loses the stated domestic detail.
In combat 甘さ can mean soft-hearted kindness or leniency. “Generosity” is awkward but defensibly conveys the compassionate impulse Rin says she suppresses.
The English possessive is awkward, but it still attributes the radiance to Saber’s class rather than to Saber personally. The person-versus-role distinction remains intelligible.
The Japanese itself presents the attempted call metonymically as a voice that stops and does not explicitly say it dies in Shirou’s throat. The English preserves that interruption in context.
