畏れ covers fear, dread, or awe, and “horrified” is somewhat stronger but remains within the fearful side of its range. The deliberately uncertain anger-versus-fear reading is retained.
The hatred and spitting narration is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its deletion from base and all-ages witnesses is an edition difference, not evidence of an unsupported insertion.
Here the Japanese deliberately moves from 魔術 to the broader 神秘 within one explanation. Rendering both as “magic” erases that observable change in scope.
A conception that “violates reality” is a defensible natural paraphrase for one that encroaches upon or erodes reality. It weakens the metaphor but preserves the governing supernatural relation.
ある魔術 means some or a certain unnamed art. “That one magic” wrongly makes it sound previously identified or uniquely designated.
Existential “there’s” with a plural complement is common informal English. More importantly, the sentence clearly and accurately states that twenty remain.
こなす in this present scene describes Shirou steadily working through the assignment; “finish” prematurely asserts completion.
つれない criticizes Shirou as cold or unfriendly. “Don’t be angry” instead invents anger and changes Shinji’s social reproach.
いっぱしな人殺し means a proper, accomplished, or full-fledged killer, and the emphatic comparison with 僕より supports “a better murderer than I am.” The wording is defensible despite its ugliness.
目を瞑ってやってた means Shinji claims to have knowingly turned a blind eye. “Let you go about Sakura” is malformed enough to obscure both that tolerated conduct and his possessive claim of indulgence.
蠕動 denotes peristaltic churning or contraction; “crawls around” instead suggests the stomach itself moving about and is materially malformed.
もつれる describes the feet tangling or stumbling, not trembling; the English changes loss of coordination into shaking.
This sentence is present in the supplied raw Original Japanese, so it is an Original-edition line rather than an unsupported restoration.
校舎のまわり means the area surrounding the school building. “Around the schoolyard” relocates and narrows the expanse of red.
“Rot away” is within the lexical and figurative range of 朽ち果てる, especially in this deliberately gruesome description; it does not necessarily assert postmortem decomposition.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly contains the scattered-garbage comparison. Its absence from the later branch does not make it unsupported in an Original-edition comparator.
重ねる here means mentally superimposing the fallen students on remembered wreckage. “Add them to the wreckage” changes that relation and leaves an awkward fragment.
The melting, oozing, keloid-like arms, and dead-fish eyes occur in the supplied raw Original Japanese. They are an edition variant, not invented pathology.
The capitalization is a presentation blemish after a line break, not a demonstrable mistranslation of the emotion or agency; the English still says anger takes control of his body.
死んだんじゃねえの speculates that Taiga has already died or may already be dead. “She’ll die” incorrectly postpones the possible death.
撃鉄 is specifically a firearm’s hammer falling. A generic hammer striking loses both the mechanism and the trigger metaphor.
魔術回路を通した時 refers to running power through or engaging a Magic Circuit; it does not describe inserting a circuit into Shirou.

Rendering 魔術 as “magic” is a defensible terminology choice, particularly where this translation contrasts it with 魔法 as “sorcery.” The Japanese alone does not require the later standardized term “Magecraft.”
The explicit no-danger sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its omission from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence of an unsupported English insertion.
こめかみ is the temple, not the forehead. The English moves the third blade’s anatomical target.
The English preserves the black overwhelming the red but omits 禍々しい, the explicit ominous or baleful quality central to Shirou’s immediate terror.

The displayed Japanese supports only an image of being brutally killed, but the English is explicitly branch-conditioned and no raw Original Japanese candidate for this page is supplied. The witnesses cannot exclude a decapitation-specific Original variant.
In context Shirou selects the left side as his route, then observes Rider’s left fist react. “Her target is my left side” assigns the tactical choice to Rider instead.
延髄 is the medulla oblongata. “Afterbrain” is an obsolete broader anatomical term and does not clearly identify the precise site pierced.
愛でる means admiring, appreciating, or cherishing the flower. “Touching” replaces that aesthetic attitude with a merely physical act.
The neck-skin taunt appears verbatim in the supplied raw Original Japanese. It is an Original-edition line, although commented out in the later Japanese branch.
“Healing magic” accurately conveys 治療魔術 under this translation’s defensible terminology scheme, and the English plainly retains Shinji as the person lacking the ability.
In the context of a mortally wounded victim, 楽にしてやれ is an order to finish him off or put him out of his misery. “Let him be at ease” is ambiguous and materially weakens the lethal command.
The supplied raw Original Japanese uses 溶かす, literally “melt.” The English mature branch therefore reflects an Original-edition variant rather than inventing melting from 蝕む.
The Japanese identifies a heavy chain specifically. “Metallic sound” removes the concrete chain noise accompanying Rider lifting Shirou.
The Japanese gives a repeated grating bodily sound. The English substitutes an unsupported hallway echo and does not reproduce the continuous ギチギチ effect.

The pronoun is awkward but naturally refers to the wounded arm/body acting as a shield, which agrees with the following Japanese statement that Shirou’s body reacts without conscious will. The alleged agency reversal is not established.

Despite stiff English, both parts of the contrast remain explicit: conscious will is absent and the body reacts solely from the urge not to die. This is a style problem, not a material semantic error.
“I would be no match for them” is a normal English paraphrase of 戦闘にすらならない and conveys that Shirou cannot meaningfully contend with a Servant.
脳天 can specify the crown, but “head” is an accurate ordinary generalization. The surrounding downward strike and attempt to avert a vital hit remain comprehensible.
English can describe a tongue-clicking sound as a “cluck,” especially one expressing irritation. The phrase is awkward but does not materially change the action or emotion.
“Die falling” is unidiomatic, but it still conveys Rider’s command that Shirou die by falling. The accusation concerns polish and composure more than a demonstrable change of meaning.
“Even without anything” is incomplete and fails to state that merely leaving Shirou alone would suffice for blood loss to kill him.

Rendering the repeated このまま as rhetorical “Like this?” fragments is defensible. With the script’s dash command restored, the final question is coherent, so the claimed broken syntax is partly an extraction artifact.
悔しさ identifies bitter frustration as the reason he grits his teeth. “In vain” instead comments on the act’s futility and drops the stated emotion.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly says he feels as though anger will drive him insane. “Going insane” is therefore the correct Original-edition branch, not an invention.
のか marks a pointed reported question challenging Shirou’s absolute nonviolence. The unfinished English if-clause does not preserve that interrogative relation.
誰を means “whom.” “What to punish” changes an accountable person into a thing and is semantically incorrect.
凶行 is the violent outrage or atrocity itself. “The cause of this” changes the object Shirou intends to stop into an unspecified cause.
空間のうねり describes an undulation or distortion of space. “A winding occurs in space” is unclear and can suggest an object winding within space rather than space warping.

“Sorcery” is a defensible established rendering of 魔法, especially since the same translation uses “magic” for 魔術. “Literally” is softened to “must have,” but the technical-category accusation is not demonstrated.
イカレる means the organs are wrecked or rendered dysfunctional. “Will explode” invents a specific mechanism and incorrectly presents it as future damage.

Saber reluctantly swallowing her objection amounts in context to accepting Shirou’s decision. The English omits the reluctant manner, but the preceding resistance and ensuing compliance preserve it sufficiently.
In this combat context, “I’ll get Shinji” naturally means Shirou will pursue or deal with him. It is a defensible idiomatic rendering of 叩く rather than a factual weakening.
空間のうねり is a spatial undulation or distortion. The noun “winding” is unclear and does not reliably express space itself warping.
“Sorcery” is a defensible technical rendering of 魔法 within a translation that distinguishes it from 魔術 as “magic.” The alleged category error is therefore not established.
“Forgetting about me” is awkward but pragmatically conveys putting Shirou aside in favor of the urgent priority. The following clause correctly states that Rider and Shinji must be defeated quickly.

The English states the resulting acquiescence, while the surrounding exchange already makes Saber’s reluctance clear. Omitting the swallowed-words image is not enough to make the paraphrase materially false.
Although “blocked my fall” is awkward, it can mean breaking or cushioning the fall, and the stated purpose—avoiding a headfirst impact—matches 受身を取る in context.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly describes an enormous quantity of blood. The intensified English is an Original-edition reading, not unsupported content.

展開する can mean opening or spreading out. Together with the next sentence’s blades bursting outward, “My chest is open” is a defensible compressed rendering rather than a demonstrable static-wound error.
A planted bomb whose switch is activated by impact is naturally paraphrased as a bomb that “went off” from the impact. The result is made explicit without materially changing the causal metaphor.

A narrower error survives: the English loses ささくれだった, the splintered or jagged texture of the rib image. The singular-number accusation is weaker because アバラ骨 may be collective and the English immediately describes a group of swords.
The ruby reads 腹 as なか, “inside.” “Stomach” ignores that governing reading and relocates the swords to an organ or abdominal area.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly says Shirou’s left hand had already melted. The English mature branch reflects that Original variant rather than inventing an anatomical event.
鉛 explicitly makes the heart “leaden,” adding oppressive physical weight to the final stoppage. The English omits this decisive image entirely.
“Don’t go too far” is an idiomatic contextual rendering of 深追いはするな: do not pursue or press the engagement too far. It need not refer merely to distance.
叩き斬る means to hack or cut down by striking. “Smack away” changes the shadows from being cut down to merely being knocked aside.
The Japanese tracks one arm—Shinji extends it, Shirou kicks that arm, pins it, and breaks it. The English pluralizes the limb twice and disrupts that continuity.

The supplied raw Original says 残った腕, “the remaining arm,” and the scene already distinguishes the limbs in use. “My other arm” is a defensible contextual explicitation, not an unsupported contradiction.

The Japanese itself presents lack of resistance to killing a fellow magus as elementary magus knowledge Shinji was never taught. An exclusively first-person reading is not grammatically required, so the English generalization is defensible.
The narration is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference and does not make the Original-comparator English unsupported.
“Shinto” is the romanized place name 新都, and “the church in Shinto” grammatically identifies it as a location. The sentence does not claim the church belongs to the Shinto religion.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly adds the possibility that Shinji built the field to defeat other Masters. The English Classic branch therefore reflects an Original-edition line.
従える means to command, control, or keep in submission. “Worked with” recasts Shinji’s desired authority over a Servant as neutral cooperation.
The stated object is the Command Spells, and 剥ぎ取る means forcibly stripping them away. “Have that arm cut off” adds explicit amputation not established by the supplied Japanese.

The English is awkward and omits the visible act of tilting his head, so a narrower presentation/gesture complaint survives. The claim that it loses his sincerity does not: the following sentence explicitly says he is not acting and genuinely does not understand.

Although 叱咤 is sharper than “voice,” Saber’s quoted warning immediately precedes the reference and supplies its urgency. The contextual paraphrase does not materially alter Shirou’s reflexive response.
一番弟子 can denote the first, foremost, or senior disciple. In a dojo setting, “senior student” preserves the mock hierarchy and is a defensible equivalent.
Although 肉球 literally means paw pads, “paws” is a normal concise rendering for the paw-mark motif in a stamp joke. The image and punchline remain clear.
“Please be rest assured” is ungrammatical; the error plainly damages Rider’s otherwise controlled reassurance.
あろうことか marks shocked disbelief at an outrageous act, whereas “for some reason” instead suggests an unknown motive.
“In one breath” can idiomatically mean in one continuous, uninterrupted action; although awkward here, it is not the unrelated bodily measure alleged.
The English omits 白い, losing an explicit visual feature of Rider’s neck against her black clothing.
ではないのか presents Shirou’s fearful inference as a question; “will … disappear” states it as certain immediately before it proves wrong.
The line is present in the supplied Original Japanese, so it is not unsupported in an Original-edition comparison merely because later witnesses comment it out.
“Looks creepy” substantially weakens both たとえようもなく and the malign force of 禍々しい.
“Big” and “lump” fall within the ordinary senses of 強大 and 塊. The result is inelegant, but the accusation is chiefly stylistic preference rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
“Seems small” retains inferiority but omits the explicit dismissive judgment that the earlier field looks like a child’s trick.
巻き込まれる means being caught up in or exposed to the attack; “in the way” incorrectly makes Shirou an obstruction.
In this combat context, “defeat you here” can defensibly render 引導を渡す as decisively finishing an opponent; requiring an explicit statement of killing is overly narrow.
“Run taking my Master” is conspicuously malformed English for Rider’s straightforward statement that she will flee with Shinji.
The preceding English already says Shirou is “forced to feel it”; “I feel like” then introduces what he senses. Narrative present for the passage is also defensible.
“Remains of cruel destruction” is awkward, but it conveys a惨状-like aftermath, and “cruel” is within 無惨な’s range. The alleged factual change is not established.
The firearm metaphor can be understood as a tensioned hammer being released or returning; the Japanese does not clearly establish the precise mechanical reversal alleged.
The translation omits both the mock question about knowing the Japanese expression and Taiga’s dojo address “Disciple Number One.”
The English still contrasts an ordinary rose ingredient with a real Rafflesia flower. Reducing “rose petals” to “a rose” is minor shorthand, not the material loss alleged.
“Closing years” is malformed, and “starts to make new products” omits 乱造, the indiscriminate churning-out central to Taiga’s joke.
“Irrational choices” conveys the absurd choice setup and the player’s yielding to it; omission of the exact number three is too minor to establish a material error here.
In Taiga’s rhetorical かな, she is effectively concluding that even Shirou dies from such a fall. The categorical English is a defensible comic paraphrase.
The supplied raw Original witness explicitly contains both “a mountain of corpses” and “people crumbling.” These are Original-edition text, not unsupported additions.
被る depicts Shirou putting on or assuming Kiritsugu’s phantom image; “acquire” instead treats the illusion as an object obtained and loses that thematic metaphor.
The English omits 夢見ていた entirely and reduces concealed dreaming or hope to an unspecified refusal to realize something.
The narrower defect is grammatical: the verb should be “follow up,” not the hyphenated “follow-up.” “Went” still makes clear that Kirei physically went to the school.
Although みたい marks secondhand appearance, the whole sentence remains Rin’s report, and omitting “apparently” is a defensible natural-English compression rather than a material certainty shift.
息を吐いて explicitly describes exhaling in relief; “take a deep breath” conventionally describes inhaling and reverses the physical action.
“My body isn’t my body” naturally conveys alienation from an unfamiliar bodily state. It is less concrete than 自分の知らない物 but remains a defensible paraphrase.
The dangling English construction obscures that Shirou himself was saved and recognized his need for Saber; it instead makes “asking” and “being saved” appear to modify the words.
正座 is literally a Japanese formal sitting posture, and “sitting Japanese-style” is an underspecific but recognizable rendering, not a materially false one.
“Instantly” preserves immediacy but omits the explicitly forceful, long-strided manner of Saber’s approach.
追いつめて here means driving Saber into severe emotional distress; “causing me so much trouble” reduces that to inconvenience.
“Hear you out” can mean listening to the whole explanation, and the preceding refusal to accept excuses preserves the pressure. “Totally” is slangy, but the alleged reversal is overstated.
持ち直した asks whether Shirou has rallied from the immediate crisis, not whether his serious injuries are fully healed.
Both declarations occur in the supplied Original Japanese. Their absence from base/all-ages witnesses is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
The raw Original witness reads 守り通せば良かった, directly supporting the Classic branch’s “protected her.” The accusation relies on the later-edition 力になれば wording.
The adjacent Japanese explicitly calls the act 握手, so “shake her hand” is normal English explicitation of the reciprocal offered-hand gesture.
The next page explicitly identifies the clasp as 握手, and “certain feeling” attempts 確かな感触. The wording is awkward but does not support the claimed categorical distortion.
Standalone colloquial って can function as Shirou’s startled “wait/hey” reaction to Rin’s sudden interruption, not only as a literal quotative “she says.”
The English retains Saber’s happiness but omits the narrator’s explicit observation that such visible pleasure is unusual for her once again.
“Scatter” can describe clothes being violently blown apart or dispersed. It is awkward diction, but it does not demonstrably contradict 消し飛ぶ.
押しつける means foisting unwanted clothes on Rin; “forcing me to wear” adds control over her act of wearing them.
The sigh is present in the supplied Original Japanese, and a resigned “…Okay” is a defensible contextual rendering of はあ after Saber’s explanation.
気が抜ける means becoming deflated or losing tension; “feel let down” instead normally expresses disappointment.
The raw Original witness explicitly says Shirou’s arms would have required amputation below the elbows. The English Classic branch follows that edition rather than inventing surgery.
The ruby identifies the damaged body as “bones,” while “body” leaves the location vague; “strains” also does not convey the explicit distortions of 歪み.
悔やむ can mean lament or mourn as well as regret, especially amid reflection on mass harm. The English remains within its lexical range.
死傷者 covers both deaths and injuries; “nobody died” drops the injury component of Shirou’s stated recollection.

In a list of anticipated aftereffects, “long-term physical disabilities” can reasonably express prolonged bodily dysfunction. The alleged permanent intensification is not required by the English phrase.
記憶障害 specifically identifies memory impairment; “mental damage” replaces it with a materially broader, undefined condition.
The raw Original witness explicitly says some students’ skin had melted. The Classic English follows Original-edition wording rather than inventing a mechanism.
The English omits 体が弱って and therefore loses the stated link between Shirou’s weakened body and his heart beginning to voice nonsense.

The raw English retains an interruption marker, and “do so” naturally supplies the already stated action of pursuing the ideal. This is defensible English explicitation, not a demonstrably invented maxim.
The clear surviving error is anatomical: 左肩 is the left shoulder, not the left arm. Mentioning a bone crack is contextually inferable and less securely erroneous.
ドロドロ gives a grotesque liquefied or mush-like bodily sensation; “weak” removes that concrete image entirely.
The declaration is active in the supplied raw Original witness. Its being commented out in the archived later-edition Japanese does not make it unsupported for this comparator.
捕まえる means catching or capturing Shinji; “find” reduces the intended seizure to merely locating him.
The narration is present and active in the supplied Original witness, so its Classic inclusion is an edition difference rather than unsupported content.
The English conveys Shirou’s realization of stupidity but omits 小さくなる, his figurative shrinking or deflation under Rin’s reaction.
In context Shirou is solemn because he sees a tactical danger; “grave face” is a defensible description of 気の乗らない顔 rather than a materially different state.
The stronger conclusion is present in the supplied Original Japanese and raw Original witness. Its later deletion is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The translation consistently uses “magic” for 魔術 and “sorcery” for 魔法 in this exchange. That legacy terminology preserves a distinction, so requiring “Magecraft” is glossary preference.
神業 is an idiom for extraordinary or godlike skill, and “godly” can carry that same nonliteral evaluative sense. No literal divinity is asserted.
A narrower error survives: まず qualifies the practical near-immunity, whereas “No … can” makes it absolute. Using “magic” for 魔術 is consistent legacy terminology, not independently erroneous.
“Divine mystery” is a defensible legacy rendering of the occult technical term 神秘, used consistently within the rule. The added English modifier does not by itself prove a changed proposition.

The finding misaligns the words: in the full Japanese, 魔法使い is Rin’s initial exclamation, while “Rider is a magus” corresponds to the following 魔術師だって. The highlighted phrase does not translate the cited term.
Within the translation’s own sorcery/magic distinction, “magus” denotes an ordinary 魔術師 and therefore fails to express 魔法使い, a practitioner of the exceptional category under discussion.
胸をなで下ろす is a conventional idiom for feeling or showing relief; “gives a relieved sigh” is a natural English paraphrase and need not assert literal chest-stroking.
“Sorcery” is the translation’s consistent label for 魔法 in this exchange. It preserves the exceptional condition even though modern terminology might prefer “Magic.”
As elsewhere in the passage, “sorcery” consistently represents 魔法. The accusation enforces a preferred glossary rather than showing a semantic error.
“You are misinterpreting that” and the placement of “only” produce malformed, difficult-to-parse English for Rin’s straightforward exception condition.

“Magic” is used consistently for 魔術, while the sentence still presents it as the remaining ranged means and explains its interaction with Magic Resistance. This is terminological preference, not demonstrated mistranslation.
直接干渉 literally permits “direct intervention/interference,” and the English immediately specifies that it means shooting an arrow of magical energy. The attack is not left unidentified.
出し抜く means outmaneuvering, outwitting, or getting past Saber; “can even kill Saber” invents a substantially stronger lethal capability.
The Japanese refers generically to borrowing a weapon used by a Servant; “she” instead makes Saber the weapon’s user and changes the proposed method.
霊格 denotes spiritual rank or standing, not the weapon being in spirit form. The English changes the stated reason it can wound a Servant.

The loose Japanese coordination can support either apposition or alternative possibilities, and 宝具そのものに効果がある物 can be read nearly as the English renders it. The accusation’s governing interpretation is not demonstrable.
“Comments” omits the explicit description of Saber answering with an indescribable expression, a visible cue reinforced by her unfinished comparison and the next page.

The preceding English explicitly says “weapons to defeat people,” while “other beings” can defensibly refer to individual targets rather than armies, including nonhuman Servants. A material broadening is not established.
“Others” fails to express the technical contrast between Noble Phantasms effective against individual persons and those effective against armies.
The English entirely omits Rin’s hypothesis that the Noble Phantasm’s great power probably entails substantial restrictions on its use.
The omitted subject is Saber: she would be blown away before swinging her sword. In English, “it” naturally makes the sword the thing blown away.
The allegedly restored sentence is present verbatim in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The governing Original Japanese supplies only the general statement about lifelong injuries; the detailed skin, necrosis, and blindness list has no support in the supplied Original witness.

In context, “not the type to stop when he’s beaten” defensibly conveys that Shinji will not quietly accept defeat and cease acting. It is less idiomatic than the Japanese but not a demonstrable material change.
The line is not unsupported: it appears in the governing Original Japanese. A narrower criticism survives because “take revenge” omits the specific claim that Shinji pays a blow back double.
The duplicated opening is produced by flattening mutually exclusive English script branches. It is an extraction artifact, not the translation presented in either branch.
潜伏 means lying low or hiding. “Resting at home” removes concealment and weakens the observation that Shinji is too agitated to remain hidden there.
“For Sakura’s best” is malformed English for “best for Sakura” and mars the explicit conclusion that Shirou considers this course best for her as well.
“There’s no findings” has an obvious number disagreement, and “findings” poorly conveys the absence of a promising response or lead.
“For a while” can denote a short pause and does not necessarily contradict 少しだけ. The claimed material extension of time is not established.
The apparent truncation comes from stripping the script’s line-dash command after “wron”; it represents an interrupted “wrong—,” matching Saber’s cut-off Japanese question.
頭 is Shirou’s head; “face” relocates the gesture to a different body part during his dizzy spell.
“Could touch her shoulder if I leaned” naturally describes how close they are and does not assert that Shirou intentionally touches her. It adequately paraphrases the hypothetical shoulder contact.
“Heyno” results from stripping the dash command between two interrupted starts (“Hey—no”). It is not evidence that the translated script fused ordinary words.
The English preserves the joke that no normal man could remain calm beside such a beautiful girl. Its indirect phrasing is a defensible paraphrase of Shirou’s masculine self-judgment.
“It seems you should” remains tentative rather than categorical and reasonably renders Saber wondering whether lying down would be preferable.
Both languages deliberately trail into an interruption. The script’s stripped dash command supplied the English termination after “and”; it is not an accidentally unfinished grammatical sentence.
材木 means lumber or timbers. “Woods” normally denotes a forest and changes the residential fire’s charred structural remains into different scenery.
A senkō hanabi is a small handheld firework, so “small firework” is a broader but defensible rendering. Requiring “sparkler” is lexical preference rather than a factual correction.

The archived English contains conditional mature/all-ages alternatives, and the supplied raw Original candidate itself has 焦げた亡骸. The displayed coexistence of “corpses” and “wreckage” is branch flattening, not an unsupported translation insertion.
The two phrasings are mutually exclusive conditional branches flattened into one field, not two sentences printed together in a single intended edition.
ところどころ means “in places.” “All over my body” materially exaggerates the extent of the burns.
The Japanese describes an especially sharp, hot sensation in his chest. The English asserts a broad burn across the chest instead, changing both perception and extent.

The supplied raw Original branch explicitly mentions inflamed flesh and grasping the heart; the alternative “innards” fragment comes from flattened edition branches. The accused additions are therefore not demonstrably invented translation content.

Although dated and awkward, “manly” falls within the possible sense of 潔く as facing death bravely or resolutely. The following “did not panic” preserves the composure, so the alleged factual change is not demonstrable.
薄れていく here describes Shirou’s fading self, consciousness, or existence as death approaches. “Grew thinner” incorrectly makes it bodily thinness.
The Japanese states only his determination to continue seeking help and then breaks off. It does not state that he physically reached out his hands.
In the immediate transition out of the recollection, “wake up suddenly” is a natural contextual rendering of abruptly bolting upright. The next pages explicitly confirm that Shirou had been asleep.
The narration is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its omission or commenting in later editions does not make it unsupported in this Original-edition comparison.
Shirou concedes that falling asleep was his own fault. “It was bad for me” instead describes harm to him and removes that admission of responsibility.
“In hindsight opinion” is malformed English and does not idiomatically express Shirou’s objection that Saber’s conclusion is merely retrospective.
The entire passage is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its later-edition deactivation is irrelevant to whether mirror moon translated unsupported Original content.
養子 means an adopted child. “Foster child” normally denotes a different, potentially temporary family and legal relationship.
The clause identifies Shirou as one who survived there but does not grammatically assert that he was the sole survivor. “The one person” adds exclusivity.
“Ehwell” is caused by stripping the interruption dash between “Eh” and “well.” The underlying English represents Shirou restarting his answer, as does the Japanese.
“SoEmiya” is a normalization artifact caused by removal of the script’s long-dash command between “So” and “Emiya,” not a fused word in the intended presentation.
報いる here means repaying or honoring the dead through prevention. “Retribution” normally introduces punishment or vengeance, which is not Shirou’s stated ethic.
Shirou’s aside is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base and all-ages is an edition difference, not restored unsupported content.
In this construction, “became confident about it” can mean that Saber became convinced. It is awkward English but does not demonstrably reduce 確信 to mere self-confidence.
それ refers to Shirou’s lack of self-preservation as the apparent sin. The English instead makes the act of stating that fact criminal, reversing the object of condemnation.
Japanese omits the grammatical subject: Saber naturally means that their remaining there is burdening Shirou. “We … by being here” is normal English explicitation, not a shift from place agency.
“Butfor” results from stripping the dash command between the interrupted clauses. The intended English hinge is “but—for some reason,” matching the Japanese contradiction.
“Acting like she doesn’t care” describes Saber’s outward performance, not necessarily her true emotion, and reasonably paraphrases behaving as though the conversation had not happened.
The sensation explicitly pricks Shirou’s skin. “Pierces my heart” relocates it internally and suggests an emotional experience.
消えかけている means pedestrian traffic is nearly gone, not wholly absent. Calling the district empty conflicts with the next page’s sparse remaining pedestrians.
Shinto is the established romanization of the proper-name district 新都, and the surrounding office-building context identifies it as a place. Capitalization alone does not turn it into the religion.

While “streets” or “sidewalk” would be cleaner, “roads” can broadly denote the urban ways along which pedestrians are walking. The accusation’s claim that it necessarily places them in vehicle lanes is too strong.
The English preserves the warning but omits Saber’s specific reason for overriding the expectation of safety in public: given this particular opponent, ordinary assumptions may not hold.
In the lip-licking context, フ is a short amused or predatory exhalation such as “heh.” “Huh” ordinarily signals surprise or puzzlement and changes Rider’s entrance.
The Japanese specifies that Rider descended to sever Shirou’s neck. “Kill” omits the exact violent action that explains the overhead interception.
“Fighter aircrafts’ dogfight” uses an incorrect plural and an awkward possessive, making the culminating comparison conspicuously malformed.
In combat English, “get Shinji” can naturally mean reach, attack, or take him down, which is the strategic alternative expressed by 叩く. The alleged softening is not demonstrable.
The English explicitly says they rise by kicking off the walls, so “fly higher” can function as vivid motion language without asserting free flight. The constrained mechanism remains present.
The governing page says an observer could barely tell that collisions were occurring; it does not describe visible tracks. The uncertain raw candidate cannot displace the designated Original witness.
The Japanese contrasts continuing upward until momentum is lost with losing momentum and falling. The English’s “rather than falling” collapses that sequence and produces a misleading relation.
Although the explicit enumeration mentions the sides and above, the same English clause says “from every direction,” which includes below. No actual directional exclusion is asserted.
火花 is a spark, not a firework. Enlarging Saber into “an exploding firework” changes the compact bursting-spark image used for her sharp ricochets.

苦手 can idiomatically mean disliking or being uncomfortable with something, and the following narration explicitly supplies Saber’s tactical inexperience. “Don’t like high places” is a defensible taunt.
楽にしてあげる is a conventional euphemistic death threat here. “Allow you comfort” is unidiomatic and fails to convey the poised promise to put Saber out of her misery.
必殺の状況 is a sure-kill or decisively lethal setup. “Ideal position” reduces it to generic positional advantage and removes the expected killing blow.
呆れる carries negative exasperation or incredulity that bare “amazed” weakens, but the precise self-directed object asserted by the finding remains implicit.
愚直 means foolishly or inflexibly straightforward; “honest” omits the explicit critical edge central to Saber’s mixed frustration and concern.
The supposedly restored simile is present in the governing Original Japanese; its absence from later editions does not make it an insertion.
“Divine mystery” is a defensible fixed rendering of the technical 神秘 and need not assert a separate religious property.
悔しい expresses vexation, chagrin, or frustrated humiliation, not generic sadness; the surrounding helplessness confirms that distinction.
The English preserves the duration but completely omits the distinctive oppressive tactile image modifying those sixty seconds.
百メートル is approximately one hundred meters, whereas “a few hundred meters” multiplies the stated height.
“Rapid succession” preserves speed but omits the expressly pendular back-and-forth pattern of the light.
不甲斐なさ can encompass fecklessness, weakness, or cowardice; in his self-reproach, “cowardice” is a defensible contextual rendering.
Although awkward English, “darkness of the inactive lights” still conveys that the electric lights are out; no material factual change occurs.
The emphatic negative with surprise naturally supports incredulous English such as “That couldn’t be”; it does not necessarily weaken Shirou’s recognition.
“As if there is nothing living” closely conveys the atmospheric fragment saying no living thing exists there; impossibility of life is not explicitly stated.
良くならない is nonpast and can naturally mean “won’t get better”; the surrounding statement still makes clear that Rin accomplished no recovery.
“Puffing because it doesn’t have enough oxygen” explicitly communicates labored breathing and is a defensible, if awkward, rendering of 喘いでいる.
In context, “heal” acceptably means restore a depleted Servant, and the immediately following alternatives specify magical-energy replenishment.
For supernatural consumption, “absorb their souls” is a normal paraphrase of 魂を食べる and retains the predatory act through “attack people.”
この手 does not require singular English, and 抱いていた can describe holding or carrying Saber; the clause is clumsy but substantively accurate.
In this self-rebuke, “How selfish of me” is a natural paraphrase for indulging a self-serving, conveniently hopeful thought.
浮かない顔 specifically indicates a gloomy, troubled, or downcast look; “serious expression” omits the visible unhappiness prompting Illya’s question.
“Amazed at my stupidity” communicates incredulous self-reproach and is defensible for 呆れる in this context, despite being less idiomatic than “exasperated.”
The rhetorical address is natural conversational explicitation of Illya’s spoken observation and still states that Shirou has no protection.
The English opens Illya’s quotation but never closes it before narration resumes, an objective dialogue-boundary error confirmed by the Japanese closing bracket.
“Seeps in into” is grammatically erroneous, and gradual “seeping” also misrepresents the image of murderous intent suddenly kindling in her gaze.
ひたり adds quiet contact texture, but “fingers touch my chest” accurately conveys the action; omitting this mimetic nuance is not a material error.
途切れた denotes vision cutting out, not gradually fading; the later ブツリ reinforces an ordered sequence of abrupt sensory and conscious cessation.
権利 can be rendered as “right” or “privilege”; “natural privilege” is awkward but still conveys Illya’s asserted entitlement.
素体 denotes a base body, substrate, or vessel; “prime field” is a categorical mistranslation that obscures the transfer’s recipient.
“In the next few minutes” is an ordinary English rendering of uncertainty about what one will become after that short interval; the alleged distinction is immaterial.
削減 means reduce or mitigate, while “nullified” wrongly makes the wall’s protection absolute.
The English omits the explicit fact that Saber cannot even execute a breakfall, materially reducing her loss of control under the impact.
In this high-speed pass, “trail” can defensibly denote the damaging wake left by the attack and preserves that it erodes her defense even when she evades.
“Divine mystery” can function as the translator’s fixed English term for 神秘; the supplied text does not prove that it separately attributes divinity.
Lowercase “magic” is a defensible broad English rendering of 魔術; no supplied contrasting use of 魔法 or binding glossary establishes the alleged category collapse.
Using “divine mystery” consistently for 神秘 is a permissible terminology choice and does not demonstrably alter the rule’s comparative relation.
“Magic” can validly translate 魔術 here, while the English retains the comparison between power accumulated through knowledge and through longevity.
“The last five hundred years” wrongly describes a historical period; the Japanese instead sets roughly five hundred years as the maximum human scale.
業が深い is a condemnatory reference to deep karma or sin; “profound deeds” can sound neutral or admiring and loses that judgment.
Rider identifies herself as something that was an enemy of Saber’s kind; “like your enemy” changes identity and former status into resemblance.
“My boy” is a conventional affectionate way to address an animal and defensibly conveys 仔; the contextual Pegasus referent prevents human-specific confusion.
The English is clumsy but does communicate that a normal Pegasus reaches the demonic-beast class within the broader fantastic-race category.
“Black cavalry” is awkward metonymy, but the singular demonstrative and following feminine pronoun unambiguously identify Rider; no material category confusion results.
As elsewhere, “divine mystery” is a defensible lexicalization of the technical 神秘 rather than a demonstrable added religious claim.
“Enough magical energy to have come from a few hundred magi” functions as a quantitative comparison and does not necessarily assert actual donors.
The line is present and active in the governing Original Japanese; its later commenting-out is an edition difference, not an unsupported mirrorMoon insertion.
Shirou’s run toward Saber is expressly present in the governing Original Japanese, although removed from the later base and all-ages witnesses.
The fragment criticism is largely stylistic and mirrors the Japanese cadence, but “likely” weakens 当然 from an inevitable or natural development to mere probability.
Although awkward and less image-specific, “his expression is worried about Saber” preserves the substantive meaning that his visible concern is solely for her.
一際大きく describes an especially large or forceful wingbeat, not an increased beating rate; “faster” invents the wrong physical change.
The object is contextually a rein, so identifying its function in English is normal explicitation; the Japanese does not require prolonged uncertainty about it.
The English preserves the will contrast through “its own intentions” and elliptical “Rider’s”; only the ruby’s additional “finger” reading is genuinely lost.
In combat, “defeat the enemy” is an acceptable rendering of 討ち滅ぼす; “annihilate” would be stronger, but the difference is tonal rather than factual.
“Cast” can mean uttering or invoking a name as part of a supernatural release; loss of the weaving metaphor alone is not a material error.
The Japanese equates a Noble Phantasm with the miracle released through its True Name; “bears a miracle” incorrectly makes the miracle a separate contained object.
The allegedly restored definition is present in the governing Original Japanese and was only removed or commented out in later editions.
Lowercase “earth” naturally means ground or land, so the English does not necessarily assert planetary destruction; the accusation overreads the wording.
“Develop” can describe seals unfolding or emerging, and the retained box-opening simile makes the intended process clear despite awkward diction.
星 can denote a star or planet, and “assembly” still communicates gathered light; the supplied Japanese cannot establish that “planet” is an erroneous narrowing.
大断層 is a vast fault, fissure, or chasm; “great disorder” erases the permanent physical scar through the city.
おかしな means strange, odd, or irrational, not insignificant; the English changes the quality of Shirou’s disordered thoughts into triviality.
“Simplest of the answers” is not necessarily ungrammatical, but “avoid” weakens Shirou’s desperate desire to deny the obvious conclusion.
The aligned Original witness explicitly contains Shirou being confronted with how different Saber is from himself; this is an edition-dependent line, not an insertion.
“Who’s there?” occurs in the governing Original Japanese and is merely commented out in the later archived edition.
The English omits ひきつりながら, which explicitly depicts Shinji twitching or contorting as he stares at the burning book.
弟子一号 literally identifies the first disciple, so “senior student” is a defensible naturalization of that relative status despite losing the numbered title.
ボケとツッコミ names the comic fool and straight-man roles; “straight man and foil” mistranslates the first role and leaves the pair conceptually muddled.
The supplied Original script witness contains the canopy-bed and erotic-CG exchange; its absence from base and all-ages text is an edition difference.
“See through the whole battle” is awkward but can mean following the battle to its outcome, which adequately conveys the gameplay instruction.
無愛想 can describe curt, brusque, or unfriendly manner, making “blunt” a defensible characterization of taciturn Leysritt.
German “Tiger” is orthographically identical to English “Tiger”; the following “danke” preserves the multilingual cue, so this is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
“Though” is an objective typo for “through,” leaving the movement clause grammatically defective even though its intended meaning remains recoverable.

The English correctly reconstructs the full name and predicate. Its preceding hyphen follows the action list; it does not split or corrupt “Matou Shinji,” while the Japanese line break is a presentation/script effect.
“The fact the he” is a genuine grammatical typo in an otherwise accurate statement of Shinji’s priorities.

In this context, “not to kill them quickly” defensibly expresses an order to prolong the encounter rather than finish the victims readily. The omitted Japanese object can also encompass Saber and Shirou, so the plural is not demonstrably wrong.

有り得ない can describe something inconceivable or highly unexpected rather than literally impossible. “An unlikely sound” is weaker prose, but remains a defensible contextual rendering rather than a material factual error.
The English drops 楽しげな, removing the explicit pleasure in the laughter immediately before Illya’s lethal appearance.
“Terminated” is stylistically clinical, but it can denote Shinji being decisively destroyed or killed and does not contradict 消滅 in this violent context.
The standalone “Because” clause is a deliberate literary fragment whose explanation is completed by the following sentence about the echoing footsteps. Its causal meaning remains clear.

感覚 can cover perception or mental faculties, and “my mind freezes” is a natural expression of shock before the body reacts automatically. The accusation treats one possible literal wording as mandatory.
激しく describes intense, violent, or rapid breathing, not irregular rhythm. “Irregular” changes the stated symptom despite preserving general illness.
“Heavy breathing” is a normal English rendering of labored or distressed breathing and conveys the suffering implied by 苦しげ in this context.
The English omits 倒れ伏した, leaving out the explicit fact that the Saber who remains is lying collapsed.
As in the parallel passage, 激しく states intense or rapid breathing; “irregular” substitutes a different respiratory quality.
“Ow!” is a natural English exclamation upon touching something painfully hot. The immediately following sentences explicitly identify the abnormal heat, so no consequential recognition is lost.
“Heavy breathing” naturally denotes labored breathing and is defensible for 苦しげな呼吸; the surrounding fever scene makes the distress unambiguous.
Japanese omits the subject, while Shirou is already carrying Saber. “I’m going home right away” does not imply that he is leaving her behind and fits his immediate departure for home.
Following “no feeling of victory,” shifting to Shirou’s awareness of Saber in his arms is a natural cohesive paraphrase. Saber’s painful breathing and physical presence remain explicit.
そうか is an acknowledgment such as “I see,” not an apology. “Sorry” invents a different opening speech act.
良くならない can naturally be rendered “won’t get well/better,” especially when Rin is denying that her limited treatment will cure Saber. The context does not force a permanent prognosis.
The allegedly restored narration is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from the base and all-ages witnesses is an edition difference, not unsupported English content.
The English attaches “I thought” to Shirou’s expedition, making that fact sound uncertain, and fails to express the Japanese sequence “when you returned, Saber was in that condition.”
Both Rin’s suggestive silence and Shirou’s inference appear in the governing Original Japanese. Their omission from later-edition witnesses does not make the English unsupported.
The two English fragments mirror the Japanese’s deliberately interrupted 「それは。」 followed by confirmation. Read together, “That’s… certainly what Saber told me” communicates the recognition cleanly.

The apparent duplicated “Phantasm” comes from flattening mutually exclusive English edition branches. The supplied raw script shows only one branch would display, so this is not an in-game translation defect.

The English changes the specific goal of restoring Saber’s former condition into a general rule about healing a completely depleted Servant. The preceding Japanese expressly says Saber still has magical energy.
The joined “That’ssomething” is an extraction artifact caused by stripping the supplied line command between the words, not a defect in the rendered translation.
The whole deliberation beat occurs in the governing Original Japanese. Its later removal from base/all-ages is an edition difference and cannot support an unsupported-insertion accusation here.
The repeated “near” results from flattening mutually exclusive conditional branches in the supplied English script. Only one occurrence would display in a selected edition.
The deadline is present in the governing Original Japanese even though it is commented out in the base witness. It is therefore an Original-edition line, not an unsupported insertion.
小王国 specifically means small kingdoms. “Smaller countries” loses the monarchical structure and turns absolute smallness into a comparative description.
“The same air” is awkward but intelligibly conveys that the knight sensed the same aura or quality in the girl as in his lord. This is a style problem, not a demonstrable material mistranslation.
The source explicitly names Britain, whereas the borrowed Arthurian formula substitutes England, a different polity.
一番多く means killing the greatest number or more people than anyone else. “Kills everyone” instead asserts total indiscriminate slaughter.

“Not even notice” is a defensible rendering of 一顧だにされまい, literally not giving the appearance a glance or consideration. The next sentence’s hypothetical recognition of her sex does not make this rhetorical wording a factual contradiction.
In the knights’ reverential reaction, 神秘 can denote something mystical, miraculous, or divine. Capitalized technical “Mystery” is not the only responsible translation here.
“A dragon in human form” closely conveys 竜の化身, an incarnation or embodiment of a dragon. The alleged disguised-dragon distinction is not compelled by the English.
“Resting her body in the wind” is stiff, but it reasonably depicts her yielding her body to the wind while gazing into the distance. The objection is primarily stylistic.
“Selected her fate” can naturally mean that the sword chose or fixed the fate she would follow. It does not demonstrably contradict 運命を決定した.
何処に explicitly asks where the sword was lost. “How did she lose” asks about manner or cause instead.
The English omits that Shirou fell asleep while watching over Saber, an explicit action establishing his continued bedside care.

Although “uncertain” is closer to 不確かだった, describing a previously unknown true identity as “hidden” is a defensible contextual paraphrase and does not necessarily assert deliberate concealment by a particular agent.
The apparent repetition of “attitude” is caused by flattening mutually exclusive edition branches. The supplied raw script would display either the short or expanded continuation, not both.

The English does omit the vocative “Saber,” but the sentence remains spoken dialogue clearly referring to her. Calling it detached narration overstates a minor address-level loss rather than demonstrating a material error.
息を吐いて explicitly describes breathing out, here as a large sigh. “Take a deep breath” normally describes inhalation and reverses the action.
“Face” is less anatomically specific than 額 but includes the forehead, and the following page immediately specifies that he wipes his forehead. This is not a material contradiction.
In context, 都合のいい事 means a self-serving or conveniently wishful thought. “How selfish of me” is a natural expression of precisely that self-reproach.
“Before she does” naturally substitutes the nearest verb phrase, “wake up,” from the preceding sentence. It does not grammatically require Saber to be the one making a decision.

The English merges the lifeless-house description and ruined-corridor simile into the impression that the house feels abandoned, but preserves the subjective desolation that Shirou immediately attributes to his depression. The spatial compression is not materially misleading.
弓を引いていた says Archer appeared to have been drawing the bow; it does not say he fired arrows. The English assertion directly conflicts with the ensuing reveal that he used no arrows.
“Shoot a bow” is an established English expression meaning to use or discharge a bow; it does not necessarily treat the bow as the projectile. It is a defensible contextual rendering of 弓を引く.
The two instances of “but” belong to nested contrasts: “I don’t know why, but…” and “not using arrows, but only….” The sentence is clumsy but grammatically intelligible and accurate.
嫌味に can describe an offensive, spiteful, or sarcastic manner. “Offensively” is awkward but still attributes the needling quality to Archer’s lip curl rather than merely reporting Shirou’s reaction.

“Follow-through” is a recognized English translation for zanshin in archery, and the subsequent dialogue supplies its broader mental significance. Retaining the Japanese term is not required for accuracy.
The conversation is explicitly about archery, so rendering the otherwise broad 事を済ませた as taking a shot is reasonable contextual specification. The later discussion still develops the moral analogy.

A narrower aspect error survives: 当たると思えば当たっている presents the hit as already settled in the pre-release image, whereas “will hit” moves it into the future. The accusation overstates this as inventing a universal law, since Shirou’s next objection shows that the Japanese itself invites that literal reading.

After Shirou says anyone would hit every time, “Well, you hit the target every time” pragmatically singles Shirou out just as 少なくとも does. だろう here seeks acknowledgment more than it expresses genuine uncertainty.

“See this thing through until the end” is an established English idiom for carrying something through and remaining for its outcome. The added “be able to” is awkward, but the intended obligation remains recoverable and contextually clear.

“See through what happens” is awkward English, but in context it still communicates staying through and observing the consequence. The finding identifies infelicity rather than a demonstrable change in event or agency.

The standard reading of “did not intend to use it until the very end” is that Saber planned to use it at the end. Japanese instead says she apparently intended to refrain from using it all the way through.

“Honest sincerity” is redundant and less precise, but it retains the core claim that Archer speaks sincerely without his usual sarcasm. The preceding factual warning supplies the omitted connection to stating facts.
“Surely” preserves Shirou’s confidence that Saber will refuse but does not convey 頑なに, her explicit adamant or unyielding manner of refusal.
浮かない顔 specifically denotes a glum, troubled, or downcast look. “A serious expression” is emotionally broader and loses the visible dejection Illya notices.
Japanese nonpast 今日は冷える can naturally make a same-day forecast: “It’s going to be cold today.” The wording does not establish that only the present cold is intended.
消えかけてる states that Saber is already disappearing or on the verge of it. “Going to disappear” presents only a future outcome and loses the ongoing deterioration.

The fragment naturally omits a verb such as “know,” and Illya’s immediate answer explains how she knows: she was at the building watching. The context strongly supports mirror moon’s epistemic question, not the accusation’s proposed conduct question.
途切れた marks vision cutting out or being severed, reinforced by the next sentence saying sight is gone. “Fades” changes that abrupt loss into a gradual one.
The English loses both the abrupt ブツリと途切れて and the relieved culmination expressed by ようやく and くれた, replacing the merciful snap into unconsciousness with a neutral gradual fade.

殺させる is causative, but Illya controls the Servant who would perform the killing; English can naturally express that mediated agency as “I can kill you.” The actual threat and Shirou’s vulnerability remain intact.

“At all” does overstate まともに (“properly/decently”), but the surrounding lines separately say Shirou cannot face a Servant, so the finding should not imply that all contextual support for severe incapacity is absent.
滅多刺し denotes repeated stabbing or cutting, not a blunt “beating”; the following sentence expressly describes cuts across his body.

“Around me” is a loose but defensible spatial paraphrase for a disaster immediately surrounding and confronting Shirou. The accusation overstates the small loss of the “before my eyes” image as a factual change.
正義の味方 can naturally denote a hero or superhero fighting for justice. “Superhero” is a defensible cultural rendering here, not unsupported content.
The Japanese explicitly depicts Shirou’s whole body trembling. “Demanding” retains the imperative but removes that physical manifestation.
In immediate contrast with 精神の戦い, English “fighting” naturally means physical or martial fighting. It need not be read as excluding every possible kind of struggle.
“More than ever now” defensibly conveys that repeated experience has forcefully impressed the lesson on Shirou. It softens 嫌というほど but does not establish a material mistranslation.

The preceding instruction is to imagine something capable of winning, and the English immediately continues with imagined images. In that context, “what could I win with?” is a defensible paraphrase of what he must conceive.
手間を増やす can idiomatically mean expending more effort or trouble. The Japanese does not specifically require discrete additional “stages.”
技法 and 無駄だらけの魔術工程 describe the same recalled procedure in apposition. Calling it “the process” does not materially omit a separate technique.
Although カタチにすれば is literally causative, “how was it supposed to take shape?” naturally describes Shirou trying to recall his own formative procedure; his agency remains evident from context.
毛足 refers to the carpet’s pile or fibers. “A long carpet” instead describes its overall length and loses the reason one could sink ankle-deep.
For a fireplace contrasted with decoration, “actually functional” reasonably conveys that it is a working heating fixture. The omission of 今も is minor and does not demonstrate a material error.
“My mind almost falls unconscious” is malformed English; the Japanese simply says his consciousness is beginning to fade.
The English omits the full clause contrasting his present limited movement with his earlier inability to move even a fingertip.
The Japanese makes Shirou’s abduction the burden on weakened Saber. “By letting her know” adds disclosure as the causal mechanism, which the text does not state.
The adjacent Japanese establishes that Shirou met Illya that morning and that night has now fallen. “The other day” incorrectly moves the park encounter to an earlier date.
The governing Original Japanese expressly contains the glare. Its omission or commenting in later editions does not make the Original-edition English an unsupported insertion.
The pout is present in the governing Original Japanese. Later-edition commenting is an edition difference, not evidence that mirror moon invented the reaction.
樹海 can describe a vast, dense forest, and “big forest” preserves the relevant geographic meaning. Losing the metaphorical “sea” is stylistic attenuation, not a demonstrable material error.
邪魔 can denote a nuisance or interfering person. Together with “Nobody will come to save you,” “nor will there be any nuisances” still conveys that no interference will occur.

The complete calm-thought clause is present in the governing Original Japanese. The competing English endings result from flattened conditional branches identified in the supplied caveat, so neither restoration nor duplication establishes a translation error.
Both allegedly inactive lines occur in the governing Original Japanese. Their absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported restoration.
逆らう means resist, defy, or disobey. “Betray” instead presupposes loyalty and morally reframes Shirou’s refusal of Illya’s coercion.
審問 presents the question as a coercive inquisition or judgment over life and death. Adding “want to” recasts that imposed binary as Shirou’s preference.
“You don’t have Saber already” is unidiomatic English and obscures Illya’s assertion that Saber is no longer present.
The sentence about lacking freedom to push Illya away is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its later removal is an edition difference.
“Smiles” defensibly renders 笑う and クスリ need not require a clearly audible chuckle, but it does omit 愉快そう, the explicit indication that Illya is amused.

“It’s my decision if you live or not” clearly communicates Illya’s control over Shirou’s life or death, and the same page soon says “kill you” explicitly. This is not a material euphemization in context.
The English preserves refusal pressure but entirely omits 妖艶さ, the bewitching or sensual quality of Illya’s delivery.

In context, Shirou’s action is his refusal, which Illya expects him to regret after she retaliates by killing Saber and Rin. The English is a reasonable explicitation, not a reassignment of who commits the murders.
The assertion that Illya could accomplish the killings easily appears in the governing Original Japanese. Its later commenting is an edition difference.

“Cheerful” preserves visible pleasure and becomes sinister through the murder context, so the claim that it normalizes her cruelty is overstated. It does, however, lose the intensifier ひどく and the stronger sense that she is actively enjoying this.
“Taking about” is a visible typo for “talking about” in a sentence meant to convey Shirou’s sudden understanding.
The missing separation comes from a stripped line command between “Illya” and “you,” an extraction behavior expressly covered by the supplied caveat, not the archived translation text itself.
駆け引き includes bargaining or negotiation as well as tactical maneuvering. “Haggling” is somewhat narrow but contextually defensible and does not create a material factual error.
The apparent fusion is caused by removal of the line command separating “Kuh” and “damn,” which the supplied caveat identifies as a possible extraction artifact.
The Japanese specifically uses lead, the conventional image of dense dead weight. Steel is a different material and produces an inaccurate comparison.
In “I was bound … without even casting a spell,” the understood subject of “casting” is grammatically Shirou. The Japanese instead describes a paralysis imposed without an incantation.
“Dispel myself” normally means making oneself disappear or removing oneself. The Japanese means dispelling the paralysis or enchantment affecting him.
The Japanese condition is that the invading energy has not become a curse rooted in his body. The English drops 呪詛 and instead makes rootedness of ordinary magical energy the criterion.
The English omits 異なる, which identifies the old ritual as driving a separate or different nerve into his back and supports the contrast with converting existing nerves.

The “switch” is metaphorical and later said not yet to have been found. “Inside of me” is a defensible general rendering of 頭の中 here; the witnesses do not establish a materially distinct anatomical location.
“Suggest myself” is malformed for placing oneself under suggestion and can instead mean proposing oneself. The Japanese clearly describes self-suggestion.
働きかける means act or operate upon; “do anything to the world” is broad but substantially preserves the direct-versus-self-directed contrast explained in the next English sentence.
自己 means the self generally. “Your body” narrows the explanation to bodily transformation and unnecessarily changes the general magus statement into second person.
自分だけの神秘 means a Mystery particular to oneself. “Divine mystery” adds an unsupported association with divinity.

The demonstrable error is that 最初 (“first/foundational”) becomes “very simple,” and the resulting English definition is malformed. Whether 魔術 must specifically be capitalized as “Magecraft” cannot be established from this page alone.
The action is occurring immediately after a process that normally takes an hour, so “an instant” is a defensible idiomatic rendering of こんな短時間 rather than a literal claim of zero duration.
手を離す means releasing one’s grip. “Let my hands go” makes the hands themselves the released object and obscures the cord image confirmed on the next page.
The Japanese warns that the healing might cease to exist one second later, not merely fail on some later occasion. “Next time” removes the immediate uncertainty.
The Japanese gives a concrete threshold: the wrist bindings were not tight enough to stop blood flow. The English reduces this to generic looseness and changes wrists to hands.

The two English alternatives come from flattened conditional edition branches in the supplied raw witness. The caveat expressly warns that such apparent duplication is an extraction artifact rather than a translation error.
軽口 is a light or joking remark. Calling it “stupid” adds a negative judgment absent from the Japanese and loses Shirou’s coping levity.
The surrounding pages identify 乱暴なやり方 as Shirou’s brute-force magical purge. “The movement was too violent” wrongly attributes the internal damage to standing up.
Only the extremities of Shirou’s hands and feet lack sensation. “My limbs are senseless” both broadens the affected area and is poor wording for numbness.

The raw English ends with a line-command dash, corresponding to the Japanese’s deliberately suspended thought. Its disappearance in the supplied display is an extraction artifact, not a missing translated conclusion.
The Japanese is a complete past-tense narrated action. “Answer with a lie” is an isolated, subjectless present-tense fragment rather than coherent narration.
わがままを聞く means accommodating or indulging someone’s demand. “Listen to her selfishness” is nonidiomatic and changes compliance with a request into listening to an abstract trait.
“Unknown uneasiness” is awkward but grammatical and substantially conveys an anxiety of unknown character. Calling it a factual or material error overstates a stylistic weakness.
The fusion results from stripping the line command that separated “but” from “I,” an extraction behavior explicitly covered by the supplied caveat.

The next supplied page explicitly has Illya say she now knows everything about Shirou because of their contract. Broadening the smile’s knowledge anticipates that adjacent statement and is contextually supported, not personal omniscience invented from nowhere.
毒されている describes contamination, poisoning, or corruption by Illya’s magical energy. “Bound” substitutes restraint and blurs the mechanism Shirou rules out.
なった is completed aspect: Illya demands confirmation that Shirou has already become hers. “Will be mine” changes this into future possession.
The apparent fusion is caused by a stripped line command between “right” and “I’ll,” exactly the type of joined-word extraction artifact identified in the supplied caveat.
殴り倒す means striking or punching Illya down. “Push her to the side” materially softens the violence Shirou is desperate enough to contemplate.
The original body is to keep Shirou’s soul functioning, not merely contain it. “Hold your soul” removes that continuing functional role.

The main Japanese term is 転送 in both places, while the ruby differs only between アボート and アポート. The supplied witnesses do not establish two distinct procedures, so normalizing the likely spelling inconsistency is not a demonstrable error.

天衣 literally supports “heavenly garment,” and the supplied Japanese alone does not establish that a particular English proper name is mandatory. The accusation relies on external terminology rather than a proven semantic error.
The English omits Illya’s explicit insistence that she is not at fault, leaving only her subsequent justification that Shirou agreed.
落ち度 concerns Illya’s fault or culpability, while “not mistaken” instead validates the correctness of her view. The preceding claim that she is not to blame makes the shift consequential.
“Honor” omits the explicit supreme bliss of 至福 and substantially softens Sella’s claim that this exceeds what Shirou deserves.
お呼びする specifically concerns how Leysritt addresses Illya. “Speak of Milady like that” makes the rebuke vaguely about tone or content instead.
The raw English contains a line-dash command between “Liz” and “the.” Their apparent fusion is a flattened-script extraction artifact, not the translated presentation.

The sentence’s subject is the earlier “Liz—the one called Leysritt”; her dialogue interrupts that suspended construction before the verb. Leysritt’s agency is therefore recoverable just as it is in Japanese.
The ruby presents からだ (“body”) over 聴覚 (“hearing”). English retains only “body,” losing the deliberate hearing/body double reading central to Shirou’s paradox.
“Hide yourselves with Berserker” naturally conveys that Sella and Leysritt are to hide along with Berserker. The subsequent display and Berserker’s later action remain clear.
The raw English has a dash command between “but” and “I.” The apparent fusion results from stripping that command during extraction.
“Go home to Saber” makes Saber the destination and is a natural rendering of returning to where she is; it does not replace her with a residence.
身を乗り出す describes leaning or lunging out from beside the wall. “Jump from the wall to the door” invents a more definite leap between locations and alters the ambush movement.
今のセイバー expressly limits the warning to Saber in her present condition. “This is no place for you” removes that condition and sounds categorical.
両腕を合わせる means bringing the arms together to simulate restraint. “Cross my arms” ordinarily describes folding them across the chest, which is incompatible with the disguise.
“Comfortable illusion” can naturally mean an emotionally comforting or convenient illusion, not merely physical comfort. In context it conveys Shirou’s suspicion of wishful perception.
“The rope isn’t tied” describes its current untied state. The adjacent explanation that Shirou managed to free himself already establishes that he had genuinely been restrained.
“Take the enemy’s guard down” is not the normal expression for inducing carelessness and can suggest overcoming a guard. The intended causal meaning is needlessly obscured.
A dash command separates “real” and “oh” in the raw script. Their fusion appears only after the command is stripped.
As in the parallel branch, 今の identifies Saber’s present weakened state as the reason for Shirou’s objection; the English omits it.
Placed immediately after Shirou hides, “the sound … follows” adequately conveys prompt succession. It is less emphatic than 間髪いれず but does not establish a material timing error.
フ、ふわふわ is a stammer on “fluffy,” not laughter. “Ha” changes the vocal action and loses the nervous repetition.
密室トリック invokes the established “locked-room trick” expression. “Closed door trick” is nonidiomatic and blunts Shirou’s inflated mystery-story joke.
In this context 呆れきった denotes complete exasperation or incredulous disapproval. “Utterly astonished” changes Saber’s fed-up response into mere surprise.
顔を出す means poking one’s face or head out. “Take my face out of the bed” is materially malformed English and treats the face as a moved object.
The raw script contains a dash command between “Uh” and “well.” “Uhwell” is produced by command stripping rather than the translated line.
The third branch likewise states that the danger is specific to Saber as she presently is. The English again deletes that physical-condition qualification.
“The memorable day of when” is grammatically malformed, and “finally” has no counterpart in the Japanese. Both defects occur in the same celebratory sentence.
In the applause-and-congratulations exchange, “We won’t congratulate you” is a natural contextual response to Illya’s invitation. Losing the exact 迎える repetition is not a factual mistranslation.

The Original-edition witness contains Taiga’s line about Illya taking Shirou by force. The displayed English combines conditional edition variants; this is not an unsupported insertion in an Original comparator.

自分でうんって言った stresses that Shirou himself said yes and can defensibly be paraphrased as accepting willingly within Illya’s self-exculpatory claim. The accusation imports a coercion analysis not stated by this line.
“Paradise” is the governing meaning of パライソ. Translating rather than preserving its archaic loanword flavor is a register choice, not a demonstrable accuracy error.
耽美 evokes affected aestheticism or decadent beauty. “Beautiful and good” reduces it to generic approval and loses the defining comic concept.
The Japanese explicitly lists Taiga, Rin, and Sakura. “You and Sakura” accounts for Taiga and Sakura but drops Rin.
The Original-edition witness explicitly says the H-scene was cut. Its appearance in the English’s Original conditional branch is supported edition content, not an insertion.
“Buruma” directly transliterates the Japanese costume insult. Leaving a culture-specific loanword untranslated may be opaque, but it does not falsify the referent.
一番弟子 commonly denotes the first, senior, or foremost disciple. “Senior student” is within that lexical range and does not necessarily assert age-based seniority.
気合入った can mean having one’s spirit restored or being fired up. Although awkward, “it filled me with spirit” is intelligible in context, with the preceding intervention supplying the cause.
師匠以上に makes the comparison personal: Rin and Illya appear to have more trust than Taiga has with her pupil. The English instead compares their bond with master–student relationships in general.
でござる is an abrupt, conspicuous mock-samurai register and supplies the line’s punchline. The plain English assertion preserves the content but deletes that comic voice.
In this reassurance, “a normal stuffed toy” is a defensible rendering of “merely/just a stuffed toy.” It does not add a materially separate claim.
The Japanese separately states abduction and confinement. “Captured … and taken to a place like this” conveys seizure and transport but omits being imprisoned there.
失格 can directly mean disqualified as well as unfit or a failure. In Saber’s rebuke, “disqualified as a Master” is readily understood as her judgment rather than an official proceeding.
きっぱりと言う means speaking clearly, firmly, or unequivocally. “Speaks clearly” is somewhat weaker stylistically but remains within its lexical range after Saber’s categorical declaration.
思いこみ is a preconceived belief, and “prejudice” can denote precisely such a preconception without discriminatory hostility. “Selfish” also reflects 勝手な in context.
The surrounding contrast is between Saber’s current firm conduct and her earlier weakened appearance. “Saber is meant to act like this” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of こうでなくちゃいけない.

“Is she really, seriously there?” naturally conveys whether Rin is physically present as a real image and compensates for the comic incredulity. Literal retention of 実像 or Japanese politeness is not required for accuracy.
“No need for us come” lacks the required infinitive marker “to,” producing an overt grammatical error.
自分だけは makes the contrast accusatory: Shirou alone survives after burdening everyone else. Bare “and survives” loses that central barb.
The Japanese says Illya explicitly declared she would kill them before leaving. “Went out intending” preserves the goal but deletes the declaration Shirou recalls.
助かった expresses relief—roughly “what a relief” or “that saved us.” “That’s okay” instead signals acceptance or adequacy.

The alleged 俺たちは does not occur here. With 遠坂たち as the stated conditional subject, the omitted subject of 戦う can naturally remain Rin’s party, making “you would have ended up fighting her” defensible.
忍び込む explicitly means sneaking or infiltrating. “Come in like this” removes the stealth that characterizes Rin’s entry into the enemy castle.
強気 here describes Rin’s bold, aggressive nerve in choosing a drastic plan. “Direct” instead suggests straightforward communication and does not fit the repeated causal wording.

The supposedly restored reactions are present as active text in the supplied Original Japanese. Their absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion in this comparator.

The accusation about simultaneously printed competing drafts is an artifact of flattened conditional branches. A narrower error survives in the Original branch: “stupid things” loses 損な’s specific sense of repeatedly choosing self-disadvantaging ideas.
じゃないと…判らなかった says Saber was necessary for Rin to determine Shirou’s location. “Only Saber knew” instead assigns Saber pre-existing knowledge and obscures that instrumental relation.
口喧嘩も結構だが has the concessive sense “quarreling is all very well, but….” The awkward “Disputes are good, but you should stop” retains that concession and does not reverse the final instruction.
“It’s fine if I bear with it” presents the condition as manageable only through endurance, which is substantially what 我慢すれば持ちこたえられる says. It does not necessarily claim harmlessness.
Describing events as “going too fast” is a natural contextual paraphrase for being unable to grasp a sudden development. No consequential chronology change is established.
懸命に describes strenuous, desperate exertion. “Move my body earnestly” is nonidiomatic for that physical effort and substantially weakens Shirou’s condition.
The masculine-pride sentence is active in the supplied Original Japanese and raw Original witness. Its omission from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported English addition.
