The room-exit reaction appears in the supplied Original Japanese. That base/all-ages comment it out does not make its Original-edition translation unsupported.
樹海 denotes an extensive, dense forest or “sea of trees.” “A big forest” is less vivid but accurately communicates the practical geographic warning and is not a material factual change.
In this geographic exchange, “that forest” adequately identifies the particular 樹海 previously mentioned. Omitting the metaphorical “sea of trees” is a stylistic loss, not a demonstrable error.
日数 explicitly raises the possibility that a greater number of days has passed. “It might have been longer” leaves open only unspecified extra duration and loses that scale of fear.

形の上では marks a formal calendar count despite only half a day having elapsed. “Captured for a day now” conventionally asserts elapsed duration and omits the qualification, conflicting with the preceding sentence.
The quotation continues with the same speaker onto the next page and is closed there. Treating the page break as continuation does not obscure a change of speaker or meaning.
This is the continuation of Saber’s still-open quotation from the preceding English page, not unmarked narration or a new speaker. The quotation closes at the end of this page.
The faint-smile narration is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its being commented out in later editions does not make the Original-edition English unsupported.
The boiling-water description is active in the supplied Original Japanese and raw Original witness. It is an edition-specific Original line, not restored unsupported content.
The raw script selects either the Original graphic sentence followed by “But” or the later “It hurts, but” wording. Both appear together only after conditional branches are flattened.
“Needs a hand” is a normal idiom for offering assistance, and the next sentence—Saber would insist on running alone—makes the intended physical support clear.

下りていく does not itself specify running, but the party is urgently escaping and has been running through the castle. “Runs down” is a plausible contextual explicitation, not a demonstrable material choreography error.
国道 is specifically a national highway, but “main road” communicates the relevant destination in natural English. The lost administrative classification does not materially alter the escape route.
呆れた事に can introduce astonishment or incredulity, not only negative exasperation. “It’s amazing” is somewhat positive-sounding but remains defensible in Shirou’s wonder at the thirty-meter passage.
忍び笑い is a suppressed, quiet laugh, and “faint laugh” conveys its subdued audible quality. The omitted suggestion of furtiveness is too slight to establish a material error.
They had previously had their backs to the unseen enemy and have just turned around. “Turn my back on it again” naturally means turning away once more; it does not invent a post-recognition action.
力が判る can mean being able to perceive or appreciate a Servant’s strength. “Can feel the Servant’s strength” is defensible and does not necessarily posit a new supernatural detection faculty.
“Cheerful” accurately conveys the delighted mood in 愉しげに弾んでいる. It is less vivid than “bouncing with delight,” but the reduction is stylistic rather than materially false.
串刺し specifies impaling a captured insect. Generalizing this to “kill” removes the concrete act used to characterize Illya’s innocent cruelty.

The English fragment functions as an apposition to the preceding smile, while the relative clause personifies “emotion” much as the Japanese modifier does. Its awkwardness does not create a separate agency error beyond the valid loss of impalement.
詰め marks a final no-move/checkmated position. “Done for now” both loses that tactical finality and can imply only a temporary setback.
The Japanese explicitly characterizes the choice as dying in vain; “pointless” leaves the death unstated and materially softens the only remaining course.
一時的に expressly limits the release of Berserker’s reason. The English supplies no equivalent temporal limit.
Despite awkward syntax, “cold, killing her emotions” still conveys a cold voice produced by suppressing emotion. The alleged agency change is not a material mistranslation.
“Quietly nods” is a defensible description of a restrained, slight nod; substituting manner for degree does not materially change the action.
The English retains the taunt about Rin having a cute side, while the immediately preceding surprise language helps preserve the unexpectedness. The omitted nuance is minor.
とんでもない judges the proposition as outrageous or unthinkable in context, not merely unforeseen. “Unexpected” substantially weakens Shirou’s reaction.
The missing closing punctuation is attributable to the continuing-line controls, but アンタ is genuinely lost: Rin begins “Archer, you—,” not merely “Archer—.”
Here the lobby has become physically too distant for intervention; “now far away” is a natural contextual rendering of 手の届かない場所.
The demonstrative is permissible contextual recognition of a known type of weapon, and “I don’t know when he got it” preserves its sudden appearance. No false prior introduction is established.
This is Original-edition narration, not an unsupported insertion; it appears expressly in originalJa even though later editions omit it.

Although 国道 is more specifically a national highway, “main road” reasonably communicates the major road Rin is using as their escape landmark. The lost administrative classification is not material here.
The page explicitly contrasts a lack of fatigue with movement-aggravated pain. Omitting the first half obscures that his limitation is pain rather than stamina.
俯く describes Saber answering with her head lowered; it is not a nod of affirmation. The English substitutes a different visible gesture.
“As she falls” can naturally describe catching someone during the incipient fall and does not say she hits the ground. The following grab preserves the arrested fall.
手 can encompass the hand/arm in this bodily description and need not establish an exact singular count. “Small and weak” imperfectly but defensibly conveys her frail, strengthless limb.
The apparent fusion is produced by stripped line-delay controls, not the underlying translation’s meaning. It should not be certified as a translation error from this flattened witness.
In a forest, “narrow openings” can naturally denote the narrow gaps or ways Rin chooses through the trees. It remains a traversable route and is not materially different.
遠慮していた denotes reserve or reluctance to entrust her weight; “unwilling” is broad but defensible in light of Saber’s preceding resistance and reluctant compliance.
Even allowing for stripped pause controls, “I can’t, let this” fails to express the defiant fragment “this little/at this level—” and points toward a different unfinished thought.
The Japanese gives the concrete sign that Saber’s clothing is soaked with sweat. Merely saying her body is sweating removes the stated degree and visible condition.

In context, “using all her energy” is a defensible explicitation of her collapsing in a weakened, magically depleted state after using the Noble Phantasm. It does not establish a materially contradictory resource claim.
Shirou abruptly strikes his back against the tree to stop his fall. “Leaning” removes both the collision in ぶつけて and the force of the reflexive brace.
斬り殺す means killing by cutting or slashing; in this comic threat, “cut me in half” is a vivid natural paraphrase with the same lethal action, not a consequential factual invention.
“Saber speaks in my arms” is slightly unusual but readily means that she speaks while being held, accurately preserving her position.
The entire reaction is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence of mirror moon invention.
“Idiot” preserves Rin’s direct comic insult. Dropping the augmentative 大 slightly reduces force but does not amount to a material translation error.
The refusal is expressly present in originalJa. It is Original-edition prose omitted in later witnesses, not an unsupported English restoration.
でもなんでも broadens Shirou’s resolve to a Command Spell or any other means. Ending at “the Command Spell and—” does not communicate that breadth.
士郎 explicitly identifies Shirou as the person who already agreed. Addressing Saber with “You said it’s okay” assigns that authorization to the wrong character.

The supplied Original page moves directly from Shirou identifying the ruin to Rin’s explanation. The two intervening sentences about holding Saber and the building’s condition have no supplied Original counterpart.
The raw Original candidate contains this staging line verbatim on an adjacent differently numbered page. This is an alignment issue, not an unsupported insertion.

The supplied Original page contains only the concise encroachment, usable-area, and moonlight description. The added collapse, rubble, abandonment, and desecrated-corpse narration is unsupported by those witnesses.
The Japanese says only part of the second floor is usable as a room. The English invents multiple usable rooms and a ranking that makes the present one the best.
The source states that strong moonlight illuminates the interior. Seeing the night sky is a different observation and omits the room’s illumination.
A bed beside a window can also be against the wall containing that window. The English is more specific, but the supplied spatial descriptions do not demonstrate a contradictory relocation.
キザ covers affected, conceited, or ostentatiously suave behavior. Given Archer’s grand boast, “arrogant” is within its defensible contextual range, though less elegant.
The supposedly inserted delivery appears verbatim in the supplied raw Original candidate. Its absence from the later active Japanese is an edition/alignment difference.
倒す unambiguously means defeating Berserker at this place. “Get Berserker here” can instead mean bringing or obtaining him and fails to state the resolved attack.

The supplied raw Original candidate reads 左手に右拳を打ち付ける, which matches striking the left hand with the right fist. The contrary active-edition wording is an edition difference, so reversal is not established for this comparator.
In the immediate context of Rin believing Archer lost, 悔やむ naturally includes grieving or mourning him. “Mourning is over” is narrower but contextually defensible.
戦えば死ぬ is subjectless and can function as the generic “whoever fights him dies,” especially after Berserker is said to destroy everything he touches. The universal reading is defensible.
The English sentence is unquoted internal narration, so “What am I saying?” need not mean audible speech; it naturally represents Shirou rebuking his own thought.
“Replenish her stocks” naturally means supplying the needed magical energy, without necessarily asserting a complete refill. The unspecified threshold in 一定量 is adequately implicit.
庭 literally permits “yard” or “garden,” and the surrounding forest and castle make the broader extent clear. The informal choice does not materially misstate Illya’s territory.

The “herethere” fusion results from a stripped control marker between translated clauses. The underlying clauses preserve both “here” and the following “there may be,” so this is an extraction artifact.
“Like going to die” is awkward but conveys that deliberately searching the castle would amount to entering mortal danger. The lethal inference is not materially weakened.
The supplied raw Original candidate says there is exactly one other method, matching the English. The later edition’s わずかな方法 is not governing for this Original comparator.

“Correct the path” is a concise rendering of restoring the explicitly imperfect path to proper operation; the following page immediately specifies reconnection. No material technical contradiction results.
The Japanese makes placing Shirou and Saber into a shared resonance state a distinct prerequisite before reconnecting the spiritual path. That operation is wholly absent here.

The supplied Original page ends after defining the circuit as a magus’s existential value. The additional question appears only as commented later-edition text and has no supplied active Original counterpart.
“Transplanted on dying people” is clumsy, but “on” can describe performing the procedure on those patients, and the severe rejection meaning remains clear. This is not a material accuracy failure.
誰も refers contextually to the people whose survival Rin and Saber are discussing. Inclusive “we” naturally denotes that entire immediate group rather than excluding a relevant outsider.
精神の一部 is part of Shirou’s mind, spirit, or self, not part of his physical nerves. The English replaces the stated spiritual mutilation with a different anatomical loss.

The blueprint analogy is absent from the supplied active Original page, which proceeds directly from the fatal defect to permanent incompleteness. Its restoration is unsupported by that governing witness.

The source specifically describes the normal prospect of an immature magus accumulating experience and becoming fully fledged. “Hope of becoming complete” removes both experience and professional maturation.

Within the surrounding contrast between completed and deficient magi, “stay incomplete” defensibly expresses remaining 半人前. The professional implication is supplied by “as a magus” in the preceding sentence.
“Her eyes look as if they’re in regret” is awkward but readily conveys that her lowered eyes appear immersed in regret. The visual and emotional content survives.
The Japanese specifically says Shirou does not know this kind of magical formula or procedure. The generic, malformed “I don’t know how from the first place” omits that technical object.

Japanese itself describes preventing one’s mind from becoming disturbed; “without getting too disturbed” preserves that desired mental state. Passive English grammar does not transfer agency to another actor.
“Screening” can mean shielding or an intervening screen, especially in technical language. Though unnatural here, the contrast with maximizing contact makes the intended physical barrier clear.
強がる identifies Saber as putting on a brave or strong front despite her weakness. “Don’t say that” only rejects her words and drops Rin’s diagnosis of her behavior.
誤魔化す can mean disguise or conceal an emotion as well as distract oneself from it. “Hide my nervousness” is a defensible reading of Shirou’s meticulous folding.
“How hard the transplant is” can naturally encompass how difficult it is to bring the procedure to a successful outcome. The English is less explicit but not materially different.
In context, “the fight against Berserker” is the ordeal of defeating him; it preserves the future danger contrasted with this mere intermediate step. The wording is compressed, not materially false.

The supplied active Original page moves from Shirou’s reply directly to forgetting to breathe. The snow/marble and open-blouse description appears only as inactive later-edition text, with no supplied active Original support.
覆い被さる means positioning oneself over or on top of someone so as to cover them. “Get on top of Saber” is contextually and geometrically defensible, even if sexually suggestive.
同調 is the technical synchronization or attunement required by the procedure. “Sympathize” ordinarily denotes emotional fellow-feeling and misstates the magical operation.
The English is Japanese-shaped and stylistically poor, but its meaning—that Shirou cannot take in their conversation—is readily recoverable and accurate.
肌が触れあうほど marks the degree of closeness—close enough for skin to touch—without necessarily asserting completed contact. “Almost touching” is a defensible rendering.
As elsewhere in this procedure, 同調 means magical synchronization or attunement. “Sympathize with Saber” substitutes an ordinary emotional meaning.
The omitted 前に is recoverable from the explicit contrast with exiting through the back; “opposite direction” followed by “out of my chest” adequately conveys a forward/frontward exit.
Although awkward, “breathing is starting to become lively” can convey breath becoming animated or vigorous; it does not necessarily impose cheerfulness.

The Japanese makes the complete separation occur in response to the voice. The English instead supplies a distinct first-person act of answering before the separation, suggesting a reply not stated in Japanese.
“Naked” can figuratively mean exposed or stripped bare. The surrounding “no arms, legs, or self” prevents a reasonable reading of ordinary physical nudity.
“It feels like I’m running back in time” expressly retains the source’s hypothetical comparison; it does not assert literal time travel.

“Rather” contrasts being left behind with the preceding impression of running, thereby preserving the essential active-motion-versus-passive-displacement correction even without translating 翔ける separately.
鏃 specifically denotes an arrowhead, but “dart” retains the image of a small pointed projectile penetrating barriers. The distinction is not materially consequential here.
The circuit is the route along which the sparks race, not their point of origin. “Fly from” changes that spatial relation.
走馬燈 evokes the rapid panorama of memories or life review. “Concentrated life” loses that established image and reduces it to an abstract life.
“Digitalization” is supported by 数値化, so that part is not conceptually wrong. The genuine loss is 人体運営: the operation or functioning of the human body is reduced to merely “human.”
The Japanese says the immense number of junctions forms rings or circuits around the mechanisms. The English recasts the junctions merely as a means of connecting organs and omits 輪を作る.
The accusation overlooks the ruby: 思考 is explicitly read いま, so “present time” is supported. The narrower loss is the written-kanji layer “thought,” which creates a deliberate dual meaning.
The English identifies Artoria but entirely drops the explicit contrast distinguishing her circuits from Emiya Shirou’s.
“Squashed by a strong force” substantially conveys the vise-like compression, though less specifically. The narrower genuine omission is the bubbling or simmering quality expressed by ぐつぐつ.

Using “mile” as a familiar literary distance unit is a defensible localization of 里, especially because the passage’s operative contrast is between a vast distance and one unit, not an exact conversion.
In the context of a spell, “sympathizing” can denote sympathetic resonance or attunement rather than emotional compassion. It is clumsy terminology but not demonstrably the alleged semantic error.
In a path through total darkness, inability to see forward or backward naturally amounts to being unable to see anywhere relevant. The English is reasonable contextual generalization.
“There is an end to this infinite path” is readily understood as calling the apparently endless path “infinite”; the same sentence immediately denies literal infinity by announcing its end.
The mid-word cutoff is deliberate presentation, not accidental truncation: the Japanese likewise stops 辿り着く at 辿り着 before the interruption command.

The raw English places “Not a sound” inside the non-Realta conditional, while the archived Japanese merely comments it out for the later-edition branch. Its presence is therefore consistent with Original-edition branching, not an unsupported restoration.
俯瞰 can figuratively mean surveying or taking in the whole picture, not necessarily occupying a literal overhead viewpoint. “Stare at the full scenery” is awkward but conveys viewing the total scene.
“Stalled” can describe something stopped or inactive, which fits the motionless fuel reserve and the surrounding explanation that the core has ceased operating.
人間が抱く makes humans the ones harboring or conceiving the threats. “Threats to mankind” instead makes humanity the threats’ target.
貴い has a lexical range including noble, exalted, precious, venerable, and sacred. In this mythic description, “sacred star” is defensible.
“The symbol, fear and king” is grammatically malformed and fails to express clearly that the dragon reigns as the emblematic, awe-inspiring sovereign among Phantasmal Species.
幻想種 is the setting’s broader technical category, “Phantasmal Species.” Rendering it as “beasts” improperly narrows the taxonomy.
“Absurd” can idiomatically express something wildly beyond ordinary scale or standards, a viable rendering of 規格外 here; ridicule or illogic is not forced.
言語を絶する means to exceed description or beggar language. “Eradicates all words” invents an act of destroying words and supplies the wrong grammatical relation.
The omitted experiencer is the observer/eater who could not bear food remaining alive. “It cannot bear it” instead makes the food itself unable to endure something.
The source specifically identifies pain perception—read by ruby as consciousness—as what would make eating living food too cruel. Generic cruelty in “keeping it alive” loses both elements.
“Appeal my pain” is not grammatical English and does not clearly convey giving voice to or protesting one’s suffering.
かみ砕く means to bite or chew something to pieces. “Bitten on” is malformed and reduces the continuing crushing mastication to an ordinary bite.
意識 is consciousness or awareness, not the senses. The substitution changes the faculty collapsing during the ordeal.
Rendering an image that “revived” in memory as “I recall her figure” is a normal English perspective shift and preserves the event’s substantive function.
Shirou is roused or encouraged by the anguish’s significance. “I exhilarate the significance” reverses the relation and uses “exhilarate” ungrammatically.
The explicit 文字通り activates the literal pain inside 痛感 while Shirou is physically suffering. “Fully realize” conveys intensity but loses that deliberate wordplay.
The passive 守られた recalls the repeated protection bound up with Saber’s trust. “Trust she kept many times” is unidiomatic and does not convey Shirou having been protected repeatedly.
In context, “I cannot fight” naturally describes his present lack of any means to fight; it does not establish an absolute incapacity beyond the situation.
Both occurrences concern consciousness: it is shattering, yet he sharpens it like a blade. Replacing it twice with “senses” breaks the sequence about preserving awareness.
わずかでも can express even a brief duration, and the immediately preceding equation of eternity with an instant supports “even for an instant.” The claimed degree-only reading is not established.
“Delicate” can mean finely wrought or intricately detailed, not merely fragile. That sense is compatible with 緻密 and the circuit imagery.
おぼつかない describes an unsteady, hazy, or unreliable state. “Dizzy mind” is a plausible compact rendering after Shirou has just regained awareness, even if not the only choice.
The accusation ignores the ruby: 後遺症 is explicitly read トラウマ. “Could’ve been a trauma” follows that supplied reading, though its English phrasing is awkward.
しっとりした肌触り can describe pleasantly soft, smooth, or supple skin and need not mean literally wet skin. “Soft skin” is defensible in this tactile context.

どんな状態 broadly asks what situation or condition they are in. “What we’re doing” is a natural contextual paraphrase of their compromising posture and does not necessarily assert deliberate sexual activity.
意識する can mean being conscious of or self-conscious about another person. The following inability to meet eyes supplies the embarrassed nuance even if the English is stiff.
丹念 describes the care and thoroughness of the folding. “Extremely folded-up” is nonidiomatic and converts careful workmanship into physical degree.
Here 同調 denotes the magical synchronization used for the transplant. The ordinary construction “sympathized with Saber” instead states emotional fellow-feeling.
The English entirely omits Shirou closing his eyes and deliberately assessing his condition before reporting the diagnostic result.
After the preposition “between,” the object form “me” is required. “Between Saber and I” is demonstrably ungrammatical.
A “weak link” can mean a faint or tenuous connection, which is within the ordinary range of 微かなライン. It does not necessarily declare the bond defective.
In Saber’s self-reproach, “so useless” is a strong but contextually viable rendering of being so inadequate or lacking in power; the clause itself limits the judgment to this failure.
“All this was caused because I couldn’t supply you” preserves Shirou’s admission that his failure harmed Saber; the hardship is implicit in both the direct object “you” and the surrounding crisis.
スッキリする commonly means to feel better, relieved, or unburdened. The English is compatible with Shirou’s light attempt to dismiss the loss and does not necessarily assert improved medical health.

接する need not mean being physically pressed together; it can mean interacting or being together. “We spent the night dressed like that” conveys their revealing state and overnight proximity, while earlier context already establishes bodily contact.
不覚を取る can denote making a serious blunder as well as being caught off guard or defeated. “Make a mistake” is weaker in tone but remains within its contextual range.
“Not a morning person” naturally conveys Rin’s grogginess and lack of her usual sharpness; “like a different person” retains the resulting contrast. This is reasonable compression.
Given Rin’s acknowledgment followed immediately by standing up for the impending battle, “then let’s go” is defensible contextual explicitation of the elliptical じゃあ、いいわね.
“The silent forest” is a natural collective rendering of the silent trees, and “on the other side” need only mean beyond them rather than across the woodland’s full extent.
The abstract 多くの意味 can naturally become “many significant things” in English, referring to the meaningful experiences or exchanges of the night. The rendering is vague but defensible.

The Japanese itself describes reciprocal killing and annihilation, then specifies that the battle ended with the red knight’s disappearance. The English preserves that same qualification and fits Berserker’s repeated restorations.
穿たれている describes holes driven or bored through successive layers. “Many walls have been knocked down” changes penetration into wholesale collapse.

“Destroyed time” is an intensified but intelligible poetic continuation of the preceding total destruction, clarified by the next sentence about the room no longer resembling itself two hours earlier.

The apparent duplication is flattened conditional output. The Original witness has 溶解しかけている, supporting “almost melted,” while the later-edition 崩壊 branch supports “broken down”; they are not simultaneously printed alternatives in the script.
貫かれている denotes a wound piercing through the body. “Slashed” changes it to a cutting wound.

The apparent pair is conditional edition output, not an insertion followed by a competing translation. Original Japanese states that the internal organs are visible, while the later version replaces this with an abdominal cavity.
The source supplies a definite span, 半刻. “Much earlier” removes the stated duration and only gives a relative ordering.

やられる can mean being beaten, defeated, or taken down; it does not itself require “killed.” The following Japanese even characterizes Archer’s attacks as near-fatal, so “defeated six times” is defensible.
致命傷に近い expressly qualifies the attacks as approaching fatal-wound purity. “Fatal blow” removes that qualification and states the stronger result outright.
Standard English requires “a few minutes.” The missing article is an objective grammatical defect in the displayed sentence.

The fused form results from stripping the [line2] interruption command from “But[line2]restoring.” It is an extraction artifact, not evidence that the rendered game text concatenates the words accidentally.

The apparent duplication is flattened edition branching. The Original witness explicitly contains 犯すなり殺すなり, supporting “rape,” while the later edition substitutes 殺すなり弄ぶなり and the English script conditionally substitutes “toy with.”
In this threat context, “quickly” defensibly conveys killing Shirou before Illya can subject him to the especially cruel death she intends; the accusation overstates a lexical distinction.
“Smiling” omits both the small audible chuckle marked by くすり and the explicit delight marked by 愉しげ, materially flattening Illya’s enjoyment.
This is an Original-edition clause, not an unsupported insertion. The supplied raw Original witness explicitly says Saber received energy from Shirou.
The dawn narration is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its being commented out in the later base witness is an edition difference, not an Original-comparator translation error.
The apparent juxtaposition is caused by flattened conditional branches. The archived English contains mutually exclusive sensations and memories readings, not both in one displayed version.
“Made love to” and “contact with” are mutually exclusive edition branches, not one malformed phrase. The supplied raw Original also has the explicitly sexual 抱いた.
The softness-and-pleasure reflection is present in Original Japanese; its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported restoration.
The tactile and vision passages belong to mutually exclusive edition branches. Their apparent duplication results from flattening the conditional script.
The two clauses are alternative conditional renderings for different editions, not consecutive prose in the actual script presentation.
The raw English contains a line-length dash command between “Y” and “Yeah,” representing a controlled stammer. “YYeah” is an extraction artifact.
The Japanese specifies decapitation as the absolute ambush condition; generic “kill him” loses the concrete planned wound.
打ち合い contrasts with exchanging blows, whereas “outside of battle” can incorrectly suggest defeating him without combat rather than striking outside the normal exchange.
In this tactical context, “best suited for this role” is a defensible paraphrase of Rin being the one most free and able to maneuver.
The Shirou-supplied-energy clause is present in the raw Original Japanese and is paired with an Original-edition English branch. The apparent doubled clause comes from branch flattening.
The English makes the loss of bodily maintenance certain, while おそらく explicitly presents it as Saber’s probable prognosis.
The source identifies reduced purity, a measure reused in the surrounding technical discussion; “not full force” substitutes generic power and loses that distinction.
Rin says her interference would actively hinder Saber, not merely that it would provide little help; this changes the tactical consequence.
そんな気 refers to staying away from the battlefield. The English instead invents someone telling Shirou to participate, reversing the relevant condition.
“Hold up” is a loose but contextually harmless rendering of taking the branch in hand; no consequential display action is established.
“A real one” can naturally mean a proper, workable bow here. The following admission that it looks unlike Archer’s does not make that functional reading contradictory.
“Concept of creation” is an awkward but defensible rendering of the concept or ideal by which the bow was created; the alleged process/object reversal is not established decisively.
想定 includes assumptions, suppositions, and hypothetical scenarios. “Formulate every hypothesis” is stiff but remains within its lexical range.
In context, “shaped right” can mean the branch has at least been brought into the intended form, not that it is an accurate or attractive replica; the following criticism supplies the qualification.
“It’s enough for now” can idiomatically mean the present result will do and the interrupted concern can be left aside. The deferral is not materially lost.

“Normal magic” contextually denotes ordinary, nonexceptional magic and contrasts with the required maximum-purity/A-ranked attack. This is imprecise but defensible, including mirror moon’s established use of “magic” for 魔術.
The raw English has a line-length dash command between “see” and “if”; the fused “seeif” is an extraction artifact.
The source script ends the utterance with a line-length dash command rather than ordinary punctuation. Its apparent absence results from command stripping.
Shirou explicitly says 死ぬ, while Saber herself uses 消える on the next page. Replacing his direct, personal “die” with the Servant euphemism erases that deliberate emotional contrast.
“Declares” itself conveys a firm, definite statement; requiring an additional adverb for きっぱり is stylistic preference rather than a demonstrable error.
“That makes me happy” naturally refers to the immediate answer in context. It is somewhat less emphatic than ひどく but does not materially mistranslate Shirou’s reaction.
とんでもない describes Saber’s outrageous or astonishing comic observation; “ominous” introduces foreboding absent from the exchange.
Grabbing Saber’s hand as she pitches forward adequately conveys Shirou catching and supporting her; omitting the exact pulling direction and his position is not a material change here.
The Japanese and raw English end the warning with a line-length dash command. The apparently missing punctuation is produced by stripping that command.
In the immediately stated blushing context, “looks like me from earlier” plainly compares Saber’s embarrassed appearance/state to Shirou’s, not their physical features.

The possessive “Saber’s sensations” can mean Shirou’s remembered sensations of Saber, and the preceding “Her hand in mine” fixes the tactile context. It does not necessarily assign the experience to Saber.
“We start to go” is weaker than 足を速めた, but the hurried dialogue already says “hurry” and the forced retreat remains clear; the loss is minor, not material.
An English future statement can naturally express the speaker’s expectation conveyed by だろう; the slight modal tightening does not materially change the scene.

The repeated “battlefield” is only flattened conditional-branch debris, but the Original Japanese supplied for this page contains no counterpart to “suppressing my beating heart.” The finding should be narrowed to that unsupported clause.
腰が抜ける means one’s legs give way or collapsing from shock. “Lose my legs” is an unnatural literalization that suggests limb loss rather than the idiom.
“Jumping off a bridge” is a defensible localization of the Kiyomizu-stage leap idiom and preserves the desperate-commitment metaphor; the following fall into a pit still works.
ぐんにゃり adds Shirou’s comic wilting or buckling to the astronomical scale. “It’s astronomical” retains only magnitude and deletes the phrase’s central joke and reaction.
In game terminology ダメージ is mass-noun “damage.” “Damages” normally means monetary compensation and is grammatically wrong here.
The raw English contains a line-length dash command between “Uh” and “no.” Their fusion is an extraction artifact, not source presentation.
強がり is bravado or a strained show of confidence, not sincere courage. The English mischaracterizes Shirou’s bluff.
“Controls my life” naturally conveys the result of having the reins of his life. Dropping the animal image is a stylistic compression, not a factual mistranslation.
The forest is explicitly cast in a hazy white by the mist. “Darkened” reverses that visual quality.

“Must be because of him” remains a strong identification of Berserker as the pressure’s source, supported by Shirou recognizing a sensation he has felt before. The ownership/causation distinction is not material here.
俺たちの手 means Rin takes the hands of both Shirou and Saber. Singular “my hand” demonstrably removes Saber from the action.
“Too much space here” is a natural contextual rendering of excessive width in the clearing; the following range explanation makes the tactical problem clear.
In a lethal battle, やられる naturally permits “be killed,” and Rin’s warning is about their potentially fatal defeat. “Die too easily” is defensible.
The immediately preceding English says Rin is “super fast,” which carries the emphasized efficiency into her movement and climb. The competence is not materially omitted from the complete page.
This sentence is valid Original-edition text, and “quiet voice” omits the expressly stated strength in Saber’s assurance.
率いられて makes the white girl the leader of Berserker’s entrance. “Along with” reduces them to mere accompaniment and removes Illya’s agency.
殺気立つ specifically indicates bristling murderous intent. “Worked up” reduces this to generic agitation despite Saber being on the verge of attacking.
English “must have finished” is itself an inferential construction, not an assertion of witnessed fact, and appropriately renders Shirou’s self-directed か speculation.
The Japanese states that Rin and the pair parted ways, without assigning unilateral agency. “She left us behind” recasts this as Rin abandoning them.
“You two would be a burden” describes Shirou and Saber collectively as an encumbering pair; it does not require that each be independently burdensome and preserves Illya’s reasoning.
“She” and “Knowing her, she” are mutually exclusive edition branches in the raw script. Their apparent adjacency is branch-flattening debris.
森への出入り refers to people entering and leaving the forest. “Sense the boundaries” instead describes perceiving geographical edges and misstates Illya’s detection capability.
The missing separation after “still” comes from a stripped line-length dash command. The negative-question construction is also a permissible rendering of ではないか, not an independent polarity error.

The thought concerns whether Illya can still turn back or start over despite this cruelty. Making “cold-heartedness” itself something to be “recovered” assigns recovery to the wrong entity and obscures her moral recoverability.
“Nod to her words” is slightly Japanese-shaped but readily means assent to her proposal in context. This is stylistic awkwardness, not an accuracy error.
A line-length dash command separates “body” and “it’s” in the raw English. Their fusion is an extraction artifact.
The alternatives come from flattened edition branches. Crucially, the supplied raw Original Japanese says 狂いなさい, so “Go mad” is valid for this Original-edition comparator rather than an insertion.
昏い figuratively describes a dark, gloomy, or lifeless tone. “A dead voice” is a defensible ominous rendering, not a demonstrable factual change.
A line-length dash command separates “insane” and “and” in the raw English; the fused form is an extraction artifact.
The Japanese says his capabilities themselves magnify into a misshapen mass. The English instead makes Berserker’s body deform and swell while the abilities separately increase.
The repeated wording consists of mutually exclusive edition branches around a conditional. It is not duplicated in an actual selected script path.
“Uneasy” can convey fear or apprehension in Saber’s voice, and the next sentence explicitly says she shudders. The difference from 畏れ is one of degree, not a material error.
Although “attacks” alone is less exact than 迎え撃つ, the same sentence says Saber acts “as if stopping a meteor,” preserving the defensive head-on interception.
“The return of legends” is a literary paraphrase presenting legendary combat as returning in the present. Myth/legend and reenactment/return are acceptable alternatives here.

The Japanese says every one of Saber’s sword strikes is made with her whole strength. The English singularizes the countless exchanges into “a blow” and ambiguously makes that blow the thing diverted.
体力 can denote physical strength or stamina, and “remaining strength” is a defensible, if awkward, rendering of their remaining endurance. The plural follows the two combatants.
After passive “be,” the required participle is “shredded,” not “shred.” This is a demonstrable grammatical error.
Japanese 剣 is not obligatorily singular here, and the sparks arise amid the two combatants’ clashing weapons. “The swords” is contextually defensible.
“Constantly putting herself in fatal situations” conveys repeated, immediate mortal danger. It compresses the one-second and vortex imagery but does not materially alter the situation.

The source deliberately uses a noun fragment, but English “surpassing human” is still grammatically defective because singular “human” cannot serve this adjectival/comparative function without a noun.
A line-length dash command separates “appears” and “and” in the raw English. Their fusion is an extraction artifact.
ようとして marks an impending ground impact. “As she hits the ground” makes the impact completed, changing Saber’s uninterrupted recovery before her renewed charge.
A line-length dash command separates “ground” and “she” in the raw English. “Groundshe” is extraction damage, not a source-text defect.
The Japanese says creating an opening is no longer even feasible; “not even trying” instead attributes the failure to Saber's volition or effort.
The explicit probability marker is lost, making Shirou's forecast materially more certain.
じゃないか presents a forceful rhetorical realization, not mere possibility. In context, “All I’m doing is distracting Saber” is a defensible natural paraphrase of the conclusion.
The curse is present in the governing Original text; its absence from the later Japanese witnesses is an edition difference, not an English insertion.
The repeated curses belong to the governing Original edition. The apparent fused words result from stripped line commands in the supplied rendering, not demonstrable translation text.
The clipped 走って leads directly into a counterfactual about running up to Berserker. “If I ran…” is a defensible way to connect that fragment rather than a demonstrable loss of a self-command.
“Them” is contextually defensible as the combatants, but the translation genuinely omits that Berserker's back is turned, an important part of the hypothetical opportunity.

The lightning wording is present in Original, while “comes down” belongs to the alternate edition branch. Their simultaneous appearance is the supplied conditional-flattening artifact, not a translation error.
Although “cleaves the ground” would be more exact, “breaks the ground” adequately conveys the sword cutting destructively into the earth; the accusation is chiefly lexical preference.
砕ける denotes breaking or shattering under pressure, whereas “grind … down” describes gradual abrasion and changes the physical image.
“Defeat that mountain” naturally preserves the metaphorical point that the giant must be overcome with a sword. Rendering 切り崩す more literally would be stylistic refinement, not a material correction.
The English omits a stated property of the imagined sword: its edge never chips. That durability is pertinent to the weapon Shirou needs.
The two English phrasings are flattened conditional edition variants. Moreover, Original itself uses the “going mad” wording, so it is not an unsupported duplicate translation.
In this battle context, explicating that the coughing Saber doubles over “in pain” is a reasonable inference and does not contradict the Japanese.
The apparent missing separator comes from stripping the supplied line command at an intentionally suspended clause; it is not established as an error in the displayed translation.
The raw English contains a line command between the words; its removal created the apparent fusion. This is an extraction artifact, not demonstrable published typography.
The apparent “swingand” fusion is caused by a stripped line command separating the clauses, so the supplied witnesses do not establish a translation defect.
懐に入る specifically means Saber has penetrated into Berserker's close guard. Merely placing her “right in front” loses the tactical advantage that prevents his escape.
“Places both hands on her sword” reasonably conveys taking up a renewed two-handed grip. The missing “re-” nuance is not independently material.
The English omits Saber's further step into the giant immediately before her full-strength cut, removing a stated part of the maneuver.
本命 means the real, primary, or intended main attack. Calling it the “final” attack adds a distinct temporal claim not made by the Japanese.

The English witnesses contain conditional long and short incantation variants for different editions. Their consecutive appearance is the warned branch-flattening artifact, not two incantations shown together in one branch.
Original explicitly identifies the matter as 脳漿, so specifying gore is not an unsupported insertion. The surviving error is narrower: 脳漿 means brains or brain matter, not “spinal fluid.”

Original separately contains the reaction that the gore prevents unreserved celebration and the conclusion that the attack was not excessive. The apparent duplication combines edition branches rather than inventing these thoughts.
Read with the preceding “In it…,” the inversion has a subject and predicate. Referring to Berserker's face despite his head supposedly having been blown away is sufficiently faithful, if awkward.

“Something like that” naturally refers back to an external weapon such as the bow or rock, and the following sentence immediately identifies his body as the Noble Phantasm. The inference is not materially obscured.

Using the supplied ruby reading “God Hand” as the English proper name is a defensible localization choice, especially because the immediately preceding explanation explicitly discusses the twelve labors.
The Japanese expressly identifies the gods as the agents who placed the immortality curse; that causal attribution is absent from the English.
引きはがす permits forcefully pulling or tearing something away, and “they won’t even budge” makes clear that Rin is trying to break the grip rather than amputate the fingers.
“What lies ahead” frames the crushed figure as the impending result Shirou envisions. The participial “crushed” does not require that the destruction has already occurred.
吐き捨てた depicts violently casting those considerations aside. “Forget” instead suggests an involuntary lapse of memory and changes Shirou's agency.
Generalizing daikon to “a vegetable” preserves the ordinary chopping comparison and is a defensible naturalization, not a factual mistranslation.
A stripped line command accounts for the apparent fusion; the raw supplied text does not establish that “WhaShirou” appears that way in display.
Japanese often leaves number implicit, and the preceding 指 is naturally plural. Given that Shirou struck with a bow, “hands” is not demonstrably incompatible with the scene.
“Raise my face” is awkward English but accurately describes 顔をあげる. This is a fluency criticism rather than an accuracy error.
The apparent fused breaths result from a stripped line command between the vocalizations, not a demonstrated typography error in the actual script.
The missing separation is explained by the stripped line command in the raw English. The underlying sentence distinguishes Saber's exclamation from her command.
In context, “the body that should have dodged” expresses Shirou's mistaken expectation that he had evaded the blow. It is awkward but does not impose a normative duty.
The surrounding sentences clearly scope “Nothing should be impossible” to reconstructing the weapon from a model. English need not restate that scope in every sentence.
“Work” and “time” are within the ordinary contextual ranges of 制作 and 年月. The chain remains recognizable and no concrete requirement is contradicted.
その refers most naturally to the giant Shirou is glaring at: Saber is preparing behind Berserker. “Behind me” explicitly relocates her to Shirou's rear.
The English retains Saber's resolve but omits that the sight of her resolve burns itself onto Shirou's retina, removing his stated perception and the searing visual effect.

斬りかかる combines rushing in and attacking with a blade; “charges straight for Saber” conveys the attack, while the following sword-blocking sentence supplies the weapon context. The omitted cutting nuance is not materially misleading.
なぎ払う describes a broad sweeping stroke across the earth. “Breaks the ground” substitutes resulting ground damage and loses the attack's trajectory.
地に伏したまま places Saber down or prone on the ground; “on her knees” gives her a materially different, more upright posture.
死にきる adds completion: Illya means Saber at full power could have killed Berserker through his remaining lives. Plain “die” loses that resurrection-related force.

The governing Original describes scattered lumps of flesh that used to be Saber. “Pieces of meat that used to be” is therefore supported, while the competing phrase comes from flattened edition branches.
Original explicitly has Illya order Berserker to remove Shirou's legs. The alternate vague command belongs to another edition branch, so their combined appearance is a flattening artifact.
理性 is reason or rational control, not sensory perception. “Shut off my senses” changes which faculty is destroyed.
遠ざかっていく has no stated physical subject here and can describe Shirou's consciousness or perspective receding as he dies. “I’m fading” is contextually defensible.
The governing Original explicitly says Rin's body had already been crushed. “Body” and “crushed” are thus edition-supported, and “motionless” is the alternate branch flattened alongside them.
線 is metaphorical and can be rendered as a cord, line, thread, or rope. “The last rope holding me” preserves the restraint-and-snapping image without creating a factual contradiction.
Both self-reproach lines are present in the governing Original edition. Their absence from base and all-ages does not make their English translation unsupported.
The kneeling narration appears in the governing Original text, so translating it is not an unsupported restoration merely because later editions comment it out.
In this exhortation, “best imitation” is a defensible English superlative for 最強の模造品, particularly after the preceding sentence already says “Always imagine the strongest.”
筈 marks expectation: Shirou insists it should not be difficult. “Not difficult at all” removes that modality and presents categorical ease.
紅蓮 intensifies the fire image, but “my left hand feels like it’s on fire” conveys the relevant burning sensation. Loss of the color metaphor is stylistic compression, not a material accuracy error.
“Regurgitate” can mean flow or surge backward, not solely a digestive act. The sentence is ungainly, but it preserves the abnormal reverse flow of blood.
The Japanese says Shirou cannot spare any concern for the bodily crisis. “There’s no problem” instead denies that it is a problem, changing indifference into an assessment of safety.
両断 specifies being cleaved in two. “Really kill me” removes the concrete threatened bisection and substitutes a generic result.

The following Japanese clause naturally has Shirou as the omitted subject, matching blades with the sword in his hand while acting 無我夢中. Explicit “I” is normal English explicitation, not reversed agency.
格闘 can broadly mean physical fighting or combat, and the next English sentence immediately contrasts it with Shirou's mental fight. “Not made for fighting” is defensible in context.

The agency accusation is overstated: Japanese can describe the attacks Shirou had been blocking through the sword. A narrower error survives because English adds that his earlier blocking was “easy”; あっさり modifies only his being flung away now.
腕 does not obligatorily mark singular number, and the two-handed sword use permits both arms to be affected. The supplied Japanese cannot establish a one-arm-only claim.

A red, peeled-back wrist can reasonably imply exposed red flesh, and the two phrasings are conditional edition variants rather than simultaneous drafts. The unsupported surviving overstatement is that the wrist is about to tear off.
振り落とした expressly describes bringing the massive sword downward. Generic “swings” omits the finishing strike's stated trajectory.
“Closer than anything” is an idiomatic emotional superlative and does not materially contradict 誰より近く in this moment.
The English preserves an unfinished conjunction but omits the supplied clause saying Saber turns as though drawing Shirou into her motion, which establishes their shared movement.
岩の体 is a figurative description of Berserker's rock-hard body, not necessarily a material composition claim. “Hard body” preserves the operative sense.
The English says the sword engulfs him but omits the stated flash of light that actually envelops his body from within.
The Japanese describes the blade turning into sand as it vanishes. “Disappearing from the tip” both changes the locus and omits the sand transformation.
Rendering the ruby reading “Caliburn” as the proper name is a defensible localization convention; omission of the ornamental surface gloss alone is not a demonstrable factual error.
ざらり conveys a gritty or granular impression tied to the ensuing gravel-like crumbling. “Slowly” replaces that texture with an unsupported statement of speed.
“Fading into the air” preserves the dissolution simile. Omitting the air's white appearance is minor visual compression rather than a material mistranslation.

The Japanese threat itself stops at 潔く、ここで because Shirou interrupts on the next page. The incomplete English “Accept your—” deliberately mirrors that interruption rather than losing completed source content.
The governing Original contains both the restraint and the explanation that it made Illya notice them. Their absence from later editions is not evidence of unsupported English content.

Original uses the switched-off-doll simile, while the cut-string marionette belongs to the alternate edition. Their joint appearance is conditional-branch flattening, not competing drafts shown in one edition.
Original explicitly includes ようやく, supporting “finally.” Its absence from the later Japanese edition does not make it a stray insertion.
弟子一号 is the numbered role “pupil number one,” not a statement of seniority; the recurring comic title is lost.
The meaning is recoverable, but “do a full swing on me” is materially nonidiomatic English for being struck with a full swing.
当たらない says the attack missed or cannot hit her; “won’t affect me” instead describes ineffectiveness, potentially after contact.
微妙 can describe a tricky, questionable, or awkward balance, so “difficult balance” is defensible in this unwinnable-game context.
“I see” conveys the underlying acknowledgment but entirely removes the deliberately mangled, catlike にゃるぺそ joke.
Calling the option “immature, reckless” is a defensible condensation of recklessness caused by youth; it does not materially contradict the Japanese.
薄墨に染まる describes the sky’s pale ink-gray coloring. “The sky is thin” loses both the color and ink-wash image.
The English changes 戦場, a battlefield, into “a battle” and loses the rapid spatial traversal expressed by 駆け抜けた.
従える specifies cavalry she commands or has under her; “alongside” removes that command relationship.
The English continues the preceding “the only thing stretching out is…,” so it is not an isolated fragment. “Remains of battle” is also a defensible rendering of 戦場跡.
Although 湧き立たない literally concerns emotion not arising, the surrounding statement that nothing remains in her heart supports the concise “There is no emotion.”
“Bodies” already establishes death, and “defeated” is not itself false. The narrower error is omission of her agency as the one who destroyed the soldiers.
父に代わって means she replaced or acted in place of her father; “like her father” incorrectly makes it resemblance.
The allegedly unsupported sentence is present in the governing Original edition; its absence from later Japanese witnesses is an edition difference.
The ruby explicitly identifies the formation as Cataphract. Generic “cavalry” discards that specialized reading and the surface/ruby layering.
“Infantries” is uncommon and awkward here, but the plural can denote infantry forces of multiple peoples; it is not categorically ungrammatical.
In this martial context 切り捨てる means cutting down or killing every enemy, deliberately paralleling the preceding sacrifice of subjects. “Defeat” softens that force.
“Could not be” can express the speaker’s inferred conclusion rather than literal impossibility and is a defensible rendering of いなかっただろう.
幾つもの部族 specifies multiple tribal political groups. Generic “the people” removes both their multiplicity and their status as tribes.
孤立していった describes her progressively becoming isolated; “isolated herself” assigns deliberate reflexive agency absent from the sentence and contrary to the preceding social withdrawal.
Here 是非もない means that nothing can be done or that the outcome is unavoidable, not that the matter lacks moral right and wrong.
雁首そろえる is a contemptuous idiom for everyone being gathered together. “So many people around her” naturally conveys its referential meaning; preserving the bodily image is stylistic preference.
Given that they got out of hostile Illya’s forest after the Berserker battle, “escaped” is reasonable contextual explicitation of 森から出て.
“Sitting Japanese-style” is vague, but it was a conventional localization of 正座 and identifies the culturally specific posture sufficiently in context.
The accusation compares the Original-edition English branch against all-ages Japanese. The supplied Original has the sexual 体を重ねた, for which “did it with Saber” is crude but supported.
This entire passage is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its later removal from base/all-ages witnesses is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
昼 can cover noon or daytime, making “afternoon” defensible. The genuine error is changing Saber alone into inclusive “we.”
The bare “they should sleep” reads as a recommendation, whereas 寝てるんだろ is Shirou’s inference that they are probably still asleep.
The Japanese says “we” cooperated and continued makeshift training. The English makes the training Shirou’s alone and omits its improvised, stopgap quality.
The English still preserves Shirou’s immediate correction from practical “help” to “fun.” Requiring the same Japanese orthographic relation between 楽 and 楽しい is preference policing.
Generalizing shimeji as “mushroom” is defensible, but the separately listed green onion is genuinely omitted while 玉ねぎ supplies the translated ordinary onion.
The standalone repeated patting sound and the following playful kneading language are replaced by generic “mixing,” materially flattening the domestic sound play.
The exact four-hundred-gram quantity is plainly present and wholly omitted from the recipe description.
The adjacent preparation explicitly identifies 合い挽き肉, conventionally a mixed beef-and-pork mince. “Beef and pork” is therefore supported contextual explicitation, not invention.
“Japanese-style hamburger” can denote the Japanese hamburger-steak dish in context. The demonstrable surviving omission is 煮込み, the simmered or stewed preparation.
“Normally witted” is nonidiomatic and shifts quick observation or alertness toward general intelligence.
“Takes position” reasonably conveys 陣取った. The narrower loss is the emphatic comic どかーっと, which depicts her plunking herself down expansively.
The Lancer’s-Master statement occurs in the supplied Original Japanese; the different active base/all-ages wording is an edition variant.
“Conveniently altered” can naturally imply deliberate alteration for interested purposes and is within the contextual range of 改竄; demanding “falsified” is lexical preference.
Calling Arthur “the great hero of England” defensibly conveys her emblematic preeminence. The exact “byword” metaphor is nuance, not a demonstrable factual error.
守るべき marks the army she was duty-bound to protect. “That she protected” changes this normative obligation into a completed past action.

Japanese does not independently establish the betrayer’s grammatical number, so the plural accusation is too strong. The narrower loss is that 腹心 denotes a close confidant or retainer, not merely people she trusted.
殲滅した explicitly says Arthur annihilated or exterminated the attacking force. “Had to defeat them” substantially softens that destruction.
Throwing the sword into the deep lake is the ordinary means of carrying out 沈める, and the next page itself paraphrases the reported act with 湖に捨てた. No material contradiction results.
The English omits the specific in-house location where Illya is sleeping, despite that location recurring in the surrounding staging.

The English preserves Saber’s core judgment that sheltering Illya is unwise. It does, however, soften and relocate the criticism from Shirou personally being irrational to the decision abstractly being unwise.
背負って specifies that Shirou carried Illya on his back, a physical detail relevant to the later piggyback joke; generic “carried” omits it.
令呪 can function as the singular name of the Command Spell system or marking, and this sentence supplies no remaining count. A plural set cannot be established from this witness alone.
The direct glare is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference.
様子がおかしい commonly means that someone seems or is acting strange. The English does not necessarily imply deliberate suspicious conduct and is defensible here.
The direct アンタ and omitted subject identify Shirou as the person put through the ordeal. “Us” broadens the victim and changes Rin’s personal appeal to him.
言いつけてやる can mean properly instructing or telling a child what to do. In this moral-behavior context, “tell her what’s right” is a defensible paraphrase.

The following narration treats Shinji’s killing as the operative fact, so “admitted” does not newly certify it. The narrower issue is that “admitted” adds a confession or concession tone absent from neutral 言った.
行為 means Shinji’s act or conduct in his capacity as a Master. “Intentions” replaces that outward conduct with an inferred mental state.
The omitted リン is an explicit, pointed direct address that makes Illya’s insult personally targeted.
たしなみ can include modesty, decorum, manners, or ladylike propriety. “Modesty” is contextually within its lexical range and need not imply only sexual reserve.
呆れた expresses exasperation, disbelief, or being appalled, not surprise. “Shock” changes Illya’s performed attitude.
The illusion reaction appears in the governing Original Japanese. Its omission from base/all-ages is an edition change, not evidence of an English insertion.
The skirt-pinching bow likewise appears in the governing Original Japanese and therefore supports the English staging.
Shirou’s choking reaction is present in the governing Original Japanese; its later deactivation is an edition difference.
The English states anger directly but removes the imagined snapping sound at Saber’s temple, which is the sentence’s visual-auditory gag.
The Japanese idiom means that a mere Servant is in no position to object. The copied syntax “A Servant is a hundred years too early…” is malformed and obscures that insult.

“The two’s” is awkward editorial English, but a possessive noun phrase referring to the pair is possible and the reciprocal staredown remains clear. Calling it categorically ungrammatical overstates the case.
The allegedly restored manner clause is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference.
はてな depicts puzzlement, while 覗き込む is close peering into Shirou’s face. “Look … in surprise” changes the reaction and weakens the action.
さもありなん is a dry “as one would expect” or “no wonder.” Bare “Yes” loses that inferential and sardonic force.
In this Japanese-food context “hamburger” can refer to the patty dish, so the sandwich accusation is not decisive. The narrower genuine omission is the repeated patting and kneading preparation.
Although “bed/mat of needles” is more conventional, “a cushion full of needles” preserves the same image of acute discomfort and is not materially contradictory.
In context, escaping the current situation can naturally mean breaking out of or overcoming the deadlock. The English is less forceful but remains a defensible paraphrase of 現状を打破する.
“Let’s decide” is acceptable dialogue with the disputed matter supplied by context, and it substantially conveys the call to settle the issue.
If it becomes noon, morning ends. The English states the same practical deadline from the opposite temporal perspective without material distortion.
The explanatory sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese witness. Its removal from the later base/all-ages script is an edition difference.
The innocence gloss occurs in the supplied Original Japanese witness; its later commenting-out cannot make the Original-edition English unsupported.

The English first correctly says the topic is “what to do with you,” so it does not wholly obscure the others’ decision. The final “what you’re going to do” nevertheless shifts that last clause toward Illya’s agency.
The English omits 自分より小さい, the explicit comparison making Shirou’s protectiveness about a child younger or smaller than himself.
The immediately preceding sentence says the Holy Grail War is unfinished, so “until the end” has a clear contextual endpoint and reasonably condenses settlement with the remaining Masters.

The Japanese itself begins with Shirou’s intended separation and then pivots to Saber having already done it. The English’s immediate self-correction preserves the final agency; the joined word is an identified extraction artifact.
“Only bring you harm” naturally conveys that sheltering Illya has no beneficial side; separately spelling out “not one benefit” is not required for accuracy.
The Japanese describes Shirou’s chest tightening with a creaking sensation. “Grinding heart” transfers the sensation to the heart and is unclear English.
“Gasps in surprise” renders 息を呑む but materially understates the accompanying stunned, frozen state.
The supplied Original witness contains the alleged condition; its absence from the later Japanese is an edition difference, not an English insertion.
In this housing discussion, シロウのところ can naturally mean being or staying with Shirou. “I want to be with you” preserves Illya’s immediate plea.

The meaning—refusing to leave Illya in another person’s care—is clear and defensible. The narrower fault is the unidiomatic preposition in “entrust her into”; standard English would use “entrust her to” or “leave her in someone’s hands.”
The literal cat-forehead comparison is intelligible and deliberately preserves the image needed for Illya’s following rat-claw escalation. Calling it erroneous is stylistic preference.
The Japanese pointedly says Rin herself is “needlessly big,” sustaining the deliberately rude ambiguity. Supplying “your place” resolves the joke to her property and removes the personal barb.
Although てあげる carries a self-favoring attitude, “I can manage to live with Shirou” conveys Illya’s boastful condescension through a natural alternative rather than omitting it outright.
“Reminds of” lacks the required object in this construction; the sentence should say that the sight reminds Shirou of something.
Neutral “Father” drops the conspicuously irreverent and affectionate description of Kiritsugu as Shirou’s wayward old man.

決着がつく can describe reaching a conclusion or showdown, and “the match with the other Masters ends” communicates that the remaining conflict must be settled. Its wording is awkward but not materially false.
In context, “really sweet” can mean excessively kind or soft as well as preserve the literal sweetness pun. The criticism is recoverable without explicitly saying “indulgent.”
令呪 can denote the Command Spell authority collectively, and “as long as they have a Command Spell” accurately means retaining at least one. The Japanese does not require a plural here.
Tohsaka is already the unambiguous interlocutor, so omitting the sentence-final vocative is normal English compression and does not remove the question’s direction.

In this explanation, a Master’s capacity to accommodate another Servant is naturally their magical-energy capacity; the immediately following discussion explicitly concerns the magical energy needed to manifest multiple Servants.
“Call on” can mean summon in context, so that part is defensible. The narrower technical loss is replacing 英霊, Heroic Spirits, with their manifested Servant roles.
“The point … is defeated” is awkward but intelligibly conveys that reduced abilities nullify the benefit of multiple contracts. It does not materially alter Rin’s conclusion.
“Form another contract” naturally expresses contracting again, while “remaining Servant” conveys a Servant still present or surviving. No material relation is lost.
This staging is present as active prose in the supplied Original Japanese. Its omission or commenting-out in later editions cannot make it unsupported in an Original-edition comparator.

The reaction is active in the supplied Original Japanese, so restoring it is not an insertion for this comparator. “Gasped” is loose for 言葉を飲んだ but that translation issue is not the alleged unsupported-content claim.
“Special” preserves importance but removes ただ一人きり, the explicit exclusivity explaining why Berserker cannot simply be replaced.
The English reduces the narration to a speech attribution, omitting both Illya’s proud chest-thrusting pose and the comic fact that Saber and Rin had nearly begun admiring her.
“Want for me to win” is awkward or dialectal, but its meaning is unambiguous and accurately states Illya’s desire. This is not a material translation error.

The context and Saber’s preceding first-person statements make this her individual opposition. “We were objecting” falsely pluralizes the position and also generalizes the concrete act of sheltering Illya there.
邪魔者 explicitly calls Saber an unwanted nuisance or obstruction. “Saber’s here” removes that insult and substantially softens Illya’s complaint.
In context, “I can’t compromise on this” naturally expresses Shirou’s refusal to yield to or indulge Illya on this point. Naming Illya again is not necessary to preserve the decision.

The Japanese distinguishes training to protect Illya from Shirou’s prior decision to shelter her in his house. Translating both as “protect” erases that concrete responsibility and creates a false repetition.
無愛想 describes Saber’s cold or unsociable demeanor. “Acting bluntly” instead suggests verbal directness even though she is silently staring.
The brief thought is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its later commenting-out is an edition difference and cannot support an insertion accusation here.

The omitted noun is naturally resolved as the remaining Servants: Illya is dismissing the opponents against whom Shirou is training, then separately delegates the Masters to Saber. This is acceptable English explicitation.

“I lose my balance” already makes the movement involuntary, and taking a step toward the exit adequately conveys the resulting displacement. The omitted “swimming” image is stylistic rather than a material reversal of agency.
The silent-walk sentence is active in the supplied Original Japanese. Its absence from later editions does not make it unsupported in this Original comparator.
The emphatic dialogue can support a loud or screaming delivery, so “screams” is not plainly invented. The narrower genuine loss is 駄々をこねて, which characterizes her glare as part of a childish tantrum.
The sentence is active in the supplied Original Japanese, although later witnesses comment it out. It is therefore supported Original-edition content.
一本入れる here means landing a scoring blow in sparring. “I’ve never gotten Saber” is malformed and does not communicate that combat result.
The shinai transition is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its deletion from later Japanese editions is not evidence of an unsupported Original insertion.
The English conveys that the observation is unpleasant but omits スパーン, which explicitly gives Illya’s delivery a crisp, uninhibited comic snap.
In this training context and the following explanation, オトしにかかる specifically means moving to put Shirou down or knock him unconscious. Generic “attacked” loses the defining consequence.
The English retains only the knockout result while omitting Saber’s immediate step-in, the sharp impact beat, and the swordwork that strips away Shirou’s consciousness.
In the established context of Saber following through to end an exchange by knocking Shirou out, “deliver the final blow” is a defensible rendering of 追い打ち. It does not imply lethality here.
Shirou is the immediate person Saber approaches and then retreats from, so English may naturally supply him as the omitted object of こわがってる. Illya’s uncertainty remains in “it seemed more like.”
Focusing on Saber is a defensible metonymic rendering of concentrating on her shinai during their exchange; it does not create a materially different target or action in context.
The English omits Shirou’s direct observation that Saber’s answer is hesitant or evasive, then turns his tentative だろうか inference into the firmer “must feel.”
“Tackle me away when I got in too close” preserves both the close-range opening and Saber’s exploitation of it. The omitted 甘い nuance is not enough to establish a material error.
“Drove me up against the wall” can naturally denote forcefully propelling Shirou into the wall. It softens 派手に somewhat but preserves the relevant impact and recollection.
The statement is active in the supplied Original Japanese, so its absence from later-edition Japanese does not make the English unsupported for this comparator.
The Japanese depicts Saber lowering her shinai, a specific signal that she stops the bout. “Backs off” instead describes bodily retreat and changes the visible action.
“Counter-attack when I let my guard down” captures the imagined trap and retaliatory strike. The approach detail and comic sound effect are compressed, but the scenario is not materially changed.

The immediately preceding “Haa, haa, haa” already conveys Shirou’s labored breathing while he watches Saber. Omitting the additional shoulder-heaving description is compression, not a material factual error.
The Japanese is a deliberate lead-in to the next page, but “narrows her eyes seriously and taking” is grammatically broken: the coordinated verb form should be “takes.”
A subjectless narrative fragment after quoted dialogue is a permissible stylistic fragment in English, and its referent and meaning are fully clear.
English “this” merely points to the present wait or situation and does not disclose what Saber is concealing. It is normal explicitation required by the English verb construction.
The conspicuous shift to 致しましょう is plot-relevant because Shirou immediately quotes and questions that wording. Ordinary “let us eat” fails to reproduce the marked register change.
Shirou specifically identifies Saber’s altered wording, even quoting 致しましょう. “You’re acting strange” substitutes a general behavioral judgment and removes the evidence motivating his reaction.
“Forget the boxed lunch” is a defensible idiom for abandoning that menu. The narrower error is “we’ll … make,” which pluralizes the cooking even though Shirou personally says he will remake the meal.
“Bring some tea with lunch” naturally describes bringing the tea together with the already-prepared lunch. Both transported items remain clear from the page and its context.

気合いを入れていた describes effort Shirou had been putting into lunches. “Was going to … make a gorgeous lunch” converts that ongoing past practice into a future one-off plan and adds unsupported extravagance.
“As if she’s switched off” is a natural localized mechanical image that preserves Saber’s abrupt, toy-like stop. Replacing a spring mechanism with a power-switch metaphor is not a factual error.
The wandering-gaze narration is active in the supplied Original Japanese. Its commenting-out in later editions cannot establish unsupported content in an Original-edition audit.

脱兎の如く is a conventional image meaning to flee at great speed. “Runs out of the dojo” preserves the decisive action; losing the animal simile is stylistic compression rather than a material mistranslation.
“Conservative” has the ordinary sense of cautious or restrained, not only a political sense, and can describe her blows metonymically. The wording is awkward but defensible for 消極的な打ち合い.
Repeated ござる is an unmistakable mock-samurai performance. Casual “No can do” removes the period-role register that launches the following military joke.
“Last stand” captures the military atmosphere but omits the deliberately absurd claim that the river behind him has flooded, flattening the joke into a generic cliché.
“On reflex” is the normal English equivalent of answering by 脊髄反射. Dropping the literal anatomical component does not change the speed or involuntary nature of the response.
Japanese ハンバーグ denotes hamburger steak in this meal context, not hamburgers served as sandwiches. The English changes the breakfast dish.
The current training is explicitly with Saber and bamboo swords on the adjacent pages, so “we’re in the middle of the training” is a contextually complete paraphrase rather than a material omission.
Saber says the discussion has not advanced even a single move. “Has not finished” allows substantial progress and omits both her absolute complaint and its tactical metaphor.
Given Saber’s forceful ultimatum, “This is your final warning” is a natural reading of これが最後です. It need not imply a threat beyond her last emphatic demand.
A body requiring nutritional input can naturally be described as wanting energy, especially in an ordinary hunger scene. Nothing in the English explicitly turns this into magical energy.
嗜み has a lexical range including modesty, decorum, and ladylike restraint. Paired with はしたない and Illya’s romantic taunt, “modesty” is a defensible choice.
The English physiological explanation is grammatically defective: “movements of stomach” lacks the needed article or possessive construction, producing a malformed sentence.
“Energy consumption is pretty high” retains the mechanical efficiency comparison and accurately conveys poor fuel economy despite heavy intake. It is a natural reformulation of 燃費悪い.

In context, ほっといたら最後までごはん食べてる can naturally mean Saber keeps eating until the meal is finished. “Always finishes her meal” is a defensible paraphrase, with the following sentence supplying the quantity joke.
遣り込める means to defeat or get the better of someone here; “disparage” instead describes speaking contemptuously about Saber and loses Illya’s victory in the exchange.

This is Original-edition dialogue, not an unsupported restoration. The governing Original Japanese explicitly contains the no-replenishment explanation; the combined public text reflects flattened conditional branches.
The Japanese states that Saber generates less than she needs merely to exist for a day. “Enough” reverses that deficit into sufficiency.
Although awkward, “cruise through lightly” conveys 軽く流す—taking the spar lightly—and the surrounding armor and strike retain the irony. This is chiefly style criticism.

“Attacks me violently” is a defensible nonliteral rendering of the fang metaphor in a scene where Saber physically strikes Shirou without mercy. The imagery is reduced, but the action and force are retained.
The supplied raw Original witness includes 祝福して, so “congratulating” is supported by the Original edition even though the aligned base-derived page omits that word.
