The English conveys the safety advice but drops the defining numerical antithesis—one second versus a lifetime—which supplies the compact slogan and its joke.
虎ッカー is a coined tiger/Shocker-style organization name. Replacing it with the generic “Tigers” removes the identifying parody rather than merely naturalizing it.

情けない can naturally express the speaker’s shame or disappointment at another’s pathetic performance. “I am ashamed that you could not…” remains a direct rebuke and does not materially reverse the judgment.
やり返す means retaliate or pay someone back, and the context is repeated physical beating. “Retort” incorrectly confines the retaliation to words.
感心 supports Saber being impressed by the sandwich, so that portion is defensible. The narrower genuine loss is the visible repeated nodding expressed by こくこく.
The napkin action is present in the supplied Original Japanese witness. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not unsupported mirror moon content.

“Use minimal manners” is clumsy English, but it communicates that Saber will observe at least the minimum courtesy. The suggestion that it necessarily means intentionally poor etiquette overstates the error.
The sincerity narration occurs explicitly in Original Japanese. It was removed or commented out only in later editions, so it is valid Original-edition content.
The narration about Saber showing no concern for Illya occurs explicitly in Original Japanese. Its later-edition deletion does not make it unsupported in this comparator.
The entire observation is present in Original Japanese and therefore is not an unsupported insertion merely because base and all-ages comment it out.
片づけて supplies a prior action—promptly finishing or clearing up the meal—before going to the outbuilding. The English transfers all urgency to going and omits that action.
関係なしで means independently of or regardless of Berserker. “Forgetting the thing about Berserker” incorrectly turns independence of motive into forgetting.
壊死 specifically denotes tissue necrosis. “Take out one of your arms” communicates disablement but removes the concrete medical consequence Rin names.
“Carry Illya home” accurately conveys the consequential action used as proof that Shirou could move. Omitting the specific piggyback posture is a minor generalization, not a material error here.

The aligned Japanese jumps directly to Rin’s diagnosis, but the raw Original match begins two pages later, leaving the intervening Original pages unsupplied. That pagination shift and the English hentai-edition condition prevent establishing that the monologue is absent from Original.
The supplied raw Original witness contains the arm-withdrawal narration immediately after the same dialogue. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference or alignment issue.
Rin says her touch should have no effect if she is supposedly unrelated to him. “You won’t mind” changes this teasing test of his involuntary reaction into permission or tolerance.
The teasing smile appears in the supplied raw Original witness. It is later commented out, so restoring it for Original is not unsupported.
In this teasing context, “your reactions are so good” naturally means his reactions are irresistibly easy and entertaining to provoke. It softens ベタな, but remains a defensible contextual paraphrase.

The literal mummy wording preserves the Japanese proverb’s image, and Rin’s warning about becoming the mummy remains intelligible in context. Its unfamiliarity in English is a localization preference, not a factual reversal.
The supplied raw Original witness contains Rin returning cheerfully to her chair. It is absent only from the later active Japanese branch.
The Japanese rhetorically notices a teasing rate that has already been increasing day by day. “Will likely” changes that observed trend into a prediction.
“I don’t like to say this” is a plausible face-saving English preface for an awkwardly belated or obvious reminder. It loses some いまさら nuance but does not materially alter Shirou’s point.
The serious-turn narration occurs in the supplied raw Original witness. Its later-edition commenting does not make it unsupported for an Original comparator.
取り付けた says Rin installed or fitted the switch. “Turned the switch on” instead makes her operate a control that was already present, changing the stated intervention.
“What you’ve learned” is broader than 体で覚えた but remains defensible after the preceding reference to what Shirou has trained. The embodied nuance is reduced without producing a material contradiction.
難しい顔 can denote a troubled, displeased, or grave expression. “Unhappy expression” is less precise but falls within the contextual range and does not demonstrably erase an intellectual process.
The head tilt is present in the supplied raw Original witness. Its being commented out in the later Japanese script is an edition difference.

“Draw whatever I want” conveys the point of the 落書き comparison: unrestricted, easy drawing with his own materials. The lower-register scribbling image is reduced, but the explanatory meaning survives.

“Faker” is the explicit ruby reading attached to 複製者. English cannot always preserve both orthographic layers, and choosing the supplied reading is a defensible treatment rather than a mistranslation.
殺意 is murderous or killing intent, not merely hostility. “Enmity” materially suppresses the explicitly lethal intensity that also explains Shirou’s chill.

“Images of existing artwork or weapons” can naturally mean image-based reproductions modeled on those real objects, which is what イメージとして再現する states. The syntax is awkward but the technical distinction remains recoverable from the full passage.
This sentence identifies a replica woven from a mental image. “Made out of illusions” substitutes a different term and construction material, blurring the passage’s technical explanation.

“Mixing magical energy like toffee” is imprecise for kneading, but the following dagger-shaped toffee explicitly preserves the plastic candy-shaping analogy. The omission is not materially misleading.

The sentence is grammatically broken, and singular “ability” inadequately renders 性能. However “things with only shape” retains an appearance component, so the claim that appearance is wholly omitted is too broad.
何百倍 denotes hundreds of times, not exactly one hundred. The translation turns an open hundreds-fold comparison into a fixed lower value.
何百倍 again means hundreds of times. “A hundred times” incorrectly fixes the magnitude at one hundred.
The English retains only “specialists,” omitting both exclusion from the institutional center and the compensating fame as exceptional specialists.
“Can try and be the best” substantially conveys 頂点を狙える—being able to aim for the top. The contrast with lacking versatility still presents swords as Shirou’s exceptional prospect.

This is internal narration rather than clearly spoken direct address, and Japanese omits an explicit second-person pronoun. Referring to Rin as “she” is normal English explicitation; only the comic honorific register is reduced.
虚影 means a phantom or insubstantial image. “Vanity” selects an unrelated sense and breaks the label’s connection to Projection’s transient image-products.
“Have death right beside them” is awkward but transparently conveys living side by side with death. The finding identifies a fluency issue, not an accuracy failure.

In an engine analogy, “speed limit” can denote the machine’s prescribed operating limit, not only a legal road limit. The surrounding small-engine and destruction language makes the intended reading clear.
“Keep on turning the magical energy” is nonidiomatic, but it closely follows 回転させる and communicates continued cycling of energy amid circuit damage. This is primarily a fluency defect.
手足 covers the limbs, including legs, while “an arm or two” restricts the possible damage to arms. It also renders 壊れる as outright loss rather than bodily failure.

叱咤 describes a stern scolding or exhortation, which contextually supports Shirou perceiving anger directed at him. “She’s angry at me” explicates that force, while the following contrast still reveals concern.

In this bodily-damage context, 廃人 can mean a severely disabled or incapacitated person, and the period usage “cripple” conveys that warning. The Japanese does not independently establish a specifically mental ruin omitted by English.
The accusation contradicts the Japanese, which explicitly uses 処方する, “to prescribe.” The English follows that wording rather than inventing formal medical action.
Japanese number is unmarked, and どうしてこう together with この家は supports a generalized, exasperated complaint about things she puts away going missing. “Everything” is natural hyperbole in context.

The Japanese itself presents this as a characteristic pattern of Rin: she performs perfectly while preparation goes badly. “Always” is a somewhat stronger but contextually supported habitual rendering.
“Throws away” can mean casts or tosses aside, especially when followed immediately by her sitting down. Context does not require the disposal reading alleged by the finding.

Here とっくに失われた物さえ develops the preceding category as things no longer existing in the world. The English redundantly expresses temporal loss but does not demonstrably erase a separate non-temporal class.

The Japanese expressly describes bringing a real object from somewhere in the world into one’s presence and using it. “Uses things that are somewhere” omits this operative contrast with fabricated Projection.
彩色する specifies giving form or color to a human mental image. Generic “uses human images” removes the construction operation central to Rin’s contrast with ordinary magecraft.

“Violates this world/reality” is a defensible abstraction of an illusion encroaching on reality, especially since the passage repeatedly describes the world rejecting the contradiction. The erosion image is weakened but the mechanism remains.
“Explains it all” accurately states the action, though it flattens the rapid-fire delivery of まくし立てる. That is a tonal compression rather than a material factual error.

The immediately preceding clause says Berserker grabbed Rin, so “how you survived” is naturally understood as how she endured that grip. It broadens 持ちこたえた slightly without changing the question’s referent.

“Menacing smile” is a compact, defensible rendering of a smile radiating killing intent in this exaggerated comic exchange. It reduces the literal lethal wording but preserves the intimidation and joke.
“Protective cover” is vague but defensibly conveys a protective layer; the surrounding jewel context preserves its magical function.
なんだかね is a resigned or rueful reaction, not a question about why something happened; the English changes Rin’s attitude to puzzlement.
The English retains Shirou’s confidence but loses the explicit parallel that her words will be realized as effortlessly as she uttered them.
“Various medicine” is ungrammatical here; the Japanese explicitly denotes several kinds of medicine.
愕然 indicates being stunned or shocked, appreciably stronger than the generic “surprised” used at this emotional turn.
The present “is finished” omits both the retrospective aspect and とっくに, which says the partnership had ended well before this conversation.
師弟関係 specifically identifies a teacher–student relationship; “are close” substitutes an unspecified personal relationship.
Rendering the chest-out pose as “confidently” is a reasonable compressed paraphrase of the attitude it performs, not a factual mistranslation.
“I can’t leave you alone” and her resulting worry naturally imply that Shirou is unreliable; requiring the adjective explicitly is preference policing.
The sentence is present in the governing Original Japanese. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported mirror moon insertion.
“Please give me your best regards” is an unnatural calque and does not idiomatically communicate Shirou’s request for continued cooperation.
“Not know right from left” is also an English idiom for being thoroughly confused or lacking practical bearings, so the meaning remains defensible.
The motivation is present in the governing Original Japanese; its deletion in other editions cannot make its Original-edition translation unsupported.
Context makes 今のは失言 Rin’s characterization of her own preceding slip. “You let something slip” wrongly assigns it to Shirou.
English “I’m shocked” can express appalled exasperation as well as surprise; in this context it is a defensible rendering of 呆れた.
大変 describes the difficulty or burden Saber faces in dealing with Shirou; “upsetting” changes that into Saber’s emotional reaction.
The line identifies Shirou’s oblivious trait as what makes matters difficult; “upsetting” again substitutes emotional hurt for practical difficulty.
“Even now” wrongly relocates a remembered morning episode into the present, while “sits there” also omits Saber’s specific formal seiza posture.
Japanese itself uses vivid nonpast forms while recounting the morning incident. Matching that sequence with English narrative present is defensible and does not make it habitual.
Dropping a plainly inferable vocative is normal English compression. Moreover, Rin’s silence follows this question, so the explanation misstates its function.
“Must have” is an epistemic inference, not an assertion of witnessed history, and therefore preserves the speculative force of Shirou’s thought.
The English preserves the relevant proposition that the current weather is anomalously cold for the normally warm locale; omitting the already established place name is not material.
しもやけ means chilblains, whereas frostbite is a distinct and generally more severe freezing injury.
The supplied raw Original witness contains the explicit adult-version content about Shirou also being naked and physically reacting. This is an edition branch, not an unsupported insertion.
“Dumbfounded” reasonably renders the Japanese description of confused Shirou, so the state is not simply reassigned. The narrower genuine error is that Saber’s frozen manner of staring is omitted.
“While backing up” conveys the ongoing retreat. Losing the finer じりじり nuance is minor manner compression, not a demonstrable material error.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly says Shirou denies being captivated by Saber’s naked body. The body reference belongs to the Original-edition branch.

The English line is a conditional adult-version branch, but no corresponding Original Japanese branch is supplied for this page. The active all-ages wording alone cannot establish whether it is unsupported.
The visibility sentence belongs to a conditional adult branch whose Japanese source is not supplied here. Comparing it only with the active all-ages branch risks confusing editions.
The challenged wording is part of the same conditional adult branch, but only the all-ages Japanese counterpart is supplied. Its accuracy cannot be responsibly established across that edition gap.
The “obtained body” line is from an adult conditional branch for which no aligned Original Japanese is supplied. The all-ages line cannot prove an unsupported replacement.
The governing Original Japanese includes Saber lowering her head in embarrassment. Its omission from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not evidence of insertion.
Although less precise than “hard” or “firm,” “rugged” can describe a strongly built, trained body and is defensible in the immediate context.
“Really feminine” naturally conveys an emphatic perception that Saber’s body is girlish. The loss of 言葉もないほど is an intensity preference, not a material factual change.
慌ただしい describes a hectic or bustling dinner, not necessarily an emotionally exciting one.
“More approving” adds an unsupported comparison and shifts guarded acknowledgment or acceptance into positive approval.
The English entirely omits the blue shadow from the deliberately paired moonlit image of white breath and blue shadow.
“Trace, on” reproduces the explicit ruby reading and also corresponds semantically to 投影、開始. Not separately spelling out both layers in English is not by itself a material translation error.
今夜 specifically means tonight; “today’s training” incorrectly broadens the reference to the whole day.
“Analyze” is within the contextual range of 鑑定 as examining or appraising a construction. The distinct later 想定 rendering can be audited separately.
The Japanese says Shirou can turn only the necessary procedural steps into an incantation; merely “performing” those steps omits that encoding process.
暗示 denotes a suggestion or self-directed mental cue. An unspecified thing “to guide” Shirou does not preserve that incantatory mechanism.
“Change the self’s recognition” is opaque, unidiomatic English and fails to state clearly that Shirou changes his own conception while uttering the words.
想定 means supposition, assumption, or formulation here. Repeating “analyze” collapses it into the preceding, differently named 鑑定 step.
“Associate himself with Projection” is awkward but intelligibly means becoming involved with it, which is within the idiomatic force of 手を出す.
やってきていた presents Saber as having already arrived when noticed; “approaches” instead depicts ongoing motion toward Shirou.
Looking at Shirou is compatible with looking at his visibly sweaty forehead, and the next sentence supplies that focal reason. This is minor compression rather than material error.
The Japanese says Shirou’s entire body is covered in sweat; “my face is all sweaty” materially narrows its extent.
The supplied raw Original Japanese explicitly contains the gentle look at Shirou. Its absence from the later active editions is an edition difference.
The wording is awkward, but “a deed that steps into your mind” still communicates an act intruding into Shirou’s inner life. The accusation identifies style, not a material semantic error.

Given that the memory is explicitly old and concerns Shirou’s earlier life, “when I was small” is plausible contextual explicitation; describing his past through the dull things he did is also a natural paraphrase.
“Honestly” can convey Saber’s sincere, serious clarification in context. It is less exact than “earnestly” but does not materially change the exchange.
In context, “what you have done wrong” can mean the mistake Saber recognizes in Shirou’s present course; it does not necessarily enumerate past wrongful acts.
“Superhero” is a defensible natural-English rendering of the aspirational savior figure denoted by 正義の味方. Requiring the established literal phrase is terminology preference.
“Wrongdoing” denotes a culpable wrongful act, while Saber calls the underlying premise of Shirou’s ideal a mistake and immediately denies that he bears culpability for the accident.
The dramatic present “How can I answer that?” naturally renders Shirou’s continuing inability to formulate a response within the narrated scene; no substantive fact changes.
The English retains the ruby reading “dream” but loses the written word 理想, erasing the deliberate ideal/dream doubleness central to Shirou’s declaration.
余韻 is the lingering emotional afterglow of victory, not memories of the victory. The English changes present feeling into recollection.
The Japanese explicitly marks Shirou’s preceding interpretation as astonishingly mistaken; “random things” removes that corrective reversal.
“Truth” approximates the ruby reading 現実 but omits the written 過去, losing the deliberate statement that this reality is Saber’s unchangeable past.
父に代わって means succeeding or taking the place of her father, not becoming a lord resembling him.
幼さ can describe remaining childlike qualities, and “childlike features” need not exclusively mean facial anatomy. The rendering is defensible though inelegant.
Knights recounting their own 武勇 can naturally be characterized as tales of bravado. The English adds a boastful shade but does not demonstrably reverse the scene.
容認されただけ means she was merely tolerated or accepted in the role of an idol. “Idolized” instead asserts positive veneration.
少年の姿 specifically presents Arturia in a boy’s form or guise; “small kid” removes the crucial gendered public appearance.
Bringing peace to previously fighting lords is a reasonable natural paraphrase of uniting them; the political result and Arturia’s agency remain clear.
In context, the invading 異民族 are foreign enemy peoples. “Invading enemies” is a reasonable general English rendering rather than a material historical distortion.
身を粉にして means working oneself to exhaustion or grinding oneself down. “Worked hard” substantially weakens the self-destructive intensity.
The following contrast establishes that the villages are expected to be overrun by the enemy. The English instead makes the knights themselves the trampling agents.
反感 is resentment or hostility, not an organized revolt. The English prematurely turns an accumulating attitude into a political event.
“All problems” concisely includes the exhaustive foreign and domestic problems named in Japanese; the categories are generalized but the total burden and agency remain intact.
何年も emphasizes that the scene lies many years in the past; “a few years” materially compresses the stated span.
“Brave sounds” is awkward but intelligibly describes the bold or gallant sound of the cavalry. It does not create a material factual error.
In the context of Merlin’s ominous next warning, “I’m not trying to frighten her” is a defensible contextual rendering of the well-meant-advice idiom, not an unsupported change of intent.
The Japanese describes putting a hand to or taking hold of the sword, not yet taking or drawing it; the later page separately states that she drew it.
顔を背け means averting one’s face, while “turns his back” changes the physical action and also drops his troubled appearance.
In the immediately established contrast with 人の心, “threw away her heart” is a defensible contextual rendering rather than a claim that she lost every capacity for feeling.
The English distributes the suspended condition across “No matter what” and the later “Even if…waiting at the end”; the foreknown ruin remains expressed.
殺し合った explicitly depicts the two sides killing one another; “a war began” states only a more general and weaker development.
Although destruction is conveyed, “utterly destroyed” removes the conspicuous elegiac image and glorious-falling nuance of 華と散った.
In this battlefield account, 散る can idiomatically mean to fall or die; “died” is supported and need not mean mere dispersal.
“Crippled” can describe battlefield incapacitation, matching a wounded body that would not move; permanence is not necessarily asserted.

The accusation overstates a contradiction, since “no regrets—if there is one” is ordinary English. A narrower loss remains: 無念 denotes frustrated grief or an unfulfilled concern rather than the same remorse expressed by 後悔.
肩の力が抜ける is the idiom for tension leaving the shoulders. “Strength escapes her shoulders” instead suggests physical weakness and obscures her release of tension.
In context, “the end of her memories” naturally means that her remembered experience goes no farther; it does not materially imply memory loss.

The restoration accusation is false because the sentence is present in the governing Original. A narrower wording problem survives: 大降り means heavy rain or a downpour, whereas “shower” describes duration/type rather than the intended intensity.
The entire headache page is present in the governing Original, so its absence from the other editions does not make the English an unsupported restoration.
The sentence is present in the governing Original, so the restoration claim fails. The surviving issue is that “have a fit” weakens 暴れ出したくなる, an urge to lash out or run violently amok.
The surrounding lines explicitly establish anger and list what Shirou is angry at, so “makes me mad” is a contextually defensible reading of 気がヘンになる.
理解されなかった means that Artoria herself and her actions were not understood; “nobody knew about it” reduces this to lack of awareness of her efforts.
The object of 埋められる is left abstract in Japanese. “Won’t fix anything” naturally conveys that easy praise cannot fill or remedy what is lacking without materially changing the point.
清算させる concerns settling or bringing her life’s account to resolution. “Her life must be repaid” makes the life itself sound like the debt and leaves the intended beneficiary unclear.

“Superhero” is a broad but defensible English localization of 正義の味方 in Shirou’s aspiration to be a justice-serving hero; the accusation demands preferred terminology rather than identifying a factual reversal.
The plural “distortions” is awkward, but it still communicates recognition of his own warped nature; Japanese grammatical number does not establish a distinct single deformation.
The English omits the explicit characterization of Illya as an 異分子, an alien or incongruous element to whom the household has now grown accustomed.
“Is healed” ordinarily presents healing as a completed state and adequately supports the decision to end the rest period.
“Training with Saber” is accurate at the relevant level, and the surrounding exchange establishes that this is their combat/sword training; omitting 剣 here is not materially misleading.
人聞きが悪い concerns wording that gives listeners a disreputable false impression, not merely a comment that sounds unpleasant.
Given Rin’s preceding joke about Saber bullying Shirou, “get beaten up” is a defensible humorous paraphrase of being put through harsh drills.
“I wasn’t listening” naturally covers failing to hear through distraction and does not necessarily imply deliberate disregard; dropping ぼうっとしてて is minor compression.
In this domestic observation, “do not seem well” can naturally encompass the absence of vigor or spirit denoted by 覇気; it does not necessarily medicalize the line.
色どりに欠ける concerns visual color or variety in the meal, whereas “smaller” asserts reduced quantity.
The wording is stiff, but “drive some energy into you” communicates the idiomatic promise to reinvigorate Shirou, and the dojo-training context prevents a material magical-transfer reading.
The Japanese says a development has obviously already occurred; the English instead presents an assumption that the opponents are currently doing something unspecified.
The sentence begins by comparing the remaining Masters, making “the Master at Ryuudou Temple” a normal contextual explicitation of 柳洞寺のヤツ rather than an unsupported promotion.
Contrasted directly with concentrating on the search, “take time off to teach” clearly means diverting time from that work and is a defensible rendering.
危なっかしい can describe someone as unreliable, precarious, or unsafe to leave alone; the following magecraft warning supplies the danger more specifically.
The supplied raw English shows mutually exclusive realta/classic conditional branches, not two active revisions. The flattened display is an extraction artifact expressly warned about.
The Japanese explicitly marks Saber’s answer as gentle and calm; “replies like that” discards this manner entirely.
胸がもやもやして describes indistinct, clouded emotional unease. A heart beating hard is a different and unsupported physical symptom.
The source specifies a headlong charge performed with life-or-death desperation; “attack seriously” omits both the charging action and its extremity.
In Shirou’s casual first-person narration, “half-assed” is a plausible colloquial equivalent for a halfhearted or incomplete strike; the alleged register violation is subjective.
具に凝る means putting care, ingenuity, or variety into the fillings. “Elaborated on the ingredients” conventionally sounds like explaining them rather than preparing them elaborately.
The English represents her controlled breath but wholly omits that Saber first readjusts herself into formal seiza, a distinct part of the comic preparation.
After Illya tries to eat the food in one bite despite her small mouth, “eat more slowly” is a defensible practical rendering of eating more calmly or restrainedly.
The action is retained, but 仕方なげ explicitly gives Saber a resigned, put-upon manner that the bare English sentence removes.
“Someone to eat lunch with” directly expresses the present social relationship denoted by 同じお弁当を食べる仲間, even if it is less warmly phrased.
“Dumbfounded” conveys Saber’s resulting disarmed state, while Illya’s preceding warmth supplies its cause. Omitting the idiomatic image is not a material change here.
殺風景 can mean bare, plain, or lacking ornament; “too simple” is weaker but defensible, and the following warmth contrast remains intact.
“Must have felt something” remains an epistemic inference rather than an assertion of observed fact and is a natural rendering of Shirou’s conjectural question.
“Clear” can convey the unclouded quality of 晴れやか, and the immediately following unprecedented smile supplies the emotional brightness.
納得いかなげ describes apparent failure to accept or comprehend the point; “still not understanding” is supported by Saber’s immediately preceding statement that she finds it difficult to understand.
Something has newly occurred to Saber before she states the reciprocal insight, so “must have realized something” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of the unspecified 思い立った.
“Overheat” is a natural figurative rendering of becoming mentally overwhelmed or flustered by the smile; it does not impose a consequentially different event.
“Sneak a peek at Saber” preserves the indirect, furtive observation established by the previous inability to face her; omission of the exact profile angle is minor.
胸にひっかかる is idiomatic unease or something nagging at one. “Nagging at the back of my head” is natural English and need not turn the feeling into a reasoned suspicion.
Not wanting to sit idle naturally conveys the awkward restlessness of 所在がない in this context; the difference is one of phrasing, not material meaning.
座禅を組む conventionally means sitting in zazen, so “meditating” is a defensible description rather than an unsupported mental activity.
自分から can express acting voluntarily or from one’s own will. “Because she wanted to” fits Shirou’s question about what Saber herself wants and is not a demonstrable reversal.
無欲 has a legitimate lexical range including unselfish or free of self-interest; the surrounding discussion still makes Saber’s lack of personal wants clear.
報いる can mean recompensing or making amends for something, so “make up for her sad end” is a contextually supported paraphrase despite the added adjective.
The English drops 何より, Shirou’s emphatic “above all else,” and changes the particular singular wish under discussion into plural wishes.
呆れる can involve being stunned or dumbfounded by someone’s behavior, and “must have” still marks Shirou’s inference; “shocked” is imprecise but defensible.
In context Shirou has specifically misrepresented Saber’s personal motivations, so “distorted her personality” is a reasonable narrowing of his distorted conception of her.
Although 似たよう is literally “similar,” colloquial “said the same things” can denote broadly the same kind of altruistic sentiment; the parallel is not materially falsified.
努めて…接触しなかった says Archer deliberately refrained from contact. “Made no effort to talk” instead suggests passivity and narrows all contact to conversation.
The supplied raw witness places “I know” inside an edition-dependent conditional, not an exposed duplicate revision. In the Original branch it forms one coherent assessment.
恒久的 is indeed omitted from Archer’s quoted proposal, but the alleged impact is mitigated because the English explicitly calls it “permanent world peace” on the next relevant page.
いじける means sulking, becoming petulant, or nursing wounded feelings; “got timid” instead attributes fearfulness.
使役される describes being employed, commanded, or made to serve Rin. “Got summoned” replaces that subordinate service relationship with the separate summoning event.
守っている says Archer still preserves or defends the fool’s dream despite intellectually rejecting it; “chasing” makes him personally pursue it.
キザ describes affected, showy, or self-consciously suave behavior. “Snobbish” instead assigns social or class condescension absent from Rin’s joke.
The awkward English still conveys that recent experience has forced the Arthurian legend upon Shirou’s awareness; it does not demonstrably exclude realization.
Calling Merlin an incubus crossbreed already conveys the demonic basis of Rin’s description; omission of the partly redundant 悪魔じみた is a tonal compression, not a material error.
The English renders the ability to cut anything but entirely omits the separately stated property that the blade never chips.
In this rebuke over Shirou’s mistaken understanding, “foolish” is a defensible contextual rendering of being an immature or inexperienced 未熟者, not a material change of accusation.
The English conveys substantial magical energy but omits 力技, Rin’s characterization of the healing as brute-force, and substantially softens バカみたいに膨大.
“I see. Well, if you say so” is a defensible contextual expression of accepting Rin’s judgment; the ellipsis does not demonstrably reverse that acceptance.
The passive “was stolen” preserves the basic event but demonstrably omits both the enemy as thief and the fact that it happened partway through events.
“I can tell” preserves that this is Shirou’s inference from Rin’s threatening air, while “intends” is natural English explicitation. Omitting 等 is immaterial here.

The wording is stilted, but “penetrate the fortress” retains the playful stronghold metaphor and the intended breakthrough. A possible unintended innuendo is stylistic, not a demonstrated accuracy error.
The Japanese asks what they would do after obtaining the Grail; the English instead repeats the condition of winning the war and loses the question about using the prize.
使い道 concerns what use is made of the Grail, not merely who uses it. The English narrows Illya’s indifference to user identity.
ただ事ではない signals that Saber’s condition is seriously abnormal; “acting in a complicated manner” is both unclear and materially weaker, obscuring why the others stop arguing.
許容範囲 concerns the range or capacity of wishes the Grail can accommodate. Generic “powerful” changes that technical uncertainty into a power-level statement.
弱音 can denote a fainthearted complaint or weak thought, including an internal one. “Such whining fills my head” is harsh but contextually defensible.

The English awkwardly attempts to express both the ruby “oath” and the underlying holy sword. Rendering 手にした through the contextual act of drawing/taking up the sword is defensible, not an unsupported event.
Tilting her head at her own statement naturally indicates that Rin doubts or questions what she has just said, especially given the voiced contradiction. The English is a defensible explicitation.
奉られている means being enshrined or venerated as a Heroic Spirit. “Respected” reduces this supernatural posthumous status to ordinary esteem and weakens Rin’s explanation.
“I have yet to become a complete Servant” preserves both temporal incompletion and Saber’s incomplete Servant state. The alleged class-instance distinction is not established by the wording.
In context, “give their existence to the world after they die” reasonably conveys surrendering one’s posthumous self. The broader English noun does not create a material contradiction.
“Servants” follows the supplied ruby reading over 英霊. Losing the visual layering is a presentational compromise, not by itself a factual mistranslation.

The accusation overstates the agency problem: the ruby explicitly identifies Masters as “us,” and the preceding context supplies the World. The narrower error is that “debt liability” misstates 返済金額 and the English does not clearly preserve the resulting compulsory service.
使役される explicitly says they are made to serve, with a “familiar” ruby. “Summoned as heroic spirits” omits that compulsory-service relation.
The English says only that Saber became a Heroic Spirit; it omits Shirou’s supposition that she continues acting as a guardian after death.

The surrounding explanation identifies Heroic Spirits as guardians, so “become a heroic spirit” is a defensible contextual normalization of the promised guardian role rather than a material contradiction.
Though inelegant, “pay for it with life after death” can naturally mean paying with one’s posthumous existence and is clarified by the surrounding Heroic-Spirit contract discussion.
The English retains posthumous sword service but entirely omits its universal beneficiary, an explicit term of Saber’s offer.

In this deathbed passage, “a lone king whose reign ended in betrayal” is a defensible rendering of a king whose course ended through betrayal; “lone” and the immediately following last-moment sentence retain the unattended end.
The accusation misquotes the complete English: it explicitly retains “I can’t die here” and “I didn’t want an end like this.” The following conditional also matches 望んでしまっても.
“Time stopped for me” can mean that Saber’s personal time stopped and does not assert that time itself ceased universally. That reading remains compatible with the next page’s distinction.
In discussion of attaining the status of the Heroic-Spirit main body, “rank” is a defensible rendering of an ontological position or standing. It need not imply a power hierarchy.
求めた means having sought the Grail, not having obtained it. The English incorrectly makes acquisition precede the return, contradicting the described repeating cycle.
あらゆる gives unrestricted temporal scope. “Various ages” reduces that to an unspecified selection of eras in Shirou’s model.
A clone made from a cell is ordinarily understood as being produced from that cell’s genetic material. Substituting DNA preserves the analogy’s substance and creates no relevant plot distinction.
The English changes simultaneous summons across every era into repeated summons within one era, altering both simultaneity and temporal distribution.
淡々と describes an outwardly calm, matter-of-fact delivery, not lack of interest. The English assigns Saber an unsupported attitude toward her defining disclosure.
愕然と marks stunned shock and 意識が白くなる an acute blanking of consciousness. Casual “spacing out” materially weakens that force despite the surrounding physical symptoms.
The English conveys repeated combat summons but omits the explicit depersonalization into a battle-only phenomenon and softens continuing enforced service.
In the context of undoing Saber’s history, saying her ten years “can’t just disappear” defensibly conveys that they cannot be negated or rendered a lie. The ethical objection remains intact.
The English omits おまえだけ, losing Shirou’s pointed claim that Saber alone fails to recognize what is evident to others.
The supplied raw Original witness contains ふざけんな at the opening. “Don’t be ridiculous” is therefore an Original-edition line, not an unsupported mirror moon insertion.
Here 負けなかった follows betrayal and being feared, not a particular battle result; “didn’t give up” defensibly expresses that she did not yield or succumb.

“People will get happier the more they work for it” substantially preserves the proportional relationship between striving and attaining happiness. The proposed distinction is stylistic rather than factual.
The interrupted Japanese still explicitly names this battle as the object of Shirou’s full effort. The English drops that object and changes commitment into being able to try.
重い describes an acoustically heavy or weighty bell sound, for which “loud” is imprecise but plausible. This isolated timbral shift is not a demonstrable material error.
The English invents distance and omits the explicit ripple-like spreading or resounding of the scraping noise.
ガシャガシャ supplies a concrete repeated clattering sound. “Strange sound” replaces that sensory information with a generic judgment.
The Japanese image is insects swarming toward a moth-attracting lamp; “crawling around a light trap” changes both their motion and spatial relation.
The English retains multiple magical-energy sources but omits that Shirou initially senses them as originating from multiple humans, which sets up the next page’s contradiction.

“Skimming quickly” is awkward, but in the preceding context of sensing magical sources it can function as a rapid scan and still yields an approximate count. It does not necessarily assert visual inspection.
大人しく従う means to obey docilely or without protest. In context, “obey him politely” is awkward but substantially conveys compliant, well-behaved obedience.
羽交い締め describes restraining the arms from behind. The English specifies only one arm being bound, materially changing the depicted hold.

The prior page establishes that Rin covers Illya’s mouth, and the punctuation visibly represents muffled speech. “Throw out insults” preserves the abuse; the alleged narrator refusal is not specifically stated by 聞くに堪えない.
“Don’t work too hard” is an ordinary contextual rendering of 無理をする, meaning not to push or overexert oneself. The ongoing attack makes the danger unambiguous.
“I doubt my own eyes” is idiomatic English and accurately conveys being unable to believe what one sees.
“Open head” is malformed and suggests an exposed or unguarded head rather than the explicit crown/top targeted by 脳天.
Although “wasteless” is awkward, it transparently conveys 無駄のない, and 剣戟 can describe the present sword attack rather than necessarily a multi-move sequence.
The Japanese assesses the attack as lacking the ferocity suggestive of a killing blow. “Not scary” substitutes Shirou’s vague emotional reaction for that combat judgment.
“Follow me” can mean proceed behind the leader, and the following English sentence explicitly says Shirou resisted “following after her.” The protective positioning remains recoverable.
“Like bad building blocks” is clumsy but conveys the creatures’ resemblance to poorly made toy-block constructions. The accusation identifies style rather than a changed fact.

The supplied raw Original contains いや, so “No” is an edition-valid discourse marker, not unsupported. The narrower genuine omission is セイバーはともかく, the contrast between Saber’s equipment and Shirou’s ordinary wooden sword.
The supplied raw Original has a separate sentence stating that her sword is no longer invisible. Its absence from base/all-ages Japanese is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The raw Original explicitly says the golden sword was shining as it prepared to display its true power. “Glowing” is supported, while “show off” can non-boastfully mean display here.
誘いに乗る can be rendered as deliberately taking or falling for a lure. “Let’s fall for” makes the acceptance intentional, so it does not portray Shirou as unknowingly duped.
最高 is explicitly superlative. “Strong” lowers Saber’s Magic Resistance from the highest class described to merely substantial resistance.

The generic singular is not a genuine number error because the next sentence explicitly considers hundreds. The narrower error is that “dragon warrior” drops 牙 and obscures the Dragon-tooth Soldier class name.
The Japanese presents Saber’s defeating them as the likely explanation for the diminishing presences. “But” replaces that inferential relationship with contrast.
“Just like her” is an elliptical “that’s Saber for you” and can convey recognition of Saber living up to expectations. It is awkward but does not demonstrably erase the praise.
In ordinary nonclinical English, “you look depressed” can mean looking gloomy or downcast and is within the normal range of 浮かない顔. The next clause also retains his dissatisfaction.
腕 can refer broadly to the upper limb, while “hand” naturally specifies the visible Command Spell location. This does not establish a materially different placement from the supplied scene.
Looking at the left hand is a defensible physical explicitation of looking at the left arm/upper limb for the Command Spell, not a demonstrated continuity error.

The English uses an interrupted construction around Saber’s groan—“Saber enters, and… …steps in”—to reproduce the Japanese staged sentence. It is awkward but the return and chest-clutching remain clear.

“My only concern” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of exclusive attention: Rin’s warning no longer registers because Shirou focuses solely on the visibly suffering Saber. “In pain” is also supported by the preceding chest-clutching description.
The supplied raw Original witness contains the left-shoulder-to-waist wording exactly; the English line is an Original-edition branch, not an unsupported insertion.
“Numbs” denotes suppression of sensation, whereas the Japanese specifically says the clean stroke postpones when pain is felt.
The English preserves deterioration but omits the explicit point that delay will produce consequences that cannot be undone.
The snow-vehicle simile is present in the governing Original Japanese; its absence from the later-edition active text does not make its Original-branch translation an insertion.
The English still communicates Saber’s exceptional swordsmanship and is awkward rather than unintelligible. The narrower loss is 今更ながら, the sense of being made to realize it anew or belatedly.
Epistemic “must” remains an inference, so “This must be the end” is a defensible natural rendering of Shirou tentatively identifying the endpoint, not settled certainty.
“Someone” is reasonable contextual identification: the very next fragment calls the shape a distorted human figure. It does not materially alter the encounter.
“Asks unpleasantly” is awkward English but can naturally mean that Saber asks in a displeased manner; it does not reverse the experiencer or introduce a different reaction.
“I made him disappear” already expresses both deliberate causation and its completed result. Reproducing the Japanese rhetorical repetition is not necessary for accuracy.
非業 here concerns Caster’s tragic fate or unnatural misfortune, not immoral acts. “Ill acts” changes Saber’s refusal of sympathy into moral condemnation.
Although nonidiomatic, “Die here in grace” substantially conveys 潔くここで散れ—an order to die cleanly or gracefully. Calling grace unrelated overstates the problem.
“Must be X or Y” still presents two unresolved alternatives and is a normal English inference from the Japanese self-question; it does not settle which explanation is true.

The raw English contains an [atlas] macro, so the apparently empty utterance and claim that everything was omitted are extraction-sensitive. A narrower loss remains: the semantic written layer 圧迫 (“oppression”) is not represented alongside the Atlas reading.
The English is syntactically awkward, but it retains the basic simpler-magic/shorter-incantation relation. The surviving issue is unclear expression, not omission or reversal of that relation.
“No mere magus” conveys that Caster exceeds the ordinary magus role. Omitting the role/class ruby wordplay loses presentation texture but does not establish a material mistranslation here.

“These fingers lived in the Age of Gods” is synecdoche for Caster herself and her practiced craft. “I have lived in the age of gods” preserves the biographical boast, with her magic discussed immediately afterward.
つまらなそう marks Saber as bored or unimpressed. “Spits” substitutes a more heated, venomous manner and loses that specific contemptuous boredom.
“Cancelling Caster’s magic” conveys the semantic nullification as well as the supplied ruby reading “cancel”; nothing material is dropped.
“Not happy about relying on Saber” is a natural, if less literal, expression of reluctance and feeling bad about burdening her. It does not necessarily mean dissatisfaction with the plan.
Saber is directly addressing Shirou, and “you … with Rin and Illya” naturally means his group can hold out because of their strength. It does not attribute that defensive power to Shirou.
The sentence occurs as Shirou rejoins Rin and Illya, and 篭城 describes the party’s defensive action. English “we” is contextually natural even though 俺 supplies Shirou’s reason for staying.
竜牙兵 is the specific Dragon-Tooth Soldier designation. “Warriors” removes that identified familiar type from Illya’s tactical report.
浮かない顔 ordinarily describes a gloomy, dejected, or troubled look. Nonclinical “depressed” is within that range, while the next clause supplies the dissatisfaction.
In this Command Spell context, specifying “hand” from 腕 is ordinary anatomical explicitation, especially since the mark is viewed there. It does not demonstrate a consequential relocation.
左腕 can encompass the limb being inspected, while the Command Spell’s visible location licenses natural English “left hand.” The witnesses do not establish a material spatial error.

The English deliberately suspends its sentence around Saber’s groan, paralleling the Japanese topic left open by は before its later predicate. The awkward resumed entrance is not an abandoned or unsupported sentence.
In context, “My only concern” adequately conveys that nothing except the suffering Saber registers for Shirou; the immediately preceding failure to hear Rin preserves the tunnel vision.
The supplied raw Original witness has the left-shoulder-to-waist trajectory. This is an Original-edition conditional line rather than content invented by mirror moon.
The repeated translation again changes postponed pain into numbed or suppressed sensation.
身を翻す can describe rapidly turning the body to evade an attack, and the following sentence makes the backward movement clear. “Tries to dodge it” is a defensible compression.
The supplied displayed translation contains a line break, not a literal “[r]” token. The raw [r] is a script control and cannot be treated as Japanese-supported displayed prose.
The Japanese explicitly says the dagger gouges and cuts through Shirou’s spine. “Wrenched open my back” removes that specific and consequential injury.
体が泳ぐ with the rushing ひゅん depicts Shirou’s body being swept or thrown broadly off balance. Generic “moves” loses the involuntary airborne lurch.
The supplied raw Original witness reads 振り払うように, explicitly supporting “as if to shake off.” The firmer 振り払って belongs to the later-edition witness, so the accusation conflates editions.
The image specifically has Shirou’s spine repeatedly snipped with scissors; “back cut” removes both the anatomy and the iterative ジョキジョキ effect.
顔を下げたまま describes maintaining a lowered, pain-constrained posture. “Nodding” invents a discrete gesture of assent.
“From the bottom of her lungs” is awkward but conveys a voice forced from deep in Saber’s lungs. The accusation identifies stylistic infelicity rather than a demonstrable material change.
“They surround us” omits the complete tableau: wounded Shirou is on his knees while Saber stands guarding him with her sword, information central to her tactical constraint.
Saber promises to burn Caster away with the full power of her sword. Generic “defeat” removes both the method and the threat’s annihilating force.
The Japanese explicitly says Caster is intimidated first and that even the surrounding bones are cowed. The English names only the bones.
“A Master or two” is an idiomatic English minimizer corresponding to 一人ぐらい, not a literal tactical authorization for multiple survivors. The immediate referent remains Shirou.
In a passage already discussing Servants by name, “hero” is a defensible contextual shortening of 英霊 and still identifies Saber as the extraordinary combat asset Caster wants.
そこまで means the pointless chatter ends here. The English instead declares that this is the only pointless talk Caster will engage in, changing the speech act.
The Japanese explicitly predicates winning Saber over on first capturing her and implies she can then be bent by whatever means work. “Persuade” omits the capture and coercive premise.
In this domination context, “control you” is a defensible rendering of 躾る’s training or disciplining sense. It is broader and less vivid, but not a demonstrable factual error.
切れ切れ describes consciousness that has become intermittent or fragmented. “Lacerated consciousness” misapplies the physical wound sense and obscures Shirou’s fading awareness.
The English entirely omits that Shirou rises on legs from which sensation is gone, materially reducing the severity and effort of the action.
“Take the wooden sword in my hand” can naturally mean taking or establishing a grip, not necessarily picking it up from elsewhere. The loss of “regrip” is too slight to support the accusation.
嘲笑う explicitly identifies Caster’s voice as mocking or jeering. “Delighted” substitutes pleasure without conveying the hostile ridicule.

Epistemic “must have noticed” remains an inference and naturally renders the narrator’s のか speculation. The preceding page has already identified the figure as a man, so “guy” is not premature humanization.
“Must have instinctively realized” is ordinary English epistemic inference, not claimed direct access to Caster’s mind, and closely matches 直感したのか.

“Sounds emotional” is broad but accurate for a voice heightened by emotion, while her escalating loss of composure is evident from the shouted dialogue itself. This is tonal preference, not material error.
“Terrified by that pressure” is a natural rendering of the figurative psychological effect of a gaze powerful enough to tear at her heart. “It’s only natural” also corresponds to 不思議ではない.
“Must know” is epistemic and preserves Shirou’s inferred explanation expressed by のだろう; it does not convert the inference into narrator-certified fact.
The supplied displayed translation contains only a line break. The raw sound-effect marker is a script command, not displayed English prose, so treating it as leaked text is an extraction error.
The supplied raw Original witness explicitly contains the image of Caster as a heap of red flesh. The English is an Original-edition conditional branch, not an invented image.
The Japanese makes Caster’s neck the axe’s target; “head” is a concrete anatomical change and also loses the neck’s figurative attempt to voice its pain.

主 can mean an object’s owner or wearer, so a robe that has “lost its master” can refer to its absent occupant. The wording is ungrammatical, but the accusation that it necessarily means Caster’s contractual Master is unsupported.
The Japanese explicitly compares the robe’s writhing to a snake. “Like a wave” substitutes a different visual simile.
“Getting run over by a steamroller” is a natural rendering of a person being caught up in a roller. The Japanese does not require the finding’s more specific plural crushing-rollers mechanism.
Epistemic “must have” appropriately conveys Shirou’s question-based inference from のか. The following Japanese itself treats her inability to die under the swords as observed fact.
The Japanese identifies the arsenal specifically as classes of demonic swords and spears comparable to Noble Phantasms. The English reduces this to unspecified weapons that “equal” Noble Phantasms.
無尽蔵 describes apparently inexhaustible quantity, the point of Caster’s disbelief about their number. “Merciless” instead supplies an unrelated judgment about cruelty.
今までの比ではなかった says the force of Saber’s glare is beyond comparison with anything before. “Different” omits that extreme increase in intensity.
“Like yesterday for you” is figurative English for an event that feels extremely recent, not a claim that it occurred exactly one day earlier. It adequately renders つい先日 in this temporal contrast.
“Shakes her head saying it’s impossible” can describe what the gesture communicates, matching the Japanese と-marked content. It need not mean separately quoted audible dialogue.

Context can support anger, so calling that emotion wholly invented is too strong. The narrower error is that 無我夢中 explains her failure to react through frantic, heedless absorption, which “in anger” does not fully convey.
変わり種 means an unusual type or variant; “hybrid” adds a specific mixed-origin classification not stated here.
愛玩 describes self-serving fondling, petting, or toying with something regarded as owned. “Prizing a possession” makes the gaze sound valuing and omits that dehumanizing mode of enjoyment.
The number is retained, but せっかくの marks the fifth as a specially valued or welcome acquisition; that evaluative force is absent.
The Japanese retrospectively links the preceding words to an effect already produced; the English instead asks a present-tense abstract question.
心を決める requires Saber to reach a decision or resolution. “Be prepared” does not necessarily convey that demand.
迅る conveys rapid motion, so “moves quickly” is accurate though less vivid. Preferring “flashes” or “races forth” is stylistic.
身を翻す can describe swiftly turning or dodging away. In this attack context, “tries to dodge” is a defensible natural paraphrase.
The English passive construction makes the indulgence itself sound “forgiven,” obscuring that it grants unrestricted license in one particular matter.

The genuine problem is loss of the base-text meaning “without an incantation”; retaining the ruby as “no action” is not itself unsupported, and the claimed contradiction with her arm movement overreads that ruby.
“Having a nightmare” naturally conveys the appearance of being afflicted or haunted by one. The alleged loss of coercive terror is interpretive preference.
“As the same criminals” is awkward English, but it still clearly conveys that Saber and Caster now share criminal guilt; no material mistranslation is established.
呪い殺す specifically means killing by cursing, while “condemn” removes that destructive magical action; 仲良く also supplies Caster’s grotesquely friendly tone.
Using “ears” for 鼓膜 is ordinary English synecdoche in a figurative description of painfully loud laughter, not a claim that the outer ears are literally destroyed.
The supplied raw Original witness contains the brain-death wording, so this is an Original/conditional variant rather than an unsupported insertion based only on the all-ages body wording.
ザッパリやられた is comic mimetic wording for being readily or cleanly done in; “dies easily from a simple mistake” is loose but defensible, while “cut down” depends on contextual inference.
猪突猛進 describes reckless headlong behavior, and “Saber’s recklessness” is a normal contextual rendering. Loss of the boar image is stylistic compression.
気が抜ける can mean losing focus or vigilance. After falling into a trap, “not concentrating” is a defensible contextual equivalent.
The English loses one member of the deliberate three-part 色／恋／情け sequence and therefore materially truncates the wordplay.
“Keep a leash on” is the natural English coercive-animal metaphor for putting a collar on someone; the humiliating control image remains.
The Japanese categorically says not to anger Saber. “Too much” introduces an unsupported permissible degree of provocation.
本気で modifies how frightening Saber is, whereas the English intensifies her anger and weakens the result to “can get scary.” It also adds a markedly profane register.
“Almost died” adequately paraphrases 臨死体験 here, but the English genuinely omits the explicit recent timing ちょっと前.
形だけの処置 means treatment that is largely nominal or retained for form’s sake. “Just for show” is a defensible idiom and need not imply fraudulent treatment.
デタラメ can describe something bizarre, unreasonable, or abnormal. “Strange” is mild, but the following vampire comparison supplies the extraordinary force; this is chiefly tonal preference.
A hand axe is a kind of axe, and the compact weapon remains readily imaginable. The lost size specification is not a material error here.
不死身 specifically concerns apparent immortality or invulnerability. “Beyond human” replaces that concrete inability-to-kill claim with generic superhuman abnormality.
The supplied displayed English contains a line break, not a literal leaked “[r]” token. The raw command is presentation data, and the interrupted “Shir—” still conveys the realization.
Lowering one’s gaze is a form of looking away. The English is less spatially exact but remains a defensible description of the same withdrawal.
覇気 covers spirit, vigor, or force of presence. Saying her “spirit has been low” is a plausible, if less precise, rendering in this subdued context.
Something difficult to say is naturally something one does not want to discuss. Saber’s silence supports that contextual paraphrase without establishing a factual reversal.
気質 can be rendered “character” or “temperament”; the surrounding comparison between two heroic spirits makes the heroic frame clear.
一度に expressly defines a simultaneous summoning limit. “Basic limit” omits that premise, which matters to the surviving-Servant hypothesis.
The ruby makes 士郎 read “this time,” so the accusation should not insist on an explicit Shirou comparison. The English does, however, omit that Saber had been 敵なし—unmatched—when properly summoned.
というワケじゃない negates invincibility. The English drops the negation and states the direct opposite, contradicted immediately by the Berserker comparison.
“Remains from the previous war” already means continued survival from that war rather than a new summoning. The nuance of そのまま is sufficiently preserved.
“Matches what I’ve been hoping for” naturally conveys that Rin’s theory gives form to Shirou’s pre-existing hope. Requiring the literal shape metaphor is preference policing.
ハルペー denotes Harpe; “Herpe” is a demonstrable misspelling of the proper name.
お不動さん specifically refers colloquially to Fudō/Acala. “A Buddha thing” erases that recognizable referent and is religiously imprecise.
原型 means prototypes, originals, or archetypes. “Forms” loses Rin’s claim about the historical sources of demonic swords.
Although “no point” compresses the proverb, the following sentences explicitly restore the threatened damage and the joke that Shirou will chiefly suffer it. The complete page preserves the logic.
形状だけで言うなら limits the identifications to judgments from shape. “I saw” presents the named weapons more directly and omits that epistemic limitation.
The sentence is present in the supplied Original Japanese. Its omission or commenting-out in another edition does not make the Original-aligned English unsupported.
困る and 申し訳ない express awkwardness and apologetic guilt, not emotional injury. “I’m hurt” changes Shirou’s reaction.
“Hiding a tree in a forest” is an established and functionally equivalent English analogy: one item is concealed among many similar items. Literal repetition of “leaf” is not required.
In this exchange, “I think you’re useless” is readily understood as useless to the current analysis. Context supplies the situational scope of 戦力外.
The Japanese explicitly describes Shirou physically raising his arms in a banzai/surrender gesture. “I give up” preserves the abstraction but omits the comic action.
The English still pivots from the difficulty of explaining to the more fundamental question of why he thought it. “Forgetting that” is awkward, but it does not reverse the introspection.
Given the immediately preceding discussion of weapons that only imitate shape, “were perfect” naturally means perfect in form. Repeating “form” is unnecessary.
“Deflected it with my sword” conveys physically repelling and rejecting the proposal. Treating “deflected” as merely a temporary conversational parry is unwarranted in context.
真面目に can mean seriously, sincerely, or honestly. “Answers honestly” is within its lexical range, even if “earnestly” would sharpen the joke.
Eyes “laughing at” Saber and Shirou naturally conveys that Rin is using both as objects of amusement. The 肴 metaphor is localized rather than materially omitted.
一気飲み explicitly says Rin downs the bitter tea in one go. The English merely says she drinks it, losing the comic demonstration that Shirou’s retaliation does not faze her.
“Leaves in a good mood” is normal English for observing someone depart with a cheerful air. It does not improperly claim privileged access to Rin’s inner state.
和室 is more specifically a Japanese-style room, but “a room” preserves the caretaking action and destination adequately; the omitted architectural detail is not material here.
The Japanese says none of the necessary conversation with Saber has yet happened. The English instead says the intended message is mentally disorganized, a different proposition.
牽制する means checking, forestalling, or discouraging what Shirou is about to say. “Tries to block my question” is a reasonable contextual paraphrase of Saber’s preemptive response.
取り戻す means regaining or reclaiming what was lost from the present onward. “Change who you are now” substitutes a demand for identity change.
The English retains the near-fall and Shirou bracing himself with his hands. Omitting the direction “backward” is minor staging compression, not a material error.
The Japanese joint subject says Saber and Kiritsugu both survived to the final stage. “I won to the end” removes Kiritsugu from that result.

The immediately preceding page explicitly establishes that Kiritsugu was Saber’s Master ten years earlier. In that context, “my father was a Master” communicates the revelation being questioned without creating a false relation.

Here “hero” denotes the heroic entity who becomes a Servant, and the sentence explicitly retains the Servant distinction. Using canonical “Heroic Spirit” would be preferable terminology, not required for correctness.
なんであるか asks what the three communications were. The English instead asks when Kiritsugu spoke, changing the implied connection to his three orders.
情 has a broad range including feeling, emotion, affection, and human sentiment. “Anything that you would call emotion” is broad but supported, especially before the next page’s あらゆる感情を殺し.
“Object” is less exact than 道具, but the immediately preceding clause explicitly says he treated Saber “as a tool,” preserving the parallel of self-instrumentalization.
In context, “my memory” refers to the childlike adoptive father Shirou personally knew. The English’s “only truth” substantially tracks 俺にとってはそれだけが真実だ.
“Legitimate” can mean conforming to the prescribed rules or procedure, not merely morally approved. It is a defensible rendering of 正規 in this ritual context.
The highlighted English “Servants would not exist” is not in the supplied page. The actual English—“I will not be summoned unless the Holy Grail is present”—accurately reflects Saber’s statement.
The English omits the separate mock-afterlife clause that returning dead Shirou to the present world looks difficult, which supplies the premise for the “rescue corner.”
Both “pit” and “bottom of the valley” express the joke of a slight detour producing a disastrous fall. The compressed English metaphor remains accurate enough.
The surrounding English already divides responsibility between Shirou and Saber; “isn’t all hers” preserves the operative contrast. The exact half-and-half wording is not material to the joke.
In a route-choice context, “real ending” naturally means the valid or correct ending. It does not necessarily assert a materially different hierarchy of authenticity.
The proverb warns the victor to tighten the helmet straps after winning and remain vigilant. “Get your act together and win” moves the preparation before victory and loses that warning.
Japanese omits the subject, and both Taiga and Illya are hosting the dojo. Explicating the promise as plural “we” is contextually natural and not an agency error.
“Relieve Saber” is awkward, but in context it can mean relieve her worry and therefore conveys 安心させる. No contrary action or agency is introduced.
“Turning point” is a natural rendering of a consequential fork in life, while the immediately preceding contrast between the Emiya household and church preserves the two alternatives.

After pausing for a breath, going through the heavy doors is a defensible compression of putting his hand on them at the scene transition. It preserves the threshold action without a material contradiction.
In this ominous context, “feel afraid” is a defensible rendering of 緊張する; the accusation imposes an overly narrow distinction between fear and tension.
The English omits the explicit description of Kotomine speaking with bored or uninterested affect.
庭園 denotes a garden or landscaped grounds, while “park” misleadingly recategorizes the church’s inner garden.
“This … room seems to be Kotomine’s” naturally means it is his own room; omitting the word “private” does not remove that relation.
The supplied Original witness contains the alcohol line, so this is Original-edition content rather than an unsupported insertion; the displayed page has evidently followed the later-edition text.
“While sitting down” compresses the heavier nuance of settling into the sofa but preserves the relevant action; the alleged character-level distortion is not demonstrable.
苦手 expresses discomfort or difficulty dealing with Kotomine, reinforced by the following intimidation; “hate” materially intensifies it into hostility.
In this quasi-mechanical description of a Servant, “a failure” can defensibly mean a defective or malfunctioning instance; it need not judge Saber’s personal worth.
The passage expressly contrasts pre-death records with post-death memory. Rendering 記録 as “memories” erases that technical distinction and makes the explanation internally muddled.
“Must not assent to the fact” is malformed and misstates 納得がいかない, which here means that the account does not satisfy or make sense to him.

Given the immediately stated conditional agreement to become a Heroic Spirit, “hasn’t completed the contract” is a defensible contextual rendering of Shirou’s rough summary rather than a demonstrated reversal.
The ruby explicitly supplies サーヴァント as the reading of 英霊. Using “Servant” follows the voiced term; not reproducing both written and ruby layers in English is not by itself a material error.
駆り出される can mean being called or summoned out for a task, and the passive repeated summoning still permits an involuntary reading. The charge demands a preferred tonal gloss.
The Japanese specifies return to her own pre-death self, whereas “deathbed” substitutes a concrete dying place and is especially misleading for Saber’s death on a hill.
使役される means being employed or made to serve. “Be summoned” describes a different event and omits the servitude that Kotomine says awaits her.
英霊 is the defined supernatural category under discussion, not merely an ordinary hero; reducing it to “hero” obscures Shirou’s technical question.
Japanese does not obligatorily mark number here, and “the deviser” can generically mean whoever devised the system. A definite historical plurality is not established by this wording alone.
元々 describes what the system originally was or was based on; “that is just the past” fails to convey that proposition.
使役される explicitly concerns being made to serve, not merely being summoned. The English removes the central burden Shirou condemns.
The genuine problems are “loop of time” for 時間軸 and the malformed “be in two chances.” However, “two … at once” is a natural way to express non-simultaneity and does not invent a fixed total of two.
“Continues to challenge each one” already conveys proceeding through all the trials individually. It softens the idiomatic force of 虱潰し but preserves the exhaustive logic.
“She’ll continue like this unless…” expresses an indefinitely continuing condition and preserves the stated escape condition. Loss of the emphatic 一生 is tonal compression, not a material reversal.
“Many ages” is a strictly narrower quantifier than あらゆる時代, which says every or all eras.
“She will return” leaves the destination unspecified, omitting the crucial mechanism that she returns to herself immediately before her original death.
似て非なる means similar yet fundamentally different. “Spurious” instead means false or inauthentic and does not express that relation.
意思 is will or volition. “No mind” more broadly denies mentality and misstates the specific lack of autonomous agency being explained.
Although awkward, “donor” can denote a supplying source, and the surrounding sentence explicitly identifies what is supplied as magical energy. The technical function remains recoverable.
English “must have predicted” is itself an inferential construction, not an unqualified factual assertion, and reasonably corresponds to Shirou’s inference marked by か.
達したかった attributes a desire to reach this conclusion. “Was waiting to reach” substitutes passive anticipation and loses that purposive desire.
“Have become a familiar summoned in this age” awkwardly but substantially conveys acquiring the status of a familiar in this era; it need not describe a separate new summoning.
The raw [r] is a script line-break command, and the supplied rendered page shows only a line break. Treating the control code as visible published prose mistakes extraction data for translation.
“I want to” states a desire rather than a guaranteed plan and naturally remains subject to feasibility. Omitting “if possible” is compression, not an unqualified assertion that success is certain.
吐き出す can evoke vomiting, and the next page explicitly calls the reaction 吐き気. Reading this solely as psychological exposure is not compelled by the Japanese.
“Just making the vessel is” is not a complete English proposition and obscures the qualification that only making the vessel is comparatively easy.
釜 specifically supplies the cauldron image. Calling it another “vessel” erases the contrast between the mythic cauldron and the manufactured Grail vessel.
The English wholly omits the claim that the omnipotent-cauldron motif lies at the foundation of all mythologies.
“Summon” is an ordinary rendering of 降霊, and “to the artificial Holy Grail” retains the receiving object, albeit awkwardly. A distinct possession mechanism is not demonstrably lost.
ラインの黄金 refers to the Rhinegold tradition or legend. “Golden rule of the line” is an unrelated phrase produced by misparsing the proper name.
神業 praises the imitation-Grail technique as virtually divine craftsmanship; “best suited” changes exceptional accomplished skill into mere comparative suitability.
The supplied Original-edition candidate explicitly says the Church and Association were killing one another, so “bloody war” is supported by Original rather than invented from the later 係争 wording.
The English retains the Far Eastern location but omits the stated selection criterion: it was beyond the Church’s surveillance.
持ち主 identifies Tohsaka as the owner of the area’s spiritual land. “In charge of” substitutes vague administration for ownership and drops 霊地.
師 can be “master” or teacher, 大家 an acknowledged master, and “summoning” is within the contextual range of 降霊術. The repetition is stylistically poor but not a demonstrated factual error.
三すくみ denotes a three-way standoff whose members check one another. Merely saying three parties should be involved omits the intended balance-of-power structure.
“A family with history” awkwardly conveys a long-established lineage. It weakens the prestige in 名門, but that is insufficiently material for the stated accusation.

The raw witness shows mutually exclusive conditional variants, “killing each other” and “fighting.” Their concatenation is the warned-about branch-flattening artifact, not revision debris in one active line.
As a verb, “model” can mean shape or form something, so “the system to model the Servants” is an awkward but defensible rendering of 形作る.
The Japanese names both Illya’s and Tohsaka’s families as originators; the English incorrectly leaves only Illya’s family and makes it singular.
In response to the claim that Illya physically “has” the Grail, “anything with her” naturally means a carried object and preserves Shirou’s literal misunderstanding without requiring “luggage.”
“It must have been” marks an inference from Kotomine’s reaction, corresponding adequately to the tentative のか; it does not present direct knowledge.
持ち得なかった states inability to possess the qualifications. “Did not become a Master” reports only nonparticipation and loses the eligibility constraint.
“Must be satisfied” remains an epistemic inference, not certainty, and substantially reflects the tentative behavioral reading marked by のか.
The preceding English “Behind me” preserves that the words follow Shirou’s retreating back, while “asks as if confirming” accurately conveys 確認するように. The lost throwing image is stylistic nuance.
Taken with “You’re not the type to give that kind of warning,” the English clearly conveys suspicion about Kotomine’s uncharacteristic behavior. “What’s wrong?” is loose but contextually defensible.
In the immediate discussion of sustaining Saber by feeding her souls, “keep Saber” naturally means keep her present and alive. The life-and-death sense is not actually lost in context.
“Must not even care” explicitly marks Shirou’s inference about Kotomine’s reaction and therefore does not promote のか to certain fact.
Saying that Kotomine is laughing already conveys visible enjoyment in this context. 愉快そう adds color, but its compression is not a material omission.
In response to Shirou’s glare, “did I offend you?” is a defensible pragmatic rendering of Kotomine’s feigned acknowledgment that his remark was indiscreet or offensive.
“Have no right to say anything about it” idiomatically means having no standing to intervene or comment on her decision; the contextual sense of 口を出す remains clear.
“Investigate tomorrow” omits both the completion in 調べ上げる and the by-the-end-of-tomorrow deadline in 明日中に.

The teeth-gritting refusal is genuine Original-edition prose, while the simpler departure is the alternate later-edition branch. Their apparent collision is branch flattening, not an unsupported inserted variant.
“Moonlit” is a minor atmospheric explicitation compatible with the nighttime scene; the supplied Japanese does not establish a material change merely because it says “bridge at night.”
Within the repeated proposal to sustain Saber by feeding her souls, “keep Saber” naturally means keep her alive or present. The stakes remain unambiguous from context.
望む concerns Shirou hypothetically wanting the outcome; “accepted that” instead concerns assent to Kotomine’s proposal and changes the object of his conflicted thought.
The base text names the Holy Grail War, but its ruby reads こんなこと, “this kind of thing.” “This kind of war” reasonably combines the written referent with the supplied reading.
The supplied Original witness contains クソ神父, while the milder line is the alternate all-ages branch. The duplication is branch flattening, and the insult is not unsupported Original content.
呪縛 here figuratively describes the binding hold of Kotomine’s words. Replacing it with the specifically named Command Spell invents a literal magical mechanism.
きいーん describes a sustained high metallic ring. “A hard steel sound” neither reproduces that audible quality nor follows naturally from the Japanese.

“Charm” can defensibly express 魔力 metaphorically, and inability to ignore conveys its compelling effect. The narrower surviving defect is the ungrammatical “charm that make,” with some loss in shifting “could not deny” to “could not ignore.”
手を重ねる can figuratively denote joining forces, and the surrounding progression concerns when Shirou began cooperating with Saber. Insisting on a literal physical hand gesture is not warranted.
The English omits 心を重ねた後 entirely, removing the explicit emotional joining that precedes Shirou making the sword for her.
