The English preserves a compassionate smile, but “big” and “full of” drop the depth and apparent/qualified force of ような. The claim of specifically ominous depth is overdrawn.
The source explicitly presents the object as unidentified and unfathomable; “something” alone omits that deliberate first-sight uncertainty.

“Father” reasonably conveys オヤジ, but the English omits the written identification 切嗣 and loses the intimate reading/register contrast. This is a narrower presentation and nuance issue, not a complete actor error.
The source says the object only looked like a young child’s empty shell; “corpse” prematurely fixes the later revelation and changes the staged uncertainty.

The supplied Original page lacks the graphic details, but the supplied English witness contains them in a conditional mature branch. The evidence establishes an edition/branch discrepancy, not whether this mirror output is an erroneous insertion for the comparator.
破壊され means destroyed/broken, while “pierced” narrows the attack to penetration and conflicts with the source’s stated result.
The hose simile and duplicated “mouth” are unsupported by the Japanese. The source describes blood overflowing as he vomits it from his mouth.
疑問 is question/doubt, and 体を支配していたのは疑問だけ emphasizes exclusive domination. “Wonder” changes the emotional state toward amazement or curiosity.
The Japanese itself uses 亡骸 after the preceding “alive” revelation, deliberately retaining the corpse/remains image. The English follows that source wording rather than inventing the contradiction.
察しておいて and 進ませる support perceiving/anticipating dangers and helping the person proceed along the best path. “Predict” and “guide” are defensible contextual choices in an astrology passage.

The Japanese says winning the Holy Grail War was her priority, not literally the entirety of what she cared about. “All she cared about” is a real strengthening, though the underlying contrast is preserved.
“A big change in her thinking” conveys change but weakens both the intensity of 凄まじいまで and the broader emotional sense of 心境. The claim should be limited to magnitude and emotional register.
苦笑し, a self-aware wry or embarrassed smile, is omitted entirely from the mirror rendering.
ゼンマイ仕掛け evokes a wind-up mechanism/toy, whereas “robot” changes the comic image. This is a genuine metaphor shift, but not necessarily the material error claimed.
意地悪く is teasingly mean or mischievous; “evil” moralizes and intensifies it. The narrower register complaint survives, but the rendering still signals playful villainy in context.
立て込んでいる事などお見通し means Rin sees through the two characters’ complicated situation. “Knows about them” omits the complication and her perceptiveness.
落ち着いた means stabilized or settled, not necessarily recovered. “Did she not recover?” overstates Saber’s premise.
もう一杯なの states that the capacity is already full. “Still filling up” reverses the relevant state.
余分な機能 naturally means surplus or superfluous functions; calling them unimportant is supported by the immediate contrast with the least necessary function and is not a material error.
忌々しげに describes Rin speaking with vexation or resentment. “Annoyingly” instead characterizes her speech as irritating to others and changes the experiencer.
外来のマスター means an outside/externally dispatched Master, not a foreign national. “Foreigner” adds unsupported nationality.
そいつ is ungendered in this passage. “Her” assigns a female gender absent from the supplied Japanese.
The Japanese presents one combined taking of the Command Spells with the body/arm bearing them. The English breaks this into a speculative arm correction and a malformed separate clause.

生存は絶望的でしょうね is an almost hopeless prognosis; “I don’t think the Master’s alive” is close and is reinforced by the following sentence, but it shifts from prognosis to a direct belief about present life status.
English singular they is a standard ungendered pronoun and can refer to Lancer. The Japanese does not require a plural reading.

The source says the Command Spells were taken; “arm… the Command Spell” adds a visible false start, though the prior left-arm evidence makes the inference understandable. Limit the claim to an unsupported hesitation/misparse.
そのどちらかによるもの means performed by either a Master or a Servant. “Between Masters and Servants” changes the agent of transplantation into the parties between whom transfer occurs.
諜報専門 means specializing in intelligence/reconnaissance. “Only there to collect information” adds an exclusive-purpose claim, although the surrounding discussion makes information-gathering central.
The Japanese specifies the opponent who saw the Noble Phantasm and calls killing such a witness their standard practice. The English generalizes this to a rule for killing an enemy after use.
The source calls the second Servant combat-specialized and the plan a sure-win method. “Unknown Servant” and “great strategy” omit or weaken both tactical specifics.

In the stated context of fighting Servants and investigating their methods, “study their techniques” is a defensible rendering of 手口. The Japanese does not require a broader intelligence category here.
自分と士郎 identifies Saber herself and Shirou as the remaining pair to defeat. “Only have to defeat Shirou” omits Saber from the enemy’s target.
規定通りの戦い means a prescribed/rule-conforming pattern of fighting, not the enemy’s previous plan. The English changes the nature of the constraint.
取り返しの付かない状況 is an irreversible or irreparable situation. “In a danger” is both malformed and materially less severe.

The Japanese explicitly bases the comparison on the air being stagnant and ranks the church with Ryuudou Temple on that basis. The English’s malformed “stagnated with death to the same level” does not clearly preserve that relation.
虚空 is empty space/void, giving the gaze an uncanny non-object. “The distance” replaces that object with ordinary spatial distance.
The source includes both 一瞬にして and the observed girl’s figure passing like a bullet. “Runs like a bullet” preserves speed but compresses the instantaneous disappearance and viewpoint detail.
The Japanese depicts her reason flaring white-hot while her whole body is already armed, with involuntary loss of control. “Made her arm herself” assigns a more deliberate causal agency.
絶望的なまでの modifies the death scent as an extreme, despair-inducing quality; “a hopeless scent of death” is awkward but preserves that semantic relation.
何千分の一にも満たない is less than one several-thousandth, not less than one-thousandth. The numerical comparison is materially enlarged.

The supplied Original witness explicitly contains these lines, even though base/all-ages mark them inactive. Under the stated rule, their presence is an edition difference, not unsupported insertion against Original.
The Japanese expresses a feared possibility with ではないか: he may expire while she is delayed. “He is dying right now” promotes that possibility into a present fact.
The English is awkward and loses the cutting-down image of 斬り伏せる, but “reason of God” remains a plausible literal attempt at 神の道理. Narrow the claim to imagery and idiomaticity.
徒い means a follower/adherent. “God’s messenger” adds a specific messenger role not stated by the Japanese.
The supplied Original witness contains the explanatory sentence; its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference explicitly excluded by the audit rule from an unsupported-insertion charge.
吹き飛ばし can naturally be rendered “crashes through” in an action sequence, especially with the immediately stated demolished church. The force is not materially absent.
冷静に means calmly/composedly, while “softly” describes gentleness of force. The source-to-English shift is real, but the calm intention is partly conveyed by “tried to open.”

それ is contextually broad and can refer to the uncontrolled force/state, not necessarily only her legs. “Them” narrows the antecedent, though the surrounding sentence makes the legs a plausible inference.
転がり落ちるように conveys a tumbling, uncontrolled descent. “Goes down the stairs” omits that vivid loss-of-control image.
地下聖堂 is an underground sanctuary/chapel, while “temple” identifies a different type of religious building and conflicts with the church setting.
“She is straining at her limits” is a natural contextual rendering of limb tension reaching its peak. The English does not necessarily erase the physical extremity.
力の加減 means moderating or easing the force; “cannot loosen up” can idiomatically express inability to ease off in this action context.
The Japanese describes the area beneath him as wet with red blood. The English changes that static spatial observation into blood actively pouring out of him.
見境なし means indiscriminate or without restraint. “Ignoring me” changes Lancer’s reproach into a complaint about not acknowledging him, contrary to the surrounding action.

殺しきれず is an idiomatic description of failing to neutralize or bleed off the blow’s force. “Could not defeat its power” is awkward English but remains semantically recoverable and does not establish a distinct event.
The translation omits the Master-exclusive condition attached to Saber’s eyes; this is a material mental-state detail, not merely an omitted pronoun.
“Comes at Saber” omits the explicit spatial transition into Saber’s range, which marks the duel’s initiation.
殺し合い explicitly means fighting one another with lethal stakes; “fight you” removes that commitment.
戦い can be generic or count-neutral, and “battles appropriate to heroic spirits” is a defensible contextual rendering of a Servant’s heroic ideal.
The core normative meaning is present, but “easily” and especially “normal Servant” overstate the Japanese. A narrower complaint about added ease/normality survives.
この上なく marks an extreme or utmost disadvantage; the translation reduces that explicit intensity to merely unfavorable.
“Invisible sword” is a defensible descriptive rendering of the concealed sword effect here; omission of the technical label alone does not establish a material translation error.
必殺の一撃 denotes a killing or decisive lethal blow, not merely a powerful one.
日和った carries a colloquial cowardly/play-safe tone that “wait and see” softens, but the basic cautious action remains. The valid claim is tonal undertranslation, not neutralization of the whole event.
弟子一号 means “Disciple/Student Number One,” not a senior student; the English changes the role label’s numbering joke.
風紀 includes discipline, conduct, and order; “morals” is broad but idiomatic and defensible in this comic complaint.
The English shifts explicit rule-breaking toward rudeness, though the general complaint about youths’ conduct remains. The narrower loss of the rules/discipline joke is valid.
“My head accepts it” preserves the action, but drops 律儀に’s grimly dutiful personification. The accusation should be narrowed from total omission to tonal loss.
The English directly preserves the conditional and repeated exclusivity: his pain is his to endure alone.
The plural is supported by the surrounding victims’ voices and is a natural contextual rendering of この声; Japanese does not require an English singular here.

“Stabbed” narrows the gouging/excavation image, but remains a plausible English metaphor for the chest being deeply pierced by the voices. The valid claim is lexical image loss, not a wholly false event.
足り無すぎた means his means were far too inadequate; “no way” makes that insufficiency absolute and changes the degree.
応えてやる means answer/respond to the pleas, not rescue the dead. The translation changes the act he is unable to perform.

The supplied raw witness explicitly contains an edition/branch conditional between “my heart will break” and “I’ll go crazy.” The joined alternatives are identified as branch-flattening artifacts, so the accusation is not established as an unsupported insertion.
“Fix the contradiction” retains the living-dead contradiction but weakens 戻す to proper order/course. The valid issue is vagueness, not wholesale loss of the concept.

原因 can naturally identify the responsible source of the hell in context, and 償いをさせる supports an English rendering involving making that responsible party atone. “Creator” is interpretive but not demonstrably false.
“Superhero” is a defensible natural equivalent for the recurring cultural idea 正義の味方; the accusation treats a translation preference as a factual error.
The English preserves reactive cleanup and limitation but omits 効率よく, “efficiently.” That is a narrower nuance loss than the finding’s broader claim.
報いる means repay, requite, or make amends, not literally save them. The translation changes Shirou’s obligation toward the dead into rescue.
The Japanese says he lacks power to refute the man’s contemptuous reduction of 正義の味方; “only so strong” turns that categorical critique into a claim about power level.
“Right behind me” naturally expresses a voice coming from directly behind his head in first-person narration; the claimed exact-location loss is not demonstrated.
“Let us go” preserves movement but drops もう少し, the incremental “a little farther.” The complaint should be limited to that spatial detail.

The Japanese ruby simultaneously presents Kotomine’s name as written text and Shirou’s self-reading. The English preserves only the semantic “like me” relation and loses that textual identification layer.
English past tense is normal narrative tense and does not establish that the wound existed only in the past; the Japanese’s present-state meaning remains compatible.
納める means sheathe or put away the sword. “Lower your sword” changes Kotomine’s demand from ending its use to merely changing its position.
“Things have turned out like this” can naturally convey an unintended or unexpected outcome; the accusation treats an acceptable English implication as omission.
獲ろう is more concrete than “seek,” but “seek the Holy Grail” can mean pursue obtaining it in this context. The valid issue is weakened possession/obtaining force, not a wholly different proposition.
最後の殺し合い is the final mutual lethal contest; “continue fighting” removes both finality and the explicit killing stakes.

The surrounding English already conveys postponing the confrontation: they may continue, and Kotomine will accompany them if they choose. The generic final question is a contextual paraphrase, not a demonstrable omission.
“Go so far” can pragmatically refer to taking such an elaborate route, but it loses the explicit roundabout/indirect character of the scheme. Narrow the claim to that lexical loss.
“It seems” preserves ようだ, while “reluctantly” reflects 不承不承. Agreement is a reasonable inference from the observed nod in context.
連中 is plural and refers to the people who summoned them. “The thing” changes both agency and number to an inanimate singular entity.

“The vessel in which the Holy Grail will appear” preserves the vessel/Grail relation but weakens 降ろす’s ritual bringing-down/descent imagery. The accusation should not claim the whole relation is lost.
すでに and 持ち始めていよう together mean the vessel should already have begun acquiring Grail power; “should begin” shifts this to a future onset.
“Should understand” preserves the probing question but drops 薄々, the tentative/dim quality of Saber’s knowledge. It is not simply a flat assertion.
空しい concerns futility, emptiness, or pointlessness. “Sad” changes Kotomine’s argument about meaningless sacrifice into an emotional appeal.
The Japanese marks the lifting as uncertain or inferred with のか. The English states the action as fact.
The English conveys pain causing whiteness, but omits 視界がかろうじて生きていた and the return-to-white image. The complaint is a narrower descriptive loss.
下衆 can be rendered as lowly, base, or vile; “not as lowly as you” retains the direct contempt without a factual reversal.
“That will not be his true opinion” is awkward but semantically conveys that the earlier statement is not his true inner view; no material future-state error is established.
“Dark side” is a normal English metaphorical equivalent for 影 in this psychological context; it does not erase the concealed-inner-shadow idea materially.
その先にあるもの refers to what lies beyond or ahead of the fire memory. “What comes out of it” recasts this as an action producing a result.
The Japanese places the electrical sensation at the back of the neck and depicts consciousness turning inside out. The English relocates the electricity into the mind itself.
“Burned-up corpses” is a defensible English description of corpses charred by fire; the Japanese blackness is not materially contradicted.
“Though” is a grammatical typo for “through,” changing the intended spatial relation in this climactic admission.
咆える音 is the roaring sound of the quoted demand “let me out”; the English adds madness and omits the actual desperate request.
The Japanese specifies one mother pleading to take this child too. Plural mothers and children materially generalize the concrete scene.
そこまでしたからには expresses a moral consequence of having gone that far, not necessity forcing him to go that far. The logical relation is reversed.
The English retains the means-to-live condition but drops the repeated ethical claim that failing to live would make his survival a lie.
ごめんなさいと is the explicit apology he refuses to say; “I knew…” removes that thought and its deliberate withholding.
The Japanese distinguishes houses around the fire from homes struck by spreading flames. The English collapses both groups into vague proximity.
未練 is lingering attachment/regret that cannot let go, not merely affection. The emotional relation to the lost is materially softened.

The English fragment “I thought that…” is supported by the continuation’s 思った and naturally links the object fragment to the following remembrance statement; it is not demonstrably unsupported content.
In the complete context, “every single bit of it” refers back to the preceding 「その全てを」. The exhaustive reference is therefore contextually supplied by the Japanese sequence.
帰して means send back or let return, not return an object. “Give it back” confuses the victims’ plea to go home with the earlier 返して.
“Superhero” remains a defensible natural rendering of 正義の味方 in this repeated ideological context; the accusation is primarily terminology preference.
“Crumbled away as I ignored the pleas” conveys repeated erosion and the resulting loss of self, albeit with an idiomatic verb choice.
許されない supplies the guilt-driven condition that he cannot be forgiven unless he continues forward; the English omits it entirely.
The Japanese fragment says he was taught by many deaths he had not saved. The English turns deaths into people and adds a specific lesson about continuing.
胸を張って adds proud, head-held-high bodily resolve to moving forward in the dead’s place; the English omits that explicit image.
The Japanese emphasizes that these parental figures were closer to him than anyone. The English preserves parenthood but omits that defining closeness.
The command explicitly refers to a window, continuing the sealed-memory metaphor. The supplied English omits the entire page.
The Japanese identifies the pain as coming from the wound opened in his chest; “pain in my chest” removes the wound and its opening.
“Burning” conveys heat but drops the extreme “hot enough to boil” sensation. The narrower intensity-loss claim survives.
“Ragged” can naturally convey breathing that breaks irregularly and without control; だらしなく does not require a more literal adjective.
中の傷 is an internal wound, not merely pain inside. The English abstracts the wound that remains unhealed.
腫れ上がり explicitly adds swelling of the inner wound, which is absent from the English sentence.
彼女 identifies the figure as female and, in context, Saber. “A figure” removes that identity at the moment her image sustains him.
“I have to act like I’m all right” naturally conveys 大丈夫だって…張らないと as putting on a brave front; the literal chest image is not required for accuracy.
死なない means not die, not merely avoid being hurt. The translation materially weakens Shirou’s imagined reversal.
The Japanese explicitly says his thoughts have become unable to think. “With my burning head” preserves heat but omits cognitive collapse.

The English preserves the fingers’ contact with the wet floor, but drops their pain-enduring state and the splatting sound びちゃり. The broader claim that agency/contact are wholly omitted is too strong.
“They all want to go back” preserves the collective desire, while the immediately preceding “I hear their voices” supplies the vocal context. The accusation overstates the loss of the chorus.
The comparison concerns whether his longing reaches theirs, not whether his experience was equally bad. “As bad” changes the comparison’s target.
“Often” conveys repeated visits, but omits the emphatic “again and again”; the terrain itself is not omitted because “burned field” is present.
The Japanese says nobody was in the hallway, not that the hallway itself was nonexistent. The translation changes an imagined surviving space into a nonexistent structure.
司る means preside over/administer, not possess or stand beside. “With the Holy Grail” materially changes the priest’s relation to it.
The translation omits the appositional “sea of the dead” image and Shirou’s counterfactual identification with those dead.
死者 means the dead/deceased, with the ruby reading supplying “them”; “dead corpses” is redundant and shifts the people into corpses.
The bodily action of gritting his teeth is explicitly omitted.
蘇らせる is bringing the dead back to life, not regenerating their bodies.
“Take back what has happened” is an idiomatic English way to express undoing or reversing events; the accusation treats a defensible paraphrase as an error.
“Hurts my heart” is a natural emotional paraphrase of 胸を抉った; loss of the exact bodily metaphor alone does not establish a material mistranslation.
The translation omits the explicit continuation through long days after mourning.
抱えて進む means moving forward while carrying the pain and weight, not merely remembering them.
悲しく means sorrowful/sad; “painful” collapses the passage’s explicit distinction between sorrow and pain.
礎 is a foundation or cornerstone. “Constraints” reverses the positive structural function of memories.
“People” is a contextual narrowing of the deliberately broad 物 (“things/what”), but the accusation should be limited to that narrowing rather than treating the whole sentence as mistranslated.
In the surrounding passage about a chosen 道, “stray from my path” is a natural contextual rendering of not bending oneself; it is not demonstrably an error.
The wording is awkward and less clearly expresses enduring pain while speaking, but it still locates the declaration in pain; the claim should not say the endurance is wholly absent.
The English makes pain itself an object of control and omits that consciousness is desperately being held back as it fades and threatens to collapse.
蹲る describes crouching or huddling on the ground; “stay up on my knees” suggests successful upright posture and changes the physical action.
恨み言 means words of reproach or resentment left to him, not the absence of resentment itself.
The Japanese has a restrained qualification (“if one calls it sad, it was sad”); “it is sad” removes that hesitation, though the core sadness remains.
傷だらけ modifies the answer as an answer marked by Shirou’s wounded state; the translation omits that central image.
“Bore” conveys experiencing anger but weakens its explicit domination of her whole body; the narrower claim is loss of bodily-control force.
The source explicitly says he could barely see properly, while the translation substitutes only ragged breathing and omits the visual impairment.
“Controlling his tears” conveys suppression, but omits both 懸命に (“desperately”) and the tears already running; the claim should be narrowed to those losses.
“People” narrows 物 (“things/what”) in the same way as the parallel line, but the accusation should not treat that contextual explicitation as wholly indefensible.
“Stray from my path” is a natural idiomatic rendering in a passage repeatedly using 道; the English preserves the refusal to alter course.
頭を下げる can naturally be rendered as apologizing in this moral context; the accusation mistakes contextual explicitation for a semantic reversal.
“Will not change his path” is a normal English rendering of 道を曲げない and “declares” conveys 言い切った.
“Seen his” conveys access to the past, but loses the stronger mutual-sharing nuance of 共有した; the claim should be limited to that nuance.
The English leaves the object of 間違えていた implicit, but the surrounding discussion supplies the path in question; this is contextual narrowing, not a generic contradiction.
救い is salvation, not a person who saves him. “Your savior” changes the grammatical and conceptual contrast.
願い is singular here, but English plural “wishes” can function generically; the genuine claim is loss of the defining singularity, not a major change of plot.
“Save the world” is broadly compatible with 救罪, but it drops the religious/redemptive coloring; the accusation should target that tonal and lexical loss only.
The translation preserves the accusation of self-interest but turns “brandish/display ego” into a more stable-sounding trait label; the narrower claim is loss of the performative metaphor.
理性 is reason or rational judgment, not the heart. This changes what Kotomine’s argument destabilizes.
The Japanese shifts into Saber’s first-person inner voice; the English converts it into detached third-person narration.
The source is an interrupted first-person thought (“If I can obtain the Grail, I—”); the translation misparses it as a narrator phrase addressing Saber.
The source explicitly contains first-person ownership and a prior decision; “She would do anything” loses both.
“Unexpected” is correct, but あまりにも adds an extreme degree and 言葉 refers to words rather than specifically a proposal.
“Before he realizes it” naturally refers to realizing that he has died or been killed in this immediate context; the object is recoverable from the sentence.
The source identifies a boy crouching beyond the door; “a collapsed figure” removes his identity, posture, and beyond-the-door placement.
“Was shown his dark side” is a defensible rendering of being made to confront 自己の闇; the accusation overstates the difference between “dark side” and inner darkness.
手をかける specifies putting a hand to the sword; plural “hands” changes the described preparatory gesture.
倒れている explicitly says the Master is lying fallen; the translation omits that physical state.
もっともだ means reasonable or having a point; “true” is stronger epistemically, though not a total reversal.
“Redo everything” broadly conveys the wish to erase the past, but なかった事にしたい is specifically making the ruin as though it never happened; the claim should be narrowed to that distinction.
ではないか presents a counterfactual possibility (“might have”), while “must have been able” turns it into certainty.
The translation implies the abandoned heart, but omits explicit 永遠に; personal ownership is already recoverable from “she left.”
“People” narrows the deliberately broad 物, but the accusation should be limited to that narrowing rather than treating the line as wholly mistranslated.
In context, “stray from my path” is an idiomatic rendering of not bending oneself and aligns with the repeated 道 metaphor.
多くのモノ means many things; “everything” totalizes a bounded burden and changes its scale.
のたうちまわりながら describes writhing or thrashing in pain, which is omitted by the abstract “in his pain.”
The English preserves emotional pain but omits the explicit chest locus and bodily metaphor; this is a narrower imagery loss, not a wholly different event.
頑なに explicitly characterizes the refusal as stubborn or rigid; that force is omitted.
私はただ is Saber’s direct first-person self-question. The English converts it into third-person narration.
The English generalizes Saber’s self-reckoning into an impersonal maxim, but “another chance” is a defensible paraphrase of やり直し.
“Pierce her heart” is a conventional English rendering of an anguished cry strongly affecting her; the metaphorical shift alone does not prove an accuracy error.
The English omits 残酷な and the bodily image of weight gouging the chest, substantially weakening the temptation’s violence.
The source combines supreme forgiveness with self-directed salvation through erasure; “salvation by elimination” omits that structure.
想い refers to inward feelings, attachments, or sentiments. “Things” removes the human interior object of the question.
The Japanese is Saber’s first-person confession and says she has accumulated many deaths; the English makes it third-person and turns deaths into directly killing many people.
The translation omits that enduring and regretting the pain is requiem specifically for what was lost.
資格 is qualification or standing as king; “no longer a king” erases the distinction between status and identity.
承知で means knowingly or with full awareness; “believing so” changes conscious acknowledgment into belief.
The source depicts a phrase gouged into her chest; “kept to herself” replaces the physical wound image with secrecy.
The source says she may be hated by everyone; “fighting everything” changes social rejection into combat.
滅び leaves the ending’s ruin open in context, especially the country’s ruin; “her destruction” assigns it specifically to Saber.
“With that in mind” is a natural cognitive paraphrase but loses the image of holding the protected thing inside her chest/heart.
見続けよう means continue to dream/watch it through to the end; “end the dream” reverses the action.
欲しい is direct personal desire (“I want Shirou”); “favor Shirou” reduces it to comparative preference.
“Fool” preserves an insult, but 下郎 carries low-status/servile contempt that is weakened; the accusation should not require the exact archaic equivalent “cur.”
私の役割 is Saber’s first-person declaration of her own role; the English turns it into detached narration.
The source explicitly marks the dream as one-time and precious, and says Artoria saw it; the translation omits those qualifiers and changes the relation to wishing.
迷いのない explicitly characterizes the words as free of hesitation; the translation omits that decisive quality.
A wound gradually becoming smaller can naturally be rendered as beginning to heal; the accusation treats a reasonable English consequence as a contradiction.
The source says he responds to her whispered voice and grips Saber’s hand; the translation omits both the response relation and the whispered intimacy.
The source locates returning vitality in the blood-loss-dazed head; the translation invents energy entering a generally weak body.
聖堂 is sanctuary or chapel in this church setting, not a temple; the religious location is mislabeled.
おまえたち is explicitly plural: both Shirou and Saber are ordered to die. The English addresses only Shirou.
The Japanese itself asks Lancer whether fleeing would be wiser; the English preserves that suggestion and addressee. “For us” is naturally implicit.
“Outsiders” reflects the ruby reading 外部, but it drops the explicit target 協会 (the Association). The surviving claim is narrower than alleging a wholly generic reference.
早めに退場して貰った is itself Kotomine’s euphemism for removing the Master; “had the Master leave at an early stage” preserves that theatrical indirectness in context.
“Piece” preserves 手駒, but “hasten the fighting” weakens the purpose of making the mutual killing proceed smoothly. The narrower loss is genuine.
“The vessel of the soul of this war” is awkward English, but it retains the vessel/cup relation and does not establish a material mistranslation. The accusation is largely preference policing.
悠然と現れた depicts a composed, unhurried entrance; “appearing suddenly” replaces that characterization with suddenness.
聖堂 is the church sanctuary/nave, not a temple. The location is materially misidentified.
どういう事だ is a rough shocked “What is this/what do you mean?”; “what the hell” is a defensible English intensifier for Lancer’s rough register, not demonstrable factual profanity.
意見を同じくして specifically concerns sharing an opinion or position. “Shared the same feelings” shifts the basis toward emotional affinity.
“Food sufficient for him to stay here” is a defensible contextual rendering of food appropriate for his remaining; the difference between suitable and sufficient is not clearly material here.
共同戦線を張る is a joint front/alliance, while “on your mission” adds an unsupported mission. The core cooperation remains, so the narrower addition is the valid claim.
立ち塞がった says they block the route, not merely occupy locations. “By the stairs” and “standing in the temple” remove the active obstruction of escape.
人聞きが悪いな means that the account makes Kotomine look bad or gives a bad impression; it is not a command not to doubt him.
待機を命じていた means ordering Archer to remain on standby. “Here” adds a location absent from the Japanese.
今後の対策 specifies countermeasures for what follows/the future; “some sort of a plan” is broader and loses that purpose and temporal scope.
謀る covers deceiving or scheming against someone, broader than merely uttering a literal lie. The English narrows Kotomine’s denial materially.
“That guy tricked me and I came straight to the enemy’s base” still presents Shirou as having gone there himself; explicit 自分から need not be repeated in English.
長年の疑問 can refer collectively to the longstanding questions just voiced. English singular “a question long unanswered” is a permissible collective paraphrase.
The English “crime of the disaster” is malformed and fails to express asking who bears guilt for the disaster. The Japanese frames the scene as demanding responsibility.
目眩まし can be rendered as a diversion or screen; “diversion to separate you two” preserves its stated function without needing the literal visual-blinding image.
私でなくとも naturally means “even if it were not me” or “regardless of who I was”; “even if I was someone else” is awkward but semantically defensible.

釜 is literally a cauldron, but “magical vessel” remains a defensible container metaphor in English. The accusation does not establish a material error rather than imagery preference.
周囲の人間 explicitly means the people around the owner. “Everything around it” broadens human victims into all surrounding things.

“Feeding on something” preserves 食いつぶす, but the English drops 飛び上がる’s forced upward-leap metaphor. The narrower imagery loss survives.

A firm grasp can naturally imply putting more strength into an already-held hand; the slight comparative degree is a minor nuance, not a material mistranslation.

For a Servant, 消える naturally means disappearing or being dissolved; “being eliminated” is a defensible contextual explicitation, not necessarily external killing.

最短でも一分近い means nearly a minute even at the shortest, whereas “at least one minute” reverses the approximation and lengthens the minimum.

The fragmented Japanese does not establish the added profanity “damn.” However, rendering the cry as “Ow” is a defensible contextual interpretation, so the claim should be narrowed to the unsupported profanity.

The Japanese makes the mud moisten Shirou, who is parched by despair. “Drowns my despair” changes both the object and agency of the metaphor.
極光 is aurora/polar light. “Ultimate black light” replaces that visual phenomenon with an unsupported superlative.

“Offset it a bit” can imply only partial cancellation, while 相殺した states cancellation achieved, with かろうじて qualifying the difficulty. The genuine issue is weakened cancellation, not the whole comparison.
The Japanese grammatically foregrounds Gilgamesh’s unscratched armor; “without a scratch” naturally describes him as a whole. This is a real attribution shift but not a wholly different scene fact.
“Earth” is a normal English synonym for 世界 in a description of the world being covered; no material scope error is established.
“A great curse” conveys magnitude but drops the explicit maximal-scale force of 極大.
The translation retains the Grail source and remnants, but loses the “leaking” process and contemptuous dregs nuance; the accusation should be narrowed accordingly.
The extinguishing-flame image is substantially retained by “ready to go out”; explicit repetition of “flame” is not required in natural English.
“She tries to get up” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of putting strength into her limbs; it does not assert that she succeeds.
“For your benefit, not mine” preserves the contrast between おまえ and 我. The marked reading of 我 is naturally represented by “mine”; omitting the visual ruby layer is not itself a mistranslation.
「口元を吊り上げる」 can naturally be rendered as “smiles,” especially in this taunting context. The finding treats a permissible loss of gesture specificity as factual error.
自我 means preservation of selfhood or ego, not merely ordinary sanity; “keep your sanity” changes the psychological consequence materially.
“Magnificent” preserves exceptional magnitude but adds positive evaluative coloring; the narrower surviving issue is loss of the objective “out of scale” nuance.
The conditional remains hypothetical through “If” and “would,” so it is not promoted to flat fact. However, おそらく and だろう add hedging that the English weakens.
The English retains the unhinged appearance and suitability, but is malformed (“abnormaland…crazyand”) and loses the emphatic “supremely fitting” evaluation.
全ての人間 is specifically every person or human being; “everything they see” broadens the object from people to all visible things.
「天地には我のみ」 expresses an immense “I alone under heaven” formulation, not merely generic selfishness or self-esteem.
選定 is a merciless selecting or governing act, while “nature” removes the act and its agency, and “never thinks of others” is an added explanatory generalization.
婚姻を決めておく means settling or arranging the marriage while there is time; “hold our marriage now” changes this into an immediate ceremony.
“She does not say it to anyone” is a natural rendering of 誰に言い聞かせるでもなく. The supplied Japanese does not require the stronger claim that she is denying self-persuasion.
The immediately following context supplies the king as the governing subject, and “a possession” conveys 己の物. English need not repeat every Japanese subject and reflexive pronoun.
“Brings back her determination” is a defensible contextual rendering of her heart becoming firm after the taunt; the alleged temporal distinction is not demonstrably material here.
The English preserves the inverted position and arm-powered jump, but omits the body reversal and weakens 大きく to an unqualified jump.
“Not the slightest chance” naturally conveys an effectively negligible chance; insisting on the one-in-ten-thousand image is not by itself a material error.
“Best range she found earlier” preserves the tactical range but loses that it was learned through her own bodily experience and was suited specifically to interception.
“The arms … are weak” is a natural result-oriented rendering of being unable to muster strength in them; no material event or agency is reversed.
愛剣 marks Ea as Gilgamesh’s favored or beloved sword. Naming Ea alone identifies the weapon but omits that characterization.
決死の覚悟 explicitly conveys readiness to stake or face death; generic “determination” omits that mortal commitment.
覇王剣 is the overlord king’s sword, whereas “sword of separation” corresponds to the separate epithet 乖離剣 later in the supplied text.
The English gives only the ruby reading and omits the written title’s semantic content, “the star of creation that split heaven and earth.”
This finding is misaligned: page 65 contains no Enuma Elish invocation. Its Japanese begins with the approaching flash and later says only 「光と風の乱舞」.
The supplied Japanese says beheading, exile, and oppression; “castration” is unsupported, and splitting beheading into a separate execution changes the list.
自傷 means self-harm or self-injury broadly, not necessarily completed suicide; the English narrows the offense materially.
Rape is unsupported by 暴虐, but “tyranny” is a defensible rendering of that broad brutality/atrocity term. The compound accusation must be narrowed to the rape insertion.
徳 is virtue or moral merit, distinct from respect or reputation; the English changes the object being sought.
嫌悪 means disgust, aversion, or revulsion. “Hatred” changes the emotional response into hostility toward an object.
The English makes the blood an explicit agent, but this is a permissible causal paraphrase of blood circulating for the purpose of standing; the claimed agency shift is not materially established.
正義の味方 is a defining “ally/champion of justice” ideal. “Superhero” recasts that ethical formulation as a genre label.
許し means forgiveness, pardon, or absolution; “permission” changes moral absolution into authorization to act.
The English preserves relief and the final nod, but “everything was okay” expands 良かった beyond the source’s simpler “good/glad” response.
“That superhero’s son” preserves the filial relation and binds the ruby ideal to Kiritsugu; the narrower issue is only the generic “superhero” rendering of 正義の味方, not mispossession of the relation.
死んでも勝て explicitly makes death an acceptable price of victory; “no matter what” omits that instruction.

おそらくは marks the narrator’s uncertainty; the English states continuation until death as certain.

限りなく can be compressed into the stark English description “inorganic”; the alleged atmospheric loss is too subjective for a material-error verdict.

The English replaces 偉そうに見下ろしながら and とんでもなくフツーな一言 with “normal tone,” losing the scene’s haughty/ordinary-line joke.

The English omits both Saber being beside him and the fact that morning has already arrived.

“Heart beating at an abnormal rate” is less vivid, but it still conveys the pounding heartbeat; the remaining difference is tonal preference.
“Acting cool” can imply pretense, whereas あくまでクール says she remains composed; the omitted awareness clause is secondary, so narrow the claim to that implication.
見た目より explicitly makes appearance the comparison point; “sharper than I thought” removes the surface-versus-competence jab.
The English turns escaping without being noticed into generic escape and changes Shirou’s inference into a question.
“I’m glad you’re so smart” is a conversational paraphrase of praise for understanding quickly; it is not a demonstrable factual mistranslation.
きっぱりと言う can be rendered “speaks clearly” when the context is a plainly delivered boundary; this is not necessarily intelligibility rather than firmness.
The English preserves the inferred content that they are enemies; flattening rhetorical でしょ into a statement is a permissible naturalization.
今更だけどありがとう means belated thanks, not an apology for being late; the English introduces a different apology.
気がする marks a hunch, while “I’m sure” asserts certainty; とんでもない事態 is also stronger than generic “bad.”
The English omits both 大人しく and the specific formal kneeling posture 正座した.

“Grumbles” can describe a low nonverbal throat sound, and “angrily” conveys displeasure; the remaining loss is minor vocal texture.
ふん is a dismissive hmph/snort, not a hesitant laugh; “H-Heh” changes Rin’s defensive delivery.
気にくわない is a distinct judgment that she disliked the act; repeating “wasn’t in the mood” erases that reason.
The English retains a general mistake caused by confidence, but loses the competitive 失点 framing and the guard-lapse nuance of 油断.
“Flab on my mind” is awkward but preserves the intentional flab metaphor and supports Shirou’s immediate fat joke; this is not a factual error.
The English narrows both 言動 and 軽率な行動 into comments, omitting the warning about reckless conduct.
“Feel a chill” is a natural English elaboration of こわかった, and the supplied English’s line breaks may be extraction formatting rather than a semantic addition.
The English preserves standing, leaving, and 今度こそ; the omitted smooth walk toward the exit is not material enough for an error verdict.
The English broadly conveys departure, but omits この屋敷から and recasts the final statement as what she leaves behind; retain only those narrower omissions.
“The killings called the Holy Grail War” is malformed and loses 殺し合い as a structured mutual-killing contest.
実感が持てない concerns feeling the situation as real, not processing facts. “Absorb all the facts” changes the nature of Shirou’s difficulty.
The chair metaphor remains in “a single chair,” so the accusation that it becomes wholly generic is overstated. The explicit game framing is nevertheless omitted.
思惑 can cover intentions, aims, expectations, or calculations. “Expectations” is a defensible contextual choice, and no explicit participant pronoun is required in Japanese.
押し退ける can naturally be rendered as defeating or displacing opponents in this war context. The Japanese does not require a non-lethal interpretation.
The Japanese identifies people by participation status, not moral innocence. “Innocent people” changes the category and omits the explicit game relation.
The English retains the any-means condition but omits the explicit forceful intervention in 力ずくでも止める.
正義の味方 is idiomatically adaptable as “superhero” in this context. The finding treats a defensible cultural equivalent as a factual error.
“Someone” is an indefinite singular referent whose life is unjustly taken; “innocent people” pluralizes and changes the stated basis from injustice to innocence.

ひどく marks degree of suitability, not surprise. “Surprisingly suited” adds an unsupported reaction and changes the observation’s force.
“Looks at me” substantially conveys the direct gaze, so that part is overstated. The omission of 淡々と, the matter-of-fact delivery, remains a narrower valid claim.
やはり marks an expected or confirmed continuing condition; “Could it be” turns this into open speculation.
ばっと and ぶるぶる encode abruptness and emphatic shaking, both flattened by the neutral movement description.
“Terribly beautiful” is marked English but can function as an intensifier for とんでもない. Awkward style alone does not establish a material mistranslation.
“She really hits me with it” is a natural metaphor for being struck anew by her beauty in the immediate scene. Japanese passive realization does not forbid such English agency.
“I’m troubled” is vague, but context can imply unease around Saber. The narrower valid criticism is loss of the explicit interpersonal object in 彼女は苦手.
The Japanese says silence would leave things unchanged for life; the English reduces this conditional relational consequence to a generic inability to remain silent.
帰ってから means after returning, not necessarily at the moment they arrived. “The moment” adds unsupported immediacy.
俺なんかの is genuinely self-effacing and omitted, but “my Servant” still preserves the contractual relation. The claim should be limited to lost humility/register.
させられない describes inability to make Saber perform spirit-form conversion, while “turn her into one” implies Shirou transforms her. The unfavorable nuance of 生憎 is also absent.
“How she exists” can preserve some of the principle question, but the English narrows サーヴァント generally to Saber. Total collapse is overstated.
“Win” overstates 切り抜けられる and is a genuine semantic shift; “strange” is defensible for 訳の分からない, so the compound accusation needs narrowing.
旅館みたいに広い supplies a specific comparison and spatial image that “a big house” omits.
土蔵 is an earthen storehouse rather than a generic shed, so the concrete location is mistranslated.
“Japanese-style” gives some posture information, but it does not identify the formal posture 正座 precisely. The criticism should be narrowed to precision and register.
“Lose my voice at the figure” is awkward, but “lose my voice” is a defensible rendering of 言葉を忘れた and 姿 can be “figure” in literary English. This is not by itself a material error.
The English retains several physical details but weakens 凛と and the exact 正座 posture. The accusation should not claim the whole purity of the image disappears.
The concessive “Even if she is a Servant” is possible English, but なんだろうと broadens the source to any category. The claim of a wholly changed logical relation is too strong.
“If I’m with her” adds an explicit condition and makes Saber the guide preventing deviation, neither of which appears in the Japanese.
The explicit absence of agitation in 慌てた風もなく is omitted; “slowly” preserves movement speed only.
“Looks at me” conveys much of まっすぐにこっちを見ながら. The narrower surviving issue is omission of 淡々と, the flat delivery.
やはり expresses expected continuation or confirmation, whereas “Could it be” presents the condition as uncertain speculation.
ばっと and ぶるぶる add abruptness and vigorous repetition that “take a step back and shake my head” does not state.
The metaphor “she really hits me with it” can naturally express Shirou being struck anew by her beauty. The Japanese does not prohibit this contextual English agency.
The translation is vague but can be read as contextual unease. The valid narrower point is omission of the explicit difficulty with Saber in 彼女は苦手.
一生このまま means things remain this way for life if he stays silent; “can’t stay quiet forever” removes both the condition and relational consequence.
The English adds “sit down” and omits 落ち着いて. The omission of “calmly” is genuine, but the added sitting detail alone is minor.
領分 identifies combat as Saber's domain or sphere of responsibility; “duty” changes the basis from authority/competence to obligation.
後方支援に徹してください is a concrete order to devote himself to rear support. “Concentrate on your role” omits the specified role and exclusive adherence.
“When Archer attacked” and “pull her to safety” convey the remembered event and Shirou’s attempt to bring Saber away. The loss of the single-strike detail is not clearly material here.
“I can’t help it” and “You were fighting” are defensible broadly, but the English loses the specific image of Saber putting her body on the line in 体を張ってた.
The English conveys a minimum obligation but omits the explicit criterion that without doing it they could not call the relationship cooperative.
“Faith in me” is a normal English rendering of trust or confidence in this context. The religious association is not sufficient to establish a material error.
呆然 describes stunned or blank astonishment, stronger and different from ordinary surprise.
問いただす is more pointed than “ask,” but “I get nervous, so I ask” still conveys the anxious questioning act. The valid issue is loss of insistence, not omission of the question itself.
The English preserves the negative through “shakes her head,” but omits the explicit いいえ and quiet manner. The accusation should be narrowed accordingly.
The English leaves “your instruction was” incomplete and omits 的確, losing the explicit contrast between an inelegant method and an accurate instruction.
夢中 is absorbed or carried away, not necessarily desperate, and あれはあれで qualifies the positive judgment. Both are real narrower shifts, but the compound wording overstates the result.
The condition that recovery is immediate only while the Master remains健在 is omitted, making the recovery sound unconditional.
今後は establishes an ongoing future rule, while “next time” narrows the instruction to one subsequent occurrence.
The English broadens the concrete 飛び出す action into general recklessness, but “should stop” can naturally render the self-admonition. The valid claim is loss of action specificity.
はっきりさせなくちゃいけない事 explicitly says there is something he must clarify or settle; the English reduces it to mere importance.
“The moment” adds immediate timing not asserted by 帰ってから.
俺なんかの is genuinely self-deprecating and absent, but “my Servant” still preserves the relation. Limit the finding to lost humility and register.
“My blush” captures the flushing broadly, but omits the embodied heat in the head and the sudden sound-effect nuance of ぼっ. The criticism should be narrower.
The Japanese says Saber's will leaves no room for doubt or challenge; the English changes this into Shirou having no opportunity to ask her a question.
“I shall not allow defeat for my Master” is somewhat nonidiomatic but intelligibly means she will not permit defeat to befall him. The finding relies on stylistic policing.
同じ霊格 means the same spiritual rank or order as the Grail; “also spirits” preserves incorporeality but omits the stated compatibility condition.
叶えるべき願い presents a wish as one that ought or must be fulfilled; “wants granted” reduces that necessity to ordinary desire.
“Unarmed” is a conventional English rendering of 剣を持たぬ in a knightly context. The slight broadening from swordless to weaponless is not clearly material.
“Treading inside me” is opaque English for the metaphorical violation expressed by 踏みいる and obscures that the Command Spell is the price of overriding her principles.
“Angered voice” is awkward but can convey a voice filled with anger. The claim that it necessarily reduces the emotion to mere irritation is unsupported.
The source gives both overwhelming strength and lack of hesitation as the basis of the machine-like impression. The English omits strength and adds “cold fighting.”
思わず謝ってた means he found himself apologizing involuntarily. The inserted “sorry” creates a second apology not present in the Japanese.
神域 is the divine realm or domain, not an attained “rank of gods.” The English overstates Servants’ status.
卓越した能力 means outstanding ability; “supernatural abilities” adds paranormal powers and excludes ordinary human excellence.

“Heroes” is less technically precise than 英霊, but the immediate context still identifies the speakers as heroic spirits and preserves a causal relation. The claim that the causal link disappears is overstated.
まず間違いなく means almost certainly or virtually without doubt. The English states exploitation and defeat categorically, removing the explicit probability qualification.
「まるごと」は召喚対象の完全性を示すが、“true”は真正性に置き換える。
世界内で存在するための依り代を説明する一文を丸ごと落としている。
剣士・弓兵のルビ gloss を英語で反復しないのは、Saber/Archerというクラス名を示す自然な処理で、誤訳とは確定できない。
クラス付与の意味は伝わるが、「役割という殻」の比喩は失われている。ただし英訳全体が誤っているわけではない。
白兵戦という近接戦闘の限定を一般的な combat に広げ、戦術上の対比を弱めている。
「息の根を絶つ」は殺す・命を絶つという明確な含意であり、“beat”はその致死性を弱める。
“lack ability”は能力不足・劣勢を表せ、能力が全くないという絶対化まではしていない。
表示された “an / a special” は未解決の分岐が連結した英文で、文法的に壊れている。
「必殺の機会」は致命打の可能性・手段であり、“guaranteed fatal attack”は必ず当たる攻撃へ過剰化する。
英雄になる条件ではなく、象徴的武具によって英雄として特化される仕組みを一般的な herohood に平板化している。
この文脈では “heroes” でも生前に武具を持った人物を指せ、英霊と生前の関係も大筋で保持される。
思い出す対象を「青い騎士」本人に変え、「騎士の槍」という所有関係を落としている。
「あり得ない軌跡」は不可能な軌道を指すが、“incredible movements”は軌道の不可能性を失わせる。
“not fit for humans”は人間には扱えない・人間向きでないという自然な英語で、文脈上の危険性も保つ。
原文は槍としてのカテゴリ内に留まったという意味だが、“wasn’t extraordinary”は単に非凡でないという品質評価に変える。
「正体」は名前そのものより身元・正体の露見を指し、“revealing the name”に狭められている。
原文の単数の欠点を “all its weaknesses” として、全ての弱点の露見に拡大している。
あっさりと決めたことへの驚きを “so quickly” と表すのは文脈上自然で、時間だけに限定した誤訳とはいえない。
相手を “enemy” とするのは戦争文脈で許容され、“fight her”もドンパチの核心を保つ自然な一般化。
やる気満々を “ready to fight me any day” とするのは、相手が戦う気十分だという含意を自然に表している。
勝手が分からないは実際の振る舞い方が分からないという意味にもなり、“what I should be doing”は文脈に合う。
魔力というエネルギー的実体を指す原文を、呪文・術として読める “magic” に変えている。
「肩で息をつく」の身体的な荒い呼吸・肩の動きを単なるため息に縮減している。
呼吸を整えるという能動的な調整を、通常呼吸を続けるだけの指示に変えている。
原文は未知の刃物の先を疑うだけだが、“her sword”を加え、物体の正体を先取りしている。
“does not make sense”でも不一致は表せるが、原文の「話・合意の前提と違う」という交渉上の含意が弱い。
冷徹は冷淡で厳しい性質を示すが、“calm”はその圧迫的な冷酷さを弱める。
原文は視線の圧に屈しないことだが、“trying not to lose”は勝敗を競う構図を追加する。
無傷で生き残れないという条件を落とし、何もしなければ生存不能という一般命題にしている。
魔術師として避けられない戦いという前提全体が英語から抜けている。
実感が湧かないは現実感・具体的な実感の欠如であり、感情的無関心を意味する “feel anything toward” とは異なる。
無関係な人々を巻き込まないという関係性の指定が、“unnecessary people”という価値判断に変わっている。
受け売りは他人の言葉をそのまま借りた・受け売りしたという自己認識であり、“an opinion that I received”はその二次性を弱く、かつ不自然に表す。
正義の味方という倫理的理念を、ジャンル的な “superhero” に置き換えている。
直前の文脈が思考法を指しており、“how I should be now”もその採用を自然に表せる。
英訳は彼女のために得たいという核心を保つが、「是が非でも」の何としてもという強度を落としている。
調停は単なる消滅だけでなく争いを止める・収めることも含み、“stop the conflict”は文脈上許容される。
“Saber stops”は発話停止とも読めるが、単独では身体動作にも見え、原文の言葉の途切れを明確に示していない。
無関係な人間を “innocent people” とするのは文脈上の自然な説明で、非マスターを道徳的に完全無罪と断定する重大な改変とは確定できない。
神秘には「神・divine」の限定はなく、英訳が宗教的・神的な性質を追加している。
詠唱を “spells” とし、魔術と宝具の発動における詠唱／真名の対応を不正確にしている。
“use magic for a living”は魔術を生業とするという職能・実践を自然に表し、英語上の用語選択だけでは誤訳と断定できない。
“Understand? You mean, what happened just now?” は今の感覚が「把握」に当たるのかを確認する会話として十分成立する。
相手は文脈上の人物・対手を指せ、“someone”は許容される。should を shall とした点も実質的意味を変えない。
“You should not be ‘sorry’”は謝罪の場面ではないという訂正として自然で、禁止命令への重大な変質とはいえない。
“should be deciding what to do from now on”は文法的に成立し、今後の方針を決めるべきだという圧力も保持する。
前へ乗り出す動作は残るが、問いただす強い追及が単なる “asks” に弱められている。
日本語は朝食を抜いた主体を明示せず、前後の “we” は許容される補いで、単数事実の改変とは確定できない。
本来受けるはずの供給を、他の全マスターが現在行っているという比較へ変えている。
完全ではない補充を、睡眠では補充が起きないというゼロ化にしている。
エプロンを畳む動作の省略は確認できるが、場面の意味を変える物質的誤訳とはいえない。
魔力生成が活動中に限られる条件が落ち、“constantly”という無条件の説明になる。
“outside source”は自然からの供給を自己回路以外の供給源として一般化しただけで、対比の機能は保つ。
内部回路による補充という核心は保つが、少なからずという程度と「補充」の含意が弱まっている。
水量と滴下量の相関は残るが、グラスの重さに応じて栓が開くという機構説明が省かれている。
消滅という存在状態を、競技上の脱落を連想させる “elimination” に置き換えている。
サーヴァントの身体を維持できないほどの傷は、文脈上 “fatal wound” と自然に要約できる。
“lose enough magical energy” は必要量の喪失という閾値を表し、前後の消滅説明から自己維持条件も読み取れる。
再び溜まることは伝わるが、「時間が経てば」という回復の時間条件が明示されていない。
“could empty out” は危険を伴う可能性を自然に表し、危険性を単なる可能性へ実質的に変えてはいない。
封じられた魔力供給経路を、士郎が魔力を与えていないという任意の不提供に変えている。
長時間の睡眠という回復条件が落ち、“right after”だけが残っている。
無駄な消費を止めるだけになり、グラスに水滴を蓄えるという回復目標が消えている。
英語の断片文は前文を受ける文体上の処理として成立し、文法上の重大な誤りとはいえない。
「死なれたりしたら、どう謝っていいか分からない」は、死なせた場合の責任・償いをどうするかという自然な表現で、死者への会話を文字通り要求しない。
「とん、と」の軽い置き方を省いた軽微な描写差で、発話や行為の意味を変えない。
タイミングの含意は省かれるが、“Then”から直後に鳴る流れは残り、重大な内容誤りではない。
一声で日常へ反転する比喩を、タイガが出来事を意図的に捨てる行為へ変えている。
“teach”は教師としての自然な具体化だが、「面倒を見る」という世話・監督の広さを狭めている。
火事・泥棒・サーカスの三段落ちから、サーカスを落としてコミカルな列挙を弱めている。
会話を実際に短く切った原文を、切ろうとしただけの未完了行為にしている。
恥を忍ぶ姉役というタイガの演技と、電話すること自体の気恥ずかしさが落ちている。
忍ぶ・凌ぐの語呂と、タイガ側の「ライブで小ピンチ」という冗談がまとめて省略されている。
卵焼きを omelet とするのは許容されるが、甘々という誇張された反復強調は “sweet” だけで弱まる。
緊急配送は保つが、至急届けられたしの芝居がかった命令調が、単なる希望表明に弱まっている。
電話を切る機械音を、原文にない発話 “Bye” として追加している。
“Easy to make” naturally conveys the practical quickness, while the adjacent “leftovers” supplies the addition context; the alleged material omission is overstated.
“There could be exceptions” is a defensible natural rendering of an unlikely exception or contingency; the probability nuance is not reversed.
“Huge” adds an unsupported magnitude to a plain intake of air. The Japanese gives no size or force for the breath.
むっと indicates displeased or offended affect, which is absent from the neutral “looks up at me.”
The English retains pressure and looking back, but loses the gradual overawing and desperate effort; the finding should be narrowed to those manner/aspect details.
“I’m telling you to just do so” has no usable English referent and fails to render the concrete order to behave/stay quiet.
引き下がれない means she cannot yield or back down; “cannot obey” changes her self-directed refusal into obedience inability.
The Original witness itself contains this prose without a comment marker. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion in the Original comparator.
The English preserves running outside and face-slapping, but the claim should be limited to the repeated/forceful sense of バシバシ; simultaneity is reasonably conveyed by the coordination.
The English says he will apologize but omits the intended result of obtaining Saber’s forgiveness.
The phrase says Saber glares as though she plainly has something to say; “After glaring at me” removes that communicative implication.
おそらく marks probability, while “must mean” presents the inference as certain.
ぷい and 不機嫌そうに specify a petulant, displeased turn of the face; “turns away” is materially flatter.
The English conveys ongoing pressure, but omits the repeated “keeps throwing” image. The claim should not imply that all pressure or force disappears.
相手 is a context-dependent “other person/party,” not necessarily “opponent”; calling the known female Saber “the girl” is a defensible rendering, not a factual error.
The action is translated correctly, but 今度こそ本当に adds recurrence and emphatic finality. That is a genuine omission, though narrower than the accusation suggests.
“That’s good” conveys the practical evaluation, but loses the self-conscious “if you call it lucky” qualification.
ここから先は無理だ has an omitted subject and can naturally mean that proceeding farther is impossible without explicitly assigning the limit to Saber’s following or Shirou’s movement.
“I sigh and give up” adequately conveys 根負けした in this context; the outlasting implication is supplied by the surrounding sequence, not required in the English verb.
とつとつと adds a halting/plodding manner that is omitted, but “comes up to me” still accurately renders the movement itself.
“Even more angry” conveys worsening displeasure, but the finding should be narrowed to the lost intensifying/sulking metaphor; “anger” is a plausible contextual paraphrase.
“Cannot allow my Master to be in danger” preserves the prohibition, but drops the みすみす sense of knowingly or needlessly letting danger happen.
生成量 is the amount or rate of energy generation in the analogy, not merely the generic process of energy being created.
逆襲 is a comic retaliatory counterattack, whereas “consequences” removes the specific threat and its Taiga-related humor.
The English conveys a short absence but omits the direct request to wait and the causal promise of returning soon.
気を取り直して, regaining composure before looking beside him, is omitted; the remaining action is nevertheless correctly translated.
言い含めておこう means carefully explain or impress the point on her, while “I’ll tell her now” retains only the timing and basic speech act.
The Japanese identifies Shirou during sleep as the object most requiring protection; “the time that requires attention” changes the protected object and duty.
The proper place name 深山町 is omitted and replaced by an anonymous “this town,” losing concrete setting information.
口裏を合わせよう explicitly involves coordinating a shared story. “Let’s make up a story” retains joint involvement but weakens the get-our-stories-straight sense.
手際の良さ means competence or deftness in handling things, not kindness. The English changes what surprises Shirou about Rin.
“At will” is stronger than the page’s explanation, but “remove” can reasonably render 消す/解除する. The valid issue is the added ability claim, not total loss of the disappearance mechanism.
The Japanese explicitly pairs bringing the armament out with making it disappear; the English retains only taking it out.
The English already conveys nonresponse and uphill continuation, but omits the plodding manner and only partly conveys the preceding recognition of a verbal slip.
開き直る can be naturally rendered by “Oh well” in this context, and “pretend” is a reasonable rendering of reframing the situation as showing around a transfer student.
“Don’t scare me like that” is a natural playful English equivalent in context; the reciprocal nuance of っこ is tonal, not a demonstrable material reversal.
居る describes Rin’s continued presence at the place. “Has gone for over a year” uses the wrong motion and produces an incorrect residence statement.
The English preserves that the energy is associated with Tohsaka, but loses the lingering-trace image and skeptical とやら qualification.
ドジ means clumsy, careless, or accident-prone; “stupid” changes Shirou’s teasing criticism from conduct to intelligence.

The Japanese omits the subject of 入る前から, so the supplied witness does not establish whether the intended entrant is Rin, Saber, or the group. The English’s contextual choice cannot be conclusively judged here.
ちゃんと付いてこいよ is an explicit instruction to follow him properly; “let’s go in” omits that directive.
お疲れ is a routine greeting whose omission in a compact English exchange does not materially alter the proposition or relationship.
テンション高くて困ってた depicts troublesome comic hyperactivity. “We were worried” plus “edgy” recasts it as anxiety and concern.
The specific financial cause—equipment consuming funds—is omitted, leaving only an unexplained shortage.
The English preserves the joke that the grocery run is treated as exercise, and “anyone resting their arm and taking a break” adequately conveys the idle-person setup.
にんまり indicates pleased, knowing amusement rather than a neutral smile, but the finding should be limited to this tonal loss.
嫌味はいいから is a genuine bantering rebuke omitted from “just take the bag,” but the rest of the line remains substantially represented.
へそ曲げる is sulking or becoming contrary, not simply getting angry. The English preserves the predicted negative reaction but loses its childish comic form.
しごかれる refers to being put through harsh training or discipline; “chewed out” changes physical/disciplinary treatment into verbal reprimand.
観念して adds resigned acceptance of the inevitable. “Go on in” gives the action but omits that coercive comic framing.
物欲しそうに and イメージ悪すぎ make the joke about an advisor covetously eyeing students’ food and creating a terrible impression; the English neutralizes both.
The surrounding approach to the ear and private question reasonably licenses “whispers into my ear”; the Japanese comparison does not make that English rendering materially false.
無言で and the attempted-entry aspect are softened, but “coming into the archery range after me” remains a plausible rendering of the ongoing action.
チャラ is a debt/evening-the-score joke, not withdrawing a promise or condition. “Don’t take it back” changes the bargain.
巻藁 identifies a specific straw-target archery practice, not merely practice in general; the concrete activity motivating the stove request is lost.
腹痛 is stomach or abdominal pain, not specifically side pain. The English also omits the named patient 岬さん.
裏反って describes the bow’s backward/reversed curve; “like this” removes the physical defect being discussed.
The Japanese specifies the joint separating after the bow is turned over, whereas “if you break it” changes the mechanical cause and agency.
“Powder” is a defensible accessible rendering of ぎり粉, and 手が、手が滑ります can naturally be translated as one hand slipping; no material error is established.
目を白黒させて adds visible fluster or bewilderment, which is omitted, but the running action itself is correctly rendered.
In context, “was I too late?” naturally asks whether it is too late for Sakura to receive/eat the lunch; it need not mean Shirou’s arrival timing. “As well” also conveys the additional portion.
The English preserves the conditional social acceptability but omits the explicit action of resuming lunch; this is a narrower omission than a generic mistranslation.
“Since I’m here” is a natural rendering of せっかく来たんだし, and “come and eat with us” appropriately expresses 桜も食べに来てくれ in context.
The English conveys club members, their agitation at seeing Saber, and Mitsuzuri’s active explanation. “Students” is contextually accurate and “getting rowdy” is not a material distortion here.
“I’ve accomplished my goal” conveys the basic result, but omits the provisional とりあえず and the narrower “original/initial purpose” qualifier.
ずずー supplies a comic audible slurping manner that “drinks” omits, but the underlying action is correctly translated.
The English omits both the bowstring and the wind-cutting quality, reducing a two-source soundscape to arrows alone.
ついばむ is a small pecking/nibbling action, while “munching” is heavier; the issue is tonal manner rather than the food or action itself.
為か marks a tentative inference (“perhaps because”), while “must be because” is more certain. The causal inference itself remains intact.
終わらせる presents Taiga as the person who will bring practice to an end at five; “the club’s over” removes that agency.
“Saber is looking at the archery range with interest” accurately renders 興味深そうに眺めている. The parallel framing of セイバーはセイバーで is a mild discourse nuance, not a material error.

The accusation overstates the problem: in context, the prior question is what Shirou will do, so an implicit first-person continuation is defensible. However, 「それじゃあ」 is only an unfinished “then/in that case…” transition; “should” adds an obligation or decision not expressed by the Japanese.
The omitted location is incidental to the request and is recoverable from the adjacent scene; “tell Mitsuzuri-san to come here” remains accurate.
“Please stay at your leisure” is awkward stylistically, but it does convey the invitation to stay and take one’s time. This is preference policing, not a factual error.
久しぶりに adds that coaching would resume after a long interval, which is omitted, but the request for coaching remains correct.
“Watching us” narrows the object beyond the Japanese’s general observation of the archery hall. The unsupported narrowing is genuine, though the location and quiet observation remain accurate.
夕方まで explicitly sets the duration of relaxing in the clubroom; the English omits that timeline.
「稽古をつけてくる」naturally means going to teach or coach; the English preserves the instruction without a material loss.
“Relax here” is a defensible natural rendering of ここでぼけっとしてなさい; it still functions as Taiga’s instruction, not merely neutral permission.
持ちたくなったら concerns wanting to take up or hold the bow, not necessarily wanting to shoot. The English narrows the permitted action materially.
人一倍成ってる supports an appraisal of unusually good development or competence; “better than most people” is a reasonable contextual paraphrase, not demonstrably a generic mistranslation.
The Original witness explicitly contains agreement before the assessment. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
The source limits the comparison to club members and retains だろう’s modest uncertainty; “better than anyone” makes the claim universal and categorical.
The translation preserves regular training but weakens the explicit nightly routine. The surviving claim is a narrower loss of 夜 and 日課, not total loss of routine.

“Away for a while” can naturally describe being separated from the bow, and “when I used to come here” conveys his active-period results. The supplied English does not explicitly say he left the club.
会心に入る is entering the archery state of kai, not simply hitting the target. The English substitutes the physical result for the named mental state.
The English is malformed and loses the claim that proper self-training without holding a bow can itself constitute a fine state of 久/kū; “endurance is good enough” is not an adequate proposition.
拘り is the attachment or fixation that can bind him; the English reverses this into positive praise for respecting archery.
The English omits the causal warning that anything one becomes entangled in makes the flow stagnate and replaces it with unsupported advice about nodding.
難しい顔 can describe a troubled, upset, or serious expression; “upset face” is within that lexical range and is not a demonstrable factual error.
拘る here is the recurring notion of being overly fixated or attached, not merely worried. “Don’t worry too much” materially weakens Taiga’s warning.
The source has two parallel conditions—facing oneself and piercing oneself. The English retains only the first and omits the archery-specific self-piercing condition.
The English’s “shooting your mind” is unidiomatic and obscures 自分を射抜く, the central metaphor of piercing the self.
離れ行く自身 means the self that is departing, not a self that has been shot to the target. The English also produces malformed assignment of agency in the zanshin explanation.
儀礼、儀式にのっとった is explicitly rite- and ritual-governed. “According to set stages” replaces that ceremonial basis with generic procedure.
“Meditation in magic” is awkward but can defensibly render 魔術の瞑想 as magecraft-related meditation. The supplied Japanese does not force a more specific technical English term.
The alleged roller-coaster sentence is absent from the supplied page and its adjacent witnesses. This page contains the ritual-training and magecraft-meditation passage instead.
錯覚できる and the quoted 「あ、きた」 describe an illusory felt arrival of the state. “Feel it when we hit” turns that illusion into an ordinary sensation and drops the distinctive moment.
自分が綺麗になれた concerns whether the self became spiritually clean or beautiful, not whether the archer merely succeeded. The English removes that central self-refinement.
The cited circus/fire/robber sentence is absent from the supplied page and adjacent Japanese. The page instead discusses the illusory hit and self-purification.
Although the Japanese wordplay cannot be reproduced literally, the English preserves the engineered-hit versus true-shooting contrast through “with technique” and “Real shooting hits.”
The alleged telephone line is absent from the supplied page and adjacent Japanese; page19 contains Ayako’s explanation of hit technique instead.
The alleged “live crisis” reflection is not present in the supplied page or adjacent Japanese, so this finding attacks absent source text.
そんな事はないけどな is a direct rejection—“That’s not so” or “Not really”—not uncertainty about what Shirou thinks.
The alleged order-ending phone click is absent from the supplied page and adjacent Japanese; page20 contains Shirou’s stated purpose for standing at the range.
動揺 can involve being startled or surprised, and the surrounding context concerns his reaction to a rare miss. “How surprised you’d look” is a defensible contextual rendering.
今まで通りだった naturally supports “you were acting normally/as usual.” The English does not necessarily imply deliberate performance.
しれっと explicitly characterizes the delivery as nonchalant or matter-of-fact. “You said” omits that characterization, which matters to Ayako’s observation.
The English is awkward but its meaning remains recoverable: he made the shot miss because his image was of missing. This is not a material semantic error established by the Japanese.
無の境地 can defensibly be rendered “nothingness” in this philosophical martial-arts context; the accusation treats an acceptable English abstraction as factual error.
だろう marks Shirou’s interpretive inference, while “You’ve reached” states definite attainment. The English also presents the categorization as settled fact.
頷ける can idiomatically be rendered “I can nod to that,” meaning he agrees or sees the point. The awkward wording is not by itself a mistranslation.
Despite awkward repetition, “erase oneself to make the self into a circuit” preserves the self-erasure transformation and the circuit metaphor.
力の証 is proof or evidence of power, not power itself. “It is the strength of a magus” changes the logical relation.

無欲 can be naturally contrasted with selfishness in this surrounding passage, where Ayako immediately urges him to become more selfish and greedy. The alleged moralization is not demonstrably erroneous.
“Have fun” preserves the recommendation but softens ハメを外す, which specifically means cutting loose or breaking out of restraint. The narrower tone-loss claim survives.
The narration that Ayako adds an uncharacteristically elegant “understand?” is absent, along with the characterization of that register shift.
In context, “Why are you so worried about me?” is a natural rendering of why she concerns herself with him, especially after her explicit 老後の心配 remark.
みんなで騒いでた is broad, but the immediate clause concerns jokes and laughing; “we were all laughing” is a defensible contextual explicitation.
The cited sleep-and-guarding sentence is absent from the supplied page and adjacent Japanese. Page31 contains Kuzuki’s weekend departure instruction.
The wording is awkward, but it retains both the smile and rival imagery. “As if smiling to a rival” is grammatically rough rather than materially inaccurate.
The alleged Saber-fighting realization is absent from the supplied page and its adjacent Japanese. Page32 contains Ayako’s grudge and rival-smile narration.
The glass-and-faucet sentence is absent from the supplied page and adjacent witnesses. Page5 contains the archery-volume exchange.
“Get into the mentality” is a defensible contextual rendering of entering the mental state of kai; the Japanese page does not by itself require the untranslated technical label.
The alleged “gave up my day off” sentence is absent from the supplied page and adjacent Japanese. Page17 discusses kyūdō as a path requiring the bow.
目を盗んで is naturally conveyed by “sneak out”; the covert purpose is retained even without naming Saber in the English sentence.
The possible presence of Issei supplies the reciprocal context for planning together; “start thinking up strategies” is a natural English compression, not clear omission of a material participant.
先回りして待っていた states that Saber anticipated Shirou and got ahead of him to wait. “Waiting outside” omits the advance interception and the narrator’s bafflement at how she did it.
In this context, excuses is a plausible English rendering for an argument or explanation intended to convince Saber; the source does not require the objection to be valid or principled.
ヤケだ conveys exasperated, self-abandoning resignation. The English keeps the decision but removes that explicit emotional posture.
The English preserves the shoulder drop but reduces 開き直って to “give up”; that misses the comic act of brazenly accepting the situation. “Call to her” is otherwise defensible for 招く.
げげ is the doubled reaction that contrasts with the earlier げ. Rendering it as the same single “Gah” destroys the explicit setup for Saber’s next line.
Saber’s line explicitly contrasts げ with げげ. Counting two “gahs” removes the lexical doubling and its comic wordplay.
動揺 is agitation, fluster, or disturbance; “displeasure” implies annoyance toward Saber and mischaracterizes Shirou’s reaction at being caught.
The Japanese rejects secrecy as the motive: rather, Shirou simply did not want to enlarge the commotion. “Instead of just hiding things” creates a malformed and misleading contrast.
誰の目にもつかない means remaining unnoticed by anyone. “No other students” narrows the observers without support and changes the concealment claim.
お堅い describes a rigid, serious, or straight-laced manner, not necessarily personal stubbornness. The English changes the basis on which Shirou predicts compatibility.
ガラッ and 勢いよく describe the sound and force of Shirou throwing the door open. “I open the door” removes the energetic, intrusive entrance.
The source is speculative and says Shirou would feel more at ease alone than with a teacher. “Must have” removes かもしれない, while “awkward” changes relief/ease into social discomfort.
今年受験する refers to taking the entrance examination this year. The English drops the exam premise and shifts the timing to possible enrollment next year.
The source expressly requires permission to bring an outsider onto school grounds, even if the person is scheduled to take the entrance exam. The English omits that condition.
なんとなく and くれる make Taiga’s acceptance a tentative, character-specific prediction. “Fuji-nee is fine with that” states settled acceptance.
筈なのだが marks the reversal of Shirou’s expectation, and 甘い adds unexpected leniency. “Um” removes the counterexpectation and “understanding” does not preserve the leniency nuance.
The English conveys being impressed but loses the observational hedge ように. The narrower issue is unwarranted certainty, not total mistranslation of 感心.
“Curfew” is less precise than the school’s weekend dismissal time, though the following gate instruction preserves the practical deadline. The valid claim is lexical institutional imprecision.
“Saber watches him go” can naturally include watching through his departure; the omitted endpoint is a detail that English commonly compresses without changing the event materially.
呆れた conveys exasperated or dumbfounded disbelief at Saber’s behavior, not neutral surprise. The English weakens Shirou’s comic reaction materially.
