感心しているようだ describes Shirou’s impression that Saber is genuinely impressed; “praising him” changes that internal assessment into an overt speech act.

The source says the tea was brewed using student-council supplies and that Saber gives an explanation Shirou cannot understand. “We brewed” adds shared agency, drops provenance, and makes the explanation merely strange.
学んでも習えぬ means the learner cannot acquire the skill even through study or instruction; “cannot be taught” shifts the inability to the teacher’s act and omits the advanced-technique sense.
内界 is the inner world or inner realm, not specifically the inner body. The English narrows the metaphysical relation from external world/internal world to outside/anatomy.
The translation preserves the extreme scarcity but adds “student” and softens 一人いればいい方でしょう, “at best one person per generation.” The narrower rarity/precision claim survives.
The source includes 骨格 and says the body’s features constitute 神意, divine will or intention. The English omits the skeleton and substitutes “perform divine deeds,” changing being into action.
魔を退ける means repel or drive away evil. “Exterminating evil” changes the effect to destruction, and “mere footsteps” loses the deliberate footwork sense of 足運び.
The omission of 神子 is genuine, but “abnormal” can be a defensible literal rendering of 異能者. The narrower surviving claim is the lost sacral “divine child” category.

The source says such people are situated in mysteries surpassing magi without knowing magecraft. The English changes that relation into possessing “divine mysteries” surpassing magic, adding divine and losing the magus comparison.
“Such a thing” has a clear antecedent in the preceding natural-talent question; this is an acceptable English pronoun substitution, not a material obscuring of the denial.
“I believe” remains appropriately tentative, while “this is contradictory” preserves the qualification; the proposed rendering is defensible.
The English omits the second explicit negative observation, materially removing Saber’s statement that Kuzuki has no blood scent.
The source says the effect is merely accidental or coincidental, whereas the English presents everyday training as producing a positively perfect effect.
“Pure and honest life” can naturally encompass living correctly in body and mind; omission of the explicit compound is not demonstrably material here.
The accusation correctly identifies loss of technique mastery and envy, but “admirable” can convey the latter; the narrower surviving claim is that “cannot breathe perfectly” misstates 身につかない.
開き直って expresses Shirou’s resigned decision to brazenly go ahead, and that stance is absent from the English.
“Myself aside” does not render the colloquial rejection of Taiga’s attribute/category framing and makes Shirou’s reply semantically incoherent.
“Her expectation differs from mine” can naturally describe the mismatch in their purposes or aims in this context; the accusation treats a valid lexical choice as factual error.
The source deliberately says the woods may or may not rival the front grounds; the English retains only the positive possibility.
The English changes “guide her to the back hill a few minutes from the archery hall” into an unclear first-person starting point.
“Harsh comment” is a defensible natural rendering of a barbed or pointed observation; no material content is lost.
The concrete nearly-twofold discrepancy is the basis of Saber’s criticism and is omitted from “far too ambiguous.”
“I held no hope to begin with, so I cannot lose any hope” is awkward but directly preserves the source’s dry no-disappointment logic.
“Looks away” conveys the action, and the following “she’s sulking” supplies the petulant tone; the accusation double-counts a nuance already retained.
不機嫌 means displeased or in a bad mood, not disappointed; the English changes the emotional state.
顔出さない warns Saber not to appear or expose herself to notice, whereas “don’t go too close” gives a different spatial instruction.
In context, “baseball’s the strongest” naturally conveys that baseball is the school’s strongest athletic area and immediately explains why they usually play it.
主導者 is a leader or person in command; “vanguard” changes the imagined authority structure into a front-line group.
“Looks around in interest” is a natural rendering of her interested, busy inspection, and the surrounding dialogue establishes that she is searching for a sport venue.
The supplied Japanese itself uses タイム as the reading for 得点 in this explanation; describing the fifty-meter time as the relevant points is defensible.
つい does add an involuntary or impulsive “I couldn’t help it” nuance, but the English still preserves that the sport looked fun; the narrower omission survives.
The English drops the defining sword-played ball game and leaves only “a sword.”
The English preserves amusement at the image; only the visible involuntary grin is omitted, so the accusation should be narrowed to that reaction detail.
押されて can be figurative pressure or urging, and “pushes me to keep going” is a normal English equivalent rather than a proven loss of physical staging.
The English conveys Rin’s magical presence but loses the temporal residue sense of 残った; “actively filling” is an overstatement of the English, so the claim should be narrowed.
“Goes away” can describe a gradual fading and does not necessarily assert instantaneous or complete disappearance.
The preceding “only been a day” already conveys the brief interval, so the alleged omission is not supported as material.
言葉以上に explicitly emphasizes understanding beyond what was verbally said, and that emphasis is absent from the English.
“We might as well” is a natural way to express his decision and intention to show Saber around after coming this far.
“Similar sport with a sword” retains the general activity and sword, but it does omit the specific ball-play wording; the accusation should not imply the entire anecdote disappears.
The English weakens 弄びながら to merely holding the key and omits 一足先に, but “leaves” still conveys departure; the compound claim should be narrowed.
The dusk-town view is genuinely omitted, but the English list can still naturally express the group departing together; only the scenic omission is demonstrable.
“With those voices in the background” still places the send-off concurrently around their descent; the alleged loss is a tonal preference, not a factual mistranslation.
The English omits both the downhill direction and the deliberate small distance between Saber and the others, altering the scene’s spatial arrangement.
The English preserves late realization but removes Shirou’s incredulous question about why Taiga had not found it strange earlier.
The English invents an intentional coaching action by Mitsuzuri; the source only treats the earlier exchange as a possible rehearsal.
飛び回ってた頃 supplies the period when Kiritsugu was traveling around, a concrete part of Shirou’s cover story that is omitted.
“It’s natural for them to be surprised” is an idiomatic equivalent of saying it would be strange not to be surprised; the concrete quote is already supplied in the preceding dialogue.
The displayed English contains unreconciled alternative branch text (“an unusual / a strange”), which is a genuine presentation defect independent of translation preference.
“Blunt” can cover unsociable or curt behavior, and “really kind” is a defensible natural rendering of being good at heart.
The context can make “anything will happen” an English euphemism for impropriety, but it is less pointed; the surviving claim is reduced specificity, not total erasure.
Taiga’s utterance ends with a direct question seeking Shirou’s agreement, so describing it as an impolite question is defensible.
なにより marks the sister comparison as the strongest or culminating reassurance; “First of all” reverses that discourse relation.
“Once we come to the bottom” places the interruption at or after arrival, while the source places it just as they are about to finish descending and marks it as abrupt.
The English preserves silence and apparent thought, but loses the ostentatious, performative “face saying she is thinking hard”; the accusation should be limited to that comic framing.
“It might be possible in the future” can naturally convey romantic prospects in this immediate context; the idiom is generalized but not demonstrably mistranslated.
無駄に部屋が多い describes an unnecessarily excessive number of rooms, not their current emptiness; the English asserts a different fact.
鶴の一声 makes Taiga’s decisive pronouncement the cause of the household’s decision; “makes up her mind” shifts this to a private mental act.
“Protest” can fit Sakura’s practical refusal to object, but it is narrower than being unable or unauthorized to offer an opinion; retain that narrower concern.
一応納得 conveys provisional or outward acceptance, whereas “understood” changes acceptance into mere comprehension.
In かつおのたたき, たたき refers to the seared bonito preparation, not minced bonito.
“Downright sinful” is a defensible humorous English intensifier for an extravagantly unrestrained menu; this is not a demonstrable moral mistranslation.
“Perfectly made” summarizes the praise but omits the concrete shrimp and batter standards; the surviving issue is loss of detail, not contradiction of the cooking result.
“A meaning” can suggest significance, but 意思表示 more specifically indicates a deliberate expression or signal; the accusation should be narrowed to that reduced intentionality.
Omitting a repeated washing sound effect is a permissible stylistic choice in English prose and does not change the narrated action.
“Like she didn’t hear me” can naturally describe Taiga’s deliberate aloof pretense, especially alongside the absence of a reply; it does not require genuine failure to hear.
“I can’t do that” is a normal English refusal for 却下, and the following sentence supplies the stated reason; the authoritative force is not materially lost.
The English conveys that the decision is treated as settled, but it omits the breezy あっさり manner and makes the settlement impersonal; narrow the claim to those presentation nuances.
The source gives Taiga’s assurance that she will contact Sakura’s household so there is no need to worry; the English makes the call optional and drops the reassurance.
力んで構える describes Sakura tensing or bracing herself forcefully, not merely showing enthusiasm.
浴衣も人数分 explicitly adds yukata for everyone, which the English omits.
A look asking for help is a reasonable contextual rendering of asking Shirou what to do; the Japanese does not require a more helpless characterization.
野宿 means sleeping rough or camping outdoors; “in the streets” adds a specific urban-homeless setting absent from the source.
The immediately preceding phrase identifies dealing with Taiga as difficult, so “if she troubles you” is a natural contextual interpretation of the escape advice.
何かあっても supplies the contingency “even if something happens,” which the English omits while retaining only general proximity.
“Pulls Saber to her” can express the hand-pulling direction, but omits that Taiga leaves or pulls her away; the accusation should be narrowed to the omitted departure/separation.
半日 means half a day, not one day; the English doubles the time span of the household’s sudden expansion.
付き合う can naturally mean joining or accompanying the others in this sleepover context; “keep them company” is not demonstrably incompatible.
“Hotel” is a defensible functional analogy in English; translating 旅館 as a generic lodging term is not by itself a factual error.
あっさり adds an unceremonious or flat quality that is not explicit in the English, but “ended without anyone speaking” preserves the anticlimactic event.
The English omits both the “what was happening to Saber” framing and the exceptionally lively “until moments ago” contrast.
“Same house” retains co-residence but drops the immediate-proximity emphasis of すぐ近く; the accusation should not additionally infer more sexual content than the source states.
やっぱりそうですよね explicitly marks Sakura’s recognition that events match her suspicion; “Y-Yeah” reduces it to generic agreement.
The English’s “natural for them to be surprised” is an idiomatic equivalent of saying that not being surprised would be strange.
“Living with her” is already an explicit English cohabitation question and adequately conveys 同居する in this context.
Although colloquial, “gets me with a surprise attack” preserves the ambush metaphor and extreme surprise; the accusation mainly polices phrasing.
備えられます expresses conditional capability while “are well prepared” asserts a present state and loses the explicit condition’s modal force.
The source asks what Taiga is thinking; it does not question whether she is thinking at all. The English adds a sharper insult.
気になって conveys concern or preoccupation, but “thinking about them” is a defensible contextual rendering of the following list. Only the bothered nuance is clearly softened.
The English omits the completed action of putting his hand on the fusuma and changes avoiding notice into merely avoiding waking them.
切りつける explicitly gives the wind a cutting or biting physical quality that “cold” does not preserve.
おんぼろな is omitted, and “turn on” is less exact than lighting a stove, but the latter can be a defensible English description. The narrower omission claim survives.
中貫久 is presented as the named kyudo teaching whose three characters structure the explanation. Replacing it with a generic focus statement loses that organizing term.
The Japanese names or alludes to 中要秘刊集, whereas “an archery manual” removes the remembered textual provenance.

The English omits the explicit aspiration to become an archer. However, the continuing practice is recoverable from context, and “masters the true meaning” is a plausible contextual paraphrase of 具備した.
二百以上 includes exactly 200; “more than 200” excludes it. That is a definite numerical change. とかなんとか also marks the wording as approximate.
空っぽの頭 is omitted and “my mind imagines” suggests more active agency, but “pops into my brain” does preserve spontaneous emergence. The finding should be narrowed to the omitted empty-head imagery.
The English retains repetition before forgetting but omits both making the technique securely one’s own and the judgment that failing to do so would be wasteful.

練習 is explicitly practice of strengthening, while “start the strengthening magic” can suggest beginning the spell itself. The surrounding sentence limits the ambiguity, so the claim should be narrower.

The Lancer-attack circumstance is omitted, but 強化 has already appeared in the preceding sentence and the English fragment is a permissible continuation of the Japanese nominal fragment. Only the Lancer omission is demonstrable.
半眼 is not simply narrowed eyes, and 絞り出す describes forcefully squeezing the lung contents out, stronger and more complete than ordinary breathing out.
“Forget” can describe the resulting effect, and “during the process” supplies some contextual immersion. Still, 没すれば depicts becoming absorbed in the process rather than merely starting it.
The English loses the degree/result construction, the self-description as immature, and the requirement that thought be reduced to nothing until the hesitations are forgotten.

“During the process” and “same training” preserve simultaneity and activity, and “never escapes my head” conveys intrusive persistence. The explicit label 魔術師 and the judgment 雑念 are omitted, so the claim should be narrowed.
The English omits the opening clause about what had been happening to Saber and weakens the explicit contrast with the room’s extraordinary liveliness until moments earlier.
すぐ近く specifies immediate proximity, which “in the same house” does not state and which explains the narrator’s mental unease.
The English changes what Taiga is thinking into whether she thinks at all, adding an unsupported insult.
気になって carries concern or preoccupation, but “thinking about them” is defensible with the following list. The valid issue is a softened concern nuance, not the full claimed loss.
The Japanese has Shirou silence his footsteps and put his hand on the sliding door so the sleepers will not notice; the English gives only movement toward a generic door and waking avoidance.
切りつける adds a cutting or biting physical sensation to the wind, which is absent from “cold.”
The decrepit condition おんぼろな is omitted. “Turn on” is somewhat generic but can describe activating a stove, so the accusation should focus on the descriptive omission.
中貫久 is a named three-part teaching and the following lines explain its wordplay. The generic “focuses on” sentence erases that term and structure.
中要秘刊集 is the remembered title or textual reference; replacing it with an unspecified manual removes concrete provenance.
The aspiration to become an archer is omitted, but the object of continuing is inferable from context and “masters the true meaning” is not by itself demonstrably untenable.
“More than 200” is not equivalent to 二百以上, and the English also fails to preserve the explicit approximate recollection marker とかなんとか.
空っぽの頭 is omitted and active “imagines” is stronger than the source, but “pops into my brain” retains involuntary emergence. The claim should be narrowed to the empty-head imagery.
確実にモノにしなければ and 勿体ない are both omitted: secure mastery is required, because failing to capitalize on the success would be wasteful.
The source says the usual practice or training of strengthening. “Start the strengthening magic” can imply spell use, though the surrounding passage partly clarifies the intended training.

The Lancer attack is genuinely omitted, but the strengthening identity is supplied immediately before and the fragmentary English syntax mirrors the Japanese fragment. The compound finding is too broad.
半眼 and 絞り出す specify a half-lidded gaze and forceful emptying of the lungs, not merely narrowed eyes and routine exhalation.
The English reasonably describes the result as forgetting, but 没すれば is immersion in the process, not merely starting it. That narrower aspect is genuine.
The English loses the explicit immature-self reference and the construction requiring thought to become nothing to the degree that all hesitation is forgotten.
不自然な explicitly marks the darkness as abnormal or unnatural; “the darkness” removes that important characterization.
The English omits both the moonlit setting and the paradox that not even an inch ahead can be seen, reducing the passage to an ordinary dark hallway.
視界を閉ざされていた indicates vision being blocked or sealed, stronger than “cannot see well.” “Helping her” can reasonably convey the darkness as relief, so the claim should be narrowed.
The Japanese says the foul air results from herbal fragrance filling the room as smoke. The English instead makes the plant itself smell rotten and omits the smoke and causal relation.
軟膏 is changed to “potion” and セリ科 is omitted. However, “must be” can still function as an English inference, so the finding should not claim that all uncertainty was removed.
The supplied Japanese does not state drained magical energy or male impotence in this line; the English inserts a separate explanatory question before Rin’s actual response.
怨恨でもあるのかしらね is a wondering or tentative hypothesis, while “must have” presents the grudge as established.
女かな is explicitly conjectural. “Must be a woman” gives the inference greater certainty than the source.
The Japanese contrasts contacting someone now with the victims being discovered in the morning. The English changes the first action into being found now and shifts morning to tomorrow.
五十人もの人間 and 床という床 establish a scale of roughly fifty people and blood pooled across every part of the floor; the English omits the number and weakens the scope.

The apparent joined wording is the documented line-marker extraction artifact, and “a knight in red” is a defensible compression of a knight wearing a red mantle. The supplied Japanese does not establish the alleged grammar error.
The source compares the presence with the room-filling smoke and says it is wavering. The English changes smoke to air and omits the wavering motion.
まだ息があるか is a question about whether the fallen people are breathing. “They are still breathing” turns uncertainty into a definite observation.
ほぼ qualifies the attribution, indicating that nearly all the incidents are the Master’s work rather than simply saying all are.
引き分けた事 means that the battle ended in a draw. “Got away from Berserker” changes that result into an escape.
手の内を晒す is an idiom for revealing one’s capabilities or resources, and “the full scope of his power” is a defensible contextual paraphrase. The alleged strategic distortion is not demonstrable here.
The Japanese describes a bomb packed with the gunpowder called a Noble Phantasm. The English makes the Noble Phantasm itself simply the bomb and drops the packed-charge relation.

“A part of them” can defensibly render 半身 in context, especially with the lifelong relation supplied by “for their whole life.” The claimed material weakening is largely a preference about figurative force.
惜しげもなく marks destroying something precious without reluctance or regret. “Freely” primarily expresses permission or ability and loses that evaluative force.
The conditional “if they would find out” is grammatically malformed in this construction. The source supports a straightforward hypothetical: if other Servants learned of it, they would faint.
大事をとって means returning as a precaution; that reason is omitted. Rest is a plausible implication of returning while tired, so the added-rest claim should be narrowed.
雑魚たち explicitly classifies the bone-made enemies as low-level fodder. “Bone Golems” preserves the ruby reading but omits Rin’s dismissive hierarchy.

In this context “defeated” can naturally include destroying the constructs; the surrounding passage makes their destruction clear. The alleged material weakening is not established by this sentence alone.
The English’s “nor did she want it” refers to Archer’s assistance, but the Japanese separately states that Rin did not intend to expose Archer’s abilities.
つい先日まで means until the other day or very recently, not “just hours ago.” The English invents a substantially tighter timeline.
第三者 literally identifies third parties or uninvolved others; “innocent people” is a defensible contextual explicitation for the workers being wrongfully involved, not a demonstrable factual reversal.
必死に does add desperate or strenuous intensity, but the rest of the sentence preserves the nausea suppression and lip injury. The valid issue is a limited intensity omission.
The Japanese concerns actions whose outcome is already fully known; it does not say actions Rin judges objectively impossible. The English changes the governing principle.
気が済まない describes an inability to be satisfied unless she picks a fight. “You have to start the fight” omits that diagnosis of compulsion.
相手 is singular in the comparison and the context identifies Saber as the easier opponent. The English changes this to plural easy enemies.
目の仇にする means actively singling someone out as a hated or sworn enemy. “Worry about them” substantially softens that hostility.
“If they’re not going to do anything” is a defensible contextual rendering of remaining quiet and not provoking an attack; singular they does not materially obscure Saber here.
自覚もないまま means while still lacking awareness or recognition of being a Master. “Without a care” instead makes Shirou knowingly indifferent.
The English omits that Rin is answering Archer’s emotionless voice, a detail that frames the cold test before her declaration.

義理 is obligation or duty, whereas “kindness” shifts toward benevolence. However, “kindness” is a plausible contextual rendering of what she refuses to extend, so the broader tonal accusation is excessive.

手の内を晒す can mean revealing one’s capabilities or resources, and “the full scope of his power” is a plausible contextual paraphrase. The alleged quantitative-versus-strategic distortion is not demonstrable.
縁側 is specifically a veranda or engawa, so “corridor” is inaccurate. The treatment of 月を肴にする as enjoying the moon is a defensible natural paraphrase, making the compound claim too broad.
のんびり describes taking things at ease; “carelessly” adds negligence and moral criticism not present in the source.
正義の味方 is the recurring identity “ally of justice,” not simply the genre category “superhero.” “Wanted to be” also underrepresents the admiration or aspiration in 憧れてた.

Although “that man” is less explicit than 父, the immediately preceding context identifies Kiritsugu and makes the father relation clear. The remaining superhero issue is already covered by the separate finding.
“Became angry” overstates the smaller pique of むっと, and “asked” omits the retort in 言い返す.
The translation replaces the specific distant moon with an unspecified sky, omitting both object and distance.
The English is overly generic: 相づちをうつ specifically describes an agreeing acknowledgment. The repetition claim is less certain because the dialogue already supplies it.
The address 爺さん and imperative まかせろ are genuinely softened or omitted, but the broader claim about father-son intimacy is interpretive.
微笑った, with the supplied reading わら, is a smile rather than outright laughter; the distinction matters in this quiet death scene.
The English omits Kiritsugu’s acknowledgment そうか and the explicit duration 長く, removing a concrete pause before the final line.
“His life ended” is an acceptable contextual rendering of someone who never wakes again; the alleged loss of viewpoint is stylistic rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
決まった can naturally be rendered as Shirou’s decision in this retrospective context, and superhero is a defensible lexical choice for 正義の味方.
“The boy” does distance the first-person memory, and “left to the fire” is awkward, but the accusation of deliberate abandonment is not established by 残されていた alone.
“The dying child” omits the explicit unconsciousness and full-body burns, both concrete severity markers.
The translation loses the contrastive limitation “even just one,” which is central to the scene’s survivor logic.
“Big smile” is broadly compatible with 笑顔, but it weakens これ以上ない’s superlative force; the stronger claim about involuntary fulfillment is interpretive.
“The emotion I felt” is normal English explicitation, and 胸 in this idiom can be rendered as mind or heart; the alleged conscious-ownership error is overstated.
Both repeated exclusivity markers ただ一人 are omitted, erasing the deliberate symmetry between the sole rescued person and sole rescuer.
In context, そういう人間 refers to the rescuer just described, and “become like him” is a natural contextual rendering rather than a demonstrable narrowing.
The translation repeats the smile-to-laughter error in a sentence whose quiet visual action is explicit.
夢見てしまった can naturally become “yearned to become one” when the preceding fragment identifies the desired 正義の味方; the alleged identity error is not decisive.

The English reverses the structure: it makes Kiritsugu’s dream something bequeathed to Shirou, while the Japanese says Kiritsugu, whom Shirou regarded as the embodiment, had wanted to become such a person.
“The old me” can plainly mean Shirou’s former self; it need not imply his present older self or a discarded personality.
The substitution clause 代わりに is omitted, losing that Shirou takes the place of the admired man in fulfilling the dream.
“Amateur” is narrower than 未熟 and the concessive wording is awkward, but the core question—what he can do while still inexperienced—is present.
The explicit magic-like comparison is omitted from the description of Kiritsugu’s universal-happiness dream.
The English omits the garment Shirou changes out of, a concrete action detail.
In the immediate breakfast-preparation context, rendering 朝の支度 as preparing breakfast is a defensible natural specification, not a material error.
The blanket-wrapped body is replaced by a subjective feeling, and 毛布 is omitted entirely.
“Classify Fuji-nee as a girl” loses the exact 子 wordplay but conveys the joke’s conclusion; this is an unavoidable paraphrase preference, not a factual error.
世間慣れ concerns worldly experience and social navigation, not being personally sociable or outgoing.
The English removes the specific claim that Saber successfully deceived Taiga and Sakura about the situation.
The awkward English still conveys that the ordinary fact was surprisingly unexpected and that Saber is surprised; the circular phrasing is not a substantive semantic failure.
朝に弱い means being bad or weak in the mornings generally, not merely failing to rise early.
失言でした is an explicit admission of having misspoken; “Excuse me” supplies only a generic apology.
ネボスケっぷり criticizes extreme sleepyhead behavior, whereas “sleeping ability” sounds like praise for skill.
寝相の悪い omits the restless or bad sleeping posture that explains why the others slept poorly.
In context, うんうん can naturally be rendered as “I get it now” while Shirou realizes the implication; the accusation treats a normal discourse paraphrase as an error.
The narration explicitly invokes Saber’s character, the shared sleeping quarters with Taiga and others, and possible苦痛; the English reduces this to not liking Fuji-nee.
騒いでいた means making noise or being rowdy, not merely staying awake; the omitted noise motivates the separate-room offer.
The closing choice question is omitted, but the English still preserves Shirou’s conditional offer of a separate room; the claim of fully removing Saber’s agency is too strong.
親しみ can legitimately be rendered as warmth, familiarity, or intimacy in ordinary English; no romantic meaning is required by “intimacy.”
The source balances not deceiving others with not being deceived; “open-mindedness” does not express resistance to deception.
監督 means supervising or overseeing; “raised you” changes Taiga’s role into primary child-rearing.
輪をかけて毒がない praises Sakura as even more guileless or harmless, not as merely less bad than Taiga.
気になる expresses continuing concern or unease, whereas “I don’t want to know” reverses Shirou’s stance into avoidance.
“Became friends” overstates うち解けて, which more cautiously means relaxing or opening up; however, the household partners are contextually identifiable.
だろう marks a tentative conclusion, while “I’m sure” makes it categorical and “all the problems” broadens the local household issue.
仲たがい means falling out or having a relational rupture; “started disliking each other” is a weaker internal-emotion paraphrase, though the core concern remains.
“I’ve already starting” is grammatically malformed; the Japanese simply says Sakura has already begun breakfast preparation.
Given the preceding 朝ごはん and the household context, “help with breakfast” is a defensible contextual rendering of 朝の支度.
“Make the miso soup and the side dish” conveys the task; the lost briskness of やっつけちゃいます and number of side dishes are tonal or minor lexical differences.
The English omits the explicit observation that Sakura does not seem to be putting on a brave front.
“I won’t answer you unless you ask clearly” can naturally convey Sakura’s teasing refusal; the benefactive nuance of あげません is not necessarily material.
“Happy for me” can express Sakura’s contrastive question about Shirou’s happiness being directed toward her rather than Saber; the Japanese’s omitted subject permits this contextual reading.
The English preserves practical help but omits Shirou’s correction from 嬉しい to 助かる; that is genuine, though not a total mistranslation of the sentence.
“Happy for Sakura” reverses the awkward but explicit direction 俺が桜に対して嬉しい, and “forgive” is not what 認めてもらえる says.
認めてもらえる means having Sakura accept or acknowledge the unreasonable imposition; “forgive my selfish decision” adds selfishness and personal absolution.
Although Japanese leaves the subject implicit, “She’s right” is a contextually valid English explicitation after Sakura’s immediately preceding question.
“I’m sure I can be friends” strengthens the cautious 思います and upgrades 仲良くやっていける from managing to get along into friendship, but the core future compatibility remains.
The English is malformed and omits 完全に, weakening the explicit complete-reconciliation declaration.
なっちゃいました marks an unexpected outcome or “ended up”; “just because we want to” invents a deliberate motive.
The English retains beauty but drops the startling degree in ビックリするぐらい; this is a real tonal weakening, not total loss of content.
“I don’t know about being cute” can naturally express Shirou’s inability to feel or recognize Saber as cute; the alleged denial is not compelled.
“It is, but” lacks the subject and loses the repeated intensifier すごく嬉しい, producing an opaque fragment.
いびられた means being harried, bullied, or picked on; “made fun of” weakens it, while “to make her angry” adds an unsupported intention.
The English loses the conditional trigger 機嫌を損ねると and turns situational toughness into a general trait; “stubborn” is nevertheless a possible approximation of 手強い.
“She’ll be over it” substantially conveys ケロッと忘れている; the morning condition is supplied by the immediately stated previous-night fight and the proposal context.
The English omits both the forceful door-opening manner and Shirou’s act of psyching himself up before entering.
The English conveys being thrown outside but drops the spectacular comic emphasis of ものの見事に and the out-of-bounds framing of 場外.
The translation omits both the collar grab and the named 地獄車 technique, reducing a specific comic wrestling sequence to generic motion.
大トラ is a direct punning address to Taiga and is omitted from the demand for help, weakening the combative joke.
The named ロメロスペシャル is replaced by “special attack,” and the English adds Earth while losing 最強 and 専用’s absurd specificity.
The English preserves the possibility that memory returns but loses the animated ぴょこぴょこ点滅する presentation and the comic “almost but does not” structure.
“That’s a big lie” preserves the emphatic denial; the lost synonym/ruby wordplay is difficult to reproduce and does not by itself establish a translation error.
十歩 means roughly ten paces or steps, not ten feet; “at least” also hardens the approximate source.
“Pretty kind” loses the teasing 士郎にしては and the situational perceptiveness of 気が利く, but it retains a broadly positive evaluation.
しかない expresses having no alternative, while “I can endure it” presents endurance as voluntary capability.
“I don’t like it” conveys unpleasantness but loses Shirou’s evaluative sense that both girls suffering would be a needless loss or waste.
The Japanese identifies Sakura’s one-sided difficulty with people like Saber; the English invents reciprocal incompatibility between two opposing kinds.
ようだ marks Taiga’s inference or appearance-based conclusion; “they’ve made peace” states it as fact despite the residual discomfort.
The English removes Taiga’s apparent successful intervention, the qualifier なんとか, and the evidential ようだ, making the resolution categorical.
弟分 denotes a younger-brother-like junior or dependent, not an institutional student; “student” changes the relationship.
腰 specifies the lower back or waist as the injured area; the English instead attributes the inability to stand vaguely to hitting the ground.
The rendering drops the specific comic callback to the three rotations, replacing it with an indefinite event.
“Black belt” is a defensible natural approximation of 有段者 here, and “well-known swordsman” preserves 名を馳せた; the gender objection is not decisive in English.
“Everyone says” naturally conveys the multiple participants, while the following sentence explicitly preserves the four-person setting; the omitted simultaneity is not a material error.
“A group of four” retains the concrete number, and “feels rather relaxing” is a defensible rendering of 和んでしまった; the proposed “nice household scene” is interpretive preference.
The Japanese names dashi specifically; “change something” removes a concrete cooking observation.

The English can imply cooking without haste, but it does not clearly preserve the request to stop accommodating Saber’s tastes. The accusation should be narrowed to that loss, not treated as a wholly wrong equivalent.
“Using chopsticks” omits ちゃんと, which marks that Saber is holding them properly; that competence motivates Sakura’s surprise.
器用 can idiomatically be praised as being versatile or multi-talented in this context; no unsupported specific talent is asserted as fact.
The English explicitly substitutes spoon for the knife named in the Japanese comparison.
The knife-to-spoon substitution is genuine, but the subject Saber is recoverable from the immediately preceding dialogue, so that part of the accusation is overstated.

The English retains the devil/terrorist descent metaphor but omits the stealth and one-day suddenness in こっそり and ある日. The claim should identify those omissions rather than call the whole image generic.
間食 specifically means snacking between meals; “eat like that” leaves the behavior unnecessarily vague.
“Man” is a normal English exclamation of frustration in this placement. Reproducing the audible click as “Tch” is an optional tonal choice, not a demonstrable mistranslation.
神経質なまでに presents excessive finickiness, whereas “sharp on details” turns the flaw into a positive competence.
The antecedent of “it” is clear from the surrounding discussion of Sakura making snacks; omission of おやつ is a permissible English compression here.
“Twice as loud as usual” is a plausible rendering of 二倍ましで騒がしい. The alleged positive evaluation is not securely established by this phrase.
“I’m happy that she’s worried about me” can naturally express gratitude for her concern; it does not necessarily celebrate the worry itself.
The Japanese makes reduced returns conditional on the battle beginning, while “now that I’m in a war” presents the war as already underway and the result as certain.

The substantive translation wrongly changes not being able to return home into being late and omits the purpose of preventing Fuji and Sakura from worrying. The joined “Thenif” is an extraction artifact and should not be counted.
“Attract a lot of attention” covers conspicuousness but compresses the separate consequence of causing a commotion. The accusation should be limited to that compression.
The Japanese says Saber will be satisfied with the plan; “You can let me do so” recasts that acceptance as permission granted to Shirou.
The English preserves that following is unnecessary, but drops the idea of Saber straining herself. This is a narrower omission than a wholesale authority error.
必要だと思えば describes Shirou’s felt need reaching Saber through the bond, not a deliberate mental call.
“Aid” is not false, but it weakens the specific protective role expressed by 守りとなる. The claim should be narrowed to that loss.
“Its” has a clear antecedent in the Command Spell, and “backup” is supported by the supplied ruby gloss for 助け. The phrasing is awkward but the claimed missing possessor is not real.
The phrase is awkward and can obscure 命令権, but “right to absolute obedience” need not reverse the relation, and the missing punctuation is tied to the supplied line marker.
The Japanese uses 魔法, the work’s distinct technical term; “sorcery” obscures that classification.
留守を守る assigns Saber the duty of watching the house while Shirou is away, which “stay here” omits.
The Japanese says Shirou raises a hand and puts it to the entrance door; waving goodbye and opening it changes both the gesture and action state.
“Be on guard all the time” is a natural contextual rendering of exercising utmost care in one’s conduct; the alleged distinction is not materially established.
In this context “do not go near Rin” is a natural safety paraphrase for avoiding an encounter with her; it does not establish a material change in the warning.
染みついている says the Association rule is ingrained in Rin, not that an external rule currently binds her conduct.
“Greet me normally” conveys the nonchalant school-persona behavior, and omission of the illustrative おはよう is acceptable natural compression.
The source concerns judgment becoming dulled under public scrutiny; “change her decision” describes a different tactical effect.
敵視している can naturally be rendered as feeling hostility toward someone; the English does not contradict the source’s hostile stance.
とは思う marks Shirou’s opinion or supposition, while “I know” converts it into certainty.
一枚 specifies one sheet of nori, and “a dried seaweed” is not idiomatic countable English for that item.
The exact measure 一合 is omitted. However, the English assignment of cooking extra rice to Sakura is a contextually plausible naturalization, so the stronger agency accusation should be removed.
Given the explicit contrast with 平日 and the school setting, “weekends” is a defensible contextual rendering of a day off; the broader lexical range is not materially consequential here.
In context “believe in you” can mean accept Shirou’s assertion, not broad personal faith; this is a defensible English idiom.
駆けつける conveys rushing promptly to the emergency, whereas “come to me” removes that urgency.
余裕を持って says Shirou passes the gate with time to spare, an explicit calm-timing detail omitted from “go through the gate.”
“It feels like” preserves the perceptual uncertainty of ような錯覚; the English does not state the fading as an objective fact.
かもしれない is tentative possibility, while “I’m sure” asserts a definite diagnosis of stress.
ポキポキと肩を鳴らす describes audible cracking, not merely rotating the shoulders.
“After that” is understandable from context, but it drops the pause and second-look test expressed by 一呼吸おいて見ても. The claim should be framed as a minor staging omission.
“Yo” supplies the light greeting, while “I know her” is a natural contextual rendering of being acquainted; the omitted hedges are not material.
The surrounding “doesn’t reply,” looks away, and returns already convey Rin’s dismissive reaction; reproducing ふん as a sound effect is optional tonal refinement.
The English generalizes 裾 to “uniform,” but dropping みる is a normal English compression of an attempted action. Only the concrete hem detail is a surviving claim.
几帳面で神経質なまでに規則を守る describes meticulous, almost neurotic rule-following; “punctual” narrows and softens that characterization.
The English changes an existing sprawled posture into a subsequent head-placing action, but the claim that the source specifically establishes a whole-body stuck-flat state is overstated.
前に requires waking him before the lunch break ends; “when lunch is over” moves the requested time to the endpoint or later.
“At the temple” is a defensible contextual rendering of お山 here, and “had to go to bed” conveys the strictness of 絶対 without requiring a literal adverb.
“Difficulty sleeping” commonly includes trouble falling asleep and is a normal English equivalent in this context; the broader wording does not materially alter the symptom.
“You certainly got me there” is a natural rueful acknowledgment of the proverb hitting home; the accusation imposes an unnecessarily narrow English equivalent.
Remaining beside Issei through the break can naturally imply accompanying or keeping him company; the proposed wording treats an acceptable compression as factual loss.
“Man, it’s too early to be spring” is understandable and preserves the setup for the spring-sleep proverb; the omitted sigh and name are ordinary English compression.
“The student council isn’t open today” conveys the intended closure joke in natural English; retaining the commercial metaphor 店じまい is stylistic preference.
The initial period follows the supplied line marker and is an extraction/display artifact, not a semantic translation error.
愛想というものはまったくない describes total lack of affability or warmth; “quite blunt” shifts this to speech directness.
“Stops his words” is awkward English, but it clearly communicates that Kuzuki stops speaking; this is a style issue rather than an accuracy error.
The source predicts that the matter will become a criminal case, not that the school will call the police.
“Do not spread the rumor” is a plausible contextual rendering of avoiding careless discussion of a sensitive disappearance; the added “rumor” does not create a material contradiction.
無断欠席 means absence without notice or authorization, a detail omitted from “absent today.”
The source says Sakura was not informed of the circumstances; “does not know anything” broadens that into total ignorance.
The Japanese reports that the first-year said Shinji had met the missing student; the English turns this into the first-year directly seeing the pair together.
The summary says missing since yesterday and last met by Shinji; “last night” narrows the time and “last talked” narrows 会っていた to conversation.
そういった事情もある explicitly links the preceding circumstances to the expected school response; the English omits that connective relation.
下校時間 is the dismissal time, not a curfew, and また indicates that the earlier-dismissal measure will happen again.
The English adds speed and does not explicitly retain only the necessary matter, but the concise manner is partly inferable from context. The claim should be narrowed to that omission/addition.
無理にでも詳しい話を聞く means pressing for the detailed account even if force is required; “get some information” substantially weakens both points.
捕まらない means Shinji cannot be reached or found; “hasn’t been home” states a different fact.
The English omits the urgency of 至急 and weakens questioning into contacting, but “actually” is supported by 練習に参加した and is not an unsupported addition.
一年生 identifies the student as a first-year, and the Japanese supplies no gendered pronoun; “he” invents information while omitting the year.
“A quarrel” can naturally mean a verbal quarrel in English, so it does not necessarily broaden 口喧嘩 into a physical confrontation.
The preceding context supplies the dojo location, and “could’ve been there” preserves the possibility-based inference; the alleged direct identification is overstated.
“Don’t leave out the important detail” can naturally accuse Issei of evading the essential point, especially followed by the question of who the student is.
The English says Ayako returned the keys but omits that she returned them to the staff room, a concrete part of her last-known sequence.
The Japanese describes the words as difficult to say and explicitly says Issei said them; the English retains only the averted gaze.
The English’s doubled “after” is grammatically broken and omits the continuing absence in 一向に行方が知れない.
“Clubs are canceled” is ordinary English shorthand for club activities being canceled; no institutional category error is established.
The translation omits the explicit no-tardiness component of the attendance joke.
“Sick” naturally includes the stated cold; this is a defensible generalization without material distortion.
The literalized wording preserves the joke’s illness contrast; requiring an explanatory idiom paraphrase would be preference policing.
In context, raising a hand while leaving can naturally be rendered as waving goodbye; the gesture’s precise mechanics are not materially changed.
The surrounding context makes the dojo the remaining place to investigate, so “place to go” is a natural contextual rendering of the ellipsis.
“Well, duh” is colloquial, but the source supports a self-evident corrective tone; the accusation overstates the register difference.
Singular they is standard English and can refer back to explicitly named Issei; no plural referent is required.
“Nothing was wrong at all” is a natural rendering of a matter turning out to be no big deal in this context.
“I can’t go straight home” conveys that Shirou cannot simply leave without taking action; the moral force is retained.
“Firm” can describe a solid, dependable person; the accusation treats one acceptable lexical choice as a factual error.
The English states the same practical result—her classmates provide only shallow information—through a natural first-person paraphrase.
The English correctly conveys the class’s surface sick-leave story, but unsupported notification of “everyone” is an overclaim; retain only that 2-A treats it as illness.
“The classroom’s like always” is colloquial but understandable English for いつも通り; the omitted particles do not create a material error.
“Take my food” can naturally describe classmates picking at lunch with chopsticks in this teasing context.
The translation reverses the causal relation and makes sleep itself prevent rest, unlike the source’s persistent-fatigue explanation.
The time-to-spare detail is genuinely omitted, but “the gate” can naturally cover the school gate; narrow the finding to 余裕を持って.
The English turns Shirou’s denial that anything is actually wrong into a question asking whether something is strange.
“I bet it’s just me” is a colloquial tentative conjecture, not necessarily categorical certainty; it reasonably renders 気のせいかな.
The English strengthens かもしれない to “I’m sure” and shifts oversensitivity toward stress, but the general causal idea remains.
Rotating the shoulders omits the explicit cracking sound and changes the described physical action.
Persistence is retained, but the deliberate pause/relook and unidentified quality are compressed away; the claim should not imply all temporal content vanished.
“I know her” conveys face familiarity, while “Yo” supplies the light greeting; the omitted qualifiers are acceptable compression.
The dismissive turn-away remains; omission of the brief interjection is a minor tonal compression rather than a demonstrable material error.
“Punctual” narrows 几帳面, but the surrounding rule-observance sentence preserves part of the characterization; the finding should target the narrowing, not allege total loss.
The marked degree “to an almost neurotic extent” is reduced to ordinary effort, materially weakening the characterization.
ヒタヒタ is evocative and difficult to reproduce exactly; “something weird on my back” preserves the essential unease without proving mistranslation.
The English omits the circuit’s emergence along the spine, obscuring the bodily mechanism explicitly stated in the source.
“Search alone” preserves the action; the casual or inconspicuous manner is a nuance that can be compressed naturally here.
The planned return with Saber is explicitly omitted, changing the stated protection and companionship of the reinspection.
The horizon image is omitted, but the sunset and one-hour darkness estimate preserve the scene’s temporal function; this is acceptable compression.
The floor, bag, and clatter are omitted and downward walking is added, but the finding should separate those concrete alignment losses rather than treat all sound wording as erroneous.
The translation loses both the fourth-floor landing and 仁王立ち’s planted, confrontational stance, materially flattening the staging.
“Here too” is not wholly impossible in context, but it weakens the explicit surprise that Rin is still remaining at school; narrow the claim to loss of まだ残ってた.
The sigh itself and Shirou’s uncertainty remain; omission of 呆れた風に is a minor affective compression, not necessarily a material error.
“Amazed” suggests surprise or admiration, while 呆れた expresses exasperation or incredulity.
The English assigns Saber’s inability to dematerialize to Shirou, reversing the grammatical subject and obscuring Saber’s intrinsic limitation.
The contemptuous heedlessness of のこのこ is omitted from Rin’s warning about Shirou’s exposed behavior.
The English visibly fuses the interjection and following clause into malformed text.
The source includes both students and teachers; the translation removes students and narrows who may remain.
“So many times” overstates repeated telling, but the broader extent of Rin’s prior instruction is genuinely weakened; retain the latter claim.
やられに来る can naturally be rendered as coming to get killed in this imminent magical confrontation; the lethal reading is contextually defensible.
“Angrily” conveys hostile force; demanding a precise barbed-tone equivalent is a register preference without a clear factual reversal.
The tentative hypothesis in ではないのか is promoted to certainty, producing an internally awkward “Could that be? ... it must be.”
“Enough for you” can naturally convey 貴方ぐらい in context, including Rin’s assessment of Shirou’s level; the alleged omission is not decisive.
“Making it hard on yourself” is a normal idiomatic rendering of 辛いだけ and need not mean mere inconvenience.
本気で is omitted, but “Fight here?” does not necessarily erase all seriousness; the claim should target the lost “for real” emphasis, not infer lethality.
The translation deletes the source’s displaced-anger judgment and changes the sequence from declaration followed by arm movement to simply starting the fight.
“My vision is filled with light” can idiomatically describe visual obliteration or blinding; the accusation assumes a weaker effect not compelled by the English.
The four-step count remains, but the all-out diving motion is omitted and “about” adds approximation; narrow the claim to lost movement/force.
“No time to think” can idiomatically mean no time to deliberate or hesitate in an emergency; it is not necessarily a general denial of confusion.
戻ろう leaves the destination implicit; the surrounding evidence suggests returning home, but the supplied sentence itself does not establish that destination decisively.
The omitted horizon and onset nuance do not materially alter the stated sunset timing, which the next clause supplies.
The English omits the third-floor location, bag posture, and clatter and adds downward movement; these should be assessed as separate alignment losses.
“Top of the stairs” loses the fourth-floor landing and the imposing planted stance of 仁王立ち, materially changing the confrontation’s visual staging.
The transformation limitation is assigned to Shirou rather than stated as Saber’s inability to dematerialize.
The translation omits のこのこ, which characterizes Shirou’s careless or exposed wandering and sharpens Rin’s warning.
“Its Servant” can refer generically to the Servant associated with a Master; the wording is stylistically awkward but not a demonstrable factual or grammatical error.
Students are omitted from the possible remaining population, changing the concrete security inference.
“So many times” overstates repetition, but the translation does lose the extent of Rin’s prior teaching; retain only that narrower claim.
“Angrily” is a defensible rendering of a sharp hostile tone; the distinction from “barbed” is not itself a material error.
The source asks whether the mark might be a Magic Crest, while “it must be” makes the identification certain.
“Passed down my family” is malformed English and fails to express transmission through the family.
“Magic carved on here” and “filling it with magical energy” are awkward but intelligible renderings of engraving and passing magical energy through the Crest.
“Filling it with magical energy” can naturally describe supplying the Crest with energy; the mechanism remains understandable.
“Hastening mechanism” is somewhat loose but can convey the Crest’s shortcut/acceleration function in the surrounding vehicle metaphor.
The English omits 本気で and よりにもよって, but calling the source’s seriousness “lethal” overstates it; retain the lost earnestness and “of all people” emphasis.
