“Gets straight to the point” covers directness but not the no-delay force of 待ったなし; the accusation should target that narrower omission.
“Please” conveys a request and some reliance, but it omits 悪い, the apology; the claim that both reliance and entrustment disappear is too broad.
The soft unraveling sound and passive loosening are flattened, but the Japanese does not establish that Rin actively unwraps the towel; that agency claim should be removed.
The English retains proximity but omits that Rin is directly in front of Shirou examining his right arm.
The English narrows a hypothesis about casting a natural-healing spell into generic self-healing, though the surrounding healing-charm context makes it partly recoverable.
“Will heal” narrows the broad, tentative “somehow manage,” but the immediate discussion is specifically about healing, so the finding should not claim a fully unsupported interpretation.
As with the parallel occurrence, directness is retained but the no-delay nuance of 待ったなし is omitted.
“Please” still functions as a request and reliance, but it loses Shirou’s apology in 悪い.
The translation flattens the soft unraveling sound and manner, but the source does not prove that Rin herself unwraps it.
The sentence omits the explicit description of Rin directly before Shirou while examining his right arm.
“That’s not true!” is a normal emphatic English denial and can carry the comic insistence in context; dropping one intensifier is not a demonstrable material error.
The English loses the fragment, location, deep penetration, and severity expressed by the fragment being driven into Shirou’s back.
“By itself” naturally means without Rin’s intervention in this context and adequately renders the contrast in わたしが手を加えなくても.
“The only reason I can think of” remains explicitly limited to Rin’s own reasoning and does not state objective certainty; the tentative force is defensibly preserved.
“Will heal” is narrower than なんとかなる, but the preceding lines make healing the relevant interpretation; the finding should not call it an unequivocal guarantee.
“Treatment is done” conveys completion, and “my arm” is recoverable as the right arm from the surrounding page; English need not overtly reproduce the benefactive nuance of くれていた.
The displayed “UhI” is a genuine presentation defect that fuses the stammer with the following word.
In this conversational context, “What?” can naturally mean “Okay, what is it?”; the omitted permission is pragmatic rather than a material change.
The English preserves another Master’s existence but omits that this person is doing something at school.
“Doing things like what we just saw” does not clearly retain the repeated or ongoing activity in 繰り返してる.
The source assigns the rescue to Rin alone; “if we hadn’t found her” incorrectly makes Shirou a co-rescuer.
“I recall the female student” is a permissible compression of the recalled image in context; omission of 倒れていた is descriptive loss, not a material mistranslation here.
The English visibly fuses the broken interjection with “using,” unlike the stammered source presentation.
でしょうね supplies a forecast rather than categorical certainty, but “weaken and die” still conveys the causal 衰弱死 relation; only the modal strengthening is clearly supportable.
The English adds intentional “trying” and “peaceful” while losing the self-accusing calmness of 平然; the claim should be narrowed to those shifts rather than treating the whole sentence as wrong.
“You’re wrong” changes Shirou’s gentle correction of the misunderstanding into a direct accusation toward Rin.
“Beat” is defensible as a contextual rendering of 勝てない, but “never” makes the inability more permanent than the Japanese requires.
The translation conveys emotional expression but omits the constrained effort in せめてこんな台詞で、精一杯; this is a real partial omission, not total loss of the idea.
The source leaves さっきのコト unspecified, while “that previous fight” fixes an unestablished referent.
The English preserves the surprise-attack metaphor and heart-jump, but omits the lightness and outrageousness; it does not necessarily turn the metaphor into a literal attack.
“Make peace for now” can naturally mean a temporary truce, and the following dialogue clarifies its technical limits; broader reconciliation is not forced.
“Before you” is a normal English rendering of 貴方より先に and, in context, can mean before Rin deals with Shirou as her opponent; the alleged temporal ambiguity is not demonstrable.
The preceding “make peace for now” plus “cooperate” preserves the temporary truce sufficiently; English need not repeat 休戦して and its endpoint verbatim.
“Hurt innocent people” is a plausible contextual paraphrase of involving uninvolved people in a lethal sacrifice scheme, but it does strengthen 巻き込む into direct harm; that narrower shift survives.
A truce agreement can be stated in English as a promise not to attack one another; the practical content is not materially different here.
“Declares” itself conveys a decisive assertion, and “She declares so” is a defensible concise rendering of 断言する声.
“Give me your best regards” is stilted and fails to express the forward-looking request to work well together.
“At least” weakens the sardonic maximizer in せいぜい, which tells Shirou to make himself as useful as possible.
“Ungracous” can describe Rin’s deliberately rude or unkind remark; it is less vivid than 憎まれ口 but remains a defensible rendering.
In English, “firmly shakes my hand” naturally entails a reciprocal handshake and preserves the physical sincerity of the exchange.
とりとめのない describes the loose, rambling structure of the conversation, not that its subject matter is unimportant; the English changes the characterization of the talk.
“Your family” is a plausible shorthand, but it omits the circumstances or household background specified by 衛宮家の事情; the accusation should be limited to that narrowing.
The English conveys the topic shift but changes Rin’s proposal into a question and uses awkward “getting into”; the genuine issue is the omitted proposal framing and malformed idiom.
The source says Rin is entrusted with the Tohsaka house; it does not state that she is head of the family or make that status the causal premise.
The English states the capability directly, omitting the reported/evidential force of という, but the underlying timing and capability remain correct.
“Never knew” is a natural consequence of the concealment described and adequately conveys the relevant result; 知り得なかった does not require an explicit “had no means” formulation here.
The English reduces explicit knowledge of other magecraft’s names and outlines to knowing merely “a bit of other things.”
“The best magic I’ve ever done” is understandable English for the best magecraft Shirou has successfully performed; the alleged distinction is not material.
“Strengthening magic” is a defensible translation of 強化 in the supplied text; no governing witness establishes that the technical term must be “Reinforcement.”
つっこむ asks whether that was the point for a comic callout or retort, not whether it was an occasion for anger.
“Scope of our power” captures one aspect of 手の内 in this context but narrows the concealed hand to power magnitude and loses methods or capabilities.
The English omits the explicit qualification that the rule applies regardless of who the other person is.
“I could quit any time I wanted” naturally expresses the permission contained in 止めたければいつでも止めろ; the imperative need not be retained literally in reported speech.
The English drops the limiting degree あんまり and sounds more categorical, though “not be bound by rules” can still be understood as the intended warning.
The Japanese states that Shirou was trained by such a man and that Rin refuses to recognize him as a magus; the conditional “if” and “can’t approve” weaken both assertions.
“Regained her composure” is a natural contextual paraphrase of 我に返った, which can mean returning to one’s senses or composure; no material contradiction is shown.
“That what?” can function as an internal fragment wondering what Rin meant; the Japanese hesitation does not require a different grammatical form.
どうかしてた means she was briefly not herself or out of sorts, not simply that she was at fault.
“Everyone’s ways are different” is vague and omits the explicit subject of training methods, though the surrounding context makes the intended reference recoverable.
The English’s “tell you something” is vague and loses Rin’s admission that she had no standing to criticize or judge Shirou.
“A few years” narrows the emphatic duration in 何年も and weakens the sustained training expressed by 魔術を鍛えていて.
“A chill” is a normal English rendering of 背筋が寒い and can carry the menace in context; the omitted intensity is tonal attenuation, not a demonstrable material error.
“Single magus” is a defensible literal rendering of 独り身の魔術師; the claim that it specifically means institutional unaffiliation is not established by the supplied sentence.
The source says Kiritsugu made no effort in that area; “did nothing against that” suggests opposition to the principle instead of failure to make the required effort.
Using “magic” for both 魔術 and 魔術師の『魔術』 obscures the governing magecraft category in this central inheritance explanation.
“The responsibility isn’t just yours” is a natural direct-address rendering of 自分だけの物じゃなく、and the Japanese does not force the claimed false implication that Shirou inherited the Crest.
伝承者 denotes someone who carries or transmits the tradition onward, whereas “inheritor” primarily denotes someone who receives it.
The source assigns the transformation duty to the family line or house called “magus,” not to an individual magus.
The Japanese separately measures accumulated training and self-sacrifice; the English makes the sacrifice merely a means of training.
“Put myself in her place” is a natural English rendering of imagining Rin’s experience without being able to share it; the source does not require a literal identity statement.
“She looks away as she says so” adequately conveys Rin avoiding eye contact and turning away in this brief narration; the alleged sequence distinction is not materially consequential.
The English shifts どんな思い from feelings or emotional experience toward explicit thoughts, but the broader upbringing context remains; the claim should be narrowed to that affective loss.
目の仇にする can mean treating someone as an enemy or singled-out target; “considered me your enemy” is a defensible contextual rendering.
The explicit magus-domain is less clear in English, but the surrounding discussion supplies that domain; the claim that it necessarily rejects Shirou personally is overstated.
“Had to” adds necessity, while つい marks an impulsive urge and っていうか records Rin’s playful self-correction.
The narration describes an awkward groan, not silent reflection or pondering.
よく分からない is anchored to Shirou’s understanding, so “something strange” can shift perspective; however, the complaint’s incomprehensibility is substantially retained.
“I’ve been forgetting about it all along” is a natural English way to express that the fact had completely slipped his mind; the source does not require a material duration contrast.
The translation retains the near beheading but omits the distinct action of fighting or trading blows with Saber.
“Shoot” supplies an absent mechanism, while 無視して and もろともに葬り去ろうとした describe disregarding Saber and trying to annihilate both together.
嫌い ranges from dislike to hate; in this hostile context, “hate” is an acceptable English choice rather than a demonstrable strengthening error.
どうやっても can naturally become “never be able to” in English; it expresses impossibility by any means, not only a literal temporal never.
願ったり叶ったり is an emphatic idiom meaning the outcome could not suit Shirou better; “I appreciate that” materially weakens it.
The Japanese leaves Archer’s matching aversion as a question or inference, whereas “must be” presents it more categorically.

姿 can refer to outward appearance, including how someone is dressed; “dressed like he is” is a plausible contextual rendering, and the technical materialization inference is not forced by this sentence alone.
The English’s “everyone” is clarified by the school context and does not necessarily broaden the victims, but it does soften the inferential, pejorative 魂胆 and なんでしょ framing.
さっきから supplies a since-earlier duration that is omitted; “depressed” is also somewhat stronger but remains possible colloquial English.
覗き込んでくる conveys peering or leaning in, which generic “looks at me” omits, but the concern itself is retained and the materiality claim is overstated.
頼もしい specifically presents Rin’s help as reassuring and dependable; “great” gives only generic positive evaluation.
The English is awkward, but “for affirmation” still conveys Shirou asking “right?” through his gaze. The accusation of a demand for validation is too strong.
よろしくね has broad pragmatic uses, and in this immediate guarding context “Please do your best” can naturally entrust the task to Archer; the finding treats one preferred equivalent as mandatory.
The Japanese states opposition to Shirou becoming a magus, not explicitly opposition to the fact that he desired it; the English shifts the object of opposition.
仕方なく adds reluctant, no-alternative concession that is not explicit in English, though persistence as the reason for teaching is retained.
由緒正しい carries established or distinguished historical standing, which “proper lineage” renders awkwardly and incompletely; this is a narrower lexical/register issue than a wholly false translation.
らしい marks reported or inferential information, while “Actually” presents the concealment as asserted fact and also drops the corrective force of というより.
English that is permitted for human antecedents, and “came from the outside” is a normal rendering of 外からやってきた; neither is a material accuracy error here.

Although stylistically awkward, “knowledge other than the magic you can use” conveys the contrast between usable magic and broader magecraft knowledge; the finding mistakes awkward phrasing for a semantic collapse.
English “Why are you telling me something like that?” includes both the object and the addressee; “something like that” can naturally convey the emphatic extent of まで.
The translation drops なぜか, which explains Shirou’s puzzlement, and adds an unmotivated “Then.” fragment.
The following sentence makes Rin the source of the grinding sound, so rendering it as her gritting her teeth is a normal contextual inference, not a material contradiction.
“Showing enmity like never before” conveys unusually overt hostility; loss of the literal exposed image is stylistic rather than a demonstrable factual error.
The English contrast and question context preserve Shirou’s direct defense of Kiritsugu; “great” can express admirable rather than merely powerful.
気に障った can include being annoyed, and “the method Father taught me” is understandable in context as Kiritsugu’s teaching method; the prose is awkward but not materially mistranslated.
なにそれ is commonly rendered as “What is that?” in a colloquial reaction; English readers can understand it as “what do you mean,” not only an object query.
夜の住宅地 is specifically a residential district at night; “night town” is both unnatural and less specific.
七時前 means before seven, not seven o’clock.
神経が歪む is an unusual metaphor, but “my nerves are getting strained” is a defensible natural paraphrase of the bodily distress.
The source specifies vomiting stomach acid, a concrete and unusually severe bodily detail absent from “might throw up.”
“I feel hostility from behind me” preserves the source’s perception and direction; retaining the stabbing metaphor is a stylistic preference, not required accuracy.
警戒している means being wary of or on guard against Shirou, whereas “watching out for” reverses the hostility into protective concern.
The source explicitly says the hostility is intense enough to wear down Shirou’s nerves; that intensity clause is absent from the English.
実体化 is the specific act of materializing, and 放ったまま says Archer continues emitting hostility; generic “appears” loses the technical event.
殺気 is killing intent, not merely hostility, and 心得があるらしい grants Shirou some training or competence in sensing it.
The English omits both the purpose of not being overawed and the embodied emphasis of confronting Archer with his whole body.
鼻で笑う is a contemptuous snort, while やれやれ and これ見よがしに add voiced and conspicuous mockery; “smiles” materially changes the gesture.
半人前 means not fully trained or fledged; “half-ass” is malformed English and does not accurately convey that status judgment.
The English omits the explicit contrast that even without personally acting, the path still becomes blood-soaked.
大違い does express a vast difference, so generic “different” weakens degree; the core comparison remains correct.
甘すぎるきらい criticizes a tendency to be overly soft; “kind-hearted” turns that criticism into an unqualified positive trait.
The source identifies the event as a split-second fight to the death; both the instantaneous duration and mortal nature are omitted.
体たらく is a contemptuous description of a disgraceful state or performance, not a neutral “case.”
年相応に戻る means reverting to behavior appropriate to Rin’s actual age; “turns immature” adds a negative developmental judgment.
余分な事 means something extra or unnecessary; “meaningless” more strongly denies purpose or value.
The fused “cooperationbut” is an extraction/line-break artifact visible in the supplied raw witness, not a Japanese-to-English accuracy error.
“Even if he turns out to be a useless amateur” is an idiomatic conditional rendering of たとえ…でも, and the immediate addressee context supports “he”; no material change is established.
捻くれ者 can describe a cynical or contrary person; “cynical guy” is within its defensible lexical range.
In this advice context, “do not worry about” naturally means do not take the Servant’s personality into consideration; the operational force is retained.
“We are only a tool” is grammatically defective in English, but the Japanese shifts between plural 我ら and generic singular サーヴァント, so the claimed semantic collapse is overstated.
“Total” intensifies the source’s control authority, but the core statement that control belongs to the Masters is preserved; this is a narrower degree issue.
戯れ言 adds foolish or contemptible prattle that is weakened in English, but “ignore what your tool has to say” retains the dismissive command and generic tool reference is contextually acceptable.
気が済まなかった expresses that Shirou could not be satisfied until he voiced a complaint, stronger than merely wanting to complain; 一言 also limits the complaint to one remark.
The fused hesitation is explicitly associated with stripped line-break commands in the supplied raw witness; it is an extraction artifact, while the pivot is otherwise represented.
“Declares” already conveys a firm assertion, and “contemptuously” preserves 侮蔑; omission of an explicit adverbial “clearly” is not materially misleading.
“It could not be helped” directly conveys 仕方なく, and “over the course of the event” is a plausible though awkward rendering of 成り行き上.
幸せな男だ is sarcastic “fortunate/blissfully ignorant man,” not a direct accusation of stupidity; the English reverses the characterization.
The source explicitly says Heroic Spirits are thereafter passed down in people’s telling before becoming their support; oral transmission is omitted.
“Really wish” conveys the sincerity challenge, and “heroic spirits” supplies the subject; the claim treats natural English compression as a material loss.
高潔な人物 is specifically a noble or high-minded person; “pure” is broader and less ethically precise, though it can still suggest moral purity in context.
The English retains the merely protective role but weakens the passive placement and instrumental “power” imagery; this is a degree/detail loss rather than a wholly different proposition.
在るが無い物 expresses an existent-yet-nonexistent paradox; “should not exist” changes it into a normative claim about what ought to exist.
In this context “save the world” is a conventional rendering of saving the human world or humanity from crisis; the supplied Japanese does not require a planetary distinction.
The fused “spiritsthe” is an extraction artifact, but the English remains awkward and does not clearly render the Heroic Spirit/Guardian naming transition.
The English stops at loss of will and omits the decisive remainder: eternal forced labor for humanity as a mere cleaner.
突っぱねる adds blunt refusal and the Japanese presents this as Saber’s characteristic response; the English still conveys that she refuses unwanted actions.
触覚 is the specific feeler or sensory-extension metaphor, not merely an unspecified part; the technical explanatory distinction is materially blurred.
The source says the extension is given form and employed as the main body itself; the English replaces that agency and servile employment with being summoned as the “real” spirit.
サーヴァントという殻 specifically identifies the Servant shell or vessel, whereas generic “bodies” erases the system’s stated level distinction.
執念 is obsession or tenacious fixation and 無念 is unresolved regret or frustrated grievance; “desires and grudges” changes both concepts, especially 無念.
The source says the Grail can redress unfulfilled regret, while the English changes the object to desires and omits 晴らす’s redress or release.
“That must mean” strengthens the tentative interpretive question という事か, but English inference phrasing can still convey Shirou’s reasoning; this is a narrower modality issue.
The Japanese makes the Grail the agent that fulfills the Servants’ unfulfilled wishes; the English makes the Servants the agents granting wishes, reversing agency.
“A miracle” preserves the proposition that the Grail is miraculous for Heroic Spirits; the unexpected windfall image in 降って湧いた is vivid nuance, not a material factual reversal.
「サーヴァントでなくなる」naturally means becoming no longer a Servant; “quit being” is a defensible rendering, not necessarily employment framing.
In context, “I don’t have any wishes” can naturally mean no remaining wishes to fulfill after making his wish come true; the alleged broadening is not demonstrable.
興味はない states lack of interest, not lack of a wish. “Nor do I wish” collapses a distinct motivational claim into the preceding desire claim.
だろうさ is an inferential “must/probably” form here; “That must be the same” is a permissible English expression of Archer’s inference.
The narration explicitly marks Archer as 呆然—stunned or dazed. “Murmurs” omits that material reaction to the word “purpose.”
問いただす means pressing or demanding an explanation, not merely asking if curious. The generic “ask” materially weakens Archer’s challenge.
典型的な守護者 classifies Saber as a typical/archetypal Guardian. “Ideal” adds normative praise that is not present and conflicts with the following “slave” barb.
であるのなら is itself conditional: “if you are her Master.” The English accurately preserves that condition; current status need not be asserted in this clause.
薄れていく describes a fading process, while “disappears” presents completed disappearance. The aspectual change is clear in this short narration.
憎まれ口を叩く means making spiteful or barbed remarks. “Talks cynically” shifts this interpersonal provocation into a general attitude.
The separate “I’m home” line already supplies the spoken greeting, while “I don’t feel like it” reasonably conveys 気乗りしない. No material omission is established.
“I feel liveliness from the living room” is a natural rendering of perceiving a lively presence coming from it; this is not a material change in viewpoint.
くれている adds benefactive nuance, but English commonly leaves this implicit in a household context. “Preparing dinner” remains a defensible rendering.
The supplied English visibly fuses the name and predicate, producing a malformed sentence.
ぶんぶん adds vivid force, but “shake my head” is a normal English rendering of the action and does not materially reverse it.
本意 means true underlying intention or intent. “Honest opinion” changes the concealed intention Shirou is trying to understand into a sincere viewpoint.
“Everything’s been cut up” is defensible in the kitchen context, but it does omit the explicit visual arrangement of the ingredients being laid out. The claim should be narrowed to that omission.
“Cook it” is broad but can naturally include simmering, especially with stew already established. The alleged error is lexical preference rather than a changed event.
The specific location 方で/和室 is absent from the English, which leaves Saber’s sleeping place unspecified.
キッとしてます can naturally be rendered as having sharp eyes or a sharp look; the English need not preserve a literal whole-expression description.
Although 呑気 is not translated by a single adjective, “while she munches on a mandarin” preserves the carefree comic contrast with the scary remark.
The English retains the permission not to hold back but omits the explicit 体育会系 household rationale and characterization.
つかぬ事 marks the question as an abrupt, unrelated conversational pivot. “Can I ask you something?” omits that marked awkwardness.
In this dojo context, “we fought a bit” can naturally mean a brief practice bout; it does not require hostile combat.
剣道家 specifically identifies a kendo practitioner. “Swordsman” broadens the comparison and weakens the joke that Saber seems more like a kendoka despite not knowing kendo.
The English omits the explicit “over there/back where she came from” in 向こう. That is a genuine narrower omission, though its comic force is contextual rather than a major factual reversal.
The phrase is awkward English, but “swings around” does convey ブン回す and “unmatched to her size” conveys the mismatch. The defensible claim is idiomatic presentation, not a major semantic loss.

“I didn’t think the news got out” is a natural contextual rendering of Shirou not being supposed to have been informed; the alleged institutional-versus-personal distinction is not materially established.
盗み聞き explicitly means eavesdropping or overhearing improperly. “I heard about her” removes the covert and improper agency.
“Has nothing changed?” can naturally convey 一向に変化なし in this conversational context; the omitted frustration is a tonal nuance, not a demonstrable factual error.
“It’s not like this is a secret” can mean it is not absolutely or strictly secret, preserving the conversational qualification of 絶対秘密って話でもない.
保護された means she was located and taken into protection/recovered. “Was found” conveys location but omits her protected status.
じゃないかしら is tentative supposition. “I’m sure” turns the possibility that she is home into confidence.
意識が混濁している describes clouding of consciousness, a more specific condition than ordinary confusion. The English materially reduces the reported state.
In context, “it wasn’t serious” is a normal English way to confirm that Ayako suffered no grave harm; the shift from person to incident does not materially alter the reassurance.
どんな目にあったのか concerns what Ayako underwent or was subjected to. “What she got into” suggests her own involvement or agency and weakens the victim-oriented construction.
一環 explicitly makes Ayako’s experience one part of a continuing chain of ominous incidents. “Something to do with” weakens membership in that pattern to a vague connection.
The Japanese expresses not knowing whom to direct his regret toward. “I don’t know what I would’ve done” changes both the emotion and its interpersonal target.
Sakura explicitly says she stayed there and went to school, which explains why she had no information from home. The English omits the school-going detail.

The teacher source and 無断 are omitted, so a narrower omission claim survives. However, “skipped school” can be colloquial for unauthorized absence, so intentional truancy should not be asserted as certain.
見当違いな質問 can naturally be called a stupid question in English when apologizing for a mistaken assumption; the translation need not preserve the diagnostic metaphor literally.
The English “know about Nii-san more” is unidiomatic and weakens the direct relational claim that Sakura knows her brother better than anyone.
“It really helps when you’re here” can naturally describe the concrete help Sakura’s presence has provided in the current situation; the present-tense phrasing need not make it habitual.
The supplied English visibly fuses “Then” and “there,” producing a presentation error at a logical transition.
間桐の家 specifically identifies the Matou household. “Her house” removes the family-specific location and the danger being evaluated.
The supplied English visibly fuses Sakura’s startled “Eh” with “S-Senpai,” obscuring the stammered utterance.
The English conveys that the sudden request burdens her, but it weakens the certainty of に決まってる and leaves Sakura as the burdened person implicit. The claim should be narrowed to those nuances.
お言葉に甘えます means accepting and relying on the offered kindness. “I’ll do as you want” recasts grateful acceptance as obedience to Shirou’s desire.
くれた adds Shirou-oriented benefactive perspective, but English “Sakura agrees” accurately states the nod and the nuance is optional in natural English.
弱いものいじめ explicitly frames the punishment as bullying someone weaker. “Beating me up” retains violence but omits the disparity central to Shirou’s comic complaint.
三人で explicitly says three people will sleep together. The English’s “they” ambiguously refers to Fuji-nee and Sakura and obscures that arrangement.

The English conveys punishment and the practice context, but omits that Saber had awakened and leaves 体罰 as generic punishment. The claim should focus on those omissions without treating “punishment” as wholly indefensible.
“Please go ahead. I will answer anything I can” naturally conveys permission limited to what Saber can answer; the confirming question is reasonably folded into the exchange.
“Her eyes show her determination” is a defensible natural paraphrase of a decisive, unequivocal gaze. The personification claim is stylistic preference, not a material mistranslation.
The English has a visible pronoun agreement problem after plural “eyes,” and “nothing I can say” loses the explicit social opening to interject expressed by 口を挟める余地.
強くは言えない means he cannot press or insist on the point strongly. “Tell you strongly” is non-idiomatic and obscures that argumentative force.
望みを叶える means having a desire fulfilled through the Grail. “Ask for a wish from the Holy Grail” muddles the Grail’s stated function.
In context, “your words” can reasonably refer to Saber's preceding assertion about the Grail and her objective; the alleged invention of a new object of belief is not certain.
覇気 can be rendered as seeming unwell or lacking one’s usual spirit; “not seemed well” is broad but defensible in this dialogue.
藤ねえたち includes Fuji-nee and the others, whereas the English names only Fuji-nee and narrows Saber’s household integration.
本質は戦う事 means fighting itself is her essential nature, with だろう marking Shirou’s tentative inference. “True nature is revealed in her fighting” changes the proposition.
“Ended up promising a truce” can naturally describe reaching an agreement to suspend hostilities. “Truce” itself preserves the relevant relationship, so the alleged formality loss is not material.

The Japanese states a forward-looking rule: tell Saber immediately when making such an important decision and consult her if possible. The English recasts it as a past complaint about an earlier omission.
窘める adds corrective restraint, but “glares” can naturally describe a pointed reproving look in this context; the hostile reading is not compelled.
わずかに思案したあと indicates only brief or slight consideration. “After thinking for a while” lengthens the pause and changes the pacing.
当面は explicitly limits the pursuit to the immediate time being. The English omits that interim qualifier.
The English preserves ending cooperation and returning to enmity, but it does not explicitly preserve 休戦協定の白紙化. The surviving claim is a narrower omission of the formal truce framing.
“Asks to make sure” conveys confirmation, but it weakens 念入りに, the care and thoroughness of Saber’s checking. This is a narrower tonal omission, not a wholly different action.
いや can function as an interrupted hesitation or correction, and “Well” is a defensible English rendering for the cut-off utterance; rejection of the premise is not certain from the fragment alone.
筈なのに supports “It has to be the case,” and ヤツ→“he” is ordinary English handling of the dismissive third-person reference. The alleged strengthening is not material enough here.
不満そうに見つめてきた can naturally become “looks at me unhappily”; the surrounding object “at me” preserves directed displeasure, so this is not merely sadness.
The supplied English visibly fuses “all” and “I personally,” producing a malformed sentence at the causal pivot.
まだ先がある can naturally mean further events or matters remain; “more to do” is a normal contextual paraphrase and does not necessarily reduce the warning to chores.
出来るかぎり modifies the extent of cooperation—cooperate as fully as possible—not its duration. “For as long as we can” changes the scope to time.

Although the object is explicit in Japanese, the surrounding Grail War context makes “fight” understood as the relevant combat; the broad English is defensible.

“todayabout” is a visible word-boundary error.

The Japanese specifies a dry smile, not merely a smile. That qualifier supports the scene’s grimly amused tone and is omitted.
“Concerned with formality” is within the ordinary English range of 「形式に拘る」. The Japanese does not require the narrower gloss “procedural scruples.”
The English “to win” directly renders 「勝つ為に」; the repeated 「結果の為に」 is a self-correcting rhetorical repetition, not an independently necessary proposition.
「私利私欲」 explicitly marks selfish personal desires or self-interest. “For your own good” commonly suggests benevolent benefit and softens the moral judgment.
The immediately surrounding discussion is the Holy Grail War and obtaining the Grail. “Unless we win the Holy Grail War” is a defensible contextual explicitation of 「私たちが勝利しなければ」.

The Japanese presents the townspeople as being made into sacrifices and made useful to Archer’s group; it does not straightforwardly state “we will sacrifice” them as the group’s direct act. Agency is sharpened in English.
In context “I shouldn’t feel anything” is an idiomatic rendering of expecting no emotional shock from a familiar saying. It does not necessarily assert generalized numbness.
The Japanese specifically rejects a method that kills no one, 「一人も殺さない」. “Trying to save everybody” substitutes a different objective and logical condition.
「死線を共にくぐり抜けた」 gives the specific basis for Archer’s mock claim of friendship: surviving mortal danger together. “Like a friend” removes that basis.
「頼まれたって」 is contextually compatible with “even if you offer/request me to accept your help.” The English’s “even if you offer it to me” does not establish the claimed reversal as a material error.
「懐かれる」 can be rendered as being liked or taken to by someone. Given the preceding refusal of friendship, “you don’t like me” is a defensible contextual simplification.
「袈裟に斬られた」 specifies a diagonal slash from the shoulder area, while “cut at my shoulder” loses the direction and extent of the wound.
The Japanese identifies the burning sensation specifically in skin and flesh, 「肌と肉」. “My body is burning” broadens and loses that concrete wound imagery.
「後ろ歩きのまま」 explicitly says Shirou retreats while walking backward, and 「よろよろ」 adds staggering. “Slowly retreat” flattens the dangerous movement.
The passage identifies one white shortsword and then refers to it as 「ソレ」. “The plain swords” changes the number and object being watched.
「戦う意義のない」 denies meaning or significance in Shirou’s fighting, not the existence of a motive or reason to fight. The English changes Archer’s philosophical attack.
The Japanese describes another diagonal downward stroke trying to sever the body completely. It does not say Archer deliberately targets the existing shoulder wound.
A loss of the audible onomatopoeic quality is supportable, but “hard clang” is more specific than the supplied Japanese alone. The narrower claim is omission of the bang/clanging sound cue.
「血に濡れた体」 supplies tactile imagery of Shirou’s blood-soaked, slick body. “I try to lift my body” omits it entirely.
Saber’s wording attributes both the wound and the fall to the attacker through the active 「叩き落とした」. The passive English removes that agentive accusation.
「すぐ近く」 places the unknown Servant immediately beside Saber, which explains the urgency. “There’s another Servant here” omits that proximity.

“She’ll get attacked without being able to defend” conveys the immediate vulnerability expressed by 「無防備」. Loss of the explicit body-part image is a minor compression, not the claimed generic mistranslation.
The English preserves both the flower metaphor and its fleeting duration: 「刹那の花」 becomes “a flower that only appears for an instant.” “Too rude” also reasonably renders 「無粋」.
The Japanese specifies Saber’s profile, 「横顔」, and her taut present bearing, 「張り詰めよう」. The English reduces both to generic faces and adds “beautiful.”
「とんでもなく時代錯誤」 is an emphatic comic judgment that the outfit is outrageously anachronistic. “Traditionally-dressed” removes that judgment.
「言い流して、あっさり」 depicts tossing off the remark casually before turning away. The English retains only the turn.
「惜しい」 expresses regret or finding the missed satisfying duel a shame. “That is not my wish” shifts the line to a personal preference and loses the regret.
「迎撃」 is an interception or counterattack likened to a flash of light. “The sword attacks with lightning speed” changes both the action type and the grammatical agent.

The English broadens a slight raising of the blade point into readying the sword. The defensible narrower claim is loss of 「僅かに」 and the precise tip-raising gesture, not necessarily a full combat-ready transformation.
“Going for the enemy’s neck” already conveys the neck as the focused target; the English need not repeat 「だけ」 explicitly for the exclusivity to be understood.

“They attack each other with amazing techniques” is a natural paraphrase of an impressive exchange of swordplay. The accusation demands a stylistic “dazzling exchange” rather than identifying a material mistranslation.
「多少は心得がある程度」 deliberately limits Shirou to modest familiarity, whereas “my experienced eyes” presents him as substantially experienced.

“Attacks” is broader than 「太刀筋」, which refers to sword strokes or sword paths, but it still identifies Assassin’s sword action. The narrower finding is lexical broadening, not total loss of the object.
The English retains will as the source of the training, so “iron will” is not wholly omitted. A narrower valid claim is loss of the hardness or exceptional resolve in 「鉄の意思」.
The Japanese explicitly says they changed clothes so as not to wake Fuji-nee. That household precaution and Taiga’s sleeping presence are omitted.

The Japanese specifically reflects that complaining or grumbling was childish. “My immature actions for complaining” is grammatically awkward and shifts the object from the complaint to vague plural actions.

The supplied Original witness does contain 「呆れた風に言う」, although baseJa/allAgesJa omit it. Under the stated edition rule, this is not unsupported added content; only the exact rendering “utter amazement” is debatable.
「非道」 has a broad range including cruel, inhuman, or morally brutal. “Archer is not cruel” is a defensible, if narrower, English choice rather than a demonstrable factual reversal.
「気の迷い」 can be rendered idiomatically as being crazy or out of one’s mind at that moment, especially in Shirou’s comic self-denial. The line need not imply clinical insanity.
「筋がいい」 commonly means promising, talented, or having good aptitude. “You have talent” is within that lexical range and does not necessarily imply innate genius.
「アーチャーに届く技量」 naturally means reaching Archer’s level, so “be as good as Archer” is a defensible idiomatic rendering, not necessarily an improper strengthening.
This repeats the same valid range as 「筋がいい」: “talent” can mean aptitude or promise in English and is not demonstrably wrong here.
The request explicitly names sword instruction, 「剣を教えてくれ」, at a major training transition. “Teach me stuff” is conspicuously vague and drops the object.

「ぐっ」 supports a firm or tight clasp, so the English loses some physical emphasis, but “hold Saber’s hand” still identifies the action. The narrower claim is undertranslation of firmness, not omission of the hand-grip itself.
Against the supplied governing Original page, 「袖をめくると、そこには」 contains no wondering or hesitation. The added line also duplicates the sleeve-raising action.
「硬い感触」 describes how the arm feels, not what material it is made from. “It’s not steel” introduces an unsupported material claim.

The English broadens cheeks to the whole face and removes 「っぽい」’s tentative “apparently.” “Blushing” is a plausible contextual inference, so the narrower surviving claim is body-part and certainty broadening.
The Japanese depicts a girl sleeping under the same roof, while the English changes this to plural girls merely staying there. It loses both the sleep-specific embarrassment and number.

The Japanese identifies the diagonal sword wound, whole-body bruising from tumbling down stairs, and complete healing. The English reduces all of that to generic wounds and bruises and omits their causes and extent.

The Japanese says the shinai produced an unusually pleasing or clear sound, explicitly 「今までにないほど」. “Rather impressive” preserves a positive evaluation but weakens the specific sound quality and unprecedented degree.
“The clashings sound” is malformed English, and the Japanese’s flexing and striking of the two shinai, 「しなり、弾け合う」, is not represented.

「お手本」 can naturally be rendered “role model” or “example.” The English preserves the act of mentally picturing that exemplar before handling the shinai; the accusation is preference-level specificity.
“Repelling my attacks” is a defensible combat paraphrase of 捌く; the broader English does not create a material agency error.
意識が刈り取られる naturally describes being knocked unconscious; the accusation mainly polices imagery rather than meaning.
“If I become desperate” adds a condition absent from the Japanese. なんとか means somehow or barely, not desperation.
The Japanese separately describes the worst state as vision going white; rendering it again as not being knocked unconscious collapses a distinct sensory image.
“It’s true that Saber wasn’t up to par” is a reasonable concessive rendering of the narrator’s stated factor; the later disagreement remains intact.
“Take a breath” omits both the exhalation and the heat accumulated in the lungs, materially reducing the physical exertion image.
The Japanese evaluates the severity of Saber’s attacks, whereas “less scared” makes Shirou’s fear the object of comparison and adds an emotional reaction.
昨日の今日で means from yesterday to today or overnight; “in a day or two” introduces an extra day and blurs the joke’s immediacy.
師範代 is an assistant or deputy instructor, not all teachers generally; the English materially broadens the occupational reference.
The Japanese locates the improvement in Shirou’s form; the ungrammatical “movements in you” both weakens that technical judgment and is defective English.
The concrete assessment that Shirou can become a swordsman one level higher is omitted, leaving only generic improvement.
叩き落とす depicts forcibly knocking Saber’s shinai down or away; “parried” weakens the decisive physical action.
“One base entered your style” is malformed and does not convey 筋が一つ通る, a coherent line or organizing principle running through the form.
断らずとも結構 can naturally mean that Shirou need not ask or obtain Saber’s permission; the English is contextually defensible.
The Japanese specifically concerns how Saber counterattacks; “how you’re attacking” broadens this to her attacks generally.
“A deep hole” is an idiomatic equivalent for being trapped in trouble; the accusation treats a metaphor choice as a material factual error.
追及する means pressing or pursuing the issue, not merely limiting conversation; the English removes Shirou’s decision to stop pursuing Saber’s grievance.
私や is explicit: Saber includes herself among the opponents Shirou cannot face. The English omits her from the power comparison.
ぴしゃりと言い放つ marks a sharp, decisive delivery; “declares so” removes the rebuke’s force.
The rhetorical question is awkward and loses the hesitant heartwarming conclusion, but 師匠 as “master” is defensible in context. Narrow the claim to tone and phrasing.
“Ominous” adds foreboding beyond “something I did not want to hear,” although the preceding Tiger warning supports some bad-news context. The narrower tone-shift claim survives.
The resigned “まいったなあ” and the concrete act of putting his hand on the classroom door are both omitted.
倫理 is ethics, not philosophy; this changes Kuzuki’s stated subject.
“Iron teacher” is awkward but still a recognizable metaphorical rendering of 鉄壁の教師; the accusation overstates a style problem as factual error.
生徒会顧問 identifies a faculty adviser or supervisor, while “in charge of the student council” suggests direct control and overstates the role.
The English omits 覚悟の上とは言え and changes the embarrassed awkwardness of ばつが悪い into simple regret.
“Even stranger today” is a natural English rendering of the comparison being beyond yesterday’s condition; no material escalation is lost.
“Friends” is a permissible contextual rendering of 仲良くやって, especially alongside the explicit alliance in 手を組んだ; it need not assert formal friendship.
“Glares at me” preserves the hostile gaze; loss of the lingering じろじろ nuance is minor and not a material mistranslation.
The English weakens both the contrast with Shinji’s usual presentation and the extreme lack of composure expressed by あまりにも.
面白みにかける can naturally be “boring” or “not interesting”; the accusation imports an ominous personal anticipation not required by this sentence.
弁当 means a boxed lunch brought or possessed today again; “I made lunch” adds unsupported preparation and removes repetition.
The English retains secrecy but loses the huddled, mock-conspiratorial staging of 固まって秘密会議. Narrow the claim to that staging loss.
The period-drama implication and Shirou’s compliance are omitted, but “strange TV program” still conveys Gotou watched something the previous night. Treat as a compound omission, not total failure.
The translation preserves reciprocal peeking, but loses the archaic spy-register joke in 草っぷり. The narrower register-loss claim survives.
The adjacent Japanese explicitly concludes ありゃイライラしてるね, so rendering the visible change as increasing anger is a supported contextual inference, not unsupported content.
“Must want to talk to me” can express Shirou’s strong epistemic inference, not certainty; the English does not necessarily erase the probabilistic force.
躊躇う事なく explicitly characterizes Rin’s usual action as hesitationless; “drag me out” omits that contrast with her present behavior.
The English keeps the deliberately non sequitur pairing of taking a walk and eating lunch; punctuation and natural English do not erase the comic excuse.
Shirou tells Rin to find a good place; “continue with your walk” changes the instruction and removes いい場所を探してくれ.
The Japanese specifies raising the lunchbox before turning away; “wave her goodbye” invents a waving gesture and drops the lunchbox image.
はてな marks Shirou’s puzzled reaction to Rin’s accusation; “I turn around” omits that characterization.
はっきり言え is a demand for direct, clear speech, not merely permission to proceed.
The offer is specifically limited to the price of a sandwich; “some money” removes that concrete amount and comic practicality.
あんぽんたん can be naturally rendered as “idiot” or “fool”; the claimed loss of comic childishness is not demonstrable from this wording alone.
“The hallway goes quiet” and “everything resumes as if nothing happened” adequately convey sudden silence and restored commotion; the accusation demands unnecessary literalism.
The English conveys the main praise cluster, but omits the grade-specific 二年 and weakens 優等生の鑑. Narrow the claim to those lost distinctions rather than four wholly erased pillars.
“Idiot” is a defensible English equivalent for あんぽんたん and preserves the joke that Rin uttered an inappropriate childish insult; it does not erase the mechanism entirely.
The English retains 作戦会議 as a strategic meeting, but weakens 顔をかせ as a direct summons to come along. The narrower summons-loss claim survives.
“Get bashed” is a colloquial rendering of being singled out for hostile attention; it need not mean vague physical abuse and preserves the social threat.
The next sentence preserves the classroom-as-fortification idea, but “hide myself” loses the mock-siege register of 篭城. Narrow the claim to metaphor and tone.
突拍子もない can be rendered colloquially as “crazy” in this gossiping schoolboy context; it need not assert mental illness or literal madness.
The English preserves both the roof-edge day and the two senses of “go out” through “with her” and “go out with him”; the alleged omission is not established.
“Bridge” is defensible and the surrounding tense-state explanation remains, but つり橋 specifically identifies the suspension-bridge trope. Narrow the claim to loss of “suspension.”
“She’s amazing” can be sarcastic in context, while “us lowly people” preserves the mock-feudal contrast; sincerity is not established.
殺気だってた describes visible killing intent or a murderous atmosphere, not that Rin was literally about to kill; the English changes perceived menace into imminent action.
The supplied Japanese explicitly says a motor; the banana-peel alternative introduces unsupported content.
The Japanese gives the precise absurd image of a seated cartwheel and one rotation; repeated generic “flip” loses that specific physical joke.
魔弾の射手 is an allusive magic-bullet marksman epithet; “the shooter” reduces it to a generic description.
食って掛かる means to round on or confront someone aggressively; “scream at” adds shouting and does not express the specific confrontational action accurately.
“Not doing well” can naturally cover 元気がない in an observational context and does not necessarily imply illness; the accusation overstates the broadness.
“Classroom idol” is understandable, but it omits the specific Class 2-A designation and is less natural than “Class 2-A’s idol.” Narrow the claim to lost scope and awkward phrasing.
“Raiders” retains the mock-military metaphor, but “steal” changes おかずをたかりに来る from mooching or cadging side dishes to theft. Narrow the claim to that social-action shift.
As with the same supplied wording elsewhere, “crazy things” is a defensible colloquial rendering of startling unpredictability, not a factual claim of madness.
The English preserves the full-day roof-edge condition and the dating pun through its two uses of “go out”; the alleged blurring is not material.
The named trope is rendered as a bridge theory and the tense condition survives, but つり橋’s suspension-bridge specificity is lost. Narrow the claim accordingly.
The mock-feudal “lowly people” wording can support sarcastic “amazing”; the accusation cannot establish sincere praise as the English reading.
The English again turns 殺気だってた, an atmosphere of killing intent, into a claim that Rin was nearly ready to kill.
The Japanese specifies a motor in the chair; “banana peel” is unsupported variant content.
“Flip” loses the specifically seated cartwheel and one-rotation image expressed by 側転 and 一回転.
魔弾の射手 is reduced from an allusive magic-bullet marksman epithet to generic “shooter.”
食って掛かる describes angrily confronting or challenging Rin; “scream at” invents vocal intensity and omits the confrontation.
“Not doing well” is a defensible broad rendering of 元気がないように見える and need not imply illness.
The English conveys emptiness but omits the distinctive comic simile of a deserted New Year shopping street with the cuckoo of desolation calling.
“Keep my sanity” is a natural idiomatic paraphrase of failing to maintain sound thinking in this flustered romantic context; the accusation treats register choice as a factual distortion.
“Keep my face from blushing” is a normal English way to express preventing visible reddening; the cheek-versus-face distinction is not materially consequential here.
「済まされない」means the act cannot excuse or settle the matter; “it’s nothing now” changes that into a claim of insignificance.
The translation drops 浮ついていた, changing unsettled awareness into an unqualified stoppage of thought.
“My responsibility” conveys Rin’s personal responsibility. The narrower surviving issue is loss of the written マスター／わたし double reading and its register.
The English is awkward but accurately expresses that Rin’s behavior bothers Shirou more than Archer’s attack; this is not a factual inversion.
ここで切り捨てた方がいい can mean eliminate or kill in this hostile context; “decided to kill you” is a defensible contextual rendering.
手に落ちかけた describes nearly coming under Caster’s control, whereas “fell for a trap” recasts this as being deceived and weakens the agency/control relation.
“What are we doing, drinking coffee here?” is a natural English rendering of the comic rhetorical question in context, not a material factual error.
“It won’t take you five minutes” naturally conveys that five minutes is sufficient for the trip; the accusation polices phrasing rather than meaning.
“Request” can naturally describe Rin’s devilish proposal to have Shirou buy the coffee; the causal and comic force remains.
“My father” correctly identifies Kiritsugu’s relation. A narrower omission remains: the explicit name and familiar オヤジ／切嗣 presentation are not retained.
二次成長期 is a specific developmental threshold, not merely general bodily maturity.
The English is malformed and omits 一人前, which qualifies Rin as a fully fledged magus.
子供の頃から means from childhood; “from the time we’re born” moves the stated starting point earlier.
The Japanese asks why Shirou is being brought into Rin’s comparison, not why she is asking him a question.
The English paraphrases the scale metaphor as putting lives on the line and accepting risk. Loss of the image is not by itself a material error.
“When we fail” broadens 赤点, but the surrounding perfect-score context preserves the school-performance joke. The claim should be narrowed to loss of the explicit failing-grade wording.
The English preserves a contrast between difficulty and harshness, so “reversed near-synonyms” overstates the defect. It nevertheless maps 厳しい／辛い imprecisely.
“Harsh nor severe” collapses 辛い and 厳しい into overlapping severity terms and loses the painful-versus-severe distinction.
The bare declarative is a formative resolve to become like Kiritsugu; “I want to be” weakens it into present desire.
独学でここまできた specifically praises reaching this point through self-study, not merely possessing personal skill.
胸を張って describes Rin’s proud posture while speaking; the translation reverses the actor and turns it into an instruction to Shirou.
“Any container” is a permissible broad English rendering of 色んな器 in this context; it does not necessarily assert unlimited capacity.
左手 identifies the left hand specifically; “left arm” changes the displayed body part.
神秘 is the setting’s specific notion of Mystery; “anything special” removes the technical proposition.
移し替えられる means transfer or move between vessels; “store” changes the capability being described.
後継ぎになったら means becoming the heir, not succeeding in a general sense.
“Foolish” can convey silly behavior, but it weakens the specific affectionate clumsiness of ドジ. The surviving claim is lexical and tonal, not necessarily an intelligence judgment.
The source refers to the connection between mage lineages; “another magus” wrongly presents Shinji as an individual magus before that is established.
魔術師の家系 refers to mage families or lineages, not individual magi with personal histories.
今朝知った explicitly says Rin herself learned it this morning; the English omits that timing and discovery.
The English retains the assumption that Shinji could not be a Master, but weakens the complacent タカをくくっていた attitude. The accusation should not claim the whole qualification disappears.
“Not do anything” is broader than 大人しくしておけ, which means keep quiet or stay out of trouble. The narrower overbreadth claim survives.
The Japanese says Shirou cannot simply accept the account and leave the matter there; “I can’t stop her here” changes the object and agency.
“Magic” is a permissible natural English rendering of 魔術 here, especially in this supplied translation’s established terminology; the accusation treats terminology preference as factual error.
発現した means the abnormal phenomenon manifested or appeared; “the disorder is revealed” implies disclosure of a preexisting condition.
The Japanese describes an attempted effect on consciousness, while the English states a completed bodily numbness.
昏睡 is coma or comatose unconsciousness; “faint” materially weakens the stated outcome.
錯覚させる can be rendered as making someone hallucinate or misperceive in colloquial English; the wording is awkward but the accusation overstates a clinical distinction.
嫌悪 is disgust or revulsion, not hatred toward another person.
四階 is an explicit location and is absent from the English sentence.
“It doesn’t mean we won’t make it” is a natural double-negative equivalent of “it may not be too late yet.”

The supplied raw witness identifies the convulsing/foaming text as a conditional English branch; the same page also contains the matching limp/clouded-eyes branch. This cannot be treated as an invented insertion without branch alignment.
“Melting” is explicitly part of the conditional English branch, while the supplied English also contains “solidified.” The branch flattening cannot be certified as a translation reversal.
The alleged melting/plaster passage belongs to the conditional English variant documented in the supplied witness material; it is not safely attributable to the governing Japanese alignment.

The added giant-stomach image is likewise contained in the conditional branch, while the governing Japanese describes wax-like reflected light. Branch flattening makes the accusation unsupported as stated.
息を殺している means Rin holds or suppresses her breath; “is astonished” states a different reaction.
元凶を叩いて止めさせる is an urgent plan to strike down the source and force the field to stop, not merely retrieve a cause.
手分けして explicitly proposes splitting up the search, which the English omits.
“Grab Tohsaka” is a natural English paraphrase of taking her hand and pulling her into motion; the hand detail is not materially reversed.
The Japanese is Shirou’s internal objection—calling Saber now will be too late—not a statement that Rin said they should call Saber.
“Usual cool” is colloquial but can naturally mean usual composure; it preserves the claim that Rin has not fully recovered her calm.
確実に勝利できる expresses certainty, while “should be able to beat” introduces uncertainty.
“Release it” is a valid natural rendering of unraveling or releasing a Command Spell; the accusation demands preservation of metaphor rather than meaning.
The English conveys clearing thoughts, and omission of the ruby’s written pun is not by itself a translation error without a demonstrated semantic loss.
The source specifies the back of the left hand, while the English gives only “my hand.”
歪み is a distortion or spatial deformation; “void” changes the phenomenon into an absence or empty space.
“Detect magic” can naturally encompass sensing traces of magecraft; the supplied English does not assert a different object of detection.
“Pretty good too” preserves competence but weakens 負けてない, Rin’s explicit claim that she is not inferior in this area.
The English’s “has to be” contradicts the explicit uncertainty in 断定はできないけど.
The English preserves the two alternatives, but adds waiting and omits 駆けつける’s urgent rushing. The accusation should be narrowed to that agency/urgency shift.
“Release it” is an acceptable natural rendering of 紐解く in this operational instruction; the concrete metaphor is not required for semantic accuracy.
“Eliminate any thoughts” conveys clearing 雑念; the ruby’s layered presentation is a textual nuance, not demonstrably a material mistranslation here.
The English omits the exact location, 左手の甲, of the Command Spell’s burning expenditure.
“Void” is not an equivalent of the stated heavy distortion 歪み.
“Detect magic” is a natural contextual rendering of sensing magecraft traces; the accusation treats a lexical choice as a categorical factual error.
“Pretty good too” conveys ability but weakens Rin’s parity claim in 負けてない; the broader accusation should be narrowed to that degree-of-confidence shift.
“Has to be” contradicts Rin’s explicit statement that she cannot determine it with certainty.
Adds waiting to an either/or statement and weakens Archer’s active response by making his arrival something they must await.
“Strengthening magic” is a defensible rendering of 強化 in this context; the Japanese does not require a capitalized technique name.
か marks tentative identification, whereas “exactly like” presents the comparison as categorical.
“Take another leg while I’m at it” preserves the casual appropriation and comic tone adequately.
人形 identifies the enemies as dolls or constructed figures; “things” omits that material classification.
“A kind of a familiar” is awkward but semantically conveys ゴーレム as a familiar-type entity; number is not materially wrong.
“The bones” reduces bone puppets to loose bones and removes their constructed animated nature.
“Creature” is broader than 人形 and loses the repeated construct/doll classification.
悲壮 denotes tragic or grim pathos, not ordinary sadness.
逃走 is flight or the urge to flee; “cowardice” moralizes a survival response.
二つの武器 explicitly says two weapons, not swords; the objects are chair legs.
The English supplies an unspecified male model, while 見よう見まね leaves the model and manner unexpressed.
薙ぎ払う describes sweeping or clearing aside, not simply smashing the fourth enemy.
今までにないほど marks unprecedented severity; “smashed” does not preserve that escalation.
叩きつけた is a forceful slam against the exposed torso, not a generic attack.
The Japanese stresses that the count does not decrease despite destruction; “there are more” loses that causal pressure.
“Why don’t you guys run out?” can naturally preserve the stock-depletion joke in context; this is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
The supplied ruby explicitly contributes 灰 and 塵 readings, which the English omits entirely.
Relief is a reasonable English inference from the sigh and shoulder-dropping after thanking Shirou; this is normal explicitation, not a factual error.
“Pure hell” is idiomatic enough, and “here” is a contextually defensible rendering of そこ; the complaint is stylistic.
Hallucinations can naturally describe unreal perceived sounds, and “moanings” is awkward wording rather than a material semantic error.
The supplied Original-edition witness contains this image, so it is an edition difference rather than an unsupported insertion.
The Japanese deliberately leaves the emotion unspecified; “in horror” fixes one emotion not stated by the narrator.
“On his butt” is colloquial but accurately represents 尻餅をつき; the objection is register preference.
詰め寄る conveys closing in or pressing toward someone, whereas “goes near” neutralizes Rin’s threatening movement.
僕じゃない does not identify the victim’s gender; “her” reveals Rider before the staged discovery.
倒れ伏した describes collapsed students, not a confirmed diagnosis of unconsciousness.
間の抜けた can mean vacant, dazed, or stunned; “a stunned voice” is a defensible contextual rendering.
万力 is a vise; a jack is a different implement.
“Ripped off” weakens the gouging-out nuance, but “by crushing it” preserves the mechanism; the broader accusation overstates the loss.
“Disappears from this world” is a natural contextual rendering of a Servant 消滅 and does not materially contradict the technical event.
やはり supports “as I thought,” while らしい supplies the surrounding apparent/inferential qualification; the English preserves both.
騒ぎ can mean commotion or panic in this school incident; “causing this panic” is an acceptable contextual choice.
“You’re next” naturally implies the attacker’s future targeting, and “I’m sure” conveys 必ず; no material weakening is established.
“Harmless insect” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of the image and is supported by the immediate explanation of Shinji’s harmlessness.
見苦しい means unsightly or undignified, not merely annoying; the contemptuous visual judgment is changed.
“That’s the only value in you right now” is grammatical and accurately conveys その程度の価値しかない.
“Lost her calmness” directly and adequately conveys 我を失っている; the alleged degree difference is preference-level.
歯を噛む refers to gritting or clenching teeth; “biting her lips” changes the bodily action.
The English preserves recognition of Rin but omits the specific profile and usual-public-face framing; it does not erase the entire recognition.
一人前の魔術師 means a full-fledged or competent magus; “mature magus” shifts professional qualification into age or personality.
“Magic” is a defensible general translation of 魔術 here; the supplied Japanese does not itself require a technical glossary distinction.
