“Dislike” is a defensible plain-English rendering of feeling uncomfortable or having difficulty with someone.
“Tense voice” falls within the contextual range of 「硬い声」; the finding treats a plausible lexical choice as a factual change.
The Japanese marks Shirou’s inference tentatively with 「のだろう」, while “must know” promotes it to necessity.
“Statue-like” is a natural resemblance-based rendering of 「岩のような巨人」.
The source’s 「言動」 includes conduct as well as words; “sounded” narrows that to verbal impression.
The Japanese concerns unreasonable terms, not the amount of compensation requested.
“Most dangerous for you” preserves the practical self/other contrast even without a separate clause for Rin.
The explicit insult 「馬鹿」 is omitted again.
“Would be” can retain certainty within the stated hypothetical; it does not necessarily weaken 「間違いなく」 to a prediction.
“Optimistic thought” is a defensible natural rendering of an idealistic proposal in context.
The epithet 「希代」 is omitted again.
“Natural enemy” can idiomatically convey someone one simply cannot handle, matching the Kirei analogy.
“Dislike” is a defensible simplification of 「苦手意識を持つ」 and does not materially reverse the meaning.
“Tense voice” is within the contextual lexical range of 「硬い声」; the claimed anxiety substitution is not demonstrable.
In context, 「相手」 can refer collectively to Illya and Berserker; “such monsters” is a natural contextual rendering, not proven number error.
“Proper girl” can mean decent or well-behaved and is a defensible rendering of 「ちゃんとした子」.
The English compresses two Japanese noun phrases into one, but “someone you haven’t met yet” still conveys the core category; only the rhetorical doubling is demonstrably lost.
「自身の信条を変えた」 concerns changing convictions, not merely changing sides or allegiance.
“My mind darkens” is a natural English metaphor for emotions sinking; the source does not require a literal emotion noun.
The source supports freezing or becoming completely cold; “cools down” weakens the intensity and can suggest calming, but does not erase the cold image entirely.
The Japanese declares a contrast in identity, while “I will swear here” invents an oath and does not translate 「違う」.
The source separates the survival purpose from the possibility that the path was ultimately right; the English combines them into “the right choice to survive.”
「綺麗事」 means pretty moral platitudes or empty fine words, not ideals themselves.
「反発しあっていた」 explicitly describes reciprocal opposition; “I opposed him” makes the conflict one-sided.
The source names Kiritsugu and the concept 「正義の味方」; “my father” and “superhero” replace both with different labels.
「歩けなくなる」 preserves a continuing path metaphor; “keep standing” changes it to a physical posture metaphor.
The English adds a room as the container and loses the explicit contrast between darkness and words remaining undissolved.
The image of mud-like, heavy sleep is omitted.
The English retains heaviness and bodily assault, but weakens the whole-body, bear-down image in 「全身にのし掛かって」.
The Japanese directly identifies the sensation as a scream; “No” inserts a corrective denial not present in 「それは」.
“Done her best to win” conveys effort toward victory, but weakens the exclusive purpose and full-force emphasis of 「勝利する為だけに全力を尽してきた」.
「搾取」 is exploitation or predation, not neutral collection.
“Sacrifices” can refer to human victims, so the core is retained, but it broadens the concrete human-pillar mechanism in 「人柱」.
“Do the forbidden” is malformed and loses the explicit object/action of breaking taboos.
The source says the arts debased her into a witch; “skills that labeled her” changes moral self-degradation into external labeling.
The English omits the recoil-on-the-victim curse mechanism and the stated practice of calling down calamity.
「気が違う」 denotes losing one’s mind; “go crazy for” is the English idiom of enthusiastic desire and changes the force.
The ability to intervene in the human world is omitted from the second-life description.
The output contains a clear spacing error, and it also weakens the explicitly total release of vigilance in 「あらゆる警戒を解いて」.
“A chanced meeting” is malformed English for 「その偶然」 and fails to express a chance encounter naturally.
白い modifies her established limbs; 凍えていた means chilled/frozen by the winter rain. The translation incorrectly makes whiteness a result of cold and drops the chilling.
面影は皆無だった says there was no trace or resemblance left even in her magical power. Adding “amount” narrows this to quantity and changes the comparison.
“Lifeline that allows them to stay in this world” is a defensible natural rendering of magical energy sustaining a Servant’s existence; this is not a demonstrable factual error.
The missing separator produces the visibly fused and grammatically defective “SheServant Caster.”
代償 is the price or cost paid for gaining freedom, not compensation received for it. The causal direction is reversed.
寝首をかいた describes killing the unsuspecting or sleeping Master. “Betrayed” omits the concrete murder and the ambush-like circumstance.
The English still presents her own misjudgment as amusing; “to see how badly” is an idiomatic paraphrase, not proof of an external observer or changed experiencer.
自滅 means self-destruction or destroying oneself. “Kill each other” adds mutual killing that the Japanese does not state.
疎む can naturally be rendered as treating someone coldly, especially with the following insult. The accusation demands a stronger wording than the Japanese requires.
“Filled the man’s conceit” is a malformed English collocation; the Japanese clearly says she continually gratified his pride or ego.
令呪 can be treated generically in English; singular “the Command Spell” does not demonstrably assert that only one spell remained.
The extraction visibly fuses “words” and “to,” damaging the sentence at a central explanatory transition.
現世 is the present/living world, not a historical age. “Passport to this age” shifts the metaphysical destination and conflicts with the supplied witness.
“Treated unreasonably” can mean treated unfairly or unjustly in this context. The accusation treats a defensible lexical alternative as a factual weakening.
神という選定者 is singular: the selector called a god or the god-selector. “The gods” pluralizes the selecting agent.
八つ裂きにし specifically says tearing the brother into eight pieces. “Cut apart” removes the explicit number and extremity.

The English is unidiomatic and shifts role into identity, but it still conveys that people demanded she be a witch. The narrower surviving claim is malformed wording and loss of “role,” not total semantic failure.

The phrasing is awkward and weakens 受け皿’s receptacle/scapegoat function, but “on the receiving end” still conveys being made to bear dark superstition. The accusation should be narrowed to role and collocation.
The Japanese says she vowed to become that imposed figure and make them realize its ugliness. The translation replaces the deliberate embodiment with ugliness merely attributed to their wishes.
咎 means guilt, blame, or culpability. Replacing it with aesthetic ugliness changes the accusation’s moral content.

The Japanese states that she continues revenge without a wish of her own; it does not explicitly state active unwillingness. “Against her will” is an added intensification, though the rest is accurate.
意識 is consciousness or awareness on the verge of collapse. “Barely able to stand” relocates the condition to bodily balance.
The source specifies spattered blood and the area below the waist. “Covered in blood” removes both location and type of staining.
何をするか is what this person will do, as confirmed by the following possible responses. “What such a person did” changes the expected future reaction into a past act.
The missing separator creates the malformed fusion “that manthe man.”
与えられた事を成す means carrying out what is assigned or given. “Whatever whim took him” invents self-directed impulse and reverses the characterization.

The surrounding English immediately specifies that he accepted her request to become Master and her disclosure of identity. “Accepted her” is a normal compact rendering of the omitted object, not necessarily romantic acceptance.

The page’s direct Japanese witness gives only the non-explicit sentence, but the supplied Original candidates include the sexual-contract passage elsewhere: 「彼流に言うのなら神仏の前での行為」 and 「それで契約は完了した」. Their page alignment is expressly uncertified, so an unsupported-insertion verdict cannot be established responsibly.

The direct page witness does not contain the sexual request, while supplied Original candidate text contains an explicit contract episode. Because the candidate alignment is expressly uncertain, this cannot be certified as invented content.

The supplied Original candidate includes the corresponding explicit dialogue, but its alignment is not certified and the page witness itself omits it. The accusation cannot responsibly be decided as unsupported insertion.

The supplied evidence contains an Original-only explicit branch candidate, including 「それで契約は完了した」, but not with certified page alignment. This is an edition/alignment question, not demonstrable invention.

The supplied Original candidate includes the Buddha/Asura/Bodhisattva material, while the direct page witness does not. Since the candidate is expressly not certified alignment, unsupported-content cannot be established.

鬼門 can naturally be rendered as a demonic or dangerous place for Servants. The following Japanese explains that entering the temple nevertheless makes it an excellent summoning site; no material contradiction is shown.
鉄壁の守り is an ironclad or impregnable defense. “Best protection” changes an absolute defensive characterization into a vague ranking.
諦めがついた means she could resign herself or accept the outcome if the miracles were absent. “Would have been fine” turns resignation into emotional contentment.
嘆息した explicitly says she sighed while judging that everything she did failed. The English retains the judgment but omits the sigh and its weary delivery.
The English preserves the hypothetical effort but broadens one definite wish into “any wish.” The surviving claim is overgeneralization, not total mistranslation.
かみ合わないお互いの存在 describes the two existences failing to mesh. “Do not get along well” reduces an existential mismatch to ordinary interpersonal friction.

希代 can mean rare, extraordinary, or exceptional; “rare witch” is a defensible though plain rendering. The accusation demands a stronger stylistic register rather than identifying a clear mistranslation.
もう敵なんていない states that no enemies remain. “Nothing to fear” changes an objective roster claim into a subjective emotional claim.
軽口 identifies Archer’s flippant or glib remark. The English omits that tone, which matters to how the statement’s apparent truth is interpreted.
使役できない means can be made to serve or commanded, not summoned. The English changes the authority relationship into a summoning rule.
“Determined by” can idiomatically mean governed or conditioned by and does not necessarily assert total causation. The accusation overreads a reasonable English formulation.
人間霊 restricts the candidates to human spirits. “Anyone with powers” broadens this to any powered being and drops the spirit restriction.
肝に銘じて口をききなさい is a severe command to engrave the fact in mind before speaking. The English is awkward and substantially weakens that command.
陥落 means fall, defeat, or subjugation. “Surrenders” adds voluntary capitulation and changes the coercive agency.
The missing space visibly fuses “But” and “the” into “Butthe.”
疲労 is accumulated fatigue or exhaustion, not productive hard work. The English reverses the image from depletion to achievement.
懺悔 is repentance or confession, and the Japanese presents an impersonal stylized statement about the path. “I do not have regrets” changes both concept and construction.
我はそこで自身をなくした means “there I lost my very self.” “My self lost its self” is malformed and changes the agent of loss.
焼け跡 means burned remains or ruins after the fire. “Burning field” suggests an area still actively burning.
思ってしまった conveys that he could not help thinking it despite himself. “Considered it” removes that involuntary emotional force.
正義の味方 is the work’s specific ideal of an ally of justice, not simply a superhero. The pop-culture substitution materially changes the concept.

The complete English page preserves the crooked paths and explicitly says “I’ve been repeating this for ten years.” “I’m taking the long way” is a natural compressed paraphrase, not a demonstrable loss of repetition.

“I will ... at times” can express a recurring expectation or general pattern in this monologue. The English retains both choosing wrong paths and losing things; the tense difference is not materially established as an error.
The source requires showing the singular meaning of having survived. “Present meanings for everything” multiplies and redirects that obligation toward separate losses.
The source explicitly compares the entire overcast sky to one dusted with ash. “A clouded one” omits both the ash-linked image and total coverage.
The English retains the landmine joke; stepping on a mine conventionally conveys the frozen or immobilized posture. The accusation treats an implicit consequence as a required literal repetition.

“Far from the city” is broadly compatible with the location, but it omits the explicit city-limits/outside-city detail. The claim should be narrowed to geographic specificity rather than calling the translation wholly wrong.
樹海 and まだ人の手が入っていない describe a vast sea of trees untouched by humans. “Unkempt woodland” changes pristine wilderness into neglected maintenance.
The extraction fuses the epithet and class name into “giantBerserker,” a clear presentation error.
The English is serviceable but generalizes a Boston bag packed with various items to “a big bag.” The surviving issue is omission of concrete prop detail, not a materially false loadout.
“In mine” leaves an unidiomatic and incomplete substitute for “in one hand.” The source explicitly identifies the hand holding the shinai bag.

Highway can be a normal English rendering of 国道, not necessarily a limited-access expressway. The supplied Japanese itself distinguishes 国道 from 高速道路, but the English wording does not prove the accused meaning.
十数メートル is roughly ten-odd meters; “more than a few meters” materially reduces the stated visible distance.
管理が行き届いている can naturally be contextualized as the forest being under surveillance, especially after 識別; the accusation treats an acceptable contextual rendering as a factual error.
The missing separator produces malformed English and obscures the two-part hesitation/interjection.
The English has subject–verb disagreement and an unnatural preposition, so the warning is materially malformed.
“Light” conveys mildness, but the dry greeting comparison in 挨拶程度 is lost.
The English preserves the contrast between fighting and talking but omits the explicit callback to Rin’s earlier statement.
“Vast place” is a defensible rendering of the seemingly infinite trees, and the dead-vegetation contrast appears in the adjacent sentence; “only people” is normal English for 生きている人間 here.
The English retains the corpse simile, so “literal dead grass” overstates the error; however, 冬の草木 includes winter vegetation, not only grass, and that scope is narrowed.
The head noun is plural: “rows ... make,” not “rows ... makes.”
The concrete temporal anchor that noon had long passed is omitted.
円形の空間 describes a circular space; “dome” introduces an enclosed architectural structure not stated here.
The English conveys peaceful intent through “as a sign,” but it loses the openness/confidence nuance of 堂々と; this is a narrower tonal omission, not total omission of the plan.
The interjection and hesitation are fused into malformed text.
The translation omits both the second-floor target and the specific flying-kick action.
The Japanese explicitly states that the window was kicked apart; “breaks” removes the actor and cause.
The fused “Butwould” is a real presentation error, but calling battle instead of sword clash is defensible in context; the compound accusation must be narrowed.
The missing separator fuses the tactical identification with the conclusion into malformed prose.
The source identifies Berserker as one side of the battle, while the translation identifies Illyasviel.
The location and its apposition are fused into malformed English.
取り返しの付かない describes an irreversible or irreparable event, not merely something terrible.
剣戟 specifically evokes a ferocious clash of swords; “battle” removes the weapon-specific acoustic image.
吹き抜け is an open atrium/void over the hall, not a stairwell leading down to it.
Given the preceding escape sentence, “either way” can naturally paraphrase the equal outcome whether together or alone; “stand a chance” need not mean combat specifically.
“There’s no point in staying together” is a natural explicitation of だから分かれる in the stated survival calculation, not unsupported content.
懇願 is a plea or entreaty; “wish” substantially weakens the supplicating tone of Rin’s warning.
“Go around” can naturally mean take a detour; the alleged loss of 大 is not sufficiently material in this context.
The translation omits that Rin arrived at the same time as Shirou, a concrete spatial and timing detail.
声を押し殺す means deliberately suppressing one’s voice, whereas “gasp” describes an audible involuntary reaction.
比ではない compares the roar’s harrowing intensity with before; “louder” changes the comparison to volume.
The English weakens 肩を震わせ and especially 泣き叫ぶ一歩手前 into generic shivering and near tears, losing the imminent vocal breakdown.
舞う presents the swords’ visual motion as dancing or whirling; “released” reduces that image to mere launch.
貫く means pierce or run through, not merely attack.
湯水の如く can be rendered as a continuous or gushing stream in this attack context; the English is a defensible image, not a proven reversal of the idiom.
“Pieces are blown from his body” can naturally convey the body being blown apart; the accusation demands a degree of explicitness the Japanese wording does not require.
蘇り means revival or resurrection; “regenerates” normally describes healing or regrowth and obscures the discrete return from death.
The English retains the smile, so total omission is overstated; it does, however, weaken the pleasure/amusement in 楽しげに.
The source explicitly specifies revival at the place of death; “regenerative powers” loses both revival and the on-the-spot timing.
The English conveys killing as the sole purpose but omits the important qualification that the battle has no order or restraint.
敵を屠り殺す states the offensive aim of slaughtering the enemy; “advances on his enemy” does not expressly preserve that purpose.
“Standing there” can convey the stopped position and the later context supplies provocation, but the deliberate halt in あえて歩を止め is weakened.
The local English omits the dull-witted judgment, though the surrounding passage already conveys Berserker’s foolish advance; the accusation should not claim complete loss of that characterization.
暗愚の輩 is a benighted or foolish person, not “dogshit”; the conditional branch adds extreme profanity unsupported by the Japanese witness.
The source dehumanizes Berserker as a thing made only to fight; “You can only fight” changes that judgment about nature into an ability limitation.
奔る describes the Noble Phantasms racing or rushing forth; “emerge from space” changes the motion and adds an unsupported source.
指令を下した means he issues commands to the weapons; “readies” removes his act of commanding them.
The Japanese makes Gilgamesh the experiencer of the stifling discomfort; the English assigns unpleasantness to Berserker.
大部分にその命を奪われた means most of the weapons take his life; “loses most of his life” changes the agency and relation.
“Dying already” is a plausible rendering of an effectively dead body in context, but it weakens the completed/dead-state force of 死に体; the accusation should be narrower.
The source asks how a mere target still retains its shape; “survived my attack” changes the focus from bodily integrity to survival.
“Body slashed” and “limbs pierced” are defensible natural generalizations of flesh damage and pierced legs; no material action is contradicted.
The shield metaphor plus the following statement about taking all attacks preserves the protective function against the weapon rain; the accusation treats distributed context as omission.
In this explicitly life-or-death contest, “the one to win” is a defensible rendering of the one who achieves the goal and survives; the surrounding English states the life condition.
The source uses a concessive even-if construction; the English leaves “Even if” dangling and then asserts the hopelessness as fact.
“Coming out of his tenth death” naturally conveys surpassing or emerging beyond the tenth death; the number and cumulative-death image remain.
“Not yet been raised against the man” plus “rips through the air” conveys the first execution of the attack; the accusation overstates this as mere posture.
The Japanese targets the rock-like neck with constriction; “tear off the head” changes both the body part and the action.
“Commands Berserker to retreat using her Command Spell” is a normal contextual rendering of 強制撤去を命じる; the spell’s force is already explicit in the sentence.
“Transportation” can cover the movement, but the explicit spatial-transfer/teleportation specification in 空間転移 is narrowed; this is a technical omission rather than a wholly false translation.
English narrative present can describe a just-completed event, and the surrounding scene clearly treats it as over; the tense difference is not materially misleading here.
The Japanese describes a form that could only be taken for a grotesque object; “after becoming” turns perception/comparison into literal transformation.
“Check if he is alive” is a natural idiomatic rendering of checking for 息, and the following English explicitly preserves the breathing point.
英雄としての精度 concerns quality or caliber as a hero, not simply physical strength; “stronger” changes the comparison.
墓標となった links the giant body to a grave marker; “giant corpse” removes that death-image and metaphor.
The euphemistic Japanese supports loss of the girl’s light/sight, but the mature branch’s specific eye-slashing method is an added inference; the all-ages wording does not make that addition.
“Impales” alone weakens 仕留める, but the immediately following “dies for sure this time” restores the killing result; the claim should be limited to the local verb.
絞った声 describes a strained, constricted voice; “I yell” loses the bodily effort and vocal condition.
制止の声 is a cry attempting to restrain him, not a successful physical stop; the English falsely assigns Shirou successful agency.
“Death” is a natural English personification in this simile; the Japanese does not require an article or a literal deity translation.
“My body wants to go out” is a natural compression of the involuntary urge expressed by the limbs, and the following page separately specifies the feet and arms.
自分 is singular and refers to Shirou himself; “we’ll be the ones” changes the number and redistributes the anticipated victim.
The supplied page explicitly contains the corresponding arm-reaching line; the accusation overlooks the complete page staging.
火を点し is figurative imagery for the feet’s urgent impulse, and “on fire from wanting to jump out” is an idiomatic equivalent.
The English preserves the urge to cross the terrace but omits the wing-like 羽ばたき image; this is a narrower imagery loss, not loss of the entire impulse.
心 can refer to mind, spirit, or emotional faculties; “my mind has broken” is a defensible rendering of this psychological simile.
“Gone crazy” is an interpretive paraphrase of emotional or mental collapse, not an established unsupported assertion; 心 has this semantic range.
意思 is more precisely will or resolve, so “mind” blurs the object being suppressed; however, the parallel “kill my voice and kill my mind” can still convey deliberate mental self-suppression.
見殺した means leaving someone to die or allowing them to be killed, not personally killing the girl.

The explicit “girl’s heart” occurs only in the flattened conditional branch; the governing Japanese withholds the noun, so the branch-specific insertion is genuine but the finding cannot be applied to the all-ages wording.
The Japanese makes the blank brain cause the whole body to shake; the English makes the brain itself the shaking subject and loses 全身.
The English retains anger but loses both its belated emergence and its unbearable quality.
「盗み見をする不届き者」describes an illicit peeper or impertinent spy. “Watching this spectacle” adds an object and weakens the accusation.
The Japanese itself is a deliberately fragmentary literary time-opening; “Going back over a month” conveys the intended temporal relation.
“Gray” is a plausible atmospheric paraphrase, but the translation drops the explicit long-standing loss of blue in 久しい and 忘れている.
山間 means a mountainous region or valley among mountains, not a location inside one hidden mountain. The spatial relation is changed.
神秘はカラのまま can naturally be rendered as the mystery within remaining empty or absent. The English is awkward but its relation is intelligible and not a demonstrable logical inversion.
“Foreseeable” is not quite 見えた, which is an end coming into sight, but the sentence is understandable; the accusation of malformed fatalism is overstated.
The English retains the contrast between rightful owners and ordinary providers. “Donate help” is an imperfect choice for 提供者, but it does not erase the loss of status.
執念 has a legitimate range including tenacity or relentless persistence, and “abnormal” preserves 常軌を逸していた. The accusation treats one preferred gloss as mandatory.
とうに正気を失っていた explicitly says they had long since lost their sanity. “Obsessed” preserves fixation but materially weakens that diagnosis.
余裕 can mean available time or leeway. In this sequence “did not have time” is a defensible contextual rendering, even if less precise than “no leeway.”
“Total failure” can convey a devastating defeat, so the charge of broadly weakened severity is too strong. It does, however, omit the explicit unprecedented comparison in かつてないほど.
The supplied Japanese witnesses include an alternate Original branch with 妻と娘. This is branch/edition content, not an unsupported translation insertion into the daughter-only branch.
作品 is a created work or product of the clan. “Their family, with their perfected Magic Circuits” changes that crafted work into the biological family collectively possessing circuits.
令呪 can function as a generic collective term; the singular English noun does not necessarily assert that only one mark exists, especially with “engraved all over.”
The causative ～させる legitimately permits “let” or “allow.” The surrounding English also identifies the attacking entities as enemies, so the alleged agency reversal is not established.
“She screamed in anguish, but allowed him to attack” preserves the pain-versus-action contrast and is a natural English rendering of the compressed Japanese construction.
嘆く means lament or complain, not merely murmur, and the English construction is materially malformed and obscures the contrast between lamenting and hating the cause.
The English communicates hostility and using Berserker as an outlet, but “insulted” is narrower than 憎み. The surviving claim is a lexical weakening, not total loss of the relationship.
消えていた states that the pain had disappeared, whereas “had lessened” leaves residual pain and weakens the completed result.
The Japanese specifies dependable allies and beloved friends. “Friends or collaborators” drops both relational qualifiers that define what Illya denies herself.
The Japanese concerns deceiving herself about things that could never be given to her. “Fated to have nothing” broadens this into total predestined deprivation.
返り血 and 真紅 specify both the source of the blood and the vivid crimson color. “Covered in blood” loses both details.
The supplied Original witness has a branch describing beasts biting off the neck, forehead, and limbs. The alleged extra injury is therefore not unsupported invention.
The Japanese repeatedly localizes the injury to her own arm. “Her body was destroyed” expands that into total bodily destruction.
彼を死なせない為に gives the specific purpose of preventing his death. “For his sake” is materially broader and omits that protective aim.
The supplied Original branch explicitly contains the eye-gashing action. It is not an unsupported mature-branch invention against the Japanese evidence.
破かれた describes a lung being torn or ruptured. “Pierced” substitutes a puncture mechanism and changes the injury description.
どこにそれだけの力が残っていたのか asks rhetorically where such strength could have remained, not how much strength remained.
“Charges at” conveys a forceful lunge, but it omits the attempted seizure in 掴みかかる. This is a narrow action-detail loss rather than a wholly different event.
“Is thrust” conveys the lance attack but not the poetic rapid-motion image in 奔る. The surviving claim is loss of motion/force, not a complete mistranslation.
“The heart-piercing lance impales the giant” naturally entails entry into his chest and preserves the attack and target. The alleged omission is not materially established.
Narrative present is a normal English dramatic tense and “That ends it” can render the completed beat in context. Japanese tense does not require past English here.
粛正 is a purge or violent corrective punishment. “Regulation” reduces the force to administrative governance.
砂と化して means turning into sand, not merely crumbling like sand as a comparison. The material transformation is weakened.
The supplied Original witness has an alternate branch explicitly stating that both eyes were crushed. The repeated mature rendering is therefore branch evidence, not unsupported invention.
不撓不屈 means unbowed, unyielding, and indomitable. “Invincible” shifts moral endurance into combat invulnerability.
The Japanese centers on her fingertips being enveloped in a definite tactile sensation. “The hand touches something” broadens the body part and removes the enveloping, certain contact.
すがりついた means clung to or clung desperately to the hard body. “Crawls to the hard figure” describes approach and omits the culminating embrace.
自分にはもう確かめられない expresses inability to verify the fact for herself. “She cannot see anymore” repeats blindness and removes the epistemic dependence on touch.
“Wanted for him to pick her up” is not standard English; “wanted him to pick her up” is required. The finding correctly identifies a grammatical defect.
乗せられるような気がした describes a felt or imagined palm already being placed on her head. “He’ll rest” shifts the sensation into a future action.
幸せに意識を閉じた means she happily closed or lost consciousness. “Peacefully falls asleep” removes the happiness and changes consciousness-loss into sleep.
安らかに and 白い are both absent from “the girl that went to sleep.” The calm, color, and exposed death tableau are materially flattened.
“What could happen to me” can naturally cover consequences beyond the immediate danger, so the English is not demonstrably a duplicate formulation.
The supplied Original branch explicitly identifies the extracted object as the girl's heart. This is branch/edition content, not an unsupported inference.
The Japanese explicitly ends with 正気が消えた, loss of sanity. The supplied English stops at fear and murderous desire and omits that endpoint.
The Japanese has two structures and two actions: piercing the castle wall and bringing down the great-hall wall. “Destroys the wall” collapses both.
家ほどもある specifies rubble as large as a house. “A big piece” materially removes the lethal scale.
The supplied Original witness includes an alternate branch with 気が狂う. The English line is therefore not necessarily an unsupported diagnosis replacing the blood-boiling branch.
Even allowing for the alternate branch, the supplied rendering of 不能なまでにかき回している omits the point that the conflicting impulses churn the brain until it can no longer function.
In context “that is nothing” can mean the fighting will amounts to nothing or is worthless, which is a defensible rendering of 話にならん. It is awkward, not clearly false.
だろう itself supplies modal expectation, so “should come down” is compatible with the Japanese. It does not falsely convert an absolute certainty into uncertainty.
正反対の壁際 places Shinji against the wall opposite the narrator. “The other side of the wall” suggests separation by or beyond a wall and changes the layout.
ライダーの時はそうだった means “in Rider’s case” or “when it came to Rider.” The Japanese does not say Rider was killed.
The Japanese uses singular 剣 in this immediate projection context. “Swords” broadens the object, though the core act of projection remains correct.
偉い can cover highest status, authority, or power. Given the immediate situation, “who’s the most powerful here” is a permissible contextual rendering, not a proven combat-only claim.
このままじゃ確実に死ぬ means he will certainly die if the present situation continues. “You’ll die now” removes both the condition and the explicit certainty.

The mature branch adds vulgar language and an assault justification absent from the supplied familial-normality line.
唆す covers enticing, tempting, or seducing in context; seducing is a defensible contextual choice, not demonstrably an error.
The mature branch adds mutual instrumental or sexual use of Sakura, whereas the supplied Japanese accuses Shirou only of trying to gain leverage over Shinji.
The Japanese fragment is split across page boundaries, and the adjacent mirror text explicitly contains Calmly says that. Omission of 平然と is therefore not established.
I seriously is an incomplete mature-branch thought with no corresponding content in the supplied Japanese fragment.
The mature branch inserts an explicit sexual taunt; the supplied Japanese instead accuses Shirou of hiding behind his sister.
The English weakens the specific furtive-hiding and cowardice accusation into a generic bad act.
Want to kill Shinji is an explicit mature-branch thought not supported by the supplied continuation.

The supplied Japanese is syntactically continued from 慎二は、平然と、 and the adjacent mirror preserves Shinji as the actor through the branch-separated fragments. The alleged reassignment is not established.

The English does shift inability to become calm toward inability to stop acting, but the surrounding clenched-fist context makes that a plausible paraphrase; the finding should be narrowed to this nuance.
我慢できない is inability to tolerate the situation, while the English makes the object self-restraint and adds that trying to restrain himself is wrong.
Tighter is a minor contextual intensification of clenching, not a demonstrable material error in 拳を握り締める.
A mocking smile and waiting for an attack are reasonable contextual renderings of twisting his mouth mockingly and bracing himself.
The English simplifies thoughts heated white-hot by anger to anger itself, but the core emotional state remains; the claim should be limited to loss of the mental-image nuance.
ここで手を上げてどうする is naturally rendered by the rhetorical What good will it do in context, where the contemplated violence is already clear.

The English preserves the people and action but omits the ruby-marked relational emphasis of Shinji as Sakura's older brother. That is a narrower nuance omission, not necessarily the main governing reason for restraint.
The source explicitly characterizes Sakura's intervention as a crying or screaming voice; the English reduces it to a neutral voice.
Get myself together is idiomatic English for regaining composure or returning to oneself, and with her voice is understandable despite being less polished.
English trembling can describe slight trembling without asserting a large movement; omission of 小さく is not by itself a material mistranslation.
The mature branch adds a request to repeat Sakura's words, replacing the supplied staged choice between staying and returning home.
Listening to an opinion is a defensible natural rendering of respecting it in this manipulative context; the difference is not a demonstrable factual reversal.
Anything you say broadens the supplied promise to obey what Shinji says, and it occurs in the mature branch absent from this Japanese witness.
The mature branch again changes obeying Shinji into the unlimited anything I say.
The mirror retains the silent pause as an ellipsis and then explicitly states that Sakura nods.
Determined attributes independent resolve to Sakura, whereas そこまで言われちゃ refers to the extent of what she has said in a coercive exchange.
I won't take you home is a normal rendering of refraining from taking Sakura back; the preceding forced retrieval context remains available and need not be repeated.
The mature branch changes Shinji's personal boast that he is magnanimous into a general rule about big brothers respecting wishes.
The English retains just a joke but omits Shinji's specific claim that it was a joke tailored to the atmosphere.
The English loses the specific judgment of being 陰湿, but generic bad opinion still preserves the social consequence; the finding should not imply total loss of the accusation.
The mature branch replaces permission to return whenever Sakura wishes with a warning to remember her coerced promise.
The English omits the cutting-board and onomatopoeic detail, but unbroken sound of chopping still conveys the isolated continuing noise; the claim should be narrowed.
The Japanese makes the kitchen itself extremely awkward, while the English assigns that atmosphere causally to the chopping sound. This changes the stated relation.
Ohyeah. is visibly malformed and fails to represent the hesitant Ah—yeah utterance.
The English omits that Sakura continues helping with the meal, a concrete action in the Japanese.
Pushing herself is a natural rendering of a face showing that she is forcing herself; the English does not assert an unrelated condition.
気を遣わせないように can naturally mean sparing Shirou worry or concern, so the English is within the phrase's contextual range.
Got hurt changes emotional and physical distress expressed by まいっている into a completed physical injury, relying on the unsupported assault branch.
The English drops the explicit qualification that Sakura's smile may be only a brave front.
The Japanese unfinished thought is about returning Sakura's smile; the English preserves incompletion but loses the reciprocal object and adds an awkward self-correction.
落ちる音 describes the sound of the bowl falling; breaking assigns a different event before the later description of fragments.
Sinks to a sitting position naturally conveys the loss of support at the knees; omission of the soft-thud sound is a minor stylistic loss, not the alleged material sequence error.
熱っ is an exclamation of heat on realizing her fever, not a cry of pain.
Raise her off the floor is a defensible rendering of 抱き起こす; the following Japanese supplies the carrying-in-arms context but does not require that wording in the first sentence.
しっかりしろ is an urgent plea for Sakura to stay conscious or respond, not merely another greeting.
What's going on is a natural contextual rendering of Sakura asking what happened to her, especially after she addresses Senpai in confusion.
The English retains effort but omits both Sakura's hazy consciousness and her straining to remain alert while speaking.
Something omits the qualifier that Sakura is trying to form coherent or proper words, but the basic attempt to speak remains.
Still sick is a normal English equivalent of a cold not yet having cleared; the specific diagnosis is not materially lost.
I'm fine is a natural reassurance for saying that this much is manageable; it need not be read as an absolute medical claim.
I overworked her can naturally express Shirou's self-blame for making or allowing her to push herself all day; the agency accusation is overstated.
The Japanese's rough, active command to put her straight into bed and make her sleep is softened into taking her to bed and merely resting.
The mirror conveys giving up, lowered head, and obedience. The contrastive but is ordinary English coordination, not a false opposition of the Japanese facts.
The Japanese cautiously assesses that the fever has not risen much; the English broadens this into saying the overall condition is not very bad.
客間 is the guest room, not Sakura's room; the possessive household status is added by the English.
The Japanese says it is time to begin preparing for patrol, while the English says patrol itself is beginning and skips the preparation stage.
The Japanese offers a tentative possibility that Taiga had an errand; must be busy tonight is more confident and broader than that hedge.
新都 is read Shinto and functions here as a location name; capitalized Shinto does not establish that the religion was intended or that the place was mistranslated.
The explicit urgency of finding the Master even one day sooner is omitted from the English.
The English omits the explicit not-yet-seen qualifier, but the omission is a narrower informational loss rather than proof that encounter history is materially recast.
一昨日 means the day before yesterday, not yesterday; the English changes the stated temporal reference.
Pretending to be normal citizens is a natural contextual explication of pretending indifference while waiting to sense the enemy; no tactical reversal is shown.
In a patrol context, no notable response or useful lead is naturally summarized as not finding anything; this is acceptable paraphrase.
Japanese does not require an English plural here; the change can be treated as a mass or general change, and subtle is reasonably implicit in context.
No conspicuous magical energy is a defensible contextual rendering of no conspicuous residue of magical energy; the alleged residue-versus-energy distinction is not material here.
Must be no Masters remains an inferential modal and the ellipsis preserves uncertainty; it is not demonstrably a categorical certainty replacing ようなのだが.
Desolate is a natural atmospheric rendering of the station area having very few people; the English does not assert a different factual crowd condition.
引き上げましょう means withdraw/leave, and “go home for tonight” preserves both the destination and the temporal retirement; omitting 大人しく is not a material error.
ターミナル can naturally be rendered as a station in this transport context; the accusation treats a defensible English hypernym/narrowing as factual error.
The translation omits the modifiers 乾いた and だけ, but “empty station” and echoing footsteps still convey the isolated soundscape; the finding overstates the loss of isolation.

The conditional scenario remains a feared possibility: “I fear that Servants have more freedom” naturally generalizes the risk, while “without anyone noticing” and the victims’ lack of resistance are substantially retained by context.
動きにくい can mean difficulty acting or operating, not merely physical movement. “Won’t be able to do anything so easily” is an idiomatic rendering that retains the limitation and hedging.
The English expands the checked area from around the house to the whole town, changing a concrete geographic scope.
念の為 explicitly gives the precautionary reason for stopping at the Matou residence, and that reason is omitted.
消えてから states disappearance, whereas “eliminated” conventionally asserts defeat or destruction. That is a material change in Caster’s status.
様子を見ている supports “keeping watch” or monitoring the situation, and “I believe” preserves Saber’s tentative inference; it does not require the narrower governing paraphrase.
“Caster’s energy” is understandable as magical energy in this explicitly magical context. The accusation demands an adjective that English context naturally supplies.
The source says the magical network was spread throughout the town, but the translation inserts Shinto, relocating it to a different city.

ほとんど消えている indicates near-complete disappearance, while “fading away” emphasizes an ongoing process; however, fading can still imply substantial disappearance, so the accusation should be narrowed to lost completion/degree.
Calling the town’s victims “innocent people” is a normal contextual explicitation of civilians who may become victims, not a material contradiction.

The English relative clause makes the temporal status somewhat future-oriented, but plural Masters is a normal generic rendering of the Japanese generic singular. The surviving issue is temporal/aspectual nuance, not the whole claim.
“As though we’re trapped inside a still image” is an ordinary metaphorical rendering of the uncanny stillness; it need not assert literal entrapment.

“There is nothing wrong with this area” is an idiomatic contextual rendering of no detected abnormality, especially alongside the earlier “I do not see anything abnormal”; the finding treats ordinary English smoothing as absolutization.

The Japanese expresses readiness to rush to Sakura at any time; “if she needs help” is an understandable pragmatic condition for rushing to help, but it is an added condition and should be identified narrowly rather than as a wholesale weakening.
体調が優れない can naturally be rendered as being sick or unwell, and the surrounding scene explicitly establishes Sakura’s fever and Shirou’s exhaustion.

The source states that Shirou’s magical energy is still not full; the translation turns that present deficiency into an inferred benefit of extra rest. The added prediction is real, but the underlying deficiency remains.
The explicit instruction to rest already appears immediately before this line: “so please rest for tonight.” The translation omits the comparison to Sakura, but not the rest instruction itself.
“Reaches out for her tea” preserves the reach and naturally implies the teacup; sitting in the living room is staging detail, not a material mistranslation.
The source deliberately combines a sulky quality with expectation. The translation retains expectation but drops 拗ねたような, materially flattening the comic attitude.
苦笑しながら explicitly describes Shirou’s wry/amused smile while recognizing the request; the translation removes that reaction.
鞭 is a whip, not a rigid stick. The English changes the physical image of the flame passing through Shirou’s spine.
大きく is omitted, while “with relief” is a plausible contextual interpretation of the exhalation after the pain. The surviving claim is a loss of scale/intensity, not wholly invented emotion.

ここのところ疎かにしていた means recently neglected; “skipped ... for the past few days” adds both total omission and a specific duration. The translation remains broadly plausible but the accusation should be narrowed to degree/time.
形成 describes forming/establishing the magical circuit, whereas “activating my Magic Circuit” describes operating an already fixed circuit. This is a technical action change.
The Japanese says Shirou can only prepare a weapon in advance through Reinforcement. “The only weapon I can use” changes the restriction into a claim about a singular weapon.
活路 is an avenue of survival or escape in this tactical context; “be able to do something” removes the explicit prospect of finding a way to survive.
効率のいい means efficient/effective, not necessarily fast. “Quickly” narrows one possible aspect of efficiency, but the core idea of a better method remains.
ゆったりとした足音 can naturally be explicated as a person walking slowly or unhurriedly; the source’s sound-based description does not prohibit this English formulation.
ほのかに marks a slight or faint improvement in complexion, while “much better” substantially increases the degree and broadens complexion into overall condition.
正体不明のダメージ is the comic image of an unidentified damage/impact. “Takes me completely by surprise” replaces that physicalized image with ordinary surprise.
The extracted “OhYeah” is malformed English and does not correctly represent the flustered Japanese interjection ああ before 起きてる.
The repetition in 良かった良かった is omitted, but “That’s good” still conveys the basic relief. The valid claim is tonal reduction, not disappearance of the sentiment.
少しは means at least somewhat, which is omitted; “this place” is a reasonable contextual object for これ, so the finding should focus on degree rather than treating the object as wholly unsupported.
ちゃんと直ったんですね praises the completed, proper repair. “This was fixable” changes that completed achievement into a general possibility.
直し始めの頃 ... サジ投げてた says he began repairing it and nearly gave up because it was a wreck. “Almost didn’t bother trying since it was so old” changes both the timing and the reason.
非難めいた is reproachful-sounding rather than unqualified criticism. “Criticizing” is broadly defensible, but the tentative tonal qualification is lost.
The English preserves anger toward both Sakura and himself, but adds equality through “just as” and omits 恐い顔, the visible frightening expression. Only those narrower changes survive.
反省した naturally includes remorse or being sorry, and ほんとに悪いコトをした captures the thought that she did something truly wrong. The English is a defensible paraphrase.
穏やか can naturally be rendered as composed or calm. “Perfectly” is an arguable degree choice, but the accusation does not establish a material shift rather than ordinary lexical variation.
気を張っている can idiomatically mean putting on a strong or brave face, and the contrast with usual Sakura is retained. “Merely” does not require a false claim that she is pretending.
The translation omits 少し and the connective trigger それで, but “I remember when I was a child” remains a natural contextual rendering of the recollection.
The Japanese specifically concerns withholding her true feelings; “if I didn’t say anything” broadens that into total silence, losing the emotional object of the suppression.
Japanese leaves the object implicit in 心配かけたくなくて, and “anyone” is a normal English rendering of that implicit others. The following reference to her father and brother preserves the family context.
あんまり聞いたことない is naturally expressed as not hearing much about something; English present tense does not establish a materially different ongoing habit.
照れ隠しに states the purpose of scratching his cheek: hiding embarrassment. “So I scratch my cheek” changes concealment into a mere causal reaction.
男としてどうかと思った expresses self-conscious doubt about what his unchanged behavior says as a man; “failure as a man” intensifies it into a categorical judgment, but the underlying self-doubt remains.
パトロールの真似事 means an imitation or make-believe patrol. “I thought I was patrolling” turns pretend activity into a mistaken belief that it was real patrolling.
The English retains same-age children and older opponents but drops わずかに, the point that the opponents were only slightly older. This is a real degree omission, not the wholesale loss alleged.
いたよーないなかったよーな explicitly preserves playful uncertainty about whether such a devilishly clever peer existed. The English states that the person was present.
連れ出してくれる can be naturally rendered as “drag her outside” in the figurative sense of coaxing or making a shy person go out; the accusation treats ordinary idiom as coercive force.
特訓 can suggest intensive or special training, which “trained” does not explicitly mark, but daily training remains an acceptable rendering of the imagined activity.
元気だせー、って supplies Shirou’s imagined encouragement while running with Sakura. The English keeps the activities but omits that motive and quoted encouragement.
The source’s 子分 is adequately rendered as “sidekick” in this playful hierarchy; no separate finding here establishes a material error beyond lexical preference.
The preceding question already says “adopted into the Emiya family,” and “I’m adopted” confirms that answer. Omitting the repeated name Kiritsugu is not a material loss in this immediate alignment.
イヤなコト naturally covers things one did not like or found unpleasant. “Things you didn’t like” is somewhat less forceful but remains a defensible English alternative in Sakura’s tentative question.
入れ知恵 means giving someone an idea or putting an interpretation in their head; “give you the wrong idea” is supported by the following clarification and remains tentative through “might’ve.”
The translation retains the initial period with “when I first came here” but omits the explicit duration of one year. The valid finding is loss of duration, not total loss of the appearance period.
耐え続けた makes enduring the healing period central. “Spent healing my wounds” removes the hardship and passive endurance that qualify the first year.
The source says he kept pursuing Kiritsugu in order to learn magecraft. The translation replaces that pursuit and purpose with studying magic in order to resemble him.
意味 is the meaning/significance of being the sole survivor, not the causal reason why survival occurred. “Reason why I survived” changes the existential question.
“That night” is a natural contextual reference to the preceding fire, and Japanese narration commonly leaves that event implicit. The supplied witnesses do not establish a material falsehood.
正義の味方 can be naturally adapted as “superhero” in this child-oriented conversational context. It is a cultural/lexical choice, not demonstrably a false category here.
気持ちのまま断言した adds sincere, decisive manner to the answer; the English preserves the answer but omits that narrative characterization. The omission is narrower than a changed proposition.
まっすぐで、かっこいい praises directness and admirable character. “Sure of yourself” shifts the praise to confidence, which is a different trait.
The translation retains embarrassment but omits the usual visible response of averting his eyes. That is a genuine behavioral omission, though not a complete loss of the sentence’s meaning.
胸に届いた can idiomatically be rendered as words “hitting” someone deeply; “hit me so much” need not imply literal force or violence. The accusation polices a normal metaphor.

The English comparative can naturally mean he would be angrier with Sakura than with anyone else, so the alleged reversal is not established. It does, however, omit the stronger degree marker 何倍も and remains somewhat ambiguous.
先輩になら、いいです is oblique acceptance—if it is Senpai, that is acceptable. “I’d want you to do that” explicitly expresses desire for the scolding, changing her guarded formulation.
The English omits the bodily cue 首をかしげる, but “makes me think that something like this happened before” accurately conveys the incomplete recognition that prompts it.
The English’s memory failure is a defensible explication of not remembering what the smile was, but it omits the small puzzled head tilt. The finding should be limited to that physical omission.
もぐりこみ means slipping/getting under the bedding. “Lie on my futon” changes the physical position.
ひっかかっていたものが取れた is a metaphor for a mental snag coming loose; “a sudden flash of insight” is a natural English paraphrase of the resulting realization, not necessarily an invented event.
“Obstinacy you would never expect from her” preserves the contrast with the Sakura previously known, even if it does not spell out the temporal frame. The accusation overstates the weakening.
The extracted “I gave upwell” is grammatically malformed. The correction structure in the Japanese requires a coherent “I gave up—or rather...” formulation.

English attachment makes “which Kiritsugu used to use” modify the shed, not the house/key, creating a materially misleading relation. Japanese has Kiritsugu modifying the house whose key Shirou stored in the shed.
The immediately preceding context identifies the object as an old house key, so “such a gift” does not erase the practical meaning of 合鍵. It is a natural anaphoric compression.
うちを使ってくれ invites Sakura to use the Emiya home freely. “Use this” narrows the invitation to the key as an object, changing the household-access proposition.
「柔らかく」は穏やか・温かい微笑みも許す。warm smile is a defensible natural rendering, not a factual insertion.
満ち足りた can naturally be rendered as satisfied/contented. The accusation treats an acceptable lexical choice as an error.
The English conveys sleepiness but weakens 虚脱感, the accompanying sense of depletion or lassitude. The claim should be limited to loss of that nuance, not a total mistranslation.
Sleeping is the practical means of taking the rest needed for recovery, and the surrounding text supports this natural paraphrase. No material contradiction is established.
“Instead of pushing myself” captures avoiding overexertion but does not explicitly preserve carrying fatigue forward. A narrower omission claim survives.
The fall onto the futon is retained. Omitting the minor sound effect ばふ is tonal compression, not a demonstrable material error.
“Feeling better” broadens the specific fever concern, but it remains a plausible contextual paraphrase. The surviving claim is loss of medical specificity, not false content.
“Tomorrow” preserves the day but drops the immediacy of すぐに. This is a limited temporal omission, not total loss of the intended thanks.
“I drop my eyelids” can describe eyelids falling or closing and does not necessarily assert deliberate action. The Japanese does not establish the alleged agency error.
The English preserves the sunlight/sleeping comparison as a gentle atmosphere metaphor. Recasting the Japanese metaphor as “sunny-day” gentleness is defensible natural paraphrase.
亡き後 states that Caster is dead or deceased; “has disappeared” removes that explicit status and materially changes the fact.
The English is awkward and can suggest purpose, but “to leave the temple empty” can also express the result of departure. A narrower awkward-result relation claim survives.
関係者 includes affiliated personnel generally, not merely monks. “Nor monks” materially narrows who is barred from entry.
“A real stinker” is a natural rough English intensifier for the extreme-stench idiom. Loss of the literal nose-bending imagery is not itself a factual error.
“The place that should be desolate” can convey an uninhabited precinct in context. The alleged loss is stylistic and the precinct is still clearly the setting.
“Sturdily-built” preserves 屈強な肉体, but drops 無駄のない and turns the described body into “the man.” The narrower omission claim is supportable.
The source explicitly gives the comic quantitative escalation of fifty percent and calls the field uglier; “too crude” omits both the figure and the core judgment.
上品だった predicates Caster herself, while “her work was much more polished” changes the object of comparison to her workmanship. That is a material referent shift.
無造作に adds a casual, unconcerned manner that “looks around” omits. The claim should be narrowed to loss of movemental attitude, not a wholly different action.
“His objectives are to gain information and to keep watch” accurately conveys 諜報・監視 as his principal functions in context. The grammatical reframing is harmless.
The English strengthens 仕方がない into “cannot disobey,” but still preserves his unwilling obedience to the Master. The surviving claim is overstatement of compulsion.
“Accomplish the mission” broadly conveys producing the ordered result but loses the emphasis on the result being as requested. This is a narrowing, not a wholly false rendering.
“What a racket” naturally expresses repeated irritating noise and rough annoyance. Literal repetition of キイキイ is not required for accuracy.
“Master of wind” is idiomatic English for someone understood as a wind-user. 読んでたんだ is preserved as “I thought.”
“Used water instead” interprets 水気の女 as an elemental technique, while the Japanese is a figurative characterization of a water-associated woman. A narrower figurative-to-technical shift is genuine.
The English makes spiders and leeches literal inhabitants, while 輩 marks them as insulting characterizations of lurking sorts. The animal imagery remains, but the target is shifted.
The displayed English is grammatically broken and fails to express the Japanese hypothetical repetition. This is a demonstrable output error, not a stylistic preference.
言い聞かせるように can mean speaking to make someone understand or persuade them. “As if to persuade” is within the normal lexical range; baiting is not forced by the Japanese.
面ァしてやがる is an idiomatic “looks as if” insult. “Looks like he was raised by beasts” is a permissible English realization of that implied background.
砂虫 literally supports “sandworm” as an ordinary English compound. The fantasy-creature connotation is not an unsupported factual addition here.

“From the darkness” preserves the source, but “rays of light” and omission of 凶器 weaken the weapons-launched-from-lightless-darkness image. The claim should focus on that loss, not call the whole line wrong.
A sweep by Lancer’s lance is a normal English way to render a lance-wielded sweep by Lancer. The Japanese does not require the agent to remain only implicit.
The English retains throwing but drops that the dagger was designed primarily for aimed shots. That is a genuine functional omission, though the weapon type remains correct.
“Eyes and throat” preserves the plural eye target and general anatomy, but omits 寸分の狂いもなく and broadens 喉笛 to throat. The surviving issue is loss of exact targeting.
The English retains darkness before Lancer but drops the hall and faintly visible reveal. This is a real descriptive omission, not complete loss of the scene position.
口上 refers to an opening verbal declaration or ritual exchange, not an external signal. “Without a signal” materially changes what is absent.
The English captures strange vocalization but turns のか into a categorical “lacking human words” and adds “inhuman.” The genuine claim is loss of tentativeness and added force.
The Japanese leaves the axis of equivalence broad, whereas “precision” selects one interpretation. Context supports high accuracy, but the accusation should be limited to unjustified narrowing.
飛び交いながら describes flying or darting through the darkness; “as he runs” supplies unsupported running and changes the movement imagery.
針の穴さえ通す is explicit hyperbole for extraordinary precision and is central to the following puzzle. “The daggers” omits a material tactical premise.

The English preserves firing between spear swings and accuracy, but does not explicitly retain 急所, the vital target. The claim should not add a separate blind-spot meaning beyond the supplied Japanese.
The English preserves the shift to killing intent but omits that the earlier hostility merely watched the skull. The surviving error is loss of the prior restraint, not total loss of transition.
踏み込む can describe a forceful forward charge in this combat context. “Counter to Lancer’s charge” is an acceptable dynamic paraphrase.
The English conveys a slight spear movement, but “swing” is broader than merely moving the spearhead a tiny amount. The surviving claim is overstatement of motion size.
“Take his life” conveys lethal intent but removes the concrete neck-thrust image. The claim should be narrowed to loss of anatomical staging.
The English retains the opening between strikes but omits that the dagger is thrown at Lancer’s throat. The danger is weakened, though the counter-timing remains.
“In one motion” conveys simultaneity but omits 一呼吸 and the explicit “completely.” This is a limited compression of timing and rhythm.
“Useless against me” is stronger than 上手くない, which says projectiles are a poor match or do not work well. The narrower claim is overstatement of absoluteness.
素顔を隠す describes the enemy’s true face as concealed by the mask; “who is now hiding his face” suggests a newly deliberate action. The claim should be limited to that agency/temporal shift.
腕 is an arm, not a hand, and 封じられた indicates bound or sealed rather than merely covered. Both anatomical extent and restraint are materially weakened.
The English preserves darkness but omits the separate white skull-mask concealment and the “not yet clearly visible” uncertainty. A layered-concealment omission survives.
ではなかったか is a tentative observational question, not a categorical assertion. “His face is flat and utterly featureless” removes that uncertainty and overstates the description.
The Japanese explicitly keeps undiminished killing intent directed at Lancer. “His hostility is still emitting” is malformed and loses both agency and lethal direction.
The surrounding English preserves visibility but not the specific distance condition その距離から. The accusation should target broadened range, not claim that all context was lost.
“Sinks down” preserves the action but omits the spider comparison that links the opponent’s movement style to the surrounding animal imagery. This is a local descriptive omission.
The English preserves an upward leap and immediacy but drops the scale and open-air/void imagery of 大きく虚空に. The claim should be narrower.
“Movements are those of a spider, snake, or scorpion” is a normal English rendering of the figurative footwork comparison. Generic “movements” does not create a factual contradiction.
The English turns 瞬発力, explosive acceleration, into “charge” and adds an explicit fastest claim. The core superiority is retained, so this is an over-specific paraphrase issue.
分の刻 can support “a minute” in English, and the broader prolonged-pursuit idea remains. The supplied Japanese does not require plural minutes.
“It is a disgrace” is an idiomatic realization of あってはならない事, an unacceptable or impossible outcome. The emotional coloring is not demonstrably false in context.
The displayed English contains the abandoned “destroyed” fragment before “aimed for,” producing an objectively malformed sentence and corrupting たしかに喉を狙った.
水蜘蛛 is specifically a water strider/assassin image, while “spider” is broader and loses the water-strider comparison. The issue is lexical specificity, not total scene failure.

In context, “his speed is far greater” naturally refers to Lancer and preserves the comparison with the previously mentioned spider-like enemy. The Japanese does not require the English to repeat every noun.
付け根 means the roots or attachment points of the limbs, not joints. The English changes the intended anatomical target in a combat-relevant way.
The Japanese presents limb roots and major arteries in apposition; the English asserts that joints are where the arteries lie, adding a broader anatomical relation not stated by the source.

“Their lifeforce is magical energy” conveys the primary-power contrast in context; the omitted explicit word 血液 is recoverable from the immediately following artery discussion and is not a material error.
The English prints two overlapping alternatives for one Japanese sentence, creating conspicuous duplicated and contradictory prose. This is a demonstrable malformed output.
One English branch says “loss of a limb,” but the immediately duplicated branch correctly says “disabling their limbs.” The accusation cannot stand as an unqualified claim about the complete output.

“Stopping a Servant’s limb” is an acceptable contextual paraphrase of immobilizing movement, even if the duplicated alternative elsewhere is faulty. The specific surviving sentence is not clearly mistranslated.
“Hashish, huh?” is unsupported by the supplied Japanese and the line is visibly abandoned before a second translation restarts the sentence. This is a clear extraction/branch corruption.
痛覚を殺す手 is a method or condition suppressing pain; “pain-killer” narrows it toward a medicine, but can be a contextual paraphrase. The claim should be limited to that narrowing.
The Japanese marks the interval until the next blow begins, while “will strike in two more seconds” can imply impact. The temporal aspect is weakened but not wholly reversed.
The source says he is about to make one slash at the fleeing enemy’s left thigh; “thrusts at his left leg” changes action, target specificity, and the interrupted completion.
水面が跳ねる can naturally become water splashing or leaping upward. “Explodes upward” is vivid but still within English depiction of the sudden splash.

The source deliberately presents a singular unidentified thin black thing, while “tendrils” supplies a plural concrete form. The surrounding pages support tentacle-like imagery, so the claim should be narrowed to premature specification.
