ない means no Magecraft value, whereas “low magical value” introduces a nonzero degree and changes the statement’s polarity.
“Such a small garden” preserves the relevant size judgment; omitting the cat’s-forehead idiom is a stylistic/image loss, not necessarily a material mistranslation.
連中 refers distantly to those people, while “you people” directly generalizes the contempt to Shirou or the addressee’s group.
The Japanese gives a class-based prescription that such places should be left to servants; “You have servants” asserts that Shirou actually possesses them.
“Downcast” captures 元気のない, but the English omits that Shirou calls out toward her back, changing the staging from action to observation.
長年 explicitly establishes years of sustained resentment; “has a grudge against” omits that duration and persistence.
The Japanese describes revenge as the only way she could confront him; “only wanted to kill him” changes a mode of confrontation into a simple desire.
“Forever” adds permanence not stated explicitly, but the translation still preserves that the opportunity had been lost; the accusation should be limited to the added intensifier.
The source says the two must part before night or fighting will result; “unless I leave this place” assigns the condition specifically to Illya leaving the house.
The source contrasts a familiar town and familiar roads with walking as if for the first time; “through the streets” removes that contrast.
“Foremost” adds an explicit top ranking, while the Japanese only asks how important Illya is among many matters; the narrower ranking addition is genuine.
“Convince her to forfeit” is idiomatic English for persuading her to withdraw, with the war object recoverable from context; the claim of grammatical incompleteness is preference policing.
“Deep tenacities” is an unnatural rendering of deep, obsessive fixation and weakens the characterization of the two families’ 執念.
解放す is to free or release Illya from her vengeful heart; “quench her desire” instead suggests suppressing or satisfying that desire.
The English’s Servant-under-a-Command-Spell comparison is a defensible paraphrase of answering Illya’s wish through the Command Spell conceit; “anything” is supported by the immediate setup.
The Japanese supports a boundary before マスター, but the supplied caveat says joined English words may be extraction artifacts rather than translation errors.
In this setting, 刻印 can defensibly be rendered as “Crest,” especially in a Master/Command Spell context; the accusation assumes an impermissibly narrow gloss.
The English preserves direct eye contact but omits the physical act of bending down, which is a real staging loss though not a change to the proposition being sworn.
息を呑む is conventionally rendered as gasping or catching one’s breath; unlike 呼吸を止めて, “gasps” is not a reversal here.
心からの笑顔 describes sincerity or heartfelt feeling, whereas “a big smile” changes the quality into physical size.
連れていって explicitly contains the concrete request to be taken somewhere; “I want……” removes that clue.
幾らでも付き合ってやれる expresses willingness to accompany her as much or as often as needed; “easily able to do” changes quantity and relational willingness into ease.
“I’ve always wanted” retains duration, but 憧れてた carries stronger yearning or idealization than simply wanting to do an activity; the accusation should be narrowed to tonal weakening.
一番 marks the thing she most wants Shirou to do, while “what I want from you right now” replaces that superlative priority with a temporary time reference.
The source foregrounds all the courage Illya mustered in making the request; the English omits that emotional basis for Shirou’s response.
一番の願い identifies this as Illya’s greatest wish, not merely one wish; the superlative is removed.
The English retains the knightly duty and obligation, but omits 精一杯’s “with all his effort” force; this is a degree loss, not disappearance of the commitment.
The Japanese establishes a boundary before 俺, but the supplied caveat leaves open whether the joined English words are an extraction artifact.
望めば幾らでも叶う says ordinary fulfillment was available whenever and as often as she wished; “an everyday event” omits that painful availability.
The source says Illya desired ordinary everyday life itself, not merely one everyday event; the English reduces the thematic object of her wish.
The Japanese explicitly suspends both enemy and ally categories; “not like Masters” does not preserve that temporary removal of combatant roles.
“Familiar scenery” preserves part of the image, but omits the familiar shops and the stronger 見飽きた sense of scenery seen to weariness.
The accusation relies on baseJa, but the governing Original witness itself contains 「―――ふん、もったいつけやがって」; this is an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.
床に届くほど explicitly says the hair is long enough to reach the floor; “Long hair” omits that concrete extent.
密室の底 identifies the bottom of an enclosed room; “the bottom of hell” introduces an unsupported infernal metaphor and changes the location.
誠実なまでに supplies the narrator’s pointed irony that the entirely false words approach sincerity; “covered with lies” omits that paradox.
The fused “sadand” is a presentation/extraction artifact around a stripped line marker, not evidence of a Japanese-to-English mistranslation.
“Finally” preserves delayed realization, but the unwanted/regretful force of 気付いてしまった is weakened. The accusation should target that narrower tonal omission.
“The end comes” omits the explicit inevitability or matter-of-course quality conveyed by 当然のように.
The English never states that Illya’s own requested drink remains stored in her coat pocket, losing the concrete symbolic detail.
“Lift” can idiomatically mean ending or dismissing a spell, so the broad accusation is overstated; at most it adds a removal mechanism not explicit in おしまいにする.
“Resolutely” is a plausible tonal paraphrase, but it does not directly preserve the absence of lingering attachment. The narrower loss of 未練 should survive.
新都 is a proper place name and “Shinto” is a defensible romanization in this setting; the Japanese does not establish that this rendering is an unrelated word.
“Far better than…” is a natural interrupted comparative for ここよりもっと and preserves Shirou’s offer of greater scope or appeal elsewhere; the alleged intrinsic-value shift is overstated.
“Set in stone” adds deterministic immutability. The Japanese says she understood the situation clearly before meeting, not that the relationship was immutable.
“Her wishes” can naturally refer to the desired ordinary life in context, so the accusation of discarding all wishes is too broad; however, the specific framing as 幻想 is weakened.
“A place without destination or backtrack” is conspicuously unidiomatic and fails to express the natural terminal image of nowhere to go and no return.
“A distant scenery is in front of me” is grammatically defective English; the Japanese supports a distant scene or landscape lying before him.
The English contrast omits the decisive predicate that Illya’s figure appears impossible, materially truncating the image.
The translation omits both the powder-snow detail and its weak, frail quality before retaining only the prediction that it will stop.
“Completely surrounded in white snow” loses だけ and あんなにも: the source emphasizes that only the area around Illya is extraordinarily white.
The English reverses the relation: the Japanese presents ordinary snow as what delights her most, not Shirou’s inability to understand her enjoyment.
“I was praised that…” is ungrammatical English and does not clearly express praise for her hair’s being white and girlish.
The Japanese explicitly says he knows without a reason; “By watching her” invents a visual basis for the inference.
“Already know” is weaker than the emphatic long-ago realization in とっくに気がついている, especially in this retrospective context.
“Pursued him” can mean continued to follow him and is a natural rendering of その背中を追い続けた; the alleged aggressive sense is not compelled.
“Leaves the park” turns 消えていった’s disappearance-from-view imagery into ordinary departure, weakening the supernatural/vanishing transition immediately before the snow fades.
The source identifies the departing figure as a symbol of winter; the English replaces that image with an unsupported causal theory about her presence sustaining snowfall.
“I’ll have her forgive me” can naturally mean obtaining her lenience, and the Japanese itself expresses that intention with もらおう. The controlling-agency accusation is overread.
“Cover for yourself with simple words” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of trying to end the matter with an inadequate apology; the Japanese criticism of easy words remains.
The fused “EhIllya” is a stripped-boundary presentation artifact; the supplied Japanese has a separate interjection and name.
The source says Illya runs off before Shirou has time to stop her. “Without waiting for a response” changes the relevant action to waiting for a reply.
The English omits the emphatic contrast 追いつくどころか and the point that he loses sight even of her back.
“Make it up to her” can cover apology and recompense, so the accusation of wholly generic amends is too strong; it does, however, omit the explicit promise-breaking and Illya-pleasing components.
“Floor” is a defensible audience-oriented rendering of tatami, but “lying face-up” is omitted. The finding should be narrowed to posture rather than treating both details as lost.
“Was sick” is understandable shorthand for having a cold, but it loses the qualified, cold-like condition in 風邪ぎみ. The categorical-broadening claim should be narrowed.
“Helped around with my house” can mean helping with the household, not service on Shirou’s property. The possessive reading is not compelled.
“Go past the living room” can naturally describe crossing or passing through it; the Japanese does not require a different route.
“Carefully” conveys deliberate care, but the explicit quietness and purpose of avoiding waking her are not stated. The accusation should target that narrower omission.
“Empty eyes” is a defensible visual paraphrase of a gaze suggesting the mind is elsewhere; it need not imply emotional or lifeless emptiness.
色っぽい has a legitimate lexical range including sexy, alluring, or erotic. “Erotic” is a tonal choice, not demonstrable mistranslation here.
The fused “Umher” is a stripped-boundary presentation artifact, not a translation error; the Japanese itself has the relevant continuation after その.
言い訳をする means making an excuse, whereas “try to explain myself” removes the self-justifying quality that motivates Shirou’s unease.
The translation preserves the wrapping action but drops the light, soft manner in ふわりと. This is a narrower tonal omission, not necessarily a major scene alteration.
The English omits the concrete fingers extended toward or around his neck and replaces them with abstract awareness of femininity.
The source’s woman’s body directly before him forcing itself into view is replaced by an added abstract effort to ignore femininity.
The English generalizes the explicit object of Shirou’s gaze, 桜の体, to Sakura as a person.
“Streams down her neck” is a defensible rendering of 髪が首筋から流れる; the alleged change of origin is not material or clearly wrong.
“Breasts are pushing up her shirt” adds a clothing interaction absent from the source’s description of a full, taut chest.
“Mature woman’s body” preserves adulthood but omits the explicit realization that it had grown without Shirou noticing.
The English omits the enclosing location of Sakura’s hands around his neck.
“Our faces near each other” is a normal English rendering of the scene’s reciprocal proximity; Japanese subject omission does not establish a material agency error.
良識 means good sense or moral restraint, not sensory faculties. “Boring senses” is a clear lexical mistranslation.
これからも marks a continuing prospective prohibition, while “shouldn’t have noticed” shifts it into past regret.
The English retains pounding but omits the near-painful quality explicitly conveyed by 痛いとさえ思える.
“Land on top of the table” omits 油断なく, the explicit guarded or alert manner completing the mock-combat gag.
気が動転してた denotes being flustered or thrown into confusion, materially stronger than being merely surprised.
“Her hands are lowered” omits both hands being outstretched, their dropping to the floor, and the soft flop indicated by ぱたん.
The English says Saber is well rested but omits the explicit recovery link to yesterday’s rest.
“Kill myself” is a natural English paraphrase of the exaggerated self-punishment in 腹を切ってた; preserving literal seppuku imagery is not required for accuracy here.
申し訳なくて expresses remorse or feeling unforgivably sorry toward Sakura, not merely private embarrassment or shame.
The page context is the entryway, and “I see Sakura’s shoes” naturally conveys the inference. Omitting an easily recoverable location is not a material error.
“Floor” is a defensible rendering of tatami, but the face-up posture あお向け is omitted. The claim should be narrowed to that posture.
“Having her head on the table” preserves the table contrast but omits the face-down posture in 突っ伏して. The accusation should not treat the whole contrast as lost.
“Was sick” is understandable shorthand for a cold, but it loses the qualified 風邪ぎみ nuance. The claim should be narrowed to that broadening.
“Helped around with my house” can mean helped with the household; the source does not force the accusatory property/service interpretation.
“My room” is a plausible contextual explicitation by the first-person narrator inside his household; the Japanese does not establish a materially false location.
“Carefully drape” conveys care but omits the explicit quietness and purpose of not waking her. That narrower omission is genuine.
“Empty eyes” can naturally depict a mind-elsewhere, drowsy gaze; the supplied Japanese does not require the stronger emotional-emptiness reading.
The comparison and prior perception are retained, and erotic is within the range of 色っぽい. Repeated “gesture” is not a material mistranslation.

The English reasonably identifies the contextual referent as Sakura’s arms, but this removes the source’s initially indirect perception as 白いもの. The claim should target that loss of indirection, not assert an outright factual error.
The source explicitly stages fingers at his neck and the woman’s body before his eyes; the English replaces both concrete elements with abstract femininity.
“No matter how hard I try to ignore it” is a natural explication of 否応なしに, meaning the perception forces itself on him. The accusation treats normal English explicitation as unsupported invention.
The English says the eyes prove she is half-asleep but omits their specific languid, unfocused quality in とろんとした.
The Japanese object is こんなの, the situation or embrace, while “shake her off me” makes Sakura herself the object and adds a more forceful personal action.
“Streams down her neck” is a defensible rendering of the hair flowing from the nape; the alleged continuous-motion distinction is overstated.
The English invents breasts pushing against a shirt, whereas the source only describes a full, taut chest.
The English conveys maturity but omits that Sakura’s body grew without Shirou noticing.
良識 is moral common sense or restraint, not plural senses. This is a clear lexical error.
“Pounding” omits the explicit near-painful intensity of the heartbeat.
The source says he lands without letting his guard down; the English drops that guarded manner.
“A bit surprised” materially weakens 気が動転してた, which describes severe fluster or confusion.
“Slowly” captures reduced speed, but のそのそ also conveys sluggish, awkward physical comedy. The claim should be narrowed to that manner loss.
The English omits both outstretched arms, their audible drop to the floor, and the soft flop in ぱたん.
手合わせ can naturally be rendered as training with someone, especially in this dojo context; “train with you” does not materially deny sparring.
「セイバーに見られなかった事」states that Saber did not see it/them; “us like that” is contextual English explicitation, not demonstrably false.
“Kill myself” conveys self-punishment, but omits the concrete belly-cutting/seppuku image.
申し訳なくて expresses apologetic guilt or remorse; “out of shame” changes the stated motive.
“Put the bandage on” is a natural rendering of wrapping/taping the finger; the action remains clear.
The translation conveys taping but omits the repeated winding rhythm and sound-symbolic presentation.
ところどころ means scattered or localized parts, not the whole body.
The Japanese says bathing is impossible in this condition; “tonight” adds an explicit time limit absent from これじゃ.
じろり can describe a sharp dissatisfied look, so “glares” is within the lexical range.
The English preserves silence but omits the explicit reason: Shirou can only fall silent because he feels apologetic or guilty.
“Empty space” loses the concrete image of looking only at the sky, though it retains absent-mindedness.
気迫 is fighting spirit or force, and locating its absence in attacks is a natural contextual rendering of Saber’s criticism.
心臓がおかしくなりそう can naturally become “my heart jumps” in this attraction-and-anxiety context; the accusation treats one acceptable paraphrase as error.
胃がもたれた means his stomach feels heavy or indigestible from overeating; that supporting symptom is omitted.
咄嗟に means reflexively or without deliberation, but “quickly” adequately conveys the immediate movement in context.
台所に立つ can naturally be rendered as standing up to go to the kitchen to prepare tea; the preparation remains explicit in the dialogue.
寝姿 is the sight or posture of her sleeping, not simply her body; the English narrows the remembered image.
温めで, especially with the supplied lukewarm ruby, can function naturally as “not too hot”; this preserves the practical request.
寝みだれた姿 specifies her earlier disheveled sleeping appearance; “how she looked earlier” drops both concrete modifiers.
柔らかそうだった means her lips looked or seemed soft, retaining an appearance-based hedge that “her soft lips” states as fact.
The Japanese says みっともない, shameful or disgraceful; the mature branch inserts the categorical diagnosis “lust.”
先輩として接してきた can naturally be rendered “acted as her Senpai”; no material role-performance claim is established.
“Always” is not explicit, although the surrounding retrospective context can support an ongoing difference in affection.
The translation invents egg and replaces pork tsukune with generic meatloaf, while losing the grilled-vegetable accompaniment.
戻っていった means Sakura returns to her established usual place; “sits down” omits that household continuity.
食後のお茶が嬉しいのか is tentative and specifically concerns after-dinner tea; “must enjoy tea” generalizes and removes the uncertainty.
シロウの強化 is naturally “strengthening Shirou” in this training context; the accusation assumes a technical confusion not established by this page.
考慮する means they will now consider or devise a survival method; “we will train you to survive” turns planning into already-determined execution.
The source utterance is うわ, an exclamation, while the later reference calls it a sigh; “Whoa” is a defensible rendering of the utterance itself.
そ、そうなのですか can express stunned disbelief; “Are you serious?” is a natural English realization rather than a demonstrable factual reversal.
The English is a fragment and omits the important contrastive posture 正座したまま while rendering labored breathing awkwardly.
なんでしょうか is literally “what is it?” but “what’s wrong?” is a natural response to being shaken and does not necessarily imply blame.
The embarrassed smile is retained, but あはは and the laugh-as-action are omitted.
“Bows” preserves the physical action; omitting the small sound-symbolic manner ぺこり is a minor presentation choice, not a material error.
午後十時 is ten p.m., not eleven.
気付かれない means without Sakura noticing; “not to wake” assumes sleep and changes the concealment condition.
昨夜の遅れ means last night’s delay, not merely yesterday.
The source says new harm spread by exploiting post-defeat complacency; “continued to suffer while my guard was down” loses both newness and the expanding harm.
その手を伸ばす deliberately withholds the renewed action; “collecting energy from people” supplies an unsupported specific activity.
新都 can validly be rendered Shinto as a place name, and 深山町→Miyama City is an acceptable localization; the finding also incorrectly fuses the separate 東 clause with the town name.
The supplied English visibly fuses the east clause with the following inference, producing malformed text.
意識が割れかける describes consciousness nearly splitting or fragmenting; “break my mind” is a materially different and unnatural mental claim.
The English drops 軽い and the bodily location 喉元, changing slight dizziness plus throat discomfort into generic discomfort and dizziness.
The English lacks a grammatical subject/finite structure for the scene description and is visibly malformed.
新手 can mean new opponents or enemies in this hostile encounter; “New enemies?” is contextually defensible.
The appositional phrase is visibly fused as “old manMatou Zouken,” a presentation and grammar defect.

押さえつけて白状させる means pin down and force a confession; “beat a confession out” adds beating/assault not stated.
The supplied English breaks the narrator’s conceit into malformed fragments, making the back itself appear to scold him.
The phrase “Just as how” is ungrammatical English, independent of the underlying comparison.
モノ deliberately keeps the referent object-like and uncertain before the reveal; “someone” prematurely humanizes it.
残っていやがった means it remained or was still there; it does not assert biological life.
外装 is an exterior shell or casing, an important technical distinction from ordinary appearance.
意思である魂 is an appositional description of the soul as the seat of volition, not two independently absent entities.
別のもので補っただけ states that the corpse was supplemented with another substance; “made from Caster’s corpse” omits the mechanism.
程度 disparages Rider as being of Shinji’s paltry caliber; “Shinji’s Rider” omits that calibration.
亡骸 can mean corpse or remains, and “trifling with her corpse” adequately conveys 弄ぶ in this condemnation.
“Trash” is stronger and more contemptuous than merely something no longer used, though the dehumanizing utilitarian sense remains.
The English weakens 外道 with “heretic” and “brute,” but the basic conditional relation between Zouken’s practice and Saber’s fate remains intelligible.
屈服させる means force into submission; “make you my slave” adds a more specific status, especially in the mature branch.
食わせ says to feed Saber’s body to the worms; “eat you alive” adds that she is alive during the consumption.
The English has number and construction problems: うぬら is plural, and 心ない人形と化すがうぬらの為 is becoming mindless dolls for their benefit, not “to turn you” in a malformed infinitive.
魔術 is the setting-specific Magecraft term; general “magic” loses the technical distinction relevant to the scene.
外装 again identifies the manipulated exterior shell, not Caster’s actual body.
The ruby reading on 帰還る is きえ, explicitly supporting disappearance/vanishing; “completely disappears” is therefore defensible in this wordplay.
The source identifies a terrestrial magus as the potential desecrating agent; the English omits that agent entirely.
受け持った means took charge of or handled Caster; “took care of” is a defensible contextual rendering and need not imply completed disposal.
The English conveys the resulting severance but omits the source’s horizontal sweeping action and one-line trajectory.
The mature branch specifies blood and entrails, while the Japanese deliberately leaves the emitted substance unidentified.
這っていた only says the lower-body-less old man crawled; arms and an intention to escape Archer are added.
みだらに modifies the manner of spilling; “something obscene” turns that manner into a property of the unidentified substance.
The supplied English visibly fuses “crushed” and “and,” producing malformed boundary text.
高く響く can describe a high or sharply resounding heartbeat; “higher pitch” is an available English interpretation, though less literal.
The source says the body rejects the command to flee even though it understands before the head; generic refusal to move loses that specific paradox.
The English omits the triggering condition 出会ってしまったからには and the categorical “never,” weakening the scene’s inescapability.
In context, “probably is not even alive” is a natural rendering of a thing that cannot even be a living creature; no material distinction is established.
懐かしい expresses nostalgia or an uncanny feeling of the past, stronger and more temporally charged than ordinary familiarity.
The English conveys withdrawal from the park but omits いち早く, the emphasis that Zouken was the first or quickest to leave.
The source depicts him whipping or driving his dying body onward through fear; “fear drove him” omits the bodily exertion and violence.
“Limbs” is a normal English rendering of 手足 and preserves the absence of arms/legs; itemized wording is not materially required.
“It points at Tohsaka” conveys the shadow’s directional action; omitting an explicit “tip” is acceptable compression here.
In the immediate attack context, “lashes out” is a defensible dynamic rendering of the shadow extending suddenly, not a demonstrable factual error.
弾き飛ばす denotes forcefully knocking or sending Rin flying; “push aside” materially weakens the rescue’s force and displacement.
The English retains water and impact but omits the salient dump-truck comparison and the explicit identification of the impacting flow as 水流.
The translation omits both head-first engulfment and the already-deep-sea state, replacing them with ordinary ongoing sinking.
生命活動 refers to vital bodily activity being progressively cut off root and branch; “cuts off my life” shifts this to life itself and loses the process.

The ruby is deliberately ambiguous: キミガワルイ can evoke “you are bad/at fault” or “creepy/disgusting.” “It’s wrong” may be an interpretive rendering, but the supplied witnesses do not establish one intended resolution.

Japanese sequences Shirou standing on the shadow, Rin thinking he had fallen, and then noticing the shadow gone; the English compresses and reorders these events.
倒れた means fell or collapsed; “fainted” adds a specific loss of consciousness not stated in this observation.
The raw script marks 南の空 and 南西の方角 as a line replacement, not necessarily two sequential directions. “Looks southwest” is consistent with the selected wording.
随分と長く emphasizes a subjectively very long duration, important to the following under-ten-seconds contrast; “for a while” noticeably weakens it.
“Supports me” naturally conveys lending a shoulder to a fallen person; omitting the exact posture is not a material error here.
敵対行為 refers to treating further approach as a hostile act, not declaring Rin herself an enemy; the English changes the object of hostility.
The adjacent dialogue identifies the relevant circumstances as the current truce, so this contextual narrowing is defensible rather than an established mistranslation.
“At peace right now” can naturally describe the bounded non-hostility of 休戦中, especially with the following “until we defeat Caster.”
約束 can be rendered as a promise, and “I promised her” is a natural English explicitation of Shirou’s agreement with Rin; mutuality is not grammatically explicit here.

The valid narrower issue is loss of the specific ague/fever comparison in 瘧; the claim of simply stronger certainty is overstated because “the most it can do” retains a limiting qualification.

The English still identifies Shirou as Archer’s gaze target (“me”); the omitted 他の誰でもない is emphatic rhetoric, not a material loss of who is seen.
相手をさせられる broadly means being made to deal with or confront it; “fight it” is contextually supported for a Servant confronting this threat.
守護者 is a common noun in the supplied Japanese, and lowercase “guardian” is a defensible English rendering; capitalization alone cannot establish an accuracy error.
“It’s not that hopeless” naturally preserves the speaker’s qualification and self-correction in そう悲観したものではないか.
瘧 is a specific ague-like fever, not an unrestricted “disease”; the generalization weakens the hallucinated fever image and its link to the next sentence.
The source specifies fever-bearing mosquitoes; “plagued maggots” changes both the creature and the fever-vector relation.
体内に発生して says the mosquitoes arise or breed inside the body; “filling my whole body” omits that internal-generation image.
“Filling my whole body” adequately conveys dense occupation extending through the body, including the fingertips; the remaining detail is not demonstrably material here.
辛くなる can mean become painful, difficult, or burdensome; “You’ll hurt Senpai” is a natural rendering and need not assert physical injury.
“I could still bear that” is a normal English explicitation of the implied contrast in それだけならよかったのに; it does not materially contradict the source.

Forlorn hope can idiomatically mean a slim or slender hope, and clinging already conveys its precariousness; this is not a factual error.
The English collapses both calculation and compromise into selfishness, removing two distinct parts of Rin’s ethical criticism.
The written subject is 衛宮士郎 while the ruby reads as I; retaining only the first-person reading removes the deliberate identity-layer presentation.
The written word is 過去, read through the ruby as reality. The English preserves reality but deletes the written past, which is central to the identity/history equation.
Blown away preserves the threat’s force, but omits the specific trajectory from the base and rolling all the way outside. The accusation should be limited to that detail loss.
売り言葉に買い言葉 describes hostile provocation answered with provocation; give-and-take suggests neutral reciprocity and loses the escalation.
Kirei says he must tell Shirou specifically because Rin left without listening; somebody removes the stated recipient and motivation.
The Japanese describes literally extracting forty percent of her nerves while alive. The English turns it into a simile and omits 生きたまま.
The written phrase says maintaining her own function, with Servant as the ruby reading. The English keeps only the ruby and changes the technical claim.
The strobe-lamp simile preserves the sudden visual shock and resulting dizziness; changing passive exposure to looking into it is an acceptable natural paraphrase here.
The English conveys severe impact and difficulty standing, but omits the explicit pain and deliberate effort not to stagger. The claim should be narrowed to those omissions.
The Japanese leaves both persuasion and the head movement uncertain; the English asserts understanding and changes a slight head tilt into a confirming nod.
引き止める means stop or hold Sakura back, not merely locate her; the English changes Shirou’s immediate protective aim.
体温を確かめる is checking Sakura’s body temperature. Feel her warmth shifts the concrete check toward generalized or romantic physical warmth.
The Japanese is Shirou’s fragmentary location search; the English adds a generic second-person hypothetical and shifts the thought’s perspective.
町 identifies Miyama as a town/district, while “City” changes its administrative and spatial scale in this Fuyuki context.
The omission of the rain being freezing is genuine, but the claimed sexual reading of “exposing her body” is an interpretive risk, not a demonstrated mistranslation.
The English’s “seen” loses the Japanese auditory framing, though “desperateness” is awkward rather than wholly unintelligible.
“Actions” narrows shame directed at oneself, but “criminal” can reasonably render 罪人; only the self-versus-actions shift is established.
“I shouldn’t [approach] until she raises her head” naturally preserves the prohibition and its condition; dropping emphatic 決して is not material here.
Plural “hands” is a minor English rendering of 手, and Sakura’s role as recipient is clear from context; this does not establish a material shift.
The English omits the clear, forceful delivery in はっきりと言い捨てた and makes hatred specifically self-loathing, although that interpretation is supported by context rather than wholly invented.
The supplied Original witness explicitly contains the virginity and first-time statements; they are not invented insertions in the Original-edition branch.

自虐的 describes self-directed punishment; “masochistic” can be nonsexual, but its common pleasure/sexual association makes the framing misleading without the categorical claim that it necessarily asserts pleasure.

自分が分からなくなる is losing one’s grasp of oneself, whereas “go crazy” materially recasts it as generic madness.

The Japanese says Sakura becomes even sadder; the English changes the internal emotion into an increased intensity of crying.
The English supplies “her pain” and “what I’ve done,” while Japanese leaves それ and 後悔した tied to the surrounding realization, not a specified pain or deed.
取り乱す means lose composure or become distraught again; “go crazy” materially intensifies and pathologizes the statement.
“By force” preserves 強引に, but the concrete hand-pulling image is omitted; the broader coercion claim is too strong as stated.
“Ending it all” wrongly introduces suicidal ambiguity, but the repeated temporal element is grounded in the nearby 毎晩毎晩; the claim should be narrowed to the relationship-ending mistranslation.
The supplied Original witness explicitly includes the knife-at-the-wrist action, so this is not an invented mature-branch detail.
The English omits no longer being sad and incorrectly confines the crying to nighttime; 毎晩毎晩 modifies the recurring thought, not a nighttime limit on crying.
“Cold body” can naturally mean a body chilled through; the supplied Japanese does not require a stronger English adjective to preserve the event.
“Your superhero” preserves Sakura-directed exclusivity, and superhero is a defensible contextual rendering of 正義の味方.
The English turns cold, rigid Sakura into a person characterized by stubbornness and omits 冷たく; the added personality judgment is materially different.

“Her sensation” wrongly makes Sakura the possessor rather than translating the sensation of holding her, while “warmth” is a defensible rendering of 肌の熱さ; the compound claim overstates the heat issue.

The supplied Japanese deliberately writes 他人 while giving it the ruby reading わたし; “given me” preserves the spoken reading but drops the written contrast and its agency joke.
拡縮する describes unusually forceful expansion and contraction, not audible loudness; the physical image is changed.
The Japanese names the restraint as 誓約, while “the bind” omits that oath/vow connection despite retaining a generic restraint.
従者 can directly mean servant or subordinate, and the English uses lowercase “servant”; the supplied text does not establish confusion with the Servant class.
“I can’t even tell her to wait” naturally communicates inability to say the word in context; the physical cause is already evident from the surrounding immobilization.
After Rin passes them, “Tohsaka leaves” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of her figure disappearing from view; no supernatural disappearance is required by 姿が消える.
The Japanese stresses moving at the earliest possible moment; “hoping that it’s not too late” substitutes an added deadline concern for that urgency.

The English makes restraint no longer necessary, while Japanese says the reason Shirou opposed Rin has already been lost, preserving the devastating causal realization.

かっ込んだ means hurriedly shoveling or wolfing down food, and the scene already has him eating; “start eating” loses both force and aspect.

山盛りで explicitly says the returned bowl is heaped full, a concrete quantity and visual part of the failed-retreat gag.

どうでしょうか is contextually compatible with wondering what to do, immediately followed by Rider offering to leave; “What shall I do?” is not demonstrably false.
目に付く can pragmatically mean being conspicuous or bothersome in someone’s field of attention; “annoying him” is a defensible contextual gloss, not clear invented content.

どことなく qualifies the resemblance as vague or somehow perceived; “really similar” removes that qualification.
Given that Shirou is looking at Rider, “if I keep looking at her” is a natural contextual expression of the condition that their eyes meet.

浮気性 can naturally be insultingly rendered as “a cheater,” and “fall for anyone with a pretty face” is an idiomatic expansion of being weak for beautiful women.
不機嫌 can include anger or an angry-looking mood in this jealous exchange; “angry” is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
“As a person, not a woman” is idiomatic English for denying that gender is the basis of his liking; it does not necessarily deny that Rider is a woman.
殺気 is killing intent or a lethal aura, substantially stronger and more specific than ordinary hostility.

信じられる is an explicit judgment of trust in Rider’s protective intention, not merely Shirou sensing her determination.

“I can’t quite figure out how to deal with her” is idiomatic English for finding someone difficult to deal with; it does not necessarily introduce procedural uncertainty.
The English omits Rider’s conspicuously formal seiza posture and the fact that she is alone while the others eat.
“How humans consume nutrition” is a defensible paraphrase of human-style nourishment; the accusation draws an overly rigid distinction between nourishment and its manner.
作法 can naturally be translated as manners in a dining context; “do not suit me” accurately renders 合いません.
ご飯を食べる can mean eating a meal or ordinary food, and the surrounding domestic context makes “first time eating” defensible without asserting Rider has never consumed anything.

The English omits the explicit living-room vantage, but “watches” still conveys 見守る and “happily” can cover the animation; the accusation overstates the loss.

“Only reason” changes 一つ, and “meet Tohsaka” removes the explicit combat alliance.

元気に振舞っている describes Sakura deliberately acting well or cheerfully, not merely appearing medically healthy.
The Japanese says Shirou’s side has no available countermeasure; “it’ll all be over” adds a definite final defeat.
The plural worms are flattened, but “activate” can reasonably render 動かせる in this technical context; the claim about concrete commanded motion is too strong.
その事実 refers to Sakura’s stated prognosis, whereas “what I’m doing” substitutes Shirou’s activity as the concealed information.

つき合い means Saber went along with or indulged Shirou’s selfishness; “fighting for my selfish goals” changes the relational agency into instrumental service.

Here セーブ means restraining or suppressing magical output, not merely conserving magical energy for later.

The Japanese uses 手, singular, while the English specifies multiple hands.
Both the breath-holding and the act of clinging to the washbasin are omitted.
In the vomiting context, “everything in her stomach” is a defensible contextual rendering of what she expels; the alleged emotional image is interpretive rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
“From the shoulder down” is a natural anatomical resolution of 根元から in this arm-loss context.
自虐する describes self-reproach, not audible yelling, and does not by itself mean masochism.
The English preserves the chill but omits its specified location on her back; this is a narrower bodily-detail omission, not a major semantic reversal.
The source evaluates how reckless the wish was; the English changes that into a question about whether carelessness caused it.
“Sharp pain in her stomach” loses both the cut-to-pieces simile and the broader abdominal reference.
傷 is an injury or wound; “scratch” materially minimizes the throat injury.
The English retains the punishment interpretation, but weakens the explicit self-reproach in 自らを責める; “malformed causal language” overstates the defect.
数十分後 specifies several tens of minutes, not merely an unspecified interval.
“She breathes heavily” is a normal English paraphrase of the panting sound and is supported by the following description of her breathing and shoulders.
The marathon itself conventionally supplies the long-distance scale; omitting the explicit number of kilometers is not a material error here.
The English preserves apology but omits the lowered/downcast posture; that narrower visual omission survives, while the accusation should not imply the entire expression is lost.
“She truly wishes” is a defensible natural rendering of sincere, unfeigned concern; the absolute emphasis is softened but not materially reversed.
“A face with a crooked smile” loses that the mirror shows her profile and shifts the active mouth distortion into a more static description.
たりぃ expresses weariness or “what a drag,” not specifically boredom.
The Japanese is deliberately corrupted comic text, so its exact rebuking function cannot be established from the supplied witness. “Hah!” at least preserves an exclamation.
“The worst sulking I’ve seen” is an idiomatic rendering of an unprecedented degree of sulking, not necessarily a moral judgment.
報われない means receiving no reward, recompense, or fulfillment; “not fair” changes the complaint into a general fairness judgment.
“Died together in a friendly manner” preserves the grotesque ironic use of 仲良く, even if the English is stylistically awkward.
“Radiating from” makes the shoulder the heat’s source, whereas the Japanese says heat invades through the shoulder base.
“A plague of microscopic bugs” can naturally describe a mass of tiny insects; the added collective image is not a material unsupported claim.
The Japanese is conditional and prospective: if attention lapses, he will be charred before he knows it. The English makes that completed injury and adds a realization event.
The English paraphrases the gradual and forceful progression; loss of sound-symbolic texture alone is not a factual translation error.
“Flood into” can convey unrestrained invasive entry in context; the alleged personification is not required for an accurate English rendering.
The fused phrase “the entrancethe hole” is grammatically broken and fails to express the opening that should let the insects out.
“Something I don’t know” is understandable but less precise than something of unknowable or unidentifiable nature; the surviving claim is lexical weakening, not total loss of alienness.
“Shouldn’t have” can mean knowledge he is not supposed or able to possess, not merely morally forbidden knowledge.
“A blacksmith heroic spirit” is an unnatural noun pile and obscures that Archer was a Heroic Spirit whose trade was smithing.
いくらでも expresses unlimited quantity or repeated reproduction; “duplicates everything” shifts this toward totality and drops the unlimited scope.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 創造理念 as イメージ, making “an image in the caster’s mind” a defensible contextual rendering rather than a demonstrable error.
“Manage this skill” can mean handle or master it; the command to use it competently is substantially preserved.
“This body” is a normal rendering of この身, and “will destroy” preserves 必ず’s certainty in English.
In context, the foreign “thing” being shown, memorized, and used is naturally understood as another person’s ability; this is contextual explicitation, not an unsupported invention.
English “can’t” can idiomatically express a prohibition, so “You can’t put time out of order” preserves the instruction not to distort time.
“Destroy the regularity” is both unnatural English and less accurate than disturbing order, the direct sense of 秩序を乱す.
“Our eyes meet” preserves the event but omits はた’s abrupt, sudden beat; the narrower written-presentation claim survives.
“I’m glad” preserves the emotion but omits the explicit emphasis of 本当に; this is a minor degree loss rather than a major mistranslation.
The English gives the resulting embrace but omits the rushing, headfirst impact and the sound-symbolic ばふ.
The dialogue already repeats “I’m glad,” and “repeats herself over and over” accurately describes the narration’s repeated よかった.
The English retains crying but omits 泣きつく’s clinging appeal and 大人しくしているしかない’s specific response of staying quietly still.
The causative construction permits an inferred operator, and the scene supplies Kirei as that operator; “put on another one” need not mean clothing.
The Japanese says he was just about to ask her to explain what happened; “As I speak” loses both the imminent interruption and the request.
抑えつける is a physical instruction to pin or restrain the arm; “repress” is abstract and obscures the action.
The Japanese asks him to identify what the foreign object is; “the origin of the pain” substitutes a different diagnostic target.
“Big hospital clothes” is unnatural and loses both the bagginess and the patient-garment sense of だぼだぼの病人服.
“Leave with Shirou” can naturally mean go out or depart together in this room context; it does not materially contradict 外に出る.
The source explicitly says he was stripped naked; “removes the coverings” sanitizes the completed exposure.
“Wrapped cloth” preserves the wrapping but not the explicit many-layer detail; the claim should be narrowed to that omission.
The English conveys foreignness but changes “something other than myself” into a stricter bodily-part claim; the alleged contradiction with later integration is overstated.
“Opposing the natural Providence” is awkward and adds theological coloring, but it still conveys attachment against natural order; the claim should not call the sentence wholly malformed.
意思 can mean will or wish; “in accordance with Archer’s wish” is a normal contextual rendering of respecting his own will.
消滅した means vanished or disappeared in this context; “eliminated” can imply that another party defeated or removed Archer.
The English states persistence but omits that the severed heroic-spirit flesh was incarnated in the present world using Shirou’s magical energy.
The source says neither had long to live; “would have died” removes the limited remaining duration.
肉体 literally supports “body,” and the immediate context is an intact body used for the transplant; the English does not demonstrably claim the whole body was transplanted.
“Divine” adds religious coloring absent from 神秘, but the core claim that this mystery lies outside magecraft remains; the accusation should be narrowed.
“Succeeded in shape” is malformed English and obscures success only in outward form before the expected shock death.
この二人なら identifies Shirou and Archer as a pair; singular “he” obscures the pair’s reciprocal compatibility and recovery.
“Sadly” conveys sadness but loses the source’s vague or impressionistic なんとなく; the narrower uncertainty-loss claim survives.
瓜二つ naturally supports “look this alike,” and the characters’ identities make “twin brothers” contextually appropriate; the accusation treats a defensible idiom as factual error.
“I flex ... to test his words” can describe attempting to tense the arm, not successful movement; the following text explicitly establishes that it does not move.
“Dead meat” adds death and flesh imagery absent from the neutral 塊, changing the description of an insensate mass.
The source says 腕, arm; “hand” narrows the affected limb.
“A piece of metal” is a defensible generalization of an iron lump in English; the material metaphor remains intact.
“Tin man” is a natural English way to express a person made of tin and does not require a specific literary allusion.
“Constricted” can mean constrained or restricted; in context it conveys the arm’s lack of freedom, even if “disabled” would be plainer.
“Familiarize with your body” is an ungrammatical intransitive construction; the arm should adapt or become accustomed to the body.
“Heal well enough to give you no trouble in leading an ordinary life” is a natural paraphrase of recovery sufficient for ordinary life, not a material overstatement.
“Swallow” is a defensible metaphorical rendering of being engulfed or caught up in the arm’s power; the accusation treats imagery preference as a factual error.
“Break down” conveys bodily collapse, but it does omit the explicit internal direction. The narrower omission claim survives; the broader visceral characterization is overstated.
The English renders pain and attempted activation, but does not preserve the repeated “each time” cadence. The claim that recoil becomes merely generic is too strong.
The source explicitly describes the shroud as one that kills or suppresses magical energy; naming only Martin drops a stated functional property.
“Infringement” can mean encroachment, not only legal rights violation. It is awkward English, but the accusation does not establish a material semantic error.
一人前になって means becoming fully fledged or competent; “master magus” is a possible English rendering and no rank assertion is demonstrably added by the Japanese.
自滅する explicitly presents self-destruction, whereas “be consumed” makes Shirou only a passive victim and loses the contrast with becoming competent.
The English states the practical implication of abandoning the rescued life. It is less specific, but the supplied prose does not prove a materially different conclusion.
“Talk like that” preserves the inference that Shirou is lively enough to reassure Kirei, but omits the cheeky backtalk nuance. The finding should be narrowed to characterization loss.
The source says the entire left arm is immobile; “left hand” narrows the affected body part.
The English invents a specific shoulder placement that is absent from the source, which only says he draped or put on the jacket provisionally.
“It’s already nighttime” conveys the temporal result but omits the unnoticed transition in いつのまにか. This is a real nuance omission, not necessarily a major factual error.
“Do your best” is broad enough to fit the warning, but it loses the specific instruction to maneuver or handle the situation skillfully.
Japanese 命 is number-neutral and the surrounding group context permits “our lives”; the plural is not demonstrably an erroneous distribution of risk.
“The war is a failure” can naturally describe a war whose operative structure has broken down. The contextual meaning is retained despite less literal wording.
“Shuts her mouth” is awkward, but it does convey that Rin stops speaking. This is not enough to establish a material mistranslation.
“The last two standing” is a normal contextual rendering of the two remaining Masters and does not materially change who is meant.
In context, “it’s already over” can mean functionally or practically over, matching the surrounding ほぼ決まっている. It need not assert completed finality.

The semantic relation is preserved, but “There is no benefit to kill” is grammatically defective English. The accusation should be limited to grammar, not a substantial loss of the concessive premise.
立て篭もる specifically recommends barricading or holding up defensively; “stay in your mansion” omits that tactical posture.
“Would be wise” is a natural English way to recommend the correct course, especially with だろう. The alleged categorical softening is not demonstrable as a material error.
赴いた means went or ventured to a place of death, while “stayed on the battlefield” changes the movement and setting; “shamelessly” also changes のこのこ’s nonchalant tone.
“Cannot give up easily” accurately conveys 白旗はあげられない. Omitting the white-flag image is a stylistic loss, not a false proposition.
“Looks away” directly describes the same action. The doubled gesture and huff are tonal detail, but the accusation presents that detail as a factual mistranslation.

The English compresses the premise that someone will win anyway into “has to win,” but the resulting winner restriction is still understood. The surviving issue is omission of the conditional premise, not necessarily a changed preference into necessity.
The English retains Rin’s wish to save Sakura but omits なんだかんだ言って, which marks the contrast with her stated posture. The accusation should not claim that the motive itself was lost.
目的 is not obligatorily singular in English translation; “goals” can naturally refer to Shirou’s purposes without changing the scene’s meaning.
小物 is contempt for Zouken’s caliber or stature—a petty small fry—not a claim that he is simply physically or generally weak.
The Japanese leaves the existence of some strategy as an inference or possibility; the English adds certainty and explicitly assigns devising it to Shirou and Rin.
“Look at each other silently” gives the event, but omits つい, the sense that the mutual gaze happens unintentionally or before they realize it.
保護を受けない naturally supports “not asking for protection” in this context; the English makes the practical custody situation explicit without changing the reason for leaving.
“I have to refuse” is a conventional conversational rendering of いいけど、行かない and does not necessarily invent an external compulsion.
問いただす means pressing Rin for an explanation using only his gaze; the English recasts this as merely staring because he is confused and loses the nonverbal question.
こっちに振るな means not to throw or hand the awkward issue over to Shirou, not a general wish to avoid interference.
戻しては makes the return an act of sending or putting Illya back under someone’s custody; “she goes back” shifts that agency to Illya.
The source completes the comic sequence with another emphatic refusal. “I’m sorry” turns that refusal into an apology and loses the repeated pattern.
“I’m going to do things myself” is a natural rendering of 一人でやってく and clearly expresses self-sufficiency; childishness is a preference judgment.
The English strengthens 嫌われたものね to “still hates you,” especially through “hates”; however, the adjacent page confirms that Rin is deliberately framing Illya as disliking Shirou.
“Tiny house” plus “doesn’t want to stay” reasonably conveys 狭苦しくて御免: cramped and emphatically rejected. The alleged loss is mainly stylistic.
“Get away from Shirou” can mean keep away or separate from him, and the unfinished sentence leaves the reason open. The supplied context does not establish an erroneous aversion reading.
責め立てる is forceful reproach or pressure, while “calmly criticizes” substantially understates Rin’s cold, deliberate attack.
“Don’t want Shirou” can introduce unwanted romantic or possessive ambiguity, but in context it also naturally means not wanting to be with him. The claim should be limited to added ambiguity.
“Smiles gently” reflects 穏やかに but omits the satisfied “ふふん” signal. The narrower tonal omission survives; “gently” is not itself false.
“Whose house is Illya going to?” is a complete, natural English question and preserves the speaker’s uncertainty; the trailing ellipsis is retained as hesitation, not truncation.
知りたがる says Kirei wants to know Sakura’s condition; “concerned” adds an emotional motive not asserted in the Japanese. The narrower explicitation claim is valid.
“What’s going on?” is a normal English expression for the suspicious change-of-heart implied by どんな風の吹き回しだよ; the idiom need not be translated literally.
危うい体 means a dangerous or precarious physical condition, and “critical condition” is a defensible contextual rendering rather than a provably clinical diagnosis.
愚行 explicitly condemns the suicidal conduct as folly. The English preserves the suicide comparison but drops Kirei’s judgment of the act.
娘 can refer to a young woman or girl; “woman” is not demonstrably incompatible with Kirei’s reference to Sakura.
“Save a life” can naturally render 生かす in this aphoristic context, and the following “satisfy one’s desire” preserves Kirei’s provocative framing rather than making it altruistic.
“Criticism” is broader and less pointed than 皮肉, which specifically indicates irony or sarcasm. The genuine issue is loss of ironic register, not total loss of Kirei’s provocation.
“Forgive you for what you did yesterday” is a natural contextual rendering of Rin saying she will let yesterday’s matter pass; it does not establish a different event or agency.
“Pompous” accurately conveys 偉そう, and the following sentence preserves the contrast with her words. Omitting the chest-puffing visual is not a material semantic error here.
The English states cooperation but underplays あげてもいい, Rin’s deliberately condescending “I’ll do you the favor” posture. The issue is voice and stance, not the offer itself.
それまで explicitly limits the alliance until their shared objective is reached; the English leaves the duration indefinite.
“Continues angrily” conveys agitation but omits the complaining look and the rapid, rattling delivery in まくし立てる. The narrower delivery-characterization claim is valid.
“A great fortune” conveys good luck but drops the explicit superlative “more than anything.” This is an emphasis loss, not a reversal of meaning.
はしゃいでる describes Shirou’s outwardly carried-away or giddy behavior; “too happy” preserves emotion but shifts it into a quantity of happiness.
“Retreats quickly” conveys hurried backward movement. The panic and comic sound effect are tonal details, not a materially different action.
じろじろと見る marks conspicuous, sustained scrutiny, while “looks at” reduces it to a neutral glance.
“Since it’s a matter of course” is stiff but semantically exact for そりゃ当然; the accusation is a style complaint.

The English labels Rin’s outrageous assertion as a demand, while the narration says she flatly declares an outrageous thing. The narrower speech-act mismatch survives, but the request is plausibly demand-like in context.
“Try to figure out what Tohsaka means” preserves the actual mental action. The omitted トンチ comic-method nuance is not enough to establish a factual mistranslation.
“Claim his ownership” is grammatically ambiguous or malformed and does not clearly mean claim ownership over him, unlike 所有権を言い出す in this context.
“After all” can convey Shirou’s wry conclusion despite Illya’s usual behavior; the frequency nuance of 時に is minor and the accusation overstates it.
“There’s no way he can be yours” naturally conveys that Illya refuses to hand Shirou over; the transfer action is implicit in the ownership context.
“Went berserk” is a standard English rendering of being on the verge of 暴れる; the possible Berserker resonance is not enough to make it an error.
The source explicitly contrasts letting Shirou live with killing him. “Keep him alive or not” euphemizes and obscures the explicit killing authority.
The teeth-grinding image is a creative equivalent for the intense, creaking tension of the mutual glare. The accusation identifies an image substitution, not a material change in the scene.
The English omits Shirou’s furrowed-brow strain and renders waiting for a decision as waiting for an ending. The narrower omission survives, though the event remains understandable.
言い合い can mean an argument or verbal fight, and “fighting solves nothing” is understandable in the surrounding quarrel context.
イヤがってる concerns Shirou’s objection to the proposed arrangement, while “you don’t want her” makes the objection personal toward Rin.
“You’re mine, right?” is a natural coaxing confirmation of わたしのものでいいんだよね and retains the preferred-answer question form.

The mature branch’s “pervert” is more explicit than the deliberately vague ソッチ系, but the supplied English also contains the faithful “into that kind of thing?” branch. The claim must be limited to one flattened branch.

The supplied raw English shows an if/else branch flattened into the displayed output; the duplicated fragment is an extraction artifact, consistent with the stated witness caveat, not a second Japanese question.
“I’m glad you understand” adds explicit gladness, while 分かってるじゃない is primarily Rin’s face-saving acknowledgment that Shirou understood. The narrower added-emotion claim survives.
運命共同体 is an emotionally weighted claim of sharing a common fate; “we’re working together now” reduces it to practical cooperation.
預けた分 refers to the portion or burden Archer entrusted, not that Archer gave everything specifically for Shirou. The English changes both scope and relation.
The source includes both exact repayment and the uneasy-conscience idiom; the English preserves only a bare duty to return the borrowed thing.
“Archer’s” is a reasonable contextual explicitation of アーチャーによって補われた; the Japanese identifies Archer as the source/agent without forbidding the possessive reading.
The English changes an ongoing contract at disappearance into failure to fulfill the contract.
The source has one promise Archer could not fulfill; the English pluralizes it and removes the explicit non-fulfillment.
The simple “hugs” omits both the vigorous impact-like manner and the accompanying sound effect.
The older-brother role is reasonably conveyed, but “like how happy she is” weakens 無条件に嬉しい from unconditional happiness to a preference.
“Really mad” is a defensible natural rendering of the degree of anger; the lost idiomatic flavor is not by itself a factual error.
The English narrows 小さい子 to girls, though the omitted “that sort of taste” is substantially conveyed by the insinuating question and context.
フラレた can mean rejected, not necessarily dumped from an established relationship; “get dumped” therefore overstates the relational presupposition, though the romantic rejection is retained.
嫌われた means being disliked or rejected, not necessarily hated; “hates” materially intensifies Illya’s claim.
“Talk like a grown-up” reasonably captures the precocious element of マセ, but drops the direct brat insult in ガキ.
The conditional protection remains, but これからは explicitly marks a new ongoing arrangement and is not stated in the English.
“Makes a big smile” conveys the prominent smile; loss of the exact sound-effect-like manner and superlative is tonal compression, not a material mistranslation.
The English makes Shirou ask what Rin means, whereas the Japanese repeats “why” as his own uncertainty about his choice.
“Made my choice without thinking” is a defensible natural paraphrase of answering intuitively in this context.
Given the immediately preceding taunt about liking small children, “have a thing for little girls” reasonably makes the existing insinuation explicit.
なんとなくそう思ったから means the answer somehow seemed right; “because I felt like it” changes that intuition into arbitrary willingness to speak.
認めてあげてもいい is prospective acknowledgment or concession, not waiving an offense.
The Japanese asks what Rin is trying to acknowledge; “letting slide” carries forward the preceding mistranslation of leniency.
The source delegates future policy or strategy, not everything generally.
俺の考えじゃ限界がある concerns the limits of his reasoning, whereas “I don’t know all that much” asserts limited knowledge.
運命共同体 expresses a bond bound by common fate; “we’re cooperating” reduces it to practical collaboration.
As with the parallel line, “Archer’s” is a reasonable contextual explicitation of Archer supplementing the arm, not demonstrable fabrication.
契約したまま describes Archer disappearing while the contract remained in force, not failing to complete it.
引き継がなくてはいけない expresses obligation or necessity; “only right” weakens it to propriety.
堂に入ってる describes practiced, assured competence or looking fully at home in the role; “firm” is a different quality.
なんか抜けてる indicates an absentminded or missing quality; “pretty loose” is an imprecise and misleading personality description.
大げさに explicitly marks the sigh as exaggerated or performative, which disappears from “Tohsaka sighs.”
蓋 is literally a lid or cover; the English replaces the physical sealed-container image with an abstract secret.
“Kischur’s keepsake” preserves the relevant person and inheritance relation in natural English; reproducing the written-title/ruby contrast is not required here.
“Kischur’s keepsake” is a defensible contextual rendering of Tohsaka’s teacher’s legacy, especially with the proper name already supplied by the ruby.
キレイそう is an appearance judgment—seems or looks beautiful—not an auditory one; “sounds pretty” changes the sensory modality.
偶像 can be rendered as a statue in the chapel context; the accusation treats one possible religious connotation as mandatory.
“Cheerfully” can naturally convey questioning in an amused, enjoying manner; the exact degree of relish is tonal rather than a demonstrable factual error.
“Laughs” is a broad but defensible rendering of 笑う; the low chuckling manner is a minor tonal nuance.
“The fact that he has no wish” remains tied to the priest’s stated words and does not materially alter the mockery’s target.
The source limits the Grail to answers it itself deems good to questions arising within oneself; “desired outcome for one’s own question” loses both constraints.
自身を叶える concerns self-fulfillment or realization by the person, not merely receiving an answer.
The Japanese says a person cannot be saved by fulfilling the wish personally; the English assigns the agency to the wish itself.
十年以上 means more than ten years, not exactly ten years.
とやら distances the narrator from the label “wish,” while the English states it straightforwardly.
その祈り通り refers to growing according to the prayer, not simply according to the father’s expectations.
The English preserves the core childhood incomprehension; omitting the head-tilt gesture is compression of a physical cue rather than a material meaning error.
体を起こし means raising or sitting up one’s body; “raised his head” substitutes a different bodily action.
悩むべきだろう carries normative self-reproach or distress—he ought to be troubled by the delay—rather than merely wondering.
The English leaves the final clause without its object and fails to state that the boy could never feel the father’s beautiful things to be beautiful.
“A common man’s sense of morality” plus recognizing goodness as right reasonably conveys 道徳を信じ; the accusation demands unnecessary lexical duplication.
心 is the specific heart or inner capacity he sought; “something” removes that central bodily-emotional referent.
The source imagines a bodily place capable of containing the missing heart; the English replaces that receptacle with a generic search for something in the body.
信徒 means believers or the faithful, not missionaries.
精神的苦行 is spiritual or mental ascetic discipline, not ordinary mental pain.
求め続けた心 is the heart he had continued seeking; “epiphany” changes the object into an insight.
“The sense to feel normal happiness” is awkward but can naturally express lacking the capacity for ordinary felt happiness; the distinction is not decisive.
“Such a mind” is a defensible English rendering of 思考回路; preserving the mechanical circuitry metaphor is stylistic rather than mandatory.
The English follows the ruby reading “world,” but the written 常識 layer—common sense—is genuinely omitted; that is a narrower loss than claiming the whole rendering is false.
“Tried his best” is a normal English equivalent for staking one’s whole effort on overcoming the problem; the stronger metaphorical register is optional.
人生を説く means teaching or expounding a way of life; “preach life” is opaque and changes the predicate into an unnatural doctrine.
“Rules of God” and “followed the law” together retain both religious teaching and discipline; the separation is a defensible paraphrase.
The missing boundary in “Yesat” is a visible punctuation/segmentation error.
The source says he affirms his abnormal self by intoxication with transgression; “satisfying his urges” changes that self-directed relation.
The Japanese asks what it means to lack even the choice to turn from good to evil; “what was wrong with him” adds a judgment not present in the question.
“Defective” is defensible in the surrounding discussion, where Kirei repeatedly characterizes himself as 欠陥者; the English does not invent the general defect theme.
The English changes the parallel rhetorical acts—telling, expounding, and judging—into unrelated “call,” “acknowledgment,” and “trial.”
罪 is sin or guilt, and 所在 asks where its locus or responsibility lies; “where the crime was” is malformed and materially changes the concept.
The source depicts anger with nowhere to bring the blow down; “towards something unknown” invents an unknown target and removes the suspended striking image.
The English visibly joins the title and name as “priestKotomine.”
不快感 means discomfort, displeasure, or aversion; “hatred” materially intensifies Kirei’s stated reaction.
此度の結末 naturally permits “the outcome this time”; specifying the end of the Holy Grail War is supported by the surrounding context and is not demonstrably false.
“Actions behind the scenes” retains the covert aspect of 暗躍; the loss of its stronger scheming nuance is not clearly material here.
“Never hatched” is a defensible rendering of the written 孵る image; the alternate ruby association need not be fully reproduced in English.
The English reasonably conveys bringing forth an answer-capable thing, but it loses the source’s birth imagery; the claim of direct creative agency is too strong.
The Japanese expresses astonishment that this normally indifferent man could make such a face; the English merely describes the man’s lack of interest.
答えは近い is a confident assertion that the answer is near; “should come soon” adds qualification and shifts it toward prediction.
“Fallen angel” preserves the central image, but the specific 織天 designation is flattened into generic angelic wording.
天 can naturally be rendered as sky in this visual context; treating the omitted written Heaven layer as a mandatory separate English proposition overstates the claim.
“Unlively” is awkward English, but it still conveys that the town lacks vitality; this is a style issue rather than an accuracy failure.
“Desolate and devoid of any human presence” naturally conveys the vanished inhabited warmth and signs of life, even without reproducing the metaphor literally.
The Japanese locates the onset after he began climbing the slope; “ever since I got to this hill” shifts it toward arrival at the hill.
The translation omits that the arm was attached forcibly.
The rendering is genuinely nonidiomatic English for breathing that will not settle.
It omits 大きく, weakening the stated degree of departure from normal temperature.
It loses the shoulder origin, stabbing onset, and sound-effect force.
“Where the pain is coming from” can naturally mean its cause or mechanism, especially with the following explanation; this is not necessarily a location claim.
“Overheats” omits the specific accumulation-to-capacity mechanism described before the excess heat is discharged.
The English plausibly renders 腹 as “stomach” and the injury as tearing, but it does omit the wholesale-removal force of 根こそぎ.
The translation changes a near-crushing injury into completed crushing.
The passive relation is reversed: Japanese has his body pierced by or through his own arm, not his body acting as the weapon.
The greeting “ただいま” is omitted, but “while I still look well” is a defensible contextual rendering of returning in a healthy-looking state.
“Rest for today” is a somewhat loose but defensible rendering of wanting to rest for now; the body object is not materially lost in context.
“Says something with difficulty” can naturally convey faltering speech; the accusation demands unnecessary explicitness.
“Can’t even move the fingers” states absolute inability and broadens 指先, whereas the Japanese says the fingertips do not move properly.
The translation drops both the act of telling and Sakura as its recipient.
In this context, “insensitivity” is a defensible contextual explication of Shirou’s foolishness toward Sakura, not a demonstrable mistranslation.
The Japanese itself says 桜の言う通りだけど違う; “you’re right, but you’re wrong” is a natural rendering of that elliptical correction.
“Bluff” can mean pretending confidence to conceal weakness and is supported by the next sentence about pretending to be fine.
The sarcastic retrospective self-rebuke is turned into an apparent present instruction not to tell Sakura.
“Turned out fine” overstates 腕はなんとかなった, which means the arm was somehow managed, not that it became fully fine.
カッコ良かった has a broad range including “looked cool” or “was impressive”; “looked really good” is defensible in this admiring context.
The English adds an unstated plan and does not preserve that Illya was rescued, but inadequately.
“Being alive is good enough” preserves the evaluative meaning of passing with survival; retaining the school-grade metaphor is stylistic, not required accuracy.

良くない says sending her there is objectionable or improper; the English invents safety as Shinji’s stated reason.
The Japanese explicitly makes Emiya the surveillance target. “That house” shifts the target from person to location.
“If she left” is a normal hypothetical rendering of conditional 離れてしまう; it does not necessarily assert that the departure already occurred.
夕方 means evening or late afternoon, not afternoon as the current scene time. The English moves the scene earlier.
The English is grammatically poor, but “it reacts slow” still conveys that the arm’s response is slow while it moves. This is copyediting, not a material Japanese error.
かじき is a broader billfish term and “swordfish” narrows it, though swordfish is a common culinary rendering. The finding should treat this as lexical narrowing, not an unequivocal factual error.
The doubled Japanese quotation marks indicate simultaneous voices, but one English line can naturally represent a group greeting. The typography loss is not necessarily material.
顔を合わす specifically means meet face to face; “spending time around” broadens the speculation, but the avoidance implication remains.
土蔵 is an earthen or traditional storehouse; “shed” is a broad, less precise location term, but the finding should not treat it as wholly unsupported content.
In this cooking context, the English’s “good at Western/Japanese food” is a natural interpretation of the contrast introduced by 得意 and 洋食・和食派.
The dish reference “it” can naturally denote the fried kajiki cut or dish; omitting 切り身 is minor compression, not a material mistranslation.
甘く煮た explicitly supplies the sweet-simmered setup that contrasts with Sakura’s report of no sweetness. “The potatoes” omits that relevant detail.
The unfinished noun phrase reacts to the possibility of such a mistake before tasting; “I made such a stupid mistake” turns possibility into an admitted fact.
“Tastes normal” conveys lack of anomaly but omits いつも通り, the comparison with Shirou’s established usual seasoning.
A 隠し味 conventionally is an ingredient intended to bring out or deepen flavor. The English’s functional gloss is defensible.
“Sweet” preserves the basic taste but omits ちょうどいい, the claim that the sweetness is well-calibrated or just right.
伸ばす describes extending chopsticks toward the dish to test it; “reaches out for seconds” adds a second serving before that has occurred.
味付けの薄いところ means a lightly seasoned portion. “A piece that wasn’t simmered” changes weak seasoning into lack of cooking.
“Keeps eating” can naturally cover resuming the meal after the brief interruption; the restart aspect is not materially lost in context.
とんでもなく元気 means exceptionally energetic; “seemed well enough” materially weakens the conspicuous vigor.
美味しそうに indicates apparent enjoyment or relish, which “kept eating” omits.
“Finished off the food” naturally covers both the rice and side dishes; the category distinction is not materially lost.
The source explicitly identifies the shadow as unknown; “the black shadow” removes that plot-relevant uncertainty.
ために expresses purpose, and “so that there won’t be more victims” states the patrol’s preventive aim, not a guaranteed result.
としても is concessive or hypothetical; the English incorrectly states Sakura is definitely Zouken’s only target.
目障りだろう predicts that their presence would be a nuisance; “we should get in his way” makes interference their intention.
The source says the same kind of thing could happen in town; “our encounter” narrows it to a personal confrontation.
The English omits the object of 余裕 and produces a malformed generic statement instead of saying they lack time or composure for serious discussion.
The sentence break before “but” is a clear English punctuation and grammar defect.
Given the immediately established Zouken attack, naming him as the implied attacker and “somebody else” is normal contextual explicitation, not unsupported content.
“Acting defiantly” can naturally render an oddly quarrelsome, confrontational manner; the alleged authority relation is not required by the English word.
The omitted ばか is Shirou’s affectionate, exasperated characterization of Rin and colors the coda.
The conditional specifically concerns taking a half-hearted or ambiguous attitude; “If we aren’t” is both incomplete and semantically underspecified.
The Japanese refers to the fact of Sakura being taken in by Matou, not unspecified events after adoption; “adopted to” is also malformed.
騙そうとしてる means trying to deceive someone else, while “convince herself” reverses the target and agency.
歯の浮く describes embarrassingly saccharine or sentimental praise, not socially arrogant or snobby speech.
In context, “She has to be my enemy” is a defensible idiomatic rendering of Rin’s declared enemy stance, even if it adds a shade of necessity.
ズカズカ conveys forceful, heavy strides; “starts to walk” removes the physical and comic-emotional manner.
怪しいか marks the murder label as questionable; “you really can’t call it murder” changes doubt into inability.
The English retains four separate areas and a large spill; it does not necessarily collapse them into one undifferentiated spill.
じゃない explicitly recalls Rin’s prior denial of Zouken’s involvement; “might be Zouken’s doing” reverses that polarity.

The English is somewhat stronger, but “it doesn’t seem that way” can still express the contextual conclusion that the evidence differs from the shadow’s activity; the accusation should be limited to loss of qualification.
荒れ地 describes the transformed wasteland-like physical setting; “site of the tragedy” replaces that concrete image with a generic location.
The source reports no notable activity in Shinto, whereas “we didn’t find anything” makes it a failure of the patrol’s search.
生々しい can include vivid, immediate, visceral reality; “vivid” is within its lexical range and is not necessarily a positive visual sense.
The explicit coldness of the riverside wind is omitted from the late-night atmosphere.
帰路につく only says they set out homeward; “trudge” adds weary, heavy movement.

In the explanatory conditional, “will feed on such excess energy first” is a normal English rendering of preferential consumption; Japanese does not require a present-tense formulation or explicit plural worms.
組み立てられない concerns constructing or forming magecraft, not merely being unable to use magic in general.
The source presents the bird as able to fly the open sky as a bird; “potential to fly” weakens that counterfactual capability and loses 大空.
刻印虫 can be rendered as a singular collective or infestation in English; “the crest worm” is not alone demonstrably a one-worm claim.
The Japanese makes Rin’s smile the visible cause or manner of her striking gentleness; “kindness” removes that concrete action.
暇さえあれば means whenever she had free time, conveying sustained watchfulness that “I watched her” omits.
毎日のように means almost every day or day after day, not an unqualified every day.
“I can’t deny what she’s saying” can naturally express being immediately convinced by the claim; the alleged reluctant argumentative concession is not compelled.
