The English preserves the condition but drops たまに, so a narrower frequency-qualification omission survives; it does not necessarily assert frequent visits.
The English adds concealment and makes 危うい into “dangerous,” but “dangerous truth” can be a defensible contextual rendering; limit the claim to concealedness and loss of precariousness.
どさんと depicts a heavy drop with a thud; “I sit down” removes the physical weight and discouragement.
打倒できる means can defeat or overcome, not merely match or hold one’s own against.
The cataphoric あの二人 must contrast the other two threats; “those two” most naturally points back to Zouken and Assassin and creates ambiguity.
街に犠牲者が出た以上 refers to casualties having already appeared; “as long as there are victims” changes the completed trigger into an ongoing condition.
済まされる状況じゃない means they cannot let matters end with the excuse of defeat; the English has an unclear plural object and malformed relation.
The blood starts flowing again as the binding loosens; “flows into my arm” invents a direction absent from the source.
剣山 is the dense spiked implement used as the tactile comparison; “mountain of swords” gives a different physical image.
The source deliberately collides tremendous speed with deceleration; “impossible crawl” removes that distortion and adds an unsupported impossibility judgment.
“Fantastic” can cover wildly imaginative imagery, so the semantic accusation is overstated; however, the English loses the frenzied register and leaves “with fantastic image” grammatically defective.
The Japanese includes kneeling, a falling head, a thud, and tatami; “my head striking the floor” substantially reduces the action.

“A natural fear for any living thing” is awkward and ambiguous, but the context can recover the intended organism-inherent fear; the claim should target ambiguity rather than assert a definite reversal.
The source explicitly says he does not reject death because he wants to live and therefore does not want to die; the English omits the second half of that relation.
“Tie the knot tight so it’ll never come loose again” conveys the result and desperation; omission of repeated pulling is a minor compression, not a material error.
嗚咽 is sobbing or choked sobs escaping while crying, not a generic groan.
The source stresses that merely loosening slightly and exposing only the shoulder is sufficient; the English omits both minimizers.
“Crumbled away” can describe ragged fragmentation and does not necessarily mean total disappearance; the accusation overstates the contrast.
The ruby makes 廃線 read as カラダ, preserving both body and abandoned-railway imagery; English retains only “body.”
“My breath is running wild” is awkward but intelligibly conveys uncontrolled or harsh breathing; this is a stylistic preference, not a factual mistranslation.
The source says he endures the pain with an unclear or disordered head; “bearing the strange pain” omits that mental state.
The source specifies inability to remember even how to direct thought back one second; the English broadens this to recollection of anything in the past.
In present-tense English, “the pain goes away” can describe the pain receding; the alleged completion contrast is not decisive.
断絶した and なんとかヒトまとめにする depict severed consciousness being laboriously gathered into a human whole; “gather up my consciousness” loses that distortion and effort.
“Chopped onions” retains the knife action, so the accusation that the knife is removed is too broad; it does omit the tap-tap rhythm in タンタンと.
The repeated sizzling sound is an explicit sensory beat in the cooking hallucination and is omitted entirely.
The source produces a misshapen but coherent damaged/stir-fried thing; “complete the dish” sanitizes and reverses that image.
The Japanese describes a head worked over by other hands to an almost meddlesome extent; “good for nothing” replaces that invasive history with a different judgment.
“Nobody relies on something that’s not there” is a defensible aphoristic paraphrase, but it drops the explicit idea that doing so is already outside proper order.
一生涯をかけて means over the whole course of a lifetime; “using all my life” is malformed and obscures the commitment.
未練がましく marks lingering attachment or reluctance; “still hold on” preserves the action but not its emotional qualification.
こめかみ is the temple, not the forehead.
The ruby reads written 撃鉄 as トリガー, deliberately fusing hammer and trigger; English preserves only the reading.
A gun firing once activated already conveys the source’s predetermined mechanical function and inevitability; the alleged omission is not material.
“Hold my breath” is a defensible rendering of 息を潜め; the narrower surviving issue is omission of the dim setting in 薄闇.
空白 means blank or vacant, not white; the English invents a wall color.
もう一度, 強く, and 左腕 are explicit repetition, force, and side details; “clutching my arm” omits all three.
弱音を飲み込んで means swallowing an unworthy expression of weakness; “my whimpering finished” invents audible whimpering and changes the action.
“The sound of footsteps” accurately conveys the event; the wooden hallway is incidental scene detail whose omission is not materially misleading.
“I wake up my dozing mind” is awkward English but preserves rousing a drowsy consciousness; the distinction is not mistranslated materially.
The source denies sensing any presence at all; the English instead frames the issue as not knowing the person’s identity.
“Door” is a defensible generic English rendering of 襖; architectural specificity alone does not establish a material error here.
The source has Sakura hesitantly open the fusuma before entering; the English omits both her hesitation and her act of opening it.
The English drops the explicit self-blaming manner of Sakura’s apology.
“Pain she has to go through” omits the bodily thirst and gasping image.
“Forgot about Sakura” can naturally mean forgetting her condition or need; the surrounding “reason why Sakura’s here” supplies that reading.
“Sucking blood” is a defensible contextual rendering of 血を飲む, especially in the immediately following feeding scene.
“Indecent” is a normal English equivalent for an atmosphere of moral transgression or taboo.
The hand-to-arm substitution is a real narrowing issue, but “tried to move” is an arguable rendering of the involuntary movement and should not be bundled as equally certain.
A syringe is a defensible natural paraphrase for a needle-based blood-transfer device; the omitted tube is not demonstrably material here.
The English presents the fragmentary internal thought as an external speaker saying it, changing its source and presentation.
“I don’t need this arm” can naturally convey that the arm is excessive or unnecessary for him; the accusation overstates the distinction.
“Waste your life” adds an evaluative judgment absent from the parallel statement that his life will be invaded and spent sealing it.
“Even just its timer will be enough” can grammatically mean that removing the timed circuit alone is sufficient; “timer” is an acceptable contextual shortening of 時限回路.
景気よく describes a vigorous or abundant flow, whereas “more quickly” reduces the observation to speed.
“As though her fright had been just an act” introduces the unsupported idea that Sakura’s earlier fear was performed; “as thought” is also a visible English error.
“Greedily” is a defensible contextual rendering of visible, hungry desire and need not impose a separate moral judgment.
“As if some sleek beast has taken Sakura’s form” preserves the simile and does not assert literal possession or replacement.
Blood on or between the lips is a natural English visualization of 血が唇に滴る in this immediate feeding context; the charge is too exacting.
The contact location is plainly changed from fingers to the arm; “softness” versus “smoothness” is a less decisive lexical issue.
The English removes the specific image of pleasure making his bodily form unable to hold together.
The translation retains loss of strength but omits the separate sensation that the shoulder feels about to come out of joint.
“Can barely feel” is a plausible consequence, but it narrows uncertainty about the arm’s state into a specific sensory deficit.
Expanding the contrasting hands to arms is a natural contextual metonymy in a passage already describing both arms; the contrast remains intact.
The English states a plain embrace and omits 知らずに, which marks that Shirou draws Sakura close without consciously intending it.
The English syntax makes the honey pleasure exceed both Sakura’s body and the lips, whereas Japanese groups the lips and honey pleasure together as what intoxicates him more than her body.
“Energy” is an acceptable English rendering of 活力; the distinction from magical energy is contextual rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
English normally transfers the personified eyes’ attempted check into “I try to see”; the protective meaning remains.
In the consciousness-shutdown context, “I can’t think of anything” is a defensible natural broadening of being unable to think about what comes afterward.
“Tired” materially weakens the explicit description of a body exhausted to its core.
The supplied mirrorMoon page is not blank; it contains “It is in a red sea.” The accusation attacks a different archived extraction state.
“Aquarium” can describe a submerged tank-like environment; the alleged display-versus-confinement distinction is not decisive in English.
The English preserves the dense substance but changes its clinging contact with the throat into inward flow; this is a narrower image shift, not necessarily a total mistranslation.
“Has to be” strengthens the modality of ようだった, though the inferential underwater conclusion remains present.
“Painful” can express 苦しい, but it loses some of the respiratory distress that contrasts with the separate line about pain.
The English changes a normative description of what the creature ought to be from into a claim about its past residence.
The bodily location is explicitly the throat, not the lungs.
The target changes from the peacefully sleeping cityscape to its townspeople, and hatred becomes cursing.
“It hurts” is possible for 苦しい, but it obscures the deliberate distinction from 痛み and weakens the suffocating distress.

The supplied page text describes smooth entrancing coloration, but the supplied raw Original witness contains a variant explicitly mentioning blood and red coloration. The alignment and edition status conflict.
The supplied mirrorMoon page contains the repeated “Need more” text; the blank-page accusation does not attack the supplied translation.

The supplied page text lacks an object, but the supplied raw Original witness has “crushing” and blood imagery matching the English branch. Because the witness notes uncertified alignment and branch flattening, this cannot be screened confidently as an insertion.
“Air hurts” is a defensible contextual rendering of the deliberately unnatural phrase 酸素が苦しい; the accusation treats an awkward Japanese expression as if only one English wording were possible.
The Japanese characterizes the pressure as light or insubstantial, not emotionally indifferent.
“Watertight protection” conveys the imagined function of 耐水服; omitting the clothing noun is not demonstrably material here.
The Japanese limits the intended target to one part of the city, while the English says the whole town.

The supplied page text says deep crimson without naming blood, but the supplied raw Original witness explicitly says the hands are covered in blood. The finding depends on an unresolved edition/alignment difference.
The English retains spilling parts but omits the endpoint where she becomes empty and ceases to move.
“All the parts ... will spill out” omits the self-disgusting manner adverb 無様に.
“Makes it only a few steps” asserts completion where 数歩も歩けない explicitly says she cannot walk even a few steps.
“Braces herself” conveys using the desk for support, but it softens the collapsing body and desperate effort to remain upright.
“Greed” is an available contextual rendering of 欲望 in this hunger-driven passage, though “desire” would also be possible.
“Hot skin” is a plausible embodied paraphrase in context, but it narrows 身体 from the whole body to one surface.
The English preserves the first thought that something is wrong but omits the repeated, explicitly self-directed judgment.
“Probably empty” omits the emphatic repetition とてもとても and weakens the stated degree of emptiness.
In context, “she doesn’t want anyone else” naturally understands the omitted object as anyone else filling her; the prior sentence supplies that relation.
“For much longer” weakens the explicit indefinite permanence of remaining his forever in that state.
The Japanese imagines time, emotion, other people, and everything disappearing, not merely being paid as costs.
The Japanese says the dizziness is not caused by the bizarre fantasy; “not so far-fetched” instead judges that fantasy’s plausibility.
The English captures sincere enjoyment and the frightening realization, but omits the explicit fleeting and unguarded framing in 一瞬、本当に素直に.
“Go mad” escalates 心までおかしくなり始めている from the mind beginning to go wrong to explicit madness.
嗚咽 is a muffled sob or sobbing sound through bitten lips, not an unqualified moan escaping the mouth.
The English retains lifelong bed confinement but omits the explicit loss of limb function.
“Trouble” can mean causing someone serious distress in English; the accusation treats a lexical choice as necessarily trivial inconvenience.
“Disfunction” is a misspelling in the supplied English; the Japanese clearly concerns this malfunction or breakdown.
The English drops この場所で, removing the specific warm place in which she wants to keep smiling at him.
The English reverses the relation: Japanese identifies the one person who wishes Sakura happiness, whom her happiness would ruin.
The English omits disappearing before anyone learns what is happening, which is explicit in the Japanese.
“Best choice” can naturally mean the morally right or correct choice in context; the alleged distinction is not decisive.
“So why?” is a natural English realization of the preceding isolated why-me fragment, especially with the following sentence specifying the ordinary desire.
“Forbidden” adds an external prohibitor, while the Japanese describes being cut off or severed; the deprivation claim survives but the agency claim should be narrowed.
The English loses both the plea for forgiveness or permission and the limited additional duration in もう少し赦されていたい.
“Justifies her decision” is supported by the surrounding choice, but it weakens 弁解する into a more settled and neutral justification.
The Japanese restricts the lack of a happy exit to この道, while the English generalizes it to all happy endings.
とうに means already or long since; “another nightmare” adds a separate nightmare not stated in the supplied Japanese.
The English conveys slow awakening of the mind but leaves the separately repeated slow bodily rising implicit.
The English preserves the immediate generic lateness and then reproduces Shirou’s correction that school lateness is not literally applicable.
“Get changed” is a normal concise rendering, and the surrounding sentence still identifies the wrapped left arm during that act.
土蔵 is an earthen storehouse or warehouse; “shed” materially changes the setting’s building type.
“The sky is nice” omits the concrete observation that the entire overhead sky is perfectly clear.
第一声 can refer to the first words or remark arising in one’s mind and does not require a false internal-versus-spoken distinction here.
“Prickling grass” plus running barefoot conveys the physical sensation; omission of the explicit endurance verb is not clearly material in this context.
四分弱 means just under four minutes; “Four minutes after” states an unqualified four-minute interval and loses the sub-four qualification.
“Wiping my feet” naturally conveys the action; English need not state the dirt as a separate object, especially with the preceding bare-foot context.
“Sick again” broadens the explicit fever recurrence, but the accusation should be narrowed to loss of symptom specificity rather than treating the rendering as wholly false.
たどたどしい can include awkward or faltering speech; “sounds awkward” is a defensible contextual rendering, though less specific.

The Japanese has mumbling and embarrassed delivery. “Trails off” can represent the broken delivery, but “furiously” overstates 恥ずかしそうに and the claim should be narrowed to that intensification/loss of mumbling.
The boiling-point metaphor is omitted, but the surrounding blood-rush and no-blood-below-the-neck imagery conveys the same comic escalation; this is stylistic compression.
The translation reverses a confirming nod into a head shake, changing the answer to whether the event was real.
In this personification, “my mind” can naturally render 理性; the passage still assigns the labeling action to Shirou’s rational consciousness.
The Japanese depicts Shirou forcing down a heat-dizzy head; “Ignoring the blazing heat” changes active self-control into passive disregard.
The Japanese explicitly describes a smile that produces a ticklish, bashful reaction in Shirou; the English retains only the smile and lethal reply.
The hypothetical has three interruptions, including seeing Illya’s face. The English omits that first condition entirely.
激甘モード is an intensely sugary romantic mode; “lost it for real” replaces that specific comic-affectionate state with generic loss of control.
“Runny” is a reasonable rendering of 半熟目, and “cut tomatoes” adequately conveys the prepared tomatoes. The omitted degree modifiers are not materially misleading here.
The Japanese names Sakura or Rin as possible cooking teachers; the English retains only Rin and therefore removes one explicit alternative.
くい adds a small gaze-shift manner, but “looks at the TV” accurately states the action; treating the minor gesture as a material error is preference policing.
“Already seen” can naturally carry the remembered-news meaning; とっくの昔に adds temporal coloring but its omission is not a substantive mistranslation.
“My mind sharpens up” conveys the sudden return to focus. The omitted speed and slack-versus-tight metaphor are descriptive nuances, not a changed proposition.
The Japanese says the incident is classified alongside unexplained mass-poisoning cases; the English replaces that cause-category with comas, changing the report’s factual classification.
“Incidence” is an awkward and less idiomatic event noun than “incident,” but the sentence still conveys an occurrence of unexplained comas; the claim should not imply a major factual change.
The Japanese explicitly says victims are still being transported to hospitals. That ongoing emergency detail is absent from the English.
“It looks like about a tenth” already conveys the provisional, current-status force of とりあえず and 落ち着きそう.
“My mind freezes” is a defensible natural English rendering of 意識が凍る in a first-person interior reaction; no consequential agency change follows.
段違いの犠牲者 means casualties on a markedly greater scale than before, not merely that there are more victims now.
かねない marks a serious possibility or risk. “Will be swallowed” turns that warning into a definite prediction.
The English is an imperative fragment and omits both the cloth wrapping and 強く, whereas the Japanese narrates Shirou’s tight grip on the wrapped arm.
殺されたのか asks whether the missing people were killed; “dead” removes the explicit violent agency and cause.
“I can move it fine” can naturally mean it has recovered enough for ordinary movement, matching 普通に動かせるぐらいにはなった.
“Understand Archer’s arm” can idiomatically mean understand the arm specifically in its Archer identity; the English does not make the question wholly generic.
The Japanese says merely exposing the skin is sufficient to cause collapse; “let this arm free” implies a fuller unbinding and loses that minimal-trigger relation.
The ruby supplies the shell reading over 世界, creating a self/world boundary image. “The world” alone removes that meaning-bearing layer.
The English can support “obliteration” as a paraphrase of an absolute end, but it omits the explicit image of the world shrinking; that narrower omission survives.
The ruby reads 魔法 as “miracle,” while the written word supplies the technical Magic category. “Miracle” alone loses the deliberate two-layer terminology.
“In terror” is contextually plausible, but 震える頭 explicitly presents a physically trembling head; the valid claim is loss of that bodily image, not necessarily a complete mistranslation.
移して can describe transferring or transplanting a Magic Crest; “transplanted my crest” does not require that the whole crest was moved.
手ごたえ is a felt response, sign, or tangible result Shirou should notice. “It should be working now” changes that subjective expected feedback into operational proof.
制御 can include suppressing or restraining in this arm context; “suppress his arm” is a defensible narrowing, especially given the surrounding restraint discussion.
困る is reasonably rendered by “trouble me,” but 勝手に adds dying on one’s own or heedlessly. The surviving claim is omission of that qualification, not loss of the whole prohibition.
“Projection magic” is a standard and accurate rendering of 投影魔術; “magecraft” is one terminology preference, not a demonstrable semantic error here.
“Half in doubt” is understandable but awkward English. The Japanese meaning is otherwise preserved, so the claim should be limited to idiomatic quality.
伝えるのはリンの役目 is responsibility to tell or convey the information; “your role to ask” changes that duty into questioning Shirou.

The Japanese compares the required magecraft use with Servants and describes a Conceptual Armament that replaces and defeats spiritual Servants. The English shifts the comparison onto the weapon generally and drops the magecraft axis.
The Japanese explicitly specifies defeating Servants as spiritual entities; “in place of Servants” does not express that defeat function or ontology.
魂魄としての重み is spiritual or soul-essence weight. “The weight of its concept” substitutes the preceding conceptual category and changes the stated basis of effect.
The Japanese deliberately writes 魂砕き while reading it as Outbreaker, preserving both semantic layers. The English retains only the reading.
短剣 identifies the requested inherited object as a short blade or dagger; replacing it with the class term Conceptual Weapon loses concrete object identity.
“Destroyed” can naturally mean completely destroyed in this hypothetical context; “no trace” adds a nuance but the accusation overstates the difference as a material weakening.
“An imitation that breaks easily” reasonably conveys the defective, fragile imitation; the hastily-made and immediate-timing modifiers are nonessential compression here.
戦い方次第 makes success contingent on how they fight after producing the sword. “We can manage a fight” turns that tactical contingency into a general capability.
The equation metaphor is stylistic imagery, while “the simplest and surest way to win” preserves the stated evaluative proposition and register sufficiently.
ならば／あるなら makes Archer’s knowledge a condition: if it is available, Shirou can trace it. “You now have” asserts settled possession instead.
The English preserves Shirou’s lack of confidence but drops the explicit reason that he lacks experiential confirmation. The narrower causal-omission claim is valid.
より上位の複製者 explicitly ranks Archer as a superior replicator. “Archer’s theory” omits that characterization.
The Japanese says Shirou can shape a replica whose capabilities resemble the original. “Get close to it” loses both the object and the capability-specific qualification.
The English retains blueprint analysis but omits that Illya performs it through Reading. This is a real technical-detail omission, though not a loss of the main action.
大師父の護符 is the great forefather’s talisman, with pass as its reading. “My master’s path” changes person, object, and ruby sense.
In context, a flaw in the Projection image naturally manifests as a flawed projected weapon; this is a defensible metonymic rendering, not a proven relocation of the defect.
土蔵 is specifically an earthen storehouse, so “shed” loses architectural specificity, but the accusation should be narrowed to that setting detail rather than treating the comparison as wholly wrong.
“Fix it in place with your image” can naturally compress superimposing the image and stabilizing the result; both operations remain inferable in the sentence.
The ruby writes 投影 while reading it as イメージ, linking Shirou’s Projection to “image.” “Your image” retains only the reading and loses the technical Projection layer.
“Train” and “practice” can imply intensive preparation in context; omission of 猛 is a degree nuance, not a material change to the planned regimen.

“Talk” is a defensible narrowing of communication, and “refreshing” is an interpretive addition. The valid narrower issue is the added refreshment and reduced broader interaction, not a wholly false translation.
指 is singular; “her fingers” changes the number of fingers involved in Shirou’s recollection.
客間 is a guest room, not Sakura’s own room. The English changes the location’s ownership/status.
“Confirm everything one last time” is a natural contextual expansion of a final confirmation/check and does not materially change Rin’s intent.

The Japanese describes Servant Archer’s poison mixing into Shirou’s body; “his influence will poison you” preserves the danger metaphor but loses the bodily-admixture formulation. That narrower loss survives.
倣う can mean learn from, follow, or emulate. “Imitate his magic” is a defensible rendering in this training context.
頼もしい expresses reassurance or confidence in Rin’s dependable instruction; “promising” is less personal and less reassuring, but still broadly positive. Narrow the claim to tonal/relational weakening.
倣う means learn or emulate Archer’s magecraft, whereas “Using Archer’s magic” suggests direct use of Archer’s magic and collapses the stated distinction from using the arm.
“My mind freezes” preserves the sudden interruption of Shirou’s thought; omission of 浮かれていた is a tonal compression rather than a changed event or relation.
The Japanese says the arm continued trembling; “in the corner” is an unsupported location added by the English.
The Japanese describes exerting all his physical force, nearly enough to roar. “Muster all my resolve” abstracts away both force and the near-roar image.
“I didn’t think you’d be okay with taking the Shroud off” can naturally express Rin’s surprise at his accepting answer; it does not necessarily assert an unspoken private willingness.
“Pleased” conveys the unusually positive reaction to Shirou’s refusal; loss of the superlative degree is tonal understatement, not a material reversal.
“Tie you down” idiomatically conveys tightly immobilizing someone and need not enumerate the whole body; the hypothetical force remains intact.
気持ち can cover Shirou’s feelings, attitude, or disposition regarding the proposal. “What you thought” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of what she wanted to know.
思わないで prohibits even thinking about removal; “don’t ever say” restricts the prohibition to speech and materially weakens the safety instruction.
A plea naturally entails earnestness, and “sounds more like a plea” is an idiomatic way to characterize the warning’s manner. The core contrast is preserved.
“Grasp” can mean hold firmly, and the surrounding arm context preserves the physical action. The omitted degree of tightness is minor.
Imitating Archer’s magic is a defensible paraphrase of 倣う; the specialized term magecraft is not mandatory here.
The English conveys extraction of Archer’s magic but generalizes the technical object. The accusation should be limited to loss of structure-specific wording.
The proposal’s explicit acknowledgment that it is unreasonable or risky is omitted, affecting Rin’s awareness of the danger.
The English retains preparation for backlash but loses the specified degree of backlash and shifts endurance toward familiarity.
Learn his techniques is defensible for 倣う, but it does generalize the specific magecraft-structure object.
The English can rely on the established arm for left-arm reference, but it omits the explicit maximum-effort qualification.
The body experiencing the technique can naturally express 身に染みさせる; the alleged weakening is not demonstrable.
The English still instructs Shirou not to attempt understanding the technique; its reassuring phrasing does not reverse the prohibition.
Japanese number is unmarked, so singular hand is not itself an error, but the firm pressure in 押し付ける is weakened.
The best-meditation qualification is minor instruction texture, while the core command to meditate is preserved.
The English introduces a condition that is absent from the Japanese: engulfment follows failure to try hard enough, whereas the source says it will certainly occur.
Senses is less precise than consciousness, but can broadly express internal composure. The surviving issue is technical lexical imprecision, not a wholly different action.
The English replaces explicit pseudo-nerve construction and the short timescale with an unspecified step.
The wording is awkward, but it still conveys a voice that cannot be heard clearly. This is not the asserted material mistranslation.
Bitter can describe harsh or cutting treatment in context; the finding imposes an unsupported personal-emotion distinction on 辛辣.
The English conveys cornering and awareness of uneasiness, but omits the burden of guilt or indebtedness and explicit lack of mercy.
Pushing her resolve is a natural English rendering of rallying herself; preserving the Japanese bodily metaphor is not required.
Cuts off retains force but loses the single-utterance and cutting-down emphasis. The accusation should not claim that all decisiveness disappears.
The English recasts Rider’s active protection of the house as merely staying there without fighting, changing the action under discussion.
Under Zouken’s control conveys subordination but weakens the instrumental pawn metaphor. The narrower issue is loss of being used as Zouken’s piece.
The English changes Sakura’s suspected individual betrayal into a plural mutual outcome.
Vagueness conveys deterioration but loses the specific image of memory breaking into pieces.
The English mentions nightmares but omits that even her only source of rest now provides no repose and consists of frightening dreams.
Go crazy is a natural contextual rendering of losing one’s reason; the alleged stigma issue is preference policing.
No magical energy is a normal contextual rendering of a body deficient in magical energy and need not assert literal zero.
The English preserves the strain-to-concern relation but loses the explicit more-strain, more-concern escalation.
The English changes a deeper bow of the head into lowering the gaze, describing a different bodily action.
The smallness of the nod is minor gesture texture; She nods accurately conveys the event.
The English removes both Rin’s summoning agency and the repeated-today element.
Teaching him magic is a defensible rendering of 魔術講座 in dialogue; magecraft is not mandatory terminology.
The English omits that the flow is one-way and continues even while Shirou sleeps, both operationally relevant conditions.
Washed away changes total collapse and disintegration without a trace into mere displacement by water.
The English omits that the sister is Sakura’s own ideal, a material psychological qualifier in the confrontation.
Set limitations does not express the temporal window of making the weapon before Shirou reaches his critical limit.
Mind is possible for 心, and other side broadly conveys contrast, but the heart-versus-role distinction becomes vague.
The English invents an external collective law where the Japanese refers to discipline or code as a magus.
The English makes Rin the giver, while the Japanese says Shirou received the arm from Rin’s Archer.
No right to object narrows Rin’s sweeping denial of Shirou’s right to speak in the matter.
The English retains endurance but omits Shirou’s continuing acceptance of the arm, which supports Rin’s argument.
It can refer to Rin’s retreating action, so the English is not wholly unclear, but it loses the explicit visual referent of her retreating back.
Japanese colloquial の can support an emotionally questioning utterance; the question mark is not a demonstrable reversal of meaning.
The English omits both Rin’s face and the extreme immediate proximity specified by the Japanese.
Talk in a big voice is unidiomatic English for producing a loud voice and is a clear usage error.
Don’t like spicy food can naturally ask about inability to tolerate spicy food; it need not assert mere aesthetic preference.
The English changes after nine into exactly nine o’clock.
The English fragment is ungrammatical and fails to form a coherent equivalent of unknown knowledge being inside his head.
Hit can include tapping, but it loses コツコツ’s repeated light-tapping manner. The accusation should not require a wholly different self-harm event.
Gone makes the dizziness completely disappear, while the Japanese says it has merely subsided for now.
The English retains Shirou’s prior statement but omits the effortful brow-furrowing and only indirectly conveys that he volunteered himself.
Japanese leaves the agent of restoring the Shroud unmarked; we is a natural contextual English choice, not demonstrably invented agency.
A bit dizzy conveys part of the state, but omits the accompanying fogginess expressed by ぼんやり.
すごい is context-sensitive and can express surprise at an unusual or remarkable comparison; weird is defensible.
The running action is preserved, but the light comic scampering manner of たたーっと is flattened.
Chatters happily can naturally describe a cheerful utterance here and does not necessarily assert habitual or rapid speech.
Tofu is normally a mass noun in this sentence; tofus is a clear English usage error.
The English retains following but omits the noisy, cumbersome physical manner expressed by ドタドタ.
The Japanese wonders whether Shirou in this flustered state pleases Illya, while the English shifts the object to an undefined it.
Walking beside me can naturally convey following closely in English context; the degree nuance is not a material error.
The English omits the supermarket shopping bags in Illya’s hands, removing a concrete part of the scene.
A familiar melody can include vague recognition from somewhere; the English does not materially overstate the passage.
Familiar conveys recognition but loses the nostalgia expressed by 懐かしい.
Kind can poetically describe a song’s gentle quality; this is stylistic preference, not factual error.
The English turns the speculative のではないかと construction into an asserted fact.
No companion to speak with on the way home is narrowed into the broader claim that Illya had no friends.
A カーブミラー is a convex roadside traffic mirror, not a concave mirror.
The English retains closed-eye singing but omits the explicit dreamlike comparison.
The English substitutes earlier singing for the buoyant movement home specified in the imagined family picture.
Call out to her can naturally function as calling to stop or get her attention in this sequence; the alleged material omission is not established.
Hang out is a defensible natural rendering of remaining together and interacting in this ordinary outing; the register objection is preference policing.
The English changes true feelings into concealment of Illya’s whole self or identity.
The English retains the lie but omits the causal relation that Illya’s conduct enabled Shirou to continue participating in it.
The English coordination is malformed and obscures Illya’s resigned companionship toward their end.
The English adds an active preference to like the relationship and want to ignore the issue, while the Japanese expresses conditional acceptance and letting it remain unspoken.
Go crazy is a natural contextual rendering of おかしくなる in this deterioration sequence; the register objection is not sufficient.
Bright smile conveys radiance but omits the flower simile. The narrower surviving claim is loss of imagery, not loss of the refusal itself.
Live a bit longer is a natural contextual rendering of 少しは生きられる, especially in a discussion of lifespan.
In this immediate sacrifice-and-survival context, no longer there naturally implicates death; making that implication explicit is defensible.
Vexing can fit mild frustration, but it shifts the wistful disappointment of 残念 toward irritation. The claim should be narrowed to tonal drift.
The English omits the strict limitation that fate might have changed only a tiny amount.
The repeated technical term 投影魔術 is rendered as “projection magic,” erasing the magecraft terminology in the stated contrast.

「その事」 refers to the immediately preceding claim about manifesting the shape of the mind; “nature” is a defensible paraphrase. The narrower surviving issue is the continued flattening of 魔術 terminology.
いっぱいいっぱい means being overwhelmed by concern for himself, Sakura, and Illya. “Everything that’s happened with” naturally covers those matters and is not necessarily an event-history substitution.
甲高い is literally high-pitched, but the later dropped-plate context makes “crashing” a plausible contextual concretization. It is a nonliteral choice, not by itself a material error.
Although the wording is omitted literally, “crashing sound” already supplies a harsh or unpleasant auditory quality; the accusation treats a paraphrase as total omission.
夕方 can cover late afternoon, and the adjacent timing is before six. “This afternoon” is somewhat less precise but within the source’s temporal range.
The furrowed brow is genuinely omitted, but this is a minor visual-detail loss rather than proof that the scene’s core concern or frustration is mistranslated.
本人たっての希望 is an emphatic personal wish; “as she requested” preserves Sakura’s agency but softens that emphasis. The narrower tonal-attenuation claim survives.
The English retains the return home but drops that Sakura had been waiting in the living room. That is a concrete action and location, not merely omitted Japanese flavor.
過ぎ means after two, whereas “around two” permits before or approximately at two and changes the chronology.
寝かせつけた can mean getting someone settled or putting them to sleep; in the afternoon context, “take a nap” is a reasonable English specification, not demonstrably unsupported.
The English omits Shirou’s return to the living room and his finding Sakura already cooking there, collapsing a concrete sequence into a temporal clause.
やせ我慢 and 強がり can describe putting on a brave front or bluffing. “Bluffing” need not imply deliberate deception and is defensible here.
The English retains refusal of help from both people, but omits the source’s special emphasis on Rin and weakens 絶対に. Narrow the claim to that emphasis.
The Japanese explicitly makes both Shirou and Sakura surprised by Rin’s reaction; “I’m stunned” removes Sakura as an experiencer.
“I want to keep doing it” preserves the continuing role, but drops the exclusive force of これだけは. The claim should be narrowed to loss of that emphasis.
The bodily-heaviness clause is omitted, but “you” is a normal English rendering of the implied addressee and “only make you uneasy” preserves the central anxiety. This is a narrowed detail loss.
ムキになって conveys becoming heated or worked up; “started to criticize” preserves the action but loses that emotional intensity. This is tonal attenuation, not a wholesale mistranslation.
The English omits both Sakura’s conspicuous confidence and her brisk, efficient arranging, which matter to the contrast with her later impairment.
手が込んでる can naturally be rendered “complicated” in the sense of elaborate or labor-intensive. Awkward style alone does not establish a factual error.

The compound accusation overstates the problem: “steamed shrimp wrap” elsewhere conveys 包み蒸し, and English allows count plurals such as “shrimps.” A narrower criticism may target the awkward conditional duplication and “ethnic-styled,” not the claimed wholesale omission.

The English conveys confidence, deliciousness, and high spirits, but weakens the boastful chest-puffing and the explicit comparison with earlier cooking. Narrow the claim to that lost presentation/comparison.
The doubled Japanese utterance and spontaneous force are not fully represented, but the English still states that all three diners clap. Only the voice-count and spontaneity losses are supportable.
“Steamed dumplings” is an acceptable English equivalent for シューマイ, so the generalization is not inherently erroneous. A narrower omission claim could note that the whole-small-shrimp detail is lost.

“Looks pretty” preserves the basic beauty and the garnish list, but the explicit exquisite balance is softened or omitted. The accusation should not claim that all presentation information disappeared.
“I freeze” is a normal English description of an involuntary reaction at the moment the chopsticks stop; it need not assert literal whole-body paralysis.
こわばらせた describes involuntary stiffening, whereas “make a sour face” adds an overt disgusted expression and changes the reaction’s character.
The source explicitly denies that the food is bad; “none of the food is good” contradicts that measured judgment and is then only partially softened by “not terrible.”
The source says Shirou watches Sakura without letting her notice. “I keep looking at her” removes that concealment, which explains the protective context.
The English implies reaching for the chopsticks, but omits the deliberate resolve in 意を決して. The specific target is recoverable from context, so the accusation should be narrowed.
The English retains the falling chopsticks, hurried recovery, and reach for the bowl, but omits the small sound and the explicit face-saving purpose. It is not a total action omission.
指の自由がきかない can reasonably be explained in English as fingers being numb or unresponsive; “numb” is a defensible rejected alternative, not invented plot content.
The English preserves the repeated forgetting but drops the important immediacy of something known only seconds earlier. This is a real narrowing, not a total change of recurrence.
非情に徹して conveys steeling himself to be ruthless; “I stopped her” preserves the outcome but loses the severity and protective self-hardening.

The surrounding line explicitly tells Sakura to sleep, and the narration explains that lying down without moving may restore her fingers. “Sleep and rest” is a natural paraphrase of that context, not a material reversal.
Looking down is a possible way of averting one’s gaze, and the adjacent lip-biting context supports that natural English rendering. The Japanese does not specify the direction of the averted gaze.
しばらくは gives a temporary duration—depend on others for a while—whereas “a bit” changes it to a degree of reliance and loses the temporal limit.
食器 is collective/plural tableware. “A plate seven times” suggests one plate repeatedly dropped and materially narrows the stated seven incidents.
The English retains the conclusion that illness remains, but omits the source’s explanation that small residual signs reveal it. Narrow the claim to loss of that evidential detail.
完全に治る means complete recovery, broader than the fever merely breaking. The English narrows the condition for returning to the kitchen.
客間 is specifically the guest room. “Her room” changes the destination into a room represented as Sakura’s own.
玄関 can naturally be rendered “door” or “at the door” in English as the entrance location; the source does not require a correction of material scene geography.
途端 and すぐ indicate immediate sleep, while “soon after” weakens that immediacy. The narrower timing-attenuation claim survives, but the event remains correctly translated.
The supplied English page is blank where the Japanese contains the recalled prognosis. This is a complete omission of consequential information.
The source states that materializing the Servant risks Rider becoming unable to fight in an emergency; the English shifts this consequence to Sakura intentionally saving energy.
馬鹿なことを can naturally be rendered “How stupid” as dismissal of the question or thought; the following “Of course I want to say something” supplies the anchor.
倒れたら means if they are defeated or fall, not necessarily die, and 助からない concerns Sakura being unable to be saved. The English changes both agency and stakes.
無関係な人間 identifies people uninvolved in the war, not necessarily morally innocent. “Innocent” changes the factual criterion Rin invokes.
Japanese leaves the encounter’s target implicit; “find them” is normal English pronoun resolution for the enemy or phenomenon and is not a demonstrable pluralization error.
最後には一回だけ means that by the end he succeeded once; “on your last try” implies the success specifically occurred on the final attempt. Narrow to that added attempt-sequence implication.
“If I was that into it” and “that’s probably why” convey excessive concentration and the resulting failure to notice time; the loss-of-time explanation is not absent.
夕方 can be rendered as late afternoon, especially with the surrounding before-six timing. This is within normal lexical range.
The ruins simile is omitted, but “deepest silence, deepest sleep” preserves the established extreme baseline. Narrow the claim to loss of the specific ruins image.
The source emphasizes that the silence easily passes beyond a limit that should not be surpassable. “Quieter even than that” omits both the ease and paradoxical limit.
In context, “the streetlamps are off” is a normal English inference from 街灯まで真っ暗 and does not materially assert a different scene cause.
睨んでいる is more intense than neutral looking, so the English softens Rin’s gaze. This is a genuine tonal loss, but not the wholesale scene change alleged.
郊外一歩手前 places the town just before the suburbs; “right into the suburbs” moves it across that boundary.

The English retains the black-wall image and its obstructing effect, but omits the source’s “as if saying nothing lies ahead” warning. The accusation should not call the remaining visual rendering ordinary obstruction alone.
The English preserves passing through and discovering what happened, but drops the explicit entry into a familiar townscape. This is a narrower omission than claimed.
軒 counts physical houses, not households. The English changes the observed buildings into demographic units.
“Standing in the darkness” can naturally convey houses remaining unchanged in the night; 沈んでいる is a literary image whose exact metaphor need not be preserved literally.
In a passage surveying multiple houses, “broken doors” is a natural collective English rendering of the generic entrance condition; the source does not require one literal door.
The English conveys the absence of broken windows but omits the source’s explicit claim that nobody entered by breaking one. Narrow to that agency/action omission.
“Take everything out of these houses” conveys removal of the contents, but walls and the vivid scooping-up image are lost. Narrow to those omitted details.
百人以上 means more than one hundred, not “the hundreds,” which normally suggests several hundred and overstates the population.
表札 is the household nameplate, not a gate. The English replaces a specific identifying feature with a different object.
The source explicitly has Rin search the first floor before going upstairs; the English omits that stage.
“More barren” is a natural adjectival rendering of looking like a wasteland and retains the comparative devastation. The accusation demands a literal noun image without showing a material loss.
胸焼けがしそうな gives the residue an oppressive bodily effect; “traces of magical energy” removes that sensory reaction.
The source says the black afterimage remains visibly in form or color; “stuck everywhere” omits that persistent visible remainder.
清潔な惨状 deliberately combines cleanliness with devastation. “This disaster” removes that central contradiction.
“Desolate” can naturally describe an uninhabited town, and “engulfed” can convey being consumed or swallowed by the shadow. The metaphorical choices are defensible.
あってはいけない expresses that the suspected relation must not be allowed to exist; “It’s impossible” changes that refusal into an epistemic impossibility.
塊 is a concentrated mass or lump, not merely an amount. The English removes the shadow’s concrete, concentrated substance.
“Engulf a town” is a defensible English rendering of a force consuming or swallowing a town, especially after the preceding English already uses “eating.”
と思う marks Shirou’s tentative assessment that nothing was taken. “It didn’t take anything” states that assessment as fact.
“Must’ve been hungry” still marks an inference, not certainty, and reasonably conveys the speculative なのか. The omitted intensity of よっぽど is at most a minor nuance.
「有機物」means organic material, not only living material; the English’s “what was” strongly implies what was alive.
「でしょう」marks Rin’s consoling inference as probable; “There was no time” states it categorically.
The source explicitly classifies the phenomenon as magecraft-like; the English only presents an analogy to Rider’s field.
「魔力」is magical energy/power, not the magical technique itself. The English changes the detected object.
“Magic” is a defensible natural rendering of 「魔術」 here, and “ordinary action” adequately conveys 「ただの挙動」; this is terminology preference, not a demonstrated error.
「らしい」presents satiation as an inference from the shadow’s disappearance; “is satisfied” removes that uncertainty.
The Japanese specifically says victims resulted despite patrolling; “damage” erases the human-casualty relation.
「なにかしら行動」means any action or move, not specifically an attack directed at victims.
「判ってはいた」states prior knowledge or recognition; “I suspected it” weakens that asserted knowledge.
「でしょうね」makes the monster forecast probable rather than certain; “It’ll be” removes the prediction’s modality.

“Enjoying the spectacle” is a plausible contextual paraphrase of sightseeing/touring, and the following correction preserves the intended contrast; the accusation treats stylistic choice as factual error.
The English preserves continued willingness to fight, but it does omit the admiring/compassionate force of 「健気にも」. The claim should be limited to tonal omission.
「人でなくなったモノ」denotes entities/things no longer human; “inhuman minds” changes the ontological category to minds.
「良かれと思い」means believing it was for the best, not explicitly for Zouken’s own good.
“Eliminate” conveys the action of 「刈り取る」, but loses the deliberate reaping/cultivation metaphor. The finding should target that metaphorical framing, not the basic meaning.
「嗤う」has a marked mocking/scornful force that plain “laughs” does not necessarily convey.
The Japanese makes the old man the subject, with the white skull accompanying him and the pair blending into darkness; the English pluralizes the subjects and omits the darkness.
「その視線」is singular and follows the old man; “They are watching” incorrectly assigns the gaze to both figures.
「小さかろう」concerns how small or minor an obstacle is, not how weak an enemy is.
「手に負えない」means unmanageable, and 「排除」means remove/eliminate; neither entails being too strong to fight or assassination.
The source calls it an unwritten law to be strictly observed. “A rule he must obey” omits both marked qualities.
“We can kill them here” is idiomatic English for proposing that killing is possible or acceptable in the situation; it need not assert mere capability.
The Japanese uses a singular omitted subject in Zouken’s statement; “we let them live” pluralizes his deliberate agency.
「齢五百を超える」explicitly gives an age exceeding five hundred, which the English omits.
「疎まれ」means being shunned or regarded with aversion; “ignored” materially weakens the social hostility.
The source specifies the world inhabited by the ally, making hatred of that world implicate the ally; the English drops that relation.
「愛欲」is more charged than neutral “love,” suggesting passionate/erotic attachment. The surviving claim should be narrowed to loss of that charged register.
The Japanese itself leaves the agent of 「されよう」implicit; “no matter what happens to it” is a defensible way to preserve that unspecified passive condition.
“He made it last so long” is a defensible rendering of 「あそこまで保たせてくれた」; the source does not require a specific “breaking-point” or progress metaphor.

The English’s later “sadism and joy” preserves some pleasure, but it omits the hearty/gleeful laugh and intoxication with his own scheme. The claim should be limited to tonal and self-satisfaction loss.
The source says only 「骨頭」, a bare skull; “white” adds an unsupported attribute and risks conflating it with the separately named white skull.
The English conveys accumulated training fatigue and delayed onset, but loses the debt metaphor and 「一気に」’s all-at-once force. Narrow the finding to those omitted nuances.
「のか」marks Shirou’s self-questioning; “My mind must be” turns it into a conclusion.
“Pass out” can colloquially mean fall asleep from exhaustion, so it is not necessarily a change to involuntary loss of consciousness.
「客間」is the guest room, not Sakura’s own room; the English changes the location.
「使役してない」describes Sakura not employing/commanding Rider; “Rider not taking form” shifts the agency to Rider’s manifestation.
「廃墟」is ruins or a devastated district, not merely empty houses.
The English preserves the habit and proper futon-laying, but “current state” is vague where the Japanese specifically says his head is not functioning adequately.
“Enough composure” is a plausible rendering of 「余裕」, but it shifts the image from a small opening/space for thought to emotional composure. Limit the claim to that nuance.
「簡単に終わっていた」describes ease, not that the whole day ended quickly or in a flash.
“Losing her freedom” is a broad paraphrase, but the Japanese specifically describes Sakura’s body increasingly failing to obey. Narrow the claim to loss of bodily-control specificity.
「体を蝕まれ」states physical erosion of Sakura’s body by the Crest Worms; the English retains only magical-energy depletion.
「とうの昔に」means long ago, not merely already.
「起きてきちゃいました」says the noise woke her and she got up; “came since I heard sounds” omits the waking event.
「我慢して損をして」means suppressing what she wants to say and suffering disadvantage; “is at a loss” changes the result.
The source says she tries hard to smile; “smiles at me” removes effort and adds Shirou as the smile’s target.
「眠れそう」means it seems/looks likely she can sleep well; “I can sleep well” is more definite.
「あってたまるものか」is an emphatic refusal to allow the possibility, not a neutral factual claim that she cannot differ.
「ちゃんと眠ってたか」asks whether she slept properly; “like I told you” invents a prior instruction.
「いえ」is “no,” directly answering whether she disliked it; “Yes” reverses the polarity.
“Do this with Sakura” preserves the deliberately deictic 「こうして」 in context; it is vague but not demonstrably mistranslated.
“Hold Sakura many times” is awkward but grammatically intelligible and accurately preserves 「何度も」; this is style preference, not a material error.
The source makes Sakura the active seeker/desirer; “needs to be satisfied” changes her agency into a passive need.
“Want it more” conveys comparative intensity, but loses 「満ち足りず」’s state of being unfulfilled and adds an undefined object. Narrow the claim accordingly.
“Sakura’s warmth on my hand” naturally describes feeling her body heat through the palm while holding her hand; this is not a material relocation.
The English correctly says he falls asleep but omits only the depth emphasized by 「深い」; this is a limited descriptive omission, not a major event error.
The source explicitly contrasts an aroused/excited head regaining composure at the brink of sleep; “haze clears” removes those states and the sleep-threshold setting.
「桜に溺れる」means losing oneself or drowning in Sakura; “indulging in Sakura” adds a different moral/sexual framing.
「認めてしまった」is an unwilling admission/acknowledgment; “confirm” changes it into evidentiary verification, while “finally” alters 「決定的に」.
Japanese uses 見る for dreams, and “seeing the dream” is understandable English in this context; it is somewhat literal but not a material accuracy error.
The English preserves walking but omits the wet/soft pattering manner encoded by 「ヒタヒタと」. Limit the claim to that atmospheric detail.
“From behind” preserves the basic position but omits 「少し」’s measured slight separation. This is a spatial nuance, not a total observer-position loss.
“Over and over” preserves repetition, but omits the recent sustained-period sense of 「ここのところずっと」.
“Intimacy” can express affinity/familiarity, but is stronger than the explicitly slight 「少しだけ親近感」. Narrow the claim to strength/register.
The source states that merely wandering outside at night causes the food to come toward her; the English omits both the nocturnal condition and mechanism.
「心」has a broad range including mind, heart, spirit, and soul; “body and soul” is a defensible literary rendering, not an unsupported technical substitution.
「くすくすと」adds giggling and 「歌ってゴーゴー」is a playful sing-song refrain; “Sing and go” flattens both voice and playfulness.
“Seems to be happy” correctly retains 「そうだ」’s appearance/inference, but drops the degree marker 「とても」. Limit the claim to loss of intensity.
The English retains her willingness to continue, but omits the limited “a little longer” duration and the benefactive nuance of 「見続けてあげても」.
“Panics” conveys severe disturbance, but omits the narrator’s pitying evaluation 「見ていて可哀相なほど」. Narrow the claim to lost sympathy/evaluation.
“The actual thing” remains deliberately vague and is a reasonable English rendering of deictic 「アレ」; it does not necessarily invent a resolved referent.
「死にゆく前に」explicitly places the curse before her impending death; the English omits that timing.
「滅多刺し」means being stabbed repeatedly/savagely, and 「刃物」specifies blades; “showered with weapons” preserves neither detail reliably.
The source’s paradox depends on Sakura being the observer watching from behind; the English omits that spatial identity.
“Cut up” can mean mutilated, but is weaker than the shredded/torn-apart force of 「ズタズタ」. Narrow the claim to severity loss.
「みっともない」means unsightly, shameful, or pathetic; “obscene” introduces a sexual/moral judgment absent from the source.
The Japanese says the body connected to the legs hangs loosely; the English reverses the dependency and makes the legs dangle from the body.
The Japanese contains an explicit line; the supplied English page is blank, so the entire utterance is omitted.
Snapping the fingers immediately before using the oversized blade can naturally be rendered as summoning it; this is ordinary English explicitation, not a demonstrable contradiction.
The broken Japanese plea explicitly includes Sakura herself and remaining together in that state; “I’ll really” drops the shared-destruction fragment.
「夢から」 means “from the dream”; rendering it as “The dream” loses the deliberate fragment and its relation to escape.
「磔にされた」 supplies the pinned/crucified image that explains the woman’s posture; “like a bug” omits it.
未練がましく denotes desperate, lingering attachment. “Frantically” is a defensible rendering of the desperate manner and does not necessarily assert speed.
見てくれた means that Shirou finally saw or acknowledged her; “accepted me” adds a distinct conclusion about acceptance.
The Japanese makes Shirou the one Sakura wanted to touch her. “Feel more of me” reverses the direction and changes the object.
The Japanese is uncertain, asking whether she can no longer see; “must not see” presents a stronger inference and is also grammatically ambiguous as a prohibition.
The English does omit the final dreamlike state, but “babbles” is an overstatement rather than the whole claim; 口にする only says she voices the wish.
先輩は is the broken subject of the unfinished clause. “Nee-san will” makes the sister the subject and drops Shirou’s role.
断頭の剣 is a sword of decapitation/beheading, not a guillotine, which changes the weapon.
覚める事なく explicitly says her consciousness vanishes without waking; that condition is absent from the English.
The English conveys taking longer, but omits 少しだけ and changes the past observation into present tense; the claim that the whole sentence is blank is false.
The supplied English explicitly translates the sentence as “It hurts. It doesn’t heal because it’s not enough.” The alleged blank is not present.
The Japanese describes the Hero King’s soul-weight as equivalent to hundreds of thousands of people. “Energy worth ... souls” changes both the measure and comparison.
The English explicitly renders the repeated insufficiency; the alleged omission is contradicted by the supplied mirror text.
飼育箱 is a box or enclosure. “Breeding area” broadens the concrete container motif and can introduce a different connotation.
燃え爛れる町の中で depicts a town burning and being consumed; “in the fire” removes the townscape and its destructive imagery.

The supplied Japanese witness exposes only the suffix るのか？, so it establishes an unfinished question but not the missing accusation’s verb or full content. The precise omission cannot be certified from this page.
裏切るのか？ is directly and naturally rendered as “Are you going to betray?”
The ruby reading オヤジ adds Shirou’s intimate “old man/Dad” relation to the written name Kiritsugu. The English retains only the name.
年月 refers to the span of years/time in Shirou’s life, not merely days. “Days” materially shortens the duration.
使われ続け is passive: Shirou’s years continued to be used/spent. “I let others use me” adds unspecified agents and voluntary permission.
The English directly preserves the accusation and former-self referent.
穿たれた presents the shadow as bored or pierced into the sky. “The shadow in the sky” removes that violent image.
自らを肯定してきた means he affirmed or validated himself for those purposes; “because you save” recasts the purpose as a record of successful rescue.
無関係に巻き込まれていく means people uninvolved in the matter being dragged in, not necessarily morally innocent people.
The English preserves the conditional lead-in, so it is not wholly blank, but it omits the trailing おまえは that leaves the accusation hanging on “you...”.
The supplied English directly states that Emiya Shirou will be judged by himself.
The tentative bodily explanation まだ血が巡っていないのか is absent. The English gives only the memory failure.
ぽんぽん indicates repeated light pats, while “I tap” can be read as a generic or single tap. The narrower claim is omission of the repeated-pat manner, not a wholly different action.
感触 means the tactile feel of Sakura’s body, while “her sensation is cold” assigns the sensation awkwardly to Sakura and obscures the narrator’s tactile evidence.
ぼんやりした頭のまま supplies Shirou’s dazed state, and 体を起こして means sit or raise himself, not the unnatural “raise my body.”
The Japanese specifies a tight grip maintained so Sakura would not go anywhere. “Held on” omits both tightness and protective motive.
避けようとして says he tried to avoid the table before striking it. The English omits the failed evasive attempt.
“My thoughts are ten seconds in the future” is a natural English paraphrase of experiencing the world ten seconds later when attempting deep thought; the temporal distortion remains.
The Japanese attributes the poor circulation to his just-awakened head and says it is impaired, not that blood categorically will not flow.
踵を返す means turn back/on one’s heel, and “head back to the living room” naturally conveys the reversal toward the prior location.
そんな悠長な真似するか is naturally expressed as rejecting an easygoing or leisurely action; the English preserves Rin’s indignant dismissal without requiring a stable trait reading.
居間に運んでから specifies that Sakura was carried into the living room. “Carried Sakura in” leaves the destination unspecified.
The English conveys the return to proper functioning, but omits that the numbness came from just waking. Its degree of recovery is not clearly less definite.
なんとかまともには戻った is qualified as having somehow returned to something like normal. “I’m fine now” overstates the recovery.
ペタンって床に座っただけ includes both sitting on the floor and the abrupt plopping manner. “Just sat down” loses both details.
客間 is the guest room, not Sakura’s own room. The English changes the room’s identity.
The English does omit 和室, the Japanese-style room, but the supplied finding overstates its function: the closet and clothing search remain clear without it.
イヤというほど追究した conveys pursuing the issue to an oppressive, sickening excess. “For all that time” retains duration but loses that intensity.
掘り出しても is specifically a digging-out metaphor, which “find” omits, but “try to find what’s not there” still conveys the futility; the claim should be narrowed to imagery loss.
さあ can naturally mean “I don’t know” in this distancing reply; the English does not materially assert a different factual state.
客間 again identifies the destination as the guest room. “Sakura’s room” changes it into her private room.
ベッドの上 explicitly places Sakura on the bed; the English omits this scene-setting fragment.
少し苦しげな is qualified as slightly labored or strained. “Breathing hard” can convey labored breathing but intensifies it and drops the qualification.
何処にいたって says that wherever Shirou happens to be, he will come. “I’ll go anywhere for you” changes a location condition into a sweeping promise.
看病 includes looking after a sick person, and “treating you” can function as natural English for caring for someone in this medical context; the accusation treats one possible nuance as mandatory.
“Sit level with Sakura” can naturally mean position himself at her eye level, preserving the purpose of matching her gaze.
ああ is affirmative here: Shirou confirms that Rin is being considerate. Beginning with “No” reverses the response.
身が持たないだろ、俺も桜も is naturally paraphrased as “we can’t manage/endure it”; “we” preserves both named experiencers in context.
心底満足そうな笑顔 is reasonably conveyed by “Her satisfied expression”; the omitted wholehearted degree is tonal nuance, not a demonstrable material error here.
体力の低下 can naturally be rendered as exhaustion or reduced stamina in Sakura’s conversational report; “just” is a defensible colloquial minimizer in context.
そうであってもらわないと困る says Shirou needs the positive result—that her magical energy is sufficient—not merely information about it.
The English omits 右手 and replaces 元気づける with “a show of confidence.” The valid claim is this purpose shift; the right-side detail alone is minor.
悔しい expresses painful frustration or distress, and “I hate that I can’t” is a natural emotional rendering, not necessarily hatred of the situation.
拘っている means being fixated on or clinging to the role. “Concerned about her role” substantially weakens the psychological rigidity.
今まで通りの間桐桜 means Matou Sakura as she has been until now. “Normal Matou Sakura” adds a normativity judgment absent from the Japanese.
許されない says even that role is not permitted or allowed to her. “Can’t manage” changes external deprivation into personal inability.
損だぞ supplies the joke that she loses out unless she rests like a sick person. “Has to rest like one” omits that comic loss-or-benefit logic.
The English preserves the joking delivery, and “plan” suggests a real intention, but it does not explicitly preserve 本気で—the sincerity of the policy.
大人しくしてる means staying quiet or behaving oneself, not literally doing nothing. The later burner exception limits the overstatement, so the claim should target the breadth of “won’t do anything.”
鍋 specifically means a cooking pot, while “pan or something” broadens and weakens the object. This is a narrower lexical-drift claim, not a major change to the domestic action.
真っ先に means first of all or as the very first act after recovery. “Once I get well” omits that priority.
The English conveys the departure position generally, but omits the concrete detail of putting a hand on the doorknob. The claim should not imply that “stop at the door” is wholly unrelated.
先に目が覚めた means she woke before Shirou. “I woke up early” changes the relative order into an absolute time characterization.
The English preserves naturalness and the comparison with Shirou’s question, but drops 明るさ, the brightness or cheerfulness of the delivery.
The Japanese specifies magical experience extracted from Archer’s left arm. The English generalizes both 魔術 and 左腕.
The surface text says 他人の特殊呪文 while the ruby gives Archer’s original spell. Rendering only the ruby reading loses the deliberate written-presentation contrast.
口ずさみ易い means easy to chant or hum. “Familiar” describes recognition, not ease of utterance.
おそらくは marks Shirou’s estimate or uncertainty. “Succeeds half the time” presents the estimate as a fixed rate.
本物の真似事をさらに作り上げる preserves a nested imitation of the genuine original. “A copy of something” leaves that central object relation unspecified.
妄想 is delusion or fantasy in Shirou’s self-denigrating judgment. “Imagination” is materially more neutral.
自滅 means self-destruction or self-ruin; “suicide” adds intentional self-killing and a narrower agency claim.
納まったままだ says the trigger remains housed or contained inside. “Still there” omits the containment that matters to the following switch logic.
考え出せる筈もない expresses that devising such a method is effectively impossible for him. “I have no idea” weakens this into present ignorance.
The bodily heaviness accompanying Shirou’s viewing is omitted; this is more than ordinary scene compression.
“Yesterday” broadens the specific nighttime time reference.
Both the exact count and the broader building category are changed.
“Survivors” retains escaping harm but drops that these were surrounding residents, which matters to who failed to notice the neighbors.
The nearly-sixty scale is absent from the remembrance ritual.
胸に刻む is an ordinary idiom for committing something to one’s heart or mind; “in my mind” is a defensible rendering, not a factual bodily-locus error.
“People I know” includes mere acquaintances and does not preserve the closeness specified by 身近な.
The Japanese identifies the entity that performed the completed act; “causing it” changes that relation and aspect.
The assertion that this is sure as well as painless is reduced to painless salvation alone.
The broadcast is specifically and clearly reporting the damage situation, not merely informing him of the incident in general.
悔やむ means regret or lament what happened; “mourn” shifts the act toward grieving victims.
“Her reasoning doesn’t sound right” naturally conveys that the stated explanation fails as a satisfactory reason; the accusation treats an acceptable paraphrase as a logical error.
The acceptance is explicitly based on the tea being made with special effort or consideration, which disappears in the English.
仕切り直す is restarting or resetting the situation, not specifically composing oneself.
おまけ makes Shirou an added bonus or extra; accidental presence is a different relation.
The English omits that they are facing one another while drinking, an explicit element of the quiet companionship.
The English loses both the sigh-like bodily release and the heartfelt relief expressed by 心から一息つけた.
“Smiling” is within the normal range for ニヤけて in context; the claim mainly polices comic nuance rather than identifying a material mistranslation.
油断ならない describes mutual inability to lower one’s guard; “dangerous relationship” shifts this toward external danger.
The Japanese makes Shirou’s becoming a Master the condition for his beginning to speak with Rin; “we became Masters” adds a shared condition.
The counterfactual subject is Shirou’s becoming a Master, but the English assigns it to the speaker.
The English omits both the prior time boundary and the one-sidedness of Shirou’s admiration.
照れくさそうに is an indefinite embarrassed manner; “blushes” asserts a specific physical reaction absent from the Japanese.
The English omits Shirou’s surprised “Why?” reaction before Rin nods.
The Japanese marks Shirou’s own first-year period; “when we were in the first year” suggests a shared school year.
“Likes to strike back three or four times as hard” can describe her readiness or characteristic retaliation, not necessarily enjoyment; the accusation overreads “likes.”
In direct dialogue the target is implicit, and “let me grumble a bit” is a defensible natural rendering of the teasing complaint; the omitted benefactive nuance is not material here.
The English retains the school entrance but omits the more exact “just after exiting” and the field-edge location. The broad claim that both anchors became merely “the school entrance” is too broad.
腐れ縁 conveys an unpleasant, hard-to-escape association, not merely the neutral fact of having known someone since then.
天敵同士 expresses reciprocal natural-enemy hostility, substantially stronger than simply being unable to get along.
因縁, reinforced by the surrounding hostility, denotes a fraught long-standing entanglement; “a long relationship” neutralizes it.
The English preserves the movement from apparent resolution to renewed complication with “unraveled” and “tangled”; loss of the temperature pun is a translation choice, not an unrelated meaning.
The Japanese only says that someone who was not a member came there; shooting arrows is added content.
The narrator objects to the way Rin identified or confirmed him, not merely to her opinion of him.
一目で判った specifies recognition at a glance, which is absent from generic remembering.
与えていた can naturally describe an impact continuing or accumulating over the intervening period; “you’ve been giving me damage” is defensible in context.
Rin directly corrects envy into feeling defeated; “probably wasn’t” adds uncertainty not present in the correction.
The English omits both passing straight by and the briskness of going home quickly.
そんな無駄 identifies the futile effort specifically; “such a thing” removes the trait Rin is contrasting with Shirou.
すっぱり手を引く emphasizes a clean, decisive withdrawal, while “give up” recasts her deliberate policy as defeat or surrender.
“She’s proud of how she is” can naturally entail confidence in that self; the alleged separate omission is not materially demonstrable.
The English retains childhood but drops the condition of being young enough to waver or be troubled by such questions.
The sunset color is atmospheric detail, and its omission does not establish a material mistranslation of the stated proposition.
The Japanese explicitly contrasts Shirou with an enemy; the English removes that relational correction.
製鉄 specifies forging steel, while “creating the framework” removes the material and metalworking process.
看病 means caring for or nursing the sick; merely watching Sakura materially reduces the requested action.
安心できる describes Shirou’s subjective reassurance, not an objective comparison that Sakura is simply better.
大人しい legitimately covers quiet, subdued, docile, or calm behavior; “calm” is a defensible contextual choice.
じゃないか is tentative or inferential, whereas “I’m sure” makes the recovery prediction certain and adds “in no time.”
人並み以上 states that both capacities exceed the human norm; “more than enough” changes comparison with the average into present sufficiency.
ズタズタ describes muscles torn to shreds, substantially more specific and catastrophic than merely being badly damaged.
刻印虫 has no overt singular/plural marking in the supplied Japanese; “the crest worm” cannot by itself establish a numerical mistranslation.
他の何か is an unknown other thing, not necessarily a person, and 切り刻まれた applies to Sakura’s body generally rather than only her limbs.
The Japanese combines surface brain wording with a 心 reading and retains possibility; “destroyed her sanity” collapses the written ambiguity and strengthens the psychological result.
“Affirmation” adequately conveys swallowing an utterance of agreement; the exact wording “of course” is not required for the sentence’s function.
殺気だった can naturally be rendered as becoming murderous or wanting to kill in this context; the English does not establish a materially different target beyond the surrounding exchange.
“Her words turn cold” is a normal English personification of speaking coldly, and omission of “slightly” is minor tonal compression.
The preceding context explicitly says “impossible for me,” so “I don’t do impossible things” is a defensible contextual rendering of her personal feasibility rule.
Given the immediately preceding discussion of protecting Sakura until the end, “not possible to let her go on” is a reasonable contextual explication of the unstated threshold in もう無理.
平行線 describes continuing irreconcilable positions; “enemies” turns disagreement into an outright enemy relationship.
The Japanese addresses Shirou’s action with an omitted subject; “we have to” adds a joint obligation and changes agency.
別物 means entirely separate things or entities; the English adds the unsupported classification “enemies.”
ガラクタ presents Sakura’s body as useless junk or scrap from her alienated perspective; “broken” reduces this to physical damage.
“Her head feels light” is a defensible natural rendering of the floating, woozy フワフワ description; the alleged dissociation distinction is not decisive here.
The Japanese specifically names her hand, while the English changes the impaired body part to the entire arm.
The English omits both the fingers’ impaired movement and the force sufficient to tear the sheets.
“Spoken of lightly” can naturally mean casually or without visible emotion, which is within 淡々と’s range; this is not a demonstrable factual reversal.
The English removes the concrete schoolyard setting and sunset timing from the remembered event.
The ruby explicitly makes surface 彼女 intimate as Sakura’s “I”; “another girl” replaces that focalized self-reference with detached third person.
The Japanese says the plea cannot reach its intended target as well as being inaudible; “none can hear” loses the failed-reach relation.
The ruby presents the treasured memory as a rare item or possession and the Japanese foregrounds it as Sakura’s sole advantage; the English removes that presentation.
記憶 can be an uncounted mass noun in English, and “recollections” is a defensible stylistic plural; singularity is not materially established here.
The same refusal is explicitly conveyed later on the page by 「今は何も聞きたくない」; the omission is a permissible compression of repeated thought.
The ruby gives 魔力 a spirit or mind reading, creating a deliberate body/psychology relation that the English’s purely magical wording omits.
目を潰す means crushing or blinding the eyes, not simply covering them; the English substantially sanitizes the imagined self-harm.
In context the English can mean the words are said to the person who least wants to hear them, which is a defensible reading of 言ってほしくない人; the alleged agency confusion is not decisive.
The English deliberately follows the ruby reading 世界 and preserves 明るい as “light”; choosing that layer over the surface 居間 is defensible for this wordplay.
The omitted distance is a minor spatial modifier, while the translated “world of light” preserves the central exclusion image; this does not reach material-error level.
“Eyes are hot” is a natural English rendering of heated eyelids in the context of imminent tears; the body-part distinction is not materially misleading.
