The Japanese explicitly adds that Sakura is crying alone, an isolation detail absent from “she’s crying.”
“As Tohsaka’s magus” naturally expresses responsibility in that capacity; it does not make Rin literally owned by Tohsaka.
The Japanese says Shirou is being placed in the same position as Rin, not turned against Sakura. The English adds an adversarial relation.
酷い is a judgment that Rin’s conduct is cruel or awful; repeating Sakura’s hatred changes that judgment into another statement of emotion.
消えればいい can naturally be rendered “should disappear” when reporting Rin’s desired outcome; the accusation treats a normal English implication as an unsupported addition.
それでいい means that Sakura’s disappearance would be sufficient or acceptable, not that she is directly obligated to disappear. “Should” strengthens the self-obligation.
The recurrence/no-more force of もう is weakened, but “anything” is a defensible way to supply the omitted object. The narrower issue is loss of “any more,” not a wholly universal claim.
“Warm people” is defensible, but it omits the temporal qualification “up to now.” The supplied explanation overstates this as an inherent or privileged quality.

“They didn’t object” is a natural elliptical rendering, and the following sentence supplies the intended reference through agreement with her. The quoted self-marking is nuance, not a demonstrable factual error.
我慢しない means she will no longer restrain or endure herself; “merciless” changes that into a claim about cruelty.
この手で explicitly presents her own hand as the instrument of the interrupted threat; the English omits that agency.
何度も explicitly indicates repeated expulsion from the mouth. “Coughs it out” presents only a single act and also weakens 吐き出した.
The Japanese has Sakura, implicitly, turning her own delusions into blood while suffering. Making “pain” the grammatical agent changes the causal and agency relation.
だめみたいです is a self-assessment that she seems to be no good or beyond help; “I can’t” changes it into an unspecified inability.
In this context, いいコトとわるいコト can naturally be rendered “good and evil”; the English moral wording is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
正しい concerns what is right or correct, not what is merely good. The English loses the explicit distinction from the preceding good/bad clause.
The fragment identifies Illya as the same kind of being as Sakura, as clarified by the following vessel description. “The same girl as her” is unclear and does not establish that shared status.
The ruby explicitly reads 魂 as もの, giving Illya’s wording an objectifying “thing” force. “Such a soul” loses that written presentation.
“Already sufficient” is a natural contextual rendering of being full or sated enough, especially when two Servants remain; the alleged difference is mainly stylistic.
“Her head cools down” is a defensible natural rendering of 頭の芯が冷えていく in the fever context; the claimed loss of core/progression is not materially established.
“Clear my head” is a normal English paraphrase of resting one’s mind; it preserves the immediate desire to recover mentally.
猶予 means leeway, grace period, or time to spare. “Postponement” incorrectly describes an act of delaying rather than the available time.
The Japanese specifies Sakura and what comes next. “Everything” removes both stated objects and materially broadens the decision.
だな is a confirmation-seeking ending, approximately “Emiya Shirou, right?” A bare declarative name removes the speaker’s confirmation.
すぐ近く explicitly places the voice immediately nearby. “Within this room” retains location but omits the frightening proximity.
“Alien tone” can naturally convey an impersonal, inorganic, nonhuman quality; the English choice is within the lexical range of 無機質 in context.
髑髏の面 means a skull mask. “White skull” invents whiteness and removes the mask.
隠密が生業 identifies covert action or stealth as Assassin’s profession, not killing people as his specialty.
“Then you just want to talk?” remains a clearly sarcastic reaction in context. Requiring the literal phrase “small talk” is register preference rather than a material error.
The English omits kicking off the tatami and rolling from the hallway to the courtyard, and changes the movement geometry to a dash.
話に乗る can idiomatically mean going along with or accepting someone’s proposal; “go along with him” is defensible in this immediate context.
間桐の屋敷 can be rendered “the Matou household” when referring to the family residence; the surrounding destination context prevents a necessary family-unit reading.
The Japanese explicitly leaves both the proposal’s content and whether the meeting itself is a trap unresolved. The English retains only trap uncertainty.
向かい合える means face or confront Zouken directly. “Talk with” narrows a potentially hostile confrontation to conversation.
こっちには余裕なんてない literally concerns having no leeway, but “I don’t really have a choice” is a natural contextual rendering of the resulting urgency.
一切の気配を立てず describes vanishing without making the slightest detectable presence, a specific stealth effect omitted in English.
間桐邸へ can naturally be rendered as heading to the Matou household or residence; this is not demonstrably a family-unit mistranslation.
日中だというのに supplies the contrast “despite it being daytime,” which is absent from the English and explains the ominous atmosphere.
小倅 is a contemptuous “brat,” “whelp,” or similar insult. “Successor” invents a lineage role and removes the insult.
殺意はない specifically denies murderous intent. “No hostility” is broader and conflicts with the contempt described immediately afterward.
The prose emphasizes Zouken’s composure because he has no intention of killing Shirou alone at this point. The English reverses this into confidence in his ability to kill at any time.
敵意 is directed hostility toward Zouken, not merely Shirou’s internal anger as an emotion.
打ち倒す means knock down or defeat, not explicitly kill. The English adds lethal intent.
殺される前に gives the specific condition “before being killed.” “Before anything can happen” removes the stated mortal threat.
自滅 means self-destruction or collapse, not simply death; the English removes the mechanism Zouken describes.
桜は一体 is an interrupted question about what Sakura actually is. “What did you do to her?” changes ontology into Zouken’s past action.
魂の物質化 is the technical concept “materialization of the soul.” “Put shape to the soul” weakens the technical revelation.
十年前の戦いの折 places the intervention during the battle ten years earlier; “after the war” changes the timing.
The omission of 回収した is genuine, but 移植した can defensibly be rendered “embedded” or “implanted.” Narrow the claim to lost recovery provenance.
“Made sure she can function as a human” can idiomatically express arranging for Sakura to live as a human; the claimed reduction is tonal rather than a demonstrable factual reversal.
八割がた means roughly eighty percent, not one eighth. This is an objective numerical error.

The supplied English visibly contains flattened conditional branch output (“tool/catalyst”); its core vessel-to-gate relation is present, so the malformed extraction cannot responsibly establish a translation error.
The English preserves laughter but drops its evidently amused quality. The narrower surviving issue is loss of manner/register, not omission of the act itself.
小倅 again means “brat” or “whelp.” “Heir” invents succession and removes Zouken’s belittling address.
天寿を全うする means completing one’s natural lifespan. “Lives as a human” omits the intended lifespan condition.
魂を収める器 describes a vessel that contains or houses souls. “Collect souls” shifts the function to active gathering.
“That end” is a normal English rendering of a destination or goal in context; the supplied Japanese does not force the technical noun “Seat” in English.
無様に生き続けておる is Zouken’s self-characterizing admission that he continues living disgracefully or wretchedly; the English drops that tone.
後継者たち is plural successors, and によって presents them as the means through which the goal is achieved. The English reduces this to one successor used by Zouken.
だったはず expresses an expectation or supposed state. “Was prepared to be” makes the nonadaptability sound like an intentional preparation rather than an expected limitation.
自滅せず specifically says Sakura did not self-destruct. “Still lives” loses the described failure mode.
The Japanese says Shirou forgets Assassin, whom Zouken commands. The English turns this into merely a possibility of intervention.
人間 can be generic in English, so “human lives” is a defensible natural pluralization; the Japanese does not establish a required singular reference to Sakura here.
The English preserves the backward stagger but omits the prior forward step. The accusation should be narrowed to that omitted motion, not claim that recoil itself disappears.
拳 is specifically a raised fist, the weapon of the attempted punch. “Arm” broadens and weakens that immediate aggressive image.
敵意 toward Zouken is a directed hostility that precedes regret. “In place of anger” changes both the object and the temporal relation.
ようなもの marks an analogy or qualified characterization (“it was like calming it”), while the English states literal nightly calming. Narrow the claim to loss of qualification.
心臓が痙攣する describes a convulsion or spasm of the heart, not merely a loud heartbeat.
“Gate” is supported by the ruby reading 門, so that part is not an error. The narrower issue is omission of the explicit outside-world relation in 外に通じる.
“A world where every wish comes true” is a natural paraphrase of a place where all wishes are fulfilled; the Japanese does not require literal “place” or potential “can be granted.”
壊れる means break, collapse, or be destroyed; “dies” narrows the outcome and adds a definite death claim. 不始末 does support the idea of a mishap, but not necessarily death.
手塩にかけた means painstakingly raised, tended, or cultivated. “The Holy Grail I made” removes Zouken’s possessive cultivation language.
身近にいたおぬしならば explicitly grounds Shirou’s recognition in having been close to Sakura; the English omits that basis.
罪は桜に及ぶ means the guilt or consequences extend to Sakura. “The crime is Sakura’s” assigns direct ownership instead.
“Took Sakura’s form” can convey much of 原型にし, so the accusation overstates the error. A narrower issue is that the prototype/model relation is less explicit in English.
The Japanese says the shadow blocks Zouken’s approach while explicitly denying that it has will. “Does not want me” assigns desire and contradicts the next clause.
この体では means that this body, separated from Sakura, cannot regulate the shadow. The English changes the object from the shadow to Sakura and omits the bodily qualifier.
Japanese number is unmarked here; 刻印虫 can be rendered as the technical singular “Crest Worm” without proving a numerical error.
覚えなどない is a memory-framed denial (“I have no recollection of using…”), not the categorical assertion “I have never used.”
奔流 is a torrent or powerful rushing flow. “Strong onflow” is malformed and substantially weakens the force image.
A genuine technical omission survives: the Grail had been borrowing Sakura’s unconscious. However, “appear” can reasonably render 浮上する here, so the claimed directional omission is overstated.
倒す can mean defeat, take down, or kill depending on context. In this lethal confrontation, “kill me” is a defensible contextual rendering, not a demonstrable factual change.
The English is awkward, but it retains both the Greater Grail’s completion and the limited gate-opening timing. The elliptical Japanese does not establish the alleged reversal of apposition.
聞こえなかった directly permits “couldn’t hear.” The reeling context may imply failure to register mentally, but it does not make the English’s literal wording erroneous.
The closing physical reaction is wholly absent: Shirou clenches his back teeth while framing the question, conveying bodily strain beyond the question alone.
This is an edition difference. The supplied raw Original has 命を捧げよう, which directly supports “give her life”; the judgment wording belongs to the later witnesses.
万人 normally has universal scope, but “thousands” is a defensible rhetorical localization of the many-versus-one maxim in this immediate context. It does not materially alter Zouken’s argument.

The surrounding dialogue is explicitly urging Shirou to kill Sakura, and the next sentence identifies her as his enemy. Rendering the maxim as ending one evil life is forceful contextual explicitation, not unsupported narrative content.
The translation reduces the corridor to merely “distorted” and omits the conspicuous image of it bending limply like candy.
“When I walk or lean against the wall” naturally conveys the feet-floor and hand-wall contacts, while “don’t feel anything” acceptably paraphrases the absence of any definite sensation.
“Ugly” can figuratively characterize a horrible situation or experience, not only visual appearance. It is within the contextual range of 酷い.
The Japanese does more than call the outcome fate: Zouken says Sakura will be made to resign herself to it. The coercive acceptance encoded by 諦めて貰おう is omitted.
“A hollow being, like a mere puppet” already communicates passive, empty existence. Omitting the literal “merely being there” is acceptable compression rather than a material error.
“Stumble” naturally conveys advancing on unstable legs that threaten to give way. The English is compressed but not materially weaker or contradictory.
Sakura’s sleeping state is a contextual modifier, not essential to who must not learn of the meeting. Naming Sakura without repeating that state remains accurate.
The referent of “notice” is naturally recoverable from Shirou’s stated need to return home and the immediately preceding discussion of his absence. English need not repeat it.
The page already says “I chose to ally with Sakura,” and “be with Sakura” then varies the repeated Japanese wording while preserving the contrast with becoming a hero of justice.
多く means “many” and supplies no number. “Hundreds” introduces a specific scale not established by the supplied Japanese.
に他ならない states identity—breaking the oath is nothing other than self-denial. “It is like” changes that categorical equivalence into mere resemblance.
The passive English still identifies what supported Shirou as the source of rejection through “by everything that has supported you.” モノ can also encompass an abstract or collective “everything.”
The Japanese expressly locates the unforgivability at the moment of death. “Never” broadens the duration but does not preserve that decisive deathbed frame.
In context, people killed despite being unrelated to the conflict are naturally described as innocent victims. This is ordinary English explicitation, not an incompatible moral judgment.
The Japanese equates Shirou’s inaction with personally setting the fire. The English instead equates him with an abstract cause, removing the imagined act and direct agency.
In this life-or-death context, protecting the one person is the means of keeping her alive. The English is a defensible natural paraphrase of 生かそう.
倒す has a context-sensitive range that includes killing an enemy. With Shirou discussing how to confront a lethal monster, “no way to kill him” is defensible.
“A monster one can’t talk with” is awkward but contextually means that discussion or negotiation will not get through to him, which is the force of 話し合いなど通じない.
“Nearly a thousand swords” accurately preserves the repertoire’s object and scale. Omitting the descriptive subclasses 名剣・魔剣 is a loss of detail, not a material mistranslation here.
The English omits the explicit heaviness of Shirou’s body, a physical symptom emphasized as he gives his weight over to the tatami.
Dropping “a little” from the ordinary self-assessment “I’m tired” is minor natural compression and does not establish a materially different degree of exhaustion.
見舞い can involve visiting, checking on, or tending to someone ill. Given the porridge dish and wet towel, “treated Sakura” can defensibly mean cared for her rather than medical treatment.
The Japanese assigns Sakura and Illya to two distinct spaces, a guest room and a Japanese-style room. “Guest rooms” incorrectly collapses them into one room category.
“She starts cutting” removes the entire crisp rhythmic sound and its light, competent quality, weakening the deliberate contrast with the violent chopping on the next page.
“Cutting lots of green peppers” preserves the action and quantity. Omitting the exact julienne technique is a minor culinary detail, not independently a material error.
ブツ切り denotes rough, coarse chunks, reinforced by 豪快に. “Dicing” instead describes relatively small, orderly cubes and changes the comic cutting style.
After the vegetable and meat signals, “What’s she making?” naturally expresses Shirou’s “Which is it?” reaction. The contradiction remains available from the adjacent context.
The grumbling manner is omitted, but this is a minor delivery detail; the preceding question and movement remain intact and no factual or logical error results.
“The lights go off” ordinarily presents a spontaneous event unless an agent is supplied. The English does not imply that somebody deliberately switched them off.
In ordinary English, switches “not responding” means operating them fails to produce the expected light. This is a natural paraphrase of lights not coming on when switched.
The English omits the explicit reservation that Zouken’s ability is a separate question; the Japanese establishes only that Assassin crossed effortlessly.
“Illya’s room” accurately identifies the destination by its occupant. Loss of the architectural label 和室 is nonmaterial in this sentence.
Dinner preparation is the salient ongoing activity established on the preceding pages. Supplying “the preparations” is normal English explicitation of the omitted Japanese object.
A shoji functions here as the room’s sliding door or partition. Calling it a door generalizes the fixture but does not misstage the action materially.
The Japanese explicitly shows brutally splattered bloodstains. “Scattered red” suppresses both the identification as blood and the gruesome force of 無残に飛び散った.

The real error is the loss of 見えた気がした, which makes the perception tentative; the English presents the sight definitely. Calling the silver threads “hair” is a plausible contextual identification and should be dropped from the accusation.
“Illya is not human anymore” combines the surface 人間 and ruby イリヤ in one English proposition. Although typography is flattened, the intended personhood/humanity equation is substantially preserved.
“Cool down my head” retains the cooling metaphor and naturally conveys regaining control. It is less hyperbolic than 急速冷凍 but not a materially different action.
The English preserves Shirou’s urgent exit through the yard. Omitting the explicit observation that it is the shortest route is minor spatial compression.
いてはならないモノ can naturally describe something that ought not exist, not solely something forbidden from this particular location. The English is within its contextual range.
把握する means grasp or comprehend the questions. “Answer” advances Shirou to solving them, whereas the attack comes before he can even process them.
The Japanese says a night without light leaves no means of escaping the shadow. The English instead makes “the dark night” itself the thing to escape, obscuring the illumination-dependent mechanism.
“Rips me open” preserves the violent opening motion of めくり開けられる, and the following forced-bud sentence retains the opening image. “Peel” or “pry” would be alternatives, not mandatory corrections.
びゅうびゅう depicts repeated forceful whooshing or whirling. “Flutter” conventionally suggests gentle movement and materially weakens the violence of the dismemberment image.
“Your body is as bad as Sakura’s” naturally compares the seriousness of their physical conditions. In context it communicates danger rather than an unrelated vague judgment.
“I’m fine as long as” is ordinary English for claiming that nothing serious will happen under the stated condition. The condition involving the cloth is fully preserved.
As an immediate response to “nothing,” “No way!” naturally rejects Shirou’s denial. The following reference to his empty eyes makes the rebuttal’s basis explicit.
The prior English sentence already says Illya scolded him, and “if that’s the case” refers to his ridiculous expression. The omitted nouns remain unambiguously recoverable by normal anaphora.
つい考え込んじまった describes inadvertently falling into prolonged thought or brooding. “I had to think” instead presents the thinking as necessary or deliberate.
The Japanese says Shirou cannot remain empty or vacant. “I can’t empty my head” reverses the state change and says he cannot become mentally empty.
まいった has a broad rueful range including “you’ve got me,” “damn,” or “crap.” In this internal reaction to unexpected kindness, the English is defensible.
手を引く readily functions as an idiom for guiding or helping someone, and ダメになっている can describe being emotionally down or in a bad state. The English captures that sense.
The ruby supplies the technical reading “homunculus,” while the written layer explains it as “artificial human.” Giving only “Homunculus” loses the deliberate explanatory equation.

The demonstrable surviving error is omission of 稀に: powerful circuits occur only sometimes, not categorically. Singular “Circuit” can function as technical English, while the made/born issue is separately encoded by the edition and ruby.
The Japanese deliberately writes “made” but assigns it the reading “born.” The English retains manufacture alone and loses that technical-human doubleness.
The English condition—having the specialized Grail function regardless of what the vessel is made as—substantially conveys that it need not be human and may even be a stew pot.

帰還 means return, whereas “retrieving” remains another acquisition verb close to 回収. Although the following sentence mentions returning through the Grail, the explicit terminological correction is mistranslated.

“Should have collected all of them” naturally expresses the counterfactual outcome in the current war. The Japanese’s standing ordinary arrangement is less explicit in English, but its practical meaning is preserved.

In context, “when I noticed” can naturally mean “when I became aware of it,” by which point the taking was evident. The English is somewhat loose but does not demonstrably place the taking at that instant.
The English immediately identifies the subject as the soul of a Heroic Spirit and then says the class shell was lost. The resulting soul state is conveyed; only the adjective “pure” is omitted.

The preceding sentences repeatedly identify the subject as the Holy Grail, so “the soul of the container itself” contextually preserves the Grail/container equation despite flattening the ruby presentation.
走らない states that no extra program runs alongside the Grail function. “You don’t need” changes an operational exclusion into a judgment that such programs are merely unnecessary.
The repeated comparative construction describes progressively cutting more human functions as more Servants accumulate. “Once I collect many” replaces that gradient with a single threshold.
The Japanese specifies a proportional increase in precision corresponding to the sacrificed limb energy. “Manage them” omits both precise control and that proportional relationship.

The Japanese redirects the components forming Illya’s personality into computation. The English substitutes power formerly used to construct a human form, changing both the consumed resource and mechanism.
The Japanese specifically describes Sakura being progressively rewritten. “Sakura is forced to” conveys coercion but leaves an implied forced switch, omitting the ongoing replacement mechanism.
Normalizing name-based self-reference to “me/myself” is a conventional English character-voice adjustment. The line still makes remaining Illya’s own self the issue.
The sentence-final かな marks Illya’s assessment as tentative. The English states categorically that no human functions need be cut, increasing certainty about a technically important limit.
From Shirou’s perspective, “lose Illya” naturally covers Illya herself becoming absent or erased. It does not necessarily assert physical death and fits the preceding personhood discussion.
The Japanese explicitly calls the embrace one-sided, indicating absent reciprocity. The English preserves gentle contact but presents only Shirou’s manner of holding her.
“What I must protect” ordinarily denotes an ongoing obligation, especially in this vow-centered context. Omitting the aspectual suffix 通す does not independently create a material error.
師範代 is the deputy/assistant instructor, distinct from the 師しょー addressed elsewhere as master; “You’re the master” changes the recurring rank joke.
Taiga’s conspicuous ワシ／帰るで／するんや switch is unmarked in English, leaving the immediately following dialect question without an English trigger.
“See a challenger while I was alive” preserves the before-death meaning, while omitting the extra 生 wordplay is comic compression rather than a material factual error.
“The name of this dead end” communicates that the named game segment is ominous; dropping ブロック does not materially alter the reference here.
正体がない can mean having no identifiable nature or identity; “mysterious things like this” is a defensible contextual rendering, not necessarily a claim that the entity is formless.
“Buruma” transliterates ブルマ accurately. Its accessibility or localization is a terminology preference, not a factual mistranslation.

The line presents Illya as a 強キャラ in terms of a moe index ten times Taiga’s; “moe power is ten times stronger” is a compressed comic paraphrase rather than a demonstrable separation of two statistics.
根こそぎ describes taking or consuming the target wholesale; “fully satisfied” states only a result and removes Taiga’s attempt to offer Illya for consumption.
“Turning defiant” is defensible for 開き直ってきた. The narrower surviving issue is omission of タイガもさるもの, the commentator’s acknowledgment that Taiga is proving formidable.
マトモに limits the warning to engaging the shadow straightforwardly or head-on; the English instead warns that fighting it at all necessarily loses.
The Japanese proverb concerns entering danger to obtain a prize and also supplies a literal tiger image appropriate to Tiger Dojo. “No pain, no gain” changes that relation to enduring hardship.
Katakana ワタシ plus sentence-final ネー marks a sudden pseudo-foreign performance. The grammatical English retains the tap-out but removes that conspicuous voice gag.
Illya says she may become 師範代, the assistant/deputy instructor, not the dojo’s master.
“Fill my heart with ice” is a natural metaphorical paraphrase of deliberately freezing one’s heart; filling it also supplies a completed result, so the alleged material weakening is not established.
“Even more troubled herself” retains the comparison to Shirou’s already stated distress, and “troubled” is contextually within the emotional range of 苦しむ.
The surrounding English says Sakura’s face brightens, that she is glad he came, and that she smiles happily. Omitting 穏やかに is compression, not a material reversal of her affect.
なんとか limits her recovery to barely managing to raise herself. “She can sit up on her own” states the ability without that important physical limitation.
なんでもない話 can naturally mean inconsequential or meaningless talk in this context; “meaningless things” is slightly blunt but not a demonstrable factual error.
実感が湧く筈がない is explicitly negative: Shirou cannot feel the prognosis is real. “I can believe” reverses that judgment.
The entire exchange concerns colds, for which being bedridden with fever is a normal contextual explicitation. The added cause does not materially distort Sakura’s health claim here.

Although awkward, “How can you have spirit during a cold?” continues Shirou’s explicit puzzlement over what 気合 could mean as a cold remedy; the active-treatment sense remains recoverable from the adjacent lines.

The English is awkward but preserves Shirou’s self-correction and his question about applying “spirit” during a cold. The accusation identifies a stylistic deficiency, not a material change of proposition.
The English conveys embarrassment but entirely omits both the performed “えへへ” and Shirou’s observation that this kind of shy laugh is unusual for Sakura.
“Energetic child” is within the range of わんぱく and need not be treated as a factual reversal. The narrower loss is the playful pseudo-statistic 指数が高かった.
得体の知れない characterizes the medicine as unknowable or suspect, directly supporting the surrounding discussion of distrust. Referring to it merely as “it” removes that quality.
“Seeing her smile makes me imagine” still makes the impression involuntary and caused by Sakura’s appearance. It is a milder image than 錯覚に襲われた but preserves the actual mistaken impression.
“Silence” is a defensible rendering of 押し止める, and hope versus wish is not a material distinction here. The narrower genuine loss is 必死に, the desperation of his suppression.

The awkward Japanese instructs Sakura to answer without assuming feasibility. “Don’t worry about if it’s possible or not” communicates that pragmatic point and does not promise that fulfillment remains open.
The English replaces a specific suppressed impulse—to seize or hold Sakura—with a generic statement about keeping feelings frozen, omitting both the desired act and what restraint prevents.

まだ何もしていない omits its grammatical subject. The supplied pages skip intervening narration after the quoted observation about Sakura, so they cannot securely establish whether this is Shirou’s inaction or Sakura’s.
“A closed world” followed by its consisting only of the Emiya and Matou houses already communicates severe confinement. Dropping the redundant 狭い does not materially alter the image.
The Japanese omits the subject of なかった, and in Shirou’s invitation “we’ve never gone anywhere for fun” is a defensible contextual reading of their shared history.
アタフタ describes an outwardly flustered, agitated reaction. “She thinks in confusion” turns that visible behavior into quiet cognition.

English “must have found” is itself an epistemic inference rather than an asserted observation. Sentence-final のか is tentative, but the translation has not promoted the conclusion to an unqualified fact.

Although “anywhere” would be more exact, the immediately preceding question is where Sakura wants to go, so “anything” is readily understood as any choice of destination and causes no material broadening.
ささやか describes the wish as modest or small, whereas “trivial” can dismiss it as unimportant. That evaluative shift conflicts with the scene’s sympathetic emphasis on Sakura’s modest desire.
先輩と makes Shirou’s company an explicit part of Sakura’s wish. The English retains the outing but omits whom she wants beside her.
Dropping the staging adverb ゆっくり does not change who rises or what occurs and is too slight to constitute a material translation error.
The English retains the condition with “if we can really do that,” and “how great” naturally expresses how happy fulfillment would make him. The awkward auxiliary does not turn it into certainty.
Calling the guest room “her room” can naturally identify the room Sakura is presently occupying without asserting ownership or permanence; the alleged status change is not established.
幾らでも says the modest wish could be realized freely, readily, or any number of times once April comes. The English reduces this to a single bare possibility of fulfillment.

心 can denote heart, mind, or inner self, and “frozen mind” remains a defensible rendering in this emotional context. Maintaining the same English metaphor would be stylistically preferable but is not uniquely required.
“Spent the whole day making” describes an ongoing manufacturing process and does not claim the jeweled sword was completed. It can encompass 型どり without the alleged stage reversal.
The English preserves the epistemic prediction with “should.” Omitting the readily contextual prior-case basis is compression, not a material change to the prediction itself.
どんな顔をしているのか concerns what expression Sakura is wearing. “I can’t even see Sakura’s face” instead asserts literal visual invisibility.
こうしている間 means while Shirou remains in his present state; after suppressing trembling and commanding himself to decide, “while I hesitate” is a supported contextual explicitation.
倒す has a broad range including defeating, bringing down, or killing an enemy. In this lethal decision scene, “kill it” is a defensible contextual choice rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
罪を犯してしまった depicts Sakura as already having ended up committing the sin unwillingly, and as one of those harmed. The English instead predicts multiple future crimes.

Falling eye-first onto a flathead screwdriver already conveys the grotesque accident and implicitly requires an exposed, upward-facing tool. Omitting its protrusion from the ground is nonmaterial compression.

“Blinding pain” can mean pain capable of blinding as well as overwhelmingly intense pain, and the adjacent eye-first screwdriver image preserves the blindness association. No definite promotion is established.
The fingers are not merely bending abnormally; they appear to be bent backward by 不思議な力, which motivates the following comparison to cinematic psychic powers. That apparent agency is omitted.
Rendering eyelids that tremble “as though frightened” as “shaking in fear” is normal English explicitation in this immediate death-threat context, not an irresponsible promotion of uncertain emotion.
Japanese withholds the possessor of 白い首筋, and the next page reveals that the bleeding throat is Shirou’s. Adding “her” prematurely resolves the deliberately staged target ambiguity as Sakura.
“Drop to my knees” is an ordinary English description of involuntary collapse and does not inherently imply controlled kneeling. It adequately renders 膝から落ちた here.
“Tried to use the knife against” preserves the attempted attack, while the downward motion was already shown on the preceding pages. Its compression in this recap is not materially misleading.
桜以上に無防備な modifies Shirou as the dagger’s target; it does not state why Rider attacks. Adding “because” invents a causal relation.
In the immediate context of a fatal throat wound, “I don’t feel any pain” is a natural rendering of 苦しくはない. The broader lexical range does not establish a material narrowing.
気がする commonly maps to English “feel,” so “I feel relieved” need not assert an objective fact. The English loses the emphatic さえ but preserves the subjective sensation.

To “atone for Sakura’s sin” already means undertaking atonement concerning her culpability, and the future “will” naturally carries practical ability. The benefactive concern is not materially absent.
滲む allows blood to seep, well, or spread visibly; describing it as dripping along the gripping fingers is a plausible physical rendering, not a consequential change.
“The sob rising in my throat” describes where the rising sob is being suppressed and does not firmly assert that it originated there. The omitted deep-chest detail is not materially misleading.
Using “eyes” for hot eyelids is ordinary English synecdoche, especially for restrained tears; it does not materially change Shirou’s physical state.
“My path was set” defensibly paraphrases the already-decided answer. The narrower genuine loss is 致命的なまでに, which gives that determination a fatal or ruinous degree.
The supplied mirrorMoon text is not blank: it explicitly contains “Are you going to betray?” The accusation therefore attacks an omission that did not occur.
“My body is wracked” is strong, bodily language for being violently afflicted by the contradictory thoughts. It compresses the cutting image but does not weakly reduce it to ordinary worry.
“A selfish superhero” preserves the accusation’s central characterization. The missing もとから and にすぎない intensify scope and degree but do not create a materially different judgment.
私情 can encompass private desires, wishes, attachments, or feelings. “His own wishes” is a defensible choice in the contrast between Kiritsugu’s ideal and personal motives.
私情 also permits private interest or personal motive, and the passage intentionally condemns saving one person solely for that motive. “Self-interest” is pointed but lexically defensible.
“Idea” reasonably renders the ruby reading おもい. The narrower loss is the written surface 自分, which overlays that conviction with Shirou’s identity and cannot be seen in the English.
“Piercing my heart” is a defensible figurative rendering of 胸を打つ. The genuine omission is 立ち止まる自分: the decade-long self confronts the present self who has stopped.

The Japanese coordinates the dead people’s voices and Shirou’s weeping survivor-self as objects of betrayal. The English makes only the self the object and invents that he survived by ignoring those voices.
“That atonement” refers back to the dead and the fire in the immediately preceding passage, so its recipients remain contextually clear. Repeating them is not required for accuracy.
取り繕って無視できる describes disguising, glossing over, and then ignoring the sin. “Can’t make amends” instead concerns whether the sin can be expiated, changing the proposition.

The supplied Japanese does not securely say the ideal sustained Shirou; 支えてきた can make Shirou the implied actor who upheld it. The narrower supported issue is that English omits this additional relationship of maintaining or supporting the ideal.
裏切るとも omits its object and therefore specifies neither grammatical number nor a unique singular referent. “Them” is a contextual explicitation, not demonstrable pluralization of Japanese grammar.
“I won’t even care if I have to live by deceiving myself” naturally expresses that Sakura’s smile makes that cost acceptable. It is an idiomatic paraphrase of それでいい, not simple apathy.
間違いはない can naturally be rendered “there’s nothing wrong with it,” with “it” referring to この思い. The English need not imply universal moral innocence rather than conviction in the feeling.
“I need Sakura. Sakura needs me” preserves the exact reciprocal relationship. Recasting the Japanese nominal fragments as natural English clauses does not materially erase their identity focus.

The preceding English explicitly says Shirou will pull the knife back; “right when I’m about to…” directly continues that stated action. The ellipsis does not leave his abandonment of the strike unproved in the supplied context.

The English does blur the contrast between Shirou coming to kill Sakura and Sakura having driven him to it. However, “sadness” is a defensible explicitation of her pained, clouded expression, so that part of the accusation should be removed.
The English entirely omits the concrete description that Sakura’s face is on the verge of tears.
Shirou’s internal question about whether Sakura truly means what she said has no English counterpart.
“Fear” conveys only one component; Sakura’s pleading tone and the fact that her fear cannot be hidden are both omitted.
「追い詰められていた」describes being psychologically driven into a corner, appreciably stronger than merely being preoccupied.
The English reduces Sakura’s resolve to an unspecified “determination,” omitting both her feigned sleep and her purpose of keeping Shirou alive.
The Japanese concerns what will happen or be present tomorrow; “what tomorrow is” instead creates an awkward abstraction and disrupts the yesterday/tomorrow parallel.
The simple “asked for help” omits 「ずっと」, which expressly says that Sakura kept pleading throughout the experience.
“Ignored everything, thinking it’s just a dream” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of deliberately looking away from the dream and its implications; it retains both denial and volition.
In this nontechnical emotional context, “curse them” is within the lexical range of bearing resentment or ill will toward them. It does not demonstrably introduce a distinct action.
Japanese conventionally uses 「夢を見る」 for having a dream, and “the one who watches it” is awkward but still identifies Sakura as its experiencer rather than demonstrably separating her from it.
Given the surrounding catalogue of memory and temporal disintegration, “forget about you” is a defensible rendering of Sakura ceasing to know or recognize Shirou.

“Become the bad guy” naturally conveys becoming her bad or villainous self, especially immediately after Sakura says she will become an 「悪者」. The English is less explicit about split selfhood but not materially wrong.
The Japanese itself euphemistically omits Sakura as the object of 「終わらせる」. In context, English “you can finish it” clearly gives Shirou the agency and refers to ending her life.
Although maximum force is retained, the English omits the distinct, desperate image of holding her as though clawing at her back.
Fear of dying does not fully convey the separately stated fact that Sakura does not want to die; that explicit desire to live is omitted.

As a reply to Sakura’s warning that he will regret it, “It’s too late” pragmatically means that he already does. The following sentence immediately specifies his existing regret, so the meaning is preserved.
“A quiet sobbing” is awkward but possible as a nominal fragment, matching the fragmentary Japanese narration. This is stylistic infelicity, not a demonstrable translation error.
The quoted words are plainly a promise to protect Sakura, so identifying the speech act as a promise is a reasonable contextual rendering of the neutral 「声をかける」.
「桜の味方」means Sakura’s ally or someone on her side. “Sakura’s superhero” imports the distinct hero role and loses the route-defining contrast with being an ally of justice.

This sentence summarizes the repeated protection declaration, and the immediately preceding scene already presents that declaration twice in English. The repetition is not materially lost from the sequence.
“Darkness” is a normal broad rendering for 「薄闇」 in this scene; the alleged shift to absolute or full darkness is not compelled by the English word.
With a vocalized 「ぁ」 and 「苦しげに」, describing the escaped pained breath as a moan is within the contextual range and does not demonstrably exaggerate it.

“Threw away his self” is awkward English, but “self” can denote identity or principles and the phrase still conveys Shirou’s self-abandonment. It is not ungrammatical enough to sustain the stated accusation.
「向き合えなくなる」means being unable to face or engage Shirou directly and honestly. “Not be able to see him again” instead suggests loss of future contact.
「心」can denote the heart, mind, or psyche. In this context of Shirou abandoning his former self and principles, “mind” is a defensible choice rather than a categorical mistranslation.

The Japanese naturally permits “there is someone who said he would protect even someone like me.” Thus the English protector reading is well supported; the finding’s protected-remnant parsing is not established.

“While she still remains” reasonably paraphrases the persistence of Sakura’s form or identity. It loses some metaphorical texture and 「少しでも」, but does not reduce the phrase specifically to biological survival.
“Something that cannot be returned” is grammatical and can mean something that cannot be restored or brought back. It is awkward but preserves the irreversible loss.

For a mortal speaker, being unable to atone “with the life that remains to her” substantially conveys being unable to atone however long she continues living. The supposed finite/unlimited opposition is not material here.
In its established time-unit sense, 「半刻」is half of a two-hour koku, approximately one hour, not half an hour.
「わかる」itself can mean “know” or “tell,” and the next English sentence explains her sensitivity to hostility. The English does not materially convert a hedged belief into fact.
「殺意」specifically denotes an intention to kill. “Hostility” is broader and removes that lethal specificity from the description of Shirou’s emotional state.
“Blazing” is incompatible with the image of cold wind whistling or passing through a hollow and appears to mistranslate the force conveyed by 「びゅうびゅう」.
The English gives only the unsuccessful result, omitting the emphatic concession that her trembling continued no matter how hard she tried to stop it.
「全部一緒になって受ける」can mean accepting all the past and future sins together as a whole; it does not unambiguously require “bearing them together with her.” The English preserves the core acceptance.
“The school in the sunset” slightly broadens 「校庭」 but preserves the remembered school setting. This minor spatial compression is not a material error.

Omitting the compact modifier 「遠い」loses a shade of spatial or mnemonic distance, but the surrounding sunset memory and formerly unknown runner retain the scene’s perspective. This is not demonstrably material.
「ずっと」and 「叶えてきた」describe an ongoing fulfillment maintained through her repeated visits. “Made her wish come true” recasts it as a single completed achievement.
The vow is to stand on Sakura’s side, not to become her superhero. The substitution erases the deliberate distinction between 「桜の味方」 and the story’s hero-of-justice role.
The English repeatedly identifies Shirou only as “him” or “the boy,” omitting Sakura’s appositive identification of him as her precious person.
The English omits the entire circumstance that Sakura’s continuity of consciousness will break unless she keeps herself mentally braced.
「手をあげる」sets the condition at raising a hand against or attacking Sakura. “Tried to take your life” narrows Rider’s stated intervention threshold to an attempted killing.

Using “you” is normal English pronominalization, and “no matter what you may become” followed by Sakura’s identity question preserves the paradox. Repetition of the proper name is not required for accuracy.

The Japanese leaves the person subject to the prohibition unstated. In English, “she” can refer to the silent Rider in the immediately preceding sentence, so a definite misattribution to Sakura is not established.
Japanese normally leaves number unmarked, and 「拳を握る」can describe clenching one or both fists. The text does not decisively establish a single fist.
The side is omitted in this one sentence, but the immediately following page explicitly identifies the changed hand as her left hand. The Command Spell connection therefore remains clear.
Within Fate’s technical terminology, 「魔術」denotes magecraft, distinct from true 「魔法」. Generic “magic” erases that established distinction in a technical warning.
Grammatically, 「弱々しくも」most naturally qualifies the eyes or gaze themselves, not Sakura’s body. The English is awkward but preserves a weak-looking yet determined magus’s gaze.
“The impossible has occurred” is a categorical and arguably more dramatic rendering of something deemed impossible; it does not weaken the claim.
“Ornamental guillotine” conveys that it was displayed, while the immediately following remarks about Sakura’s taste preserve the hobby joke and attribution to her.
“The instant someone got on it” is broader than lying down but adequately communicates the bed-triggered transformation. The unspecified person does not materially alter the gag.
“Direct offense” is stiff but grammatical, and “offense” can mean a criminal act. The murder-mystery sense remains clear from the surrounding attempted killing.
The wall placement is a minor physical detail; “knife-throwing security system” still supplies a coherent locked-room mechanism and preserves the joke’s operative cause.
Because the two characters are advancing knowingly absurd theories, “speculation” is within the contextual range of 「推理」 and does not erase the detective parody.
After “It goes like this,” the fragment “Going back to yesterday morning” functions as a natural temporal transition and accurately locates the case’s origin.
In theatrical mystery language, “haunted mansion” is a defensible genre-level rendering of 「呪われた館」. The distinction is not consequential to the joke or events.
The English is clumsy, but “never again do a one-time ridiculous Tiger Dojo” remains understandable as a request not to stage another such one-off stunt. It is not logically contradictory.
“Wake up up” contains an unmistakable duplicated word absent from the Japanese.
The Japanese says dawn has just arrived and expressly describes the sky as still dim. “The day is dawning” changes the aspect and omits the dimness.
“Must mean” expresses a strong contextual identification rather than meaningful doubt, and is a natural way to explain the omitted subject in Rin’s preceding Japanese sentence.
「被害」broadly denotes harm, damage, or casualties. In a sentence explicitly quantifying people, “hundreds of people getting hurt” is a defensible contextual rendering.
The guest-room location is omitted, but the essential contrast—that Sakura and Illya are asleep while Shirou and Rin are alone—is fully preserved. No consequential error results.
「出来る」already expresses Rin’s expectation that the framework will be ready today. 「なんとか」adds difficulty, but its omission does not demonstrably convert uncertainty into certainty.
In the context of an ongoing supernatural war, “settle our match with Zouken” is an awkward but defensible rendering of bringing their contest to a decisive conclusion.
In supernatural English, “summoned by the Holy Grail” falls within the plausible range of being called by it. The Japanese does not establish that only a nontechnical attraction is intended.
“Already” retains prior knowledge but omits the emphatic temporal distance of 「とっくの昔に」—that Shirou suspects Rin knew long ago.
The English still says they cannot rely on obtaining a Grail whose acquisition is uncertain. “Ourselves” naturally supplies the agents from context without materially changing the logic.
Calling Shirou a “liability in your condition” naturally means that his condition will cause trouble for the group, closely matching 「わたしたちが困る」 and Rin’s blunt tone.
In the immediate context of sleeplessness, pallor, and dark circles, “so tired” is a defensible contextual rendering of being badly worn down under 「参ってた」.
「夕方」means evening or late afternoon approaching evening; unqualified “in the afternoon” moves the promised wake-up materially earlier.

The genuine omission is 「即興」: English does not say Rin expects to improvise the technique on the spot. However, “something like sleep suggestion” reasonably reflects the limiting 「ぐらいなら」, so the alleged additional weakening should be dropped.
The Japanese anticipates Rin teasingly asking whether Shirou wants to try it. “She might test it on me” instead suggests that Rin might perform the test on him without obtaining his agreement.
“Sensitive” is within the ordinary range of 「神経質」, especially when immediately qualified by his ability to sleep. The narrower high-strung wording is a preference, not required meaning.
In context, taking Rin’s offer to care for Sakura is precisely how Shirou accepts and relies on her kindness. The relational implication is preserved pragmatically.

When Sakura is already in bed and might try to get up, “put her back in bed” is a natural contextual rendering of making her settle down and sleep. The Japanese does not require magically induced sleep.
In the general statement about genius-type people, 「相手」can mean the people dealing with them collectively. “Everyone else” is a defensible idiomatic generalization.

Although this sentence says “together again,” the immediately preceding English page explicitly states that Shirou wants them “back to being sisters.” The restoration of sisterhood is therefore not lost in context.
The English replaces Sakura’s valuation of the restored relationship as a gift with a limit on Shirou’s own capacity.
“Protect her until the Holy Grail War ends” naturally conveys sustained protection through the endpoint; 守りきる does not require separate English wording.
Although awkward, “wait for the duration of the war” can defensibly mean waiting until the war’s allotted duration expires; the operative endpoint is retained.
Rin is the stated challenger, whereas “we’ll challenge” expressly makes the action joint.
Japanese omits the agent of 倒せる. Supplying “we” is a contextually natural English explicitation and does not contradict who may participate.
“Came from the Holy Grail” preserves the essential source relation. Losing the overflow metaphor is compression, not a demonstrable material error here.
The Japanese tentatively asks whether erasure is possible only through one of two targets; the English instead states actions Shirou personally must perform.
Rendering only the written 魔力 loses the explicit reading “electricity,” which extends the projector-and-power-source analogy.
欠片 is not grammatically plural here. “A piece of the Holy Grail” is fully supported by the Japanese.
Japanese does not establish a plural count, and 少量 treats the worms quantitatively. The awkward mass use of “crest worm” does not prove the alleged number error.
最後まで残った means Kirei remained through the end, not that he was the sole final Master. “One of the last surviving Masters” is contextually compatible.
無意識 can denote the unconscious or subconscious mind. “Sakura’s subconscious form” is awkward but defensible in this psychological manifestation context.
調合 is preparing or compounding medicine, not the administrative act of filling prescriptions.
“Gets up” omits the explicitly rough, forceful manner that expresses Rin’s anger.
弱っている covers being physically run-down or exhausted, and the surrounding concern is precisely Shirou’s depleted condition. “Exhausted” is defensible.
The next sentence explicitly says Rin is hurrying to catch Shirou, so “dashes down the stairs” is reasonable contextual explicitation rather than unsupported action.
言いつける means to tell or instruct Sakura. “Check on Sakura” changes the immediate intended communication into a welfare check.
The omitted “this morning” is already recoverable from the immediate morning-care context and does not materially alter the fact that the temperature remains unchecked.
時間にしてほんの一分だ has no overt verb marking the minute as elapsed or prospective. The adjacent context permits either time since Shirou left or time needed to visit Sakura.
The Japanese places Shirou’s wheezing stop partway down the slope; the English moves it to the bottom and adds resting.
“The worst part” is a natural emphatic rendering of Rin’s repeated 厄介 construction identifying his unawareness as the troublesome point.

The preceding sentence supports calling Rin the strongest or most energetic, and “natural” reflects 当然. The genuine loss is that the others are temporarily downed comrades, not generically weaker members.
Rider is lying in the bed as a decoy, but the Japanese never says she is asleep. The English adds that state.
“She’s the one causing us the trouble” preserves Rin’s assignment of blame to Sakura; “the one” substantially conveys the exclusivity expressed by 一方的に.
In this angry context, gritting her teeth is a natural English realization of the audible 歯の鳴る音, whose precise physical cause is not otherwise specified.
受け流す includes letting an attack or provocation pass without engagement. “Ignores it coolly” defensibly conveys Rider’s composed nonreaction.
技量 can be rendered as ability or skill, and the explicit contrast with “instincts” still distinguishes trained capability from intuition.
潔い can describe accepting defeat cleanly or gracefully. Given Rider’s surprise that Rin will not resist, “graceful” is contextually defensible.
The sigh is explicitly ostentatious or performed for Rider’s notice; plain “sighs” loses that calculated manner.
“Looks down” adequately conveys the restrained gesture. Omitting the minor degree marker わずかに is not a material mistranslation.
The Japanese locates the distress in Sakura’s lungs and describes labored breathing; “chest hurts” changes both anatomy and symptom.
The English omits Sakura physically pressing down over her chest as she tries to restrain her heart.
“For a while now” reasonably conveys ずいぶん前から. The narrower genuine omission is 慌ただしく, the heart’s frantic manner of signaling.
The English still personifies the heart as protesting, so that part of the accusation is overstated. It does lose the elderly ワシ register and the claim that the heart will die before anything else.
トゲ covers thorns, spines, or sharp needle-like points. “Swallowing needles” is an acceptable rendering of the pain image.
倒れる can mean collapsing or losing consciousness, and the surrounding pages explicitly describe Sakura’s fading consciousness. The English is defensible.
The Japanese visibly pivots from third-person “she” to Sakura’s “I”; the English supplies only first person and loses that focalization shift.
自分に決着をつける means settling matters with herself. “Settle my match” is malformed and fails to identify that reflexive object.

“Stop the old man … even if it costs me my life” preserves the practical substance of 刺し違えてでも: stopping Zouken despite her own likely death. Requiring a literal mutual-kill formulation is preference policing.
食事時 means at mealtime generally. The English invents both nightly frequency and a regular dinner encounter with Zouken.
Singular “scheme” can collectively cover all of Zouken’s plans. The genuine omission is とりあえずは, which makes the ending provisional or limited to the immediate situation.
Here 拒絶 is the refusal Sakura plans to express by saying no to Zouken. “Disobey” is a defensible contextual rendering of that refusal, not a reversal of agency.
Applied to a house, 陰湿 permits a damp, gloomy, dank atmosphere as well as figurative oppressiveness. “Damp” is within its contextual range and not demonstrably a lexical mistake.
回収 treats Sakura instrumentally as something to retrieve or collect. The ordinary relational phrase “wants me back” loses that deliberate objectifying force.
The entire passage is Sakura’s internal reasoning, so the English assertion remains implicitly attributed to her. Repeating “I think” is unnecessary English explicitation.
“No matter how far I run” naturally expresses becoming arbitrarily far away in parallel with hiding. The essential claim—that distance cannot prevent Zouken finding her—remains intact.
としても makes Sakura’s resistant intent hypothetical for the argument. “The possibility that I might resist” accurately preserves that hypothetical status.
The simple present “He only treats me as a tool” naturally describes his established pattern, especially after “always watching” and “never considers.” The history is not materially erased.
If the priest removed some of the worms, their quantity inside Sakura was reduced. The English preserves that causal meaning, and Japanese does not independently establish the alleged plural form.
Omitting さっきから loses a small temporal nuance but does not change Zouken’s already-established awareness of Sakura’s arrival and solitude.
The antecedent of それ is Shirou’s disordered breathing and resulting difficulty running, not his overall fatigue.
Using the rounded figure “five kilometers” for 五キロ近い is normal English approximation in this context and creates no material factual discrepancy.
The English omits Shirou’s explicit resolve to extract the information by force if necessary.
The infinitive “admirable enough to come pray to God” keeps the judgment tied to pious behavior rather than asserting Shirou lacks general worth.
余裕がない can mean lacking emotional composure, and “disturbed” is a defensible observation immediately followed by Kotomine’s separate comment on Shirou’s body.
調整された means adjusted, tuned, or prepared. “Coordinated” is an incorrect and syntactically defective description of Zouken’s modification of the Grail.
In immediate dialogue, “I stop” can naturally mean Shirou stops speaking. It is vaguer than 言葉に詰まる but preserves the speechless pause without contradicting the Japanese.
English ellipsis supplies the antecedent correctly: “you don’t have a reason to [protect her].” That directly preserves そんな理由’s comparison with Shirou’s motive.
The Japanese emphasizes both potential birth and an entity actively striving to be born. “What has not yet come into existence” reduces this to a static absence.
The raw English contains “And[line3]he”; the joined display is caused by stripping the line command, exactly the extraction artifact warned about, not a translation typo.
The Japanese specifically states Zouken’s leakage model, which Kotomine is about to correct. Neutral “appearing through” blurs that technical premise.
“Gate” preserves the ruby reading of 聖杯 but omits the written identification of that Grail/gate as Sakura herself, leaving its source unspecified.
蝕む depicts something invasively eating away at or corroding Sakura; generic “ruining” discards that bodily process.
“Vision wavers” is a natural rendering of the perceptual distortion conveyed by the figurative 視界が軋む. Preserving the literal creaking image is a stylistic preference.
“This is too ridiculous to be true” directly voices Shirou’s rejection, and the following “But” preserves its reversal. An explicit verb meaning “deny” is unnecessary.

The English is awkward but retains a vortex that directs interpretation toward slaughter. The supplied Japanese does not establish the accusation’s proposed paraphrase as the uniquely correct logical parse.
認める can mean recognize, accept, or approve. In contrast with Kiritsugu rejecting the Grail’s evil, “still found the Holy Grail worthy” is a defensible contextual rendering.
In context, “the cause of it” refers back to the witnessed catastrophe and adequately identifies its cause. The loss of the emphatic 全て is not materially misleading.
くべる depicts souls being fed or cast into the cup like fuel. “Receives” removes that sacrificial, fuel-like operation.
“A small amount of poison” accurately conveys the minute quantity emphasized by 一粒. Requiring “one grain” is overly literal.
広大 describes vast extent, not magnificence or worth. The English replaces one side of the depth-and-vastness pairing with an evaluative quality.

The article “a” retains grammatical singularity, so singular number is not wholly omitted. The genuine loss is 一人, whose human counter marks the contaminant as one person rather than an impersonal substance.
“Too narrow” directly preserves the Japanese’s own spatial metaphor for inadequate capacity. Explicating it as capacity would be clearer, but the literal metaphor is not incorrect.
The English gives only the written ontological label “phenomenon” and loses its ruby reading as “thing/entity.”
“Expected baby” is an established English expression for a child not yet born and adequately conveys 出産予定児, despite sounding unusual in this supernatural context.
“Legitimately made” can mean validly or properly made and is compatible with 正しく作られた in this discussion of a properly constituted Grail.
“Its birth” followed by “come into this world” conventionally expresses passing from nonexistence into existence, so the ontological transition is conveyed.
“Birth” plus “come into this world” substantially preserves the combined ideas of being born and beginning to exist, even without reproducing the graphic ruby construction.
“Master” preserves the ruby but loses the written 寄り代, which identifies Sakura technically as the curse’s vessel or host.
“The power is completely succeeded” is not grammatical English for a completed transfer or inheritance and obscures whose succession is being completed.
The English obscures that the Grail itself is an unsuitable vessel; plural “they” most naturally refers only to the curses and therefore misstates the compatibility relation.
“Something” omits 依り代, the technical host/vessel relation central to how the curse acquires form.
“Give it shape” directly conveys 象どれる here. Failure to reproduce the kanji/ruby interplay is a presentation loss, not by itself a material mistranslation.
For a flesh mass, “expanding” is a defensible description of the result of 増殖; it does not establish a materially different event.
The parallel imperatives distinguish demanding the conclusion from Kotomine and ordering himself to comprehend it. “Let me know” makes both requests to Kotomine.

The relative clause grammatically describes Sakura herself as a human raised as a magical circuit. The proposed reading that only the implanted material was cultivated is not established by the Japanese.
The supplied spelling is 触覚, ordinarily “sense of touch,” not 触角, “feeler/antenna.” The accusation substitutes a reading not demonstrated by the witness.
Although awkward, “she still has command” conveys that command remains Sakura’s, and the immediately following Master–Servant explanation clarifies the authority involved.
The English conveys the written 殺人嗜好 but drops the supplied ruby ほうこうせい, which deliberately characterizes the curse's killing impulse as its orientation or directionality.
“Will be given birth” is malformed English and fails to state cleanly that the darkness Sakura carries will itself be born.

The preceding English explicitly identifies the black shadow, and “beneath its darkness” remains a comprehensible reference to that manifested shadow. This is loose wording, not a demonstrated change of identity.
“Clutch my chest” omits the explicit extremity of pressing hard enough to gouge the flesh.
In context, “force myself to breathe” naturally conveys resuming impaired breathing after the shock. The fading-breath image is compressed, but the action is not materially changed.
発生 can mean occurrence or emergence, and the adjacent English immediately speaks of what “has yet to exist.” The birth threshold remains recoverable from the complete passage.
“Created from the host” adequately conveys that the shadow was formed from Sakura, especially after the preceding discussion repeatedly establishes shape and form.
The Japanese says both guilt and punishment are to be assigned. “Punishment for its crime” instead treats guilt as already settled, weakening Kotomine's claim that judgment follows birth.
“Not yet been born” accurately conveys the relevant status of 孵らざる. Omitting the hatching image is not a factual change.
Together with “not yet been born,” “cannot be punished” reasonably expresses that the being cannot yet be held answerable. The alleged temporal relation remains clear from context.
The Japanese denies the existence of a clear definition of evil in human society; the English instead denies the existence of a clearly evil entity.
The English omits the predicate “absolute evil,” leaving Kotomine's rhetorical conclusion materially incomplete.
Kotomine merely refuses to reject the possibility of Sakura's transformation; the English attributes the stronger positive position that she should transform.
“Declaration of hostility” is a defensible functional rendering of 宣戦布告 in this confrontation, not merely an unspecified hostile feeling.
“Embryo” and “fetus” are neighboring developmental terms, and nothing in the supplied context establishes a stage for which this choice produces a material factual error.
俺たち expressly denotes Shirou's side, whereas “I” reduces the surviving alternative to Shirou alone.
The Japanese makes transformation the outcome Kotomine will not force upon Sakura. Coordinating “forcing” and “altering” presents them as separate actions and blurs that relation.
口出しする can mean to object or interject verbally. In this dialogue, “I will not say anything” reasonably conveys that Kotomine will not contest Shirou's interpretation.
“Health” is a natural contextual rendering of concern for Sakura's body, while the joined “healthno” is identified by the supplied caveat as a likely stripped line-command artifact.
After “We're clearly enemies,” the ellipsis in “I still can't tell for certain” plainly concerns Kotomine's allegiance. The alternatives remain inferable without material distortion.
The Japanese explicitly stresses the paradox that Kotomine is advising Shirou despite being his enemy; the English sentence omits that adversarial relation.
In this context 少しでも耐えられる naturally permits “endure ... for a bit,” since the next phrase expressly identifies the resulting short interval. No material distinction is lost.
The genuine loss is that the second entity uses Sakura's body as its vessel. Japanese does not obligatorily mark 刻印虫 as plural, and “baby” is supported by Kotomine's continuing birth analogy.
The explicit condition “if [the controller] fails” is lost, and the English gives the resulting repetition to an unclear impersonal “it.”
アテがある can naturally mean having some hope, prospect, or recourse. Rin is immediately identified as that recourse, so “one hope” is defensible.
容易だろう predicts that the synchronization and mitigation should be easy, not merely possible. “Reaction” also makes the Grail's recoil less specific.
The English retains that persuading Rin must happen upon returning. Omitting the idiomatic emphasis “first thing” is minor compression, not a material error here.
認めない can mean “do not accept/approve,” and 言い分 can be a stated opinion or position. The English is awkward but substantively defensible.
After Shirou says goodbye and Kotomine tells him to wait, “I stop” naturally means stopping his departure. The omitted body-part image does not change the action.
Returning the favor is the natural action by which Shirou cancels the debt he feels he owes. The English preserves the reciprocal logic.

In the argument, the unalterable fact that Sakura ate people supplies the basis for the continuing label “sinner.” The English paraphrases the conduct behind 人食い without materially changing Kotomine's claim.
The immediately preceding 辛かろう frames the alternative in terms of suffering, so “less painful” is a contextually apt rendering of 楽.
The preceding sentence identifies Sakura's offense as killing many people. In context, 奪われた者たち refers naturally to those victims; a broader injured class is not established.
“Must repay the victims with something of equal value” preserves the conditional necessity expressed by saying they will not be appeased without equivalent repayment.
The Japanese externalizes the pressure as every conventional norm continually insisting; “my morals” internalizes it as Shirou's personal ethic and drops the persistence.
すまないという気持ち denotes guilt, apology, or feeling one has wronged the lost; “pity” instead describes compassion directed downward at them.
“Many more” omits the explicit prediction that the death toll will be dozens of times greater.
In this disaster context, “innocent people” is a natural English characterization of people wholly uninvolved in the conflict, not a contradictory substitution.
Despite awkward phrasing, “bleed out of my eyes” can straightforwardly mean blood coming out through the eyes. The context does not require the fatal-exsanguination sense alleged by the finding.
The Japanese itself uses detached comparative fragments, and the next English sentence connects them to humanity surpassing its limits. Reordering “farther” and “wider” is immaterial.
“Definite evil” is neither idiomatic nor equivalent to the categorical “absolute evil” expressed by 絶対の悪.
拾い上げた states that Kiritsugu did pick the discarded thing back up; “trying to” changes the completed action into an attempt.

The omitted object is recoverable from the preceding contrast as the human feelings or capacities Kiritsugu possessed. “Anything” turns that specific congenital deprivation into universal inability to obtain things.
“Have it both ways” reasonably conveys Shirou's insistence on realizing otherwise incompatible outcomes together; Kotomine's criticism already makes the expression pejorative.
後天的 means acquired rather than congenital. “It is posteriori” is malformed and invokes an unrelated epistemological expression.
Once Sakura's mind is gone and her body occupied, “save her” naturally means getting Sakura herself back. The complete sentence preserves that personhood context.

Although “parasite” generalizes the first clause, the next English sentence identifies the main body as a worm and explains its bodily possession. Across the complete page, the insect nature is not lost.
The Japanese identifies a brain worm that functions as the vessel of Zouken's soul. “The worm with his soul” omits both the brain specification and the vessel relation.
“Tiny” replaces the concrete and potentially significant palm-sized scale with indefinite smallness.
陽性 and 陰性 can directly denote positive and negative polarity. The conditional “If Rin is...” also retains the comparison's tentative framework, despite awkward English.
手を出してきた describes making a move against or laying hands on Shirou; neutral “contacted you” removes the hostile intervention.

The Japanese distinguishes withstanding the hatching from the maternal vessel consequently avoiding death. The English collapses this into the tautology “if she survives, she should not die” and omits 母胎.
“Do not let Zouken have her” naturally conveys preventing Sakura from being handed into Zouken's possession. The active-transfer nuance does not produce a material change here.
The English preserves the two relevant propositions: nothing is observably wrong and there is no indication of danger. The more concrete “mixed in” image is nonmaterial compression.
“I have a bad feeling” directly conveys the premonition. Omitting the fleeting bodily metaphor of brushing his back is stylistic compression, not an accuracy error.
“Her room” can naturally mean the room Illya is using, without asserting ownership. The English omits that it is Japanese-style, but no material contradiction is demonstrated.
English possessive location can denote Rin's currently assigned room, including a guest room; it does not necessarily invent permanent ownership. The lost room type is minor here.
The Japanese specifies an intuitive warning that something is missing. Generic “uneasiness” removes the concrete absence that anticipates finding Sakura gone.
“Her figure disappears” accurately reports Rider's vanishing. The illusion simile and abrupt verb add imagery but do not establish a materially different event.
“Has been glaring at me until now” can naturally mean continuously up to just before the present exchange, and the next sentence explicitly says Rider fled when Shirou entered.

The Japanese attributes Rin's coldness to resignation followed by acceptance of an unwelcome outcome. “Cold disinterest” instead characterizes her as lacking concern, while only partially retaining resignation.
ようだから marks Rin's chronology as an inference—Sakura appears to have been absent already. The English presents that timing as certain fact.
“It’s already been two hours” naturally states that two hours have elapsed by now and need not imply stopwatch precision. It adequately conveys もう二時間は経つ.
The English conveys uncertainty but loses the specific failed categorical denial: Shirou cannot bring himself to say that Sakura could not possibly be hiding anything.
“She” identifies Sakura naturally in English. Omitting the postposed あの子 loses a shade of address but does not materially alter Rin’s accusation or relationship to Sakura.
In context, “give up” and “it’s all over” are defensible paraphrases of Rin’s unspoken もういいでしょう and the ending her eyes urge Shirou to accept.

Japanese leaves the understood subject of 納得いくまで unstated, while 言い合ってやる can support arguing it out for Rin’s benefit. “As long as you like” is defensible; the finding cannot establish that Shirou alone controls the endpoint.
Treating the unexpected voice metonymically as an unexpected caller is a natural English paraphrase, especially when the following page identifies Illya.
The sentence-final のか marks Shirou’s tentative self-question. “Must understand” replaces that uncertainty with a substantially more confident conclusion.
決着をつける can mean bringing something to an end, and the very next sentence explicitly says Sakura left 自分を消すため. Rendering the intended settlement as ending herself is contextually supported.
想ってる can mean the Sakura Shirou has in mind, not necessarily an explicit declaration of love. “The Sakura you know” conveys that conception, though it loses the Japanese verb contrast.
The English conveys the substantive point—that Illya is speaking about herself through Sakura. Losing the name/sound formulation is stylistic compression, not a factual mistranslation.
After saying he does not understand complicated matters, 俺にはそれだけだ naturally means that this is the sole consideration that matters to him. “That’s all I care about” is defensible in context.
Japanese depicts Illya as though gazing into the distance. The English instead makes her see off an unspecified distant object, changing the image and action.
“All the running” conveys accumulated exertion. The omitted “since morning” is a minor temporal detail, not a material contradiction or unsupported reading.
Shirou is setting foot on the staircase to the second floor, with the creaking attached to that action. The English assigns the sound to the floor and leaves him merely approaching the stairs.
A skylight is glazing above the landing; “the glass above the landing” is less specific but accurately describes the visible medium and scene.
“Simple” reasonably renders 飾り気のない, while “suited for Sakura” naturally conveys that this quality is 桜らしい. The characterization remains intact.

The apparent concatenation is an extraction artifact where the script’s line-break command was stripped. The archived English preserves two coordinated descriptions, so this is not a translation error.
The English replaces the described reaction with an internal emotional state and entirely omits Sakura turning her face away and twisting her body.
抵抗 is active resistance, not another variety of loathing. Substituting “loathing” erases Sakura’s physical and volitional refusal.
伸ばしかけた marks an action only begun: Shinji had started to extend the hand. “Outstretched” presents it as already fully extended.
“Surprise” is broader and less forceful than 呆然, but it remains within the relevant astonishment range. This is tonal preference rather than a material error.
“Stares resolutely back” naturally communicates that Sakura summons courage to return his gaze. The claim that Japanese specifically depicts a limited reserve is not established.
The Japanese explicitly has Sakura backing away. “Standing before him” removes her retreat and turns a dynamic act of resistance into a static position.
Shinji is venting rage directly at Sakura, and the supplied Original-edition candidate makes the ensuing assault explicit. “On her” is contextually supported, not an unsupported new victim or action.
“His fury is unstoppable” accurately states the meaning of the broken-dam metaphor. Omitting the image is literary compression, not a factual translation error.
“Denied by” can mean rejected or refused by Sakura and retains her as the agent. It is awkward, but it does not necessarily turn the passage into denial of an unspecified possession.
The repeated “he laughs” while mocking Sakura’s futile resistance already conveys enjoyment. Dropping 楽しげに is a minor tonal compression.
恨む here denotes longstanding resentment or a grudge against the world. “Has cursed” instead suggests an unspecified act of cursing and obscures the sustained emotional state.
“Strength floods out of her body” is an idiomatic, vivid rendering of being unable to put strength into the body, reinforced immediately by her loss of will to resist.
