The English generalizes the onomatopoeic snap, but still accurately reports the sudden sound in the air. The lost sound texture alone is not a material error.
The pencil-like “line” is the very fine wound just described, so retaining it as the subject does not change the physical event. The English is clumsy, but its meaning remains recoverable.
The English does repeat the dream basis: first “she saw plenty in her dreams,” then “she saw it in her dream…” The apparent joined text is caused by a stripped line-break command.
The English counterfactual hindsight is a natural reformulation of Sakura concluding that, if the act leaves her feeling nothing, she should have done it earlier. The practical meaning is unchanged.
Japanese explicitly contrasts present 楽しい with past 楽しかった. Repeating only “It was fun” erases the tense distinction that prompts Sakura’s recognition of earlier killings.
The explicit わたし marks Sakura’s inward first-person realization. Changing it to “she” removes that deliberate shift into her immediate self-recognition.
夜な夜な means repeatedly, night after night. “Through the night” instead describes duration within a night and loses the repeated pattern.
The Japanese establishes repeated nightly roaming, whereas “wandered through the night” can describe a single night. This changes the temporal pattern of Sakura’s killings.
The comparative clause describes Sakura herself crumbling more and more as she laughs. The English omits that collapse and transfers the comparison to the quantity of tears.
Japanese says her tears will not stop; the English instead says progressively more tears flow as she laughs. Duration and comparison are materially rearranged.
In this breakdown scene, “regressing mentally” is a defensible contextual rendering of feeling progressively more 馬鹿. It is somewhat clinical but preserves the perceived mental deterioration.
楽 can express comfort, relief, or freedom from strain. “Comforting” is within that contextual range and is not a demonstrable change of state.

The supplied Original-edition candidate explicitly describes her face as contorted by crazed laughter. “Manic grin” is therefore supported by the governing edition, even though the base/all-ages wording is milder.
もう動かない states that the dead Shinji no longer moves. Calling him merely “silent” weakens this explicit physical finality.
The immediately preceding “Fu—Fufu” represents the little giggles denoted by クスクス. The manner is present in the English scene even though the narration does not label it again.
English readily permits an understood object after “killed so many”; in this context it unambiguously means people. No human victims are semantically removed.

The English first identifies it as “her own shadow,” then appositively calls it the black shadow that ate people. That sequence does not clearly assert a wholly separate entity, although it loses the ruby’s explicit self-identification.
Japanese makes Sakura the agent who desperately restrained herself. The English assigns that effort to “someone,” reversing agency and turning self-restraint into external prevention.

The English has not omitted the protective purpose; it moved “trying hard not to turn her into it” onto the preceding “someone.” That reassignment is the separate agency error, but the purpose itself remains expressed.

そんなもの refers to the restraint and companionship just enumerated: Sakura concludes those efforts were all futile. “There was never any hope for her” instead makes an absolute claim about Sakura’s prospects.
Despite awkward wording, “stays as darkness” and “shows up as a presence” communicate that it manifests as a presence without taking visible form. The restriction is recoverable.
Zouken’s preceding line is a declaration, not a question, and 頷くまでもない says it no longer warrants even a nod. The English explicitly invents a question.
苦しい bodily suffering can naturally be summarized as bodily pain, and 楽になった as that pain going away. The later onset of burning pain does not make this immediate relief contradictory.

“She knows” adequately conveys strong certainty, so that accusation is overstated. A narrower error remains: the English omits that her claim to be strongest is specifically scoped to this war/battle.

倒す can include killing, and the supplied Original-edition continuation explicitly imagines gruesomely killing the threatening figures. “Kills” is supported rather than invented; “everyone” naturally summarizes the plural targets.

The governing Original-edition candidate is stronger than ordinary joy, saying the imagined act nearly brings Sakura to climax. “Greatest joy” is therefore not an unsupported intensification for this comparator.
何度も何度も describes Rin recurring again and again in Sakura’s fantasy. “Foremost” expresses prominence instead and discards the repetition.

敬愛 combines affection with esteem and can be rendered contextually as deep love or adoration. “The relative she loves the most” is narrower but remains a defensible translation, not a factual reversal.
“Only been half a day” idiomatically emphasizes that very little time has passed and is a reasonable approximation of “not even half a day.” The small boundary difference is not material here.
From Zouken’s elderly, contemptuous voice, “the Emiya boy” can function as a belittling address. “Brat” or “whelp” would be stronger, but the English is defensible.

The preceding sentence already states that Zouken laughs, so describing him as laughing with a hideous face naturally combines the two Japanese observations. The distortion is softened but not materially contradicted.
“Put her mind to it” means apply deliberate attention or effort. その気にさせる instead means inducing Sakura into the required willingness or state, so the English uses the wrong idiom.
Breaking Sakura down is a defensible contextual rendering of breaching the emotional dam restraining her. The metaphor is lost, but the intended psychological collapse remains.
この世に makes the world itself the object of Sakura’s despair. “Despair in this world” instead most directly locates despair within the world and obscures that target.
“Persistent” can denote continuing to endure despite difficulty and is within the contextual range of 我慢強い. It is less precise than “patient” or “long-suffering,” but not demonstrably false.
“My nerves condense” is non-idiomatic but transparently preserves the Japanese metaphor of nerves drawing into concentrated readiness. This is a fluency problem rather than a material accuracy error.
“I wanted you to betray her” already makes Shirou the person personally performing the betrayal. The instrumental emphasis of おぬしの手で is implicit in the English agent construction.
The blow is delivered through Shirou’s hand, so placing magical energy there is a natural physical explicitation. The loss of ありったけ weakens intensity but does not materially change the action.
The plural worms “have been crushed,” followed by Zouken saying his voice will soon fail, already conveys extensive destruction. Omitting 軒並み is minor compression.

In this exchange, wagging one’s tail means willingly doing Zouken a service, and the next line identifies raising Sakura as the unintended service. “Do anything for you” preserves that conversational point, though not the insult’s imagery.
After killing her brother, “cannot turn back” is an idiomatic contextual rendering of being unable to stop her present course. It does not materially reverse 立ち止まる here.
“That will be the end” conveys the substantive consequence of 詰み—that the position is finished and no effective response remains. Losing the chess/shogi metaphor is stylistic.

“Sorcery” is mirrorMoon’s established localization term for 魔法, used to distinguish it from ordinary magecraft. “Third Sorcery” is therefore a terminology choice, not evidence that the underlying concept was mistranslated.
耳障り can mean irritating or unpleasant to hear, so “annoying” is within range. 哄笑’s loudness is compressed, but the line still describes Zouken’s objectionable laughter echoing.
Zouken is the immediately established source of the laughter, and its audibility is retained. Omitting his repeated name and the room-wide resonance is natural contextual compression.
The Japanese targets 俺たち, not Shirou alone, and 見下す adds literal or figurative looking down on them. “Watching me” loses both the plural target and Zouken’s superiority.

The Japanese fragment establishes that something urgent takes precedence over Zouken’s ravings. “There’s no time to let … drivel get to me” naturally expresses the same immediate prioritization, even though it explicates the transition differently.
“Turned dark” is a defensible direct rendering of 黒化; the supplied Japanese does not establish that a fixed English technical term was mandatory.
“Once” can introduce the same future condition as ～れば, especially in Zouken’s confident warning; it does not necessarily assert that capture is certain.
Given the desperate sprint and fear for Illya, “frantically” is a natural contextual rendering of his single-minded urgency, not necessarily loss of composure.
The English retains the worms but drops the explicit description of them as Zouken’s operative limbs, a meaningful statement about their agency.
“Too much” naturally conveys the regret inherent in 浪費してしまった and the urgent context; no distinct quantified extent is asserted.
In context Sakura is seeking Illya, so “before Sakura finds Illya” defensibly expresses the anticipated face-to-face encounter without materially changing the event.
Saying the gray light “dulls” the red eyes naturally conveys the shadowing effect; the visual meaning is condensed rather than omitted.
The English identifies Illyasviel by name, while the immediately preceding line already describes her silver hair. The surface/ruby information is preserved across the passage.
“Giant cavern” is lexically possible for 大空洞, but the translation genuinely omits the ruby alias “テンノサカズキ” and fails to present the location’s dual name.
The Japanese says activation has begun, whereas “already activated” presents activation as an achieved state.
The English keeps the ruby sense “rules” but omits the written-text identification of the Grail War as a ritual, losing the deliberate dual reading.
The Japanese describes something appearing or coming to dwell inside despite the gate remaining unopened; the English instead makes preexisting contents emerge outward.
滑稽ね is Illya’s explicit judgment that the outcome is ridiculous or absurd, not merely a description of her disbelief.
“Even if she tried” preserves inability but omits the specific contemplated action: going to mediate or arbitrate.
Although awkward and uncommon, transitive “excels her” communicates that Sakura surpasses Illya in Grail ability; the comparison is not materially blurred.
“Completely different” is a natural emphasis of the sharp same-versus-different contrast and does not introduce a demonstrably new kind of distinction.
The Japanese places Illya standing in the courtyard and specifies Sakura reaching toward her shoulder; the English invents sitting on the porch and omits the target.
腕 can focus on the arm or limb in motion, while “her hand stops” is a natural rendering in the established reaching gesture and causes no material action change.
“Watch over” can mean to observe attentively, and “as if to watch over the confrontation” does not necessarily assign Illya a protective role.
Sakura euphemistically says she came to “invite” Illya; “coming for Illya” removes that deliberate framing and anticipates Rin’s accusation of kidnapping.
The English conveys mockery but omits Sakura’s additional accusation that Rin first fixes or categorically decides what Sakura is.
The grammatical object of 守りたがってた is Sakura: the unnamed person wanted to protect her. The English reverses that relationship.
今まで and the repeated “same failure” support an established habitual pattern; “the same mistake you always made” is a defensible paraphrase.
“Takes a step back” is an ordinary concrete rendering of retreating slightly; it does not establish a materially greater retreat.
焦り denotes alarm, impatience, or anxious urgency, not hesitation or indecision. The English changes the state that emboldens Sakura.
The English reduces the class-marked “Knight of the Sword” to a male-coded swordsman and mishandles the description of black corruption.
多少 permits a limited amount of rough handling; “as rough as you like” removes that limitation.
The surrounding passage treats the oily shadow and mud as manifestations of the same substance. Calling it “mud” here is contextually defensible, not a changed agent.
The English omits the striking technical formulation that figures Rin herself as “the Magic Circuit called Tohsaka Rin” being absorbed.
Absent a supplied terminology scheme requiring “magecraft,” generic “magic” is a defensible translation of 魔術 and still attributes the technique to Sakura.
無尽蔵 commonly means inexhaustible, limitless, or infinite; “infinite” is within its normal lexical range, especially beside the bottomless-monster imagery.
The Japanese questions whether even a Servant could defeat Sakura; the English asserts categorical inability and substitutes merely matching her for defeating her.
In context, “she doesn’t have such a thing” naturally conveys that no equivalent supply source has been made or made available to Rin; the tactical conclusion is unchanged.
唇を歪める can describe curling one’s lips into a distorted or malicious smile, and the passage immediately says Sakura smiles at Rin.
The English omits 可愛く, which supplies the taunt’s belittling instruction that Rin flee “cutely.”
“Quickly” reasonably renders 一息のうちに, and covering the whole house necessarily includes the courtyard. The lost escalation is stylistic rather than a material factual error.

“Violates” can render invasive damage in this context, so sexualization is not demonstrable. The narrower error is that the English omits ドロドロに, obscuring the organs’ liquefying or slurry-like corruption.
“Chest heaving” is a normal physical rendering of labored, pained breathing and preserves Rin’s exhausted condition despite not specifying an audible exhalation.
The narration explicitly says Sakura is convinced she will be killed next time, while the English reduces that belief to losing the fight.
The Japanese presents Rin’s conduct as the model Sakura believes she must follow; it does not say Rin previously attempted this killing. The English invents that past attempt.
Japanese 掌 is unmarked for grammatical number. The supplied sentence alone cannot establish that only one palm is intended, so plural English is not demonstrably erroneous.
陰湿 describes something sinister, insidious, gloomy, or malign here. “Damp” substitutes a physical moisture quality for that oppressive character.
A palm is part of the hand, and “pointing her hand” naturally conveys the attack pose without changing its agency or direction.
どれも covers all the separately presented concerns in the yard, not a fixed pair. “Them both” unjustifiably reduces that scope.

The genuine error is omission of the need to treat Rin immediately. Describing her apparent condition as life-threatening is a plausible contextual inference, so that part of the accusation is too strong.
The English reports only silence and omits that Shirou has physically lifted Rin into his arms before receiving no response.
“Gelatinous” is a defensible description of mud that behaves like an elastic liquid, and the following rubber comparison preserves the intended physical paradox.
“I panic and frantically” reasonably conveys 混乱 and being on the verge of 錯乱; the English preserves the threatened loss of composure in natural idiom.
In this taunt, “someone as weak as you” naturally refers to Shirou’s inadequate capability, including his technical skill; it does not clearly assert physical weakness.
The Japanese says Shirou’s fragmented, wildly disordered thoughts stop. Nothing states that he is enraged, so “my rage turns to ice” invents both emotion and metaphor.
慌てる can encompass being flustered, panicked, or confused under pressure. “Confused” is contextually defensible as Sakura’s observation of Shirou’s state.

The witnesses conflict by edition: the designated page has 口を出す, but the supplied raw Original candidate has 叱る, which directly supports the PC branch’s “scold.” Because that raw alignment is expressly uncertified, the accusation cannot be resolved responsibly.
“A chill runs down my back” is a conventional English rendering of the same involuntary shudder and raised-hair reaction, followed by the text’s explicit escalation beyond a chill.
The Japanese supplies precise spinal endpoints—the medulla oblongata and coccyx. “Brain” and “waist” change both anatomical locations substantially.
The apparent “machineis” joining is an extraction artifact: the supplied raw English contains display commands between “machine” and “is Sakura.” It is not source translation prose run together.
“Every cell … screams a warning, trying to defrost” conveys intense, desperate effort even without a separate adverb corresponding to 必死に.
殺意 is explicit killing intent. Generic hostility removes the immediate lethal intent that explains Shirou’s terror.
The Japanese complains that Shirou would not look exclusively at Sakura; “everyone but me” instead implies he attended to everyone while wholly excluding her.
“It tells me” is an awkward but understandable personification of the forbidden thought forming in Shirou’s mind; the denial that the figure is not Sakura remains intact.
先輩の前から消える can idiomatically mean removing oneself from his presence. “Get away from you” is a defensible contextual paraphrase, not necessarily a denial of self-erasure.
“Shadow picture” is an established literal sense of 影絵 and remains intelligible with “stage”; “shadow play” would be more idiomatic but is not uniquely correct.
The Japanese foregrounds Shirou acting with his thoughts in tatters. “By instinct” introduces a different cause for the action and drops that damaged cognition.
弾き飛ばす indicates knocking or sending Rin flying clear; a simple push materially weakens the force and displacement.
The attack explicitly falls from overhead. “Sweeps over me” changes its described trajectory.
“That knowledge wouldn’t let me move my body” is a natural paraphrase of the fact preventing Shirou’s body from being commanded to evade; the guilt-caused paralysis is preserved.
真っ白 describes Shirou’s blank mental state during exposure. The English instead interprets it as the darkness striking him directly, changing the condition of the warning.
“Warmth fades away” omits both the instantaneous speed and the explicit approach to zero body temperature.
The Japanese says every breath brings Shirou close to losing consciousness. The English makes breathing an effort sufficient to render him unconscious, altering both completion and causation.

裏切り explicitly frames Rider’s conduct as betrayal from Sakura’s perspective. “Opposing her” retains the immediate action but loses the relational and emotional force established by Rider’s prior loyalty.
The English drops the explicit restriction to Sakura in her present state, making the acts generically meaningless rather than meaningless for her now.
八つ当たり specifically means directing one’s anger at other targets; “throwing a tantrum” loses that displaced-aggression relation.
大人しく explicitly promises quiet, compliant accompaniment, an important condition of Illya’s offer that “I’ll go with you” omits.
“Without emotion” is a defensible contextual rendering of 淡々と, which can describe dispassionate or affectless delivery; the Japanese does not establish the alleged overstatement.
The English conveys inability but entirely omits Shirou’s attempt to marshal all his conscious faculties despite his condition.
The genuine loss is the irresistible-force nuance of 仕方がない. English plural “them” can contextually cover the people denoted by みんな, so loss of universal scope is not demonstrated.
乗ってあげます marks a knowing, volitional decision to go along; “fall for” instead represents Sakura as deceived by the smooth talk.
The omission of Shirou remaining on his knees is genuine and materially weakens his incapacity. Calling “Sakura!” a scream is plausible from the punctuation and need not be treated as unsupported.
The condition is simply Shirou being before Sakura; English adds the narrower requirement that he actively obstruct her.
“Sakura leaves” is a concise, defensible rendering of her receding in this departure scene; loss of the progressive image is stylistic compression, not a factual reversal.
In context, “take Sakura’s hand” naturally includes grasping and leading her away, so it defensibly conveys the attempted action expressed by 手を引っ張る.
Japanese names nausea and chills as separate symptoms. “Cold nausea” conflates them and is not a normal equivalent for 悪寒.
だった makes Saber’s silence a preceding state; English instead attaches silence to her present sword-pointing immediately after she has spoken.
Both versions give a figurative disappearance into the shadow. “The shadow” is contextually Sakura’s, and changing the visual simile from sinking to fading is acceptable paraphrase.
A cut-string puppet’s limbs falling produces the whole-body collapse expressed in English; “my body drops” is a natural non-contradictory generalization.
The separated Japanese fragments form くそ, while the separated English fragments “Da” and “mn” form “Damn.” The finding mistakes intentional interrupted presentation for corruption.
目蓋に焼き付いて離れない is an image persisting before one’s eyes or in memory; “sticks in my mind” is a normal idiomatic paraphrase.
胸に刻む is conventionally rendered “keep firmly in mind” or “take to heart”; “Please keep that in mind” preserves the injunction adequately.
The English preserves that she served as Shirou’s sword through the very end. The benefactive nuance of くれた adds appreciation but its non-explicitation is not a material error.
“A meaning to why you survived” is awkward but defensibly expresses purpose or significance in the fact of survival; it need not assert a mechanical cause.
Japanese predicates meaning as a consequence of having survived; English instead adds a reason that Shirou “must keep living,” changing the logical object of that meaning.

The rescue-seat metaphor describes one person’s salvation becoming possible through everyone else’s sacrifice; stating that one person was saved conveys the contextual result without a material contradiction.
“Superhero” is a defensible localization of 正義の味方, and “can save anyone” is within the normal range of 誰をも救える.
Despite awkward wording, “denied his battle because it was wrong” naturally means repudiating the battle as wrong, not denying that it occurred.
“Was left alone” need not imply deliberate abandonment and naturally describes the result of Kiritsugu’s death: the formerly shared path became Shirou’s alone.
In context, “leaving the dream to you” defensibly conveys Kiritsugu dying with his dream and hopes invested in Shirou; no material agency reversal is established.
The apparent joining results from stripped line-break or dash commands; the underlying English deliberately separates “Yeah” from “I’m relieved.”
今までの自分 denotes Shirou’s identity or self up to this point, not merely the totality of his past actions.
English loses the written 罪/read ツケ debt–sin overlay as well as 必ず’s certainty and the emphasis on Shirou himself being judged.
“Using all my life” is unidiomatic English, but it still communicates devoting one’s entire life to continuing atonement; no material mistranslation is established.
English omits the explicit worm-damage simile and weakens the pointed contrast between the killed self and the still-living self being eaten away.
The English preserves only the ruby reading “shield” and entirely loses the simultaneously written image of a saint’s burial.
English omits the governing condition that erosion continues for as long as the arm remains attached, and also drops 確実に’s certainty.
The defensible core “lived seeking revenge” does not preserve だけ or the image of revenge sustaining her heart. The added “but” is a plausible contextual connection, not demonstrably false.
The swallowed words are the proposal “let’s live together.” English misattaches “so that we could live together” as the purpose of swallowing them, reversing the relation.
“What about the match is decided?” is grammatically malformed and fails to express the clear defiant relation “So what if the outcome is decided?”
The apparent run-together text is an extraction artifact, but the English still reduces “why is Kotomine here?” to merely recognizing or questioning his name.
“Dead on your feet” strongly denotes extreme exhaustion or debilitation, and the following explicit risk of two corpses supplies the medical severity.
“There’s nothing wrong with my body” is the direct natural equivalent of Shirou’s present self-assessment 体に異状はない; the continuing arm condition does not invalidate that translation.
“Energy” can naturally mean physical stamina, but English wrongly makes that energy itself what the shadow swallowed and omits the large amount being shaved away.
“Three in the morning” is reasonable conversational rounding of 三時過ぎ, especially beside the approximate twelve-hour duration; no material timing error follows.
長椅子 is a bench, couch, or other long seat suitable for lying down, not an ordinary chair.
In contrast with “magical energy,” ordinary “energy” naturally denotes Shirou’s bodily stamina and preserves the distinction sufficiently.
“The land is good for her” is a natural, if broad, way to convey that the Tohsaka soil suits or is compatible with Rin.
昼 can denote daytime or the afternoon period as well as noon; “tomorrow afternoon” is within its contextual lexical range.
Japanese nouns do not obligatorily mark number, and 吸血種 can refer collectively to vampire-kind. “Home to vampires” is therefore defensible.
一晩 specifically means one night or overnight, whereas “for a day” gives a different duration.
減らず口 denotes persistent impudent backtalk; describing Rin as returning to her “impudent self” is a natural metonymic paraphrase in this joke.
踏み止まる can figuratively mean holding back or hesitating as well as physically stopping; the English fits Shirou’s resolve to act immediately.
相手 denotes the opposition he expects to face, and the next page immediately enumerates several people; plural “these people” is reasonable contextual explicitation.

The preceding lines enumerate Sakura, Saber, Zouken, and Assassin as the assembled opposition. “All my enemies” loses the board metaphor but conveys the tactical inference without a demonstrated factual error.
勝敗が決した means that winning and losing—the victor and outcome—are settled. “The victor is decided” is a defensible equivalent here.
刻印虫 is not morphologically marked for number in Japanese; this sentence alone cannot establish that singular English contradicts the governing witness.
“I stop” naturally conveys 足が止まる in English; specifying the feet would be optional bodily imagery, not omitted event information.
私程度 means someone of Kotomine’s level or capabilities. Referring to “my powers” conveys why his participation should help, though it trims the dry self-deprecation.
In this context, “I’m happy for any help” idiomatically means that additional assistance is welcome and unobjectionable; it does not materially alter Shirou’s position.
相容れぬ covers being unable to reconcile, agree, or understand one another. “We can never understand each other” is narrower but defensible in context.
“Mutual benefit” is a standard contextual expression of aligned interests: each party benefits because their interests temporarily coincide.
Modern English “they” may be singular and gender-neutral, so it does not establish that the one referent of ヤツ was changed into multiple opponents.
Japanese says Shirou can no longer see any meaning or significance in getting up; English instead says he lacks will and desire, changing existential justification into volition.
English narrative present commonly renders Japanese past-tense narration, and “ends here” still presents the endpoint as reached before the following denial that it began.
Although なにより is literally “above all,” the following claim that the war never began undercuts the statement that it ended; “or rather” is a defensible rendering of that rhetorical progression.
少なからず is emphatic litotes meaning a considerable or no-small connection; “some relation” materially weakens its stated degree.
The English preserves their joint departure but omits the explicit impression that they act as though they had arranged it together without speaking.
Not looking at each other naturally entails not seeing each other’s expressions. The English generalization loses a small image but does not change the guarded interaction materially.
The page later establishes the car and that Kotomine arranged it, so transportation is not wholly omitted. The urgent speed expressed by 飛ばして is genuinely absent.
“Car” is an accurate hypernym for 黒塗りの外車. Omitting its color and foreign make reduces descriptive specificity but does not create a material factual error.
協力する can mean helping someone as well as mutual cooperation; after Kotomine offers assistance, “how are you going to help me?” is normal contextual explicitation.
得体の知れない can describe someone suspicious, mysterious, or of unknown character. “A suspicious student” is within its lexical range from a taxi driver’s perspective.
The explicit 淡々と characterizes Kotomine’s matter-of-fact delivery of a grim contingency; English reports only that he gives orders and loses that tonal information.
A stick-like object is conventionally long and thin, and the adjacent description confirms a slender, lengthened weapon. This is reasonable visual explicitation, not unsupported reshaping.
The ruby explicitly reads 細剣 as レイピア, so “like a rapier” directly preserves the supplied Japanese rather than inventing a classification.

A dagger “made into a sword” naturally conveys lengthening it beyond dagger size, especially after the object has already been identified as a slender sword; the omitted 長剣 is not materially misleading.
In ordinary firearms context, 鉛弾 is naturally rendered “bullets”; the generic English does not necessarily assert that every conceivable projectile material is ineffective.
Lack of relevant training is a reasonable contextual explanation of why submachine guns would be hard for Shirou to handle, and it does not contradict 扱い辛い.
“About a kilo” is an ordinary approximation encompassing a weight slightly below one kilogram; it does not assert an exact kilogram.
Absent a mandated English terminology scheme, “magic” is a normal broad translation of 魔術, and the sentence still clearly distinguishes it from sacrament.
専売特許 is idiomatic here for the Church’s specialty or stock-in-trade; “exclusive right” wrongly frames expertise as an entitlement or monopoly.
Using one’s magic “on that sword” naturally conveys applying it to the weapon, including its blade. The layering image in 載せる is compressed but not materially contradicted.
“We’ll think about that after we get there” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of dealing with the possibility if it proves real; it does not materially contradict Kirei’s pragmatic acceptance.
The Japanese promises only that they can find some clue about Sakura’s destination, while “find out where” presents the destination itself as discoverable.
Although 短く marks the breath as brief, a deep breath is naturally understood as a short, bounded action; the English preserves the substantive action without a material distortion.
あっち denotes the opposing side, so explicating it as plural “they” and saying that side “has Saber” is natural English, not an invented possessive group.
The English omits the defining circumstance that Sakura has become “like that,” weakening Shirou’s concern about how to face her transformed state.
From Shirou’s viewpoint, 衛宮の家 is his home; “my house” identifies the same destination without changing ownership or household membership.
おまえの方が is explicitly comparative and naturally means that Shirou understands it better than Kirei does. The English comparison is supported.
“Let it go this time” closely conveys 今回は諦めろ, and the following sentences make clear that Kirei is postponing the confrontation rather than permanently abandoning Sakura.
こちらで means protection by their side or group, whereas “under your care” specifically assigns Illya to Shirou, an actor and custody relation the Japanese does not state.
猶予 is additional time or leeway. “We will have our chance” instead asserts an opportunity and does not communicate that rescuing Illya buys time.

In immediate context Sakura has threatened to kill Illya, and the coordinated next clause explicitly names Sakura. “I won’t let her die” is a natural rendering of the passive-causative commitment, not a material change of agency.
二時間強 means more than two hours, not exactly two; the quantitative excess is dropped.
The English remains explicitly conditional. Omitting the emphatic low-probability nuance of 万が一 does not make the fight expected.
“Black Sakura” functions intelligibly as an adjectival label for Sakura in her blackened state. Capitalization and nominal compression do not establish a material categorical change.
The question naturally echoes the preceding English term “Black Sakura.” Although 黒化 is literally blackening, the exchange still challenges what Kirei means by that state.
繋ぎとめる specifically means keeping Sakura’s psyche tethered or from slipping away. Generic “protect” removes the continuity mechanism central to Kirei’s explanation.
その refers directly to the just-described act of tethering Sakura’s psyche. “Protect her mind” repeats the broader mistranslation and loses that reference.
“Slowly turning” preserves the ongoing gradual transformation. 刻一刻と adds a moment-by-moment emphasis, but its omission is not a materially different temporal claim.
共感 has the lexical sense “sympathy” as well as affinity or correspondence. In this metaphysical context the wording is awkward, but it is not demonstrably an emotional-compassion claim.
胎内 specifically means the womb or uterine interior. “From her body” removes the literal pregnancy premise Kirei is rejecting.
For a supernatural entity, “energy” is a defensible contextual rendering of metaphorical 栄養, the sustenance Sakura supplies. The biological metaphor is softened but the operative meaning remains.
Here 実像 contrasts with a formless entity and can naturally be rendered as concrete “form.” Requiring “real image” would be lexical preference rather than a demonstrated error.
“Host” is within the contextual range of 依り代 for a person through whom an entity is sustained and manifested. The surrounding sentence supplies the relevant anchoring function.
大頭脳たる modifies 魔法陣: it is a magic circle functioning as the great brain. “The magic circle and the brain” grammatically coordinates them as separate items.
“Summon … into” adequately conveys 降霊させる in context. The repeated Grail terminology is also present in Japanese and distinguishes the summoned Grail from the human-prepared receptacle through syntax.
The English is repetitive, but so is the Japanese contrast between humanly caused and human-made cause. Awkwardness and retained abstraction are not factual mistranslation.
The supplied ruby explicitly gives 起動式 the reading まほうじん (“magic circle”), so “magic circle” is directly licensed by the Original witness.

犯している permits “invading” or “violating,” and locating a supernatural invasion in Sakura’s body is a reasonable explicitation given the bodily markings in context. It does not expressly deny psychological effects.
遠坂 can denote the Tohsaka house or lineage, and “supervisors of this land” substantially conveys its formal management role. The plural family wording does not create a contradictory authority.
Saying the successor “should know” naturally compresses the inference that the information should have been taught to her; no competing source of knowledge is asserted.
A singular predicative role can apply distributively to two people: both are to be used and discarded in the capacity of the Holy Grail. The English does not necessarily merge them into one vessel.

起動式 is explicitly read as “magic circle” elsewhere on the supplied pages, and 成就 can mean its completion or realization. Context makes this the ritual circle’s successful completion, not mere construction.

The raw witness contains a line-dash command between “Sakura” and “no.” The fused “Sakurano” is the warned-about command-stripping artifact, while the underlying translation retains the self-correction.
“Unlike Zouken” expressly scopes “no wish” by comparison, preserving the statement that Kirei lacks a wish like Zouken’s rather than denying every possible desire.
私とて例外なく means that even Kirei is no exception. “I will die just like everybody else” is a normal explicitation of that comparison, not unsupported new information.
The rhetorical ではないのか advances Kirei’s conclusion strongly, and “it must be” is a defensible English rhetorical formulation. “The desire” also preserves the single focus of 一念 in substance.
得る can be rendered “earn,” and “just by existing” immediately makes clear that no labor or moral merit is required. The sentence’s governing proposition is preserved.
The Japanese distinguishes learning what is enjoyable from possessing a faculty that accepts what is right. The English makes both objects of “learn” and omits the stated faculty.

In context, “the person’s knowledge” can denote what the person has learned, and the preceding English already describes that developmental learning. The lexical shift does not materially reverse the argument.
“The ‘self’ that raised you” can naturally mean one’s own self shaping or cultivating oneself; generic second person does not require a separate external actor.
“Receiving birth” is unnatural English, but it still plainly communicates that being born carries no guilt. This is a fluency defect, not a material accuracy error.

魔 can contextually be rendered as “evil,” so the entity-versus-abstraction accusation is not conclusive. A narrower aspect error remains: 生まれようとしている is trying or about to be born, while “will be born” makes the outcome categorical.
In this context, freeing Sakura “from Zouken” naturally means freeing her from his control. The English does not state that control is the only form of exploitation involved.
“Lives that cannot coexist” is a natural abstract rendering of two incompatible living beings or existences, especially parallel to the preceding abstract 思想. It preserves their irreconcilability.
The preceding “right now” supplies the situational scope, and “an ally better than anyone” conveys that no available ally surpasses him. The comparison is awkward but not materially globalized.
“After twelve tries, I finally found” can conventionally mean success on the twelfth attempt; it does not necessarily posit a thirteenth taxi.

The immediately preceding and following English sentences both identify the forest as the destination. Calling it “the outskirts” in the intervening sentence avoids repetition without losing where Shirou is going.
In combat context, “no way to match the shadow” means no way to contend with or overcome it, a defensible paraphrase of having no way to break the deadlock.
The English omits the essential qualification that Sakura has become “like that,” reducing Shirou’s question about facing her transformed state to a generic question about acting on her.
二時間強 specifies more than two hours; the English removes that quantitative excess.
“The scene Illya showed me” directly expresses that Illya enabled the viewing. The later reference to seeing through her eyes supplies the precise mechanism.
Because the prior sentence explicitly says Shirou saw the castle through Illya’s eyes, “just like I remembered” naturally refers to that earlier vision and preserves its unchanged appearance.
“No watch anywhere” accurately generalizes the absence of guards at both walls and gate. It compresses spatial detail but does not make a false claim or obscure the tactical point.
二階から上 explicitly includes the second floor and higher floors. The English restricts the preferred window to the second floor alone.
門 is a gate, particularly in this castle context. “Back door” changes the proposed point of entry to a different architectural feature.
The Japanese says Sakura or her magical energy is afflicted or invaded by the markings. “The crest took control” turns that condition into completed agency and domination not stated here.

“Lower grounds” is awkward, but within the castle it remains understandable as lower levels, and the next sentence identifies the first floor. This is chiefly an idiom problem, not a material factual error.
The Japanese explicitly makes rescuing Illya a prerequisite to confronting Sakura. The English omits that required sequence.

“Come across a storeroom” is a reasonable narrative compression of finding and entering a storage-like room; the following page unmistakably places Shirou inside it. The firm noun is also supported by his immediate storage-room inference.
Epistemic “must be” expresses an inference from the clutter rather than established certainty, which is compatible with Shirou’s tentative 物置なのか.
The English omits the incidental fact that the room is stone-built, but this descriptive compression does not materially alter the room, action, or inference under dispute.

The English compresses the basis on which Shirou remembers Sella’s name, but supplying the correctly recognized name is normal narrative economy and does not create unsupported knowledge material to the scene.
世話係 covers caretaker or attendant, and “servant” is contextually defensible for Sella’s household role. It does not negate her caregiving duties.
The bow and Sella’s highly formal speech already convey pointed politeness. Omitting an explicit adverb for 慇懃 is a tonal compression, not a demonstrable material error.
淡々と can mean dispassionately or without outward emotion. “Talks without emotion” is somewhat strong but remains within the phrase’s contextual range.
The Japanese makes the words Shirou intended to ask seize up, specifically indicating failed speech. “I freeze” transfers the reaction to his whole person and omits the arrested question.
息を呑む describes catching one’s breath. “Bothers me” replaces that immediate physical reaction with a different emotional judgment.
“It feels like they’re sisters” remains explicitly an impression rather than a factual assertion. Dropping か何か does not make literal sisterhood certain.
“Servant” is a contextually acceptable broad rendering of Sella’s attendant or caretaker role and does not erase the appeal to her responsibility toward Illya.
“How rude” reasonably conveys Sella’s rebuke of Shirou’s undue familiarity. It is broader than 気安い but pragmatically accurate in this exchange.
In context, “freed” naturally means gotten out of the dangerous castle, matching the causative 逃がす. It need not imply formal release from imprisonment.
A dagger 飛来した is a projectile sent flying toward Shirou; “fired at me” naturally explicitates its trajectory, confirmed by the immediate hit, without committing to a specific firing apparatus.
“My legs give way” can describe momentary buckling or staggering and does not require collapse. Shirou’s subsequent retreat is compatible with 足がよろける.
目を眩ませ describes severe pain dazzling or blinding Shirou. “Pain wracks my body” relocates the stated effect from his vision to generalized bodily pain.
The Japanese presents a white skull mask appearing to float in darkness. The English instead makes a skull emit light and omits that it is a mask.
“A dagger has pierced my chest” conveys penetration and the continuing injury. Omitting the intensifier 深々と loses degree but does not materially change the wound described.
Japanese honorifics are not obligatorily reproduced individually in English, and the detached “the magus” can carry the pointed register here. The accusation is honorific-preservation preference.
Japanese 手 is not grammatically marked as singular here and can refer generically to one or both hands. The supplied Japanese cannot establish the accusation that exactly one hand was used.

Rendering Taiga’s third-person self-reference as “I” is normal English conversion; the mock-parental claim remains intact, so treating the lost “big sister” wording as a factual mistranslation is too strong.
“Without dying” already means reaching the ending with zero deaths; “even once” would add emphasis, not a distinct challenge condition.
“Determined” loses the explicitly masculine, valorous dojo register of 漢気, reducing a characterful requirement to generic resolve.
English “you” may be plural, while “wish you luck” is a normal rendering of 健闘を祈る. The accusation demands unnecessary literal martial phrasing.
The supplied mirrorMoon page is not blank: it renders the cry as “AhAh, ahah.” The alleged total omission does not exist.
The supplied mirrorMoon page renders the cry as “AhAh, ahah”; line-command flattening explains the joined presentation, not an omission.
The supplied English contains “Hauh, ahahh, ah!” and therefore does not omit the active cry.
The cry is present as “Ah…… Ua… ah… aaahh, ah……”; the finding attacks a nonexistent blank page.
The English explicitly renders this cry as “Uh…… Ah… ah… ah……!”
The English explicitly renders the cry as “AhAhhh, ahhhh……!!!!”; its joined typography is not omission.
空間 denotes one constructed space here, whereas “rooms” introduces an unsupported plural and changes the immediate setting.
The decisive error is “burned away”: 崩壊していく says the space collapses. “Meaningless” can cover some of the two purposelessness phrases, so the omission claim should be narrowed.
本来 states an inherent nature: the shadow ordinarily has no real form. “Formerly shapeless” instead creates a past state and suggests that condition has ended.
“Figure” is defensible because this sentence leaves the subject implicit, but the English does omit 立ち, changing standing hunched over into simply curling up.
“Desolate” is immediately explicated by “Nobody has lived here,” so the lack of inhabitants is preserved across the complete page. “Forgotten by everyone” is a defensible rendering of 永く忘れられた.
“The shadow’s kingdom” is an ordinary English rendering of the Japanese genitive 影の国 and does not necessarily assert stronger sovereignty.
The Japanese locates the incompatibility specifically in embodied existence “in this world.” “Having a physical form” broadens it into embodiment as such.
“Engulfed” defensibly conveys cognitive takeover, but it loses のみ: her thinking is being narrowed to bodily pain and the destructive impulse alone.
自己を苛む苦しみ is not necessarily a distinct psychological category; it can restate the suffering afflicting her. Given the preceding 肉体の痛み, “physical pain” is a defensible condensation.
“Pain” can naturally denote emotional anguish in “the pain of having her existence denied.” Requiring “tragic grief” overstates the lexical distinction.
猛毒 specifies extremely virulent or deadly poison; unmodified “poisonous” materially weakens its severity.
“Deep-sea” is not invented: the supplied ruby assigns 異界 the reading しんかい. The English chooses that authored layer, even though it does not preserve the surface/ruby wordplay.
The English retains loss of sanity but omits the separately stated loss or forgetting of self.

The English twice identifies her pain and says she keeps appealing to the world about it. Changing the embedded fragment into indirect narration is a defensible structural paraphrase, not omission of the complaint.
The English represents the indifferent outside world but omits the second relation: that the world does not understand her.
Using “she” for the known female referent is normal English explicitation. The sentence’s more consequential point—that her identity as Matou Sakura persisted—is preserved.
“The vessel” omits 肉 and therefore loses the explicit bodily or fleshly nature of the vessel Zouken expects Sakura to become.
“Cowardice” lies within the ordinary range of simply lacking 度胸, especially in Zouken’s contemptuous characterization.
抱え込む describes taking in and retaining the Servants; “controls” instead suggests active command. The surrounding lines emphasize captivity and keeping them alive.
The English replaces the specifically named Lesser Grail with generic “Holy Grail,” obscuring the stated Lesser/Greater Grail relation.
“Tool” is authorized by the ruby reading どうぐ, so it is not an invented replacement. The narrower loss is that the surface text 聖杯 (“Grail”) and its dual reading disappear.
English “immortality” conventionally encompasses not aging and not dying; the Japanese compound need not be mechanically split into two English properties.
The Japanese expressly distinguishes general hostility from murderous intent. “People with hostility” erases the specifically lethal trigger.
The English removes both Assassin’s epistemic qualification (“I do not think”) and 唯々諾々, which specifies meek, unquestioning compliance.
殺気 is killing intent or a murderous aura, not generic hostility. That distinction matters in Assassin’s description of approaching Sakura.
“Laughs” accurately conveys the event; 呵々 adds hearty or loud manner, but demanding “guffaw” is a minor tonal preference rather than a material error.
The indirect English retains Zouken as the addressee through “me,” but it omits Sakura’s quoted “Grandfather,” an explicit familial address tied to his eleven-year regression taunt.
壺毒 with the reading こどく names the poison-jar ordeal, not ordinary solitude. “Pain and solitude” discards the concrete ritual-horror reference.
“Begging for her life” is a plausible contextual rendering of her life-or-death desperation, but the English genuinely omits that she appeals specifically to her grandfather.
作品 means Zouken’s work or creation; “masterpiece” adds an unsupported judgment that it is his supreme work.
ついてこなかった means Sakura’s psyche failed to keep up with the conditioning or bodily development. Adding “follow me” wrongly makes Zouken the object and suggests personal disobedience.
無情 can mean unfeeling or emotionless; “emotionlessly” is a defensible description of Assassin’s cold gaze, not neutralization of a clearly distinct meaning.
The referent of アレ is plainly Sakura, so supplying “her” is normal English pronoun explicitation rather than unsupported identification.
The Japanese reports Illya meekly nodding assent. “She does not mind what we do” instead asserts broad indifference and removes the observable, potentially coerced agreement.
本来の姿になって means become or assume her proper form. “Keep her original form” reverses that change into preservation of her current state.
Japanese omits the object, with Illya supplied by context. English “them” can function as singular, gender-neutral reference and does not demonstrably pluralize the target.
Although awkward, “cannot take it back” communicates that Illya’s death would be irreversible. This is an English-style complaint, not a factual reversal.

The raw English places a line-break/dash command between “duty” and “Assassin.” Their fusion in the supplied flattened display is an extraction artifact explicitly warned about, not a translation error.
“Hurried out” is a defensible rendering of 飛び出した in a sentence that also preserves “without hesitation.” “Burst out” would be stronger but is not required for accuracy.
手をすり抜け is idiomatic here: the intruders evade Zouken’s control or defenses. “Slipped through the unwary magus’s guard” preserves that contextual sense.
Cooperating with Zouken’s side is contextually implicit, and “even if he doesn’t force her” retains the voluntary contrast of 自分から. The supplied English is a defensible explicitation.
“Land of the origin” retains only a vague source notion and omits 心臓, the explicit heart imagery identifying the ritual site.
“Two dark figures emerge” adequately conveys the darkness taking visible form from the black swamp. Omitting the exact pool-bottom detail is minor spatial compression, not a material error.
The Japanese deliberately makes both the joy and pain dark. Bare “Pleasure” loses the ominous emotional quality and the paired 昏い／暗い contrast.
なんて supports an incredulous, contemptuous fragment, for which a rhetorical English question is natural. “He came to be eaten?” preserves the mocked initiative in context.
The hound does not literally transform into wind; 突風となって figuratively conveys its sudden speed. “Disappears with a sudden gust” is a defensible naturalization of that image.
In context, “who that is” refers to the person Berserker is confronting. It conveys his inability to identify the target without needing the noun “opponent.”
笑い声 explicitly denotes audible laughter, and くすり specifies a small chuckle. “She smiles” changes the sound into a silent expression.
The English omits Sakura’s continuing state of being wrapped or clothed in shadow as she leaves.
The dead character is Shirou, already rendered as “he” in the preceding English line. Supplying his gender in the diagnosis is ordinary contextual explicitation.

The Japanese leaves the opponent unstated, and the supplied dojo page does not establish whether English “them” has a singular or plural antecedent in the preceding bad-end scene. The causal wording is awkward but understandable.
“Join hands with someone” is established English for cooperating or teaming up. It may be less idiomatic tactically, but it accurately conveys 手を組む.
The Japanese specifically invokes the standard formula of shōnen manga; generic “a manga” removes the genre that defines the joke.
“Everyone’s part of the family” naturally conveys the inclusive maxim 人類みな兄弟 in comic English; it does not materially alter the intended universal fraternity.
“Don’t talk too honestly” is awkward but preserves the joke that Illya has stated the candid truth aloud. The accusation is stylistic rather than a demonstrable meaning error.
The complete English sentence explicitly says the castle was seen “through Illya’s eyes”; “just like I remembered” therefore refers to that shared vision rather than replacing it.
“No watch anywhere” generalizes the walls-and-gate detail but preserves the operative fact that the castle has no guards. The lost escalation is not a material contradiction.
The condition is reversed: 気付かれている means they may already have been detected, whereas the English says the defenders do not know they are there.
正門 is the castle’s main gate, not an ordinary front door; the English changes a significant architectural entry point.
通じる相手ではない means such a leisurely method would not work against this enemy. “They aren’t the sort to fall for” is a natural contextual paraphrase, not necessarily an invented deception.
有無を言わせぬ means extracting Illya without allowing objection or resistance. “Escape immediately” conveys speed but omits that coercive condition.
にやりとした声 describes audible pleased or amused affect; “A happy voice,” reinforced by 楽しげ in the next sentence, is broad but defensible rather than factually wrong.
“This tone” refers directly back to the preceding “A happy voice,” so the emotional quality remains available across the complete page rather than being omitted.
“Walking down the street” is a standard English idiom for walking along an ordinary road; “down” does not necessarily introduce downward movement.
だからこそ makes the slow pace the reason for Kirei’s weighty stability. English “slow, but stable” instead presents stability despite the slowness and omits ズッシリ’s physical weight.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 足場 as ポイント, authorizing “points.” The English may be technical or terse, but it does not replace the authored terminology without basis.
“The sword” identifies the already established weapon; repeating that Kirei lent it is redundant contextual information, not a material omission on this page.
The ruby reads 壁 as いし (“stone”), so describing the rough masonry as “rocks” is not unsupported invention, though “stonework” would be more precise.
“A puzzle of improvisation” is somewhat stiff but accurately conveys a puzzle full of improvised decisions. This is style criticism, not a factual error.
In this climbing context, “target” can naturally denote the intended hold or placement; it does not materially add an external target.
Construing 力加減 as gripping force is plausible, but “handle” is unsupported and misidentifies the wall hold.
The English excludes the expressly stated middle slopes and therefore narrows the normal climbing region materially.
In the mountain context, “high places” defensibly conveys 高層. The surviving problem is the awkward plural–singular agreement in “high places are ... a sacred place.”
“Not enough oxygen” directly conveys oxygen becoming insufficient; omission of the intensifier 絶対的に does not create a material factual change.
Although 無酸素 is not repeated in the last English sentence, the immediately preceding oxygen-shortage and oxygen-deprivation statements supply the defining condition.
“A scratch would turn into necrosis” is awkward but can naturally mean that the injured area becomes necrotic; the consequence remains intact.
The English entirely omits the progressive loss of bodily function with every step, a substantive part of the described extremity.
In climbing language, using the fingers only to the first joint reasonably corresponds to relying on the fingertips or distal finger segments.
“Small foothold” loses the explicit extreme that it is not even toe-sized, materially weakening the precariousness.
The Japanese specifically invokes a wall-clinging lizard; changing it to a spider alters the stated animal image and joke.
The raw witness contains a line-command between “Hey” and “are”; the apparent concatenation results from command stripping, not the translated script.
Grabbing the wall with both hands and then swinging naturally implies supporting or suspending himself by those hands; the action is not materially changed.
“Swing my body at the window” omits both the pendulum comparison and the repeated back-and-forth buildup before entry.
許容範囲 is a judgment of tolerability, not whether the danger matched an expectation; the English substitutes a different evaluative standard.
“False smile” is a normal rendering of a consciously put-on or artificial smile and need not imply malicious deception.
The English drops the explicit callback to Illya’s face at their first meeting and also substitutes coldness for composed self-presentation.
“Slap her across the cheek” states the same action and does not inherently imply great force; omission of the sound effect alone is not a material error.
The English omits “even Shirou,” erasing Illya’s concession that his privileged closeness normally grants him special latitude.
“Bad girl” is a defensible colloquial rendering of 不良娘; the accusation’s specifically daughter-like interpretation is not grammatically required.
English “but” preserves the central concessive opposition between happiness at seeing Illya and genuine anger; the alleged logical loss is overstated.
The simplification to “I’m really angry” removes the explicit image of his blanked-out mind itself nevertheless sustaining the anger.
Being unwilling to remain in the present situation is a defensible contextual reading. The genuine loss is 少しでも, which says even the slightest reluctance suffices.
嫌 can cover dislike or hatred, so the lexical accusation is too rigid. “I’m not hating it” is nevertheless an unnatural progressive rendering of her denial.
“Is made to be” can describe what the body was designed or constituted to be; it does not necessarily assert ongoing creation.
Japanese leaves the user of the Grail’s power implicit, and Illya is the natural contextual subject; supplying “I” is ordinary English explicitation.
In this discussion of sacrificing herself for Sakura, “someone else” is a contextually defensible realization of the broad 何か rather than an unsupported invention.
Here sacrificing Illya herself as the Grail entails sacrificing her life; “your life” is a defensible natural-English explicitation.
The Japanese itself prints the complete utterance for the reader and then says Shirou could not hear it clearly. Reproducing that structure is not a contradiction.
After “we cannot beat Sakura,” the omitted object of 逃げられない can naturally remain Sakura; “run away from her” is defensible explicitation.
好きにさせている means allowing Illya to act as she pleases; in the castle setting, “letting me roam freely” is a reasonable contextual paraphrase.
見逃してもらえる supports the prediction that Shirou will be spared or overlooked, while まだ can carry “for now”; the English is defensible in context.
The explicit demand that Shirou leave immediately is reduced to an unqualified instruction to go back.
This is Shirou’s internal assessment of his available choices; “no alternative in my mind” adequately conveys that no other option exists for him.
ぼんやり describes an unfocused or dazed gaze, whereas “in surprise” supplies a distinct emotional cause not stated by the Japanese.
The English omits 無防備, an explicit indication that Illya’s hand and posture are unguarded when Shirou takes it.
“Light” removes すぎる, which marks her body as disturbingly or excessively light rather than merely light.
呆れた ranges through exasperation, disbelief, and being taken aback; “I’m stunned” is awkward in tone but remains lexically defensible here.
トテトテ adds childlike sound symbolism, but “starts to walk without resisting” preserves the material action; this is a stylistic compression.
Because Shirou is already holding her hand, “closes her hand over mine” naturally expresses a reciprocal grasp, and happiness is retained; only a minor gentleness modifier is lost.
This is Shirou’s internal assessment of his available choices; “no alternative in my mind” adequately conveys that no other option exists for him.
ぼんやり describes an unfocused or dazed gaze, whereas “in surprise” supplies a distinct emotional cause not stated by the Japanese.
The English omits 無防備, an explicit indication that Illya’s hand and posture are unguarded when Shirou takes it.
“Light” removes すぎる, which marks her body as disturbingly or excessively light rather than merely light.
呆れた can express exasperated astonishment or being taken aback, so “I’m stunned” is a defensible, if less idiomatic, choice.
The omitted トテトテ is childlike sound symbolism, but the English preserves the complete material action and lack of resistance.
“Closes her hand over mine” contextually conveys grasping back, and 幸福そうに is retained; omission of そっと alone is not material.
As internal narration, “no alternative in my mind” reasonably conveys that Shirou presently recognizes no other available choice.
The source gives Illya an unfocused, dazed manner; “in surprise” replaces that manner with an inferred emotion.
The English drops the explicit description of Illya’s hand as unguarded at the moment of contact.
The excessive degree in 軽すぎる is significant and is lost when the body is described as merely light.
呆れた permits an astonished or exasperated “I’m stunned”; the proposed affectionate-exasperation reading is contextual, not the only lexical possibility.
Omitting the childlike gait sound トテトテ is stylistic compression rather than a material mistranslation of the action.
The prior handholding makes “closes her hand over mine” reciprocal, while “happily” preserves the principal affect; only the minor modifier そっと is absent.
The cloak’s flutter is a visual embellishment omitted from an otherwise accurate entrance; its absence does not materially alter action, agency, or context.
The raw English contains a line command between “Wha” and “Illya”; the apparent splice is an extraction artifact from stripping that command.
“Kotomine has already landed” followed by “Illya is in his arms” preserves that she reached the ground while held; the sequence remains clear.
Inferring a hard slap from the conspicuously loud バチン that can be heard from the upper floor is a natural, context-supported explicitation.
The source compares the castle with Japanese apartment-building scale, reinforced by the マンション ruby; “normal house” changes both building type and comparison.
A possible crack in a leg bone is escalated into definitively breaking both legs, changing both severity and number.
Although 痺れ is more specifically numbness or tingling, “pain” is a defensible generalization after the fall, and the preceding English already states that his feet are numb.
“Right when I started the jump” substantially matches the instant of jumping down. The genuine omission is that vertigo specifically caused the near-faint.
“The sword I left here” identifies the same sword, while the surrounding climbing sequence supplies when and why it was left; the omitted timing is not material.
“Ruthless” is defensible for 無慈悲, but “honorable” does not translate 親切; it removes the paradoxical characterization as kind or considerate yet merciless.
“Every last ounce ... from my body” preserves total bodily depletion and the squeezing image; omitting the cell metaphor is stylistic compression.
In context, “forget about him” idiomatically tells Illya to abandon hope or reliance on Berserker, a defensible rendering of 諦めろ.
“The whole three hours” presents a set duration, while 最短 specifies that three hours is the best-case minimum—a meaningful tactical constraint.
The Japanese says the pursuing darkness has drawn immediately close; “is overtaking us” instead asserts that it is catching or passing them.
The gradual increase in the pursuer’s speed is explicitly stated and tactically important but absent from the English image.
The Japanese compares the pursuer with Shirou’s own full speed. “Ours” incorrectly includes Illya despite the preceding statement that he slowed to her pace.
“He’ll catch up” retains certainty, and idiomatic “in a minute” can mean within roughly a minute or very soon; the accusation overstates the distinction.
Immediately after “get on my back,” saying one little girl’s weight is no problem is a natural explicitation of イリヤ一人ならどうってことない.
The singular “this sword” already conveys one weapon, and “borrowed” conveys 借り受けただけ. The genuine loss is that 細剣 specifies a slender sword.
The English removes the specific image of his conscious upper half being noisily stamped into fragments and obliterated like construction machinery.
Kotomine had gone ahead and then returned to them; “walks over” omits the tactically significant doubling back.
The English omits that Kotomine takes Illya without permitting either person to object or answer.
“Per seven seconds” is unusual but intelligible rate grammar. The narrower error is that 七秒台 means somewhere in the seven-second range, not exactly seven seconds.
With the following heartbeat-like どくん, “throbs” is a defensible natural rendering of the arm’s rhythmic vibration.
“Throbs” carries the beat and “it feels like” carries the abnormal sensation. The surviving loss is 大きく, the impression that the arm swells greatly.
Although “flowing into me” softens 侵している locally, the same page immediately calls the influx an overdose and poison, preserving its hostile bodily character.

The range-exceeding Geiger-counter image survives in “too great … to measure,” so that portion of the accusation is overstated. The humorous aside describing the counter as vaguely cool-looking is genuinely omitted.
“Not as much as you” is an intelligible elliptical retort to “are you really human?” Japanese likewise leaves the compared property unstated, implying that Shirou is the stranger case.
Rendering the trees as pebbles beneath Berserker’s feet naturally conveys that they are negligible obstacles; the following sentence supplies the pursuit context.
The English preserves Kotomine’s disinterest but omits the reason Shirou finds it remarkable: in their present circumstances this should be welcomed as good fortune.
Although “killing intent” is more literal, “hostility” is a defensible contextual rendering of 殺気 during an imminent attack and does not create a factual contradiction.
The Japanese itself metonymically says that a white skull was seen; it does not explicitly say “mask” here. Context permits English to retain that image unchanged.
振りかぶる supports an overhead throwing wind-up, so that direction is not invented. The narrower valid issue is omission of 僅かに, which makes the movement explicitly slight.
“Fired without any indication” is a natural generalization of a throw displaying no arm-raising motion and preserves the operative fact that the release was visually imperceptible.
一瞥 literally indicates a brief glance, but the stated displeasure and clouded brow make “glares” a defensible contextual description rather than a material mistranslation.
Calling the weapons daggers is supported by the adjacent page’s 短剣. The surviving issue is that “three daggers” drops the vivid 電光 imagery describing them as streaks or flashes of lightning.
The ruby reads 山の主 as アサシン, creating a deliberate title/readings interplay. Translating only “assassin” erases the written “lord of the mountain” formulation and makes the standard generic.
The surrounding weapons justify associating the flashes with blades, so “sword flashes” is not wholly invented. It nevertheless omits the explicit violet-lightning image of 紫電.
斬って捨てた depicts the priest cutting the projectiles down; “knocked them all aside” changes that destructive cutting action into deflection.

“Destroying everything in its path” conveys ongoing destruction, so the accusation overstates that loss. It does omit that the seemingly random destruction functions as a way of probing for their location.
In Kotomine’s dismissive response, “meaningless warning” is a loose but defensible rendering of an unnecessary or superfluous warning; the core dismissal is unchanged.
Here 生業 defines what belongs to a priest’s professional role. “Duty” communicates that role distinction adequately in the surrounding explanation of what priests do.
全なるもの describes totality, completeness, or all-encompassing divinity, not knowledge. “All-knowing” substitutes omniscience for the stated attribute.
聖霊 explicitly identifies a holy/divine spirit. Rendering it merely as “a spirit” removes the religious qualifier and genericizes the claim.
The English mentions only disgrace to the created world, omitting the separate claim that demons defile human beings, expressly identified as God’s own children.
The English preserves necessity and lovability but omits 被造物, the doctrinal assertion that even demons are created beings within the Lord’s constructed world.
In this abstract moral contrast, “brings out” can naturally express 鍛える as developing or eliciting human goodness and evil. The parallel doctrine remains intact.
The grotesque 悲劇喜劇 pairing—tragedy and comedy or tragicomedy—is reduced to tragedies alone, losing the deliberate comic half of the formulation.
錯覚させた says humanity was made to mistake Heaven as powerless. “Realize how powerless God is” turns that expressly mistaken perception into a fact.

使徒 can legitimately be translated “apostles,” and “carry out the will of God” substantially conveys acting as proxies. The narrower omission is 赦された: these human agents were exceptionally permitted or sanctioned.
魔 has a broad range encompassing demons, supernatural evil, and darkness. “Drive away darkness” is a defensible figurative rendering in this doctrinal passage.
移り身 can denote quick change, adaptability, or evasive versatility. The surrounding insult keeps the mocking force, so “adaptable as the snake” is not demonstrably false.
白い髑髏 is itself the text’s metonym for Assassin, so “white skull” is faithful. 嘲笑う occurs after an openly mocking speech, making “laughs” a defensible contextual compression.
数個 unambiguously means several Command Spells. The singular “a Command Spell” is a number error.
代行者 is the same named office previously rendered “Executors.” Switching to capitalized “Agents” obscures that established institutional term.
The source specifies Berserker’s receding footsteps, but “crashing into the distance” is a contextually supported rendering of the sound made by the gigantic pursuer moving destructively away.
以前のおぬしならば explicitly contrasts Kirei’s present conduct with what the former Kirei would have done. “You could have” removes that characterization and presents only an available tactic.
In the immediate contrast with an uncharacteristic 善行, “moved by kindness” is a defensible interpretation of being swayed by 情; emotional compassion is not excluded by the Japanese.
The unseen old magus is already established by the dialogue and immediately responds. Omitting the repeated addressee from the speech tag causes no material ambiguity.
“No sign of hostility” is broader than literal “without even kindling killing intent,” but it preserves Kirei’s complete lack of outward aggression in context and is not materially contradictory.
じき and the passive 殺される state that both men will shortly be killed. “Die eventually” removes both the imminence and the external lethal agency.
“Do something for yourself” naturally conveys taking action for one’s own ends. The preceding “business” supplies the specific objective, so the paraphrase does not materially alter Kirei’s motive.
The archived English contains a line-formatting command between “Then” and “it”; the joined form is the warned-about extraction artifact, not source translation prose.
間に合わん gives a specific temporal reason: even after defeating Assassin, Kirei would not reach Shirou in time. “I can do nothing” replaces that with unspecified incapacity.
“Melts into the forest without trace” is a natural visual paraphrase of camouflaging among the trees and completely disappearing; it does not require literal melting.
Although 穿つ supplies a piercing or driving action, the English immediately says the priest’s sword clashes with the thrown daggers. Static possession does not replace the action of the full sentence.
何処まで戦うか asks how far or how long Kirei can continue fighting. “See through the battle” is unnatural and fails to state that limit being observed.
The accusation overlooks the supplied ruby: 死の天使 is explicitly read マラク・アル・マウト. The English transliteration therefore comes directly from the Japanese presentation.
The archived English has a line-formatting command between “faster” and “run.” The concatenation “fasterrun” results from stripped script markup, not the rendered translation.
The valid issue is omission of 股から, which locates the threatened snapping at the crotch or hip. Calling “bones are screaming to break” independently erroneous is largely stylistic.
“Already” reasonably conveys とっくに in context, and the following statement that the distance might be twice that makes clear he may have run well beyond five kilometres.
“So short of breath that I can’t think” is natural experiential English for an oxygen-starved brain failing to function; it preserves the causal physical state.
“Full speed without slowing down” already communicates sustained maximal exertion. Omitting the idiomatic intensifier これでもか does not materially change the action.
The antecedent is the pursuing presence established immediately around this line. “It won’t go away” intelligibly conveys that it will not recede or become more distant.
心筋 is specifically cardiac muscle. “My heart and muscles” incorrectly splits it into the heart plus muscles generally, broadening the anatomical scope.
A presence “getting larger” idiomatically means becoming stronger, more imposing, or nearer, not necessarily increasing in physical dimensions. The central escalation is preserved.
弱音 can encompass weak, defeatist thoughts as well as spoken complaints. “Won’t think negative thoughts” is a natural paraphrase of running until such weakness is mentally blanked out.
The grammatical subjects are reversed: Japanese says the body reacts faster than the heart or conscious mind, whereas English says the mind reacts before the body.
“Frantic warning” reasonably conveys the desperate intensity of a warning delivered with one’s whole being. The fuller idiom is compressed, but no distinct factual content is contradicted.
Feet sliding to a halt through dirt is a natural physical rendering of stopping while gouging the earth. The force is somewhat compressed but the action is not materially changed.
The Japanese identifies the weapon specifically as a Black Key, an established named armament. Calling it merely “the sword” discards that identity despite using the term elsewhere.
Japanese does not grammatically mark 魔術回路 as plural here, and 発現させる permits bringing forth or producing a circuit. The asserted plural activation is not established by this sentence alone.

The English explicitly retains the empty-mind point with “without even thinking,” so it does not reverse that aspect. It does replace traversing every process simultaneously with the vaguer and misleading “manufacture everything.”
The Japanese explicitly describes a two-handed block or resistance. The English retains maximal strength but omits the concrete combat stance.
粉砕された is rhetorical in a passage where Shirou is flung away rather than literally pulverized. “Sent flying” followed by “all it took was one blow” preserves the operative event and emphasis.

The English describes the impact travelling through the sword into and throughout Shirou’s body from head to toe. Omitting the intermediate mention of both arms is compression, not a material change of injury.
対抗した一撃 can naturally be rendered as the blow or attack Shirou made in opposition, while “with all my might” is an ordinary equivalent for committing his whole being and everything he has.
一方的に粉砕された describes Shirou’s utmost resistance being overwhelmingly crushed. “Deflected like nothing” changes destruction into a comparatively non-destructive parry.
In this context 絶望的 means escape has no realistic hope; “impossible” is a conventional, defensible English expression of that practical conclusion rather than a distinct categorical claim.
受け入れそうになった marks an incomplete threshold—Shirou was about to accept the fate. “I accept my fate” incorrectly presents the acceptance as completed before the interruption.
愕然 denotes being shocked, aghast, or stunned; “crying in disbelief” is an apt contextual rendering of that reaction to Berserker’s transformed state.
咄嗟に emphasizes an immediate, instinctive response. In this emergency action, “frantically reach out” is a defensible natural paraphrase and does not materially alter what Shirou does.
Japanese says even the single breath available to him makes his body feel ready to burst. “If I take another” invents a second breath and changes the condition of the paradox.
Kicking off the ground is the concrete means of resuming his run. “Gives me the strength to run” is a natural contextual paraphrase, not a conflicting action.
総動員 means mobilizing the full complement of magical circuits. “All of my Magic Circuit” is both grammatically malformed and incorrectly singular in this construction.
侵食され depicts Berserker’s whole body being invaded, eroded, or corrupted by the black mud. “Covered” reduces that active bodily corruption to a surface coating.
“Hostility” is broader than literal killing intent, but in describing red eyes whose sole function is to radiate aggression, it remains a defensible contextual translation without factual reversal.
