The immediately preceding page identifies the corrupting substance as black mud, making “mud” a reasonable contextual explicitation of the black shadow rather than proof of a different entity.
The images not registering in Berserker’s eyeballs is figurative evidence that he cannot visually recognize Shirou or Illya. The English states that intended consequence naturally.
The raising of the axe-sword explicitly occurs together with Berserker’s roar. That accompanying action and sound are absent from the English sentence.
最期の時を迎えた means reaching one’s final moment. “End his life” assigns Kirei apparent agency and readily suggests suicide despite the enemy-inflicted danger.
Whiteness is contextually established elsewhere, so supplying it is not unsupported. The narrower loss is かすむ: the skull is hazy or indistinct in the distance, not merely present ahead.
神父服 can straightforwardly mean the priest’s outfit, and “slashed up” conveys extensive cutting in natural English. The clerical identity is already explicit in the surrounding sentence.

サーヴァントを向こうに takes the Servant as the opponent, while よく保った means holding out well. “Lasting this long against a Servant” accurately conveys the construction; it does not mean maintaining physical separation.
A laugh that “echoes through the sky” naturally conveys the spatial effect of the guffaw filling or covering the sky. The imagery is adapted, but its scale and force remain.

The English retains both the vital-point targeting and the secondary measuring function through “go for…vital spots” and “also.” “Strength” can denote overall capability here; losing the ruler metaphor is chiefly stylistic.
At a range reachable only by thrown weapons, saying only projectile weapons are useful is a defensible contextual paraphrase of the same combat limitation.
The English lists damaged limbs and bodily fatigue but entirely omits the culminating effort to drive the heart near rupture.
魔 can carry demonic, malign, or evil associations. “Evil arm” is imprecise terminology but not an indefensible meaning in this supernatural context.
“Just a chore…bringing him no joy” already conveys mundane, habitual, joyless work. The unexpressed 日常 nuance is not a material factual omission.
“At least twenty” is marginally less exact than “more than twenty,” but it communicates the same approximate quantity in ordinary prose and is not a material error.
The English preserves surviving the attacks and reaching the ruin but removes the explicit movement through and out of the forest.
Although all seven being dodged is retained, both their bullet-like launch and their subsequent disappearance are absent.
“Grace” can mean mercy or clemency, and “show him some grace” is contextually intelligible as granting a merciful end.
眉間 is the point between the eyebrows, not the temple; the English materially relocates the first target.
“Lightning flashes” conveys the projectiles’ appearance but omits the tactically important facts that all three were released at exactly the same time and in one breath.

“Fatal attack” is not an exact technical label for 必至, but the following English immediately defines it as a move that guarantees killing and victory, while the feint and unavoidable consequence remain explicit.

“Is developed” is awkward English, but 展開 can describe deployment or manifestation, and the sentence remains intelligible as the cursed arm forming the one-winged spear. A material mechanical contradiction is not established.
“Wounded” is broader than 出血した but defensibly encompasses the prey’s bleeding condition; the accusation is one of preferred specificity.
Two ken is roughly 3.6 metres, and three metres is a coarse but ordinary localized approximation. The difference does not materially change the described short jump.
The finding ignores the ruby: 告げる is explicitly read セット. Rendering the spoken cue as “Set” follows the supplied pronunciation rather than mistranslating it.

相打ち狙い directly supports aiming for a double kill, and the immediately preceding certainty of Kirei’s own death supplies the self-sacrificial context. The English is compressed but not materially different.
The Japanese makes the hit conditional on releasing the Black Keys from Kirei’s present posture; the English turns that conditional tactical assessment into an unconditional prediction.

“Pierce through Assassin, sticking to the tree behind him” naturally describes the blades penetrating him and lodging in the tree, which entails pinning him there. The immobilization is not materially lost.
The Japanese likens the absurd upward-moving Kirei himself to a cannon projectile. The English instead calls the action inhuman and compares it to a cannon firing, altering both evaluation and image.

“Amassing his strength and releasing it” compresses the repetition and drawn-bow image but preserves the operative action, followed by the explicit ten-metre burst. This is loss of texture, not a demonstrable material error.
Neutral observation does not convey that Zouken was sadistically enjoying what he regarded as the priest’s execution.
The supplied raw English contains “Hm[line4]What”; the apparent fusion results from stripping a presentation command. It is an extraction artifact rather than translation evidence.
“This has always been his announced intention” conveys an intention held from the beginning, and the singular formulation adequately carries the exclusive target in context.

“Slams his head against the wall” naturally implies continued physical control of the head, especially after the preceding page explicitly has Kirei seize it. Omitting the grip’s exact形態 is not material here.
The raw English is “Ha[line4]I see”; the malformed “HaI” was produced by stripping the line command, not by the translation itself.
In the ruin context, “the stones” can naturally denote the stone wall, while “smear of blood” is a defensible rendering of 血の跡. No consequential spatial change is established.
描かれていく itself invites a drawing/painting image. Saying the blood and flesh “paint a picture” is an expressive paraphrase, not an unsupported coherent object or factual change.
“Ground away against the stone” preserves the operative abrasion and destruction. The explicit file metaphor is lost, but that is chiefly figurative compression rather than a material mistranslation.
許しはここに is a declaration that forgiveness is present here. “Ask for forgiveness here” changes it into a command directed at the victim.
The ruby supplies the liturgical pronunciation, but the displayed text specifically asks mercy for “this soul.” Retaining only “Kyrie eleison” loses that soul-specific written layer.

“Cut off” conveys the laughter’s cessation, and the following English sentence depicts the unseen form withering away. The alleged abrupt-versus-gradual distinction is not sufficiently material in the complete passage.
The decisive defect is the complete omission of 目には見えぬ重み. “Withers away” is a loose but defensible rendering of the form growing faint, so that part of the accusation should be dropped.
The Japanese describes a magical foundation fixed into the world. “The systematic basis of their magic” loses that ontological relation and muddles what is being classified.
対霊魔術 identifies a technical category of magecraft. Calling it merely a “weapon against spirits” changes the stated classification.
“Wandering souls” omits the defining description that the soul has left its flesh and wanders while decaying and maddened.
“Eliminates” adequately conveys the practical result of returning the soul to nothing. The more cosmological phrasing is lost, but the English does not assert a contrary destination.
Calling him a five-hundred-year-old magus reasonably conveys that he lived five hundred years. The surviving error is 妄念: an obsessive or deluded fixation is reduced to an ordinary “wish.”
判らず states failed or impossible recognition. “Doesn’t even try” instead attributes a deliberate refusal to identify Illya.
The interrupted ～ようと leaves Berserker about to bring the sword down. “Before he swings his sword” presents the swing as the completed next action.

The unpunctuated fevered sequence 血液麻薬推進剤 can support an asyndetic accumulation of blood, narcotic, and propellant imagery. The witnesses do not establish the finding’s single-compound parse as uniquely governing.
大剣 is still a sword, and the established weapon and surrounding pages supply its scale and axe-sword identity. Using “sword” here is reduced specificity, not a material error.

The complete page already says “I block it” immediately before the cited sentence. Thus the successful block is not omitted, and the weapon is recoverable from the adjacent identification and next page.
The raw English contains mutually exclusive if/else renderings of the same utterance. Flattening both branches created the apparent duplicate, so this is an extraction artifact.
“Slides across the ground like trash” preserves the uncontrolled ground motion and comparison. Omitting the additional rolling manner is minor compression, not a material error.
The nonpast 無くなる in this stream of consciousness can describe consciousness presently disappearing. “My consciousness is fading” is a defensible aspectual rendering.
The Japanese specifically has Shirou desperately gather together his own scattered self. “Gather up everything” removes both the fragmented-self image and the desperation.

The Japanese can straightforwardly state that projection has already halved his intelligence, followed by the chill that it may never return. The finding’s claim that even the halving is only a feared future possibility is not established.
In a passage about losing thought and consciousness, rendering 我 as “my mind” is a reasonable English explicitation of the self undergoing mental dissolution, not a demonstrable contradiction.

ギラつく can describe a fierce glare as well as glittering, and the source explicitly says the eyes act as though searching for the Shirou he knocked away. The alleged invented scanning is present in Japanese.
The English identifies the external injuries as branch scratches; slight oozing is a minor severity qualification consistent with those scratches, not a materially missing injury.
苦しい permits “pain/distress,” and the surrounding English explicitly describes gasping and oxygen deprivation. The awkward tongue image remains substantially represented rather than reversed.
After explicitly stating that his body has no oxygen, “I want air” is natural English for wanting a satisfactory breath. The concrete respiratory need is clear from the full sentence.
The raw script contains a line-control command between “body” and “I.” Their fusion in the flattened witness is an extraction artifact rather than malformed authored translation.
“I don’t really want to know what condition it’s in” naturally paraphrases refusing to make a cool-headed diagnosis of his internal condition. No material assessment is changed.
“Get out of his range to regain my breath” preserves the necessary withdrawal and purpose. 一分 can function as a brief interval here, so omitting its nominal length is not material.
The preceding page has Shirou holding Illya’s hand; describing her pulling back as denying his assistance is a natural contextual rendering of rejecting that offered hand.
The English reduces Berserker to being behind Illya and entirely omits that he is actively trying to set his aim on them.
俺は俺で is a contrastive “as for me/in my case,” not a self-identification. “I’m myself” is nonsensical and disrupts the sentence’s relation to Illya’s situation.
“She hits my head” retains the action. ぽかぽか adds repeated light or ineffectual thumping, but losing that manner is tonal compression rather than a material factual error.
“Pull her close” is a common contextual paraphrase for drawing someone into an embrace. The firmness marker ぎゅっと is softened, but the interpersonal action is not materially changed.
Retaining the culturally specific address “Onii-chan” is a localization choice, and the same sentence immediately explains its meaning through “older brother” and “younger sister.”
異常 has a lexical range including strange, unusual, and abnormal. “A bit strange” matches 少し、異常だった without denying the later physical abnormality.

“Lungs are burning from lack of air” is an embodied paraphrase of suffering from oxygen deprivation in a passage explicitly about breathing. It adds localization but does not contradict the condition.
“My heart’s gone on strike” naturally implies cessation and uses a perfect construction indicating an already-entered state. Omitting explicit さっきから and 完全に does not materially reverse it.
The reciprocal grip is not verbalized, but the ongoing hand-holding context and reference to Illya’s fingers make contact clear. This is a minor gesture omission rather than a material error.
“Unnaturally hot” is a plausible English way to convey heat intense enough to be frightening or alarming. It does not establish a specific diagnosis contrary to the Japanese.
“Mad, senseless” does not preserve the specific imposed conditions that all five senses are sealed and even his reason has been taken away.
In context, “Thoughts are useless” naturally refers to the intrusive thoughts just mentioned as an impediment to escaping. It need not be read as a universal condemnation of thought.
“Somehow” conveys the anomalous, unexplained nature of the gained distance, while the prior running supplies Shirou’s participation. The English does not clearly claim deliberate success.
With trembling legs during flight, specifying that his remaining movement is running is normal contextual explicitation. “About ten metres” is a reasonable approximation of just under ten.
The raw English contains a line-control marker between “Well” and “hiding.” The joined form was produced by command stripping and is not a translation defect.
The depression was gouged by Saber’s Noble Phantasm and is subsequently used like a trench. Calling it a crater is a reasonable contextual rendering, not an unsupported impact event.
Calling a trench-like hole “the trench” is ordinary English compression, especially as it is used for cover. No consequential difference in terrain is created.
The English retains both bodily rest and relaxation; “I relax” can naturally cover the mind. The omitted absolute-limit modifier weakens intensity but does not create a material error.
“Track us down and kill us” substantially encompasses pursuit and capture before death. The narrower surviving issue is that plain “kill” drops the explicit brutality of 惨殺する.

The preceding English sentence already identifies her voice as suppressed, while “frantically hugging herself so she won’t be a burden” retains her strenuous self-restraint and motive. The page as a whole preserves the claim.

The displayed 赤布 is explicitly assigned the ruby reading ひだりうで. Translating the intended reading as “my left arm” follows supplied Japanese presentation, even though it sacrifices the visual cloth layer.
The bound arm is literally the dangerous combat power under discussion, so calling the sole breakthrough measure a “weapon” is a natural contextual explicitation rather than a changed plan.

Untying the cloth is precisely what releases the arm’s power, and the next page explicitly describes removing the red cloth. “Released my arm” compresses action and function without materially changing the choice.
頭に locates the metaphorical firing mechanism at Shirou's head; “in my head” instead places it inside him. The following gun-in-mouth image confirms the intended external threat.
The substantive modifier 得体の知れない, describing the shadow as unknown or uncanny, is entirely absent from “the shadow.”
外に出る specifically says Shirou will go outside or emerge from the hollow; generic “I’m going” loses that tactical movement.
Sentence-final いいな asks for Illya's assent or acknowledgment. The English presents only a declaration.

The Japanese literally contrasts dying with being killed before that happens; it does not state that Shirou's identity will be destroyed. The English follows the supplied wording, however paradoxical it sounds.
The supplied raw English contains a line-length pause command between “Eh” and “Shirou”; “EhShirou” is a flattened-extraction artifact, not the translated presentation.
The Japanese explicitly identifies Shirou's right hand, a meaningful contrast with his dangerous left arm; the English omits it.
The English conveys departure but omits that Shirou advances within the fissure, an explicit part of the scene's spatial staging.
“So she doesn’t get involved in the fight” naturally describes preventing Illya from being caught up in it. It loses the emphasis of 万が一にも but does not change her into a voluntary participant.
The source specifies both the left shoulder and the named Holy Shroud; “the knot by my shoulder” omits both details.
The defensible core is narrower: “tight” omits the exceptional degree expressed by 際立って強く. Calling the tied portion a wrist knot is a reasonable contextual rendering.
何十倍 means tens or dozens of times, not exactly ten times. The English materially reduces and fixes the magnitude.
“If I’ll be sane or not” is not an idiomatic English embedded question and is left as a malformed subordinate fragment; the intended concern is whether he can remain sane.
The repetition 怖くて怖くて and たまらない express overwhelming, unbearable terror. Plain “I’m scared” substantially flattens that force.
In context, “lose my sanity and forget about Illya and Sakura” is a defensible paraphrase of no longer knowing himself or the girls, especially with the following fear of forgetting his vow.
“Them” is normal English explicitation: Illya and Sakura are the immediately preceding referents and the omitted object of 守る.
“Give in to the pain” is an ordinary rendering of being unable to endure it, not necessarily a voluntary surrender. The surrounding text already identifies the arm as the source.
The supplied raw English places a line-length pause command between “Yeah” and “that’s”; the fused form is an extraction artifact.

“There’s something I can’t give up, and that’s why I continue to live” preserves both the unyielding value and Shirou's continued existence for its sake. The missing explicit “unchanged” is not a material reversal.
力を篭める describes applying or concentrating force into the red binding. Merely putting a hand on it changes the physical action immediately before it is torn away.

The accusation cannot establish that “cloth” was merely truncated, because the Japanese instead names Shirou's right arm. A genuine error remains: “clot” is unsupported and malformed, while 右腕 is not conveyed.
“Faster than a hundred meters per second” accurately conveys exceeding that threshold. Omitting 優に's margin is minor compression, not a material numerical error.
“Therefore” is a reasonable connective after the description of an unsurvivable gale; it does not materially alter the escalation that this is no longer wind.
“Groan in protest” can naturally mean voicing anguish while physically resisting. It does not necessarily reduce 抵抗 to a verbal objection.
The supplied raw English explicitly contains all four aligned forward commands. Their absence from the flattened mirrorMoon field is an extraction/presentation artifact, not a translation omission.
“My body lost already” is genuinely ungrammatical, but it can still be read as the body having already lost rather than as the body being lost. Only the malformed English is securely established.
心 can denote mind, heart, or spirit. In this surrounding sequence about sanity and consciousness, “mind” is a defensible lexical choice and preserves the opposition between bodily and mental defeat.
“Use that to move forward” conveys the functional meaning of using the recovered sensation as a basis for advancing. Omitting the literal foothold metaphor is acceptable paraphrase.
The Japanese says both consciousness and vision fade; the English mentions only vision.
To “grit” one's teeth already denotes pressing or grinding them together and adequately renders 歯を鳴らした. The sound need not be separately explicated.
振り向いた means that the knight turned or glanced back. “Turned away” reverses the direction of that movement.
The surface text identifies accumulated punishment or consequences, reinforced by the ruby ツケ. “Crimes I’ve accumulated” changes those consequences into Shirou's offenses.
如く makes the manner of his limbs cutting the wind analogous to wielding a great sword. The English instead makes the limbs themselves analogous to swords.
“Pass” is defensible for 突破 in this context, so loss of the breakthrough is overstated. A narrower error remains: 赤い背中 specifically presents Archer's red back, not a generic figure.
距離にして三十メートル is an estimated battlefield distance, not an expressly exact measurement. “About thirty meters” is defensible.
憑依経験 refers to the experience borne or embedded in the projected object, conventionally its wielding history; “growth experience” is a different concept.
物質 explicitly classifies this as material Projection, contrasting it with the following Reality Marble description. That classification is absent from the English.
In this sword battle, “if I’m cut, I’ll be killed as before” is reasonably compressed as remaining vulnerable to a killing blow. “One blow” does not materially broaden the claim in context.
The Noble Phantasm best suited to the situation is naturally the one best suited to the intended use arising from that situation. The phrasing is broader but not materially different.
“Put all my magical energy into my left arm” preserves the complete transfer and total quantity. Losing 叩き込む's violent manner is tonal compression rather than a factual error.
寸分違わず explicitly says the sword is perceived without the slightest deviation. The English omits this exactness from the scan.
The supplied raw English has a line-length dash command between “But” and “my”; “Butmy” is caused by flattening that presentation command.

“The strength of my enemy” conveys that the enemy's strength is reproduced, and the surrounding weapon-projection context supplies the accompanying relation. Omitting 怪力's intensity is not enough to establish a material error.
The English preserves the substantive event—that part of his brain explodes. Omitting the brief onomatopoeic snap is a minor sound-detail loss, not a material mistranslation.

In this bodily-collapse context, “my bones break” is a defensible rendering of the skeletal frame giving way, while “overflowing magical energy” adequately conveys energy flowing beyond what the body can withstand.
The source itself uses the unusual apple-peel comparison. “Unsightly like apple skin” is awkward but intelligible and substantially faithful, not a fabricated image.
殺意 is specifically intent to kill, stronger and more precise than general hostility. The English removes the explicitly murderous object of the converging intent.
In context, treating Shirou's magecraft use as identifying an enemy and recognizing it as a threat are functionally equivalent reasons for Berserker to focus on him.
Japanese bare nouns do not establish singular number, and “they” plausibly refers to Berserker's eyes from the preceding page. The narrower genuine omission is 黒い, the image's blackness.
The governing Japanese says the giant remains unchanged while in a state of rage. “Insane” substitutes a different condition already discussed separately later in the passage.
“His body is rotting” naturally encompasses his body as a whole, and 腐敗させながら itself describes an ongoing condition. The accusation's claim of completed damage is unsupported.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 投影魔術 as トレース, so “Tracing” follows the original presentation. “Won’t do the trick” colloquially but accurately conveys that it cannot reach the required level.
The English preserves the ruby pronunciation but loses the simultaneously displayed meaning “Projection, loaded.” That deliberate dual-layer presentation is substantive.
The comma can carry the pause visible in the surface phrase 投影、装填 while rendering the ruby words. It does not materially change the command into direct address.
体内 places the twenty-seven circuits in Shirou's body. The English incorrectly attaches “in my head” to those circuits, confusing them with the preceding nine mental targets.
The English retains only the ruby “Set / Nine Lives Blade Works,” omitting the displayed claims that all Projection processes are complete and that the result is Shooting the Hundred Heads.
The supplied raw English places a line-length pause command between “Set” and “Nine Lives.” Their fusion in the flattened field is an extraction artifact.
Although 健在 is stronger than mere survival, the complete English page first says “He doesn’t fall,” which supplies his continued combat capability. The page does not reduce him to passive survival.
八割 is eighty percent. “An eighth” is 12.5 percent and directly reverses the scale of Berserker's bodily loss.
殺された explicitly describes Berserker as already killed despite still moving. The English omits that paradoxical status.
With Shirou as the continuing subject, 胸元 is his own chest level. English “his chest” most naturally refers to the recently named Berserker and misplaces the preparatory position.
臆面もなしに explicitly characterizes Shirou's use of the privilege as unabashed or shameless. The English preserves full output but omits that characterization.
こめかみ identifies the temple, the precise point the blade will graze. “Head” materially generalizes the fight choreography.
The complete English page does convey death (“will be the end”) and mentions the sword tip in the final sentence. The surviving omission is the exact “only a few millimeters” margin.
“Destroy the ground” is a natural English rendering of the personifying hyperbole “kill even the earth” and preserves the physical scale without introducing a factual difference.

The Japanese itself uses the nonpast “at the instant my head is blown away”; the following reversal makes its anticipatory status clear. The English mirrors that construction rather than independently asserting completed decapitation.

The hollow has functioned as shelter, so calling it “cover” is a reasonable contextual paraphrase of emerging from the depression. Berserker's blindness does not make shelter from the battle irrelevant.
The Japanese explicitly describes Berserker's eyes as devoid of reason. The English staring action omits that important quality.
情 can mean compassion, sympathy, or mercy, particularly while delivering a killing blow. “Without hesitation or mercy” is a defensible rendering, not an unsupported moralization.
The English grammatically makes the fading eyes the thing “telling” Shirou, preserving the source's figurative silent communication rather than presenting spoken dialogue.
The complete English page already states that Illya went out to stop him, and “wondering what she could say” naturally develops 言葉など思いつかず. Only the literal back image is compressed.
“Yet still followed after him” conveys that her inability to remain behind led her outside. The loss of 耐え切れなくなって's emotional threshold is tonal compression, not a materially different action.

であった places the protector role in the past relative to his disappearance. “Who once protected her” is a defensible English expression of that completed role, with the immediate context preserving its recency.
背中 specifically leaves Shirou's back in Illya's view, continuing the passage's repeated back motif. “The figure” removes that concrete image.
煩悶 includes mental anguish or torment, so “agonies” is within its lexical range. The immediately preceding “no doubt left” also preserves the deliberative context.
The Japanese distinguishes an appearance like another person from a body that has actually become something else. The English collapses both into merely looking like someone else's body.
尊い can legitimately mean sacred, precious, or noble, while 結末 can mean an end or conclusion. “End with no return” does not necessarily assert immediate death.

Japanese 蛇 is number-neutral here, so the singular-versus-plural accusation is unproven. A narrower problem survives: 電気製 means made of electricity, whereas “with electricity” treats electricity as an accompaniment.
“Wriggling around like mad” is a defensible naturalization of a snake moving violently throughout the body. It changes the literal bouncing motion but preserves the chaotic pain image.
腰を落とす can mean lowering oneself or sitting down, and the preceding page says Shirou can barely remain standing. Rendering it as resting is contextually defensible; a combat crouch is not established.
Defeat can naturally express 撃退 in the sense of beating an attacker back; it does not necessarily imply killing or total conquest.

The preceding page explicitly has Saber approaching Shirou. Thus once I am within range can describe the point at which her approach brings him within her striking range without making Shirou the mover.
躱す specifically concerns evading Saber's cut. Fight back instead suggests counteraction and loses the stated inability even to dodge.
その持ち主 requires the Noble Phantasm's own possessor, whereas an appropriate user is a looser qualification. The unsupported masculine pronoun further narrows the referent.

In context, being supplied with sufficient magical energy after release from Shirou reasonably entails having a powerful source. The English preserves the operative contrast with Shirou's inadequate supply.
斬り伏せにくる directly presents Saber as coming to cut Shirou down. Her subsequent decision to leave does not turn this sentence into merely a prediction.
The Japanese contains only an interrupted initial syllable, こ—, with no recoverable propositional content. Representing the interruption by a dash alone is defensible and not a material omission.
自滅する identifies Shirou as bringing about his own destruction. Someone who will soon die preserves the outcome but removes that agency and characterization.
The concrete action is already stated at the start of the page as I can't call out to her. The final condensed sentence relies on that established referent rather than materially omitting it.
五体満足 means remaining physically whole or unimpaired. Physical defects is awkward English, but it conveys the bodily impairment at issue and is not a factual change.
戦闘不能 means unable to continue fighting and does not entail death. The English materially escalates the contemplated outcome.
The supplied raw English places a line-dash command between Saber and no. Their fusion in the flattened witness is an extraction artifact, not the translated script's wording.
Loudly is a reasonable natural rendering of the subjectively 巨大 heartbeat, so that part of the accusation is overstated. A narrower omission remains: the creaking quality ギシギシ is absent.
Red with blood preserves the vermilion staining, contrary to part of the explanation. A narrower issue remains: cloak is not established by 黒衣 and loses the black-clothing contrast.
No longer there conveys that Assassin had already departed by the time Kirei turned. Omitting the added emphasis of とうに is minor compression, not a material temporal error.
こちら naturally denotes this world or this side, and 干渉 can be rendered tamper or interfere. Uses worms also retains their instrumental role; catalyst-level precision is not materially lost here.

In this spiritual-body context, 強い括りで留まっていた can plausibly describe Zouken being strongly bound or anchored here despite being human. The proposed category-of-being reading is not uniquely established.
Within an explicitly Christian Church and exorcism context, the Bible is a reasonable explicitation of 経典 rather than a demonstrable mistranslation.
Not so foolish as that is an idiomatic rendering of 酔狂ではない, meaning he is not mad, quixotic, or foolish enough to avenge Zouken. The accusation imposes an unnecessarily narrow nuance.
地獄の天使 identifies an angel of Hell, matching Zabaniya's name. Fallen angel is a different theological category not stated by the Japanese.
The English retains creation and substitution but omits both exact identity with the target's heart and the stated counter-mirror relation that effects the swap.

The Japanese does not explicitly identify the target of Assassin's resentment, so claiming outward resentment overstates the evidence. Still, self-deprecation is an unsupported interpretation of a hateful or bitter tongue-click.
Although 殺気 is literally killing intent, hostility is a conventional contextual rendering for the threatening aura being emitted. The scene retains its cessation and no contrary action is asserted.
Must be satisfied remains an epistemic inference, not an assertion of known fact. It is somewhat stronger than のか but does not eliminate the narrator's inferential stance.
乗り物 here denotes Sakura's body as the vehicle or host Zouken would occupy. Tool removes the specific bodily-possession relationship central to the sentence.
The supplied ruby explicitly assigns the reading マスター to 寄り代. Rendering the ruby reading as Master is therefore supported by the Original Japanese, even though the base text also evokes a vessel.

The alleged leaked command is not present in the supplied mirrorMoon page text, while the raw witness identifies it as layout syntax. The accusation therefore attacks an extraction or command representation rather than displayed translation text.
Closes his eyes preserves the physical action, and the next page expressly says he fell asleep. Omitting the brief sleep-like staging from this sentence is nonmaterial compression.
十年以上も前 places this portion of Kirei's past at least ten years, and naturally more than ten years, earlier. Exactly ten years ago removes that open duration.
青年期 has a flexible range covering youth and early adulthood and can include one's teenage years. The supplied context does not establish an age that makes teenage years demonstrably false.
Purgatory can figuratively denote a severe ordeal or prolonged suffering. The plural is awkward, but together with sufferings it conveys 苦行、苦悩 without a demonstrable factual change.
The Japanese states that no one fails to dream of such peace, even while hating it. Can only dream instead suggests that dreaming is all one can do, adding unattainability or limitation.
絶望は近かった presents despair as drawing near or nearing culmination. Was in despair makes it an already established state and loses that progression.
The raw English contains a line-dash command between Then and there. Their fusion in the flattened page text is an extraction artifact rather than an authored spacing error.
Relatively quickly is weaker prose than あまりにも速やか, but it preserves the rapid arrival of the end. The difference is tonal degree rather than a demonstrable material error.
The Japanese explicitly situates her final look within consciousness that is fading away. The English removes this physical and temporal condition altogether.
The English explicitly preserves that neither her voice nor her face can be recalled. Losing the rhetorical はおろか／さえ scale is stylistic compression, not a factual omission.

The preceding English sentence already says the answer should be hidden forever, preserving permanence. Stopped searching for answers is a defensible contextual paraphrase of permanently refusing to reach the answer.
The English retains feeding on others' misfortune but entirely omits the further relation that he becomes fulfilled in proportion to the world's corruption.
Following Kirei's attempt to walk onward, is interrupted by a girl naturally means that she stops or intercepts him. It does not contradict the physical path obstruction.

The English substantially retains both magical-energy quantity and presence, so the claimed semantic collapse is overstated. A narrower grammatical defect remains in coordinating two subjects with singular is and awkwardly attaching both to magical energy.

The visible transformation supplies the bodily component, while the English states that change of this degree additionally requires her mind's attunement. The operative body-versus-mind condition remains inferable and is not materially reversed.
The English retains Rin's trouble-free life but omits Sakura's explicit assertion that her sister differs from her in every respect, a salient part of the comparison.
思い知らせる is retaliatory: Sakura will teach them a painful lesson or make them understand what they did. Merely making them realize she exists substantially weakens and redirects the threat.
昏い explicitly gives the pleasure a dark or sinister coloration. Sacred reverses that coloration without support.

One of the qualities to adapt is clumsy English, but it still communicates that her darkness is a quality enabling adaptation. Technical aptitude is a preferable phrasing, not a demonstrably different fact.
そうとしか思えない itself says the change appears explicable only that way. The English presents the same apparent conclusion, then immediately marks its reversal with But and Kirei's denial.
The raw witness places a line-dash command after Eh. The apparent fusion with What is caused by command stripping in the flattened text.
それは真実だったのか leaves the accusation as an explicit question. He's absolutely right converts that uncertainty into unequivocal authorial confirmation.
Grits her teeth conventionally includes forceful clenching or grinding. Omitting the standalone onomatopoeic ぎり does not remove the represented action.
侵食 here is the shadow's physical encroachment or corrosion across the ground. Infringement is a legalistic false friend that obscures the actual phenomenon.
Covers the ground in an instant conveys speed but omits the explicit statement that this speed is beyond comparison with the shadow's previous behavior.

The Japanese describes Sakura's unilateral position to make others painfully understand or experience the consequence. Anyone and whatever I want instead asserts arbitrary control over both target and content.
She smiles cruelly naturally condenses a cruel smile appearing at her lips. The precise corner-of-mouth staging is a minor visual detail, not a material translation error.
Quickly backs away conveys rapid opening of distance, which is the operative sense of 急速に間合いを離す. Omitting the idiomatic one-breath measure is nonmaterial compression.
一足 can denote a single bound or movement as well as a literal step. One jump is plausible in this rapid disengagement and does not contradict the action established by context.
笑い声 expressly identifies an audible little laugh or giggle. A smile changes the sensory mode from sound to sight.
The adjacent English immediately says He rolls down, so rolling motion is not actually omitted from the sequence. A narrower omission remains: 力なく, his powerless or limp condition, is absent.
The red mass being expelled from his mouth is plainly blood in the surrounding passage. Coughing up blood is a natural rendering that loses concrete imagery but not the event or substance.
Read as a whole, the English says he cannot stop coughing up blood and that every attempted breath brings more to his throat. It retains both repeated expulsion and its unceasing character.
The raw English has a line-dash command between Ha and I see. The fusion occurs only when that command is stripped by extraction.

The supplied raw script places the two phrasings in mutually exclusive mature and all-ages branches. Their apparent duplication results from flattening conditional branches, exactly as the witness caveat warns.
The Japanese measures the amount against dust accumulated in a room corner, an absolutely minute quantity. The English instead makes it small only relative to Sakura's enormous total power.
可憐 can describe dainty, delicate, or slender-looking fingers. Slender preserves a plausible physical aspect; the alleged lost dissonance is a stylistic preference, not a factual error.
ごきん is an onomatopoeic hard crack or crunch, and crushing sound is compatible with the immediately described squeezing of Kirei's body. It is less vivid but not materially false.
Will die in the next second naturally denotes death within roughly the coming second. The distinction from taking less than one second is too slight to support a material timing error here.

The supplied raw Original witness for this same surrounding block explicitly contains blood being expelled. The blood sentence is an Original-edition reading omitted from the base/all-ages text, not unsupported invention.
Earlier Japanese identifies Sakura's garment as her shadow itself. Referring to the manifested black clothing as the shadow on her body is therefore contextually supported.
Outfit is an accurate hypernym for 神父服, and both the character and his priestly identity are already explicit in context. The loss of clothing specificity is not a material factual error.
The English retains Illya’s guidance but drops the explanatory characterization that she is the forest’s master, which establishes why her guidance is effective.
In context, “the car I arrived in” naturally identifies the car used for the journey to the forest; the direction is not materially obscured.
“Filthy” can cover the mud but not the separate fact that both are covered in wounds.
The generic “a ride like this” entirely loses Shirou’s comic comparison of their coercive hitchhiking to robbery.
夕方 denotes evening or dusk here, reinforced by the setting sun; “afternoon” moves the stated time earlier.
いた presents Illya as having been beside him. “Standing beside me” instead asserts her present location immediately before the text reveals her absence.
In the context of eating dinner, “get energy” is a defensible natural paraphrase of taking in nourishment, not a factual substitution.
おかげでいい思いしちゃった broadly means that she benefited or had a pleasant experience; “I’m glad we did” adequately conveys that positive result.
The two-person count is omitted, but the adjacent dialogue already establishes that Shirou and Illya ate together; “dishes in the sink” preserves the relevant evidence of the forgotten meal.
“Some groceries” is an ordinary uncounted expression and does not affirm a small quantity. Losing いっぱい is minor emphasis, not a material error.
The supplied raw script shows a pause command between the words; “Hmyeah” is produced by stripping that command, an identified extraction artifact rather than the translation text.
Given that he finds himself on the floor, the English naturally conveys the result of 倒れていた. Explicitly saying “collapsed” is not required.
Although this sentence says only “chest,” the immediately following English sentence specifies “the left side of my chest,” so the location is preserved in the complete passage.
“My life is draining out” preserves the central loss of life force. The narrower surviving criticism is that it drops the pulsing, blood-substitution image.
“Rebelling” reasonably renders the rejection response, but the English loses the more specific mechanism: an abnormal sensation is transmitted from the arm and affects the nearest part of the chest.
The English concisely preserves the stated mechanism: events fail to remain when Shirou passes time without maintaining concentration.
The finding points to the wrong phrase: 『衛宮士郎』 has no ruby. The actual loss occurs later, where written 自分 is read きおく; “memories” preserves the reading but not the self/memory overlap.
“Only pain” removes the concrete severity threshold—pain comparable to having his chest pierced—and leaves the relation to equally intense concentration underspecified.
“Every time I relax” broadens the trigger and omits the specific warning that his experienced images are about to skip.
The next sentence immediately identifies the occasion on which the pendant appeared, so “that day” is normal contextual explicitation of いつか rather than a false fact.
The accusation ignores the supplied ruby: 魔術 is explicitly read きょうか, “strengthening.” The English follows that governing presentation.
The context uniquely identifies Rin as the other person at school. Using “she” is normal English explicitation of the omitted Japanese subject, not an unsupported recognition.
“Save a life” is a natural English rendering of saving a person who is near death; it does not materially abstract or change the act.
嬉しい and 楽しい substantially overlap here, and “happy things” naturally covers both pleasant and enjoyable thoughts.
In the immediate context of bodily self-destruction, “fatal” is a defensible rendering of 決定的. The following sentence still marks the mechanism as Shirou’s subjective expectation.
Here 無限の剣製 can naturally describe limitless sword production inside his body; the Japanese does not unambiguously say that the named Reality Marble itself is constructed there.
“Instantly” is an inferential intensifier, but being internally impaled by a thousand swords is presented as fatal. It does not create a material contradiction.
それなりに qualifies Shirou’s acceptance as partial or limited; “the whole situation” reverses that qualification.
助かる ordinarily means both “survive” and “be saved.” The passive English is lexically and contextually defensible.
“I can’t just die selfishly” naturally conveys that, after his promise, he has no license to die on his own. The omitted personification is stylistic rather than factual.
まいってたら can mean being in bad shape, and “look after her” is a normal contextual rendering of 手当てをしてやる. The alleged medical weakening is not demonstrable.
The English preserves the communicative action and target. The small repeated quality implied by ちょいちょい is nonmaterial gesture detail.
“About an hour ago” is compatible with conversational 一時間前. Omission of ほんの’s “just/only” emphasis does not materially change the timing.
数分後 gives a specific imminent horizon of only minutes. “At any time” removes that bounded urgency.
人一倍 means stricter than for ordinary people, whereas “a little strictness” expressly weakens the required degree.
安心 expresses Illya’s relief or ability to rest easy; “grateful” substitutes a different emotional response.
In context Shirou is defending his haste, and 間に合ったかどうか expresses doubt about whether they would have made it. “I don’t think” is a defensible natural realization of that doubt.
“Important choice” is somewhat less evocative than 重い選択 but remains a plausible contextual rendering; the accusation is chiefly tonal preference.
The immediately preceding exchange identifies Rin and Illya, so “the conversation” clearly refers to their back-and-forth and does not generalize the cause materially.
受胎 is the specific conception/gestation event that transforms Sakura. “Once that happens” leaves the trigger ambiguous after a sentence about Avenger’s birth.
In this context “the strange word” naturally means a word strange to the listeners. It need not assert that the term is intrinsically strange.
The supplied raw English contains a pause command between “Avenger” and “an”; their fusion is a command-stripping extraction artifact.
The immediately preceding page already calls Avenger a rule-breaking “violation.” The omitted repetition of 喚んではいけなかった adds emphasis but no new material prohibition.
In context, definite “the information” means the information relevant to understanding events. The Japanese does not establish that unrestricted extraction is being alleged in English.
The source assigns the duty specifically to Illya; “we” materially redistributes her personal responsibility to a group.
To “make something into one’s enemy” can naturally mean choosing or regarding it as an enemy; it does not necessarily claim the group created the threat.
“Stares at us” preserves the square, direct gaze. The narrower loss is the 挑むように characterization that makes the look explicitly challenging.
決まり事 means the ostensible rules or conventions, not the war’s ostensible reason. The English changes the type of explanation Illya is giving.

In this summary of the familiar Holy Grail War, calling the seven summoned Heroic Spirits “Servants” is normal contextual terminology; the Japanese does not establish the claimed pre-contract error here.
“Host” is a standard and semantically adequate English rendering of 依り代 in this context. Calling the hosted spirits Servants is likewise contextually established.

The source refers to the human who will obtain the Grail. “The summoner” narrows this to a specific procedural role not stated here and is awkward beside the assertion that the Grail summons the spirits.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 聖杯探求者 as マスターとサーヴァント. “Other Masters and Servants” correctly follows that reading.
The supplied raw English separates the two layers with a pause command. “spiritsServants” is a known artifact of stripping that command, not a translation error.
The English already describes the spirits as outside this world’s logic yet able to influence it, preserving the substance of 外界の力 rather than omitting their external nature.
For a ritual whose objective is to realize an otherwise impossible phenomenon, “create a phenomenon” is a natural English rendering of obtaining that result, not a material change of goal.
The English never clearly states the defining operation: materializing the otherwise-disappearing human soul. “Bringing it about” has no secure antecedent for that omitted mechanism.
The raw script contains a pause command after the stammered S, so “SSorceries” is an extraction artifact. The plural is also defensible after the preceding reference to five sorceries.
Using “Sorcery” as this translation’s chosen term for 魔法 is a glossary choice, not an error by itself; the passage consistently contrasts it with “magic” for 魔術.
The English consistently uses “Sorcery” for 魔法 and “magic” for 魔術 in the very sentence at issue. Demanding a later standardized glossary is preference policing, not evidence of mistranslation.
The English preserves the operative fact that Shirou is not even an Association member and therefore cannot know the details. The omitted self-deprecating buildup is nonmaterial rhetoric.
四人足らず means fewer than or just under four. “About four” permits four or more and loses the stated upper bound.
The supplied ruby reads 英霊召喚の基盤 as システム. “The system” follows the marked reading, while the surrounding discussion supplies its summoning referent.
“Aren’t alive as part of this world or time” adequately conveys that Servants do not live here as beings belonging to this earth and age. The abstraction is not a factual change.

The Japanese says the being remains a spiritual body and can independently affect the material world. “Can take a spirit form” changes that persistent state into an ability and omits 単体’s independence.
“Elevates a soul to the next level of life” is a reasonable compression of making the soul itself a living being and advancing it as life; the transformation is implicit, not contradicted.
The raw English has a pause command between “step” and “that’s.” Their fusion results from the supplied extraction process.
“Administrated” is uncommon where “administered” or “managed” would be more idiomatic, but it is intelligible and does not mistranslate 管理地 materially.
The Japanese says no path is connected; “the path is obstructed” instead presupposes an existing route blocked by something, changing the spatial mechanism of the analogy.
炉心 can denote the core of a furnace or reactor. “Reactor core” is a valid technical rendering for the component that powers the Greater Grail, not necessarily a nuclear embellishment.
The marked description of Heroic Spirits as visitors from “outside” supplies the reason their return can open a hole. The English omits that technical status.
In the Grail context, “your wish isn’t granted” is a natural rendering of failing to obtain what one desires. It does not materially alter the point that opening the hole is insufficient.
The supplied raw English has a pause command between “But” and “the”; “Butthe” is an extraction artifact.
In “I see. So … must,” English must functions as an inferential modal, preserving Rin’s deduction rather than presenting prior confirmed knowledge.
The next sentence defines the 代償 as giving the spirits what they desire so they will answer. In that persuasive exchange, “incentive” is semantically defensible.

The immediately preceding line identifies the rule as Masters killing one another, and earlier exposition states that they fight until one magus remains. “Last magus standing” is supported contextual explicitation.
The source locates the power at the apex described by dimensional theory. “Governs dimensional theory” instead makes the theory itself the object of that power’s rule.
“My father” is licensed by the ruby reading オヤジ attached to 切嗣; using the familial relation is not an unsupported replacement of the name.
Lowercasing an English common-noun rendering is an orthographic/style choice, not a demonstrable mistranslation of the institution.

The genuine issue is narrower: “convinced her” implies persuasion or agreement, whereas the Japanese only suggests that Shirou hit a vulnerable point and Rin fell silent. Shirou’s causal role is already evident from context.
English normally requires a pronoun, and Avenger is already being treated as a Servant/Heroic Spirit. “He” is defensible contextual explicitation despite Japanese pronoun omission.
“Souls” is licensed by the ruby たましい over 魔力. The surviving error is omission of 無色の力, the specification that this power is normally colorless.

The fixed-term complaint about “Sorcery” is a terminology preference, but なりつつある explicitly describes an ongoing process; the English apposition presents it as a successful example without preserving that aspect.
The subject is specifically the Greater Grail, and the English calls it merely “The Holy Grail” before distinguishing the Great Holy Grail later in the same sentence.

In context, “can use” is a defensible natural rendering of being capable of accomplishing the Third Magic. “Sorcery” is mirror moon’s established terminology rather than an independently demonstrable meaning error here.
英霊 is the defined Heroic Spirit category, not merely an unspecified spirit; that category is directly relevant to the surrounding explanation of what the Grail can summon.
“A foreign folklore” is genuinely unidiomatic because “folklore” is ordinarily uncountable. Bare “as catalyst” is awkward but can occur in English, so that part is not decisively erroneous.
手の内にある中で limits the choice to the worst evil available to the Einzberns; “the worst evil possible” incorrectly removes that constraint.
容認者 denotes one who accepts, permits, or acknowledges evil. “Embodiment of evil” substitutes a materially different relation.
Naming the readily identifiable Zoroastrian god of light is normal English explicitation and does not contradict or materially change the Japanese description.
相応しい can mean suitable or appropriate as well as worthy; in a Grail-selection context, “compatible” is a defensible rendering rather than a demonstrated technical invention.
The base text explicitly classifies the referent as 絶対悪 while the ruby supplies the reading アンリマユ. Rendering only the ruby name loses the meaningful “absolute evil” layer.

現れた can describe a hero emerging or existing within the village, and the surrounding account identifies him with that community. “Lived in” is a defensible contextual paraphrase without a material contradiction.
The Japanese expressly characterizes the villagers as poor as well as isolated; the English omits the material poverty.
The English loses the severe claim that these people are “less than human” and that this pride is what makes them human, reducing it to a kind of pride they knew.
殺戮 specifically means slaughter or massacre. General “conflict” substantially softens the violent human function being rejected.
The Japanese calls these all functions attached to humans from the outset. “Such human concerns” loses both their innate character and the totalizing すべて.
In a passage about humanity’s inability to detach itself from evil, “evil is in us from birth” is a reasonable explicitation of 悪とは元からあるもの, not a material new proposition.
悪い事ができない concerns inability to perform evil deeds. “Cannot be evil” changes conduct into an essential state, which matters to the villagers’ faulty logic.
“Cursed words” can naturally denote words or formulas bearing a curse; it does not necessarily assert that the words themselves are victims of a curse.
“Every sin imaginable” is a defensible paraphrase of every sin the villagers could know or conceive, preserving the limit of their conceptual inventory.

The surrounding account repeatedly frames the victim as bearing “all the evil in this world,” and immediately defines the village as a small but complete world. The English explicitation is contextually supported.
The English preserves their claimed righteousness but omits the explicit moral license that they remain good no matter what they do, a central part of the villagers’ reasoning.

The supplied witnesses conflict: the page-level Japanese has 崩壊, while the closely matching raw Original candidate has 発狂, which directly supports “went insane.” The candidate is expressly not certified alignment, so the edition basis cannot be settled responsibly.
In this context, refusing him death until his natural lifespan ends can reasonably be expressed as making him survive until old age. The English does not materially alter the duration.
The English retains irrational hatred but entirely omits his imposed status as humanity’s enemy and the continuing act of killing him.
世界中の人間 expressly extends the supposed proof to humanity throughout the world; “their goodness” most naturally restricts it to the villagers.

“His existence pardoned everyone of their evil deeds” preserves the operative indulgence: people are absolved despite their wrongdoing. The omitted repetition and quoted judgment are intensification, not a separate material claim.
The Japanese identifies the entity as the form of a curse called a “wish,” created by primordial human thought. “A curse made by a concept” loses that central wish–curse identity.
この世の悪 is the universal role “the evil of this world.” “Their evil” instead makes him represent the particular evil belonging to other people.
“Merely constructed by the people around him” substantially conveys 想いだけで構成された, and the omitted impossibility is explicitly restored on the adjacent page as “An existence that should not be.”
“Raw magical energy” is a reasonable natural rendering of energy stripped of personality and direction. The surrounding contrast with Angra Mainyu’s imposed purpose remains intelligible.
In context, “a heroic spirit that others wished for” can naturally mean a spirit wished into existence, especially after the immediately preceding explanation that people constructed him.
The English replaces the entity’s present lack of sex, personality, and even humanity with a statement about how the former human was treated. That is a substantial ontological mistranslation.
生まれる事になった describes the entity being set to be born in the form people desired. “Was finally given flesh” makes embodiment complete and omits the wish-determined form.
In context 人間の理想 is humanity’s long-held ideal—the externalization of evil—not an exemplary or ideal individual human. The English changes the concept’s possessor and object.
“That’s what that shadow is” naturally identifies the entity underlying the shadow. Requiring a literal “true body” is not necessary to preserve the relation in this context.
得ようとする means the entity is trying or about to obtain form. “Finally obtained form” incorrectly makes the still-preventable incarnation complete.
The surrounding account makes this an injunction or wish imposed by others—“be evil.” “Wanting only to be evil” instead assigns the desire to Angra Mainyu.
The ruby explicitly gives 宝具 the reading のうりょく, “ability.” The English follows that supplied reading rather than arbitrarily replacing the term.
占拠 means occupation or takeover, not tainting. The substitution blurs Rin’s correction from the Grail being occupied to its granted wish already being fixed.
“Leaking from” reasonably describes the shadow’s movement out of the Grail; 出ようとしていた need not imply conscious agency. The emergence and danger remain clear.
The Japanese concerns Angra Mainyu being incarnated through the Grail. “Formed inside” changes that prospective incarnation into an already completed internal formation.
“Use Sakura to obtain Angra Mainyu” preserves the instrumental plan, while the preceding page already explains the link and extraction on emergence. Loss of the fishing metaphor is chiefly stylistic.
Angra Mainyu is the immediately named object and is repeated in the next sentence, so “the taint of the magical energy” is contextually understood as coming from it rather than becoming generic.
The ruby reads 本体 as むし, explicitly licensing “worm.” The English also retains its function as the bearer of Zouken’s soul, so the true-body distinction is not erased.

“Angra Mainyu” is licensed by the ruby over 架空の魔物, so naming it is not an unsupported substitution. The narrower surviving issue is loss of the base-text description “imaginary monster,” whose materialized soul defines the prospective body.

“A living example” is a defensible expression for a successful instance produced by materialization of a soul. The “Sorcery” objection is terminology policing rather than a demonstrated local meaning error.
貶める explicitly describes a downward transformation from a perfect god into an imperfect god. “Tainting” conveys corruption but omits the stated resulting imperfect divinity.
The English says only that Sakura’s creation kills. It omits that it acts as Sakura’s proxy, the relation underlying Shirou’s belief that those deaths would burden her.

“Master” is explicitly licensed by the ruby reading over 寄り代, so it is not simply a mistaken substitution. The narrower issue is that the surface meaning “vessel/host” is lost, weakening why Sakura’s death would prevent emergence.
Because Sakura and Zouken will stand in the way, saying the Grail cannot be destroyed without defeating them is a reasonable contextual inference from being unable to avoid them.
Here “the world where Sakura is” directly identifies the underground cavern just named. “That’s where Sakura is” is a natural contextual translation, and the alleged loaded metaphor is not compelled.
The Japanese specifies letting out only a slight breath. “Take a deep breath” changes both the scale and potentially the direction of the breathing action.
“Settles my thoughts” can naturally mean organizing or bringing thoughts into clarity, and the immediately preceding context identifies which thoughts are involved.
嘘はない modifies the words Shirou said to Tohsaka. The English instead declares that Tohsaka is not lying, reversing whose truthfulness is at issue.

“My entire body is numb with fear” naturally compresses the spine-to-fingertips bodily range and the numbing fear. It loses some texture and the separate pressure term, but not enough to sustain the broad material-error accusation.
以前 compares the shadow with its own former state. “Unlike anything I’ve ever seen” instead compares it with Shirou’s entire experience, materially changing the reference point.
The complete page already says immediately beforehand that it is “a shadow shaped like her.” The final “virtual image” therefore does not omit the Sakura-model relation from the passage as a whole.
偉くなったものね is a sarcastic “you’ve become important/high-and-mighty”; “you’ve gotten arrogant” is a natural taunting equivalent in this exchange.
The single quotation marks can mark the word Shirou reads in Sakura’s gaze rather than spoken dialogue. The surrounding silence and preceding “Her eyes look at me” keep the appeal clearly implied.
“Say anything to her” is a natural rendering of calling out or addressing Sakura, and weakening resolve without qualification still includes even a slight weakening. The differences are not material.
侮蔑 is explicit contempt, distinct from mere coldness. The English retains the cold voice but removes Sakura’s contemptuous stance toward Rin.
The English preserves total coldness and lack of concern but omits 見下しきった, the explicit characterization of Rin’s voice as completely contemptuous or looking down on Sakura.

Angra Mainyu’s former male human identity has already been established at length, so “him” is normal English pronoun explicitation. The finding does not allege the separate loss of the “that child” relational metaphor.
「今夜」identifies this specific night, whereas “for one night” states an abstract duration and can shift the deadline.

“Take his life with mine” defensibly expresses killing the entity at the cost of Sakura’s own life. The context can also support masculine reference; the alleged loss of mutual destruction is not decisive here.
The narration specifically repeats 「刺し違える」, reciprocal fatal combat. “Kill him using her life” instead makes her life an instrument and does not clearly preserve the entity killing her in return.
“Tohsaka trembles a bit” is a natural compression of her shoulder trembling slightly; it does not necessarily assert a materially different whole-body action.
In this context, 「我慢できなくなる」 means losing the ability to restrain or endure herself, and “run out of patience” is a defensible English rendering rather than necessarily irritation.
“Kill the Servant … along with you” can convey taking the Servant with Sakura in death, so the agency accusation is overstated. The explicit fact that Sakura inherited its power is genuinely omitted.
「変わりきる姿」is the appearance Sakura will have after changing completely. “See me change” instead foregrounds witnessing the transformation process.
The shadow is pleading for them not to pursue it. “By letting us go” makes the shadow’s release of them the means of salvation, reversing the requested action.
「アンリマユと刺し違える」means killing Angra Mainyu while being killed in the exchange. “Kill herself along with” recasts this as Sakura-directed suicide and obscures the reciprocal attack.
Rin’s declaration is personally voiced: she will go and kill Sakura. Repeated “we” transfers that commitment to a group without support in the line.
“Her sister” preserves the central kinship. Omitting the already-established biological and younger-sister specifications is normal contextual compression, not a material contradiction.
“Tohsaka’s magus” is awkward English, but in context it remains intelligible as the Tohsaka family’s magus. The finding establishes a stylistic problem, not a material mistranslation.
English permits the object of “kill” to be contextually elided, and “you’re telling me to run” makes Rin the intended target readily recoverable.

Japanese does not grammatically mark a singular subject here. Given Shirou and Rin’s joint plan to go, “we” is a defensible contextual explicitation, despite Rin’s subsequent personal promise to kill Sakura.
“Make a good face” is stiffly literal but still refers transparently to Sakura’s displayed expression. The complaint is primarily about naturalness, not factual accuracy.
“Smiles violently” awkwardly but plausibly conveys the terrifying intensity of 「凄絶」. The distinct quiet chuckle marked by 「くすり」 is genuinely omitted.
Present-tense “recedes” can describe the shadow going away in narrative English and does not necessarily assert that the withdrawal remains incomplete.
In the immediate context of Sakura telling them to flee far away, “run” naturally conveys leaving town. The lost geographic wording is not enough to establish a material error.
After Rin offers Shirou the option of fleeing town, “I won’t run away” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of his refusal to stop participating in the fight.
“Doing things you can’t do” substantially preserves covering Rin’s limitations. The narrower genuine omission is 「最後まで」, Shirou’s commitment to continue that support through the end.

“Sakura’s superhero” preserves both the heroic-justice concept and its restriction to Sakura. It is a defensible localization of the recurring phrase, even if another terminology might better preserve series consistency.
Rin’s utterance both mentions Sakura’s killings and asks whether saving her is justice. Calling that decisive utterance an “inquiry” is contextually defensible.
「言い逃れ」specifically concerns evasion through excuses or words. “A sin I can’t talk myself out of” closely reproduces that sense rather than improperly narrowing it.
“The part of her that wants to kill herself” is a natural way to include Sakura’s suicidal aspect within the whole denoted by 「ひっくるめて」; it need not assert a literal divided-self model.
“Tell her what I think” reasonably conveys giving his feelings verbal form. It does omit the explicit pride and confidence of 「胸を張って」.
Rin is conceding after an argument with Shirou, so “You beat me” is a normal and well-supported English explicitation of 「負けた」.
「もう口出ししない」is a continuing promise not to interfere or object any further. “Not going to say anything now” can be read as only temporary silence and weakens that concession.
The cheek action depicts comic irritation, and “looks angry” conveys that emotional display. The loss of the precise visual manner is compression rather than a demonstrably false assertion.
“Leaves” accurately reports Rin’s departure. Omitting that she goes into the detached annex and the figurative 「消えていった」 is incidental scene-detail compression.
“The uneasiness in my chest goes away” preserves the governing emotional event. Size, obstruction, and melting are imagery-level losses, not a material reversal.
The preceding text already uses 「助ける」for saving Sakura; here 「立ち直らせる」specifically means helping her recover or regain herself. Repeating generic “save” erases that distinction.

The Japanese coordination permits more than one scope reading: the midnight phrase certainly governs finishing preparations, but it may also pragmatically govern the subsequent assault. These witnesses do not decisively prove the narrower accusation.
“As close as we’re going to get” naturally conveys an Azoth sword made or chosen to resemble the jeweled sword as closely as possible. Deliberate modeling remains inferable.
The action of handing Shirou the dagger is preserved. Dropping the tiny handoff utterance 「はい」 does not materially change the event.

“A ritualistic equipment” is grammatically poor, but the preceding noun “dagger” still identifies the concrete object and its ritual function accurately. This is editing quality, not a material meaning error.
“How much magical energy is stored” preserves both magnitude and the stored state, while Shirou’s ability to sense it despite being an amateur implies that the amount is exceptional.
The English broadly preserves the comparison but changes 「何百倍」, hundreds of times, into one hundred times. It also drops the concrete palmful scale.
In a joke contrasting apparent generosity with strictness over money, “stingy” is within the contextual range of 「お金に関してはすごく厳しい」 and is not demonstrably a false character judgment.
「飛んだり跳ねたり」describes vigorous physical movement idiomatically; “manage to move around” is broader but accurately states the mobility Rin retains.

The technical term “magic” may reflect translation convention, but the source specifically says Rin’s magical energy has not recovered. “I haven’t healed” incorrectly makes general bodily recovery the stated limiting quantity.
Here 「領域外」can idiomatically mean beyond normal bounds rather than a formally named technical category. “Absurd powers” conveys that extraordinary scale in context.
「部屋」does not specify Shirou’s private room, and the narration explicitly has Rin head toward the living room. “Your room” invents a destination contradicted by the same page.
Saying she must be present “in case something happens” pragmatically conveys Rin’s proposed backup function. The active-support nuance is compressed but not materially lost.

Japanese leaves the possessor of the concession implicit. In a negotiation between Illya and Rin, collective “we” is a defensible English framing and does not contradict an explicitly personal marker.
「はた、と…閃いた」marks a sudden idea arising as Shirou starts to follow. The English replaces that cognition with a deliberate decision to ask a question.
In this casual departure line, “go do my best” is a defensible idiomatic rendering of putting spirit into the task. The exact self-bracing flavor is stylistic.
Within this scene, “after everything is over” naturally refers to the ongoing Holy Grail War. The endpoint remains contextually unambiguous.
“A dagger that’s just like it” can colloquially mean one modeled after or resembling it; it need not claim technical equivalence to the original jeweled sword.
The source says the inherited record should have seen the sword in the old man’s hand. Saying only that the sword “was there” removes both the wielder and the recorded observation.

The pressure is specifically caused by tracing backward into a two-hundred-year-old record. “The pressure of two hundred years” instead suggests an undifferentiated temporal weight and omits the traversal mechanism.
The English preserves trembling arms but omits the substantial physical action that those arms are embracing Shirou from directly in front.

“Within her memory” is a natural description of being included in the record, especially after the preceding pages call that record Illya’s memory. Spatial wording does not materially reverse inclusion.

The source distinguishes self-damage beyond applicability of ordinary pain from the rotating layers of pain into which Shirou falls. The English’s malformed sequence turns this into pain being absent or irrelevant and injury swallowing him.
Assigning the radius to the rock surface is not itself wrong. The genuine losses are its mortar-like basin shape and the fact that dozens of multilayered markings cover it.
An “observatory” can denote a large observation installation or apparatus, fitting the Arizona-desert comparison. The repeated intensifier is compressed into “large,” not contradicted.
「蜘蛛の巣」is the visible web structure. “Spider’s nest” substitutes a different object and damages the circuit-web image.
The transitive 「従えた」places Makiri and Tohsaka in Justeaze’s following or attendance. “Accompanied by” reduces that directional hierarchy to neutral company.

Terminological objection to “sorcery” is not decisive under older Fate localization conventions. The real error is that 「試みる」states an attempt, while the English presents ongoing reenactment and attaches it directly to Justeaze.
「マキリや遠坂だけでは」means that Makiri and Tohsaka alone are insufficient. The English instead makes them fellow knowers alongside the old man, reversing their grammatical role.
The surrounding lines establish a shrinking body and lowered viewpoint within the record. “Ripped in half” invents violent bisection rather than the perceived body becoming half-sized.
The old man is looking down on the Greater Grail and watching events unfold. “Standing in front of” both relocates him and omits his sustained observation.
“Sears through my eyes and into my brain” conveys severe burning that penetrates the eyes and reaches the brain. It is less anatomical, but it does not materially sanitize the destructive escalation.
「しかできない」affirmatively preserves analysis and Projection as the only thing Shirou can do. The English inserts “can’t” and reverses that capability.

The source escalates from something like another planet to something like an entirely different star system. “Alien technology” replaces that comparison with an unsupported technological classification.
“Modern man” preserves the governing contrast between present humanity and knowledge from the far future. The infancy metaphor is lost, but the factual temporal relation remains.
「脳神経」means cerebral or cranial nerves, not multiple brains. “My brains” is both anatomically wrong and malformed English.
The accusation attacks a blank page that is not present in the supplied translation. Mirror moon explicitly renders both the stop and return commands as “Stop! Come back, Shirou…!”

“Back out now” is a natural contextual paraphrase of refusing to return after Illya orders him back. The repetition is omitted, but that tonal compression does not establish a material change of decision or movement.
The supplied mirror-moon text is not blank: “Give up…! Do you want to disappear, Shirou!?” preserves both Illya’s command and her warning that he may vanish.
Although “pushed back” is milder than 「跳ね飛ばされた」in isolation, the next English sentence explicitly says Shirou is flying and lands on his back, preserving the violent displacement as a whole.
In context, “it paid off” naturally means the dangerous action produced the successful Projection. That is a defensible paraphrase of 「上手くいった」, not a different causal claim.
“Points at my face” accurately preserves Illya’s accusatory pointing gesture. Generalizing the target from the nose tip to the face is minor visual compression, not a material error.
“Wouldn’t cut paper” is a normal English concretization of a blade apparently unable to cut things at all. Paper is not in the Japanese, but the idiom does not contradict the broader inability.
The English is grammatically malformed and misconstrues 剣製, which denotes sword-making/creation rather than a plural noun phrase blade works.
The concessive description of Rin as junior or inexperienced is wholly omitted, removing the exceptional contrast with wielding the Second.
Running to put them on trial is a loose but defensible institutional paraphrase of every department mobilizing for a trial; it need not describe literal running.
屈折 means refraction. Refractory denotes resistance or intractability and gives the named phenomenon the wrong technical meaning.
Sorcerer is a defensible term for 魔法使い and can preserve its contrast with magus. A narrower issue remains: pursue leaves vague the endpoint explicitly expressed by たどり着く.
Sorcerer is a conventional and defensible rendering of 魔法使い, especially where the English separately uses magus for 魔術師; the categorical distinction is not necessarily lost.
The Japanese identifies clouding or blurring vision when his guard relaxes, whereas dizziness is a broader and different symptom.
The English retains some agency through Shirou clenching his fist, so the experience is not wholly passive. It nevertheless omits the explicit act of driving the pendant into his flesh.
言葉 can mean words, speech, or language. In this comprehension contrast, a language he does not understand is a natural rendering rather than an unsupported resolution.
記憶がとぶ describes a break or missing stretch of memory, not merely indistinct recollection. Vague materially understates the discontinuity.
飛びついてくる describes Rin springing or lunging at him. Grabs me substitutes the later contact and omits the abrupt movement contrasted with its perceived slowness.
何処で asks where he found it; the English instead asks why he picked it up.
忘れられない presents the event as unforgettable, making his failure to retrieve it paradoxical. Shouldn’t forget instead suggests an obligation.
Until the end is a natural contextual rendering of 最期まで and can readily denote the end of his life; the Japanese does not require the explicit word death.
They’re the same is ordinary English for two objects looking identical and need not assert numerical identity. Rin’s correction concerns their remaining contents, not their appearance.
Although awkward, meaning behind the usage conveys that the pendant’s having been used is significant. The causal inference is blurred stylistically, not reversed or lost.
