Walks off with Illya preserves their departure but omits Rin’s concrete action of taking Illya by the hand.
In a command addressed directly to Shirou, your room is normal English explicitation of 部屋 and does not establish a materially unsupported location.
殺気 is killing intent or a murderous aura. Outright hostility substantially reduces the deliberately lethal hyperbole of Rin’s anger.
I guess I’m saved already qualifies the claim and reasonably conveys 助かったといえば助かった. Calling it unqualified casual relief overstates the difference.
The paired 丁寧に丹念に stresses careful, painstaking examination. Find out omits that methodical quality in a dangerous bodily self-check.
Before I start moving preserves the practical condition that he must assess himself first. The loss of 下手に is a nuance of caution, not a materially different logical relation here.
Have to go, in Shirou’s immediate recollection, adequately conveys present urgency. Omitting an explicit now is not a material temporal error.
倒れてる describes being down or collapsed, while lying states only posture and obscures the involuntary physical failure being questioned.
The English says only that he realizes he is in the shed, omitting that he finds himself sprawled there in an undignified posture.
Is hurting is a permissible, if less vivid, rendering of the persistent aching expressed by ジクジク. The accusation is chiefly intensity preference.
You… is a natural interrupted fragment, and Rider’s immediate answer, I was watching you, supplies the all-this-time relation. No material information is lost across the exchange.
The grammatical subject 貴方 is Shirou and サクラ is the target of harm. The English reverses them and says Sakura is trying to harm Shirou.
Lightly is imperfect in isolation, but the immediately following She speaks without emotion explicitly restores the dispassionate quality of 淡々 and 事務的.
殺気 denotes killing intent, not merely hostility. The added creeping bodily phrasing can reflect ぞわり, but the lethal force is still weakened.
倒される can mean being brought down or killed, and Rider has explicitly announced that she came to kill him. Killed is defensible in this immediate context.
One step is defensible for 一足 in context, but the English does omit the explicitly backward direction of Shirou’s escape leap.
The Japanese states only that Rider’s closing speed exceeds Shirou’s retreat speed. Long before adds an unsupported, much larger timing margin.
The affect may be unreadable as anger or disappointment, but 殺気 still expressly denotes killing intent. Hostility weakens that lethal force.
The English retains the snake comparison but omits the defining image of Rider standing in darkness and watching her prey.
Signs of her attack accurately conveys the functional meaning of the figurative snake raising its head. Losing the carried metaphor is a stylistic compression, not a demonstrable factual error.
The page immediately renders his excitement as the rush of evasion and his accelerating heartbeat. The affect is redistributed rather than materially omitted.
A superior opponent’s attack accurately identifies Rider contextually and subsumes the dagger strike. The abstraction is not a material change to the action.
The English preserves the successful escape but omits that Shirou achieved it by exploiting an opening, a concrete tactical relation.
Pleasure lies within the lexical range of 喜ぶ and refers here to his satisfaction at escaping. It does not necessarily introduce a sensual meaning.
Coming after me directly expresses pursuit, so the English preserves 追って来る. Mentioning emergence from the shed is supplied by the visible setting.
The comparison with her arrival is omitted, but She disappears into the night preserves the event itself. The surviving complaint is a minor literary-detail omission, not a material accuracy error.
Presence disappears can naturally describe a sensed presence fading beyond detection; it need not mean an instantaneous physical disappearance. The following departure context supports that reading.
If my suspicion is correct is an idiomatic equivalent of if my interpretation is not mistaken. Both preserve Shirou’s uncertainty.
Japanese leaves the beneficiary unstated. Given the group effort to save Sakura, us is a normal contextual explicitation rather than an unsupported change.
やり過ごす means getting through, evading, or weathering the encounter. Can’t match Rider instead asserts a general parity comparison.
Can’t afford is idiomatic for being unable to bear the cost or consequence and, with any more, adequately conveys that further Projection exceeds his limit.
Take chances is a defensible English expression for gambling under uncertainty, and the surrounding threat of death supplies the desperation of イチかバチか.
Not daring to take his eyes off Rider naturally explicates the sustained vigilance in 見据えたまま. It need not impute cowardice or a materially new constraint.
The ruby reads 投影 as ぶき, explicitly presenting the Projection as a weapon. Delaying weapon creation until the last second is therefore a defensible rendering.
Rider stepping into Shirou’s space is the onset of her attack here. The English generalizes the physical trigger but preserves the intended response timing.
Project something and counter omits three concrete elements: completing a sword, doing so in zero seconds, and meeting Rider with full force.
Projection is the established name of the technique and can stand naturally for 投影魔術 in dialogue. Repeating the category magecraft is not necessary for accuracy.
使いこなせない means being unable to use or handle something proficiently or to its full capability. Cannot use you to your full potential closely matches it.
殺気 specifically identifies killing intent growing faint. Hostility is broader and removes the immediate lethal quality of what subsides.
引き下がる can mean stepping back or backing down, while her fading killing intent supports relaxes. The English adequately conveys her ready disengagement.
健在 concerns Saber remaining alive, intact, or viable. Were here reduces that counterfactual condition to mere physical presence and is misleading given her altered status.
Presence disappears can describe Rider’s aura receding beyond perception, especially with the following inference that she left the grounds. Instantaneous disappearance is not required.
The English conveys that Rider leaves the property but entirely omits the explicit gesture that she does so without looking back.
If my suspicion is correct preserves the same self-doubt as if my belief is not mistaken; the change is idiomatic rather than substantive.
The Japanese does not state an indirect object. In the shared plan to save Sakura, help us is a reasonable contextual rendering of lending assistance.
The Japanese frames the recollection tentatively through 確か and the self-questioning 問われたのではなかったか. The English states the memory directly.
The English retains fighting to the end but wholly omits the unconditional test no matter what happens.
守ろうとする expresses intention or an attempt to protect. Want to protect is a defensible rendering of that volitional construction in context.
取り戻す specifically means getting or reclaiming Sakura back. Save her conveys the broad goal but loses the stated idea that Sakura has been displaced or taken from them.
全力で排除する says he will remove or eliminate the obstruction with all his strength. Do whatever it takes to kill you makes death the explicit objective and changes 全力で into different wording.
The English omits the adverbial brevity of 短く but preserves the statement and ensuing departure. This is a minor delivery detail, not a material error.
姿を消す can idiomatically mean leaving or disappearing from someone’s presence; it does not by itself establish a sudden occult vanishing.
In this departure scene, 返ってくる気配はない naturally means there is no sign Rider will come back. It does not say 返事 or otherwise clearly refer to an answering voice.
As in the parallel scene, 確か and 問われたのではなかったか make this a tentative reconstruction, while the English presents it as direct recollection.
The cited governing reading incorrectly substitutes fighting for the supplied Japanese’s not giving up. A narrower valid claim remains: the English omits 何があっても, the no-matter-what condition.
Want to protect is a reasonable rendering of the intention or attempted action expressed by 守ろうとする; it does not materially erase Rider’s protective stance.
Save Sakura conveys rescue generally but omits the more specific aim in 取り戻す of reclaiming or getting Sakura back.
The source threatens full-force removal of Rider as an obstacle, not explicitly killing her at any cost. The English hardens both the method and objective.
The omitted 短く supplies a clipped delivery, but its absence does not materially alter the retained statement or action.
姿を消す permits the ordinary sense of departing from sight or presence. She leaves is therefore defensible without evidence of supernatural suddenness.
The surrounding narration concerns Rider physically departing to fight alone, so no indication she’ll return is a natural reading of 返ってくる気配はない.
The English preserves remaining Sakura’s ally through the end but omits the emphatic condition whatever may happen.
Please help us omits 今だけでも, which explicitly limits Shirou’s request to cooperation for the present occasion.
Care for Sakura naturally means holding her dear and can carry sincere concern. Omitting the intensifier 本当に slightly reduces emphasis but does not create a material mistranslation.
いつぞや denotes an unspecified earlier occasion, and “the other day” can function as a loose recollection rather than a precise date. The English is defensible in this context.
The Japanese identifies Rider as the strongest card for protecting Sakura; the English syntax instead apposes “Sakura’s strongest card” to Saber’s Noble Phantasm.

囚われた literally means captured or caught, but “consumed by Sakura” is a defensible contextual description of the Servants absorbed and transformed by her shadow. The following embodiment explanation remains intact.
The contextual attribution to Sakura is defensible, but the English wrongly generalizes the singular statement about Saber into plural “bodies” and “they.”
Although 魔術品 is broader than “weapons,” the preceding question specifically concerns weapons capable of harming Servants, so the contextual narrowing is defensible.
Japanese normally leaves noun number unstated. “Their shadows” can naturally denote the black covering associated with the affected Servants and does not establish a contradictory plurality.
“I’m just making sure” is an ordinary idiomatic rendering of taking a precaution, especially immediately after saying nobody is listening.
確かに itself supports “definitely/indeed,” while Rider and the object of the breakthrough are recoverable from the proposed plan and surrounding discussion. These are normal English explicitations.
The issue is specifically how far Rider can trust Shirou’s skill, not her general personal trust in him. The English loses that calibrated tactical assessment.
戸惑い indicates momentary uncertainty, and portraying the accompanying finger-to-mouth gesture as thinking is a defensible natural paraphrase, not a demonstrable material change.
承知しました is a controlled, formal acknowledgment. “Fair enough” is conspicuously casual and concessive, altering Rider’s established register.
The English preserves Shirou’s surprise but omits 可憐, the explicit description of Rider’s smile as strikingly lovely or charming.
The Japanese presents the visual convergence of the clock hands. “The clock strikes” invents an audible chime and replaces that image.
The English retains the pendant but omits that it is the one Rin instructed or told Shirou to take, removing a concrete part of their preparation.
俺の希望 modifies the decision to have Illya remain behind. “She’s my hope” instead makes Illya herself an abstract source of hope.
Because Shirou is human, “human functionality” reasonably conveys his functions as a living organism. It is awkward English but does not materially contradict the Japanese.
“Eroding” naturally conveys functions being progressively worn away and retains the incremental deterioration expressed by 少しずつこそぎ落ちている.
頃 gives an approximate time around dawn, whereas “before the day breaks” imposes a firm earlier deadline.
ごうごう describes a powerful roaring sound, for which wind “howling” is a conventional English rendering. The source’s acoustic force is not demonstrably lost.
Rin describes going to the Greater Grail as a destination. “If we want the Great Holy Grail” instead suggests wanting or obtaining the object.
山の中へ入っていく means proceeding into the mountainous interior. “Climb the mountain” adds upward movement, contrary to the stated descent and the following terrain.
The raw witness contains “Hm” followed by a line-dash command before “it.” The joined “Hmit” is an extraction artifact, not malformed translated prose.
A pitfall is a kind of concealed pit, and “just be a pit” retains the practical joke that an entrance would not simply be a hole. The distinction is too slight to establish material error.
枯れ木 can straightforwardly mean dead or withered trees. 冬 permits a seasonal reading but does not make “dead trees” demonstrably false.
“No sign of human influence” is a natural contextual paraphrase for the absence of artificial or manufactured objects in the clearing.
Calling チロチロと流れる小川 a “small stream” compresses minor descriptive motion but preserves the object and scene; this is not a material mistranslation.
Shirou uses the sound as a guide while actively straining his eyes. The English replaces that visual scrutiny with deciding which direction to search.
In context, “a rocky outcropping” can reasonably summarize the ground or formation of overlapping rocks from which the water emerges; the following page supplies its geometry.
“Big enough for one person to fit through” conveys a single-person opening and can pragmatically imply its tightness. Omitting ようやく is a minor degree loss, not a material error.
The Japanese says an entrant would encounter rock almost immediately inside. The English invents a huge boulder blocking the entrance, changing both location and scale.
After explicitly saying the rock has no tactile presence, “goes through the space instead” adequately conveys passage through the apparent rock. Its awkwardness does not create a contradictory event.
The central action is still a deep breath. Omitting 小さく loses only a slight manner qualification and does not materially change the scene.
かつん denotes a discrete hard click or knock. “Scraping” changes it into a continuous friction sound.

“Using my hands” reasonably renders 手探り, and the surrounding sentences establish a steep downward cave surface. Calling that wet surface rocks and making the descent explicit is defensible contextual phrasing.
The English states that it is dark and preserves uncertainty about how far downward the underground path continues. It compresses the Japanese syntax without losing its governing spatial uncertainty.
In a sentence about saving Sakura, “better to have two people” naturally means that two improve the likelihood of success. It is a defensible rendering of 方が確実.

The omitted Japanese subject is naturally Shirou, as the immediately following text specifies what he promised. “Made a promise with her” is awkward but does not falsely erase a demonstrated mutual promisor.

“The victor” has a definite, readily recoverable field: the surrounding lines discuss their earlier alliance and Rin winning the ongoing Holy Grail War. Repetition of the contest name is not required in English.
In the context of a former schoolgirl crush, “the girl I used to admire” is a defensible restrained rendering of 好きだった女の子, which need not mean explicit love.
“Faithful” is within the range of 律儀, and the immediately preceding discussion of promises makes conscientious promise-keeping the natural reading rather than romantic fidelity.
The English reduces the line to generic descent, omitting both the abyss image and 淡々, their controlled, matter-of-fact manner after the conversation ends.
進んだ measures distance traveled along the spiral passage. “Over a hundred meters underground” instead asserts vertical depth.
体の感覚で supplies the basis for an estimate already rendered as Shirou’s thought. Its omission is minor compression and does not alter the estimate’s content.
生々しい describes disturbing rawness or visceral immediacy. “Lively” instead suggests ordinary animation and weakens the revulsion developed on the next page.

The alleged separation of od and mana is not decisive because the English can be read as coordinated descriptions of the same phenomenon. The clear surviving error is “almost visible”: 視覚化できるほど says the outpouring is sufficient to be visible.
汚物 means filth, refuse, or a foul substance. “Something rotten” introduces decay, distorting the intended revulsion at an obscenely excessive manifestation of life.
意識が切れる describes consciousness cutting out abruptly. “Fades away” makes the loss gradual.

呼び起こす can naturally mean rousing oneself or restoring alertness. Given the surrounding threat of lost consciousness, “clear my head” is a defensible English paraphrase rather than merely ordinary calm.
生暖かい is lukewarm or unpleasantly warm, while 撫でる is a stroking motion. “Warm wind hits” changes both the temperature’s nuance and the action.
“About as big as the schoolground” is a natural shorthand for the cavern’s horizontal span, with its height separately stated next. It does not demonstrably assert a conflicting geometry.
“Unforgettable” directly reverses 忘れられた, which describes an abandoned or forgotten underground hall.
殺気 specifically denotes killing or murderous intent, not merely hostile feeling. The English weakens Saber’s expressly lethal presence.

The full page already identifies Saber as gatekeeper, executioner, and remover of intruders. “The strongest Servant Sakura has” is therefore a defensible contextual restatement rather than an erasure of her protective role.
The preceding English sentence already says Rin intends to fight “head-on,” and the visible gem sword supplies the sword context. The shorter second sentence is not materially misleading.
Saber pointedly frames Rin drawing her sword against her as a possible “mistake.” The generic “do not attack me” removes that condition and its controlled, sardonic warning.
“Stops Tohsaka in her tracks” can idiomatically describe the effect of Saber’s verbal admonition and does not state that Saber physically restrained her.
“We” preserves that both Shirou and Rin understand, while “right away” reasonably conveys that no question is needed. The loss of しまった is too slight to establish material error.

In “anyone that passes by here,” “by here” can naturally mean through the guarded location rather than merely nearby. The gatekeeping context prevents the alleged ambiguity from becoming a factual error.
“She must be serious” is a normal English expression of Rin’s realization from Saber’s confirmation. It does not materially weaken or contradict 本気なんだ.
The Japanese deliberately withholds the object of 信頼; the next page explicitly calls the line “目的語抜き.” Supplying “you” removes Shirou’s intended confusion and the guarded comic beat.
“Right before she disappears” adequately conveys Rin vanishing from view as she enters the darkness. The loss of the blending metaphor is stylistic compression, not a material factual error.
The English reports only that Rin disappears, omitting the expressly purposeful detail that she continues deeper without turning back.
“In short” still marks the sentence as Shirou’s interpretation, and “told me to come help her while she keeps Sakura at bay” conveys the practical content of Rin’s indirect encouragement.
殺気 is specifically murderous or killing intent. Rendering its sudden swelling as generic “hostility” materially softens the onset of Saber’s lethal pressure.
With the immediately preceding sentence describing her hostility, “doesn’t have to hold back” naturally refers to suppressing that aggression. It is a defensible contextual paraphrase.
手を出す means to attack or use force, and the preceding dialogue establishes Saber’s assigned elimination duty. “Your job to kill” is a blunt but contextually supported explicitation.
Shirou is speaking directly to Saber, so “I wouldn’t listen” naturally means he would not listen to her. The source of the warnings is not actually obscured in context.
Here 一分 is read いちぶ and denotes one tenth. “A tenth of her powers” is therefore textually supported, not an invented ratio.

“The battle doesn’t start when the blades first meet” naturally expresses that Shirou’s real contest begins before any comparison of sword technique. It preserves the tactical hierarchy in idiomatic English.
“Do you crave death so badly?” idiomatically conveys Saber’s taunt that Shirou seems eager to be killed sooner. Omitting the literal one-second formulation is not a material change.
In a waiting contest, “lose patience” is a standard rendering of becoming unable to endure any longer. It does not require frivolous impatience.
打倒した explicitly says Shirou defeated Berserker. “When I fought Berserker” removes the prior success that motivates treating Projection as a possible tactic now.
Even allowing for the intentionally fractured presentation, the Japanese explicitly protects both sensation and thought. The English retains only “the senses,” omitting 思考.
The English still calls the paired swords Archer’s lifelong symbol and says he wielded them throughout his life. Its altered syntax does not materially contradict the identity association.

The material objection is not fully decisive because 錬鉄 can be rendered broadly as forged iron or steel in this stylized description. The genuine loss is 夫婦剣: “twin blades” omits their expressly married or mated-pair relation.
“Strong swords,” immediately followed by their ability to withstand Saber’s blows, adequately communicates their proven sturdiness. Rendering the idiom 折紙つき literally is not necessary.
無駄 can cover wasted effort or energy, and the following explanation concerns the costly projection of a powerful Noble Phantasm. The supplied resource is contextually defensible.
“Holds the sword” reasonably entails gripping its hilt, so that part is not a material error. The narrower omission is 音もなく, Saber’s explicitly soundless movement.
Shirou has just been told his body will last only minutes, so “my dying body” is a defensible contextual paraphrase of being on the verge of collapse, not an unsupported diagnosis.
The direction is redistributed, not omitted: the same page ends with “swing down with all my might,” preserving the descending Bakuya strike.
“Everything I have” substitutes general effort or strength for the specifically named consciousness being concentrated into the arm, a meaningful distinction in this sequence.
The English preserves the thrust and target but entirely omits that it happens too quickly for Shirou even to see.
Although awkward, “moves like a superhuman” defensibly conveys 超人的 motion; 翻る does not establish one indispensable, precisely defined maneuver here.
Successful defense is conveyed by “blocked,” but 三十余 is more than thirty and 確実に殺せる describes reliably lethal precision, both weakened in English.
In this combat context, rendering the body’s inability to execute borrowed experience as the limbs failing to keep up is a defensible physical concretization.
“Battle experience” is contextually the executable combat expertise reproduced with the swords; it does not materially contradict 戦闘技術.
The immediately preceding references to Archer’s combat experience and the swords constrain “abilities” to fighting ability, making the broader word harmless in context.
The ruby いちげき supports associating the cost with each strike, so the alleged trigger change is not established. A narrower issue remains: “wavers” softens vision being progressively削られる.
“Shift into high gear and step on the gas” naturally carries the same figurative acceleration; 踏み砕く adds hyperbolic force but its loss is tonal compression, not a material factual error.
The English omits both explicit benefits of drawing further: fighting longer and fighting more strongly.
The complete English does distinguish the actions: Saber first “pushed me away,” after which Shirou “jumped back to regroup.” The opening fragment is merely a redundant summary.
The Japanese specifies the resulting interval as ten meters, not the distance traversed by Shirou’s jump. English turns state into movement distance.

Context permits “these swords” to mean the sword attacks rather than Shirou’s held weapons, so that accusation is speculative. The English does, however, lose どんなに—the willingness to take any number or extent of nonfatal blows.
受ける can mean receive, withstand, or block an attack. Given that Shirou has been parrying Saber and counts five forthcoming exchanges, “block five more attacks” is defensible.
よく吠える is a contemptuous, animalizing taunt. The explanatory English question removes that conspicuous hostility from Saber’s direct speech.
“This next exchange” is supported by このまま打ち合えば、次は. The surviving error is that English loses the written sword/ruby body construction and Saber’s threat to pulverize him together with it.

The Japanese makes the one remaining Projection his means of victory, with 投影 itself glossed as “sword.” English instead says he will use swords already possessed, disrupting the reserved-resource logic.
“Broken and crazy” is rough but remains within the lexical force of thoughts warped and collapsed to an extreme degree; the psychiatric objection overstates the distinction.
“Greatest protection” is a natural metonym for Sakura’s strongest guardian, whose identity as Saber is explicit in the surrounding text.
“Her Master” unambiguously identifies Sakura in this tactical discussion and accurately expresses the relationship motivating Saber’s return.
The Japanese says the heart or mind is no longer Shirou’s own. “A mind without a self” changes that alienation or loss of ownership into the absence of any self.
“My wish” transparently refers to saving Sakura in the immediately preceding sentence. This is normal English anaphora, not loss of the concrete goal.
In context, “give her the chance” naturally expresses enabling Rin to carry the rescue onward; it does not contradict the succession implied by 繋げる.
“Will do it” expresses confidence and its object—saving Sakura—is explicit in the same sentence. Repeating Sakura and adding “surely” are not necessary for accuracy.

読み込むする is visibly malformed, but the witnesses do not prove that the defect intentionally represents cognitive collapse rather than a source typo or ruby construction. Repairing it is defensible, and “weapons” is supported by the next sentence.
“Full capabilities” is a natural rendering of not yet grasping the weapon’s 性能; “full” does not establish a materially different degree of partial knowledge.
“Mind” is within the contextual range of 意識 here, where a percentage of Shirou’s remaining awareness or conscious self is being measured.
The surrounding lines make the forgetting involuntary and catastrophic, including loss of his own name. English first-person grammar does not turn it into ordinary deliberate agency.

必至 can denote an inevitable or unavoidable winning state as well as desperation or necessity. In a passage seeking a 必殺 technique, “guarantee a kill” is a defensible reading, not a demonstrable overstatement.
“Get him through” can idiomatically mean prevail through the battles, so the victory/survival contrast is overstated. A narrower inflation remains: 多く means “many,” not necessarily “countless.”
イド participates in wordplay with drawing water from a well. “The well of experience” preserves the operative reservoir metaphor; choosing that side of the layered wordplay is defensible.

Within this telegraphic list of tactical instructions, “keep to the basic technique” is a defensible implied command. The omitted Japanese subject does not conclusively require a descriptive English sentence.

The first four English lines follow the special ruby readings supplied when the verse is spoken, rather than arbitrarily replacing its written images. The final “shared life” remains wrong: both the writing and later ruby indicate separation/death or an inability to share heaven.
Lowering the hips is a conventional readying motion, so “readies herself” accurately conveys the action’s function; omission of the exact posture is minor staging compression.
The English retains the contrast that all other names are gone and leaves the enemy’s name unfinished with an ellipsis. “Is called…” naturally represents recall on the verge of completion.
敵上 can mean at or over the enemy’s position; it does not decisively require an intersection spatially above her body. The neck target also supports crossing at her location.
撃ち砕く an iron mass describes smashing force, whereas “steel-penetrating” changes both the material image and the mode of destruction.
“Hero” falls within the range of 豪傑 as a heroic or exceptionally mighty warrior, especially in this mythic combat register.
“She escaped the attack” conveys that the tactic failed, and the next English sentence explicitly restores her active role in redirecting both swords behind her. No evasion-only account results.

The incantation explicitly carries the foreign-language rubies フリーズ and アウト. “Freeze, out” is stylized command terminology rather than ordinary prose, and the following manifestation makes the release function clear.

The page says Projection is already complete and that prepared Kanshou and Bakuya are now created again. Treating the prepared element as their Projection image is a defensible technical explicitation, not an unsupported new event.
届かない commonly means failing to reach or measure up to someone figuratively. Saber’s “cannot match me” is a defensible boast about the Noble Phantasm’s insufficiency.
“Cognition-like” does not mean resembling prediction of the future and produces an incoherent description of Saber’s instinct.
The Japanese explicitly says Bakuya is shattered against Saber’s sword. Reporting only a block omits the weapon’s destruction.

The English is awkward but correctly states that Saber destroys the Bakuya used for Shirou’s attack. 正面から斬り伏せにいった means he attacked to cut her down head-on, not necessarily one uniquely specified downward motion.
打ち砕いた explicitly records that Saber shattered the final strike or its weapon. “Blocks” omits that destruction immediately before the text accounts for all weapons being broken.
“An instant” naturally denotes a moment shorter than a second and adequately conveys 一秒に満たない刹那 in this rapid exchange.

The immediately preceding English describes the surprise attack from behind and the simultaneous strike to Saber’s exposed chest. The four-blade geometry therefore remains clear even though the recap does not repeat “front and rear.”
“Back where we started” is an idiom for returning to the prior state or deadlock, not necessarily to literal starting positions. It is compatible with 元に戻る here.

“I still have more” conveys a move beyond the apparent deadlock, and the next page immediately reveals another pair created in his empty hands. The preparation and hand-based reveal remain clear across the page break.
三度目 is explicitly glossed by the ruby げんかい, “limit.” English follows that governing spoken reading, while the prior text already establishes this as the third Projection.
The Original-branch English says they embrace heaven together, directly reversing the ruby’s negated “we do not embrace heaven together.”

This accusation targets the Realta conditional English branch, while the requested comparator is the Original edition. Its appearance beside the Original line is a documented branch-flattening artifact, not an Original-branch translation finding.
最後の最後で naturally means “at the very end” or “in the final moments.” Given Shirou’s imminent loss of consciousness and self, the English does not necessarily assert bodily death.
“I’ll sleep a bit” preserves both the decision to sleep and its brief duration. The omitted sinking simile is literary imagery, not a material change in event or agency.

In this combat context, saying all her limbs are occupied naturally communicates that she has no bodily means free to respond; the preceding English also states that her body cannot follow her thought.
“Has to crush her head or heart” already conveys that decisive destruction of one target is required. 確実に reinforces certainty but does not add a separate omitted procedure.

Having no choice but to submit to a finishing blow in her current state reasonably entails temporary incapacity. “Any finishing blows” is clumsy number handling but does not materially change her vulnerability.
命に関わる can describe a fatal or potentially fatal wound. A fatal wound need not prevent immediate movement, so the following qualification does not make the English diagnosis contradictory.
“Impending death” reasonably conveys Saber’s coming disappearance, but the English omits the explicit few-second interval and the nostalgic manner in which she addresses Shirou.

In a passage saying that no person remains despite biological life, “mind was destroyed” is a defensible contextual rendering of 意思—the will or conscious agency constituting Shirou’s remaining personhood.

“Die meaninglessly” broadly conveys the futility of failing to reach Saber. The narrower genuine change is that 命を捨てて describes deliberately throwing life away, stronger than merely risking it, and the personal failure to reach her is no longer explicit.
English assigns using everything to the hero. Japanese assigns every effort and sacrifice to the challengers, whom the hero then cuts down as effortlessly as breathing.
Saber’s prone condition is already established by her fall and uninterrupted incapacitation. “She looks up” is compatible with looking upward while lying down, so no contrary posture is introduced.
“A tremor rumbles” preserves a conspicuous distant vibration. Losing the intensifier 一際 is a small degree adjustment, not a demonstrable material error.

The Japanese conditional is rhetorical: if she feels anything, it is only pity. “Only the slightest trace of pity” naturally conveys that restricted emotional content rather than adding a materially new certainty.
“The clock strikes midnight” is a conventional natural paraphrase of all clock hands reaching the top as midnight arrives. The added auditory idiom does not alter the promised time or ensuing action.
The English retains the pendant but omits that Rin specifically instructed Shirou to bring it, removing its planned provenance and Rin’s agency.
俺の希望 refers to Shirou’s own wish that Illya remain behind. “She’s my hope” instead makes Illya an embodiment or source of hope.

For the human Shirou, “human functionality” awkwardly but intelligibly denotes his functioning as a living organism. The witnesses do not establish a materially narrower category of abstract humanness.
Erosion is itself gradual wearing or stripping away and fits 少しずつこそぎ落ちている. The difference in physical imagery is not a material change to the deterioration.
夜が明ける頃 means around the time dawn breaks, not necessarily before it. English creates a stricter deadline.
The Japanese locates the silence specifically in the living room. Expanding it to the whole house erases the first location in the subsequent room-by-room farewell sequence.
Describing the morning scene as part of Shirou’s life for the full year and a half substantially conveys its sustained familiarity and closeness; the omitted いつも is not a material contradiction.
追いかける背中 idiomatically means pursuing someone’s example or trying to become like them. “Hoping to be like Kiritsugu,” coupled with nightly training, preserves that sense.
“Trained hard every night” preserves sustained, intense effort. 無我夢中 adds absorbed single-mindedness, but its compression is tonal rather than a factual error.
面影 can denote a remembered face, visage, or lingering image. “Sakura’s face” is an acceptable concrete rendering in this memory scene.
細切れ describes consciousness on the verge of fragmentation into discontinuous pieces. “Fading” changes that specified mode of cognitive destruction into simple diminution.
Although stylistically awkward, “ambiguous in my head” communicates that the ten years have become vague and uncertain in Shirou’s memory, which is within the range of あやふや.

“Taking a firm grip on my consciousness” naturally conveys keeping a failing consciousness together. It loses the wire metaphor, but does not replace it with mere resolve or materially reverse the meaning.

The genuine error is aspect: 繰り返す describes something still being repeated, whereas “I’ll do it again now” presents a new future act. The omitted Japanese subject does not establish the accusation that mutual agency was reassigned solely to Shirou.
何処に向かう為 asks what destination the hope pointed toward. “What was it used for?” instead asks its instrumental purpose and removes the directional question.
大往生 can idiomatically denote a peaceful or fulfilled death. In this comic postmortem context, “peaceful in a way” is a defensible rendering rather than a factual reversal.
一本とってる says Shirou scored a point or clean success against Saber, not that he won the entire fight; the surrounding bad-ending discussion makes that inflation especially clear.

The Japanese uses written 強敵 with the reading とも, while the English substitutes an ally/anally sound joke. This is a substantial localization, but it recreates the page’s punning exchange and is not demonstrably erroneous merely for using different wordplay.

“Anally” is an invented replacement for the untranslatable とも／トモヨ joke, but it functions with the preceding “ally.” Losing the food remark is a localization tradeoff, not enough to establish a factual translation error.
すぐ can mean either immediately or quickly. “She quickly runs away” is within its normal range and does not demonstrably change the event.
The accusation attacks a blank page that is not present in the supplied mirrorMoon witness, which explicitly translates the altar sentence.
封殺 is forceful imagery, but “the wind’s stagnant” accurately states the resulting unnatural stillness. The loss of the violent metaphor is stylistic compression, not a material mistranslation.
The English omits both the wall-seeping relation and 悉く, changing an exhaustive statement about every droplet into an unquantified description of drops already on the walls.
The Japanese categorically describes the visitors as nonhuman. “No human would come” instead states a hypothetical reluctance and does not assert who actually visits.
The English preserves worship and flight from sunlight but entirely omits seeking salvation and reduces the snake-and-scorpion catalogue to serpents.
The English says only that Assassin lost his Master, omitting the expressly stated agent responsible for that loss, Kirei Kotomine.
Three ken is about 5.45 metres, so rounding it to five metres is reasonable. The preceding page places the girl in Assassin’s path, making “in front of” a defensible spatial explicitation.
応えられた states that Assassin’s call was answered. “The call reaches him” instead describes a call reaching someone and obscures the answer-response relation supplied by Zouken’s speech.

退治された筈 can naturally be rendered “was supposedly killed,” particularly because the following lines explain that only a worm manifestation was destroyed. The apparent contradiction is part of the reveal, not necessarily an error.
With no narrower comparison class stated, “the safest place on earth” is an idiomatic English rendering of 最も安全な場所, not a meaningful new geographical claim.
The Japanese identifies the true body specifically as a worm and says it must be crushed. “Unless the main body is destroyed” suppresses the concrete identity central to the explanation.

手足 is itself a figurative use of “limbs” for Zouken’s external extensions. Translating it as “my limbs” preserves that metaphor, whose nonliteral nature is clear from the surrounding worm-body explanation.
Here 肉 means replacement flesh or bodily material. “Find a new body” accurately conveys what Zouken must procure and is not a factual sanitization of the action.

Berserker has been lost because he was defeated. In the immediate context, “now that Berserker is defeated” conveys the operative reason a new bodyguard is needed without materially changing possession or agency.

Calling 絶対者 the person with absolute control over Sakura is supported explicitly by the following page’s 絶対的な支配力 and her established inability to disobey him. This is contextual explicitation, not an unsupported invention.
ワシの言葉が聞けぬ is an idiomatic demand meaning “won’t you listen/obey?” rather than a literal hearing test. “Are you disobeying me?” fits Zouken’s intent and the following narration.

The English conveys the two losses but weakens the specific charge: Sakura let Illya escape through her own 不手際. The surviving issue is omission of that escape-and-incompetence framing, not omission of the losses themselves.

念 has a broad range including psychic force, will, or power. In this supernatural context, “such a great power within her” is defensible and the sentence still connects that burden to her apparent collapse.
“A weak girl” directly renders 脆弱な小娘; “girl” already conveys youth, while weakness and Assassin’s dismissive judgment remain present. Requiring “little” is register preference.
“Disappointed, yet happy” preserves both simultaneously genuine emotions. Omitting the repeated 心底 reduces emphasis but does not materially alter Zouken’s emotional state.

意識 can denote consciousness, awareness, or mind. “Her mind has been swallowed” is compatible with the surrounding discussion of shattered mentality and vanished reason; the Japanese does not itself establish the finding’s claimed temporary, locally reversible state.
食らう explicitly casts Zouken’s possession as devouring his granddaughter. “Take over” gives the result but removes the predatory act and its force from Zouken’s own language.

The English twice locates Zouken’s laughter as coming from Sakura’s throat, adequately conveying that he is producing it through her body. Requiring the anatomical term “vocal cords” is overly literal.
“Give you the glory” reasonably conveys 譲る: Zouken presents the glory as something he wished to let Sakura have. The claimed concession relation is not materially absent.

“Did not succeed in time” conveys the central point of 間に合わなかった—that the ritual failed to meet the required timing. The Japanese does not require the narrower preparation-only interpretation asserted by the finding.
The English retains the internal origin but omits 逃れようのない, an explicit statement that Sakura cannot escape the will approaching from her own heart.
擬似神経体 denotes a pseudo-neural body, structure, or entity. Calling it one “false nerve” materially reduces the organism-like anchor to an ordinary singular nerve.

In English, “hasn’t changed yet” can naturally mean the change is not complete, especially with “yet” and the surrounding transformation context. It does not necessarily assert that no change has begun.
The English conveys appropriation of Sakura’s flesh but omits Zouken’s explicit rationalization that he will replace her supposedly vanished reason as the body’s controlling master.

よくぞ耐え抜き praises exceptional endurance despite her status as an experimental creation. “Endured more than I expected from an experiment” is a natural rendering of that evaluative force and retains her objectification.
愉しませた means entertained, gratified, or pleased him. “You have done well to please me” falls within that range and does not demonstrably reverse her role or his enjoyment.
血管を這う describes movement crawling through the blood vessels. “Writhing blood vessels” instead makes the vessels themselves move and loses the parasite’s crawling relation.
目を覚ましていた is resultative: the speaking girl had awakened or was awake. “Wakes up” places the awakening after her preceding spoken declaration and changes the reveal’s temporal relation.
踏み止まる figuratively means hold out, resist, or persist rather than succumb. “You still persist” is concise but semantically appropriate in direct contrast with 呑まれてしまった.
The order specifically makes Sakura contract with Assassin in Zouken’s place. The English omits ワシの代わりに and therefore the transfer of contractor role.
一撃のもとに attributes the compression to a single blow. “In an instant” preserves speed but changes the stated attack mechanics.
In this taunt, “Such a disappointment” is a defensible idiomatic expression of finding him つまらない—dull, trivial, or a letdown. The contempt remains clear.

In “regain your name,” “your” unambiguously marks the name as Assassin’s even though the Grail is the grammatical agent. English permits an agent to recover something for its owner; no possessive reversal occurs.
主 means lord or master, not an age-marked old man. “Old man of the mountain” substitutes a different title for Sakura’s 山の主 address.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 本物 as ハサン. Naming Hassan in English therefore translates Japanese evidence rather than adding a withheld identity.
狂乱 is frenzy, delirious agitation, or madness. “Fury” substitutes anger for the stated near-frenzied mental disintegration.
The English preserves surprise versus fear but omits that the first possible cause is the sudden atrocity, that the fear is indescribable, and that either cause explains his frenzy.
The English retains dismissing Assassin but omits 可哀想, Sakura’s explicit and chilling claim that withholding leave would be pitiful for him.

The displayed English has flattened conditional branches. The supplied raw Original candidate itself describes actual gouging and nerve-shredding, so “tore her nerves” is supported for that edition rather than disproved by the all-ages-style branch.

The middle Japanese category is the thing that calls itself her grandfather. English replaces that with “what used to be her grandfather,” duplicating past identity and losing the self-claimed relationship.
寄生する expressly describes parasitizing Sakura’s heart. “Planted himself” conveys placement but not the ongoing host-parasite relation explaining Zouken’s chosen body.
“Swallowed” is a normal figurative rendering of being consumed and is already the scene’s established image for engulfment. It does not materially deny Zouken’s predatory takeover.
反旗を翻す means rebel or turn against one’s ruler and can reasonably be expressed as betraying him. Although “rebelled” would preserve the idiom more closely, “betrayed” is not a factual reversal.
門は全て can mean the entirety of the Gate or all authority over it, not necessarily multiple gates. The following page uses singular 門を開ける, so the finding cannot establish a number error.
汚物 denotes filth, excrement, or contaminating matter. “Trash” retains contempt but removes the specifically bodily and unclean revulsion with which Zouken is described.

“Hand” is an acceptable broader rendering of 掌, so loss of the palm distinction is not material. The narrower genuine omission is こびりついた: the blood is caked or stuck to her palm, not merely present on it.
“Empty puppet” preserves the core puppet-and-emptiness comparison, so the broad thematic accusation is overstated. It does omit the concrete severed-string detail.
いつまでも笑い続けた explicitly says she continued laughing indefinitely. The English simple “laughs” removes both continuation and duration from the scene’s final action.

In Japanese, the crouching-giant comparison describes the temple’s size, while the alien force is a separate impression it produces. English attaches the simile to its emitting plural “powers,” altering both relations.
For a roaring wind, “howling” is a natural English equivalent of ごうごう. The omitted personification of kicking the atmosphere is imagery compression, not a material error.

The English identifies these as Masters who want the Holy Grail and immediately contrasts their gate with the Greater Grail below. That context preserves the limiting distinction despite not separately translating ただ as “merely.”

The Japanese identifies this land itself as an optimal spiritual vein for Servants. English instead makes the area contain a ley line and adds a potentially global “most suitable … in the land” comparison.
回復は容易い asserts that recovery will be easy. “I can recover” states only possibility and removes Rider’s confidence about ease.
The raw English contains a line-control marker between “Hm” and “it.” Their visible fusion is the warned-about extraction artifact, not evidence of the underlying translation’s grammar.

In context, “a pit” can naturally denote the hole or pitfall Rin contrasts with a designed entrance. The trap nuance is less explicit, but the joke’s operative contrast remains and no material error is shown.
枯れ木 normally means withered or dead trees and can describe winter-bare trees. “Dead trees” is within its lexical range; seasonal dormancy is not conclusively asserted.

In a visual inventory of the clearing, “no sign of human influence” is a natural paraphrase of there being no man-made objects. It broadens wording slightly without changing the scene’s practical claim.
Calling it “a small stream” already entails flowing water. Omitting the light trickling manner チロチロ is minor descriptive compression, not a material error.

In relation to a watercourse, “above the stream” can mean farther upstream, which fits 先 and the subsequent discovery of its source. The supplied context does not establish a contradictory spatial placement.
The Japanese explanatory のだ identifies the source of a sound Shirou cannot see. “Must’ve taken off” naturally expresses his inference from that metallic sound rather than contradicting the action.
Japanese says that after entering, one would immediately encounter rock ahead. English invents a single huge boulder blocking the entrance, conflicting with the already stated person-sized opening.
かつん denotes a discrete click or clack. “Scraping” changes it into sustained friction and adds an unsupported hard-surface explanation.

In the rocky, steep cave, “wet rock” is a reasonable contextual specification of the ground, and “using my hands” conveys 手探り sufficiently. The wording is less precise about feeling one’s way but not materially contradictory.
In this practical rescue comparison, “better to have two people” naturally conveys that two make success more reliable. The certainty rationale remains clear from the preceding need for Rin’s help.

The subject of 約束した is omitted, and the next page explicitly describes Shirou’s promise to make Rin the victor. “I made a promise with her” is therefore fully defensible; the Japanese does not establish that Rin alone made it.

The immediately preceding and following pages identify the promise and its Holy Grail War context. “Make her the victor” has an unambiguous contest referent here, so repeating the contest name is unnecessary explicitation rather than an omission error.
好きだった女の子 is a direct personal admission that Rin was the girl he liked, with romantic force in context. “Used to admire” redirects that feeling toward esteem and materially weakens the admission.
見れず marks inability, whereas “without looking” ordinarily suggests a choice not to look; the darkness makes that agency shift consequential.
The Japanese measures distance traveled along the spiral, not vertical depth; “a hundred meters underground” changes the geometry.
“Accomodate” is misspelled and “widens up” is nonstandard English; the underlying meaning remains recognizable but the language defect is real.
In this life-force context, “too lively” defensibly conveys an excessive, disturbing vividness; “raw” would retain more texture but is not uniquely required.
The Japanese describes mana being poured out in visible-scale quantities; “so strong that it’s almost visible” omits the ongoing uncontrolled outflow.
汚物 denotes filth, waste, or a contaminating foul substance, not merely something decayed; “rotten” changes the central image.
“No words to say to her” is a reasonable contextual explicitation of the subjectless かける言葉はない; the following sentence separately preserves the mutual silence.
“Look out for your own safety first” naturally expresses prioritizing one’s survival in this explicitly lethal setting.
“To the back” is awkward but can represent 奥; the narrower valid issue is that 点々, the intermittent trail of drops, is omitted.
“My consciousness fades away” is a defensible English rendering of losing consciousness; 切れる does not by itself require a formally instantaneous cutoff.
With the preceding lines already stating that he may disappear, using pain to “clear my mind” defensibly paraphrases rousing himself back to alertness.
“Warm” is broader and less ominous than 生暖かい, but remains within its lexical range; the alleged bodily quality is contextual interpretation.
撫でる is a gentle stroking motion, so “hits” is a genuine force change; plural “cheeks” is normal English and not an established number error.
横幅 explicitly limits the school-ground comparison to the cavern’s width; “as big as” applies it to overall size.
忘れられた means forgotten or abandoned; “unforgettable” directly reverses that description.
殺気 specifically denotes murderous intent or a killing aura; generic “hostility” materially softens Saber’s lethal posture.
“Turned black” can naturally describe Saber’s transformation into her blackened form; it need not mean only a literal color change.
The preceding English sentence preserves Rin’s resolve and head-on intent, but the second sentence does omit まともに斬り合う, the direct exchange of sword blows.
控えている can mean waiting or standing by, and the enemies beyond Saber are contextually waiting for the party; “in reserve” is not the only defensible rendering.
The Japanese pointedly frames attacking Saber as a mistaken choice of target; the plain request removes that ironic warning.
“Stops Tohsaka in her tracks” is an idiom for the effect of Saber’s verbal admonition and does not necessarily assert physical restraint.
“Comprehend … right away” adequately conveys immediate understanding without clarification; the unasked-question and しまった nuances are not material omissions here.
Rin is muttering about the absent Sakura, so “she must be serious” preserves the realization; omitting the rhetorical name is not a material agency change.
Shirou is directly addressed and immediately told to meet Rin’s expectations, making “I believe in you” a normal and well-supported English explicitation.
目的語 explicitly invokes a missing grammatical object; the English replaces that metalinguistic joke with a complaint about missing instructions.
The English omits the explicit farewell gesture that Rin leaves without looking back.
“That gave me strength” is a natural contextual paraphrase of being fired up or having one’s fighting spirit renewed.
The valid loss is that 遠まわしに応援してくれた describes indirect encouragement, while “told me” makes it direct; coming while Rin restrains Sakura reasonably implies helping her.
殺気 explicitly identifies Saber’s swelling killing intent, not merely generalized hostility.
Japanese その手 does not establish a contrastive one-handed grip, and a two-handed sword grip is contextually possible; the plural cannot be certified as an error.
The English preserves full power and killing but omits the explicit intention to finish them in one strike.
認識しあった is reciprocal: Shirou and Saber mutually recognized the irreversible fact, whereas the English assigns realization only to Shirou.
The English drops the explicit identification of Zouken as the root cause behind the remaining opposition.
“Motions me back with one hand” can naturally describe Rider causing Shirou to move behind her; the Japanese does not conclusively establish pushing or bodily contact.
The Japanese locates sword aura or fighting energy rising from the blade’s point; “hostility” substitutes an emotion and removes its weapon-originating manifestation.
“Repel Mystic Eyes” can mean ward off or resist their effect, which is a defensible functional rendering of 魔眼除け rather than necessarily an active counterattack.
Rider is female, while “cavalryman” conventionally denotes a male cavalry soldier; the source’s 騎兵 is gender-neutral.
高速 means high speed; “light speed” introduces a much stronger literal magnitude absent from this sentence.
動体視力 specifically concerns visually tracking motion; “human reactions cannot perceive it” both generalizes the limitation and gives perception to reactions.
The same English sentence uses “her,” so “swordsman” is plainly functioning as a generic class label rather than asserting that Saber is male.
Rendering a smile at the corner of the mouth as “a smile on her face” is ordinary English generalization without a material change in expression.
The complete English page explicitly names “Tohsaka Rin” in its second sentence, so the alleged removal of the viewpoint identification did not occur.
For an apparently endless overhead canopy, “impossibly high” is a defensible spatial paraphrase; the Japanese does not uniquely specify horizontal boundlessness.
戦い can denote either a battle or a war, and the Greater Grail is contextually the beginning and endpoint of the wider Holy Grail conflict.
Although awkward, “has been activated for two hundred years” can denote remaining active over that period and does not demonstrably contradict continued operation.
The English genuinely omits that the energy leaks from an unidentified “something”; however, 波 need not be treated as grammatically plural.
最中 read さなか means the midst or middle, not necessarily an innermost superlative; the English is clumsy but preserves a center-to-middle relation.
回廊 is a corridor or gallery, so “circuit” is a genuine lexical error; treating 天の杯 through the established “Heaven’s Feel” title is less conclusively erroneous without terminology context.
くみ上げる describes drawing magical energy from the reserve; the English instead describes casting whatever magic the magi wish.
The Japanese explicitly concedes that a finite limit may exist and calls the supply practically inexhaustible; the English’s unqualified “infinite” removes that distinction.
The English retains the premonition of death but wholly omits the overwhelming demonstrated disparity in fighting strength that also threatens Rin’s resolve.
“Keeping her spirits up” is a defensible functional paraphrase of using banter to cool the fear and prevent her resolve from breaking.
自分を見失う means losing sight of oneself or losing oneself; “lost her mind” strengthens Rin’s dismissive diagnosis into outright insanity.
The preceding English identifies Zouken as Rin’s greatest enemy, so calling Sakura’s fight unimportant adequately conveys her view of it as secondary cleanup, despite compressing the chronology.
The English collapses two distinct operations—imagination shaping the shadow and wishes incarnating it—and omits incarnation in flesh.
The ruby explicitly reads 寄り代 as マスター, authorizing “Master,” and “depends on” reasonably conveys 委ねられる in this explanatory context.
The English retains emitting the curse but omits Sakura’s separate function of giving the released curse directionality.
In sequence, “it” clearly refers to the released gem sword and “the being above her” to Sakura; reversing the grammatical framing preserves whether the sword can match her.

The two categories are distinguished by their functions, so describing the implements as having “two functions” is imprecise but does not materially misstate the classification developed in the following lines.
The complete English sentence immediately explains that the backup supplements the magus’s energy and strengthens the spell, preserving the relationship alleged to be missing.
神秘 is the setting’s technical “Mystery”; adding “divine” introduces a religious or divine character not stated here.
“Magic she’s not capable of ordinarily” naturally means an effect beyond the user’s unaided capacity, matching 再現できない; the broader “magic” terminology alone does not prove an error here.
使役 covers commanding, controlling, or making a being serve, so “enslaves” is forceful but defensible; singular 聖獣 can also be generalized in English.
The ruby explicitly supplies キャンセル over 初期化, directly supporting “cancels”; insisting on only the surface-word mechanism ignores the supplied reading.
The immediately preceding alternatives scope “nothing” to the two weapon types, and “match Sakura” naturally conveys being effective against her.
昏い殺気 is explicitly dark killing intent; “hostile tension” removes both the lethal content and the darkness.
生気 is vitality or life force, not atmospheric air; “warm air” removes the corrupt vital-energy phenomenon filling the cavern.
クスリ can mark a small private smile as well as a slight chuckle; “smiles gracefully” preserves the expressly stated elegant smile and is defensible.
飼い犬 literally means a kept or pet dog, and “his own pet dog” retains the ownership reversal; “hound” is not demanded by the Japanese.
The English preserves binding but omits that Zouken occupied the explicit role of Sakura’s ruler or controller.
The active statement “you killed him” already assigns Sakura direct personal agency; omitting “with your own hand” only removes emphasis.
The raw English contains a line-break command between “So” and “as”; their fusion in the supplied display is the warned extraction artifact, not a translation typo.
The preceding English clause already says Rin will not disappear “from within me,” and “in my mind” is a defensible clarification of Sakura’s internalized torment.
“Words … heavy as slime” naturally renders the sticky heaviness of Sakura’s utterance while retaining its contradiction with her light singsong delivery; the metaphor is supported by 粘りつく.
“Awe” is a standard lexical rendering of 畏怖, which combines fear with awed reverence; the Japanese does not expressly identify it solely as Sakura’s fear of Rin.
The ruby makes 潰して read あそんで, deliberately superimposing “crushing” on “playing”; English retains only ordinary fun and loses the murderous wordplay.

The displayed English has flattened mutually exclusive eating/drinking branches, while the supplied page Japanese has 呑み込む and 飲む but the raw Original candidate has 食べる and 食べない. These conflicting edition witnesses cannot establish which wording the comparator should accuse.
In this identity-focused exchange, “I’m different now” is a natural English paraphrase of Sakura saying that her way or state of being has changed.
The raw English has a line-break command between the repeated “I” and “I’m,” so “II’m” is an extraction artifact; the surrounding dialogue already establishes that Sakura has become strong.
泣きじゃくる describes a sobbing child pleading from desperation; “petulant” instead characterizes spoiled irritability and materially changes the emotional judgment.
関 can naturally mean a barrier, hurdle, or obstacle. “Last obstacle” preserves the question’s threshold function; calling it merely external opposition overreads the English.

The apparent alternatives are flattened conditional branches, not one malformed displayed sentence. “Sanity” corresponds to the supplied Original candidate 狂いかけた心, while “hold on herself” corresponds to 手放しかけた心; this is an edition/branch artifact.
The supplied English page and raw witness contain “Want to swallow Senpai too.” The accusation of a blank active line is contradicted by the evidence.
“Take Angra Mainyu with you” is an established English idiom for causing his death while dying oneself. It adequately conveys 刺し違える in context.
“Swallowed” is defensible for 取り込まれて, but “let yourself” adds an element of permission or culpable acquiescence not expressly present in the passive Japanese. Only that agency addition survives.
Quoted 魔 can denote an evil or demonic being, and “acknowledges … as ‘evil’” retains both the administrator context and classificatory act. “Demonic enemy” is not uniquely compelled here.

この子 is gender-neutral and can be rendered by a contextual pronoun, but these pages do not securely identify its referent or establish whether the child-like wording is essential. The male explicitation cannot be certified or disproved from these witnesses alone.
魔力 is magical energy, not “a magic.” The English apposition consequently misidentifies the absorptive energy comparable to a Noble Phantasm.

鎌首をもたげる depicts snake-like threatening elevation; “rise up to attack” is a defensible contextual paraphrase, especially as the figures immediately reach for Rin. The lost image is stylistic compression, not a demonstrable action error.
The ruby reads “this me,” but the displayed term identifies Sakura as the Heaven’s Cup. Rendering only “me” removes a substantive dual-layer occult identification.

“All possible directions” adequately generalizes front, rear, left, and right. The narrower genuine loss is that Rider is explicitly described racing on the ground while attacking through the air above it.
髪を引いて describes her hair streaming or trailing as she runs. “Her long hair blown behind her” is a natural rendering of that visible result and does not materially change its cause.
“Swordsman” has long-standing generic use for a sword fighter and does not necessarily assert that Saber is male. “Swordswoman” would be more explicit but is a preference, not a factual correction.
“Break through Saber’s guard” is defensible from 構え, 迎撃, and 打ち崩す. The narrower loss is 泰然: Saber’s composed, unruffled stance is reduced to physical firmness.

In “Saber deflects the daggers,” the definite plural naturally denotes Rider’s already-established daggers as a set. Ownership and exhaustive scope remain recoverable without mechanically adding “every one of Rider’s.”

The Japanese describes Saber reliably and progressively breaking Rider down with each returning stroke. “Striking Rider” retains the counterattack but loses the cumulative destruction marked by 確実に and 壊していく.
“Consume you” naturally conveys being burned away by approaching the star. The shift in grammatical agency does not materially alter the proximity-and-destruction image.

The English retains the racing meteor, its ephemerality, and its inability to rival the stationary star. Speed and light are natural developments of the surrounding stellar metaphor rather than unsupported factual grounds.
体を削られる can idiomatically describe accumulating bodily damage. “She’s wounded” is less vivid but accurately states the result and is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
The body being healed is Rider’s body, which Saber has wounded. The English instead says Saber sustained the wounds, reversing the injured and healed participant.

抑えきれない means Rider cannot keep Saber checked or contained. “Can’t match Saber” turns the immediate defensive suppression requirement into general parity and loses the tactic explained on the next page.
体力 permits “energy” in ordinary English as well as stamina or physical strength. Later mention of magical energy does not make this normal rendering factually wrong.
The Japanese states that both legs are beginning to collapse internally from extreme overuse. “Give in to the strain” reduces structural internal destruction to generic fatigue.
捉える predicts Saber physically catching Rider. “Catches up to Rider’s speed” instead predicts speed equivalence and omits the decisive capture.
Losing her strength and magical energy already conveys why Rider can no longer exert full power. Omitting the explicit causal restatement does not change the fatal condition.
The subject and recipient are explicit: Rider told the boy. The English reverses them and makes Shirou the forecaster.
The translation preserves cognitive loss but entirely omits the stated emotional degree—that it is becoming so severe Shirou wants to cry.
The first fragment leaves the object suspended before specifying something precious. “Everything” introduces totality absent from the Japanese and materially enlarges the feared loss.
The English marks hesitation but omits the meaningful correction from “I” to “I too,” which explicitly aligns Shirou’s effort with Rider’s, and it completes the source’s aborted たたか.
The supplied mirrorMoon page and raw English witness explicitly contain “Select, analyze.” It is not a blank-page omission.
The supplied mirrorMoon page and raw witness contain “Defer” four times. The accusation that the active page is blank is false.
The English skips the complete sentence recalling Rider’s pledge to entrust her life. Nothing elsewhere in its rendering supplies that reciprocal commitment.
“Give all I have” is a natural English equivalent of 全霊を以って, while “keep watching Rider” conveys the sustained direct attention of 直視しろ. The objection is overly literal.

翻る gives the sword a sharper turning or flashing motion, but “moves” remains factually accurate and the imminent attack is supplied by the following sentence. This is lost vividness, not a material error.
白熱する describes becoming white-hot or reaching incandescent intensity. “White out” ordinarily means blanking or losing perception, changing intensified cognition into cognitive erasure.

The supplied raw Original candidate contains the madness aphorism, while the base Japanese contains the object/subject line; the raw English places them in mature and non-mature branches respectively. Their simultaneous appearance is branch flattening, not unsupported replacement.
“Trace, Fractal” preserves only the ruby pronunciation. It omits the displayed command 投影、重装, including the substantive designation of a heavy-armament Projection mode.
混濁 can mean confusion, muddling, or chaotic admixture. “Chaos with law” is awkward but deliberately preserves the coexistence of disorder and governing law; it is not necessarily contradictory.

Despite awkward syntax, the English retains the deliberate paradox—apparent birth from nothing that is not truly from nothing—and the emergence of many similarities through expansion. The accusation overstates the semantic loss.
The English omits 刹那を抜いて, the assertion that the sword was projected with effectively no instant of elapsed time. That extraordinary timing is substantive in this accelerated Projection sequence.
“Caladbolg” preserves the ruby name but omits the displayed designation “False Spiral Sword,” which identifies the projected weapon as a variant rather than simply the original named sword.

The broken typography is substantially retained. The narrower problems are the loss of the 確実 certainty fragment and the non-idiomatic “unreturnable” for an irreparable state; the whole damaged passage is not omitted.
たたらを踏む explicitly says Saber reels or staggers after deflecting the sword. “Unable to pursue” states the consequence but removes the physical cause of the two-second opening.

The immediately preceding English sentence says “Fifty meters,” so “the gap” clearly refers to that full range. Its suddenness is also supported by the preceding two-second opening; no tactical distance is lost.

“A strongest attack” is objectively unidiomatic English, but the repeated construction still communicates answering a maximum attack with another maximum attack. Only the grammar complaint survives, not the alleged semantic failure.
The Japanese makes Saber’s blade itself incandescent while it whips up wind. The English instead makes a scorching wind emerge from the sword and omits the blade’s heating.

“Wipe out” is a defensible outcome-oriented rendering of destroying or cutting away the opposing light. With Saber’s sword already explicit, failure to repeat the cutting image is not a factual change.
組まれている is a resultative state: the magic circle has been assembled or completed and is in place. “Already completed” is a natural contextual rendering, not a demonstrable timing error.
結ばれた directly permits “bound,” “joined,” or “linked,” and “bound by blood” need not imply that blood restrains a preexisting eye. The proposed formation reading is not uniquely established.
横 can mean horizontally or at/to the side. “Readied beside her” is awkward but contextually defensible; the Japanese fragment does not uniquely compel a horizontal blade orientation.
唱じられる means the name is uttered or chanted, and magical English can describe such an invocation as being “cast.” The preceding spoken fragment makes the vocal act clear.
“Contend for supremacy” concisely conveys two lights struggling so only one can prevail. The personification is compressed, but the mutually exclusive contest is not materially changed.

Outside a rigid terminology scheme, “magic” is a normal English rendering of 魔術. The supplied Japanese establishes a distinction from 魔法 lexically, but does not make the generic English word factually wrong by itself.
Knowing what he has to use entails that the item has been selected. Here 使うべきもの and 選び出すもの describe the same chosen object, so condensing them is defensible.
成る can mean come into being, be realized, or be completed. “The projection’s completed in an instant” accurately conveys the resultative instantaneous formation.
血管 means blood vessels, not blood. The English changes anatomical structures convulsing throughout the arm into free blood “dancing,” a concrete referential error.
The English retains the convulsion but omits 弾け散りかねない—the explicit danger that the left arm may burst or fly apart.
跳弾し describes magical energy repeatedly ricocheting inside Shirou like bullets. “Explodes” replaces those successive internal rebounds with a different event.
中身 identifies Shirou’s insides or contents, reinforced by the eraser simile and progressive action. “Body” relocates the whitening to his outward physical whole and loses the internal erasure.
The raw magical energy is the force being slammed into the deadlock. “Is smashed” reverses its role and makes the energy itself the object being struck or destroyed.
四枚羽 is four wings or petals shattered by the black aurora. The English misreads the cardinal as an ordinal “fourth petal,” changes shattering to penetration, and leaves the relation malformed.
生身 explicitly stresses Rider’s unprotected flesh striking the wall at charge speed. The English preserves the collision but removes that materially heightened bodily vulnerability.

After the wall impact, saying Rider is “still on the ground” because she has used up her energy naturally conveys that she remains fallen and cannot rise. The Japanese is fuller, but the state is not removed.
死に体 is stronger than “deeply wounded,” while 充分に余力 says Saber retains ample reserve, not merely “some power.” Both opposing severity scales are materially weakened.

“Wounded and unable to fight back,” combined with Shirou already being on top of her, adequately conveys Saber’s helplessness. Omitting the additional inability to stand is redundant compression, not a changed execution choice.
準備に入ってしまった says Projection has already entered, and become committed to, its preparation phase. “Already prepared” instead presents preparation as complete.

The English first calls it “our plan,” then calls the accepted implementation “my strategy.” Given that Shirou proposed and executes it, this shift is contextually defensible and does not erase their settled cooperation.
“The greatest retreat possible” is awkward, but the next sentence explicitly places Rider at the cavern’s edge. Together the English clearly communicates withdrawal to maximum range.
Japanese 膝をつく does not establish whether one or both knees touch the ground. “Went on her knees” is awkward but a possible posture, so the numerical accusation is unsupported.

The English preserves the core anchoring action—driving a dagger into the ground to pin Saber—and the chain is explicit in surrounding sentences. The narrower error is inventing the weapon label “nail dagger” for plain 短剣 and reducing bedrock to ground.
The English says only that two seconds are sufficient, omitting what they accomplished: more than enough run-up distance for Rider’s charge. That tactical purpose is explicit and central.
The immediately preceding “Fifty meters” supplies the exact range, while the two-second withdrawal supports suddenness. “The gap” does not reduce the established tactical spacing.
“A strongest attack” is unidiomatic, but the repeated phrase still communicates answering a maximum attack with another maximum attack. Retain only the grammar criticism.
The Japanese makes the sword itself become incandescent while whipping up wind. The English transfers the heat to wind emitted by the sword and omits the blade’s thermal transformation.
“Wipe out” defensibly conveys destroying the opposing white light, and the sword relation is clear from the immediately preceding sentence. The objection chiefly demands retention of one metaphor.
The resultative 組まれている permits “has been assembled/completed.” In this prepared attack context, “already completed” does not establish a materially different chronology.
結ばれた supports “bound by blood” as well as “joined in blood.” The English does not necessarily describe blood restraining a preexisting eye, so the accusation relies on one preferred visualization.
横 may describe either horizontal orientation or position to the side. “Readied beside her” is therefore a defensible, if awkward, reading rather than a demonstrable orientation reversal.
The name is visibly being spoken in the preceding quotation, and “cast” can describe invoking it in magical English. The vocal release is not materially obscured.
“Contend for supremacy” conveys the struggle in which each light seeks to exclude the other. The omitted personifying phrasing is literary compression, not a factual error.
“Magic” is a conventional rendering of 魔術 here, and its capitalization is sentence-initial. Nothing in the English invokes or confuses this with True Magic.
使うべきもの and 選び出すもの can appositionally describe the same chosen projection. “What I have to use” defensibly compresses the decision without demonstrably deleting a separate operation.
成る permits “be completed/come about.” Since 一瞬で expressly makes the formation instantaneous, “completed in an instant” does not introduce a materially longer process.
血管 means blood vessels, not blood, and 腕中 locates the violent activity throughout the arm. The English changes the anatomy and drops that extent.
The English retains the convulsion but entirely omits 弾け散りかねない, the explicit danger that the arm may burst apart.
跳弾し describes repeated ricocheting like bullets inside the body. A generalized “explodes” loses that repeated rebounding motion.
中身 specifically identifies Shirou’s interior or contents, not his visible body. The English relocates the whitening and weakens the erasure imagery.
The passive 叩きつけられる makes the raw magical energy the force being slammed down. “Is smashed” instead makes that energy the thing struck and broken.
四枚羽 is four wings/layers, while 打ち砕かれた says the black aurora shattered them. “Fourth petal” and “penetrated through” both alter the event.
“Rider smashes against the wall” already describes Rider herself undergoing the impact. Omitting the redundant emphasis of 生身 is not a demonstrable material change here.
In context, “she’s still on the ground” after the collision and apparent mana exhaustion naturally conveys that she remains collapsed and cannot get up. The rendering is compressed but defensible.
“Deeply wounded” weakens the moribund 死に体, and “some power” materially understates 充分に余力, which says she retains ample reserve.
