“Wounded and unable to fight back” adequately conveys Saber’s total present incapacity; separately repeating that she cannot stand is contextual detail rather than a materially distinct condition.
“Bear” is defensible for suppressing or enduring かみ殺し. The narrower error is “the shredding memory,” which obscures that Shirou’s memories are progressively being scraped away.

Although now often gender-associated, “swordsman” can denote a sword fighter generically. Since 剣士 itself is gender-neutral and Saber is immediately identifiable, this is not a demonstrable mistranslation.
足 can be rendered as foot or leg, and the English preserves the comparison’s essential sense of explosive power. Generalizing the push-off to “legs” is awkward but not materially different.
“Regurgitation” is not limited to vomiting; it also denotes backward fluid flow, including blood. It is stilted but semantically available for 逆流.
“Supreme super being” is clumsy prose, but it still conveys 卓絶した超人, an exceptional or surpassing superhuman. The finding establishes a style problem, not an accuracy error.
“Sacrificing Emiya Shirou” naturally communicates that Shirou is being destroyed as the price of the power. The progressive aspect is compressed, not materially contradicted.
“Attack from the side” directly preserves 横合いから斬りつける’s flank attack. The run is supported by the preceding 疾走した and does not change the combat geometry materially.
“On the ground” is less exact than 跪いた but remains compatible with kneeling and preserves Rider’s low position. The explanation’s claimed inability to disengage is not itself stated by this phrase.
“Open side” and “left arm” preserve the exposed target, while “cut/swing at” is a defensible rendering of bringing the sword down. The alleged relational loss is not material.
“At the speed of light, the counterattack comes” still makes the counterattack lightspeed. 一撃 is a blow, and the contextual counterattack adequately conveys 斬り返される.
This accusation relies on the later-edition euphemism. The supplied Original witness explicitly says an arm flies off, so the English is not premature in the Original-edition comparator.
The supplied Original witness explicitly identifies a severed left arm. The vaguer カタマリ belongs to the altered witness; the English branch reflects the Original wording rather than inventing anatomy.
Rendering approaching footsteps as the person approaching is ordinary metonymic paraphrase. It preserves the event and does not materially overstate what Shirou perceives.

The repeated 背中、背中 is a conspicuous cognitive stutter that the English smooths away. However, the unfinished Japanese does not securely establish the finding’s stronger claim of actual blade contact on this page.
“Lost your weapon” contextualizes the conventional metaphor 牙をもがれた after Shirou loses his arm and sword. It preserves the intended combat neutralization despite dropping the imagery.
抉る is a forceful gouging into the back, whereas “pricks” substantially weakens it; “spine” also adds an anatomical target absent from the Japanese.
“With one push” already preserves the blade’s immediate lethal proximity. Omitting the supplementary measurement 数センチ is minor compression, not a material change.
A sword being “pressed against” Shirou’s back naturally communicates the felt pressure or weight of the blade. The physical oppression is not removed.
The Japanese describes consciousness that had nearly gone out, not a mind fragmented into pieces. The English substitutes a materially different mental condition.

ひどく can simply intensify an adjective as “extremely,” without necessarily marking pain or unpleasantness. “Strangely” defensibly expresses the striking contrast with his previously fading consciousness.
“Must be” remains an inferential modal, not certainty, and naturally renders Shirou’s tentative realization in 意識が戻ったのか.
The supplied ruby places し—invoking 死, death—over 俺. The English preserves only “me,” losing the deliberate written/reading collision at the execution choice.
“Click” is a functional interface localization of pressing the confirm button, especially for a PC release. The named controller glyph need not be reproduced to preserve the instruction.
“Simple choice mistakes” is loose, but in this comic tutorial context it adequately describes casual, low-stakes selection errors. The distinction does not create a material factual change.
Unqualified “Shirou can’t beat Saber” is already categorical in English. Dropping the explicit intensifier どうあっても does not weaken the stated impossibility materially.
“Powered up a lot” is a colloquial degree equivalent suited to the comic register. It is less flamboyant than 超絶 but does not alter the event or scale materially.
出番 means one’s turn, appearance, or role; “take a big part in this route” clumsily but recognizably conveys Illya’s expectation of a prominent role.
The preceding inability to compete with Sakura supplies the cause of Illya’s return. “Forced to come back” is comic contextual explicitation, not an unsupported external agent.
うたれ強い specifically means being resilient under blows or punishment. Generic “strong” loses the beating-related wordplay central to the joke.
猫を被る denotes putting on a false innocent facade. “Putting their masks on” is awkward but conveys that facade rather than materially mistranslating it.
４以下 includes a score of exactly four; “below four” excludes it. This directly changes the stated true-ending threshold.

チェスト is conventionally presented as the transliterated attack cry “Chest!/Chesto!” Elongation and exclamation already mark it as a yell, so the English does not reduce it to an ordinary anatomical reference.
“Keep up your indecisiveness” is awkward but conveys continuing or persisting in 優柔不断. The mock-heroic tone is weakened stylistically, not factually reversed.
“Holding her gaze” naturally describes maintaining eye contact in response to her look. The mutuality of 視線に応えて is sufficiently preserved.
The Japanese stresses that the remembered warmth remains alive even now. Generic “the warmth of life” removes that present survival at the moment of Saber’s death.
体温 is bodily warmth and すぐ近く means immediately nearby. “Always by my side” changes present embodied proximity into generalized companionship and omits 忘れようのない.
抉り describes gouging or wrenching memory out. “Search through my mind” reverses that violent removal into an act of looking for something.
許されない conventionally permits “will/cannot be forgiven.” The Japanese passive does not uniquely establish the proposed distinction between impermissibility and future non-forgiveness.
The English omits both 親しい, identifying personal closeness, and 少女, identifying Saber as the girl who protected him. Those details carry the sentence’s emotional contrast.

“Neither regret nor confession will bring forgiveness” is a defensible interpretation of 後悔も懺悔も許されない: neither remorse nor penitent confession can absolve him. The proposed permission reading is not exclusive.
The ruby explicitly reads the beloved 者 as エゴ. Translating only “the one I love” loses the written self-indictment that equates this singular love with egoism.
奪い続ける makes Shirou the agent continually robbing precious things away. “Sacrificing” can imply voluntary offering and materially softens that agency.
ツケ is a mounting bill or debt generated by his choices. “Losing more than I gain” instead frames the problem as Shirou’s personal cost-benefit balance.
動けなくなる may figuratively mean becoming unable to continue on this path. In context, “I know I’ll stop someday” preserves that inevitable endpoint; a specifically bodily collapse is not established.
“Swordsman” can function generically for a sword fighter despite modern gender associations. With the following feminine pronoun, it does not actually misidentify Saber’s sex.
ぼんやり marks a vague, unfocused or dazed upward look. “Eyes fixed on me” instead suggests concentrated, steady attention and also loses the upward orientation.
In an attempted fatal chest stab, rendering 胸 as “heart” is normal contextual explicitation. The adjacent execution context supports the lethal target.
対岸の火を見るように is an idiom for watching something with detached unconcern. “Without emotion or interest” directly renders its sense rather than needing the literal fire image.
鮮やかな describes vivid or brilliant golden color. “Clear, golden hair” is unnatural and does not accurately express that chromatic vividness.
The Japanese presents moving silver armor and the beauty of one particular stroke. Static “armor” plus generic plural “attacks” materially generalizes the sharply pictured memory.
“Serving as my sword to the very end” preserves Saber’s continuing role and its benefit to Shirou. English need not mechanically encode every benefactive nuance of くれた.
“Shining under the moonlight” is a natural rendering of the figurative 月の光に濡れた, describing hair saturated or bathed in moonlight. The finding chiefly enforces imagery preference.
“An eternal scene that will never be lost” already conveys a moment isolated and preserved from later change. Omitting the literal cut-out metaphor does not materially change the memory’s function.
見る影もなく says no recognizable trace of Saber’s former appearance remains. “Turned dark” preserves only the color change and loses that extreme transformation.
The Japanese says the dagger sticks or pierces into dry ground. “Falls onto the ground” omits both penetration and the explicitly dry surface, changing the physical result.
刻一刻と explicitly depicts Saber recovering moment by moment before reaching complete restoration. The English states only the endpoint and removes the ongoing recovery during Shirou’s delay.
In conjunction with “healed” and “as well,” saying her magical energy “is charged” reasonably conveys replenishment. The context supports restoration rather than merely possessing some energy.
誰か literally means “someone,” ordinarily a person, and the English question mark retains Shirou’s uncertainty about the inference. “The person” does not materially overcommit.
The scene is a rocky cavern, so “rock” is a reasonable contextual specification of 地面. Both versions describe the shadow seeping into the cave floor and disappearing.
The English omits the incidental raised-knee sleeping posture, but it preserves the essential awakening in an unfamiliar place. The finding does not establish a material narrative change.
“I won’t be able to suppress Archer’s arm after that” is already categorical. The omitted 何をしても reinforces inevitability but does not alter the stated result.
人形 can denote a human-shaped figure or doll, and “tin man” naturally expresses feeling like a human figure made of tin. A possible literary association does not make it inaccurate.
Japanese commonly omits an understood object of 呼ぶ; in this first-person scene, “someone’s calling for me” is normal explicitation supported by Shirou following the voice.
Although 生温かい has an unpleasant lukewarm nuance, “warm wind that makes me want to vomit” explicitly preserves the bodily revulsion. No material sanitization results.
English intransitive “shreds” can describe the brain undergoing destruction, not deliberate self-agency. Having thoughts crumble like a collapsing building reasonably paraphrases the erosion of 思考能力.
The Japanese locates the fierce heat at Shirou’s skin, saying it could scorch it. The English instead relocates the injury to his lungs.
The ruby reads 消化器官 as ハラノナカ, “inside the belly.” “Inside a giant stomach” reflects that supplied reading, while the cavern comparison naturally supplies enormous scale.
“Hid herself” is a defensible contextual rendering of 閉じ篭り, which can mean secluding or shutting oneself away; the accusation overstates the concealment/confinement distinction.
煙って denotes a white haze or smoky obscuration. “Intensely white” preserves whiteness but drops the haze that prevents recognition.
“Precious resource” conveys scarcity but not the explicit discrete-use limitation imposed on Shirou’s thinking.
“Looks at me with wonder” conveys the puzzlement. Omitting the rhetorical repetition is compression, not a demonstrable material mistranslation.
The Japanese specifically says the coldness strikes Shirou emotionally and leaves him unable to speak; “everything” stopping replaces both effects with a vague generalization.
The plural “them” does not convey いっぱい, which explicitly says Sakura stationed a large number at the exit.
くすりと笑う is a small audible laugh or chuckle, not merely a smile.
“From here” plus the immediately preceding cliff ascent supplies the elevated viewpoint, while “look around the cavern” is a defensible rendering of surveying it.

The Japanese describes both a black cloth and black-stained ground. English preserves the cloth’s blackness but leaves the ground’s black staining unexpressed; it does not simply transfer all blackness from ground to cloth.
After Sakura says she swallowed Rin and left no mess, “finished every bit of her body and mind” naturally conveys 残さずキレイに and the grotesque consumption context.
The aligned Original-edition witness explicitly has 処女だったんですね, while “weak” belongs to the base/all-ages text. The mature English branch reflects an edition difference, not an unsupported insertion.

The ruby reads 食材 as あのひと, supporting “the person,” while “delicious treat” and “Thanks for the food” preserve the food metaphor and gratitude. The alleged ingredient-to-banquet mechanism is overread.
破裂していく describes the remaining thought circuits progressively bursting apart; “thoughts ignite” substitutes a different physical metaphor.
In this context, progressively forgetting what he must do and who stands before him is a natural expression of 判らなくなっていく, not an ordinary-memory claim materially at odds with it.

Sakura is the unmistakable omitted subject, and English must normally complete the Japanese hanging construction. “Too far away for me to retrieve you” faithfully conveys the unrecoverable distance rather than inventing a new accusation.
取り込む can mean absorb or take in, and the immediately preceding scene repeatedly frames Sakura’s assimilation as swallowing and consumption. “Swallow” is contextually defensible.
The present perfect progressive “has been asking” already expresses continuing pleas from earlier. Failure to reproduce ばっかり literally is not a material omission here.
A tidal wave that “surges over” a person naturally describes engulfment; it does not imply harmless surface passage.
The valid error is that English makes the hearing definite and reduces 泣き叫ぶ to “weeping.” It still preserves the unresolved person as “someone,” so that part of the accusation does not survive.

The page retains “Six already” and says Rin cut down the dark curses; the adjacent page explicitly restores that every one was destroyed in one blow. No material action or count is lost across the supplied passage.
This is normal distributive English: “each giant” is compared with the class of Noble Phantasms wielded by Servants, not necessarily with several Noble Phantasms at once.
The surrounding English says Rin destroys all six with single blows while running up the cliff, already communicating apparent ease. Dropping 苦もなく is not independently material.
A blade “emitting seven prismatic colors” is awkward but conveys that the formerly colorless blade shines chromatically. This is style, not a factual error.
The Japanese technically describes the sword’s center supplying extraordinary magical energy. A generic “power surging” obscures both the resource and the provision relation.
“In her way” conveys the shadows’ entry-blocking function, and calling them the last such shadows is a reasonable inference because Rin clears them and reaches the top.
“Stares with surprise” is within the contextual range of 愕然と凝視する. It is somewhat less forceful but not a demonstrable material mistranslation.
The fused “wayit’s” is an extraction artifact: the raw script places display commands between “way” and “it’s.” “No way—it’s not possible” also naturally expresses Sakura’s broken disbelief.

Japanese nouns are not obligatorily marked for number, and モノ can refer vaguely or collectively to the presences behind Sakura. Singular number is not established firmly enough to accuse “things” of material error.
In a battle about extravagant expenditure of magical energy, “you’re not holding back” is a natural contextual equivalent of 大盤振舞 rather than a factual change.
The preceding English explicitly identifies magical energy, so “strength” naturally refers to that power; “kill one of my shadows” is also a defensible combat rendering of eliminating one.
The preceding English “is like…” preserves Sakura’s uncertainty. The genuine omission is her physical reaction of grinding her teeth.

出来そこない can describe a failed or poor version, and “poor imitation” conveys Sakura’s deficient relation to the Third Magic in this passage. “Sorcery” is a translation convention, not independently demonstrable error here.
The Japanese makes Rin herself the old man’s imitation. English instead says she uses an imitation of her master, reversing the grammatical and conceptual relation.
The ruby explicitly reads 泥棒猫 as コピーキャット, so “copycat” follows supplied Japanese evidence rather than erasing an unsupported theft meaning.
English preserves the cavern’s rumbling but entirely omits that the light and heat physically shave away its inner wall.
The governing Original witness reads 引き篭もってる, directly supporting “hiding” or “holed up.” The accusation relies on a base/all-ages edition difference.
使役する can naturally be rendered “summon” in fantasy English when shadows are being called up and directed. The context does not establish a materially different creation mechanism.
時代の一生 gives the scale as the lifetime of an era or age; unqualified “a lifetime” normally reduces that to one person’s life.
“A thousand magical energy” is grammatically malformed because “magical energy” is uncountable, and it also omits 程度’s approximation or an implied unit.
“Such a large supply” conveys the enlarged reserve, while “just a waste” preserves Rin’s contempt and the functional point of 宝の持ち腐れ. The missing bodily metaphor is stylistic compression.
魔力 bears the ruby かげ, directly supporting “shadow,” and the surrounding Japanese repeatedly describes the forces as canceling each other. The accusation ignores both ruby and context.
拮抗 is equilibrium or evenly matched opposition. “Competition” fails to convey the precise technical balance created by the sword.
The Japanese denies that Rin’s energy is being amplified, not categorically that her energy is used. English collapses that technical distinction into a broader zero-use claim.
退ける can mean repel, defeat, or get rid of an attacker; “eliminate” is within its contextual range and does not necessarily assert permanent destruction.
The preceding and following English explicitly discuss mana, so “power” here is a natural local abbreviation for atmospheric magical energy rather than a change of resource.
The governing Japanese gives 大空洞 the ruby reading せかい, expressly licensing “this world.” The accusation ignores the supplied ruby.

“A parallel world” with “the cavern there,” following the prior hypothetical second cavern, preserves the corresponding-place mechanism. Omitting the facing-mirror simile is not a material factual error.
Drawing from one parallel world at a time agrees with the later sequential-world explanation. The narrower valid omission is 毎回: English does not state that the thousand-unit draw repeats each time.
The surrounding passage establishes Sakura’s Greater-Grail reservoir as the source she draws upon. “Drawing a massive supply” is a contextual paraphrase, not a materially conflicting ownership claim.
Although awkward, “makes a path in between infinite parallel worlds” conveys connecting a route among parallel worlds, and the next sentence supplies the opening into another world.

“Another possible world” naturally conveys a world embodying another possibility, while the opening and prior parallel-world context supply its relation to the current world. The alleged loss is not materially established.
English retains energy creation when swung but omits the explicit thousand-unit quantity and that it would occur with every strike.
“The next one” has a clear antecedent in the previous page’s next parallel cavern. “Move on” idiomatically means switching sources, not bodily travel by Rin.
合わせ鏡 means mutually facing mirrors with recursive reflections. “Opposite mirrors” is nonidiomatic, obscures that image, and is paired with incorrect number agreement.
二つの事柄 refers to inexhaustible storage and indefinitely repeated supply. English instead declares the two magi themselves equal, changing the proposition.
大聖杯たる identifies this altar as the Greater Grail. Coordinating “the altar and the Great Holy Grail” incorrectly creates two threatened objects.
English immediately says continuing will make Sakura lose, which conveys the practical futility of continuing. Omitting 徒に as a separate adverb is not materially misleading.
In this established cavern setting, “the room will cave in” naturally describes the enclosing cavern collapsing; “cave in” directly conveys 崩壊.
Here 敵の正体 is the newly revealed nature of Rin’s otherwise inexplicable power. “Origin of her enemy’s power” is a contextually supported explicitation.
“Gasping for breath” reasonably compresses Sakura’s heaving shoulders and painful breathing. The genuine omission is the contrast with Rin standing calmly and composed.
“Cool your head” is an established English idiom for ceasing to be carried away or overexcited, so it conveys 舞い上がってた頭 without literal elaboration.
自らの首を絞める is idiomatic for harming oneself or worsening one’s position. “Pushing herself into a corner” is a natural nonliteral equivalent, not improper euphemism.
Rin is unmistakably the grudge’s object from the surrounding confrontation and the immediately following confession. Omitting the redundant explicit object is not a material ambiguity.
勝ちたかった is a past desire explaining Sakura’s longstanding wish for recognition. “I want to win” recasts it as a present competitive objective.
“Room with worms” loses both 暗い and the specific 蟲倉 torture-site designation, reducing the dark worm storehouse to a generic room.
The Japanese says she was treated every single day like a toy or plaything. “Treated as an object” omits the relentless duration and changes the specific abusive comparison.
“The miserable girl” plainly refers to the speaking Sakura and can function as rhetorical self-reference in English. The referent and accusation against Rin remain intact.
In this abstract context, “blind plea” can naturally mean a desperate, directionless plea with no outlet. It is a defensible paraphrase of 出口のない, not a literal claim about sight.
The Japanese expressly frames Sakura’s changing eyes and hair in comparison with Rin. English reports alteration but omits that sisterly divergence.
体に直接刻む describes instruction or magecraft being invasively engraved into Sakura’s body. “Taught my body” removes the physical inscription.
放り込まれる is being thrown or cast in, and 蟲倉 is the worm storehouse. “Put me with the worms” loses both violent confinement and the location.

The ruby reads 少女 as かげ, explicitly supporting “shadow”; English therefore does not invent that object. It does, however, lose the deliberate surface-image of the crying, clinging girl embodied in that shadow.
The apparent two renderings come from flattened conditional branches, not text printed together in play. Moreover, the aligned Original witness has 狂ってますよね, supporting the mature “I’m crazy” branch.
The aligned Original witness explicitly says her abusers acted 喜んで, supporting the mature branch’s delight. Its absence from base/all-ages is an edition difference.

“Oppressed” and “wounded” are separate conditional branch renderings exposed by flattening, not competing words simultaneously printed to the reader. The finding treats an extraction artifact as translation output.
それを is a deliberately unresolved accusative “that…” referring back to Sakura’s wounds and plea. “But” replaces the anaphoric object with an adversative relation.

The preceding English sentence, “She doesn’t feel for her at all,” directly renders 一切同情しなかった. “Not a single word of sympathy” then handles the separate 可哀想ね fragment; the finding isolates the wrong sentence.

それはそれでいいんじゃない naturally means that being a monster may be acceptable in its own way. “Doesn’t sound so bad” is a defensible colloquial rendering, with the next page explicitly retaining the cruel approval.

苦しい can denote emotional pain or suffering, and “painful” is not limited to physical pain. The surrounding lines about being cornered support a psychological reading, so the accusation imposes an unduly narrow English sense.
“Cruel treatment received” replaces terrible days Sakura lived through with treatment inflicted upon her, adding a specific external-agency relation not stated here.
“Just” preserves the limiting だけ, while “the truth” naturally represents 事実 in a passage that immediately says Rin is not lying. It does not materially endorse her judgment beyond the Japanese.
“Never thought I was blessed” is a defensible English rendering of 一度も思えた事はなかった. The potential form can suggest an inability to feel it, but it does not require a separate incapacity claim.
The Japanese places Rin’s feeling into the act of looking back at Sakura; the English explicitly relocates it to her words.
The Japanese says Rin lacks every fragment of what Sakura wanted Rin to possess. The English instead makes Sakura want everything from Rin and receive nothing, reversing both possession and desire.
The exclusion expressed by 自分だけ—Rin insisting that she alone remains clean—is absent from “she’s still pure and clean,” weakening Sakura’s contrast with herself.

Although awkward, “Rin’s weakness against Sakura” can naturally mean the particular vulnerability or soft spot she has where Sakura is concerned. The surrounding admission about entrusting their problem to Shirou prevents a necessary tactical reading.

あっさり adds ease or clean abruptness, but “At that instant” followed by “finishes the battle” already conveys the decisive suddenness. Omitting the adverb is a minor tonal compression, not a demonstrable material error.

“Monsters you had a hard time killing come back” already entails that they were believed killed, substantially conveying 倒した筈. The credits and subsequent “fin” remain intelligible despite clumsy syntax.

In context, “A monster’s gotta be immortal” can state immortality as the defining condition for being such a monster. The causal nuance of 故に is loosened, but the joke’s classification relation is not materially reversed.
拘った describes actively clinging to an unresolved attachment. “Were confined by lingering affection” makes the subject passively constrained and narrows 未練 to affection.
“Brutally honest” is a normal contextual rendering of 身もふたも無い, describing an excessively blunt, unvarnished answer. Calling it a factual character judgment is overreading.
“Thanks for bearing with us” is an idiomatic acknowledgment that the audience stayed through all forty installments. It is less complimentary than 飽きずに but remains a defensible tonal paraphrase.
The reunion is expressly conditional on 縁—if circumstances or fate bring them together. The English turns it into an unqualified invitation to meet again.
“Fully complete the game” is awkward but accurately conveys フルコンプリート. Unnatural phrasing alone is not an accuracy error.
The English omits three explicit and scene-relevant features: the legacy is irreplaceable, Rin tosses it lightly, and the motion resembles a casual game of catch.

Calling the sword “miraculous” is a reasonable condensation of its embodying a miracle beyond human reach. The fuller metaphysical formulation is lost, but the English does not state a materially different property.
怯む includes flinching or recoiling, and people can “wince from the light” because of brightness rather than injury. The English does not necessarily introduce pain.
The unqualified statement “it won’t make it in time” is already categorical in English. 絶対に intensifies it but does not create a distinct factual condition.

ホッとした can idiomatically become “sighs with relief,” so the alleged invented physical action is not decisive. The narrower valid criticism is that 少しだけ limits Sakura’s relief to only a small amount, which the English omits.
In the immediate context Sakura expects to be killed, so rendering 消えてしまえば as dying is a natural explicitation. 楽になる also supports the thought that her present pain or distress will end.
“Firmly wrapped around her” reasonably carries しっかりと and does not materially misassign it. The genuine omission is that Rin is embracing Sakura with a body on the verge of collapse.
The English states only that blood is flowing and omits 取り返しがつかないほど, which marks the blood loss as already catastrophic or irreparable.

“The voice she’s always dreamed of” can idiomatically mean the voice she has long admired or yearned for, and the next sentence identifies it specifically as Rin’s. It need not mean an imagined voice.
“Relentless” can represent 容赦がない but does not convey 皮肉屋, so Rin’s explicitly cynical or sardonic trait is omitted.
納得してみる presents Rin tentatively trying out self-acceptance or self-persuasion. “Rin’s convinced” changes that into a settled state.
“So preoccupied with that” supplies the backward connection of それだけで, while “painful” can cover emotional suffering. The relation is awkwardly expressed but not materially lost.
The treasure comparison is retained, but ようやく手に入れた specifically presents Sakura as a treasure Rin has finally obtained after long separation. That culmination is absent.

Leaving the established Japanese kinship address as “Nee-san” is a translation convention, not a meaning error. The raw supplied English also contains an internal timing break, so its apparent loss may be extraction-related.

Japanese does not obligatorily mark 花 as plural, and “a falling red flower” is a defensible rendering of the image. 舞い散った adds fluttering or scattering, but the finding’s asserted plural contrast is not established.

The English genuinely omits both the mirage comparison and the past/distanced 姉だった人 wording. Calling the latter specifically “estranged” overinterprets why Sakura frames Rin as someone who had been her sister.
その言葉 refers to Rin’s recalled statement on the preceding page. Naming them “Sakura’s words” reverses whose hidden loneliness Sakura is beginning to recognize.
“Her agony for her alone” is ungrammatical English, but its readily recoverable meaning is that her agony is hers alone. It does not materially reverse or erase the nontransferability claim.
The English retains Sakura’s admiration but entirely omits 信じ続けた, her continuing faith in Rin.

The surrounding broken utterances 「、ゃ」 and 「だ」 form the semantic response いやだ. Rendering the fragments as “No” does not invent an unrelated negation, even though it poorly reproduces their phonetic division.
The supplied English page is not blank: it contains “ButI destroyed them.” The finding attacks text that is demonstrably present, with the joined word explainable as extraction formatting.
“She destroyed it all herself” preserves Sakura’s personal agency; “herself” naturally carries 自分の手で. It compresses the shattering image but does not materially change responsibility or outcome.
抱き返す means returning another person’s embrace. The English instead invents a present attempt to embrace someone absent, losing Sakura’s failure to reciprocate before Rin fell away.

A “rumbling” that shakes the cave is a plausible sensory rendering of a transmitted 衝撃, especially as the next sentence says the cavern creaks and trembles. The missing faint-degree nuance is not materially transformative.
“Still far off” conveys the weak, distant transmission relevant to the contrast with the cavern’s trembling. Omitting an explicit “faintly” is minor compression rather than a factual error.
ぼんやりと頭に浮かんだ describes an indistinct association arising in Shirou’s mind. “Suddenly I realize” makes it abrupt and cognitively definite.
The Japanese explicitly describes Saber turning into shadow as she disappears. “Saber disappears” omits that transformation.
After the stated final Projection, the unqualified English “I won’t be able to suppress Archer’s arm” already expresses inevitable failure. 何をしても adds emphasis, not a missing condition.

The extra line is present in the supplied raw Original witness, even though it is absent from the base/all-ages page text. For this Original-edition comparator it is therefore not an unsupported insertion.
The Japanese compares the pain to having an iron rod stabbed into the leg. The English instead describes the sensation of a metal pipe protruding outward, reversing the physical image.

In this discovery scene, “She’s still there,” immediately followed by her wounds and depleted energy, reasonably conveys that Rider survived and remains present. 健在 is weakened but not materially contradicted.
眩しそう describes Rider looking up as though dazzled—literally or figuratively by Shirou. “In a daze” instead attributes cognitive disorientation.
回復 naturally means healing or recovery here, and “after she heals instead of pushing herself now” preserves the requirement that she wait until recovery. The omitted certainty nuance is minor.

Shirou is explicitly wounded throughout the adjacent pages, and “drag my wounded body” conveys impaired movement rather than replacing it with an incompatible cause. This is defensible contextual explicitation.
Leaning against a wall while walking is a natural paraphrase of advancing with a hand on it for support. The precise contact changes, but no material action or agency is lost.

In context ビシっとしたはずだ is Shirou’s minimizing insistence that the sensation was merely the sharp numbness just described. “Just a little numbness” is loose but preserves that denial before he sees the wound.

The supposedly unsupported “inside my body” is present in the supplied raw Original witness; the alternative “a gaping wound” belongs to the all-ages branch, and their simultaneous display is an acknowledged branch-flattening artifact. “Pants leg” is contextually reasonable for a thigh wound.
生暖かい is an unsettling lukewarm or tepid warmth, not simply warm, while 撫でる describes the wind brushing or caressing the body rather than hitting it.
Japanese 頬 is not obligatorily singular in this construction and can naturally correspond to “cheek” or “cheeks.” No reliable number error is established.

記録 literally favors “record,” but the supplied pages do not establish the nature of Illya’s record or whether “memory” is an acceptable contextual description of inherited recorded experience. The technical distinction cannot be certified from these witnesses alone.
受肉 is the specific process of acquiring or incarnating in flesh, and しかけてる marks that process as incipient or incomplete. “About to be born” reduces it to generic birth.
The Japanese attributes an excessive abundance of life force to the entity’s breathing and says birth is imminent. The English loses that excess and introduces the distinct image of hatching.

“Wreaking havoc on the cavern” naturally summarizes destructive, uncontrolled gouging. It omits the sound effect and Shirou’s comic insult, but that is tonal compression rather than a demonstrable material mistranslation.
The English preserves the central grotesque paradox that the eyeless fetus looks at Shirou. Omitting the adverbial ぎょろり loses manner but not a material mechanism.

English normally requires a pronoun, and the surrounding narration already treats the entity as an agent and as the Servant responsible for taking Sakura. Using “he” is contextual explicitation, not a demonstrable contradiction of Japanese gender.
中が胎盤だ identifies the black pillar’s interior itself as the placenta. “His placenta is inside the pillar” instead makes it a separate object located there.
胎盤 specifically means placenta, whereas “womb” is a different anatomical structure. The change also conflicts with the preceding statement that the pillar’s interior is the placenta.

みっともなく explicitly judges the entity’s desperation as shameful or pathetic, and 急造でいいから means even a crude rush job will do. The English omits the judgment and weakens acceptance into mere possibility.
The Japanese says a tremendous light is released and deliberately breaks at “and then.” The English replaces that event and suspended consequence with a completed inference about the light’s cause.
“The world starts to quake” already denotes substantial shaking; “quake” itself supplies the magnitude carried by 大きく. The claimed scale omission is not material.
惷動 denotes the giant shadow’s grotesque stirring or writhing as it tries to emerge. The English instead makes the cavern’s shaking the main predicate, losing the entity’s bodily movement.
予感 need not be supernatural; “imagine the worst possible outcome” is a natural rendering of a foreboding prompted by Sakura’s crying voice. “Cry” can also encompass sobbing in this context.
The English retains the all-fours scramble but omits both the comparison to someone stricken with illness and the description of the cliff as high.
The verb “crash” naturally absorbs the impact sound ドオン. Translating an isolated sound effect lexically rather than reproducing an English onomatopoeia is not an omission of the event.

In the surrounding sequence Sakura is explicitly hating and condemning herself. “Cursing her own existence” is a forceful natural rendering of 自らを罵倒していた, not a demonstrably different object of condemnation.

The Japanese separately inventories Sakura’s present self, blood-stained self, blackened self, and the black shadow connected to her. The English collapses part of that structure and incorrectly changes the connected shadow into a pillar.
半狂乱 specifies that Sakura is nearly frantic, while 憎んでいる is direct hatred. “Cursing everything” omits her mental state and changes the emotion/action.

ダメだ and 負けるな are closely linked admonitions in Sakura’s recollection, and “always told me not to lose” reasonably condenses their shared encouragement. The alleged loss is too slight and context-dependent to establish a material error.

Japanese does not independently establish grammatical plurality for 令呪, so singularization is not demonstrable. The narrower valid omission is 全身を覆った: the English does not say that the black marking covers Sakura’s entire body.
本体 identifies Sakura as the shadow’s necessary principal or core body. “Host” instead frames the shadow as a separate occupant using her as a vessel, changing the stated ontology.

Although the final English sentence summarizes the forces generally, the immediately preceding translated lines already state that Sakura tries to kill herself and the shadow prevents her. The opposed actions are therefore not removed from the complete page.

憑き物が落ちる is an established idiom for coming to one’s senses or being freed from an obsessive state, even though it invokes possession imagery. “Regained her sanity” is contextually defensible and does not necessarily blame Sakura.
叩いていたら describes physically striking or smacking Sakura, reinforced by the comic sound ぱかん. “Scolded her” replaces that imagined physical intervention with verbal reprimand.
かろうじて says Rin is only barely managing to breathe. “Still breathing” communicates survival but omits the explicit extremity of her condition.

The genuine issue is narrower: 生まれてもない means “not yet born,” whereas “not alive yet” changes birth status into nonlife. The surrounding ガキ/この子 personification makes “he” a defensible English explicitation.
“Cut through my neck” still describes a fatal severing and is a defensible rendering in the context of a cutting shadow attack; the accusation overstates the tonal difference.
“Sakura’s scream made it miss” preserves both Sakura’s causal agency and the attack’s resulting deviation; specifying its trajectory would be more literal, not materially different.
蝕む suggests consuming or eating away, and “the shadow swallowing her” is a defensible contextual image for that ongoing engulfment rather than a demonstrable factual error.
The English conveys her inability to suppress herself but entirely omits that she has no alternative except being controlled by the shadow, a material loss of coercion and agency.
Here ちゃんと is emphatic resolve, not necessarily literal “properly.” The English preserves the repetitions, dying here, and doing so alone, so the alleged material weakening is preference-level.
“I shouldn’t live” naturally conveys Sakura’s categorical judgment that she is someone who must not live. Rendering 人間だった more literally would alter framing, not establish a material contradiction.
この子 personifies the unborn entity as a child, while adjacent text calls it a ガキ. English requires a pronoun, and “he” is a contextually defensible resolution rather than an unsupported factual claim.
The archived line is “And[line4]even,” where the removed line command represents a pause/dash. “Andeven” is a flattening artifact, not a missing-space error in the translated script.
The archived English is “What[line3]What,” deliberately reproducing the Japanese repetition and pause. Its displayed concatenation is an extraction artifact, not a duplicated-word translation error.
“Can’t back out now” is an ordinary idiomatic rendering of being on a path from which one cannot turn back; it does not imply that Sakura merely refuses voluntarily.
In context, “those actions” unmistakably refers to taking many lives, while “haunt her forever” naturally conveys blame remaining in her heart. The meaning is condensed, not removed.
昏い影 is plainly metaphorical here, and “the darkness will remain within her” is a natural equivalent. Retaining the repeated shadow image would be stylistically preferable, not factually required.

“Things I have to tell her” defensibly supplies Sakura as the addressee, but it omits the explicit closing window—while Shirou can still put the necessary words into speech. The fragmentary syntax is secondary.
The Japanese unambiguously identifies the right leg, while the English says left leg.
“Everything” erases the defining relation expressed by 問われる: Shirou promises protection from everything for which Sakura will henceforth be questioned or held accountable.

“My ideal has always been to protect the one I love” substantially conveys both the enduring ideal and its object. The more literal “lived by” and 守り通す endurance are nuances, not a demonstrable material error.
“The dagger that breaks all contracts” is a reasonable contextual expansion of the epithet 契約破り, especially given the adjacent explanation of its broad nullifying and contract-breaking function.
Japanese does not grammatically establish a plural, so the singularization charge fails. A narrower loss remains: 砕け散る depicts the mark shattering and scattering, not merely disappearing.
The Japanese explicitly identifies a short dagger; the bare agent noun “contract-breaker” omits the weapon category at the point where the object is being identified.

The defensible terminology choice “magic” versus “magecraft” is not itself an error. The narrower technical shift survives: 初期化 describes resetting effects to their initial state, not simply nullifying all magic.
横たわる means lying down, and in this cavern scene “on the ground” is normal spatial explicitation with no conflicting location supplied.
まだ間に合う is commonly rendered “she’ll make it” when a speaker judges that rescue is still possible, and the following explanation supports Shirou’s confidence. This is not demonstrably false certainty.

“The Tohsaka family’s magic” is a natural rendering of inherited Tohsaka 魔術, and the immediately identified Magic Crest already conveys familial transmission. The accusation largely enforces preferred terminology.
桜がいなくても means the shadow can emerge without Sakura being present. “Without Sakura’s help” instead suggests optional cooperation, conflicting with the vessel relationship stated immediately before.

The subject “it” and the unconditional future “will emerge” already communicate autonomous eventual emergence. Omitting the crawling image reduces vividness but does not establish a material translation error.
For a personified, unborn supernatural entity, “die” is a defensible contextual rendering of ceasing to exist. 消え去る is not restricted to a technical ontological sense here.
The English preserves immediate destruction but omits 跡形もなく, which explicitly requires complete erasure without a trace.
“As near as I can” captures ギリギリまで近づいて, and “attack with great force” conveys 大火力. The missing feet and explosive register are vividness losses, not a material factual error.
The English retains cutting the entity in two but wholly omits the intended endpoint: smashing it back into its original state as a nonexistent thing.
Angra Mainyu is repeatedly personified as a child and individual in the surrounding scene. Using “he” where English requires a pronoun is defensible contextual explicitation.

The preceding “such a feat” anaphorically supplies the action and target, so “the greatest Noble Phantasm I know of” still identifies what will eliminate the monster. The Japanese restates the action more explicitly, but it is not absent in meaning.
The Japanese presents Shirou’s breathing as currently stopped. “Stopped for a moment” changes this to a completed, explicitly brief interruption, softening his ongoing physical failure.
In the immediate context the hundred meters are the distance Shirou must traverse to the target, so “I can walk this distance” is a reasonable resolution of the omitted verb in やれない距離じゃない.
The English omits that the person appears unfamiliar to Shirou, an explicit perception that motivates his struggle to recognize her on the next page.
“Stares” preserves the gaze and duration but drops 値踏みするように, which explicitly characterizes Rider as appraising or assessing Shirou.
閉じる means to close or seal the relevant thing/opening. “Destroy” fixes a different operation and object even though destruction is part of Shirou’s broader plan.
Making Sakura “his Master” naturally expresses the relational meaning of making her a Master of Angra Mainyu. The male pronoun is also supported by the scene’s sustained personification.
“I have rested enough” gives the natural cause and practical result of her stamina having recovered sufficiently. It is somewhat less physiological, but not materially contradictory.
“Make sure they’re okay first” is broad, but the same English speech immediately specifies “please treat Tohsaka.” The page as a whole preserves the medical priority rather than suppressing it.

The preceding English sentence explicitly says Rider lacks healing ability, and “But I still have to” conveys entrusting Rin to her despite that known limitation. The alleged awareness is preserved across the two sentences.
肝に銘じる is forceful, but “Please remember that” is a normal English rendering of the admonition. Calling the difference a factual loss overpolices register.
The Japanese says Rider cannot accept anyone other than Shirou as Sakura’s support. “I need you to support Sakura” requests him but loses that explicit exclusivity and Rider’s evaluative standard.
ご武運を is a conventional wish of luck in battle, and the battle context supplies the martial specificity. “Good luck” is concise but accurate, not a demonstrable register error.

“Falling rocks” naturally describes debris from the falling ceiling and collapsing cavern, while the surrounding English already states that the cavern is collapsing. The accusation treats compression as omission.
“One more thing” identifies the final remaining task, while “take care of” is a normal contextual equivalent of 後始末. The threat to be handled is already clear from the preceding pages.
“Consciousness is breaking apart” accurately conveys mental disconnection and collapse. Preserving the wire-breaking metaphor of 断線 would be more vivid, but its loss is not a material factual error.
“An impossibly vast expanse” communicates that the hundred meters have become uncrossable. 永遠 intensifies that perception, but the English does not materially reverse or obscure it.
“Strewn with rubble” substantially reduces the depicted transformation: formerly wasteland-like ground is progressively becoming a mountain of rubble.

The immediate rationale is mechanical movement: humans cannot move without taking in oxygen. Changing 動けない to “can’t live” breaks the logic of Shirou’s following thought that his altered body might move without oxygen.
The Japanese visibly fails mid-word at 動けなくな, enacting Shirou’s collapsing consciousness. The English completes the proposition and removes that deliberate interruption.
串刺し刑 denotes punishment or execution by impalement, and “an inescapable death by skewering” preserves the concrete fatal image. The distinction is tonal rather than materially factual.
The narration states that Shirou’s current body is made of swords. Substituting the incantation phrase “I am the bone of my sword” changes that literal bodily proposition.

The surrounding chronology shows that Shirou has already used Projection to free Sakura. The Japanese recalls the warning that once he projected, the time bomb would start; the English retrospective past is contextually appropriate.

A narrower error survives: 消す means erase or eliminate, whereas “beat” can mean merely defeat. Calling the referent “him” is defensible because the surrounding scene consistently personifies Angra Mainyu.
The Japanese identifies the crater itself as what is called the Greater Grail. The English apposition instead reads as though the Greater Grail stands in front of a separate crater.
“Ruddy glow” preserves only a reddish illumination; it removes both the black component and the concrete red-black flames lighting the figure.
“Desolate realm” can naturally denote an uninhabited, lifeless world and fits the scene. The categorical wording is less explicit, but the accusation does not establish a material contradiction.

“Predication” is an uncommon but valid word for an assertion or act of affirming something. It is awkward here, but it can express the contrast with speculation and is not demonstrably the alleged typo.
The curse is already treated as an individual, child, and prospective god throughout the dialogue. Resolving it as “he” in English is defensible contextual personification.

Shirou is the outside enemy and has repeatedly stated that he intends to destroy the entity. In this context, trying to kill it is the concrete means of obstructing its birth, not an unsupported alternative action.

“There is nothing to be gained” is an idiomatic rendering of no one obtaining any result, especially after Kirei says both men share the same end. A surviving beneficiary is contextual inference, not omitted lexical content.
The English omits the explicit tactical detail that Kirei would crush Shirou’s skull before Shirou could create Saber’s sword—the intended final projection.

何故も何もない dismisses the demand for a further why, and “there is no room for questions” is a defensible idiomatic response before Kirei states his sole motive. It is not a material prohibition replacing a reason.
The surrounding discourse explicitly personifies Angra Mainyu as a child, individual, and god. The male pronoun is a defensible English resolution, not a mistranslation of the killing claim.
The English entirely omits Shirou’s statement that he cannot possibly answer Kirei’s moral question, removing the transition into his admission that he has lost his former moral framework.

The Japanese says a person’s own choices determine how their coexisting moral attributes divide or which way the person inclines. “Decide which is which” instead sounds like labeling good and evil themselves.
戯れ describes goodwill shown capriciously, playfully, or on a whim. “Rare moments” replaces that motive with an unsupported claim about frequency.

The Japanese coordinates two universal denials: nothing is unwanted by everyone, and nothing is born evil. The English relative-clause chain can deny only an entity satisfying both properties, materially weakening the logic.
The English names “all evils” but omits the explicit claim that humanity’s own collective wishing raised or fashioned it, a central part of the entity’s moral origin.

In context, “someone that can only kill” reasonably conveys an entity whose sole designed purpose is killing, and the next speech explicitly states that people made it that way. The distinction is not materially lost across the passage.

“His nature is evil” is a defensible English expression of evil inhering in the entity’s very existence, especially as the following sentences explain that it was created to be evil. The male personification is contextually established.
“A pure deity that people made” omits two defining claims: it possesses nothing except evil and is a singular/one god.
The archived English is “But[line4]even,” with a pause/dash command between the words. “Buteven” is caused by command stripping, not a spacing error in the script.
自分をどう思うか asks what Angra Mainyu thinks of itself. The English prematurely narrows this to what it thinks about its actions, changing the philosophical object of self-judgment.
意思 denotes will or intention, the faculty Kirei makes relevant to moral judgment. “Emotions” substitutes a materially different mental faculty.
The Japanese condition is lamenting its own existence; the English changes this to remorse over its deeds, which is a different basis for Kirei’s moral classification.
The Japanese describes something inherently unobtainable from birth; it does not identify congenital bodily defects. The English concretizes an omitted object into a different condition.

Both concepts survive: “meaning of birth” corresponds to 誕生する意味, while “worth of worthless life” defensibly conveys the value of a valueless being’s existence. Reordering them around a colon is not a demonstrated omission.
Being separated from the external world is substantially stronger and more specific than merely being different from other people; the isolation central to the following 孤独 is weakened.
The source has Shirou force his impaired, hazy vision to function. “Shake off the vagueness” instead suggests successfully dispelling an abstract state.

“Holding my gaze” adequately conveys not looking away, so the alleged loss of unwavering gaze is overstated. The narration nevertheless omits the explicit image of his declaration being made with a dying body.
間違い denotes error, wrongness, or having been mistaken here. “Doubts” instead describes uncertainty and changes Kirei’s apparent claim that his course was not wrong.
Not wanting to accept the fact covers denial, but the separate purpose of remaining unaware through the end disappears.
The English says Kirei knows no alternative at all, omitting Shirou’s morally significant qualification that he knows no other genuinely right way to live.
澱 supplies a deliberate image of innumerable dregs or sediment. Replacing it with generic “things” erases that characterization rather than merely varying the wording.

鬱積 can mean pent-up feelings or accumulated frustration, and releasing them is a natural contextual rendering of 帳消しにする. The accounting metaphor is softened, but the alleged change of act is not demonstrable.

Although 倒す is literally “defeat,” this is explicitly a fight staking both lives, and Shirou must stop Kirei before his own life expires. “Kill him” is defensible contextual explicitation, not an unsupported new objective.
The source attributes unavoidable evasion to the chosen timing, not to the punch’s speed. The English changes the combat mechanism.

This is an edition-witness problem: the supplied raw Original candidate reads 掌, “palm,” while the archived base/all-ages text reads 拳. The English agrees with the Original wording and cannot be faulted from the base-edition form.
“A while” naturally accommodates the several-hour interval established by ここ数時間. It is less exact but does not materially alter the event or chronology.
Having the neck yanked out of the torso entails the head being ripped off; the English is a conventional, forceful rendering of the same grotesque injury rather than a different event.
もとより makes external damage a given and adds internal damage. “Instead of outside” reverses that inclusive relation and wrongly excludes external damage.

The accusation ignores the ruby ごくじょう, which supports the English judgment that the art is exceptionally good. A narrower omission remains: English does not preserve the written 秘門 sense of an esoteric or secret school.
何も宿らぬ is categorical emptiness. “Without much” changes that into partial deficiency.
The raw English places a line-dash command between “it” and “but”; the fused public text results from command stripping, not from a translated clause lacking separation.

固まった covers stiffened, fixed, seized, or hardened joints. In the surrounding transformation into blades, “fused” is strong but contextually defensible and does not establish a distinct factual condition.

The surrounding sentences identify Kirei’s bloody fist and the danger to the attacker; “the price … to attack a body made of swords” compactly preserves the causal mechanics. Barehanded smashing is compressed, not materially contradicted.
The supplied ruby explicitly reads 条件 as ハンデ. “Handicap” is therefore directly licensed by the Japanese rather than invented.
The exact one-second interval is explicit and creates an immediate scheduled release; “getting ready for the explosion” removes that timing.
自身 denotes the self or oneself, matching the contrast with an external enemy. “Your body” both narrows the stake to physical flesh and loses the broader mutual, existential formulation.
In an ongoing hand-to-hand fight, saying one fighter is “stronger” naturally means superior as a fighter. The context supplies the technical domain, so this is a defensible compression.
The participial phrase can read as a postmodifier of “my enemy,” and the immediate context makes the approaching actor unmistakable. The English is awkwardly ambiguous, not demonstrably reassigned.
妄執 is a deluded or pathological obsession, not a neutral wish. The English removes the source’s condemnation of the centuries-long fixation.
一つ means one or a single world; it supplies no diminutive judgment. Adding “small” unsupportedly reduces its scale.
In this context 意味 can naturally be rendered as the remaining purpose or point of Shirou’s existence and action. “Purpose” does not necessarily reduce it to a mere task objective.
“Breaking apart” is a natural rendering of consciousness losing continuity. It drops the literal severed-wire metaphor of 断線 but does not produce a materially different mental event.

“Impossibly vast” conveys that the hundred meters cannot be traversed. The Japanese’s 永遠 intensifies that impossibility, but the English preserves the governing effect rather than asserting mere largeness.

The English preserves the partially collapsing overhead structure and the ground’s accumulating rubble. Losing the former wasteland simile and using “pile” rather than “mountain” are descriptive compression, not a material scene error.
“Death by skewering” naturally conveys execution by impalement. Rendering 刑 through the lethal punishment itself is defensible.

This is a literal statement that Shirou’s body is made of swords amid physical blade growth. Substituting the familiar incantation’s “bone of my sword” changes that bodily fact into a different formula.
割れる ranges over cracking, splitting, and breaking; the English immediately follows “crumbling” with “shatter” twice and retains the progression into pieces. This is defensible lexical variation.
“I’ll still make it” is an idiomatic rendering of まだ間に合う, especially with the stopping condition explained in the next sentence. It need not imply certainty of completing the larger mission.
手遅れ states that saving the body is already too late. “My body’s dying” describes an ongoing process without preserving that explicit point of no return.

The surrounding passage defines loss of meaning through loss of identity and intended action. “Lose myself” is a defensible contextual rendering of that abstract deterioration, not an unrelated stable object.

The Japanese is itself a compressed fragment equating behavioral principle with its linkage to pleasure. The English is stiff but preserves that appositional anatomy and does not establish a material mistranslation.

“Would become beasts” is a conventional English rendering of being no different from beasts under the stated condition. The comparison’s force survives despite the slight shift in grammatical framing.
The source concerns remaining oneself and describes a consuming attachment to that continuity. Reducing it to wanting to retain memory removes both the broader identity and the intensity of 執着.
Memory “fading” is a natural processive rendering of memory disappearing, particularly while the loss is visibly ongoing. It does not deny the ultimate 消失.
The English retains forgetting the intended action but entirely omits losing who he is; it also weakens きっと into probability.
The Japanese specifies only that the important reason lies outside his body, not where outside it is. “Somewhere” reflects that omission, and “big reason” directly renders 大きな理由.
The repeated おまえ deliberately addresses Shirou as “you” during the dissolution of his self. Converting it to ordinary first-person resolve removes that marked perspective.
“Couldn’t breathe if I had all day” idiomatically conveys that even an entire day would not suffice for one breath. The hypothetical grammar preserves the intended time-dilated inability.

踏み止まる can mean holding oneself or arresting a fall, and the next English sentence explicitly supplies reaching for the wall to avoid falling. The physical resistance is preserved across the two sentences.

“Tiny foothold” preserves the operative scale, while “shards of my existence” is a contextual image drawn from the surrounding disintegration. The wording is florid, but the entire existence remains precariously concentrated on the foothold.
The Japanese deliberately stops on the continuative 崩れて, leaving both syntax and collapse suspended. The English completes the event as a settled finite sentence and loses that enacted interruption.
行動理由 is the reason or motive for acting. “Meaning of behavior” is not only unnatural but blurs this distinct stage into the adjacent loss of existential meaning.
The source specifically loses both what he exists for and whom he exists for. The generalized English “meaning behind my existence” omits those two relations.

Japanese nouns do not obligatorily mark number, and 腕 can refer contextually to his arms or arm-function generally. Possessive “my” is also normal English explicitation of その; singularity and alienated distance are not securely established.

“Neopallium” is an established synonym for neocortex, and the English culminates in the loss of the cerebrum, which subsumes the enumerated regions. “Language” is imprecise for 言語野, but the exhaustive brain loss remains clear.
節 can denote a verse or section, and “eight verses” is natural for sections of an incantation. The source is also a subjectless fragment, so the matching English fragment is not an independent error.

Within the explicit machine comparison, “programmed” naturally explicates 機能, and swinging the sword encompasses raising it to strike. The projected sword is identifiable from context; no material new mechanism is introduced.

残骸 can mean remains or wreckage, and the immediately preceding sentence states that Emiya Shirou has died. Calling the immobile remains a corpse is contextually defensible while the prior machine comparison remains explicit.
人工の知能 is artificial intelligence. Replacing it with human intelligence reverses the stated premise about machines functioning without artificial intelligence.

The English wrongly turns the sequence into an act of “recitation” and makes the words objectively meaningless. The accusation should be narrowed because the Japanese says Shirou can no longer understand their meaning, not that the symbols are intrinsically unreadable.
The English preserves the remembered hope but omits 果たされるべき, the explicit necessity that it be fulfilled.

“Continuous” and “never completed” preserve the unending succession and failure to come to fruition, so the explanation overstates the loss. The distinct 翻らず element—never turning or being overturned—remains omitted.
意思 is will or volition, as the following declaration demonstrates. Mere consciousness does not convey that it still possessed an intention.
The Japanese identifies worms that had established themselves underground. The English replaces that history with the unsupported present claim that the swarm fills the cavern.
“Using all the worms” omits the concrete construction: gathering every worm and combining them into a single flesh-body.
The ruby explicitly reads 本体 as よりしろ, a vessel or medium that anchors a spirit. “His soul’s vessel” therefore reflects a supplied Original reading rather than improperly generalizing it.

潰された describes being crushed or bodily destroyed twice, with unhealed damage remaining. “Killed twice” asserts two completed deaths even though the passage says his final destruction is still impending.
The English leaves the object unspecified and omits Zouken’s upward gaze. The source identifies it as the visible manifestation of eternity he almost obtained.
溶け合えず describes failure to blend or assimilate with the foreign land’s laws. “Unable to familiarize themselves” instead suggests insufficient knowledge or acquaintance.

The preceding English clause explicitly identifies “his bloodline’s end,” so “accepted fate” has extinction as its clear antecedent. 大人しく is compressed, but the claimed removal of extinction is false.

The founding seeker marks the beginning of the Makiri pursuit, so “since the start of their search” is a reasonable metonymic timeline. Omitting the individual ancestor is not a material historical contradiction here.

“Their limit” refers to the Makiri family in a passage entirely about its hereditary decline, and the next English sentence names the family. The mage-lineage constraint is compressed but recoverable and not materially changed.
衰退 means decline, not extinction. Saying the family died out by Zouken’s generation asserts a completed end that the surviving bloodline contradicts.

A frantic lifelong protest against the bloodline’s end substantially conveys his struggle to overturn the verdict that it could go no farther. The English is compressed but preserves the central ceiling and resistance.

The excess English repetitions sit inside a maturity-condition branch, while the supplied Japanese witnesses show only the shorter refrain and provide no securely aligned raw Original branch here. Given the explicit branch-flattening caveat, the displayed duplication cannot be certified as translator-added from these witnesses alone.

Regardless of the rotting/crumbling edition variant, 恨めしい says Zouken resents or curses the failing body. The English leaves only an orphaned body fragment and pain statements, losing that directed resentment.
The English retains refusing to disappear without leaving anything, but it has no equivalent for the separate refusal to die while still suffering.

A narrower error survives: “Grant the wish” changes 聞くがいい, an appeal that the Grail hear his wish, into a direct grant command. The explanation overstates the loss because “The answer being…” still partially reflects the imagined question-and-answer.

“On top of the cliff” identifies the required destination, and the surrounding inability and distance make the need to reach it clear. Omitting the explicit verb “climb” does not materially change the action.

“Leaving bits of itself behind” conveys that the crawling mass is shedding and scattering itself. The wet ビチャビチャ sound-image is lost, but that is tonal compression rather than a materially different event.
怨念 is rancorous, resentful fixation, materially darker than neutral perseverance. Repeating “tenacity” erases the deliberate turn from 執念 to malign resentment.
“Ignoring” can non-volitionally mean failing to notice or heed something. In this fixation context it defensibly paraphrases the sound not registering; deliberate choice is not necessarily asserted.

The visual tunnel-vision image is compressed, but the complete passage retains the fixation through “filled only with obsession” followed immediately by movement toward the Grail. The claim that the fixation disappears is overstated.
“Hideous monster” defensibly represents 醜怪 in context, but この世ならざる (“unearthly/not of this world”) is genuinely omitted. The surviving issue is that modifier, not an invalid monster classification.
陶然 denotes an intoxicated, enraptured, or spellbound state, not astonishment. The English materially changes Zouken’s emotional response.
“Partner” conveys companionship but entirely omits Justeaze’s identification as 天の杯 and the first-person 我が framing. That ritual identity is explicit and significant.

The English compresses the past-time comparison, but “still has the eyes he adores,” following “hasn’t faded,” substantially conveys unchanged eyes and enduring yearning. Treating the tense choice as a material factual error is too strong.
The Japanese says the thought or cognition “this is painful” stops. “Shields his mind from the pain” instead describes protection from pain itself and invents a shielding mechanism.
限界を定められ is passive: humanity has limits imposed or fixed in advance, not limits it “has set.” The English also loses 回り続ける and disconnects humanity from the command to take it outside.
自身を、人という命を is naturally read as appositional reformulation—himself, his human life—rather than two independently paired objects. “Change his human life” is compressed but defensible.
地平 literally permits “horizon,” but in this figurative destination culminating in 理想郷, “land” is a defensible rendering. The essential impossibility of imagining it remains.
In context, reaching the ideal and making it a reality describe the same sought achievement. The English is an interpretive paraphrase, not a demonstrable material change.
去る can denote death, especially for foes who disappeared over a two-hundred-year span. “Died” is contextually defensible and not contradicted by the Japanese witness.
そう在る事 means existing or continuing in that manner; after “he remained” and “kept seeking,” “a reason to exist” is a defensible contextual condensation rather than a contradictory generic purpose.

自身を継ぐ者 is grammatically a generic singular successor, so “a successor” does not falsely narrow a plural. “Bring on” can also mean cause or foster the successor’s emergence, making the cultivation accusation insufficient.

Angra Mainyu is not unsupported: it is the supplied ruby reading over 第三魔法. A narrower error remains because 間違いでしかない characterizes the produced Third Magic as nothing but an error, whereas “created by mistake” suggests accidental creation.
彼ら is explicitly plural and 試み is explicitly present. “His journey” assigns the collective project to one person and omits the attempt.
Though awkward, “history … starts its loop” substantially renders 歴史が…回っていく, while “to reach the distance” conveys aiming far away. The alleged loss of historical motion is not established.

The immediately preceding words are plainly words of resignation, and the English then identifies their familiar voice as the old magus’s. Across the complete passage, the characterization is retained despite restructuring.
覆す means overturn, reverse, or repudiate, not conceal. The Japanese says he never reverses his identity as one who condoned evil; “not hiding it” changes that ethical continuity into secrecy.
生きながらえ means surviving, while 当事者であり続けた means remaining an involved party. “Also started everything” has no support here and removes the participant-observer paradox.
A collapsing cavern canopy physically falls as rock, so being buried by “crumbling rocks” is a defensible concrete paraphrase. The overhead source is less explicit but no material event changes.
The Japanese makes the long-pursued ambition itself collapse alongside the magus. “The embodiment of his desire is destroyed” invents a separate embodiment and omits 目指し続けた, his continuing pursuit.
Given Shirou’s body transformation into swords or steel, “what my body’s made of” naturally states the resulting transformed condition. It does not introduce a materially incompatible fact.
“Pierces through me” can figuratively describe shock passing through the body. It preserves the internally transmitted impact and need not imply a literal piercing weapon.

The Japanese lists three distinct treatments of Shirou’s punches—dodged, deflected, and drawn in. The English retains only dodging and parrying, omitting the drawing-in maneuver that enables the counters.

“My vision whites out” accurately states the perceptual result. 切り刻まれる supplies violent imagery, but the proposed special link to Shirou’s sword-body is interpretive and its omission is not a demonstrable factual error.
For a failing sense, “will be cut off” naturally means it will cease functioning; it does not necessarily posit an external agent. This is a defensible rendering of sight dying out.
“Pulverize my body” ordinarily applies to the body as a whole. Although くまなく is not separately lexicalized, the exhaustive force is adequately conveyed and no localized damage is implied.

The Japanese leaves どちら context-dependent and breaks the thought off, so the finding cannot establish that it specifically contrasts body and brain. A narrower issue survives: the English selects the two fighters and completes the deliberately interrupted cognition.
わき腹 denotes the flank or side around the ribs, and “left rib” is a slightly narrowed but contextually defensible bodily localization. It does not materially alter the blow.
“Stabbing my brain” preserves the blades’ invasive, destructive action. The distinction between stabbing and repeated slicing is vividness and manner, not a demonstrated material plot error here.
“My body’s about to cry out from it” preserves the source’s personification of the whole body reacting to pain. “Cry out” is a natural English realization of 泣きそう.

吹っ飛ばされた already supports being violently flung, making the rag-doll simile ordinary embellishment rather than a conflicting event. A cave-in rock can also naturally be described as a large piece of rubble.

作り変える means remake or reconstruct, consistent with the arm overwriting his body. “Reinforce” instead suggests strengthening or supporting it and obscures the involuntary reconstruction causing brain pain.
The English omits both the explicit one-second threshold and the ensuing inability to think. Those details define the immediacy and nature of Shirou’s neural burnout.
一分後に消えてもおかしくない expresses that disappearance could readily occur by the imminent one-minute point. “Within the next minute” is a natural English rendering of that practical time window.
The English is awkward, but it retains both propositions: Kirei lacks a goal and merely follows the way of life he has upheld. The rule-like nuance of 在り方 is not wholly lost.
A body “with no future” is terminal, and “was dying” naturally expresses that condition in this context. The English does not introduce a materially different prognosis.
相打ち覚悟 explicitly states that Shirou throws the punch prepared to take a simultaneous hit. Calling it merely “my attack” omits his decisive willingness to trade blows.
“A hard shot” is colloquial English for a forceful blow, and “counterattacked” supplies the delivery. It defensibly conveys 強烈なのをぶち込まれた without materially weakening the action.
蹲る states that Shirou is crouched, huddled, or doubled over after being sent flying. The English omits that posture, altering the immediate fight staging before Kirei approaches his head.
“Looms over me” substantially conveys an enemy standing over and covering Shirou. The separate shadow image and blocking verb are compressed, but the spatial threat remains clear.

Unmarked 足 can refer generally to one’s leg or legs, while the interruption then singles out the right leg as wholly immobile. The Japanese does not conclusively establish that the other leg remains normally mobile.

足に火をつける can be literal ignition or a figurative forcing of the limb into action. The supplied prose alone does not establish flames, and “fire them up” preserves the ambiguity imperfectly but plausibly.
With death arriving in the next second, “I won’t die here” is a natural contextual explicitation of refusing to let things end this way. It does not contradict the broader wording.

Separating failure and posture into adjacent English sentences does not itself sever their relation. A narrower omission remains: the fist had reached immediately before Shirou’s face, not merely an unspecified raised position.
Sentence-final のか can mark realization or an internal inference, not necessarily unresolved doubt. English “So” likewise presents Shirou’s conclusion, while “half-dead” reasonably conveys 死に体.
In this context, having a purpose means having something one must do. “If you need to do something” is a natural paraphrase and retains Kirei’s instruction to hurry.

The accusation ignores the supplied ruby: 責務 is explicitly read のぞみ, “wish.” Rendering the performed responsibility as fulfilling one’s wish preserves the authored dual-layer reading rather than replacing it unsupportedly.

The preceding English sentence already says Kirei will not change “even on the verge of his death,” supplying the final temporal test. The following sentence then states that he remains Shirou’s enemy.
いためつける covers hurting, tormenting, or beating up. In the immediate aftermath of their fistfight, “hurting me so much” clearly carries the physical and sardonic sense.

“Rusting away” is a contextual metallic-body paraphrase of eyes nearing scrap. The English construction still grammatically applies the condition to “my eyes,” so the alleged shift to Shirou generally is not established.

“This world” is a defensible simplification of 苦界, though it loses the Buddhist coloring. The decisive surviving omission is 今度こそ, which marks that this time Kirei truly disappears after his earlier apparent death.
苦しい can directly mean physically painful or distressing, and the surrounding passage concerns bodily sensory failure. “It’s not painful” is a normal, contextually apt rendering.
“Starting to feel faint” idiomatically means beginning to lose consciousness. It is not merely generic weakness and adequately conveys the advancing inability to stay conscious.
一仕事 means a job, task, or piece of work, and “my final job” naturally conveys one final undertaking. The occupational reading is not forced in context.
“Definite end” expresses a certain and conclusive ending, a legitimate sense of 絶対の終わり. Requiring the cognate “absolute” is lexical preference rather than correction of fact.
断線 specifically evokes a severed connection or circuit cutting out. “Breaking apart” instead depicts fragmentation, changing the mechanism and imagery of Shirou’s failing consciousness.

“Crumbling down” and “becoming a pile of rubble” retain the collapse and accumulation, so the claimed loss of all three details is overstated. The genuinely omitted details are the sectional ところどころ and the ground’s former wasteland-like appearance.
